en: (re15527. (The first leaf is blank.
(The second leaf is blank.)
I salute Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the world, who, like speech and its meaning, are eternally united for the sake of the comprehension of both speech and meaning.

(The third leaf, side a) the method as stated in the *Śāradātilaka* (... the ritual manual (*kalpa*), the *Suhmaṇka-vastra* (?), (side b) the installations of Sūrya, Gaṇapati, Skanda, Durgā, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Viṣṇu, and Datta; the installation of the human [deity], initiation through knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*), worship through knowledge (*jñānapūjā*), the consecration of the teacher (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), and the sequence of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*).
The procedure for the eightfold binding, the procedure for circumambulation, the procedure for rudrākṣa beads, the procedure for sacred ash, and the procedure for the temple-prasāda.
[First Chapter] (The fourth leaf, both sides a and b, is blank.)
[Morning Meditation on Śiva] Hariḥ Om.
(1a, 1st line) (Damaged ………) I take refuge in the son of Gaṅgādhara, who is sung by Kinnaras; in the illustrious Lord of Gods. (2nd line)
Having bowed with devotion to Śivā, Vāṇī, Gaṇeśa, Ṣaṇmukha, and the Kurus, the conduct of the Śaivas for the fourth [order] is now declared.
Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, facing north...

Having become silent and performed the ritual of purification (*vibhūtidhāraṇa*), and having meditated upon the pair of the Guru’s lotus feet upon his own head, he should meditate on Śiva according to his qualification.
For it is stated in the Āgama that [Śiva] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; thus, the initiate (*samayī*) shall [meditate] within the center of the heart-lotus.

The practitioner— whether a *putraka*, a *sadāśivamūrti*, a *yogin*, or a *jñānin*— having meditated upon the forms of Māṇa-Rudra and Sadāśiva, and having contemplated the *bindu* and *nāda* at the *bhrūmadhya* and the *brahmarandhra* while cultivating the realization "I am Śiva," should bow to and praise Śiva and then rise.

Now, one might object: "The conduct beginning with rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta* is prescribed only for those of the three [upper] castes; how then can the conduct of the fourth caste be described? This is true.

"Having extracted the caste [status] of the Śūdra and others by means of the root mantra itself ending with 'svāhā'—thus three oblations—and afterwards one should speak to Śiva: 'O Blessed Supreme Lord, may this twice-born one become pure from the body born of the seed of Yoru, through both the faults of lack of food and [the fault of] ignorance,' according to the statement in the Kāmika and other Āgamas. This applies to Śūdras who are [otherwise] virtuous."
By virtue of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) that elevate one’s birth, the performance of the practices taught in the Śiva-āgamas is indeed enjoined.
(1b, first line) [This is] the ritual procedure for action (*karmavidhi*); we shall demonstrate this in detail later on.

(Dismissal) Then, having gone outside the village, prior to the performance of the necessary rites, for the sake of purification, [one should take] earth that is free from gravel, free from sand, free from anthills, and situated at the root of a tree... (second line).
Having silently taken earth that is situated in the middle of a sacred site, not burnt by fire, not located on a wall, untouched by mice and other such creatures,
situated eight finger-breadths beneath the surface of the ground, pure, and sufficient for purification— and having collected water for the purpose of cleansing after evacuation— (3rd line)
Having placed [the vessel] on a pure ground,
avoiding places near anthills, stone slabs, cremation grounds, gardens, temples, medicinal plants, sacred fields, *dūrvā* grass, *kuśa* grass, and the like,
one should [perform the rite] elsewhere in a secluded and fearless place; facing north during the day and at the twilights, and facing south at night.

In cases of eye disease, in darkness, or in a narrow place, facing whichever direction is possible, with his head covered, remaining silent, having spread out ground unfit for sacrifice, and in a fierce wind or when the directions are obscured, he—
standing there with an upright body and a concentrated mind as if seated upon a celestial chariot— should behold everything, including the Brahmins, the Moon, the Sun, and Agni.
With his eyes cast down, holding his penis between the index and middle fingers of his left hand, he should discharge both feces and urine.
Immediately thereafter, using his left hand, he should wipe the anus with sacrificial grass, wood, or a clod of earth found there;
then again with his [right hand]... (6th line)
Having gone to a clean place and leaving a space of one cubit from water, one should perform purification (*śauca*).
As for that purification: first, for the sake of removing odor and residue, [one should follow] the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*).

Having performed purification (*śauca*), and having again taken a quantity of clay sufficient for the purpose of [making it] invisible, one should place it in the right hand and apply it to the left hand;

then, excluding water, one should perform purification by applying the clay once to the penis and five times to the anus. Then, one should wash the left hand ten times, and the hands again [thoroughly].
One should wash the feet with earth and water seven times in total, once for each occasion.

This purification is prescribed for householders; for those who are dispassionate, it is fourfold. Likewise, during the day it is as stated, at night it is half, and for the sick it is half of that again. In great sacred bathing places (*mahātīrtha*), one should perform purification by drawing up water; in such cases, the purification by a continuous stream (*dhārāśauca*) must not be performed.

One should perform the cleansing with water from the hollowed palms. One should purify the remaining clay residue left over from the cleansing with water. Then, having risen and put on the *kaupīna*, one should rinse the mouth twelve times on the left side, remove the head-covering, and in another place, perform it once without mantras.
One should perform the ritual sipping of water twice with the mantra once.
(Ācamana)

For example, facing either east or north, sitting in the *kukkuṭāsana* posture with both hands between the knees, [one should take] water from a pond frequented by those of the lowest castes, or water from a small pool insufficient to quench the thirst of a cow,
or water that is turbid, or water released from a decoction, or water mixed with [impurities].

Having discarded the water that is *tāmasa* and *rājasa*, one should take pure water as at Gokarṇa; with the hand formed into the *gokarṇa* shape, grasping it between the thumb and the little finger, and having observed that the water is free from froth, insects, moss, and the like, and is no deeper than a *māṣa* bean, one should drink it three times silently through the *brahmatīrtha* in the same manner as before.
(Second line) Because of the statement, "If the water has been drawn out, one should drink water purified by a cloth," having thoroughly cleansed the vessel with a cloth and placed it on the ground,
one should tilt the vessel with the left hand while holding it in the right hand. (Third line)
Having poured it out as before, one should drink.

One should not sip water with the water remaining from washing the feet for purification; however, if no other water is available, one may pour that water slightly onto the ground and [use] the vessel...

Having placed [the water] on the ground and consecrated it by means of gazing and other rites, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana). At the time of the pure sipping, one should avoid laughing, looking at others, speaking, scratching, and so forth. One should not sip water while standing on a bed, a seat, or wooden sandals, nor while wearing a turban, nor with a garment draped over the right shoulder. This applies even when one is holding necessary items required for the occasion.
Thus one should sip water. Then, having sprinkled the head and the feet, one should wipe the two lips on the right side twice with the base of the right thumb;
then, wiping the mouth once with the three middle fingers, [one should proceed] according to the sequence to be described.
Having touched the nose, eyes, ears, and navel—
and likewise the arms in the order of right and left— with water, one should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) accompanied by mantras. To that end,
having taken water in the manner previously described, one should first [perform it] for the sake of purifying the *ātmatattva*.
"Hrāṃ ātmatattvāya svadhā" for the purification of the principle of the self; "Hrīṃ vidyātattvāya svadhā" as the second [offering] for the purification of the principle of knowledge;
and "Hūṃ śivatattvāya svadhā" for the purification of the principle of Śiva.

One should drink the third [sip]. Thus, even regarding the mantras to be mentioned hereafter, it should be understood that they are preceded by the short *praṇava* (*oṃ*), because of the statement: "In those cases as well, one should not be devoid of reverence. Then, having sprinkled the head and the feet with the *Śiva-mantra*, and having twice wiped the lips with the root of the right thumb while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra* ending in *namaḥ*.

For the sake of pleasing Bhāratī, one should wipe the lower part of the mouth with the three middle fingers while reciting that seed-syllable; for the thumb is the abode of Īśvara, and the tip of the ring finger is the abode of the digit of nectar— thus, [one should touch] each respective [part].

For the sake of purifying the locations and for the satisfaction of the respective presiding deities, one should touch, in sequence, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), eyes, ears, navel, heart, head, and arms with the thumb and ring finger. Upon touching the two lips, [one should recite] the *praṇava*.
By touching the mouth, one attains Bhāratī; by touching the nose, Prāṇa; by touching both eyes, the Moon and Sun;
and by touching both ears, the deities of the quarters.

Through the touch of the navel, Brahmā [is satisfied]; through the touch of the heart, the Destroyer; through the touch of the head, Viṣṇu; and through the touch of the [two] feet, the Aśvins—these deities become satiated. Thus it is stated in the Parākhya: "And the touch should be performed upon the Anāmikā [finger]."

With that [power], together with the thumb (aṅguṣṭha), he becomes the Lord; she is named Nāmāmṛtā, the digit of immortality. By her, whose nature is nectar and who is free from disease, the deities are satisfied.
For the performer of that ritual, these serve as the supports for the manifestation of the action:
the Goddess of Speech resides at the tip of the tongue; the Praṇava is in the cavity between the lips;
the Pārās are in the two nostrils; and the Moon and Sun are in the two eyes.

"All directions dissolve into the two ears; Brahmā dissolves into the navel; Viṣṇu [dissolves] into the heart for the sake of purification; and the two Aśvins reside in the two eyes. Thus [it is said]. On the banks of water or in the water itself, having placed the left foot on the bank and the right foot in the water, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). This is the procedure for *ācamana*.
Now, regarding the cleaning of the teeth:
one should not do so on the first, sixth, ninth, eleventh, full moon, or new moon days;
nor should one do so even after sunrise.

On days other than the new moon, the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*), and the days dedicated to the ancestors (*paitṛka-divasa*), one should perform [the cleaning] with *parṇa* leaves or grasses on those prohibited lunar days (*niṣiddha-tithi*). On these days, one becomes pure by rinsing the mouth twelve times with water. (Sixth line) However, for those who are dispassionate (*virakta*), the cleaning of the teeth must be performed after the meal on all lunar days, beginning from the first (*pratipad*). As it has been said:
"In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*,
it is stated: 'On the first lunar day, the full moon, the sixth, the ninth,
and also on the new moon— especially for one seeking liberation— one must always perform the cleaning of the teeth.'"
Householders [should offer] to you [a twig] produced from an unprohibited milky tree such as *pāmārga* or *kakubha*,
with a circumference equal to the little finger, eight finger-breadths in length, pure, moist at the joint, made of living wood, straight, cut unevenly, and ending with the word "namaḥ."
Having consecrated the tooth-stick with his heart-mantra and having softened it with his teeth, facing the east,

he should gradually clean the gums both inside and out, beginning from the upper front tooth and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction; then, having rinsed it, he should discard that stick on his left side.

Having gargled and washed both hands, one should scrape the tongue with a piece of wood of that same species— or [with something] empowered by mantras over the syllables— using the previously described procedure, and then gargle. However, one who is detached...

Having collected tooth-sticks brought by the disciples— which originate from the *karañja*, *ciribilva*, *khadira*, *arjuna*, and *śirīṣa* trees and possess the previously mentioned characteristics— one should perform the cleansing of the teeth according to the previously stated procedure. In the absence of disciples, one should do so oneself with fallen leaves.

One should avoid the ashes produced from the trees known as dhava, dhātrī, śigru, niṃba, bakata, eraṇḍa, tintriṇī, japā, and piśāca, as well as those originating from coconut, and those made of iron, clay, cloth, finger-prints, and so forth.
The Ritual for Bathing Now, the ritual for bathing is declared: for householders who wear their hair, there is bathing with clay;
for those who wear [shorn] hair, there is bathing with *āmalaka* fruit. For those who are dispassionate, bathing with clay is always prescribed in a pure location.

Having dug eight finger-breadths deep with the Astra-mantra, having extracted [the earth] with the Hṛdaya-mantra, and having filled the pit with that same [earth], one should deposit it on the bank of a sacred ford (tīrtha) with the head of the mantra ending in "namaḥ. Having purified it with the Astra-mantra, having removed grass and other debris with the Śikhā-mantra, and having divided it into three parts with the Kavaca-mantra, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), perform the renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
Having placed his right hand upon his right thigh and his left hand upon his left [thigh], while the command of Śiva, Śiva, Śambhu is being carried out— on this day,

in the second *parārdha* of the current Brahmā, in the Śvetavārāha-kalpa, in the Vaivasvata-manvantara, in the Kali-yuga, in its first quarter (*pāda*), in Jambūdvīpa, in Bhāratavarṣa, in Bharatakhaṇḍa, on the southern side of Meru, in this present time...
In the legal proceedings, in the year so-and-so, in the [southern/northern] solstice, in the season so-and-so, in the month so-and-so, in the fortnight so-and-so,
on this auspicious lunar day joined with the day of the week, the asterism, the yoga, and the karaṇa, for us... (4th line)

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of the attainment of the fourfold aims of human life (*caturvidhapuruṣārtha*), by means of the destruction of all sins along with my family, I shall perform a bath in this sacred ford (*tīrtha*)," and having risen, [he should address] the Guardian of the Field (*kṣetrapāla*) thus: "O Bhairava, salutations to you, who are exceedingly fierce and like the fire at the end of an aeon (*kalpānta*). You ought to grant me permission. Thus [he addresses] the Guardian of the Field.
Having paid homage and received permission, and having bowed to his auspicious guru and there saluted even the most eminent [elders],
he drew five lumps of earth from the ponds and lotus-pools, cast them upon the bank, and [addressed the river]: "O purifier of the three worlds, O supreme one dwelling upon the crest of Śiva!"
"O Goddess Gaṅgā, salutations to you; be present in this water.
Having thus prayed to Gaṅgā-Bhavānī, he tied the hem of his garment that was wrapped around his waist to his waist-string on the left side, and at one point, with clay...

Having smeared [the body] from the navel down to the feet, one should wash it. Taking a portion of clay of medium consistency and consecrating it seven times with the *astra-mantra*, one should smear it from the head down to the feet for the pacification of physical impurities; then, for the pacification of the impurities of the sense faculties, [one should smear] the sense organs.

Having restrained [his speech], for the sake of pacifying verbal evil, he uttered the *prāsāda* mantra; and for the sake of pacifying mental defilement, restraining his breaths within his heart and recollecting the *Śivāstra* which possesses a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālāgni*), he plunged into it as long as he was able. Then—

Having risen from within the water, performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), and made the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart, one should meditate on the twilight (*sandhyā*) as being of the nature of a blazing weapon. Having sprinkled the head three times with the *astra-gāyatrī*, and having offered three portions of the water-offering (*arghya*) with that same mantra, one should recite the *astra-gāyatrī* ten times: "We know the weapon of Śiva... (*śivāstrāyavidmahe*).

"Let us meditate upon the fire of time; may it impel our weapons. Then, having emerged from the water and taken a third part of the clay, one should stand in water reaching up to the navel, or in water as available, facing east in the morning, north at midday, and west in the evening while in rivers.
Facing the current, one should sprinkle the clay held in the hand with water,

divide it into three parts according to the sequence of East, South, and North, and as before, consecrate each portion seven times with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Then, [consecrate] the southern portion of clay either with the four-limbed mantras beginning with the *hṛdaya*, or with those beginning with *sadyojāta*.

Having consecrated [the earth] once with the Pañcabrahma mantra, or having consecrated it ten times toward the northern direction, one should then take the portion of earth from the east and so forth.

Having taken [the earth] with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should cast it toward the obstacles of the directions with the *nārācamudrā* using the [mantra] weapon in the ten directions beginning with the east. Then, having taken half of the portion of earth from the northern direction and cast it into the water for the purpose of removing all defects within the water, [one should take] the other...

For the sake of accomplishing the Śiva-tīrtha, one should sprinkle [the water] from the root-mantra all around by rotating the arms. Then, having drawn forth the nectar flowing from the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) from the location of the Bindu by means of the Aṅkuśa-mudrā, [one should recite] the Hṛdaya-mantra ending with "Namaḥ" while performing the Udbhava-mudrā.

Having placed [the earth] in water and sprinkled it, one should render it immortal (*amṛtīkuryāt*). Then, taking earth from the southern direction for the sake of pacifying physical sins, one should smear all parts of the body from the head down to the feet— using either the *Aṅga-mantra* or the *Pañca-brahma-mantra*— with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger, in due order.

Having closed the ears, eyes, and nostrils with the six-faced mudrā (*ṣaṇmukhamudrā*), and having meditated upon Śiva within the heart-lotus while recollecting the Prāsāda mantra, one should restrain the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and,
having fully immersed oneself in the Śiva-tīrtha, bathe for as long as possible. Then, having risen, [one should contemplate] the form of the moon and the sun.

Having visualized the left and right hands as Śakti and Śiva, one should repeatedly sprinkle the head with the water from the *kumbhamudrā* while reciting the *saṃhitā* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, for the sake of self-protection, [one should sprinkle] the water with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having sprinkled water all around, sipped water, performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and briefly offered libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, one should take water with the *saṃhāramudrā* while reciting the heart mantra ending in *namaḥ*, and offer three handfuls of water in joined palms.

(…) Having placed his left foot on the bank and his right foot [in the water], he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Because of such scriptural injunctions as, "One who is detached should not cause affliction to living beings, nor should he pluck flowers," the disciple should take earth brought from a mountain, a riverbank, a sacred field (*puṇyakṣetra*), the root of an *aśvattha* tree, or a pure spot, according to the previously mentioned procedure, by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).

Having smeared [the body] from the feet to the top of the head, one should perform everything except the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*). In the absence of a disciple, one should bathe by taking the mud from above oneself without causing distress, even in rivers and other such places. If one is unable to go outside the village to rivers and other such places to bathe, one may do so at home.

In the monastery, one should bathe according to the previously mentioned procedure with cold water or heated water. Bathing in well-water is superior to [bathing in] ordinary water; bathing in a pond is superior to that; bathing in a river is superior to that; and bathing in a great river such as the Gaṅgā, in a lotus pond near a temple of Śiva, or in the water used for washing the feet of the Guru—each subsequent type yields greater fruit than the preceding.

It should be so. Then, having wiped the body with a washed, damp cloth while facing south and sitting in the cock-posture (*kukkuṭāsana*), one should put on a clean loincloth (*kaupīna*) of the size of one's own buttocks that is free of holes;
holding the two fringes attached to the region of the anus with the left hand ending in *namaḥ*, [one stands] above.

One should wrap oneself only in white cloth; one must not wear red, yellow, blue, saffron, or similar garments. If one wears such [colored] clothing, one is indeed unfit for rites dedicated to the gods and their sons. If a householder should wear saffron robes, then upon seeing him, one must perform the ritual of looking at the sun (*sūryāvalokana*). However, the prohibition against householders wearing loincloths applies only to those of the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*).
One who is dispassionate, having made the ochre-colored loincloth (*kaupīna*)—characterized as previously described—and the two-fold hem of the garment equal, should wear them.

Having placed the ochre waist-wrap (*kāṣāyakaṭiveṣṭi*) over that, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Thereafter, the dispassionate one should perform the bath with sacred ash (*bhasmasnāna*). Following the Varuṇa-bath...

One becomes entitled to the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*). If one is unable to perform the water-bath (*vāruṇasnāna*), then the ash-bath alone must be performed in its place. If a yogi has attained mastery in the contemplation of Śiva (*śivabhāvanā*), he may set aside the water-bath and perform the fire-bath (*āgneyasnāna*) instead.
Thus it is stated in the Mataṅga:
"O best of sages, in this manner, having bathed daily in water according to one's capacity, one becomes qualified for the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*); not otherwise."
This is the procedure for those engaged in ritual action.
For one who repeatedly bathes with water, pain may arise; therefore, constant bathing is not desired, and one should perform the desired fire-ritual. This is the rule.
In the *Svāyambhuva*, for those who are ill,
another fire-bath (*āgneyasnāna*) is prescribed, which is declared to be equal to the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*);
it may be performed daily after the water-bath, or even as a supreme alternative.
In the *Kāmika*, it is said that the fire-based (*āgneya*) bath possesses ten times more merit than the water-based (*vāruṇa*) bath;
therefore, having abandoned the water-based bath, one should perform the fire-based bath. This is [the seventh line].
The procedure for the Śiva-yogins is as follows:
according to the Kāmika [Tantra], it should be with water for householders, while for ascetics it is performed with ashes.
In the *Parākhyatantra*, it is stated that householders should always bathe with water, while ascetics should bathe with ashes.
This is also found in the *Kriyāsāra*.
For ascetics, the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is always prescribed; for householders, bathing is the Vāruṇa rite.
And in the *Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga*:
"The abandonment of obligatory rites through the ripening of dispassion;
subsisting on alms, meditation upon Śiva, and bathing with ashes during the twilight prayers."
If it is argued that the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) for householders is mentioned in some scripture (*āgama*), that refers specifically to Brahmins. It also applies to yogis.

Furthermore, on occasions such as the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), solstices (*ayana*), transits of the sun (*saṃkrānti*), and eclipses (*grahaṇa*), even if there is contact with impurities such as feces or urine above the navel, or contact with the untouchable (*aspṛśya*), or during shaving, vomiting, or a stumble—[the ash-bath is required].
In various occasional rites (*naimittika*), the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) is indeed prescribed after the Varuna-bath;
where the man’s bath is with his clothes on, there the woman [should likewise bathe].
"One who suffers from head ailments or one who wears matted hair should always perform the bath excluding the head," according to this statement.

For auspicious women, however, purification is always achieved through a neck-bath (*kaṇṭhasnāna*) alone; for occasional rites (*naimittika*), a full bath is prescribed. For widows, on the other hand, a daily bath (*nityasnāna*) is prescribed.
Now, the procedure for the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*):

having washed one's feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and having thoroughly wiped both hands with a cloth, one sits facing north upon a seat such as a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and pays homage to Śiva and the gurus.
Having paid homage to the manifestations (*vibhūti*) residing within the treasury of manifestations— such as *kalpa*, *anukalpa*, and *upakalpa*— whose characteristics will be described hereafter,

and having taken them in the left hand with the *Śiva-mantra* and offered them with the *Śakti-mantra*; then, having poured in water purified by a cloth and consecrated through rites such as *nirīkṣaṇa*, and having covered it with the right hand, [one should perform the rite] with the five or six limbs and the five digits (*kalā*).

Having consecrated [the sacred ash] by means of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), one should take a small amount with the thumb and ring finger while reciting the word-mantra "jyoti jyoti. Having led it from the big toe up to the top of the head and scattered it, one should then stir the water and ash together with the *śiva* mantra. Then, from the feet up to the knees, [one should apply it] with: *haṃ sadyojātamūrtaye nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ*.
From the forehead up to the *brahmarandhra*: *Hoṃ*, salutation to the head of Īśāna (*īśānamūrdhne*).
From the knees down to the navel: *Hiṃ*, salutation to the secret organ of Vāmadeva (*vāmadevaguhyāya*) and to the *pratiṣṭhā* level (*kalā*).
From the navel up to the throat: *Huṃ*, salutation to the heart of Aghora (*aghorahṛdayāya*) and to the *vidyā* level (*kalā*).

Reciting "haṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa, to the Śānti-kalā, from the throat up to the forehead," and "hoṃ, obeisance to the head of Īśāna, to the Śāntyatīta-kalā, from the forehead up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra)," one should smear [the body].
With the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should slowly rub all the limbs from the feet to the head with both the right and left hands,
and perform the ritual as for a deceased person (*vadhivat*). If one has not performed the *vāruṇa* bath, one should wash the hands and feet,
cleanse the impurities from the eyes, ears, and nose with water, put on a washed *kaupīna*, perform *ācamana*, and [proceed with] the *nyāsa*.
Having performed the previously described procedure and bathed with ashes,
one should thereafter discard the loincloth worn previously, put on a washed loincloth, and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). This should not be done on impure ground, nor on a path,
nor in the presence of women or men who have excluded the gods, or those guilty of ungratefulness or great sins (mahāpātaka).
One should perform the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*) in the presence of the deity, the guru, fire, Śiva, and the scriptures. Now, as an incidental matter, the subsequent bath is described:
(the mantra-bath).
Therein, first the mantra-bath is defined. Having washed one's feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)... (line 8)

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should perform the sprinkling on the head with water consecrated by the *saṃhitā* mantra, using the *kumbha-mudrā* and the *saṃhitā* ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Next is the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*).
Having washed one's feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and executed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should—

while the mind is united with the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— utter the root mantra as far as the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*) residing at the *dvādaśānta*. Then, one should bathe the body internally and externally with the nectar-like water flowing forth from the partless Power (*niṣkalaśakti*).
Now, the bath of reverence (*gaurava-snāna*):
having become pure through the Varuṇa-bath, while reciting the *śiva-mantra*, one should bear the feet of the Guru upon one’s head. Thus says the Āgama:
"Purified, one should bear the feet of the guru upon one's head while uttering 'Śiva'. Now follows the bath with cow-hair [strainers],
which is equivalent to the Vāruṇa bath.

Having become pure, reciting the Śiva-mantra, having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and executed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), he should, while reciting the Śiva-mantra, cleanse [the image] from the head down to the feet with the tip of the tail of a cow that possesses the proper characteristics and is accompanied by her calf.
The Procedure for Wearing the Tripuṇḍra Mark.

Now, for one who is unable to bathe with ashes, who is detached [from worldly life], or who is otherwise ineligible, he states the alternative method of *uddhūlana* (dusting with ashes): having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*),
and cleansed his hands with a cloth, he takes the sacred ash (*vibhūti*), consecrates it as previously described, and applies it to the head, forehead, heart, navel, and knees.
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* with the mantras beginning with *Īśāna*. This constitutes the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*).

Now, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* at sixteen locations. Namely: with the middle, index, and ring fingers, [one applies it] to the head, forehead, heart, both arms, throat, navel, both ears, and the two elbows.
On the backs of the two wrists, the hips, and the two sides of the waist,

[an application] is prescribed for Brahmins with a measure of seven finger-breadths, using the Śiva-mantra for the sake of pleasing Śiva, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, the five Brahmās, and the eight Vidyeśvaras.
The triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) of Kṣatriyas should be five finger-breadths (*pañcāṅgula*) in measure;
likewise, one should wear the triple mark of Vaiśyas as four finger-breadths;
that of Śūdras should be three finger-breadths, and for women, it should be one finger-breadth—so says the scriptural injunction.

(8b, 1st line) The initiate (*samayin*) should wear a sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*) three finger-breadths in length with sacred ash (*udbhūlana*). Thus, one who is established in the Śiva-āśrama through the initiation of purification (*uddharaṇadīkṣā*)—namely, a Śūdra—is to be understood as being like a Kṣatriya, according to the scriptural statement. One should wear [the mark] five finger-breadths in length for the *udbhūlana*... (2nd line)

At the time of the *puṇḍraka*, one should carefully scatter upon the ground the ashes that are equal to [the size of] an atom (*paramāṇu*) and hold them. If they have fallen, one should collect them with the *hṛdayamantra*. Afterwards, having washed both hands, one should sprinkle that water upon the head from a water-pot (*kumbha*).
To express agreement with the stated meaning, he says in the *Kāmika*:
"One should duly apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark with the middle, index, and ring fingers."
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*).
It [should be applied] on the head, the throat, the forehead, the ears,
both shoulders, the elbows, the wrists, the heart, the navel, and the sides.
On the back, one should likewise establish the deities presiding over the calves:
Śiva-śakti, Sādākhya, Īśa, and the one called Vidyā.
The power of Mādinava is the Aśvins; they are remembered as sixteen.
In Ajita, there are no [others]; these two, Ātasa and Tritsa, are declared to be the two Aśvins.
On the hips, on both ears, on the two sides, and in the region of the navel.
O Janārdana, the sixteen locations for the triple marks (tripuṇḍra) have been specified as the two elbows and the two wrists.
In the *Kālottara*: "Śiva, Sadāśiva, Maheśa, and the five Brahmans, as well as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras)—these sixteen are indeed the presiding deities. Thus [it is said].
For a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), [the rite] is without initiation; likewise for men, it is accompanied by water until midday, and thereafter it is devoid of water.
According to this statement, one who dwells in the Śiva-āśrama should perform the application of sacred ash mixed with water during the three junctions of the day.
[9a, 1st line] ||The Rule for Prāṇāyāma||
Then, having sipped water according to the prescribed rule and performed the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads in the manner to be described,
one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas).
[The lowest is] lacking twelve measures, while the middling and the highest are with double [the number].
The time for each [of the three], beginning with exhalation (*recaka*), is superior when measured by three *guṇas*.
One should exhale the impure air residing in the body and situated in the ether;
then, having gradually drawn in pure air through inhalation (*pūraka*).
"One should remain like a full jar and then exhale," according to this statement;
the exhalation through the *piṅgalā* consists of twelve measures (*mātrā*), while the inhalation is through the *iḍā*.

The *kumbhaka* consists of twenty-four *mātrās*. That which is double that is the middling (*madhyaka*), and triple that is the superior (*uttama*). Among these, according to one's capacity through practice, having performed three *prāṇāyāmas* with the *Śiva-mantra* for six *mātrās*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
(The Ritual of Nyāsa):
And that [nyāsa] is threefold, distinguished by creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
Among these, a householder should perform the nyāsa by way of creation, while one who is dispassionate should perform it by way of withdrawal.
(The Procedure for the Ritual Placement of Emanation):
A householder, having purified both hands by means of the weapon-mantra ending in *phaṭ* in the sequence from left to right—
cleansing the palms and the backs of the hands— and then joining the hands together, [should place] *hāṃ śivāsanāya* with the two thumbs in the middle of the palms.
*Namaḥ*. *Hāṃ haṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the form of Śiva. (*...*) *Hāṃ hauṃ*, salutation to Śiva.

(7th line) *Hauṃ*, salutation to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*). Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), one should place [the mantra] on the head with the thumbs and index fingers, saying: *Hoṃ*, salutation to Īśāna. [Then,] from the two thumbs to the little fingers, starting with the index fingers...
Having performed the placement [of mantras] thus: *haṃ* to Tatpuruṣa, *huṃ* to Aghora, *hiṃ* to Vāmadeva, and *haṃ* to Sadyojāta;
and having performed the placement on the palms of both hands with the three middle fingers, saying *hauṃ* to the three eyes.

From the little finger to the index finger with the thumb: *hāṃ* to the heart, *namas*; *hīṃ* to the head, *namas*; *huṃ* to the crest-lock, *namas*; *haiṃ* to the armor, *namas*. With the thumbs and index fingers: *haḥ* to the weapon, *namas*. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

Having protected both hands with the *kavaca* [mantra] and joined them together in the hollowed-palm gesture (*saṃpuṭīkṛtya*), having consecrated them with the root mantra, one should place [the seed-syllable] *hāṃ* at the navel, saying:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*). Having thus meditated upon the seat of Śiva from the navel up to the heart, one should [place] *hāṃ* in the heart.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva," and having invoked the subtle form as far as the forehead, one should place "Hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*)" in the hollow of the ear; then, having contemplated the body of knowledge from the navel to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), [one recites] "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva."

Having recited the *dvādaśānta* and placed the root mantra upon the head, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) with the tips of the thumbs in a fist-bound position: *Hoṃ*, salutation to Īśāna on the head; with the thumb and index finger:
*Heṃ*, salutation to Tatpuruṣa on the face; with the thumb and middle finger: *Huṃ*, salutation to Aghora on the heart.

*Namaḥ*. With the thumb and ring finger: *Hiṃ*, salutation to Vāmadeva, the secret part. (Sixth line) With the thumb and little finger: *Haṃ*, salutation to Sadyojāta, the form. One should thus place [the mantras] in sequence upon the head, face, heart, secret part, and knees.
Then, with the thumb and little finger: *Hāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; thus at the heart. With the thumb and ring finger: *Hīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; thus on the head.
With the thumb and middle finger: *Haṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; thus on the crest-lock. With the two index fingers: *Haiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*.
Thus (line 8),
having performed the placement on the throat with the upper garment and on the space between the breasts; and having placed [the mantra] on the eyes with the three middle fingers, saying "Hauṃ,
vauṣaṭ to the three eyes," and having performed the three gestures of dispersal and clapping while uttering "Haḥ, phaṭ to the weapon," [one should proceed].

Having performed the binding of the ten directions with that mantra and the *choṭikā* gesture, and having [performed the protection] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should effect the supreme consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*) by reciting the root mantra up to its final nasal resonance (*nādānta*) with both hands, from the crown of the head down to the feet.

(The Procedure for the Ritual of Withdrawal) Now, the procedure for the ritual of withdrawal (*saṃhāranyāsa*) for one who is dispassionate is described. [This involves] the purification of the palms of the hands. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seat, the image, and the body of the root-mantra as before, [one proceeds].

Having performed the placement [of the fingers] from the little finger to the thumb with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras facing downwards, and likewise having placed [the mantras] from the heart to the [other limbs] from the little finger to the thumb; and having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) from the knees to the head, starting with *sadyojāta* and ending with *īśāna*, beginning with the heart.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] as before, one should perform the supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) from the feet up to the head.
By this ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the five short utterances—*hakāra*, *hikāra*, *hukāra*, *hekāra*, and *hokāra*—burn away all sins.
[The five long utterances are: *hākāra*, *hīkāra*, *hūkāra*, *haikāra*, [and *haiḥkāra*].
The fivefold long pronunciation of the syllable *haḥ* bestows liberation. The protracted (*pluta*) pronunciation of the syllable *hau* nourishes [the practitioner] with the nectar of supreme bliss.
As it is said in the *Sārdhatriśatikālottara*:
The short [vowel] burns away sins; the long one bestows liberation.
The prolated [vowel], adorned with a dot upon its head, causes nourishment.

O Six-faced One, the Brahmā-mantras are said to be short, while the Aṅga-mantras are long. (7th line) Thus, a mantra uttered ending with *namaḥ* brings about prosperity (*sampat*). One ending with *svāhā* is the manifestation of the powers of will, knowledge, and action (*icchājñānakriyā-śakti*). One ending with *vaṣaṭ* brings the deity being worshipped under one's control (*vaśyakara*). One ending with *hum* effects the hatred of enemies and the like, such as those [obstructing] desires. (8th line)

Ending with *vauṣaṭ*, it slays wicked beings; ending with *phaṭ*, it draws in the deities residing in the external and internal organs; ending with *svāhā*, it eradicates all obstacles; and ending with *svadhā* during pure sipping of water (*ācamana*), it brings about nourishment. In this regard—
And nourishment (*puṣṭi*) is simply clarity regarding the three principles (*tattva*).
For that very reason, mantras are uttered; and rites such as ritual placement (*nyāsa*) bring about the presence of Śiva by means of the pacification of all obstacles.
"Perform [the rite]. This has been stated in the *Mantravārttika*:
"Vaṣaṭ is for subjugation (*vaśya*); phaṭ is for eradication (*uccāṭa*); and huṃ is used both for hatred (*dveṣa*) and for killing (*māraṇa*)."
And for the pillar, "vauṣaṭ"; for attraction, "namaḥ" and "sampatkarāya."
"‘Svāhā’ is Śakti and ‘Svadhā’ is Puṣṭi; these two are the mantra-wives. Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the sequence of the Sandhyā rites.

Having placed [the water] upon the two eyes with the tips of the thumb and ring finger while reciting the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should gaze at the water; sprinkle it while reciting the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; strike it with that same [mantra]; sprinkle it again while reciting the *kavaca* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; and [visualize it] as flowing from a drop resembling a smooth moon by means of the *hṛdaya* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the *aṅkuśa* mudrā.
Having taken the nectar (amṛta), having placed it in water with the *namonta-hṛdaya* [mantra] and the *udbhava-mudrā*, having consecrated it with the *saṃhitā*,
having veiled it with the *namonta-kavaca*, and having protected it with the *huṃphaḍ-anta-astra*,
[one should worship] with the *vauṣaḍ-anta-śakti*.

Having rendered [the water] nectar-like by means of the mantra and the *dhenumudrā*, one should take that sacred water (*tīrtha*) with both hands and, while reciting once the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*— which takes the form of the *praṇava* and flows as nectar resembling the moon through the *kumbhamudrā*—

one should sprinkle it upon the head three times. Then, having enveloped one's own body with the nectar-water using the *namonta-kavaca* mantra, one should perform *kuṃbhaka* while contemplating [the deity] mentally.
One should recite the Śivasaṃhitā three times. For householders, it is the entire temple complex.
The Saṃhitā is: *Hāṃ hauṃ haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ huṃ hūṃ heṃ haiṃ hoṃ hauṃ haḥ śivāya namaḥ*.
The Niṣkala-prāsāda mantra for those who are dispassionate is: *hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ hīṃ haiṃ haḥ śivāya namaḥ*; this is the *saṃhitā*.

Then, having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should envelop one's own body with water while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *namaḥ*, and clench the hands into fists.

One should meditate upon the *sandhyā*. The power (*śakti*) of the Lord is one alone; yet, through the threefold division of Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—endowed with the three *guṇas* and presiding over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra respectively—she assumes the names Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of time (*kāla*).
Being possessed of their respective colors, vehicles, weapons, and forms, she resides at the heart, the space between the eyebrows, and the *brahma-randhra* during the three junctions of the day.

Bhavānī resides in the apertures; for one who possesses mastery, there is only the single morning *saṃdhyā*. He, however, should meditate on Brāhmī alone in the heart during both the morning and evening *saṃdhyās* of his son. In the morning, he [meditates on] Brāhmī in the heart, and in the evening, between the eyebrows.

One should meditate on Raudrī according to the power of the time. The practitioner has three junctions (*sandhyā*): at dawn, one should meditate on Brāhmī in the heart; at midday, Vaiṣṇavī between the eyebrows;
and in the evening, Raudrī in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
And one should meditate [upon her]. The fourth twilight is indeed the Supreme Power (Parāśakti); such is the traditional teaching.
Likewise, she is proclaimed as the distinct powers of Action (Kriyā) known as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī; through transformation, these very powers constitute the natures of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
Endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*), these three powers— Brahmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Śāṅkarī— are to be known by the wise as the *sandhyās*.
The *samayinī* is indeed to be known as "other" (*aparā*) by the sons and practitioners (*putrasādhaka*).
These [three goddesses] are to be meditated upon in sequence within the heart, the bindu, and the *brahmarandhra*.
Due to the influence of temporal conditions (*kālopādhi*), they possess [specific] colors, vehicles, weapons, and forms. Thus it is said.
Now, the meditation for the twilight devotions (sandhyā-dhyāna).

At dawn, one should meditate upon the Brahmin goddess, adorned with jewels and wearing jeweled garments, with a white sacred thread, matted hair, and youthful appearance; seated upon a swan and a lotus, she has four faces and eight eyes, holding a deer and a rosary in her right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in her left hands. At midday...
In the middle of the eyebrows, one should visualize Vaiṣṇavī, radiant white, wearing white garments, with a sacred thread and a garland of forest flowers,
seated upon a throne of Garuḍa and a lotus, having one face, two eyes, and four arms,
[the two] on the left and right.

One should meditate on her as being endowed with a conch, a mace, a discus, and the gesture of fearlessness. At the head of the evening twilight, one should meditate on Raudrī—dark in color, mounted upon a bull, mature, with one face and three eyes, adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon, and holding a trident, a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and a spear in her right and left hands respectively. But one who is dispassionate [should perform] the pure twilight worship.
One should meditate: at dawn, within the heart-lotus in the center of the *suṣumnā*, [one should meditate on that] whose radiance is like the mass of the rising sun;
at midday, in the lotus between the eyebrows, the form of Supreme Śiva-consciousness, shining like the moon;
at evening, in the lotus in the middle of the head, the ocean of nectar, accompanied by the half-syllable (*ardhamātrā*), whose nature is light.
At midnight, one should meditate upon the immovable, full treasury of light at the *dvādaśānta*.
This has been stated in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:
"In the heart-lotus at dawn, [one should contemplate] that which resembles a mass of rising suns; at midday, it is to be contemplated at the *nāḍī*."
(5th line) At midday, within the lotus of the eyebrows, one should contemplate Paramaśiva, whose nature is consciousness and who shines with the brilliance of Indra.
In the lotus of the crown at the time of evening, one should contemplate the light of the ocean of nectar, arising with sound,
immeasurable throughout the night, immovable, and unimpaired at the end of the twelve fingers.
"It is great," he said.
Now, the procedure for the Aghamarṣaṇa rite:

taking water that is completely full with the right hand and pouring it into the left hand, one should perform the act three times, uppermost first, with the *han-mantra*; then, having scattered drops of water upon the head with the limbs of Brahmā ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should [discard] the remainder of that water.

Having taken [the water] in the right hand and held it near the nose, one should contemplate that [water] located at the heart by means of inhalation through the *iḍā* channel; then, for the purification of the sins of speech, mind, and body, while reciting the *astra-mantra* three times and exhaling through the *piṅgalā* channel,
one should contemplate that water on the right side.
Upon a blazing vajra-stone, one should discharge [the weapon] with the *pāśupatāstra*, accompanied by a frown, like an iron arrow.
(The recitation of the Gāyatrī.
Having sipped water (*ācamana*) there and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the householder should rise; [he should meditate] upon the disk of the sun and within his own heart.
Having meditated upon the Gāyatrī within the heart—
white and non-white, wearing a sacred thread, with her right foot extended horizontally and resting upon the lotus-petal of her left foot;
She has one face and three eyes, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon;
she is draped in a black antelope skin, her limbs are well-proportioned, and she is decorated with white garments.
She holds a rosary and a boon-granting gesture in her right hands, while her left hands hold a lotus and display the gesture of fearlessness.

Having meditated thus, one should offer *arghya* three times with the mantra: "We know that Great Lord; we meditate upon Him whose speech is pure; may Śiva impel us. Then, having emerged from the water, one should surround oneself for self-protection with water while reciting the *kavaca* [armor] mantra.
Standing on the bank, one should recite [the mantra] seventeen, twenty, or one hundred and eight times.

Likewise at midday; and in the evening, having risen and offered the arghya water, one should sit and recite it. Even while wearing wet clothes, one must not recite it while standing in the middle of the water.

By reciting the Gāyatrī seven times, one becomes pure; by ten times, one attains heaven; by twenty times, one reaches the world of Śiva; and by one hundred and eight times, one is delivered from the ocean of rebirth. Thus says the Āgama.
By seven recitations, she purifies the body; by ten, she causes one to reach heaven;
but by twenty recitations, O Goddess, she leads one to the abode of Īśvara.
"By exactly one hundred and eight [recitations], one is delivered from the ocean of birth.
Having thus recited according to one's capacity, one should perform three circumambulations of oneself and a prostration. This is the general rule for the observance (*sāmānyasamaya*).

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), and so forth, using the five-syllable mantra in its gross form as will be described hereafter. However, one who is dispassionate should meditate upon Sadāśiva— who resides within the solar orb and whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss— and having offered three *arghya* oblations with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, [proceeds].
Having wrapped oneself with the upper garment as armor against the water for the sake of self-protection, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;

then, one should perform three circumambulations of oneself and a prostration. Here, one who is dispassionate may, according to his own inclination, [proceed] after receiving initiation into the Śiva-dharma.

The intended subject is indeed a renunciant of Śiva (śaivasanyāsī) who has performed renunciation according to the method taught in the scriptures, preceded by the *virajā-homa* and the *jīva-śrāddha*.
(The Procedure for Libation) Now, (3rd line).

Having washed the feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should offer libations with the tips of the fingers accompanied by the word *svāhā*: *hāṃ sarvebhyo mantrebhyaḥ svāhā*, *hāṃ ādityebhyaḥ svāhā*,
*hāṃ vasubhyaḥ svāhā*, *hāṃ rudrebhyaḥ svāhā*, *hāṃ viśvebhyaḥ svāhā*, *hāṃ sādhyebhyaḥ svāhā*, *haṃ*.
*Hāṃ* to the Rudras, *svāhā*. *Hāṃ* to the Bhṛgus, *svāhā*. *Hāṃ* to the Aṅgirases, *svāhā*.
*Hāṃ* to all the gods, *svāhā*. [Thus with the tip of the finger, using the *devatīrtha*.
*Hāṃ* obeisance to Atri. *Hāṃ* obeisance to Viśiṣṭha. *Hāṃ* obeisance to Pulastya. *Hāṃ*... [sixth line]
Salutation to Kratu. Hāṃ, salutation to Bharadvāja. Hāṃ, salutation to Viśvāmitra. Hāṃ, salutation to Pracetas.
Hāṃ, salutation to Ṛcchaka. Hāṃ, salutation to Agastya. Hāṃ, salutation to Dadhīca. Hāṃ, salutation to Durvāsas. Oṃ. (7th line)

"Salutation to all the sages (*ṛṣi*). Thus, with the joints of the *parvan*s, one should offer oblations to the sages using the *ṛṣitīrtha* [finger-tip]: "Hāṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to Sanaka; Hāṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to Sananda;
Hāṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to Sanātana; Hāṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to Sanatkumāra. (8th line)

*Vaṣaṭ! Hāṃ, to Kapila, *vaṣaṭ!* Hāṃ, to Pañcaśikha, *vaṣaṭ!* Hāṃ, to Ṛbhu, *vaṣaṭ!* Hāṃ, to all humans, *vaṣaṭ!*—thus, for humans, with the hollow of the palms (*karatalasandhi*), that is, by the human *tīrtha*. Hāṃ, to all beings (*bhūta*), *vauṣaṭ!*—thus, for the beings, with the base of the palms (*karatalamūla*), that is, by the *bhūta-tīrtha*. Hāṃ...
Svadhā to Kavyavāhana! Hāṃ, svadhā to Anala! Hāṃ, svadhā to Soma! Hāṃ, svadhā to Aryaman!
Hāṃ, svadhā to Agniṣvātta! Hāṃ, svadhā to the Barhiṣads! Hāṃ, svadhā to Ājyapa! Hāṃ, svadhā to Somapa!

With the mantra "svadhā," one should satisfy the divine ancestors (*devapitṛs*) using the root of the index finger and the *pitṛtīrtha*. Regarding the case of deceased paternal ancestors: with that same *tīrtha*, [one offers]: "Hāṃ, svadhā to the father Īśāna; Hāṃ, svadhā to the grandfather Sadāśiva;
Hāṃ, svadhā to the great-grandfather Śānta."

Hāṃ! Svadhā to all the paternal ancestors. Regarding those whose mothers have passed away: Hāṃ! Svadhā to the mothers; Hāṃ! Svadhā to the grandmothers; Hāṃ! Svadhā to the great-grandmothers; Hāṃ! Svadhā to all the maternal ancestors. Hāṃ! To all... (fifth line).

[Offer] *svadhā* to the kinsmen. Then, having offered libations with the *devatīrtha* [finger-tip] saying, "Hāṃ, *svāhā* to all my gurus," one should cast water along with *kuśa* grass onto the bank while reciting "Astrāya phaṭ"; this is the ritual purification (*mārjana*). One who is dispassionate, however, should offer libations to Śiva alone using the root mantra and the mantras of the limbs of Brahman ending in *svāhā*. Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Having performed the withdrawal with the *namonta-hṛdaya* mantra and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*,

one should withdraw the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), wash the loincloth and other items, place them upon the left forearm, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), carry out the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and pay obeisance to the preceptor and others.

Having entered a house or a monastery, having washed one's feet, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), and performed the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*), one should begin the worship of Śiva. *Śrīṃ*. Thus ends the section on purity, sipping water, and bathing in the *Kriyādīpikā* composed by the eminent teacher, the protector of the *śaiva* tradition, the foremost yogin, [whose name begins with] Śiva. (13b, line 1)
The First Chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Performance of the Śiva Twilight Rite" (Śivasandhyānuṣṭhānavidhi).
[The Procedure for the Worship of Śiva]:
Now we shall explain the sequence of the procedure for the worship of Śiva for the spiritual sons (putraka), the practitioners (sādhaka), and the teachers (ācārya).

Having brought flowers, *kuśa* grass, fuel-sticks, water, and so forth— possessing the characteristics to be described later— for the purpose of worship and fire-oblation, either by means of the disciple or having gathered them himself,

[the preceptor], standing within the enclosure of the *astra-mantra*, enters the house, washes his feet, performs the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), bathes with ashes, and again performs the ritual sipping of water.

(3rd line) Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), while mentally relinquishing the thirty-one principles beginning with Earth and ending with Māyā, [one should meditate upon] the center of the fivefold weapon-array,
which is endowed with all auspiciousness pervaded by the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*) and adorned with canopies and banners. (4th line)

Having entered the delightful place of worship— which is adorned with lamps and the like, its floor smeared with cow dung— by first stepping with the right foot, one should first worship the Sun (Bhāskara), because for a householder, the worship beginning with the Sun and ending with Caṇḍa is prescribed by the ritual injunctions.
(Sūryapūjā) Thus, having brought forth the articles of worship and standing facing the east, one should worship the Sun with the mantra:
*astrāya phaṭ*. (6th line)

Having purified the palms and backs of the hands, and having sprinkled them with water while reciting the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should perform the placement]: With the thumbs and index fingers: *aṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*. With the little finger, ring finger, middle finger, and so on, together with the thumbs: *aṃ* to the sun (*arkāya*), *namaḥ* to the head; *jvālinī* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *namaḥ*; *aṃ hṛṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *namaḥ*.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Hāṃ, salutation to the two sun-eyes" on the middle fingers of both palms,

and with "Phaṭ, salutation to the weapon" on the index fingers; having encased [the hands] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), joined them, and performed the placement with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should proceed] with the root mantra of the Sun.
Having performed the purification, one should apply the *hṛdaya-mantra* at the heart with the right thumb and ring finger joined; the *śiras-mantra* at the head;

the *śikhā-mantra* at the crest-lock; the *kavaca-mantra* from the ears and covering the face down to the middle of the breasts using both index fingers; and the *netra-mantra* on the two eyes. Then, having applied the *astra-mantra* on the palms of the hands, one should [apply it] in the ten directions.

Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the *koṭika* weapon-mantra, and having applied the root-mantra to all limbs with the *mahāmudrā*, one should visualize one's own body as the form of the sun.

One should meditate. Afterwards, having placed the *arghya* offering in a copper vessel with water mixed with red flowers and other ingredients, one should descend to the ground on one's knees, bring [the water] up to the head, and offer this *darśanārghya* while reciting: *hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ śivasūryāya namaḥ*. Then, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity. Thereafter, one should purify the *arghya* vessel with the *astra-mantra*.
"Obeisance to Khaṣolkā, who has a throbbing red bindu in the center of her forehead and a stream of nectar from her heart"— having thus filled [the vessel] with scented water,
one should then worship it with the six limbs and the root mantra, and with the *astra* and *kavaca* mantras.

Having performed the protective veiling (*rakṣāvakuṇṭhana*) with the root mantra and displayed the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*), one should worship the substances, oneself, and the ground with water using the weapon-mantra (*astra*). Then, having dispelled obstacles with flowers and the weapon-mantra upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), [one should proceed].
One should worship either a drawn eight-petaled lotus or an eight-petaled lotus fashioned from copper or other materials.
There, on the right side of the door, [one should place] "Aṃ Daṇḍine namaḥ" (Salutation to Daṇḍin).
Daṇḍin is at the right of the door, fair-complexioned, with a large belly and a beard.
Holding a pen made of collyrium and a leaf of birch-bark,
he records virtuous deeds as the witness of the karma of living beings.
On his left side, [one should worship] "Aṃ, obeisance to Piṅgala.
Piṅgala is on the left side, while Pratīhāra and Daṇḍavān are also there.
Having thus meditated and worshipped [them],...

To the northeast of the lotus: Homage to Gaṇapati. One should visualize the Lord of the Gaṇas as seated upon a red lotus throne, possessing four faces and four hands, holding a tusk, a noose, a goad, and a blue lotus.
Having meditated thus and performed worship,
[one should place] "Aṃ,
obeisance to the Gurus" in its south-eastern direction [to one who is] richly adorned with a crown of matted locks and possesses a body as white as a conch shell.
The sacred thread (brahmasūtra), joined with a yogic belt, [is worn] above the region of the navel.

Having meditated upon the supreme Guru, peaceful and bearing the mudrā known as *kṛtayoga*, and having thus meditated, one should worship him in his proper place in the center with: "Aṃ, obeisance to Prabhūtāsana. In this way, one should worship the white pedestal (*śvetapīṭha*). Then, in the four corners starting from the southeast (*āgneya*), [one should worship] Aṃ Vima...
"Oṃ, salutation to Laya; oṃ, salutation to Sāra; oṃ, salutation to Ārādhya; oṃ, salutation to Paramasukha.
Having thus visualized lions of white, red, yellow, and green colors, one should worship them. Above that, [one says]:
"Oṃ, salutation to the lotus-seat (padmāsana). In the center of the white lotus, upon the filaments starting from the east and ending in the northeast—

RĀṂ, salutation to Dīptā; RĪṂ, salutation to Sūkṣmā; RUṂ, salutation to Jayā; RŪṂ, salutation to Bhadrā. (Fifth line) REṂ, salutation to Vibhūti; RAIṂ, salutation to Vimalā; ROṂ, salutation to Amoghā; RAUṂ, salutation to Vidyutā.
In the pericarp, in the northeast, [one should worship] "Salutation to Sarvatomukhī.
These nine powers, having the form of blazing lamp-flames, are to be meditated upon.
Or else:

Having thus meditated upon them—red in color, holding lotuses and chowries in their hands, and adorned with ornaments on all their limbs—and having worshipped them, one should display the *visphurā* mudrā. In the center: *oṃ arkāsanāya namaḥ*. This is the *arkāsana*.
Having worshipped him who is mounted upon a white lotus, who has the luster of a pomegranate flower,
who possesses a shimmering great red radiance, and who stands in the center of a circular mandala;

One should meditate upon the Sun-god as having one face and two eyes, wearing red garments, with his two hands holding a clearly white lotus with its stalk resting upon his shoulder. Having thus meditated:

"Aṃ khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolkā, the solar form. Having thus projected the form upon the seat, and having bestowed the eyes with "Bhaṃ, obeisance to the two eyes of Bhānu," one should fill the joined palms with flowers and [visualize] the shimmering light drawn from the forehead...

Having meditated upon the eighth auspicious sign, one should invoke that pervading [deity] with this root mantra: *hrāṃ hrīṃ sahaśivasūryāya namaḥ*. Having invoked [the deity] with the heart-mantra and the invocation mudrā, and having established [him] on the lotus-seat with the placement mudrā, [one performs] the presence (*sannidhāna*).

Having brought [the deity] near, having restrained [it] with firmness, having displayed the *bimbamudrā*, having applied the heart-mantra and other mantras to the locations starting from the heart and ending with the hands of the Sun, having effected identity with the root mantra, and having performed the protection and veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*). (Third line)

Having performed the Amṛtamudrā and Mahāmudrā with the root mantra, and having offered water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the arghya offering with the *kaṣolka* mantra ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*, and having offered flowers, incense, unbroken rice (akṣata), and so forth with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should utter] *khaṃ khaṣo*.

"Oṃ kāya hṛdayāya namaḥ. Having thus bathed [the deity] at the heart with the *upahṛdaya* mantra, preceded by the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth, and having adorned [him] with red garments, perfumes, and other offerings, one offers three handfuls of flowers with the mantra: "Hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Śiva-Sūrya."

Having worshipped [the deity] and offered the *arghya*, one should display the *padmamudrā* and the *bimbamudrā*. Then, having worshipped the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*), and having prayed for the sake of the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhojāṅga-pūjā*), one should worship the mantras of the heart, head, crest, and armor in the directions of the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest, and in the locations such as the heart of the Sun (*sūryahṛdaya*).

One should meditate upon the limbs of the Sun as being gentle, red in color, granting boons with lotuses in their hands, adorned, and having two arms. Having thus meditated and worshipped them, one should worship his [the Sun's] eye in front of the deity, which has the form previously described.

Having meditated upon the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), which resembles a mass of lightning and has a face made terrifying by fierce fangs, in the four petals starting from the east, and having worshipped it— (8th line).

Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* for the heart and other limbs, the *goviṣāṇamudrā* for the two eyes, and the *trāsinīmudrā* for the weapon (*astra*), one should perform the worship. Thereafter, on the tips of the petals in the directions starting from the east: *saṃ somāya namaḥ*; *buṃ budhāya namaḥ*;
*bṛṃ bṛhaspataye namaḥ*.

"Bhaṃ, obeisance to Bhārgava" [and so on] at the tips of the petals starting from the southeast: "Am, obeisance to Aṅgāraka; Śaṃ, obeisance to Śanaiścara; Raṃ, obeisance to Rāhu; Kaṃ, obeisance to Ketu. And likewise: "Soma, who has the luster of the kumuda and kunda flowers; Budha, who has the radiance of refined gold."
The Guru [planet] has the luster of yellow orpiment, while Śukra resembles the Gokṣura plant.
One should meditate on Mars as red, Saturn as resembling the color of a kingfisher,
Rāhu as black with palms joined in reverence, and Ketu as having the appearance of smoke-colored light.
All of them, assuming forms at will and adorned with divine ornaments,
have their left hands placed upon their thighs and their right hands granting the gesture of fearlessness.
He saw Soma holding a white lotus, Rāhu and Ketu with palms joined in reverence;
Śani with half his body visible and hair standing erect, his eyes red with blood;
and Rāhu with a face distorted by terrible fangs. Thus.

Having meditated and performed worship, and having displayed the mudrā of salutation, one should present the offerings of incense, lamps, food, betel, and so forth, along with a mirror, parasol, fly-whisk, water for rinsing the mouth, and the arghya offering; then,
having recited the root mantra as many times as possible, [one should proceed] with the water from the arghya vessel.

Having offered [the oblation] to the Sun with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having recited the ten-fold portion for the limbs (*aṅga-mantras*), and having presented [it], [the deity] is served by Daṇḍa and others;
seated upon a throne of four lions with pure faces, he possesses the luster of a ruby due to the networks of powers (*śakti*) such as Dīptā and the rest.

May he— whose body is the form of the sun with its rays, whose limbs are the planets and the lunar mansions, who is the foremost refuge for wandering mendicants, and who is seated upon a white lotus— protect you, he who has two hands, possesses a pair of auspicious eyes, and is like Śambhu and Sūrya.

Having recited the hymn and so forth in this manner, having paid homage to the deity and performed worship, one should offer the *parāṅmukha-arghya* with the mantra ending in *khaṣolkāya svāhā*. Then, saying "Forgive me," one should [dismiss the deity] with the *nārāca-mudrā* and the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, while reciting the mantras for the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth: *khaṃ khaṣolkāya sūryamūrtaye namaḥ*.

Thus, having united him with the divine mudrā, O God of gods, one should join him to the Śiva-sun within the lotus of the heart by means of the root mantra. Then, in the northwestern direction: "Aṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa Tejas.
Thus [one visualizes] Caṇḍa, who is red, with a fierce face, and two hands displaying the lotus and the gesture of fearlessness.

Thus, contemplating [the deity], having worshipped, offered the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*), and presented the water of honor (*arghya*), one should dismiss [the deity]. Alternatively, one may dismiss [the deity] at the conclusion of the Śiva-worship.
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the Sun.
The Worship of Śiva
Having gone outside, washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), applied the *tripuṇḍra* mark, and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the teacher—
because the worship of the *adhikāra-liṅga* is for the sake of another, being intended to bestow grace upon the disciple— should perform the worship of the door and so forth,
as well as the worship of the deity together with the retinue. As for the son-initiate (*putraka*) or the practitioner (*sādhaka*)...
In the worship of the *liṅga* for one's own sake, one should not perform the worship of the door and so forth. Thus says the *Āgama*:
"Therein, the worship of the door is not prescribed, nor the offering to Caṇḍeśa;
there, no oblation is offered with a mantra, nor is there a daily festival."

The great bell (*mahāghaṇṭā*) is not prescribed, nor is the rite of concealment (*tiraskaraṇī*). The procedure for pure dance (*śuddhanṛttavidhi*) is not mentioned, as are the sun, obstacles, and likewise the teacher.
Having performed worship, the best of those who know mantras should perform the sacrifice for his own sake. Thus it is said.
(The ritual sequence for the worship of the doors:
(7th line)

Having constructed a maṇḍala in the front pavilion of the southern door of the worship hall, one should purify the general arghya vessel there with the mantra ending in *namaḥ* and the *astra-mantra*. Having placed it upon a leaf in the maṇḍala, one should fill it with pure water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra* ending in *namaḥ*.

Having worshipped with the *namaḥ* mantra, with flowers, or with the vessel, and having consecrated that [vessel] seven times with the same [mantra], one should hold the general *arghya* vessel and, through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, sequentially salute the thirty-one principles beginning with Earth and ending with Māyā by means of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). Then, with the water from the general *arghya*, [one salutes] that foremost gateway of the worship of Pure Knowledge.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should meditate thus upon Gaṇeśa on the upper right side of the *udumbara* tree:

"I praise Lambodara, who resembles a dark cloud, holding an axe and a rosary in his two upward-pointing hands, and a ladle-cake (*laḍḍuka*) and a tusk in his two lower hands, the left and the right. Having meditated in this way...
Having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," [one should worship] in the area to its north [the goddess] who is white, clad in white garments, and holding a rosary and a book.
And with her right and left hands, she holds the very gracious Sarasvatī.
Thus meditating: "Hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī"— having thus worshipped [her],
[one should visualize her] holding a *śrīphala* and a lotus with her left and right hands between those two.
She possessed a golden luster and great splendor, being bathed by two elephants with their trunks.

Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī," [one should visualize] on the right branch of oneself a red, three-eyed, matted-haired [deity] with two hands, the right and the left.
And [he saw] Nandikeśvara, bearing a rosary and a trident.

Having meditated thus, [one should say]: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin. Having worshipped him in this manner, [one should worship] the one seated upon a crocodile-throne to his north, radiant, with two hands—one on the right and one on the left—...
She is white in form, holding a blue lotus and a full water-jar.
Having meditated thus, [one should offer] "Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā.
(7th line) Having worshipped thus, on the northern branch [one should place] Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, or Mahākāla, with two hands, the left and the right.
He held a skull and a trident, and had a hideous countenance.
Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla," [one should place] a jar on his right side [with the mantra] ".................. and in both his left and right hands.
And one should visualize Yamunā holding a blue lotus.
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Yamunā. Having thus worshipped and requested protection for them, [one performs] the expulsion of obstacles.

Having performed the placement of the root-mantra (*nyastamūla*), looking upward at the divine beings with "Haḥ," and having cast a flower or a leaf with the weapon-mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ" while employing the blazing *nārāca* mudrā,
one should [ward off] those various obstacles moving through the intermediate space with the *pāśupata* weapon-mantra "Huṃ Phaṭ" by striking three times on the right side of the ground.
Having moved a short distance from the shrine room and taking refuge at its left branch, he enters within with his right foot first;
at the threshold, he says: *Haḥ astrāya dvārapālāya namaḥ*.
Having visualized the weapon in the form that will be described and having worshipped it, one should proceed by circumambulation to the southwest [and visualize]:
a fair-complexioned, pot-bellied, four-faced being with a beard, seated upon a swan,
holding a staff in his right hand and a rosary and a water-pot in his left.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with the mantra: *Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site*.

When engaged in the endeavor of propitiating Śiva at common [sites] such as riverbanks or gardens, and having constructed the worship pavilion with *kuśa* grass, *darbha* grass, and so forth, one should draw the lines according to the stated method.
One should perform the worship of the doors and so forth.
(The purification of the elements.
Thereafter, the rite for bathing (line 6).
Having procured all the materials for worship— such as pure water and other items filtered through cloth and obtained from great holy sites like the Gaṅgā—
one should sit comfortably on a seat in the northeast direction facing north, O Lord.
(7th line)

Having protected the sacrificial hall by means of the encasement in armor consisting of the ramparts of missiles, [one should perform the daily rite], according to the maxim that "all salt roasted in *rumā* [salt-earth] becomes entirely salty," because the gross body has evolved from the blood and semen of the mother and father. (8th line)

Since all food, drink, and so forth that have been consumed transform into the nature of impurity, and for the sake of purifying that [impurity] and pacifying its resulting transformations, one must perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) every day prior to the internal sacrifice; indeed, for one who has not performed the purification of the elements— (17b, first line)
If it is asked how a person has the qualification for rites beginning with the offering of the *arghya* and ending with the worship of the Sun and Brahmā,

we reply: because those [rites] such as the offering of the *arghya* constitute external sacrifice (*bāhyayajana*), they are [rendered unnecessary] by the external purification through clay-baths, the wearing of ashes, and the wearing of rudrākṣa beads.

Since purity is already established there, one indeed possesses the qualification for that [rite]. However, in the case of the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*), because the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*)—which effects internal purity—is indispensable, the *bhūtaśuddhi* must be performed. This [purification] is to be carried out according to the distinctions of the *putraka*, the *sādhaka*, and the *ācārya*, and through the divisions of gross, subtle, and supreme.
(Third line) "In three ways! Indeed,
you must never [use] weapons against Śūdras."

If it is asked, "How can there be the status of a teacher for a Śūdra, given such a profusion of scriptural statements?"— it is true that the status of a teacher does not exist with respect to all castes. However, according to the sequence of the [higher] castes, the status of a teacher does exist for those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) and so forth.
Thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras born of pure lineages—
among these, they should be known as teachers, and never others."
In the *Dviśatikālottara*:

"O Six-faced One, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those who are pure are the practitioners (*sādhakas*); however, the teachers (*ācāryas*) follow the sequence of gold [and the other metals]."
Also in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"Those belonging to the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with the Śiva-śāstra and are averse to the Paśu-śāstra are proclaimed as Ācāryas."
And elsewhere: "Gold, silver, copper, and iron—
this quartet attains [the state of gold] through the power of the mercury-transmutation (*rasavedha*)."
Just as copper pierced by mercury attains the state of being mercury on both sides,
so too the body pierced by knowledge shall never again fall into the state of a bound soul.
Through the rite of consecration for Śiva, even a stone becomes the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
since even a stone attains the state of Śiva, why indeed should a Śūdra not do so?
"The teacher of all castes shall be a guru belonging to the four castes;
this is the truth, O Great Goddess, as proclaimed in the Śiva-śāstra. (18a, first line)
"A Śūdra (who is established in his duty) is fit only for the daily *iṣṭi* sacrifice;

if he were fit for consecration (*abhiṣeka*), how much more so for installation (*sthāpanā*) and the like? This statement refers to the installation of a *liṅga* intended for another's benefit (*parārtha*).
(Regarding the ritual for the elemental level: there, the son and others (2nd line),
