having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) and having cupped their hands, [should assign] the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), deity (devatā), power (śakti), seed-syllable (bīja), and so forth, according to their respective places.

Having placed the two hands [on the body] with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having formed them into a bud-like gesture (*mukula*), one should visualize them as having the form of fire from the wrists down. Then,
having sprinkled them with the power-mantra (*śakti-mantra*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should place the seat, the image, and the root-mantra upon the palms, beginning with the thumbs.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five Brahmans, beginning with Īśāna and ending at the little finger, with the fist closed and the thumb [extended]:
*HOṂ* to the head of Īśāna, to the *Śāntyatīta* kalā, *namaḥ*; with the thumb and forefinger: *HEṂ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, to the *Śānti* kalā, *namaḥ*.

With the thumb and middle finger: *huṃ ra*, salutation to Aghora, the heart, the *vidyā* aspect. (5th line) With the thumb and ring finger: *hiṃ*, salutation to Vāmadeva, the secret organ, the *pratiṣṭhā* aspect.
With the little finger and thumb: *haṃ*, salutation to Sadyojāta, the form, the *nivṛtti* aspect. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

The sphere of space (ākāśamaṇḍala), located at the head, is circular, crystal-like in appearance, characterized by the quality of sound, the substratum of the sense of hearing, marked with the *bindu*, and its seed-syllable is *Haṃ*. Sadāśiva is its presiding deity; it is presided over by Īśāna.
The sphere of air (vāyumaṇḍala) extends from the forehead to the ears.

The hexagon is smoke-colored, possesses the qualities of sound and touch, is the locus of the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*), and is marked with six dots. Its seed-syllable is *Yaṃ*, with Maheśvara as its presiding deity; it is presided over by Tatpuruṣa. From the ears down to the navel is the fire-mandala, triangular and red-hued, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, and form; it is the locus of the sense of sight (*cakṣurindriya*).
The Svastika is its emblem; *raṃ* is its seed-syllable; Rudra is its presiding deity; it is established by the Aghora mantra.
From the navel down to the knees, it is the form of the half-moon of the water-maṇḍala; it is white in color, possesses the qualities of sound, touch, and form, and is marked with a lotus.
The seat of the sense of taste; the seed-syllable *vaṃ*; Brahmā as the presiding deity; presided over by Vāmadeva;
extending from the knees to the soles of the feet; the earth-maṇḍala, which is square, yellow in color, and possesses the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste;
the seat of the sense of smell.

The seed-syllable *laṃ* is marked with a vajra; its presiding deity is Brahmā; it is presided over by Sadyojāta. These five elements, from the feet up to the head, are mutually connected through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). One’s own body consists of the five elements beginning with earth; the seed-syllable is distinct from Brahmā and Viṣṇu, measuring four finger-breadths.
Rooted in passion, hatred, merit, demerit, and delusion; nourished by knowledge (*vidyā*) and the other [faculties]; having the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* as its core;
with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs as its branches and sub-branches;

with the perception of objects as its foliage; [having] the manifoldness of states of being (*bhāva-prapañca*) as its trunk; bearing the fruits of cognition (*buddhi*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*); it is to be enjoyed by the bird that is the Puruṣa.

Having meditated upon the form of the banyan tree with its roots above and branches below, characterized by the relationship between the enjoyed and the enjoyer, one should withdraw the Self— which pervades one's own body— by means of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) through the mantra of the Self’s form.
Within the lunar, solar, and fiery mandalas of the nectar of power (*śakti-pīyūṣa*),
having established oneself together with the inner ruler Śiva in the center of the blossomed lotus of the heart,

and having refined the individual soul (*aṇu*) by means of the mandala of the nectar of power and so forth, the purification of the self occurs through the power of the union with the energy of the Lord.
It brings about the power of the elements (*bhūtaśakti*).
As it is said in the *Kālottara*:
Having withdrawn the self by means of the mantra and the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), one should place it within the fully blossomed lotus of the heart, which pervades one's own body,
inside the nectar-mandala of the Power (*śakti*) situated within the Moon, Sun, and Fire; then, having sealed that atom (*aṇu*) with the mandalas beginning with Power.
Then, having formed the tortoise-mudrā (kūrmamudrā), one should purify the reality of the elements (bhūtatattva).
And elsewhere:
"Then, one should gradually bring the Lord of the Senses (akṣeśa), who resides in the sense organs, [into the heart]."

"One should gradually perform the purification of the self by the self within the self. Having placed five flowers or five vessels in the left hand with the mantras of the *nivṛtti*-kalā and the others, and having formed the tortoise-mudrā (*kūrmamudrā*), [one recites] first with half an inhalation (*pūraka*): *hlāṃ*.

Having mentally uttered "hlāṃ (third line) hlāṃ hlāṃ hlā(hlāṃ) nivṛttikalāyai haḥ huṃphaṭ," one should visualize one's own body as a banyan tree devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruit, with its five qualities such as fragrance and so forth removed; [this is done] by means of the latter half of the inhalation (*pūraka*).
Having mentally uttered "hvīṃ hvīṃ hvīṃ hīṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai haḥ huṃphaṭ," and having meditated upon the four qualities beginning with *utsāda*, one should,
while performing *kumbhaka* [breath retention], mentally utter "hrūṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ vidyākalāyai haḥ huṃphaṭ" and [meditate upon] the three qualities beginning with *rūpa*, which have been removed.
Having visualized that [the offering]— consisting of dry leaves and the like— is burned by the *kaulāgni* arising from all the big toes,
one should mentally utter "hyaiṃ hyaiṃ śāntikalāyai haḥ phaṭ" during the first half of the exhalation (*recaka*),
thereby removing the qualities of sound and touch.
Having visualized [the body] as reduced to ashes and dissolved by means of the supreme half-recaka breath, one should mentally utter "Hāṃ, to the Kalā beyond peace;

Haḥ Huṃ Phaṭ," and visualize it as having its quality of sound eliminated, appearing like pure crystal. Then, having visualized it as completely purified, with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should [visualize] the downward-facing lotus situated within the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Having caused [the nectar] to flow through streams of immortality that have entered the openings of all the channels, and having flooded the body both internally and externally,
one should visualize oneself within the blossomed heart-lotus as resembling the moon released from Rāhu, [pervading] the interior and exterior...
Having performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* beginning with *māṇa-śrī-karṇa*, as well as the *pañcabrahma-nyāsa*, the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*, and the *karāṅga-nyāsa*,
one should perform the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). Or, in the case of a *putraka*, having performed the visualization of the *nyāsa* as before, [one should meditate on] oneself mentally.

Having extracted [the subtle body] from one's own body and joined it with Śiva, twelve finger-breadths above the *brahmarandhra*, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) as previously described. Thus ends the procedure for the physical dimension (*ādhibhautika*).
(The Internal Ritual):
The practitioner, having performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) as before, [should proceed] from the two big toes up to the bladder; that which is above it is of two forms.
Having meditated upon the Suṣumnā as being of a single form extending to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*), joined with the Iḍā and Piṅgalā in the heart, throat, and other locations,

and consisting of a hollow bud-like lotus facing downwards; and having visualized within it the Śakti in the form of the Supreme Vyoman, from whom flows a stream of nectar both internally and externally— [in the center].
Having meditated upon one's own form as blazing with the syllable *huṃ*,
and having performed inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), one should fix the mind on the *huṃ* and exhale the breath upward while continuously uttering "huṃ phaṭ."
Having opened the knot at the top of the lotus bud and having turned it back, one should exhale through the right channel; then,
having gathered the consciousness by means of the inhalation (pūraka), one should place the *jīva*— which rests in the heart-lotus, has the form of a shimmering star,
consists of the seed-syllable ending in *saṃ*, and is enclosed within the heart— into the syllable *huṃ* at the crown of the head, [visualizing it] as the embodiment of the seed-syllable.
Having meditated upon the Person (Puruṣa), who resides within the crest of the syllable *huṃ*, who is delimited by the city of eight (*puryaṣṭaka*), solitary, and free from affliction;

and having performed the *kumbhaka* breath-retention while causing the vital air to move upward, one should proceed by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* through the sequential abandonment of the spheres beginning with Brahmā.

With a single exhalation, saying "hrūṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Self," one should unite [the self] with Śiva, who extends for twelve *mātrās* within the temple (*prāsāda*), for the purpose of experiencing the karma that is to be experienced.
This is the internal procedure (*adhyātmika-vidhi*).

(Regarding the procedure for the divine level): If it is argued that there is a requirement for another agent here, based on such statements as "one should take up the self through the sequence of withdrawal and unite it with Śiva," [the response is: having placed the self at the top of a pillar and then cast it down again, [one unites it] in the middle.

There is no contradiction, because [the act of] "I establish" is possible there, unlike in the case of verbal expression or physical gesture (*ābhilāpa-abhinaya*). One should perform the remainder as previously stated.

At the time of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Earth and ending with Sādākhya should be dissolved in reverse order into their respective causes.

One should meditate upon those [elements] that are devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) and exist in a subtle form: namely, earth in smell, water in taste, fire in form, wind in touch, and space in sound; these mantras reside in the *tāmasa* ego (*ahaṅkāra*). [The faculties] known as speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals—

The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are in the *rājasa* ego; and the mind is in the *sāttvika* ego. That [mind] is in the intellect (*buddhi*), and that [intellect] is in the consciousness (*citta*). The Great One (*mahat*) is in the *vyakta-guṇa-prakṛti* (the manifest quality-nature). And that [nature] is in passion (*rāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and the principle of the person (*puruṣa-tattva*). [Passion, etc. are in the principle of limited agency (*kalā-tattva*), and limited agency is in the principle of necessity (*niyati*). Limited agency is in the principle of illusion (*māyā-tattva*). Thus they exist in their subtle form.

Having meditated upon the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*) within the principle of Īśvara, and likewise within the principle of Sadāśiva—one should meditate on all these as existing in a subtle form. Thus, one should meditate that everything consisting of bondage is void (*śūnya*).

At the root ending with *vauṣaṭ*, from the downward-facing lotus situated within the crest-lock (*śikhā*), by means of streams of nectar flowing [downward], [one should fill] the openings of all the channels (*nāḍī*).

Having bathed the body, both external and internal, with the *tāraka* mantra— which consists of the three syllables beginning with *haṃ* and ending with *saḥ*— [one attains] the seat whose nature is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).

Having placed the *puryaṣṭaka* upon its ear with the four *kūṭas*, one should contemplate it as having descended by means of the *praṇava*. Within that, having brought down the corpse-like self residing at the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *praṇava* through the inhalation (*pūraka*) and the fivefold *kāla* according to the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), one should establish it in the form of light.
One should perform the consecration by reciting the Śakti-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, through the flow of abundant nectar overflowing from the Śakti of the jar.

The Ācārya, however, [should do so] in the locations beginning with the heart, following the sequence of the Prāsāda mantra, having abandoned the causal deities such as Brahmā and others, [and thus becoming] the embodiment of the twelve Śaktis.

One should unite [the self] with the Supreme Śiva at the end of *manana*. This concludes the procedure for the presiding deities (*adhidaivika*). Having thus become identical with Śiva, one should initiate oneself, according to the scriptural statement:

"The self initiates the self. The mantras reside in the words (*pada*), the words in the phonemes (*varṇa*); the phonemes, by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), [dissolve] into the letter *a*, and the letter *a* into the resonance (*nāda*); and the resonance into the supreme point (*parabindu*). The worlds [likewise dissolve].

Having joined the *tattvas* within the *tattvas* according to the sequence of their withdrawal, having united the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti* and the *kriyā-śakti* and others with the pure and impure *māyās*,
and having contemplated the gross body as being like a tree as previously described, [one should burn it] with the fire of time (*kālāgni*) by means of the *śivājñā* mantra.

"Burnt" means reduced to ashes, being completely liberated from all adjuncts such as those pertaining to the individual soul (*āṇava*). Having contemplated this, and having become one with Śiva within the powers (*śakti*),
he who has matured his self should again contemplate those elements that have arisen through the process of emanation for the sake of bestowing grace, using the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
By means of streams of nectar flowing from the downward-facing lotus situated within the *khikhā*, which have entered the openings of all the channels (*nāḍī*),

having flooded the entire body both external and internal, [one should meditate] with the *tāraka* mantra joined with the three measures (*mātrā*) beginning with the crocodile (*makara*) at the heart-lotus.

Having placed the seat consisting of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) in its pericarp, one should contemplate [the deity] descended by means of the *praṇava* with four parts of consciousness. Then, having brought down Śiva— who resides at the limit of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*)— into that [seat], as the self consisting of five parts by means of the *praṇava* with five parts during inhalation (*pūraka*), [one should contemplate him] in the form of light through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).

Having established [the disciple], one should consecrate them with a profuse stream of nectar flowing from the agitated Śakti by means of the utterance of the Śakti-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. If it is asked, "How can the removal of impurities residing in the body occur through mere mental visualization (*bhāvanā*) alone?", [the answer is: as in the case of one bitten by a venomous snake...

Just as the removal of poison occurs merely through the meditation on Garuḍa, so too here, through the meditation on the ritual action of the mantra, the removal of impurity and the pacification of the transformations of the elements occur; thus it is faultless. Even for one who is dispassionate, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is exactly the same.
(The Procedure for the Mātṛkānyāsa):
Thereafter, one should perform the internal and external nyāsas of the Mātṛkā, the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the thirty-eight kalās.
This is the sequence: one who is devoid of the Mātṛkānyāsa has no authority to recite mantras. (5th line)

Therefore, one should first perform the *mātṛtā-nyāsa*. The procedure for the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* is manifold; among these, because the fourth [set] pertains to the five-syllabled *prāsāda*, there is the internal *mātṛkā-nyāsa* accompanied by the five-syllabled *prāsāda*, and the external *mātṛkā-nyāsa* accompanied by [the names of] Śrīkaṇṭha and the others.
And one should perform [the internal placement]:
(The Internal Mātrkānyāsa) In the center of the Suṣumnā: Haṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva. (Line 7)
In the *mūlādhāra*, there is the tetrad: *vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saḥ*. In the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, there are six: *baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ*.
In the *maṇipūraka*, there are ten: *ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ*. In the *anāhata*, there are two: *kaṃ khaṃ*.

(........... *jaṃ*, *jhaṃ*, *ñaṃ*, *bhraṃ*, *ṭaṃ*, *ṭhaṃ*—these are twelve for purification. *am*, *ām*, *im*, *īm*, *um*, *ūm*, *ṛm*, *ṝm*, *ḷm*, *ḹm*, *em*, *aim*, *om*, *aum*, *am*, *aḥ*—these are sixteen. *Ājñā*. (21b, first line)

(............. | Thus there are fifty-one mantra-syllables. One should mentally place them upon the lotus petals of those respective locations and shapes, together with the previously mentioned five-syllable *prasāda* mantra.
Now, (line 2)
The sequence for the external placement of the Mātṛkās (*bahirmātṛkānyāsakrama*):

*Am*—salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī; thus on the head. *Ām*—salutation to Ananta and Virājā; thus on the circumference of the face. *Im*—salutation to Sūkṣma and Tṛtīyā; thus [on the third line].

In the right eye: *īṃ trimūrtaye śāṃtyai namaḥ*. In the left eye: *uṃ amareśvarāya lolākṣyai namaḥ*. In the right ear: *ūṃ astraīśāya vartulākṣyai namaḥ*. In the left ear: *ṛṃ bhārabhūtaye dīrghakoṇāyai namaḥ*. In the right nostril: [the mantra follows].
*Ṛm* to *Atithi*, *Dīrghamukhī*—*namaḥ*—in the left nostril;
*Ḷm* to *Sthāṇu*, *Gomukhī*—*namaḥ*—on the right cheek; *Ḹṃ* to *Hara*, *Navamī*—*namaḥ*—on the left cheek; likewise, *Jhadīśa*.

"Salutation to Dīrghajihvikā" (6th line). On the upper lip: "Aiṃ, salutation to Bhautika and Kuṇḍodarī. On the lower lip: "Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta and Ūrdhvakeśinī. On the upper teeth: "Ai (Aum), salutation to Anugraheśvara and Vikṛtamukhī" (7th line).
*Namaḥ*—on the lower teeth.

*Am*—to Akrūra, to the support of the flickering flame, *namaḥ*. On the root of the palate: *Aḥ*—to Mahāsena, to the art of knowledge (*vidyākalā*), *namaḥ*. Thus, on the upper palate... *kaṃ* (8th line).

"Krodhīśāya mahākālāyai namaḥ. [At the elbow: "Daṃ caṇḍāya sarasvatyai namaḥ. [At the forearm: "Gaṃ pañcāntakāya sarvasiddhiyātāyai namaḥ. [At the wrist: "Ghaṃ śivottamāya gaurīye namaḥ. [On the palm: "Im ekarudrāya trailokyavidyāyai namaḥ."
At the tip of the finger: *caṃ* to Kārma, the power of mantra, *namaḥ* on the left arm (*vāmabāhau*).

On the elbow (*kūrpare*): *etadṛśe* to Ātmaśakti, *namaḥ*. At the wrist (*maṇibandhe*): *jaṃ* to Caturānana, the element-mother (*bhūtamātṛ*), *namaḥ*. On the palm (*hastatale*): *jhaṃ* to Ajeśa, *lambodarī*, *namaḥ*. [On the fingers: *ñaṃ* to Śarva... (third line).

*Nagaryai namaḥ*—on the tip of the finger. *Aṃ someśāya khecaryai namaḥ*—at the root of the right thigh. *Ṭhaṃ lāṅgaline mañjaryai namaḥ*—on the knee. *Ḍaṃ dārukāya vikṛtarūpiṇyai namaḥ*—on the shank. *Ḍhaṃ ardhanārīśvarāya vṛkodaryai namaḥ*—on the foot. *Ṇam*... [on the other foot].

"Umākāntāya pūtanāyai namaḥ"—at the tips of the fingers. "Tam āṣāḍhāya bhadrakāl̤yai namaḥ"—at the base of the left thigh. "Thaṃ daṇḍine yoginyai namaḥ"—at the knees. "Dam atraye śaṅkhinyai namaḥ"—on the shank. "Dhaṃ mīnāya garjinyai..."—[at the]... (sixth line).
*Namaḥ*—on the foot: *naṃ meṣāya kālarātryai namaḥ* on the tips of the toes; *paṃ lohitāya kubjinyai namaḥ* on the right side; *phaṃ śikhine kapardinyai namaḥ* on the left side;
*baṃ phalaṇḍāya jayāyai namaḥ* on the region of the back; *bhaṃ dviraṇḍāya*.

"Bhadrāyai namaḥ" [is placed] below the navel; "Mahākālāya Vijayāyai namaḥ" at the navel; "Bāline Sumukheśvaryai namaḥ" on the stomach; "Raṃ Bhujaṅgeśāya Revatyai namaḥ" on the chest; "Laṃ Pinākine" [on the chest].
"Salutation to Mālatī"—below the trika.
"Vaṃ, salutation to Khaḍgeśa of the Vāyavyā"—below the two armpits. "Śaṃ, salutation to Śambaka of the Vāruṇī"—on the right breast. "Śaṃ, salutation to Śveta."

"Obeisance to Rakṣopadhāriṇī"—on the left breast. "Obeisance to Saṃsṛgava Sahajā"—between the two breasts. "Obeisance to Haṃ Lakuṭīśa Lakṣmī"—in the heart. "Obeisance to Ḷaṃ Śiva Vyāpinī"—in the anus. "Obeisance to Tacca Saviśakti Viśakti"—in the secret place. "Obeisance to Kṣaṃ Saṃvartaka Māyā"—in the private organ.

Having thus performed the placement of the letters (*varṇanyāsa*) and the placement of the feet (*padanyāsa*) beginning with Īśāna as previously described, the preceptor should thereafter perform the placement of the digits (*kalānyāsa*). (The placement of the digits:)

And that [power] is threefold, due to the distinction between being with power (*saśaktika*), without power (*viśaktika*), and pure power (*kevalaśaktika*). Among these, for the student (*brahmacārin*) of the first stage, it is the *viśaktika-kalā* of the heart and so forth; for that householder (*gṛhastha*), it is the *saśaktika-kalā*; and for the fourth [stage], it is the *kevalaśaktika-kalā*. This is because of the scriptural statement: "The thirty-eight *kalās* should be deposited."

If it is asked how the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) can be performed using only the *śaktis* [and not the *kalās*], [the answer is: because these are words (*pada*) consisting of thirty-eight *kalās*. Since they are Vedic mantras, it is appropriate to perform the *nyāsa* by means of the *kalā-śaktis* alone, setting aside the individual words. Thus: *hāṃ* (6th line).

"Obeisance to Śaśinī"—on the head. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Aṅgadā"—above the forehead. "Hām, obeisance to Iṣṭā"—on the right side of the head. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Marīci"—on the left side of the head. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Jvālinī"—in the western part. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śāntyatītakalā"—above the crest-lock (śikhā).
At the edge of the forehead: *hāṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ*. At the mouth: *hāṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ*. At the region of the right ear:
*hāṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ*. At the region of the left ear: *hāṃ*... [23a, 1st line]

*Nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ*—at the location of the western crest. *Hāṃ tamase namaḥ*—in the heart. *Hām amoghāyai namaḥ*—in the throat. *Hāṃ jayāyai namaḥ*—on the right shoulder. *Hāṃ nidrāyai namaḥ*—on the left shoulder. *Hāṃ dhṛtyai namaḥ*—in the navel. *Hāṃ kṣāntyai namaḥ*—in the belly. *Hāṃ*.

"Salutation to Smṛti"—thus on the back. "Hāṃ, salutation to Akṣayā"—thus on the wings. "Hāṃ, salutation to Rasā"—thus on the chest. "Hāṃ, salutation to Ratnī"—thus on the two private parts. "Hāṃ, salutation to Pālyā"—thus on the right thigh. "Hāṃ, salutation to Rakṣā"—thus on the left thigh. Hāṃ...

"Hāṃ, salutation to Kalā" on the right knee; "Hāṃ, salutation to Samyamī" on the left knee; "Hāṃ, salutation to Kriyā" on the right shank; "Hāṃ, salutation to Mahātṛṣṇā" on the left shank; "Hāṃ, salutation to Mohā."
Thus: on the right buttock, "Hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣayā"; on the left buttock, "Hāṃ, obeisance to Cintā"; at the region of the bladder, "Hāṃ, obeisance to Mohinī";
on the northern and southern sides.
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Grāmiṇī"—on the left side of the abdomen. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Siddhi"—on the right foot. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Ṛddhi"—on the left foot. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Dhṛti"—on the right hand.
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī"—on the left hand. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Medhā"—at the tip of the nose. "Hāṃ, obeisance to Kauntī"—on the head.
With "Hāṃ, obeisance to Svadhā," [one should touch] the right arm; with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Prajā," the left arm. Thus ends the procedure for the householder's renunciation.

But one who is dispassionate should, in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), place the *kalās* beginning with *siddhi* upon the feet and other limbs. Following that, it is stated in the *Sāntānasaṃhitā*:
"The five *kalās* belong to Īśāna; the four *kalās* belong to Puruṣa;
the eight *kalās* belong to Aghora; and Vāmadeva has thirteen."

One should know that there are eight *sadyojāta* kalās; one should place them in order, beginning with the crown (*makuṭa*). One should assign Vāmadeva with the thirteen *vāmadeva* kalās, then Aghora with the eight *aghora* kalās, and likewise the Face with the four [kalās].
"One should place the five [vowels] beginning with 'ai' and the five [consonants] beginning with 'śa' in sequence upon the feet and so forth.
Thus it is said. In some places, there is a difference in the names of the *kalā* powers; here, he provides support for the method stated above.
In the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
Śaśinī, Aṅgadā, Ceṣṭā, Marīci, and likewise Jvālinī—
these five kalā-śaktis one should place above the five heads.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti—
thus the Power (Śakti) consists of four parts, transcending [the lower levels] in her upward-facing aspect.
Tamas, moghā, jayā, nidrā, dhṛti, kṣānti, smṛti, and kṣayā—
these are the eight powers (śaktis) in Aghora; likewise, those in Vāmadeva are said to be rasa, rati, pālyā, rakṣā, kalā, saṃyamīnī, and kriyā.
Thirst, delusion, destruction, anxiety, the deluding, and likewise the bewildering;
these are proclaimed as the thirteen powers (kalās) of Vāmadeva.
"O Nandikeśvara, the power (śakti) of this [goddess] is said to consist of eight parts: Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dhṛti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Sudhā, and Prajā. (End of the seventh line) (The Inner Sacrifice).

"One who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra"— according to this scriptural statement. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner and having meditated "I am Śiva," the sons, practitioners, and teachers should perform the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*) according to the sequence of the material, the personal, and the divine.

I am Śiva, whose sacrifice is internal; he who performs external sacrifice without such contemplation, though purified by bathing and other rites, remains indeed impure and does not partake in liberation. Therefore, having abandoned the notion "I am a living soul" (jīva), one should worship Śiva only after contemplating "I am Śiva."
Thus says the scripture:
"Having performed that mental sacrifice, he who should undertake an external sacrifice is to be known as inauspicious; it is not ordained for the sake of liberation."
Having abandoned one's ordinary state of being, one should contemplate: "I am Śiva."
"As long as one equal to him has not been born, one is not capable of propitiation.

(3rd line) (The sequence for the elemental realm). First is the sequence of internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*) for the "spiritual son" (*putraka*) at the *mūlādhāra*: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the tortoise-throne (*kūrmāsana*)."

Above that: *namo 'nantāsanāya*. Down to the navel: *hāṃ namo 'nantāya* at the navel. *Hāṃ namo pṛthvīkandāya* at the navel. In its center: *hāṃ namo bījāya*, *hāṃ namo 'ṅkurāya*. Eight finger-breadths above, having the form of the thirty principles (*tattvas*): *hāṃ namo nālāya*. Above that, the secondary [directions] beginning with Agni, etc.
In the corners, one should visualize the legs of the pedestal as having the forms of lions and being white, red, yellow, and black in color.

[One should offer worship with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma; Hāṃ, obeisance to Jñāna; Hāṃ, obeisance to Vairāgya; Hāṃ, obeisance to Aiśvarya. This is the set of four starting from the southeast (gauṇa-pūrva), arranged in reverse order. [The colors are] black, white, white, red, red, and yellow.

Having visualized [them] as black in color: "HĀM, obeisance to Adharma; HĀM, obeisance to Ignorance; (7th line) HĀM, obeisance to Non-detachment; HĀM, obeisance to Lack of Sovereignty. Thus, having meditated upon the lower covering, which is the nature of impure Māyā and is yellowish-red in color: "HĀM, obeisance to the Lower Covering."

Having meditated upon the white-colored upper canopy, which is the nature of pure *māyā*, [reciting] "HĀM, obeisance to the upper canopy. Then, having meditated upon an eight-petaled white lotus above such a lion-throne,
which is the nature of pure *vidyā* and is accompanied by the seed-syllables of the eight *ya*-group consonants, [reciting] "HĀM."

(24b, 1st line) Homage to the eight petals. At the tip of each petal: "Hāṃ, homage to the solar disc. "Homage to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc. Thus [on the] right side. Above that, having visualized the filaments as the form of the principle of Īśvara: Hāṃ... (2nd line)

Salutation to the filaments (*kesara*). At the tips of the filaments: *Hāṃ*, salutation to the lunar maṇḍala; salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar maṇḍala. Thus on the left side. In the center, having visualized the pericarp (*karṇikā*) as the nature of the principle called Sādākhya: *Hāṃ*, salutation to the pericarp. At the tip of the pericarp: *Hāṃ*, salutation to the fiery maṇḍala; salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fiery maṇḍala.
Homage! At the tips of the hair-tufts, in the directions starting from the east and so forth in sequence: *hāṃ* homage to Vāmā; *hāṃ* homage to Jyeṣṭhā;
*hāṃ* homage to Raudrī; *hāṃ* homage to Kālī.
Hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī; Hāṃ, obeisance to Balavikaraṇī; Hāṃ, obeisance to Balapramathinī;
Hāṃ, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamanī—[these are] in the pericarp. Hāṃ, obeisance to Manonmanī—thus [are they].
In this manner, [one should worship] the presiding deities of the Kūrma-seat and so forth, all of them with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.

One should worship with the five services mentally. Then, through the performance of worship, meditation, and self-surrender according to the specific form—whether it be Sakala, Sakaḷākalā, or Niṣkala—one should worship that which is called Karmasāda in the center of the pericarp.
It is as follows: resembling pure crystal, endowed with the thirty-two marks.
The upper face, named Īśāna, is seated in the *baddhaparyaṅka* posture, possessing the luster of pure crystal, stainless, and having the form of a youth;
it has three eyes, is adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon, decorated with vajra earrings, and is golden-hued, three-eyed, and adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon. (8th line)
The eastern face is youthful in form, adorned with a red earring called the Puruṣa, dark-complexioned, three-eyed,
adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon, its mouth formidable with fangs,
and embellished with serpent earrings.
The right face, named Aghora, has a mature appearance; it is the color of a pomegranate flower, possesses three eyes,
is adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon, wears pearl earrings resembling a woman's face, and is the northern face named Vāmadeva,
which is white as milk and has three eyes.

The western face, known as Sadyojāta, is adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon, along with golden earrings; it is endowed with such five faces, and in its five right hands holds a trident, a vajra, a sword, an axe, and the gesture of fearlessness,
while in its left hands [it holds other implements].

In the fifth [panel], he holds a winnowing basket, a noose, a bell, fire, and a goad; he wears a tiger-skin garment, possesses all his limbs in their entirety, and is the Lord of Karmasādākhya. To his left side is [the deity] with the luster of a pearl.

Having four arms, she displays the gestures of holding a rosary, a lotus, and granting fearlessness and boons; she possesses beautiful breasts, is in the prime of youth, has faultless limbs, and wears fine silk garments.
Adorned with all ornaments, she is the bringer of all auspiciousness and the source of the origin of the entire world.

Having meditated upon Tikāriṇī and Manonmanī within the form of Sadāśiva, one should contemplate Paramaśiva as being manifested in a state of serenity within Manonmanī, and Parāśakti likewise. Thus says the Āgama: (6th line)

The lack of auspiciousness (*aśivatva*) belongs to the [five] elements beginning with Earth, and it is the same for the limbs [of the body] as well; for Śambhu has established even those [limbs] as being devoid of inherent nature (*adharmatvāt*).

Having thus worshipped [the deity] with divine ornaments—water for the feet, water for sipping, the guest-offering (*arghya*), consecration, clothing, the sacred thread, perfumes, flowers, a crown, earrings, and so forth—and having requested permission by declaring, "I shall perform the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*)," he proceeds.

Having taken the limbs of Brahmā from the form of Sadāśiva in the manner to be described, one should worship Īśāna and the others in the directions starting with Īśāna within the pericarp; Ananteśa and the others on the tips of the filaments; Nandin and the others in the middle of the petals; Indra and the others on the tips of the petals; and Vajra and the others at their outer extremities. One should worship them in sequence in the secondary directions starting with the east. Now, [an objection]:

(9th line) If it is argued that the procedure for worship of the Sun and others, Brahmā and others, Indra and others—who reside on the impure and pure paths—within the principles (*tattva*) such as Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is contradictory, [we reply]: the state of being real has been stated for those who reside on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). (25b, 1st line)

Furthermore, there is no contradiction here, as it is stated that worship is prescribed in this context specifically for those such as Sūrya, Brahmā, Indra, and others who dwell on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) and have emerged from the limbs of the Lord (*īśvara*).
As it is said in the Vātula: [text omitted].
Brahmā is born from the right limb, and Hari is born from the left limb;
Nīlarudra arises from the heart of Śiva, who is known as Śiva himself.
From a thousandth part of Maheśa, the god Rudra comes into being.
From this Great Lord, the preeminent one, Brahmā and Viṣṇu were born.
In the eyes, there is the arising of the left and right [channels];
or when it has arisen in the vital breath (prāṇa), there is the arising of the digits (kalā) and so forth in the ears.
Knowledge arose in his mouth; from his throat were born the Gaṇas;
the Six-faced One was born in his heart; and from his navel was born the God (Kumāra).
Furthermore, fifty crores of gods were born from a portion of Maheśa.
"And likewise, millions of sages arise from the pores of his skin.

Then, [one should offer] mentally incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, as well as royal honors such as the water-offering, collyrium, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the mirror, the palm-leaf fan, and the like.

Having meditated upon [the deity] and worshipped him, and having requested permission, saying, "I shall perform the fire-ritual," and having received that authorization, one should meditate on the Śiva-fire within the naturally established fire in the navel-pit (*nābhikuṇḍa*). Then, having performed the mental oblation (*manasā homa*) according to the method prescribed for the external fire-ritual, [one should contemplate] that which has an unmanifest form in the center of the eyebrows, resembling the autumnal moon.
Having meditated upon Śiva, one should attain samādhi.
(This is the internal sequence.
The practitioner, possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, [visualizes] the nature of the heart-lotus as a seat in the form of a circle consisting of the *bindu* and the letter *sa*.

Having meditated upon the nature of *nāda* as having the form of a swan’s staff (*haṃsadaṇḍa*) and shining like a lamp, one should contemplate it as the *liṅga*. Then, within that *liṅga*, one should contemplate the mantras of the stations beginning with Īśāna in the form of the previously mentioned five faces and other limbs, using the seed-syllables of the elements such as *lāṃ*.

Among the five subtle elements, such as fragrance and so forth, [the offering of] clothing, the sacred thread, perfumes, flowers, incense, various foods and edibles, betel, and so on, arises from the subtle element of earth; while water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, the arghya offering, water for ritual bathing, drinking water, and so on, arise from the subtle element of water.

Because of the subtle element of air (*vāyu-tattva*), one should offer items such as mirrors and the like, just as one offers red garments and other ornaments; because of the subtle element of space (*nabhas-tattva*), one should offer items such as yak-tail whisks (*cāmara*) and palm-leaf fans; and because of the respective utterance of their seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should accomplish the ringing of bells, hymns of praise, songs, and so forth. Having thus worshipped Sadāśiva with those various offerings, [one should perform] contraction by means of the root-wind (*mūla-vāyu*).
Having awakened the root-fire with the *viṣṇubīja* (*vaṃ*), and having pierced the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) by means of the *suṣumnā* path,

one should, by means of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), cause the fire to ascend into the ocean of nectar at the *brahmarandhra*; then, by the stream of nectar flowing from that [ocean], [one should perform the sprinkling].

One who is devoid of yoga practice should offer oblations into the navel-pit (*nābhikuṇḍa*). Drawing in the nectar through the *iḍā* channel by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), one should offer it into the fire of Śiva within the spontaneously perfected channel-pit by way of the *prāsāda* mantra. Then, at the center of the eyebrows, by way of the *prāsāda* path—
Having meditated on the form of the *bindu* as consisting of the light of knowledge, one should become identical with it.
As it is said in the Vātula:
"Nāda is declared to be the *liṅga*, and the *bindu* is cited as the *pīṭha*."
"And in the *makuṭa* [crown],
I, Śiva, always abide within the body of living beings. Thus,
"within the body" refers to the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*).
Abiding in the heart,
[one should worship] with the nectar-draught drawn up by inhalation (*pūraka*) and with the *śiva-aṇu* mantras, according to the *Śivatantrarahasyasāra*.
One should satisfy the fire of Śiva in the naturally perfected pit of the navel.
In the *Siddhāntasārāvalī* as well:
"Having thus worshipped even in the fire, one should offer oblations according to the previously mentioned yoga;
[this is done] with the *iḍā* situated in its place by means of the *sruva* ladle, and likewise with the *suṣumnā*."

(The Cosmic Order): The Teacher, however, is the pedestal (*pīṭha*) consisting of the power of form and action (*rūpa-kriyā-śakti*) residing within the heart-lotus characterized as previously described;

the *liṅga* is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Having realized oneself as that Supreme Śiva, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), through union with the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti-yoga*).
With a purified mind, one should meditate upon the limbs, minor limbs, major limbs, and sub-limbs as being the very nature of power (*śakti*), and then worship them.
For example:
[one should worship] the yogin, and likewise those who possess [the power of] *yati*, the knowers of reality (*jñānin*), and the mantra-practitioners (*mantrin*). (9th line)
For the sake of the sign of worship through meditation, the partless becomes possessed of parts.
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jāta, in this order,
are the states of Sadāśiva.
Īśānī is conceived as the supreme limit, established as the crest-jewel.
Because it is the cause for filling the universe through the functions of the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and so forth.
Because he is equal to the crooked, he is called the "Face" (*vaktra*) of the Person.

The world of saṃsāra, consisting of impurities and the like, is "terrible" (*ghora*); the All-pervasive Lord (*vibhu*), being its opposite, is renowned as "not terrible" (*aghora*), possessing this true nature and its defining characteristics.
And since the heart is indeed true being, for that very reason it is exactly so.
Because he is difficult to perceive, subtle, and consists of both vision and action,
and because he is the creator of the universe— since from him proceeds the generation of effects such as sons—
he is therefore called Vāma; and for this reason, O wise ones, he is accepted as such in this scripture.
By his mere will, [he brings about] that which consists of the expansion of his own power.
Since it attains form immediately, it is known as *mūrti* (form);
thus these five mantras are [the limbs] by which the body of Śiva is bound.
That [body] has Īśāna as its crest, the face of Puruṣa, and Ghoratman at the region of the heart.
Vāmaguhyā, Sadyāṅghri, Hākiṇī, and likewise Jananī.
With the three powers beginning with Rodhayitrī, their sense organs are fashioned;
these eight illustrious ones, beginning with Īśāna, are trident-bearers.

She is declared by Śiva to be the "Seizer" (Hāriṇī), possessing the power of all ornaments; or rather, she is so called because she seizes the throat (pudgala) and leads it to the supreme abode. Therefore, this power is called Hāriṇī by the wise.
The mother of the world, whose nature is birth, possesses immeasurable splendor.
Because she establishes the restrictive order of the atomic aggregate during dissolution,
and likewise ordains its experience of enjoyments from that very state.
These three powers, consisting of the body and the instruments [of action], are internal;
likewise, there are other mantras whose essence is Śiva.
The heart, head, crest-jewel, armor, eyes, and weapons are not on the left;
his true being is the heart, and his head is the most exalted virtue.
The state of Śiva is independent, and that which is Śikā is situated above it;
it is naturally hidden from others, even though she is capable of concealing [it].
Because it shares the same nature as armor, it is designated by that name;
since it is the seed of omniscience, one should therefore perform the gazing with it.

That which is the irresistible power of Śambhu is called the weapon of Śambhu. Thus, the thirty-eight digits beginning with Śaśin mentioned previously are the powers (*śakti*s). They are the individual limbs.
It has been stated that the trident consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*); truly, it is intended as the axe (*paraśu*).
This majesty of the Lord Khaṭvāṅgin is considered to be an impenetrable diamond.
The grace of the Lord and fearlessness are likewise praised;
there shall be prosperity, while the form of the serpent represents the noose and the nature of illusion.
They know the goad to be discolored, and the bell to be of the nature of sound. Withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) should take the form of fire, and the ash should be the *kṛti* of nooses.
These are proclaimed as being of the nature of the three qualities (*vaiguṇya*), along with their constituent parts.
This is the form known as *karmasādākhyā*.

For the purpose of meditation and worship for all [practitioners], the manifest (*sakala*) becomes the unmanifest (*niṣkala*). Having understood this specifically, one should perform every ritual action.
Thus, because of this statement, the performance of ritual action is necessarily preceded by knowledge of that [reality].
Now, the definition of the five-fold *sādākhya* is stated; [this refers to] the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*), along with its synonyms and so forth.
Śiva, who originates from the Sādākhya state, arises from a tenth part of Parāśakti;
and because he originates from Parāśakti and because of his purity, he is called Śiva.
That form, in its subtle aspect, is known as the form of light;
it is like the form of lightning in the sky, manifest and facing in all directions.
This has been declared as the Śiva-tattva, the abode of all principles (tattvas).
It is said to be the Sādākhya of Śiva; now listen for a moment, O Six-faced One!
Ādi-śakti and Śānti are synonyms for it.
From a tenth part of Ādiśakti, the manifestation of the Formless One occurs.
Because the primordial power (*ādi-śakti*) is formless, it is proclaimed as "formless.
Due to its formlessness, that form is devoid of parts (*kalā*) and is like a *liṅga*.
Resembling ten million suns, it stands in the form of a pillar of light.
The form contained within that is here called "formless" and so forth.
This indeed is the divine Liṅga, which is called the Root-Support (*mūlastha*). Everything has arisen from the Liṅga, and its dissolution is said to occur in that very place;
thus is described the creation and withdrawal of these Liṅgas.
Thus has the formless been described; now hear of the formed.
[The following are] its synonymous designations.
The state called Sādākhya arises from a tenth part of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti),
and the Jyotirmūrti is said here to arise from a tenth part of the power of will (icchā-śakti).
And because the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) possesses qualities (*guṇa*), it is therefore declared to be embodied (*mūrta*).
Because of its embodiment, it is proclaimed to be a form associated with *kalā*.
Resembling a blazing fire in appearance, it shall take the form of a divine liṅga;
in its uppermost portion, it is endowed with a single face,
possessing three eyes, a beautiful countenance, and all the necessary limbs.
Thus, the embodied *liṅga* endowed with these nine aspects has been described.
That which is called Mūrta-sādākhya is indeed said to be the agent, Sādākhya;
knowledge and Pratiṣṭhā are its synonymous designations.
From one-tenth part of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the emergence of the agent, Sādākhya, occurs. (The word "saṃbhavam" [is used as a gerund].)
Knowledge is designated as the "agent" because its intrinsic nature is that of an agent.
For knowledge, because its nature is pure, is said to resemble a crystal.
It is the divine liṅga, exceedingly long and endowed with great bulk. Abiding within that form is the Lord, the embodiment of all causes.
He has four heads, four faces, and is endowed with twelve eyes;
he possesses four mouths, four noses, and is provided with eight ears.
He has eight arms, two feet, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
In her right hands, she holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and the gesture of fearlessness.
In his left hands, he holds a noose, a serpent, a bell, and the gesture of granting boons;
he is complete in all his limbs and adorned with every ornament.
Thus, that *liṅga* endowed with Īśvara is called the agent (*kartṛ*);
it is described as the *sādhya* of the agent, and it is also called the *sādhya* of the action (*karman*).
Cessation is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); these are its synonymous designations. From a tenth part of the power of action arises that which is called *karma-sāda*.
Action is to be understood as "karman"; therefore, it is designated by the name "karman.
According to the manner of the *liṅga* and the *pīṭha*, the characteristic of what is called the "attainment of karman" (*karmasāda*) is as follows:
Nāda is to be known as the *liṅga*, and Bindu is remembered as the *pīṭha*.
The form endowed with Nāda and Bindu is called Karmasādākhyā.
The four [principles], beginning with the agent and form, are called merely *nāda*;
Liṅgaśambhu is the seat (*pīṭha*), which is declared to be Śakti. By way of the union of the womb and the phallus, it is the cause for the purpose of creating the universe.
Because it exists as a state of constant conjunction, it is illustrated as having the nature of action (karma).
The resonance (*nāda*) resides within the drop (*bindu*), while the forms reside within the resonance;
that reality resides within the forms, and Śiva resides within that reality.
The Śūnyamadhya is situated within the Nṛtta; the Śāntika is within the Nṛtta;
the Atīta is within the Śānti; and the Śāntyatīta is beyond the supreme.
This is the *liṅga* consisting of Śiva, remembered as the abode of all principles (*tattva*).
Within that *liṅga*, indeed, the world—both stationary and moving—is born.
Therefore, the characteristic mark is specifically cited as being of the nature of action;
for when action arises, there is creation, and at the end of action, there is dissolution.
This form of Karmeśa brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
through union with the five called Sāda, it is termed Karmasāda.
Through the yoga of Śiva and Sadāśiva, one always takes refuge in the form of Śiva;
for that Mahāsena indeed takes refuge in the formless Śiva-Sadākhya.
Therefore, they know that the form of the Lord of Karma is supported by the fivefold manifestation (pañcamūrti).
It should be known as the essence of all reality and is remembered as the support of all.
Indeed, because it consists of a formal mass, this is traditionally known as the "piṇḍa" (the body);
it is specifically the form of the manifest, resting upon the unmanifest and other [principles].
For that form indeed rests upon the nature of the manifest.
The form of action specifically rests upon the form of the agent;
by this very sequence, each one indeed rests [upon the next].
That which is situated in the body (*piṇḍastha*), situated within the body, and enveloped by the body—
That which is condensed by means of a mass is called a "mass" (piṇḍa) in its essential form.

The wise know this *piṇḍa* to be composed of Śiva and consisting of all the *tattvas*. It is the Lord (*deva*) consisting of the five forms (*pañcamūrti*), and it should be understood as having the nature of the five *tattvas*. Through the distinctions of the bodies of these forms, it is endowed with the five qualities (*guṇas*).
Within that body, however, there arises the manifestation of all principles (tattvas), beginning with Maheśa.
From his mouth arose the Siddhāntas together with the Tantras—
the God who consists of all knowledge and is the cause of all causes.

Thus, upon the *liṅga*, one should meditate on Karmeśa as both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*). Having thus meditated upon Sadāśiva, who is encompassed by the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), one should consecrate him with the "dead" [substance],
with the sandalwood of dispassion (*vairāgya*), with the eight flowers beginning with *ahiṃsā*, and with the incense arising from breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).

By means of the lamp of consciousness (*vijñāna*), by the oblation of the moon-nectar of the nature of sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), by the recitation (*japa*) that brings clarity as it enters the path of the *suṣumṇā*, by the various streams of [meditative] flow that purify the mind through exclusive focus on Śiva,
by the acquisition of qualities such as omniscience arising from meditation, and by the offering of oneself— thus, in this very moment...
Just as wood manifested by fire becomes the very nature of fire, so too, through the manifestation of Śiva, the self becomes the very nature of Śiva;
this is the meaning.
(In the meditation on Soma)
In the *nābhikuṇḍa*, by means of the clarified butter of nectar flowing from the agitated power (*śakti*) resembling the moon at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
one should satiate the fire of Śiva— the very nature of Śiva—
through the activity of the essential forms of the measures (*mātrā*) and sounds (*svara*) arising from the lotus-root situated in the throat (*nāpyāryasthita*).
Above the *brahmarandhra*, twelve finger-breadths higher,

[one should proceed] toward Śiva— who consists of the supreme space (*paramākāśa*), the supreme sound (*paranāda*), and the supreme power (*parāśakti*), and whose nature is existence, consciousness, bliss, and the self-luminous manifestation of both self and other—

by means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by exclusive contemplation (*ananya-bhāvanā*). This sequence of the temple (*prāsādakrama*) should be learned from the mouth of one's own guru, as it is a secret.
(5th line) It is to be performed. One who is unacquainted with temples becomes a teacher (...).
This has been stated in the Vāruṇapaddhati:

The offering of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) into the *liṅga* which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and its union with the *pīṭha* according to the prescribed rite—that is called *pratiṣṭhā*. In the hymn of praise (*pūjā-stava*), having established the pure [deity] consisting of knowledge within the mind-born *pīṭha* of action—which is the abode of Śiva known as the heart-lotus and is Having thoroughly bathed that *liṅga* with nectar-like water, and again with the waters of dispassion (*vairāgya*),
with the eight flowers of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the rest, with the incense-rite born of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and with the offering of the lamp of consciousness (*cittadīpa*).
He who, with his mind fixed thereon, offers that [nectar] as an oblation through the sacrifice of the moon consisting of sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), through the recitation of the *suṣumṇā*,
and through the ornaments arising from pure meditation (*dhyāna*) and manifold concentrations (*dhāraṇā*);
he alone is blessed and stainless, having offered it into the fire-pit of the navel which flows with the moon and consists of nectar— [he is not satisfied] by any other oblation.

Having satiated this [deity] consisting of the five elements, which has gone to the abode of Śiva, [one should worship] the all-pervading one situated in the void. That person who brings about self-realization within the Śaiva light produced from the *kanda* by means of the *śivāṇunāda* is indeed liberated and imperishable.
And elsewhere: "The goddesses Rodhinī, Kuṭilā, Rūpā, Samanā, and likewise Unmanā reside in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)."
"The power that is above them—that [power] a man should conquer within her. Thus it is said in the Vātula[-tantra]:
"He who does not know the temple whose great body consists of the five mantras..."
"One who is not endowed with the thirty-eight arts is not called an *ācārya*. Thus [it is said].
I shall now fully explain the performance of sacrifice (*yajana*) according to the rules and in proper sequence;
that is to be understood as being of two kinds, in accordance with one's qualification (*adhikāra*).

"Internal sacrifice is prescribed for ascetics (*yati*) and yogis whose external powers have ceased, while external worship is for others"— according to this statement, one who is dispassionate should perform internal sacrifice either by way of yoga or by way of knowledge. Herein is the sequence:
First is the path of yoga (*yogamārga*).
(The worship of the path of yoga) is described in the *Kāmika*:
Through worship during the disappearance of the moon and the sun, one shall accomplish the desired fruit;
when the vital breath (prāṇa) resides in the center of the Suṣumnā, one should always worship Śiva.
The meaning of this is as follows:
the moon is the *iḍā* channel, while the sun is the *piṅgalā* channel. Their cessation is the absence of inhalation and exhalation;
that itself is the *kevala-kumbhaka* (pure breath-retention). Worship therein is the very experience of Śiva, which is the desired fruit.
May the power of accomplishment fulfill you! When the vital breath has entered the aperture of the *suṣumnā*, one becomes possessed of the experience of Śiva.

Herein is the sequence: having restrained the breath, one should kindle the root-fire with the root-wind by means of the fire-seed-syllable ending in the *bindu*; then, having abandoned the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), [one proceeds].

By way of the *suṣumṇā* path, having entered the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) from the heart and so forth by abandoning the causal deities such as Brahmā and the phonemes beginning with 'A', one performs the worship of that deity who is the fire within the form of undivided light.
Now (line 8).
The sequence of knowledge is being described:
[the worship of the path of knowledge] according to the Kāmika.
One should worship the God at dawn, but never at night;
one should worship the God constantly during the day, and avoid it at night.

The meaning of this is as follows: day is conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), and night is non-cognition (*ajñāna*). Therefore, having abandoned both the state with parts (*sakalāvasthā*) and the partless state (*niṣkalāvasthā*), one should worship Śiva by means of the stainless *kalā* and so forth; this is the worship through knowledge (*jñānapūjā*). (29b) *Oṃ bhūta*: these [elements] are like living beings; freedom from the ego-sense (*māna*) is the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Poison... (first line)

Freedom from desire for sense objects; purity of substances (*dravya-śuddhi*); or alternatively, the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) through the vision of Śiva’s eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*). Purity of substances is the vision of Śiva’s pervasion into all substances. In the five-syllabled mantra consisting of three words, setting aside the two syllables of the second word which concern the category of *pāśa* (the bond), [one contemplates] the two syllables of the first word which concern the category of *pati* (the Lord).

Having understood the single syllable that is the supreme word for the category of *paśu*, and having abandoned the vocal and mental [forms], the application to the expressed object is the purification of the mantra.
Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntabodha*:
"Having omitted the word 'namaḥ', when [the mantra] is proclaimed as 'Śivāya', this is the pure five-syllabled [mantra] that illuminates one's own direct experience.
[This is from the *Śivajñāna* (4th line)].

Having perceived one's own true nature, remaining absorbed in that is the purification of the self (*ātma-śuddhi*). The purification of the *liṅga* (*liṅga-śuddhi*) is the contemplation of Śiva, whose nature is the indivisible form of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*akhaṇḍākāra-saccidānanda*), which is to be known through experience alone. Now, the sequence beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and the image (*mūrti*) is described.
(The sequence of the seat, the form, and so forth:
The Self is the Śiva-seat; the Form is truth, knowledge, and the unobscured;
the Root is supreme bliss; now the invocation is described.
For here, the manifestation of Śiva alone is traditionally known as the invocation (āvāhana).
Seizing [the deity] is the installation (sthāpana), and facing [toward him] is the presence (sannidhāna). The removal of absorption and distraction is called the firm restraint (sannirodhana).
In the *Pūjāstava*:
invocation (*āvāhana*) is the manifestation of consciousness within oneself;

installation (*sthāpana*) is the abiding of the Lord (*īśvara*) therein; presence (*sānnidhya*) is the proximity of the Self and the Lord; and confinement (*saṃrodhana*) is [the union] of oneself with Śiva.
Cessation. Hereafter I shall explain the worship of Śiva beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*):
the draining away of the two-fold *māyā* is the water for the feet, and likewise the water for sipping (*ācamana*).
The destruction of the three types of karma is the unsurpassed liberation through knowledge;
it is the great consecration, the removal of impurities, pure clothing, and freedom from veils.
The ointment is the fragrant paste of *śrīgandha*; the pair is *kyā* (*...*) and *prasūdaka*.
The incense is the fragrance of the latent impressions of ignorance; the lamp is self-luminosity.
The offering of food is the experience of Śiva, and the drinking water is well-scented.

The swallowing of the taste of flavors is said to be the "wringing of the hands" (*hastodvartana*). The swallowing of the [taste of] *khaṭvā* (or *kaṣāya*) is the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), which serves as an oral fragrance (*mukhavāsana*). The dissolution of the sound called "the struck" (*āhata*) is declared to be the hymn of praise (*layastotra*).
And he circumambulated you, who are omnipresent everywhere, together with Śambhu.
Just as water becomes of one flavor through the union of rivers and the ocean,
so too is the union of the self and Śiva proclaimed as the act of salutation.

"Just as that which is known and unknown becomes submerged within the object of knowledge, so too they call this the 'face turned toward the supreme' (*parārdhamukha*), which is the self-revelation of the Self. (4th line) Thus, following the praise of the qualification (*adhikāra*), after performing the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*) must be performed; and that is of nine kinds.

Thus is the traditional teaching: that which ends with the dance is the highest; that which ends with the song is said to be middling; and that which ends with the music is declared the lowest. These three [latter types] are called the superior ones.
This refers to the subject of the *siddhaliṅga*. It is declared that the best [type] ends with the *geya*, the lowest ends with the *geya*, and the middling would end with the *bali*.
That which ends with the *homa* is said to be the one pierced by the essence (*sara*) in the middle.
The highest oblation should end with the word "haviḥ"; the middling should end with "dhiṣ" or "pā";
and the lowest should end with "puṣpa"—this is called the triad of lowest offerings.
Thus, the ninefold worship of the *sakalākala* [liṅga] is completed.

Regarding this subject—concerning the six mobile liṅgas among the objects of the senses—at the time of receiving the Śiva-liṅga from the hand of the Guru, one should determine the manner in which the worship will be performed, beginning with the eight flowers and ending with whichever other [rite] is appropriate. (7th line)
A formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) has been made. Worship should be performed in that very manner. This occasional rite (*naimittika-adhikaraṇa*) leads to spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
Herein is the sequence: "By the command of Śiva, Śiva, and Śambhu, as it proceeds," and so forth, ending with "I shall perform the worship of Śiva" (line 8).

Having resolved [upon the ritual] at the place of worship, and having performed the method of binding the directions with three *tāla* gestures using the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having created a moat with the armor-mantra ending in *namaḥ*,
he displays the *mahāmudrā* with the power-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [thus creating] a pavilion consisting of Indra.
One should meditate [upon it].
(The general *arghya* and the *nirodha-arghya*:
Following that, with the *astra-mantra*, one should [purify] the *arghya* vessel made from any one of gold, silver, copper, or leaves such as those of the *palāśa* or *padma*.

Having washed [the vessel] while visualizing a stream of nectar flowing from the *bindu*, one should fill it with water using the heart mantra ending in *namaḥ*. Having consecrated it seven times with the weapon mantra (*astra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should sprinkle the ritual substances (*pūjā-dravya*) with that water using the armor mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, having washed the *nirodha-arghya* vessel with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*...

Having purified [the vessel] by means of inspection and other rites, one should fill it with water consisting of nectar flowing from the *bindu*-place while reciting the Heart Mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Having offered perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having worshipped it with the eight *piṣpikas*,
one should consecrate it with the *saṃhitā* mantra and perform the *avaguṇṭhana* rite.

Having protected it, one should consecrate it as nectar (*amṛtīkuryāt*). During both the withdrawal (*nirodha*) and the emission (*visarga*), one should offer this very *arghya*; however, among the *arghya* offerings for the foot-water (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should offer the special *arghya* (*viśeṣārghya*).
(The Special Arghya)

Then, having purified the special arghya vessel with the Astra-mantra and placed it upon the seat, one should fill it with pure water consisting of nectar flowing in a continuous stream from the *bindu*, using the Hṛdaya-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; then,
having cast into it the eight substances for the arghya— water, milk, sesame seeds, rice, barley, white mustard, flowers, and the tips of kuśa grass.

In that [vessel], having worshipped with the seat, the form, the root-vidyā, the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and again with the root-mantra; having consecrated it with the Śiva-gāyatrī along with the Saṃhitā; having protected it with the Astra-mantra; having sprinkled it with the Hṛdaya-mantra using the cow-seal (dhenu-mudrā); and having veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra.
One should consecrate [the water] with the Dhenu-mudrā to make it nectar.
(The Pādya):
Having filled the pādya vessel with pure water as previously described, one should add the pādya substances—uśīra, siddhārtha, dūrvā, and candana.

Having deposited [the materials], one should worship them with the Sadyojāta mantra; mark them with the Astra mantra; worship them with the Mūla mantra; consecrate them with that same [Mūla] mantra; protect them with the Astra mantra; sprinkle them with the Hṛdaya mantra; and thus render them nectar-like.
(This is the purification of the substances.)
Thereafter, having sprinkled one’s own head three times with the water of the special *arghya* while reciting the *Śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*,

and having purified the collection of substances such as water by means of *nirīkṣaṇa* and other rites, one should sprinkle them with the water of the special *arghya* while reciting the *Kavaca-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and perform the *avaguṇṭhana* and other rites after consecrating them with the *Hṛdaya-mantra* and others ending in *namaḥ*. Thereafter, [one should prepare] the pure [water] for the bathing of the Deity.
Having brought water into copper or other vessels,

having added fragrant substances, flowers, and so forth, and having consecrated it with the purificatory rites beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* (inspection), one [prepares] the flower and the special *arghya* water.

One should pour [the water] into that. Thereafter, having sprinkled the incense, the lamp, the [offering] vessel, and the bell with the special *arghya* water using the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having worshipped them with the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should worship the bell with the weapon-mantra ending in *namaḥ*. This is the purification of the substances (*dravyaśuddhi*).
Purification of the Self

Thereafter, having offered flowers in sequence—saying "Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Self" on one's own seat; "Hāṃ Bhaṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the Self" at the heart; "Hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" in the hollows of the ears and throat; and "Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to the Self" on the head—and having worshipped with the limbs beginning with the heart using the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*...

Having placed a drop of the special *arghya* water on one's own head, having made a *tilaka* mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste, and having recited the root mantra ten times, one should offer it to oneself, thinking, "I am Śiva."
"One should meditate" refers to the purification of oneself.
(The purification of the mantra occurs) during bathing, recitation, fire-offering, eating, and likewise during worship.
In meditation, in the ritual of smearing ashes, and even in the twilight worship;
"One should always remain restrained in speech regarding all necessary duties," according to this statement.

Having adopted a silence that is not contrary to worship, one should recite the mantras in the sequence of short, long, and protracted vowels, proceeding in due order from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *dvādaśānta*.

Having recited the Prāsāda mantra, beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should contemplate this mantra as consisting of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and as being eternally presided over by Śiva. Thus ends the purification of the mantra.
The Installation of the Five Products of the Cow (Pañcagavya)

Thereafter, for the purpose of bathing Śiva, the householder—whether detached or otherwise—should prepare the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*); however, one who is detached should establish them by way of withdrawal (*saṃhāramārga*). This is as follows: having drawn a square mandala with rice grains in the eastern direction, [he should arrange them] in the order of west, east, south, and north.
Having drawn four lines in each direction to form nine compartments, one should offer salutations as follows: in the central compartment, *hāṃ namaḥ śivatattvakoṣṭhāya*;

in the secondary eastern compartment, *hāṃ namaḥ sadāśivatattvakoṣṭhāya*; in the secondary southern compartment, *hāṃ namaḥ vidyātattvakoṣṭhāya*; and in the secondary northern compartment, *hāṃ namaḥ kalātattvakoṣṭhāya*.
In the western secondary square, [one should offer] "Hāṃ, obeisance to the square of the principle of masculinity. Having thus worshipped with a flower or a leaf,

one should purify the vessels with water, place them upon the squares beginning with the principle of Śiva while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra, and [offer] "Hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel of the *supratiṣṭhā* [principle]."

Thus: in the vessel of the central square, "Hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel of perfect peace" (hāṃ suśāntapātrāya namaḥ). In the vessel of the secondary northeastern square, "Hāṃ, obeisance to the radiant vessel" (hāṃ tejovatpātrāya namaḥ). In the vessels of the secondary southeastern square and so forth, "Hāṃ, obeisance to the blood-born vessel" (hāṃ raktajapātrāya namaḥ). In the vessel of the secondary northern square, "Hāṃ, obeisance to the nectar vessel" (hāṃ amṛtapātrāya namaḥ). (2nd line)
[In the] vessel of the secondary western square; having thus worshipped, [one places] cow’s milk purified by a cloth weighing five *palas* in the *supratiṣṭhā* vessel;
curd from three fruits (*triphalā*) that are not too sour in the *suśānta* vessel; fresh ghee weighing one *pala* in the *tejovat* vessel; and one *pala* [of the third substance].

Having placed the water from the *gojala* in a jewel-made vessel, the *kaṭhina* [cloth] that fell to the ground, and previously taken cow-dung the size of half a thumb in an *amṛta* vessel, one should arrange them in sequence.

One should consecrate [the materials] one, two, three, four, or five times with the mantras of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta. However, one who is detached should place them in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). Thereafter, having filled a vessel for the power (*śaktipātra*) located in the square of Gauṇeśāna with water mixed with *kuśa* grass and fragrance to the measure of one *pala*, [one should recite] the Śiva-Gāyatrī.

One should consecrate it six times with mantras. In the secondary squares of Agni, Nairṛta, and Vāyu, one should scatter powdered barley, *āmalaka*, and turmeric, ground together, using the Heart-mantra; or, in the absence of barley, use rice powder. Thereafter, [one should scatter] cow-dung in the square of Gojala.

Having mixed that [curd] with the [milk], and having added water infused with *kuśa* grass to that [mixture], one should consecrate it once with the five Brahmans, the root-mantras of the six limbs, and the Śiva-Gāyatrī. Thus ends the procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

The Ritual of the Five Nectars (Pañcāmṛtavidhi) / (The Ritual of the Śiva-Broom [Śivakūrcavidhi]) On auspicious days such as the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should consecrate the previously prepared *pañcagavya* by reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred times, and then consecrate it with a tenth part of that number using the Brahma-aṅgas and the Śiva-gāyatrī. This is the ritual of the Śiva-broom.
(The characteristics of the ball suitable for the five products of the cow):
The characteristics of the ball suitable for the five products of the cow are stated:
the dung of a black cow endowed with all auspicious marks; the urine of a blue cow; the ghee of a tawny cow.

One should take curd from a white cow and milk from a copper-colored one; or alternatively, all [substances] may be taken from a tawny cow (*kapilā*). In its absence, those possessing the auspicious marks should be taken. Cows that are barren, recently calved, afflicted by disease, or near death are impure eaters and are unfit for use.
Those who are unworthy of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
(The procedure for the five nectars *pañcāmṛta*):
As before, having made nine compartments, [one should place] the central, secondary, eastern, and southern [sections]. (32a, 1st line)

Having poured milk, curd, honey, clarified butter, sugar, [and water] into vessels situated in the south, west, north-west, and northeast, one should consecrate each one once in sequence with the mantras beginning with Īśāna and place them separately. However, for one who is detached, one should consecrate the sugar and other substances with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta and place them separately.
(Worship of Vighneśvara and the Guru):

Now, on the Ālaṅkāra seat, in the primary north-western direction, one should worship Vighneśvara facing south, either in an image made of copper or other materials, or in a temporary form made of sandalwood paste and the like. (3rd line)

Having performed the rites from invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the recitation (*japa*), ending with "Oṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ," and having worshipped [Gaṇapati], one makes the request: "O Lord, please grant that I may perform the worship of Śiva without obstacles. Then, facing south toward the principal *Īśānī* (the northeast), one worships one's own Guru or the Guru’s sandals with scents and other offerings.

Having performed the worship from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the conclusion with the *Śiva-mantra*, one should pray: "O Lord, I worship Śiva according to the path taught by you; please grant me permission. This has been stated in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*: (–) [The text continues: "O Lord, having worshipped You with devotion according to the prescribed method, I now offer this worship; O Great Lord, be pleased with me. Then, having offered the *arghya* water, one should perform the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial vessel (*pātra*). As it is said: "One should purify the sacrificial vessel with the *Śiva-mantra* and the *mūla-mantra*. Having thus purified the sacrificial vessel, one should place it upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Then, having offered the *arghya* water once more, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *tattva*s. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *bindu*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *nāda*s. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *nāda*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *śakti*s. As it is said: "One should perform the *nyāsa* of the *śakti*s, beginning with the *ādhāra-śakti* and ending with the *ājñā-śakti*, in the sacrificial vessel. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *śakti*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *ātman*s. As it is said: "One should perform the *nyāsa* of the *ātman*s, beginning with the *viśva-ātman* and ending with the *anākhya-ātman*, in the sacrificial vessel. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *ātman*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *vidyā*s. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *vidyā*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *mantra*s. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *mantra*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *tattva*s. As it is said: "One should perform the *nyāsa* of the *tattva*s, beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva, in the sacrificial vessel. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *liṅga*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *cakra*s. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *cakra*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *padma*s. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *padma*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *yonis*. As it is said: "One should perform the *nyāsa* of the *yonis*, beginning with the *ādhāra-yoni* and ending with the *ājñā-yoni*, in the sacrificial vessel. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *yonis*, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *bindu*s. As it is said: "One should perform the *nyāsa* of the *bindu*s, beginning with the *ādhāra-bindu* and ending with the *ājñā-bindu*, in the sacrificial vessel. Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *bindu*s, one should perform the *nyāsa* of the *nāda*s. As it is said: "One should perform the *nyāsa* of the *nā
One should worship the four-armed Lambodara in the northwest corner—
he who holds weapons, has the luster of a ruby, and is the supreme destroyer of obstacles.
"One should worship with devotion the Teacher, the storehouse of compassion,
the bestower of all knowledge, as if he were Śiva himself, in the northeast quarter.
Thus it is said.
Thereafter, having placed the bathing altar— made of gold, silver, or copper, or fashioned from the wood of a milk-tree, circular or square,

provided with a girdle and a cow-mouth (gomukha)— in the northeast according to the secondary directions, and having installed the deity there within the previously prepared vessel of worship, one should make it slightly illuminated while reciting the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having sprinkled the deity with the general *arghya* water and offered a flower, one should say: "Salutation to Gṛhastha-Śakti-Śiva" and "Salutation to Śiva-Śakti for the detached one," and thus display the *liṅgamudrā* and the *yonimudrā*.
Purification of the Linga

Immediately thereafter, having worshipped the throne from Śakti up to the end of Śakti, and having invoked Śiva, one should consecrate him with the five products of the cow, the five nectars, and so forth. Regarding this, some say: "Having offered the sixfold [oblation] beginning with *laṃ*, [one should visualize Him] facing westward and seated upon a bull."

Following the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the sixfold arising of the mobile [liṅga] and its seat, because the rule for the mobility of the *śiva-kumbha* and the *vardhanī* is established, that very same procedure constitutes the ritual for the worship of the mobile liṅga and its seat.
Furthermore, regarding the worship of the fixed seat, the statement concerning the *kumbha* is exactly the same. This is the measurement for mobile liṅgas.

Having worshipped the mobile seat upon the bathing altar and having consecrated [the deity] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth; having wiped [the image] with a cloth; having performed the worship of the deity upon the ornamentation seat following the ten purificatory rites beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*);

and having mentally contemplated the great consecration consisting of anointing with oil and other rites; [one should offer] the special *arghya* water from the joined palms as drops upon the top of the *liṅga*.

"Having offered [the vessel], one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth"— this is incorrect. For when the *kumbha* and *vardhanī* are stationary, having been employed for the purpose of circumambulation to dispel obstacles to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), first there is the moving seat, and afterwards...
