Both [the moving and the steady] postures must be practiced. However, for those who are by nature fickle, how can worship be performed with both moving and steady postures? For as long as there is proximity to consciousness (*cit*), movement is not appropriate. But one should keep the eyes fixed on a target (*lakṣa*) while remaining steady; thus says Somaśambhu. (5th line)

[Objection: Since it is heard in the scriptures that the movement occurring after the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the movement occurring after the firm seat (*sthirāsana*) are defects for which expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed, one should not perform the worship of the firm seat (*sthirāsanapūjā*) nor the invocation on the sacrificial altar (*vedī*). [Response: No.
"One should mentally conceive the placement of the production of the *brahmaśilā* jewel and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) according to the rule upon crystals and the like;
for this is seen in the *Piṅgalamata-vṛtti*. [This occurs] within the pervasive *ādhāraśakti*, which serves as the locus, and is eternally stable."
Because it is described as worship preceded by movement and placement according to one's desire, it is called "mobile" (*cala*), according to the words of Rāmakaṇṭha.
It should be saluted as the pervasive (*vyāpinī*), the unstable (*asthirā*), and the immovable (*acalā*). *Ḍrūṃ vaṃ hrīṃ*.
The worship of the *liṅga* for one's own sake (*ātmārtha-liṅga*) has been taught with the mantra "svāhā" from the *ādhāraśilā-mantra-liṅga*.

For those [liṅgas] together with the *ādhāraśilā*, there is always the worship on a fixed pedestal (*sthirāsana*). By such statements as "for images there is always movement" and "in that [pedestal] there is indeed movement," it is established that for the *ātmārtha-liṅga*, there is no worship on a fixed pedestal.

There is no fault whatsoever in internal movement; however, by the force of the word "firm" (*sthira*) in the expression "having firmly uprooted," it is understood that as long as the presence of consciousness (*cit*) remains, movement is not appropriate for a firm linga. (9th line)
This [procedure] also applies specifically to the installation of a fixed liṅga, because the movement to another village after the installation of a mobile liṅga is prescribed,
and because the act of formal dismissal (*atisarjana*) involves a dependency [on time],
whereas the vehicle [of the mobile liṅga] is always [present] merely by being turned toward the worshipper.
Because it is presided over by the deity, there is no fault whatsoever in its movement immediately following the invocation (*āvāhana*).
When the worshipped *liṅga* moves slightly due to contact with the hands or other parts of the body,
one should perform a hundred recitations of a formidable mantra and then proceed with the remaining rites.

This is because of the force of the phrase "by touching with the hand and so forth," which remains as the stated rule. By the touch of the hand—that is, by touching the consecration vases, the *arghya* vessel, and so on—the very trembling, quivering, shifting, moving, and flowing of what has arisen constitutes the meaning of the word "movement" (*calana*) in that context; therefore, [the rite] consists of the recitation of the *aghora* mantra and other such expiations, but not from the physical ground.

All of this regarding the transfer to another location has been explained in detail by the Ācāryas through objections and their resolutions in the *Pūjāstavavyākhyā*; therefore, it is not elaborated upon here.

Consequently, having performed the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending immediately after the worship of the five seats (*pañcāsanapūjā*) on the bathing altar (*snānavedī*)—

It has been well said that the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances should be performed; likewise, the imposition of defects upon a mobile linga or a mobile pedestal is for the purpose of leading virtuous people astray. This has also been stated in such words in the *Siddhāntaratnākara*.

For movable lingas, after the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), there is no fault whatsoever in worshiping them even without [the rite of] *ācāmana*; enough of this digression, let us return to the subject at hand.
(The Invocation)

Thereafter, having worshipped the throne beginning with the *ādhāraśakti* according to the sequence to be described, one should invoke Śiva. Invocation (*āvāhana*) is of various kinds, depending on the distinction between temporary supports (*kṣaṇikaliṅga*), such as a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and those like the *bāṇaliṅga* bestowed by a Guru. In the case of temporary supports, invocation consists of the manifestation of consciousness through the rite of the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
Invocation (*āvāhana*) consists in making [the deity] face toward [the practitioner], as in the case of the *bāṇaliṅga* and other such forms.

For a practitioner situated facing north, the face of Īśāna becomes oriented toward him. Now, one might object: "But the Tatpuruṣa face is oriented toward the east; therefore [how can it face the practitioner]?"
At the time of worship, even Īśāna must face eastward; only then is it possible for him to face the practitioner who is situated facing north. If one asks how this is so, it is explained as follows:
One should designate that direction in which the door is located as the east;
there, the face of Tatpuruṣa and the upward face should be oriented toward it.
Regarding the upward face, however, [the offerings] should be given facing it and turned away from it. Thus it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*.
Regarding the phrase "there, lying supine in the northeast": according to the *Kāmika*, it is entirely logical that this [deity], being face-upward, faces the worshipper;

that very [orientation] is the invocation (*āvāhana*), which is the vision whose form consists of will, knowledge, and action. Thereupon, [the deity] shines forth by facing its own respective [aspect].

The manifestation of consciousness (*cidabhivyakti*) is also faultless; therein lies the establishment (*sthāpana*) of the Lord (*īśvara*). (Third line) Therein, in that *liṅga*, the very stability of the Lord’s manifestation of consciousness is what constitutes "establishment" (*sthāpana*), as well as [the presence of] worship, fire-offerings, and so forth, and His facing toward it. "Establishment" (*sthāpana*) is the settling [of Him] there with devotion.
"It has been stated by the wise" (4th line).

"Proximity" (*sānnidhya*) means the presence of the Lord within the self; that is to say, proximity is the continuous succession of grace arising from the Lord's being turned toward the self. Furthermore, this "being turned toward" is simply the proximity of Śiva, and not—

In response to the inquiry as to which faces of Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna, and Tatpuruṣa are intended when it is said "facing toward," the determination of the faces is stated in order to resolve that [doubt].
(The Determination of the Faces)
In that regard, the mantrin should have a gentle countenance, his posture should be gentle,
his mind and soul should be serene and gentle, and his ritual action should be gentle;
thus it is stated in the Parākhya.
"Seated upon a black antelope skin or on a mat of grass, facing north"—thus says Brahmaśambhu.
"Seated comfortably on a seat situated to the south of the deity, facing north, with a disciplined mind. (7th line)
Thus says Somaśambhu.
"Perceiving this [world] as unborn and unique, those who are fearful of birth resort to the south-facing aspect of this Rudra for the sake of protection," so it is said in the Purāṇa.

Therefore, the worshiper faces north, while the worshiped Śiva faces south. The *liṅga* presided over by the worshiped Śiva is of two kinds, distinguished as mobile (*cala*) and immobile (*acala*). Of these two, because the fixed *liṅga* is intended for the universal grace of all people, its orientation toward a specific direction is determined at the time of constructing the temple.
The worshipper of the *cala-liṅga* faces it because it is for the sake of bestowing extraordinary grace (*sādhāraṇānugraha*).
Now, [it may be asked] in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: [text follows].
"The eastern face is that of Tatpuruṣa, situated above the heart.
Thus, Īśa and Puruṣa face westward. And [it is said]:
"Not in the east in front; nor to the north of Śambhu, which is the locus of the Woman (Śakti); nor in the west behind."

Since it has been stated, "One should worship the desired [deity] to its right," it is logical that the deity faces east and the worshipper stands in the south-eastern quarter. If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be a statement regarding [the deity] facing toward the practitioner?"—it is not so; for the statements from the *Jñānaratnāvalī* concern a fixed *liṅga* that faces east. Moreover, ...
Even though the practitioner stands facing north,
it is not contradictory for the deity to face east; such is the scriptural tradition.
One should designate as the east that direction in which the door is located;
the door that faces the liṅga is considered to be the front (the east).
In that regard, the *tatpuruṣa* face and the upward face should be facing [the practitioner].
The pedestal for the offering (*balipīṭha*), the bull, and the trident should be facing that [eastern] face.
Now, since the front of the deity—situated facing north—is to the right of the practitioner who stands facing [the east], how is it that...? (5th line)

If it is argued that [the direction] is conceived as "east" (pūrva), it is replied: by the principle that the direction which lies in front of the deity is to be understood as the east, it is entirely logical to conceive the direction in front of the deity who is standing facing south as being the east. (6th line)
By this very logic, even regarding a permanent linga, the assignment of the four directions—east and so forth—is made in each respective case based on the front side of the deity;
thus, a divine linga or an image is fashioned. Or else, another [method]... (7th line)

*Kakubhā*: In each of those [directions], the sacrificer performs the sacrifice. "Auspiciously facing north" (*śivam uttarābhimukhaḥ*): either by the word *śivam* (auspiciously) or by the word *uttarābhimukham* (facing north). It is established that the worshipper faces south and the object of worship faces north. And thus, for one facing south who has been worshipped by means of the staff-gesture (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*)... (8th line)

In the worship of the ritual arrangement of heads (*muṇḍabhaṅgi*) of Lord Sadāśiva, the faces of Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta are situated in the principal [eastern], southern, western, and northern directions respectively.
This very point is [stated in] the ninth line.

And there occurs the status of being secondary, eastern, southern, northern, or western. For a movable liṅga, this is in the secondary, northern part of the "cow-mouth" (gomukha). And the worship of Caṇḍeśvara takes place in the secondary, northeastern part itself. By this very principle, even for fixed liṅgas, it is according to the orientation of the door.

It should be understood that Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta face respectively the secondary direction (southeast), the east, the south, the north, and the west. For, by the statement beginning with "the faces of the Karmapuruṣa and others [are directed] toward the eastern sun," etc., [it is shown that] he does not abandon those directions.
The directions such as "east" are not fixed relative to that person, because they are subject to deviation; rather, whichever direction faces the face of that person is itself the east and so forth.

Therefore, the placement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), as well as the worship of the doors and enclosures, the installation of the flag, the bull, the trident, and the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*), must be performed solely with reference to the east as it is determined by the orientation of the door. Thereafter—
The sequence for the worship of the seat of Śiva.
|| Worship of the Seat ||
Anantasaman,
seated upon the tortoise-stone below, with a body white as the Ocean of Milk,
bearing the form of a sprout from a seed in her crown, bestowing boons and granting fearlessness.
Having meditated on the lower central part of the reading as "the Śakti who holds the noose and goad, Kriyā, whose form is the support," and having worshipped with "Hāṃ,
obeisance to Ādhāraśakti" upon the Brahma-stone.

Having meditated thus: "The earth is the bulbous root (*kanda*), with the *kalā* as its sole stalk and *bhāva* as its pericarp; it is cast upon the lotus of *māyā*, crowded with many petals. (HĀṂ) [6th line]

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Anantāsana," one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord situated in its center, Ananteśa, who stands pervading everything down to the very base of the netherworld; then one should worship him with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Thus, from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) up to this point constitutes a single seat.
Thus it is said in the Kāmika:
"One should contemplate the infinite seat through Ananta and the power of the support. (This refers to the Siṃhāsana.)
Hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma; Hāṃ, obeisance to Jñāna; Hāṃ, obeisance to Vairāgya; Hāṃ, obeisance to Aiśvarya.

(8th line) In the corners beginning with the southeast and ending with the northeast, [one should place] those whose forms are the powers of Ananteśvara, resembling variegated filaments, [and who are] mutually...

One should worship the deities of Dharma and the others, who face backward and resemble those who are detached, yellow, and blue, respectively, in the directions starting from the southeast and ending with the north, in due order: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Adharma;
Hāṃ, obeisance to Ignorance;
Hāṃ, obeisance to Non-detachment; Hāṃ, obeisance to Non-sovereignty. These are worshipped in sequence, beginning from the secondary direction and ending with the northern direction.

One should worship the limbs, beginning with Adharma, which are black, white, whitish-red, red, yellow, and yellowish-black in color. Above that, in the place of the girdle, one should visualize the pure Māyā as red-colored and as the lower covering, [reciting]: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the lower covering (adhaśchadana)."

One should worship in the southwest. Above that, having visualized the pure Vidyā of white complexion as the upper covering, one should worship in the northeast with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the upper covering"— this is the lion throne.
(Yogāsana):
Regarding the matter of yogic postures, the Kāmika states:
"The feet, representing the Kṛta Yuga and the others, are placed at the corners in the form of elemental beings."
The fourfold group consisting of the Unmanifest (avyakta), Niyati, Kāla, and Kalā is declared to be the Ālikās in the directions starting from the East; Keśava, however, is the central foot.
Thus, one should worship each respective Yogāsana with its own name-mantra.
One should worship according to the sequence of mantras, beginning with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Kṛta" and ending with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Keśava.
(Padmāsana).
Thereafter, (the fourth line).
Upon the lion throne is the bulb (kanda), resembling a ruby; the stalk has a luster equal to sapphire;
the sprout has the brilliance of coral; and the petals have a luster like silver.
The filaments have the luster of gold and are topped with strings of pearls;
they possess the brilliance of molten gold and contain fifty seeds within them.

One should then worship the pericarp with the sixty-four filaments. Having meditated thus: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the bulbous root; Hāṃ, obeisance to the seed; Āṃ, obeisance to the sprout; Hāṃ, obeisance to the stalk; Hāṃ, obeisance to the petals"—having thus contemplated these as being the forms of the eight Siddhis of Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā) upon the petals— [The text continues: ...upon the petals.
Upon the root-pīṭha: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the filaments. Thus, one should worship the sixty-four filaments consisting of the sixty-four *kalās* of the *Īśvara-tattva* in the inner portion of the pīṭha.
In the center of those sixty-four filaments: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
This refers to the pericarp, which has as its essence the seed-syllables of the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā, belonging to the *Sādākhya-tattva*.
Thus is the form of the lotus (*padma*).
Having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the lotus (*padmāya*)," then, on the filaments starting from the east and ending in the northeast, [one worships]: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā;
Hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; Hāṃ, obeisance to Raudrī; Hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī; Hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī; Hāṃ..."
(9th line) Salutation to Balavikaraṇī. Hāṃ, salutation to Balapramathinī. Hāṃ, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī. These are the powers presiding over the Vidyeśvaras.
Resplendent like the rising sun, three-eyed, and possessing four arms;
adorned with matted hair, a crown, and the crescent moon;
holding chowries, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and their lotus-like hands resting upon Śivā.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, [one should worship] at the base of the *liṅga* in the pericarp with the mantra: "Obeisance to Manonmanī.
[She is] resembling pure crystal, four-armed, with beautiful breasts, a beautiful body, and in the prime of youth; she whose every limb is faultless and who upholds the lineage (*kuladhāriṇī*).

One should worship her, adorned with all ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, crowns, bracelets, bangles, girdles, and anklets; holding a rosary and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in her right [hands], and a lotus and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) in her left [hands]. One should show the salutation to the nearby attendants with the mantra: *Hāṃ, obeisance to the mudrā of salutation*.
On the circumference at the tip of the petal: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the solar disc" (4th line);
thus [one worships] Bhāskara. On the southern side of the circumference at the tip of that petal is Brahmā, its presiding deity:
Brahmā has four faces, is yellow in color, and is adorned with four staff-like arms.
One should contemplate the Sun as Bhāskara, equipped with a sacrificial ladle, a staff, and a kusha grass ring.
On the southern side of the circle at the tip of the petal, one should place Brahmā as its presiding deity.

Brahmā has four faces, is yellow in color, and is adorned with four staff-like arms; he is equipped with a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), a sacrificial spoon (*sruva*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*), and a *kuśa* grass blade, and stands in the midst of a solar disc.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with the mantra: *Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc*.
Then, on the circle at the tips of the filaments: *Hāṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc*, [worship] Soma in the lunar disc.

Having meditated thus: "Viṣṇu, the lord, at the tip of the filaments on the left side—Viṣṇu has four arms, wears a garland, and holds a conch, discus, mace, and lotus; he resembles a dark blue cloud and stands in the midst of the lunar orb."
Having worshipped with "Hāṃ,

obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar maṇḍala," [one worships] with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the fire maṇḍala" on the circle at the tip of the pericarp. One should place Vahni in the fire maṇḍala and his lord Rudra in the southeastern quarter of the circle at the tip of the pericarp.
"Rudra, the blue-throated one with three eyes, situated in the midst of fire—
thus [he is described]. He has four arms, holding the mudrā of exposition, the fire of gnosis, and a trident in his hands."
Having meditated [on the deity] as being adorned with all ornaments and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one should worship with:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala. Then, in the center of the pericarp, [one worships] seven times with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the power-maṇḍala (*śaktimaṇḍala*)."
One should worship the circle of powers (*śaktimaṇḍala*), which is crooked, beautiful, shaped like crystal, and extends upwards through the honey.
This is because of the statement: "The seven Krodhas of the mantras are situated upon the seat of Śiva. (36a, first line)

Because it is the cause of the arising of the seven crores of mantras, the power (*śakti*) possesses a sevenfold curvature. In the northeastern sector of the circle of power (*śaktimaṇḍalī*), one should visualize its presiding lord, Maheśvara, who is red in color, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon, possessing three earrings, and holding a serpent, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*). Hāṃ! To Maheśvara.
"Namaḥ"— one should worship.
Upon that is the Vimalāsana, which has the form of light.

May the Great Goddess Gaṇāmbikā Gaurī impel us. One should worship with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Pure Seat. In front of that circle, one should worship the Śiva-maṇḍala with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-maṇḍala," and then worship its presiding lord, Sadāśiva, as the primary Lord of the Northeast, with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva."
The collection of seats:
"The seat that pervades thus, from the earth up to the edge of the crooked [reality]"— having contemplated this,
one should worship at the base of the pedestal with "HĀṂ, obeisance to the Śiva-seat," and then upon the *liṅga* with "HĀṂ HAṂ HĀṂ."

Having meditated upon the form of Śiva with the mantra "Salutation to the Form of Śiva"— a form consisting of radiant energy, shaped like a staff, with undivided limbs, and pervaded by the supreme point (*parabindu*) which is the essence of the Śiva-tattva— one should install it in the *liṅga*.
(This is the *daṇḍabhaṅgī* placement.)

In this form composed of staff-like radiant energy (*tejomayī-mūrti*), one should perform worship upon all the limbs, beginning with the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet: *HOṂ ĪŚĀNAMŪRDHNE NAMAḤ* (Homage to Īśāna, the Head);
*HEṂ TATPURUṢAVAKTRĀYA NAMAḤ* (Homage to Tatpuruṣa, the Face); *HUṂ AGHORAHṚDAYĀYA NAMAḤ* (Homage to Aghora, the Heart); *HIṂ VĀMADEVAGUHYĀYA* (Homage to Vāmadeva, the Secret Place).

"Oṃ, homage! Haṃ, homage to the form of Sadyojāta. Having performed the placement [of the mantras] according to the sequence of the staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*), one should perform the placement of the *kalās* (*kalānyāsa*).
"Hāṃ, homage to Śaśinī. On the head of Īśāna: "Hāṃ, homage to Aṅgadā. On the head of Tatpuruṣa: "Hāṃ, homage to Iṣṭā."
*Namaḥ*—(8th line):
*Hāṃ, to Marīcī, namaḥ* on the head of Aghora; *Hāṃ, to Jvālinī, namaḥ* on the head of Vāmadeva;
*Hāṃ, to Śāntyatītakalā, namaḥ* on the head of Sadyojāta; [and] *Hāṃ, to Śāntikalā, namaḥ* on the face of Īśāna. (9th line)
*Namaḥ*—at the face of Tatpuruṣa: *Hāṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ*. At the face of Aghora: *Hāṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ*.
At the face of Vāmadeva: *Hāṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ*. At the face of Sadyojāta: *Hāṃ tamase namaḥ*. At the heart: *Hāṃ*.
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Mohā" on the throat; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Jayā" on the right shoulder; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Rudrā" on the left shoulder;

"Hāṃ, obeisance to Dhṛti" on the navel; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣānti" on the abdomen; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Smṛti" on the back; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Rajā" on the chest; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Rati" on the private parts.
With "Hāṃ, obeisance to Pālī," [one places it] on both testicles;
with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Rakṣā," on the right thigh;
(third line) with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Kalā," on the right knee; with "Hāṃ Saṃ, obeisance to Dhaminī," on the left knee; with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Kriyā..."

*Namaḥ* at the region of the bladder; *hāṃ mohinyai namaḥ* on the right side of the abdomen; *hāṃ bhrāmiṇyai namaḥ* on the right buttock; *hāṃ kṣayāyai namaḥ* on the left buttock; *hāṃ cintāyai namaḥ* at the region of the bladder; *hāṃ mohinyai namaḥ* on the left side of the abdomen.

"Hāṃ, obeisance to Bhrāmiṇī" on the left side of the abdomen; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Siddhi" on the right foot; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Ṛddhi" on the left foot; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Dhṛti" on the right hand; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī" on the left hand; "Hāṃ... (sixth line).

"Salutation to Medhā," thus on the nose; "Hāṃ, salutation to Kānti," thus on the region of the head; "Hāṃ, salutation to Svadhā," thus on the right arm; "Hāṃ, salutation to Prajā," thus on the left arm. In this manner, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight Kalā-Śaktis.
(The Meditation on Sadāśiva): Now, the meditation on Sadāśiva.
By means of this Śākta [meditation], Śiva is to be understood as both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).
Seated upon the lion-throne of mantras, which has the earth and other elements as its curved extremities.
Resembling pure crystal, endowed with the thirty-two marks,
seated upon a lotus throne, five-faced, with three eyes in each face,
possessing vast eyes that gaze everywhere, and joined with the digit of the moon of primordial wisdom.
The face of Dhavaleśa is white, and the Tatpuruṣa face is yellow.
It is endowed with a black and terrible face, and its upper wheel is red in luster;
it has a single very white western face, and Sadyojāta is its embodied form.
Clad in a tiger skin garment, with a lordly serpent as his waist-string,
wearing a snake as a sacred thread, he is peaceful, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon.
Visualizing the form as bearing in the right hand a trident, a vajra, a sword, and an axe that grants fearlessness, and in the left hand a serpent, a noose, a bell, a fire-tipped arrow, and a goad;
having meditated thus, one should recite "Hāṃ Hau! Salutation to the body of knowledge," and then utter the mantra that pervades the aperture of Brahmā, [namely] Śiva.
Having meditated upon the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), which pervades the entire reality, resembles lightning, and has manifested within the handful of flowers,
one should worship it according to the length of the liṅga.
(This includes the rites of invocation and so forth.)
Thereafter, holding flowers in both hands and forming them into a bud, one should recite the root mantra ending with *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*),

the *nirodhinī*, the *nāda*, the *śakti*, the *vyāpinī*, the *samana*, and up to the *unmanā*. Having offered the flowers at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva by means of the invocation-mantra (*āvāhinī*), [one should contemplate] Him who is of the nature of light, partless, and all-pervading.

Having meditated upon Paraśiva, who consists of knowledge and bliss, manifested through the stages of karma and sādākhyā, and having performed the *vaṣaṭ*-limb assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) consisting of the sixfold attributes such as omniscience and so forth, [one should place Him] within the lotus of the heart by means of the *sthāpanī* [mudrā].

Having established the two forms through *sannidhānyā*, having pervaded them and contemplated them as being present (*sannibhūta*), one should restrain them with *niṣṭhurā* and offer the *nirodhārghya* for Śiva with "HĀṂ HAUṂ ŚIVĀYA NIRODHĀRGHYAṂ SVĀHĀ. Some, however, [say that one should] bring the Supreme Śiva residing at the *dvādaśānta* from there to the center of the forehead.

"Having meditated upon Śiva, who resembles ten million moons, one should, by means of the *recaka* breath, visualize him as being situated within a handful of flowers and join him to the *brahmarandhra* of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva. This they say, but it is incorrect;
for there is no coming or going at all for Śiva, who is indivisible in form, existence-consciousness-bliss, non-dual, and perfectly full. Rather, just as...

Just as fire is manifested in wood, so too Paramaśiva becomes manifest within the form of Sadāśiva through the contemplation of mantra-activity. This has been stated in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*: (8th line) [text follows].
Having thus conceived that peaceful form within it— the supreme, eternal, and true self consisting of knowledge, bliss, and happiness— [one should meditate] on the causeless [reality].
Pervading all principles, immeasurable, and incomparable;
devoid of the signified and the signifier, it lies beyond the sphere of speech and mind.
It should be specifically manifested as the unmanifest within the self that possesses parts.
It is said that "the summoning from afar" (*parāvāhana*) occurs through the application of the *śiva-mantra*.

Then, having warded off obstacles by casting flowers upon the body of Kālakarṇī with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [one forms] the *liṅga-mudrā*, the *yoni-mudrā*, and the *namaskāra-mudrā*.

Having displayed [the deity], having veiled [him] with the *namonta* armor-mantra, having worshipped the pure limbs of the God ending in *namaḥ* upon their respective parts, having consecrated [him] with the root-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, and having inflamed the mantras with the *dhenumudrā* and *mahāmudrā* using the power-mantra (*śaktimantra*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should meditate upon the God as satisfied and with a smiling face, O Lord.
Having announced, "Welcome," and having reflected upon what was said by Śiva, "Welcome, my child."

"O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World, remain present within this *liṅga* with a spirit of great affection until the conclusion of the worship. Having thus petitioned, [one recites] *hāṃ hauṃ śivāya*.

Saying "vādyannamaḥ," one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the two lotus-feet of Śiva. Saying "hāṃ hāṃ śivāya ācamanasvadhā," one should offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) to the faces of Śiva, beginning from the east. Saying "hāṃ hauṃ śivāyārghyaṃ" [and] "heti," [one offers the guest-water (*arghya*)] to the northeast of Śiva.

One should offer the *arghya* on the head at the end of each of the [mantras] beginning with *disadyojāta*. One should offer flowers on the five heads of Śiva with the mantra: *hāṃ hauṃ śivāya vauṣaṭ*.
(The consecrations and so forth.)

Having again offered incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and betel leaf, one should then pray to Śiva for the sake of the bath. In the absence of a bathing altar (*snānavedikā*), having placed the deity upon the palm of the left hand, one should perform the purification of the *liṅga* as before, seat the deity upon the pedestal, and perform the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), as well as the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Having consecrated it for the purpose of the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*), and having requested [the deity] with the words "O Śiva, arise," one should place it upon the palm of the left hand and perform the consecration.

In the absence of the substances for the great consecration, such as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, one should consecrate it with pure water while reciting the root mantra, the Brahma-mantras, and the pada-mantras.

Mantras are of three types, distinguished as *mālā* (garland), *bīja* (seed-syllable), and *pada* (word). As for the *mālāmantras*, they consist of the five [faces] beginning with Īśāna, joined with four, eight, thirteen, and eight *kalās* respectively; these belong to the Brāhmaṇas alone.
The *padamantras*, however, take the form of single words ending in the dative case, such as "Īśānamūrdhne" and so forth; and these belong to the fourth [class].

The seed-mantras consist of five short vowels and six long ones, as well as the prolated [vowel], and so forth; these are common to the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*). Therefore, within the word-mantras (*padamantra*), following that, one should offer the special *arghya*.

When substances for consecration such as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are available, one should consecrate [the deity] with the five products of the cow, and then again with pure water.

Having placed a flower upon the head and offered incense and lamps, one should anoint a crystal liṅga with water [mixed with] (*elā*) and immediately with cow’s ghee; having bathed it with pure water, rubbed it with a powder of barley or rice, and bathed it again with water, one should then bathe it with water [mixed with] *naśā* paste and *āmalaka*, using the armor-mantra ending in *namaḥ*.
Having bathed [the deity] with the *mānasī-majjā* and *abhiṣeka* mantras of the two lunar mansions (*rākā-udina*),
having worshipped the root forms (*mūrti-mūla*) upon the seat, and having offered incense and lamps,
one should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)— namely milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar— respectively, using the mantras beginning with Īśāna and ending with *namaḥ*.
Having sprinkled [the deity] again with water and bathed the deity with lukewarm water,
one should sprinkle [him] with the juice of *jambīra* and *nāraṅga* fruits,
and rub [him] with a mixture of coconut, plantain, jackfruit, mango, sugar, and honey.
Having sprinkled [the image] with sugarcane juice, coconut water, and cold water;

having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra; having smeared it with sandalwood paste and fully honored it with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*); and having offered incense and a lamp, [one should offer] either pure food or fruit.
Or having offered coconut water, thereafter having consecrated [the deity] with fragrant pure water, golden water, jewel-water, and conch-water,
having presented the special *arghya* offering, having wiped [the image] with a pure, fine, bright, and fresh cloth, and having placed it upon an auspicious throne... (8th line)
Having devotedly offered with the mind divine garments, a loincloth, a waist-thread, an outer cloth, a sacred thread, and a girdle, and having smeared the Śiva-liṅga with musk;

Having offered sandalwood mixed with snow-water, camphor, agallochum, and saffron, one should thereafter offer the ornaments for the body and so forth. In the absence of physical materials, one should offer them with a respectful mind.
Thereafter, for the destruction of the threefold suffering, [one should recite]: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self. Thus, at the base of the *liṅga*.

One should worship with three handfuls of flowers in sequence: saying "Hīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva)," at the middle part of the liṅga; and saying "Hūṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva)," at the upper part of the liṅga.
If it is asked how Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra can possibly reside within the *liṅga* whose essence is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the answer is true:

the Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra who dwell there do not belong to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). [Rather,] Śiva alone exists through the conjunction (*yoga*) of his distinctions as the active, the intent-to-act, and the capable.
He dwells under the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
As it is said in the Parākhya:
"The Supreme Lord indeed exists through various distinctions of names."
Because of its vastness and because it destroys through the sound "buṃ," it is indeed Brahman through the yoga of Śiva.
Because his nature originates from Viṣṇu, he is the source of the world and its Lord;
because he causes [the body] to wither through austerity, he is Rudra, and because of the destruction of evil, he is Uruja.
Following this, having worshipped him with the mantras of the five Brahma-padas and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), [one should worship] with garlands of flowers.
One should worship with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, tulasī, bilva leaves, and so forth.
(The procedure for leaves and flowers)
In worship, there is a distinction based on flowers, leaves, and fruits;
as it is said in the *Śivatantrarahasyasāra*:
"In this world, those flowers which are white in color are indeed of the nature of purity (*sāttvika*)."
Those that are red are characterized by *rajas*, and those that are dark are characterized by *tamas*.
That which is black is a mixture of *tamas* and *rajas*; yellow is characterized by *rajas* and *sattva*. [In the ray...]
It should be known that [an offering] characterized by *sattva* bestows liberation, while that characterized by *rajas* bestows prosperity;
a mixture of both is for the attainment of both, and flowers and leaves likewise grant growth.
(*Śivadharmottara*)
The ascetics should always perform worship with those auspicious flowers produced in the forest or with leaves grown in the woods.
With well-cooked, burst-open, fragrant fruits gathered immediately,
along with *caṃbaka* fruits, *karkandhu* jujubes, and other appropriate offerings.
Or one should worship Śiva with flowers produced from one's own delight;
[with] white, red, and likewise yellow [flowers] in Ajita.
(…) not left overnight, without holes, and free from worms, hair, and the like.
When worship is performed with all these aforementioned substances and likewise with such leaves,
it is declared to be the most excellent form of adoration, provided it is performed without black flowers.
The middle [grade] sacrifice is said to be with white and red [flowers], while the lowest is with yellow and red ones;
I shall describe those flowers, beginning with the white, in their proper order.
The white lotus, the white sun-flower, the mandāraka, the karavīraka,
the nandyāvarta, the punnāga, the mallikā, and the jasmine;
Mādhavī, kurava, droṇa, and likewise durdhūra;
bakapuṣpa, bhadrā, and similarly girikarṇī;
śrīpuṣpa, vakuḷa, and likewise loddhrapuṣpa.
Sindhuvara and Śamī flowers, combined with white sugar—these indeed [are the offerings].
Red flower, palāśa, hayamāra, pāṭalī,
the deep red bṛhatī, and after that piṇḍitaka;
likewise paṭṭikā, red utpala, and the munipuṣpa.
And the Kadamba; now hear from me of those that are red and yellow.
Campaka, karṇikāra, and likewise iraśvadhamā,
as well as hemadhūrdhuraka, kuraṇḍa, and gokṣura.
Āsana, Śaṅkhinī, and Pītapuṣpa are proclaimed [as substitutes];
likewise Nīlotpala, Viṣṇukrānti, and Atasīpuṣpa.
The *kuṇḍa* is proclaimed to be black in color and to have black flowers;
likewise, there are golden *kadamba* flowers and *jāti* flowers.
One should offer [the flowers] at night to Śiva, and the remainder should be offered day and night to the Deity.
A *nandyāvarta* should be offered in the morning, and likewise a *droṇa* at midday.
Specifically, a *jāti* flower should be offered to Śiva in the evening.
One should avoid flowers that are scentless or have an unpleasant odor.
Even if devoid of fragrance, items such as *kuśa* grass and the like are to be accepted if they are pure.
The *kuśa* blades should be grown in a single place, glossy, neither too short nor too long;
they should have seven leaves, possess both tip and root, and be shaded by a parrot.
In the *Kālottara*, one should perform worship with blue lotuses and the like, with *kunda*, *campaka*, and *jāti* flowers,
as well as with *kubja*, *dhūdhūraka*, *karvaka*, *karavīra*, and *pāṭala* flowers.
One should worship the Liṅga with Kadamba, Damanaka, and other such flowers that are fierce yet not loathsome; one should offer only fully ripened fruit.
But if even flowers are not available, one should offer leaves as well—
namely, apāmārga, kuśa, dūrvā, pañcabilva, and likewise śamī.
The single-petaled lotus, tulasī, nāgadantikā, the mango tree, as well as kṛṣṇatulasī and fragrant flowers; madhura, sahadevī, dānta, and the sprout of bhadrā.
These and other such leaves are indeed pleasing to Śiva.
One should collect bilva and both types of tulasī from all vessels;
having likewise washed the tulasī, the bilva leaf, and the golden flower,
one should worship the Supreme Lord again and again.
Uśīra, haribera, and other roots that bestow auspiciousness.
A garland made from flowers of a single color is proclaimed to be the best;
likewise, one made with flowers of many colors is proclaimed to be middling;
and a garland fashioned from flower petals is proclaimed to be the lowest.
One who worships Śiva even once with unbroken bilva leaves [attains great merit].
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva by [worshipping] Maheśāna with a garland of *tulasī* leaves, reaching down to the very base of his pedestal.

One who covers the Lord of Gods with flowers obtains the merit of giving ten million cows. One should fashion a very beautiful lotus-shaped crown upon his head, provided with a pericarp and eight petals, and joined with sixteen petals. Thus it is said.
(The Incense and other offerings):

Thereafter, taking the bell with the left hand and sounding it while offering curd, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should take the incense burner containing incense and [offer] incense to Śiva with the mantra: *hāṃ haṃ śivāya dhūpam*.

Saying "svāhā," one should cook [the offering]. Having consecrated the *ārātrika*—provided with a lamp made of cow-ghee and camphor wick—by means of the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, and having worshipped it with curd, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) while reciting the weapon-mantra ending in "namaḥ," one should take that *ārātrika* and offer it three times, saying: "The *ārātrika* for the golden armor, svāhā. Then, three times.
Having raised [the lamp] by rotating it upward and taking up the lamp-vessel, one should offer it with the mantra: *HĀM HAUṂ ŚIVĀYA DĪPAṂ SVĀHĀ*.
One should present it at the face, on the sides, and above—[the lamp] which wards off obstacles.

Having consecrated the *ārātrika*—which consists of many blazing lamps—with the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, and having worshipped it with curd and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) preceded by [the syllable] *da*, ending with the *namaḥ* mantra and the *astra* mantra; then, taking that *ārātrika*, one should offer it three times with the mantra: *haiṃ kavacāyārātrikaṃ svāhā*.
Having lifted [the deity] by rotating it upward, one should encircle the deity with water for flowers and *arghya* while reciting the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
and then place the flower along with the *arghya* water upon the night-vessel (*rātrika*).
(The worship of the limbs of enjoyment.)

Thereafter, having offered water for sipping as before and visualized the Lord as being fully satisfied, he should inform Him: "O Master, I shall worship the limbs of enjoyment; please grant me permission. Having received permission, he should worship Śiva with the root mantra, beginning from the head at the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding toward the northeast, saying: "Hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. [This is done] in the secondary Īśāna.

[One should meditate on] Īśāna, who has the luster of crystal, who is the cause of the universe, three-eyed, crowned with the moon, gentle, serene, and holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands.
Thus.
Having meditated, one should invoke [the deity], taking the Puruṣa from the mouth of Tatpuruṣa with the mantra: "Heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa.
In the east [one should place] a man resembling a crow, wearing yellow garments and a sacred thread.

Having meditated thus on the one who bears a citron and a rosary, and who has the moon as his crest-jewel, one should invoke him. Taking Aghora from the region of the heart with the mantra "Huṃ, obeisance to Aghora," [one should place him] to the right—
the three-eyed one, with the moon upon his head, gentle-hearted, and adorned with earrings.
He had tawny whiskers and hair, and a distorted face with fangs.
Adorned with a garland of skulls and decorated with snakes and scorpions, he holds in his four left hands a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, a shield, and a noose; and in his four right hands—
The trident, the battle-axe, the sword, and the staff that crushes enemies.

Having thus meditated upon [Vāmadeva], who has the appearance of a fresh cloud, is formidable, and grants all desires—one should perform the invocation. Taking Vāmadeva from the secret [part] of Vāmadeva, [one says]: "Hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva. [This is done] in the north.
Having meditated [on him] as being on the left, red, with beautiful garlands, garments, and sacred thread;
with a prominent nose and a red turban, and holding a sword and a shield—one should invoke him, taking Sadyojāta from the foot with the mantra: "Bhaṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta," in the west.
Richly adorned with green blood and fragrant garlands, wearing a white turban and white garments,
endowed with a gentle crown and the head of a child,
three-eyed, newly born, with a single white face, and holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness— thus [he is described].

Having meditated, one should perform the invocation. Alternatively: from Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha (the benevolent-eyed one), [one should invoke] those who possess the luster of pure white, gold, a bumblebee, blood, and white, [respectively], from the four-faced one.

Richly adorned with the beauty of matted locks and crowns, and decorated with serpents as ornaments and the crescent moon; in their left hands they hold a serpent, a rosary, a blue lotus, and a citron.

Having meditated thus on [the deity] holding a trident, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a sword, and a spear with hands adorned by serpents, one should perform the invocation. Taking the eye from the eyes, one says: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the eyes," in the northern part of Īśāna.
One should remember the eye of the All-pervasive Lord as having the luster of the dawn, consisting of vision and action,
and resting upon the triad of maṇḍalas beginning with fire, which embody the three principles.
The face [of the deity] is as described for the heart and other limbs, joined with the hand-held implements and so forth;
or, according to the teaching of Yogaśiva, it has one face and a trident and snake in its hands.
Thus.

Having meditated, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*). Taking from the heart that which consists of the essence of existence (*sat-bhāvātmaka*), one says "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart" in the southeast (*āgneya*). Taking from the region of the head that which is characterized by universal lordship (*sarveśatva*), one says "Hiṃ, obeisance to the Head" in the northeast (*īśāna*), to the north of the eye. Having extracted from the crest (*śikhā*) that which is the nature of Śiva not dependent on another, one says "Hṛṃ... [obeisance to the Crest].

"Obeisance to the crest-lock (*śikhā*)," [reciting this] in the southwest (*naiṛta*). Having taken the armor (*kavaca*), which is of the nature of splendor and impenetrable by others, from all the limbs with "Hraiṃ, obeisance to the armor" (*kavacāya namaḥ*) in the northwest (*vāyavya*). Having extracted the weapons (*astra*) in the form of majesty from the weapons [themselves], [one places them] in the four directions starting from the east for Tatpuruṣa and the others, on the left side, with "Haḥ, obeisance to the weapon" (*astrāya namaḥ*).
On the left side:
the heart, resembling the moon; the head, with the luster of gold;
the crest-lock, rich in the color of vermilion; and the armor, radiant as a bumblebee.
Seated upon lotus-thrones, wearing crowns of matted hair,
three-eyed, four-armed, and adorned with all ornaments;
facing Śiva, they hold the spear, the trident, and display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
Then [he saw] one with four faces, holding a weapon, possessing fangs, and having a tawny luster.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon [the deities] as having two arms and one face, granting boons and protection, or alternatively, bearing a trident and the gesture of fearlessness.

These [deities] are [worshipped] with the eight [rites], ending with the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the presentation of flowers (*puṣpadāna*), performed like those for Śiva.

One should worship by forming mental conceptions through the *saṃskāras*; or else, having recollected the entire group of eight *saṃskāras* in their collective form, one should offer the *arghya*. [The symbols] of the Brahmās beginning with Īśāna are known as the cow, the lotus, the trident, the makara, and the deer...
(third line).

One should display the gestures (mudrās) for the limbs and the gesture of salutation (namaskāramudrā). Afterwards, having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) to Śiva with the root mantra and having displayed the Great Gesture (mahāmudrā), one should contemplate the unity of mind of all [deities] together with Śiva. Thus are the Brahma-limbs [placed] upon the pericarp.
(Āvaraṇapūjā) On the tips of the petals of Anantā, at the neck of the pedestal, below the Gaṇas,
on the legs of the pedestal, and upon the stone slab, are the Lokapālas and their weapons.

Because of the statement, "The offerings and the other coverings are thus," one should worship Ananta and the others on the tips of the petals; one should worship Gaṇeśvara and the others at the neck of the pedestal; one should worship the Lokapālas at the base of the pedestal;
and one should worship their weapons upon the Brahma-stone.
(The second enclosure:
Thus, in the second enclosure,
one should worship Ananta and the others, situated at the tips of the petals starting from the southeast and ending in the northeast.
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) have four faces and ten arms like Śiva;
they carry a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, a water-pot, and a rosary;
their hands are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and they hold a trident and a lotus.
Having meditated [on them] as being, respectively, golden, fire-colored, blue, bumblebee-black, moon-white, snow-white, red, and white:
*Hāṃ*, salutation to Ananta; *Hāṃ*, salutation to Sūkṣma; *Hāṃ*, salutation to Śivottama; *Hāṃ*, salutation to Ekanetra; *Hāṃ*, salutation to Ekarudra.
Hāṃ, obeisance to Trimūrti; Hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha; Hāṃ, obeisance to Śikhaṇḍin. Having thus worshipped them—(the ninth line)—(the third enclosure).
Having meditated thus: "At the neck of the pedestal (pīṭha),
in the northeast, is Nandin, red in color, four-armed, one-faced, with three eyes, wearing matted hair,
holding a rosary and a trident, and endowed with hands in the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness."
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin. In the southeast (41b, first line): [One should] meditate thus:
"Mahākāla, whose body is black and who has abundant beard and hair, carries in his hands a staff, a sword, and a goad, and is swift. Having meditated in this way...
HĀṂ, obeisance to Mahākāla. In the south:
Bhṛṅgin is fleshless in form, white, holding a staff and a rosary;
he has three eyes, wears a topknot, and is intent on beholding the gods. Having meditated thus—
HĀṂ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin. In the southwest:
three-eyed, dwarf-shaped, elephant-faced, and pot-bellied, he carries a noose, a goad, his own tusk, and a ripe mango fruit.
O Lord of Obstacles, [he has] a trunk and two left hands, and is red; having meditated thus, [one recites]:
*hāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*.
In the western [direction]...
Having meditated thus: "The bull, bull-shaped, three-eyed, with his mind solely fixed on Rudra,
the very embodiment of Dharma, as pure as clear crystal"— [one should offer] "Hāṃ,
obeisance to the Bull" in the northwest.

Having meditated thus: "Skanda has four arms, the appearance of a child, and a golden luster; he holds a spear and a cock in his hands, and is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness," [one should recite]: *Hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda*. In the north (–).

Seated upon a lion, yellow in color, holding a trident in her two [upper] hands, the goddess wears a crown of caskets and is adorned with pearls and other ornaments. Having thus meditated, [one should recite]:
*hāṃ devyai namaḥ* in the northeast.
Caṇḍeśvara has four arms, four faces, and three eyes;
he carries a water-pot, a trident, a rosary, and an axe.

Richly adorned with a girdle of *mahoragas* and wearing bracelets fashioned from them, he has the luster of a fresh cloud; he who restrains the *samaya* and other [pledges] should be meditated upon. Having meditated thus, one should worship him with the mantra: *Hāṃ Caṇḍāya Namaḥ*.
Their vehicle is the celestial chariot; that of Gaṇeśa is the rat;
Skanda has the peacock as his mount; and Vṛṣabha stands alone.
(Fourth enclosure:
On the pedestal-base; (line 9) in the directions starting from the secondary east and ending with the northeast, in sequence—( ).
One should visualize Śakra, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, wearing a golden-colored crown,
possessing a thousand eyes, and holding a thunderbolt in his hand.
"Hāṃ! Salutation to Indra.
Having meditated thus: [him] bearing seven flames, holding a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), surrounded by garlands of fire, red in color, with a spear in hand, and seated upon a goat."

Hāṃ, obeisance to Agni. One should meditate upon Kṛtānta, the lord of the southern quarter, who is mounted upon a buffalo, holding a staff in his hand, terrifying, black in color, and bearing the noose of Time.
Having meditated thus:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Yama!
[She who has] red eyes, is mounted upon a corpse, and has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus."
Having meditated thus: "The Lord of the Rākṣasas, sword in hand, drinking the flood of blood," [one should recite] "Hāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti.
[He is] joyful, bearing a serpent-noose, with a body possessing the luster of a flood of blood.
"One should meditate upon Varuṇa, white as the moon, seated upon a sea-monster (makara). Having thus meditated, [one recites]:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa.
[He is] full-bodied, green-hued, and bearing a banner with its fringe turned downward.
Having meditated thus upon Vāyu, the life-force of all beings, seated upon a deer— reciting "Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu"—
[one should likewise meditate upon] Kubera, seated upon a man, proud and of short stature.
One should meditate on the Lord of the Northern Quarter, golden-hued, with a mace in hand; having thus visualized him, [one recites]:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera.
[Then one meditates on] Īśāna, mounted upon a bull, bearing a trident and a sword.
Having meditated thus upon the one who has the splendor of the autumnal moon, who bears the moon on his crest and holds a trident—
saying "Hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna"—
[one should place] in the northeast a yellow, stout, four-armed Brahmā with four faces.
And bearing an elephant-vehicle, a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot—having thus meditated, [one should say]:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. In the southwest (Nairṛta).

Having meditated thus: "The infinite Puṇḍarīkākṣa, endowed with a hundred heads, resembling a flash of lightning, mounted upon a tortoise, and with palms joined in reverence"—one should worship him with the mantra:
*Hāṃ Viṣṇave Namaḥ*.
(Fifth Enclosure:
Upon the Brahma-stone—having meditated thus: "A man [as large as] a diamond, rough, extremely firm, and powerful."
Hāṃ (9th line), homage to Vajra.
Śakti, however, has the form of a woman; she is red-limbed and triangular.
Hāṃ, obeisance to Śakti.
The staff is also a person, black in body with red eyes;
Hāṃ, obeisance to the staff.
The sword is a dark-blue man with wrathful eyes;
*Hāṃ*, homage to the sword.
The noose consists of a seven-hooded serpent joined with a human tail.
Hāṃ, obeisance to the noose.
The banner, however, is the yellow Puruṣa, with a face turned away and mighty arms. Hāṃ, obeisance to the banner.
The mace is a maiden of yellow luster with very full hips;
*Hāṃ, obeisance to the Mace*.
The divine trident-man has a body dark as the sky.
Hāṃ, obeisance to the Trident. In the northeast:
the divine Puruṣa, with white limbs and white eyes, is upon a lotus.
Hāṃ, obeisance to the Lotus. In the southwest:
A male deity with a dark body, bearing a hundred-spoked wheel on his heart and a wheel upon his head,
should be worshipped with the mantra "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Wheel.
To the east, all [the hands] are in the añjali gesture and situated within lotuses.
One should visualize the heads marked with the vajra and other [mudrās] in the fifth enclosure.
All the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvara) and the others stood facing the deity.
Following that, in front of the deity, [he prepared] with cow dung... (line 5).
Having smeared a square area with lime and drawn four lines in each of the four directions,
one should arrange the individual vessels and seats for the five Brahmans, the limbs [of the mantras], and so forth in their center;
having placed vessels made of gold or other materials upon those respective seats, one should provide foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, sucked, and drinks, according to one's means.

Having placed in the vessels all the side dishes available for his own consumption and more, and having consecrated them by means of inspection and other rites, sprinkled them with the water of the general *arghya*,
and empowered them with the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, he offers incense and a lamp to the Deity, saying: "O Lord, for the sake of Your grace..."

Having requested, "Please accept this food offering (*naivedya*)," and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), one should pour water into the right hand of the Deity.
Then, with the mantras beginning with Īśāna and ending with *svāhā*, one should place the food and other offerings into five separate vessels for the five faces.
In the absence of separate vessels, one should contemplate that the food and other items contained in a single vessel are accepted by the upward-facing mouth.

One should offer [the substance] with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* in the right hand, saying: "…… *dāyai namaḥ*. Having displayed the mudrā of the offering of substances (*dravyadānamudrā*) and visualized the collection of substances as complete, one should remove the *nirmālya*.

Having placed [the items] in the presence of Caṇḍeśvara, and having performed the purification of the area for the food offering (*naivedya*) by applying curd with the hands as an unguent, he offered the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) to the deity,
and presented mouth-freshener and betel leaf. (Second line)
Having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should worship the seat with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga),
or worship the form (mūrti) with the mantras of the root, heart, head, crest, armor, and weapon. (This includes the propitiation of the lamp and so forth.)
Having fumigated with either *gulgulu* resin or a ten-ingredient incense mixture containing the four types of processed substances,

and having displayed lamps of various forms ignited with cow’s ghee and cotton wicks above, below, and on the sides, one should purify the *ārātrika* lamps— provided with wicks of cow’s ghee and camphor— by means of the ritual inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and other rites.

Taking [the ashes] with both hands, saying "svāhā," and having whirled it three times upward with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should lower it, offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*),
present the ashes endowed with the four purifications (*saṃskāra*), and [offer] the mirror, umbrella, chowries, and hand-fans.
Having gratified the deity with royal services, [the priest performs] the offering of *kuśa* grass and *pavitra*:
taking *kuśa*, *dūrvā* sprouts, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers in his joined palms (*añjali*), the officiant says: *Hāṃ Hauṃ*.

"To Śiva, the lord of all principles—the principle of Śiva, the principle of knowledge, and the principle of the self—together with his limbs, [I offer] this *kuśa*-grass purifier; *svāhā*! Thus one should offer the *kuśa*-grass purifier. "Hāṃ Hauṃ!
To Śiva, the lord of all principles—the principle of the self, the principle of knowledge, and the principle of Śiva—together with his limbs, [I offer] this *kuśa*-grass purifier; *svāhā*! (7th line)
One should offer a *kuśa* purifier (*pavitraka*).
This is stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*: (—)
One should cause the purifying substance, accompanied by unbroken rice grains and especially by dūrvā grass,
to be offered while consecrated with the three truths and the root mantra.
"One who seeks worldly enjoyment [worships] the principles of Śiva and so forth, whereas one who seeks liberation does the opposite;
he performs purification and protection, which is proclaimed as the 'Pavitra' rite.
Thus [ends the section on] the handful of flowers and so forth.

Then, having worshipped Śiva with flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and having offered incense, lamps, and water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra;
then, with the *śakti* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should display the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā*. Now...
Hari should contemplate Śiva as being pleased by the worship offered by the triad beginning with Brahmā, Indra, and others.
[The Procedure for Japa]

Thereafter, having sprinkled the rosary with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having worshipped it with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Akṣamālā," one should display the rosary-mudrā. Taking the rosary, placing a flower in the left hand, and covering both hands with a cloth, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Since the whispered (*upāṃśu*), mental (*mānasa*), and spoken (*bhāṣya*) recitations yield progressively greater fruit, one should perform the recitation either in a whisper or mentally;

having consecrated the recitation and performed the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) and other rites, one should place a flower in the right hand, place that hand at the region of the heart, and rest the right knee upon the ground.
"O protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us;
may success be mine through your grace while you remain present.
Having thus recited the mantra, the practitioner of enjoyment [should stand] to the right of the deity.
It should be offered into the hand that grants boons with the water of the mantra-offering (*arghya*).
Reciting "Hāṃ Haṃ! To Śiva, together with his limbs, accept the recitation, Svāhā," one should offer the *arghya* water in three mouthfuls to Śiva using the *udbhava-mudrā*.
One should offer [the oblation] with the left hand.
This is the procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). (The daily fire-ritual:
Thereafter, having offered three handfuls of flowers, the householder, provided with the necessary implements, should perform the fire-ritual as follows:
Having requested, "O Master, I shall perform the fire-rite;

please grant me permission," and having obtained that permission, he takes the *arghya* vessel and other implements and approaches a prepared pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated in a direction other than the south, southwest, or northwest—
either facing east or north.

Having sat down in the center of the *kuṇḍa* or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should, with the *astra-mantra*, prepare three lines with *kuśa* grass pointing eastward, and then prepare one line pointing northward. If facing north, one should prepare three lines pointing northward and one line pointing eastward; then, having sprinkled [the area] with the *kavaca-mantra*, [one effects] the perfection of all purificatory rites.

Having meditated there, one should offer a seat made of darbha grass and kūrca with the heart-mantra; and upon that, [one should visualize] Vāgīśvarī Gaurī, who has the luster of a ruby, who is three-eyed and four-armed, possessing a lotus, a book, a rosary, and a water-pot, shining like a red lotus, with four hands, thick breasts, and the splendor of a pundarīka flower.

Having meditated upon Vāgīśvara and Maheśvara as holding the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), as well as the trident (*śūla*) and the noose (*pāśa*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
As it is stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"She [the consort] becomes Gaurī, the Mistress of Speech (*vāgīśī*); from the Lord of Speech (*vāgīśa*) comes Maheśvara."
The three-eyed god has four arms and a splendor like that of a ruby;
with two hands he bestows boons and fearlessness, while his other hands hold a trident and a noose.
Vāgīśī has the luster of a white lotus, possesses four hands, and has full breasts.
But she who holds a water-pot and a book, as well as a rosary and a girdle—
thereafter, *Hāṃ*, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara.

Thus, having first performed the invocation and other rites, and having offered the *arghya*, one should bring fire—produced either from the forest or from the house of a cultured person (*śiṣṭa*)—into a pure vessel. Having discarded the portion consumed by the *kavyāda* [creatures], and having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), one should [worship] with the mantra: "Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Fire."

Having taken [the fire] with the mantra by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and drawing it in through the *iḍā* channel during inhalation (*pūraka*), one should join it with the fire at the *bindu* during retention (*kumbhaka*). Having brought about unification, one should exhale through the *piṅgalā* channel with the mantra "Hrūṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire" (*vahnicaitanya*). By means of the fire-mantra, [one visualizes] the fire resembling the flame of a lamp.

Having placed the seed with the *udbhavamudrā* and worshipped it together with that [mudrā], one should contemplate: "This is the virility of the Supreme Lord and the Mistress of the Gods. Then, having contemplated Vāgīśvarī being placed within the womb-channel by Vāgīśvara, one should cast [the seed] facing oneself with the root mantra, collect it, and perform the dressing, purification, sipping of water (*ācamana*), and so forth for the Goddess.

Having offered [oblations] with the *hṛdaya* mantra and worshipped [the fire] with the *sadyojāta* mantras and others, and having offered five oblations (*āhuti*) with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should assign the name to the fire, saying: "Hāṃ! O Śivāgni, you are the consumer of oblations. Then, having visualized the fire as purified by the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), one should worship the altar-belt (*kuṇḍamekhalā*) with the water of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) while reciting the armor mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vaiṣaṭ*.

Having sprinkled [water] around the girdle and spread *kuśa* grass with tips pointing east and north in the four directions, one should worship upon those *kuśa* blades in the east, south, west, and north with:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā; Hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu;
Hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra; Hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara. Having thus worshipped and dismissed the two ancestors, [one should proceed] in the directions from the east to the northeast.

Hāṃ, obeisance to Indra; Hāṃ, obeisance to Agni; Hāṃ, obeisance to Yama; Hāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti; (second line) obeisance to Varuṇa; Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu; Hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera; Hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna.
Pointing toward the upper portion, [one offers] Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā in the northeast; pointing toward the lower portion, [one offers] in the southwest... (third line)

Having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu," and having fully honored the fire with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śivāgni," and having offered five oblations of sesame seeds with "Hāṃ Hrūṃ, svāhā to Agni," [one recites]:
"O Agni, you are the divine splendor, for you are the supreme wind."
Therefore, having established him within the lotus of your heart, I satisfy him.

Having thus prayed, one should contemplate the mouth of the fire as being the size of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having worshipped Śiva—the Śiva-fire—along with His attendants (*sāsna*) and limbs (*sāṅga*) within the lotus of the heart, at the time of the food offering (*naivedya*), one should pray: "O Blessed One, I satisfy You; grant me Your command. Thus having requested permission, [one proceeds].

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of substances such as ghee and sesame seeds with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having offered a tenth part of that for the limbs (*aṅgas*), one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the mantra *hāṃ hauṃ śivāya vauṣaṭ*. Then, having taken three morsels (*grāsa*) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* and having offered one morsel each for the limbs, [the procedure] continues again.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and worshipped Śiva with the eightfold flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), having offered the *arghya* for turning away (*parāṅmukha-arghya*), and having duly united Śiva residing in the fire with Śiva residing in the *liṅga* through the connection of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), one should dismiss Brahmā and the other deities. [The *vyāhṛtis*... (8th line)
The fourfold [set] and the fourfold beginning with fire are not written here because they pertain to the subject of the Brāhmaṇas. [One should recite]: *hrāṃ hrūṃ vahnaye namaḥ*.

One should dismiss the fire. If one is not provided with the implements for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and is incapable, one should mutter that mantra ten times. Then, with cow dung, [one should prepare] at the southeast corner of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having prepared two maṇḍalas, at the edge of the western maṇḍala, one should worship in the four directions starting from the east with the following: *hāṃ rudrebhyo namaḥ*; *hāṃ mātṛbhyo namaḥ*; *hāṃ gaṇebhyo namaḥ*; [hāṃ ... *namaḥ*. Then: *hāṃ grahebhyo namaḥ*; *hāṃ asurebhyo namaḥ*; *hāṃ rākṣasebhyo namaḥ*.

Having worshipped in the corners beginning with the northeast with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Nāgas," [one worships] in the center of the maṇḍala with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Nakṣatras; Hāṃ, obeisance to the Rāśis;
Hāṃ, obeisance to the Viśvedevas; Hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla.
(Third line)

Having worshipped in the corners beginning with the northeast (īśāna), having offered the *bali* to Rudra and the others with food mixed with water using the mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having dismissed them with the *hṛdaya-mantra* at the eastern maṇḍala: *Hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*; *Hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*; *Hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*; *Hāṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ*; *Hāṃ varuṇāya...* (4th line).

Having worshipped in the eight directions starting from the east with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Yama; Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu; Hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera; Hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna," and having worshipped in the regions of the zenith and nadir, as well as in the south and southeast, with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā; Hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu," [he should worship] with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Nīlalohita."

Having worshipped in the center of the mandala with [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*, one should offer the opening (*bila*) and dismiss [the deities] with the heart-mantra and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mantra]. For the directions: "Hāṃ! To those dwelling in the eastern direction—the lords of the directions, the hosts of spirits and mothers, Rudras, kṣetrapālas, and so forth—*svāhā*! Thus for the directions.

Having offered oblations in all directions under various names, and having offered an external oblation outside the mandala with the mantra "Hāṃ, svāhā to the crows and others who violate the commitments," [he recites]:
"Those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes..."
And those who are gentle, as well as those who dwell properly in their respective abodes—
the Mothers, those with the form of Rudra, and the lords of the Gaṇas—
likewise others who have become obstacles and are stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
May all, with well-pleased minds, accept this offering;
may they grant me constant success and protect me always from all states of existence.

Having made this request, one should dismiss [the deity] with the *saṃhāriṇī* [mantra] from the heart. Taking its splendor (*vibhūti*) and applying it as a tilaka on the forehead, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and then the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Thus concludes the procedure for the minor fire-ritual (*svalpāgnikāryavidhi*).
(Quelling the defects of deficiency and excess):

Thereafter, having gone into the presence of Śiva and worshipped him with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the Aghora mantra twenty-one times for the sake of quelling the defects of deficiency and excess; that recitation...
One should offer [the self] as before:
"O Lord, whatever action there may be—whether always well-done or ill-done—enjoy that for me while I abide at the feet of Śiva; destroy it, O Śaṅkara!"

Having made this request, one should offer it into the hand of the Bestower of Boons (*varada-hasta*). Thereafter, one should pray to the Deity: "O Lord, may whatever I have done out of delusion—whether deficient or excessive—all that become complete through your grace."
(Announcement of the Fruit of Worship) Then, having visualized the entire fruit of the worship as completely fulfilled,
one should worship Śiva with the "eight-flower offering" (aṣṭapuṣpikā), and having honored that fruit— which resembles the autumnal moon— just as one honors the recitation of mantras (japa).

Whatever merit has been earned by me through worship, recitation, fire-sacrifices, and so forth—O Supreme Lord, that fruit is offered to You. Please accept it Yourself out of Your own grace; O Lord, let this not be for my own enjoyment.

"O Maheśvara, through action, mind, and speech, you are my refuge. Having thus informed [the Lord], one should say, "O Śiva, accept the fruit of the merit of this worship, recitation, and so forth; Svāhā! and, having spoken thus, one should offer it with one's own left hand into the left [hand] of the All-pervading Lord. Thus...
O Supreme Lord, whatever merit has been earned by me through worship, recitation, fire-sacrifices, and other such acts— whether for the sake of liberation or for the enjoyment of worldly pleasures—
that fruit I now offer unto You.
"O Lord of Gods, may that fruit be mine as the means for achieving both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Having thus made this request, one should offer the fruit.
(This concludes the response to doubts concerning the subject of worship.)

Now, one might ask: since Śiva’s essential nature is eternally pure, stainless, and unsurpassed bliss, and is thus eternally [perfected], for what purpose are the offerings of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful oblation (*arghya*), ritual bathing (*abhiṣeka*), perfumes (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth, performed?

It is not performed for the sake of attaining Śiva as its own purpose; rather, it is performed with the aim of one's own purpose [which is Śiva]. In that case, does He accept the worship performed by a devotee of Śiva or not? If He accepts it, then [He would be] possessed of attachment, aversion, and so forth.
And it would be subject to modification.

If it is argued that in the absence of its appropriation, there would be no attainment of the fruit, we say: no; just as the earth, though subjected to plowing, digging, watering, and sowing by the farmer, yields its fruit for his enjoyment.

Even though one has not formally accepted [the offering], the performer enjoys a fruit corresponding to their effort. Likewise, whatever a person desiring a particular result offers—even a stone—once it sees the worship performed with devotion, it certainly becomes the bestower of a fruit corresponding to that very action.
Just as on earth, whatever root-seeds or the like are sown by someone with a desire for truth, [they yield their respective fruits].

In each case, that very fruit corresponding to its seed is experienced. Likewise, whatever service a person performs with whatever ritual materials and mantras for the sake of Śiva, out of a desire for a particular result, he alone experiences a fruit corresponding to that.
As it has been said in the Prajāstava:
"The water for washing the feet and the water for rinsing the mouth are offered to Śiva, who is established by his own nature, for the sake of one's own purification. (5th line)
The offering of the *arghya* and the presentation of flowers— this is the means for attaining the desired place.
The auspicious bath that removes the impurities of one's own self, the anointing with fragrant unguents, fine garments and ornaments,
worship with fragrant flowers and garlands, and the ritual offering of incense to Sadāśiva adorned with ornaments— [these constitute the rite].
Indeed, for the sake of the enjoyment of the individual soul (aṇu), that place [is established] as a pure abode, providing the lamp of the knowledge of Śiva.

The worship of the limbs of enjoyment is for the sake of the self’s attainment of the qualities of Śiva; furthermore, the oneness of the limbs of the Lord with the limbs of the worshipper is for the sake of the union with Śiva of the purified soul. [Therein lies] the offering of food to one who is satisfied, and the granting of many sacrifices, dwellings, and so forth.
For the sake of satisfying the mind,
O dear one, the fruit of your worship is a wonderful state of auspiciousness that brings well-being;
for one who has become pure, this gift of purity destroys the threefold suffering and leads to the accomplishment of all goals.
"Recitation [of mantras] with devotion and prostration to Śiva are the cause of attaining the sovereignty of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and others.
Thus it is stated elsewhere as well. (9th line)
Through worship one obtains a vast kingdom; through the fire-rite, prosperity;
through recitation, purification from sin; and through knowledge and meditation, one is liberated.
"But he who worships with devotion until the end of the body—he is Śiva, the burner of all karmic actions; he is called 'liberated while living'.
Thus [it is said].
(The Offering of Oneself:
Thereafter—
Salutation to Śiva, the peaceful one, the cause of the three causes.
And I offer myself to you; you are my refuge, O Supreme Lord.

Because it has been stated: "In worship, there is meditation on the *sakala* [form]; the recitation (*japa*) is both *sakala* and *niṣkala*; and in the *niṣkala*, there is the offering of the self," one should offer [the self] into the boon-granting hand of Sadāśiva, directed toward the *niṣkala* with the mantra: *HĀṂ HAUṂ ŚIVĀYA ĀTMĀNAṂ GṚHĀṆA SVĀHĀ*. Thus says the Āgama.
The root mantra, extremely clear, [is established] at the end of the heart;
having reached the splendor [of the deity], it is not other than that.
Having brought it back, one should offer it into the hand of the God who grants boons,
by means of the yoga of channel-union, into the lotus of one's own heart.
Having entered, the supreme guide should lead [the disciple] to the fulfillment of his purpose.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire world.
"Śiva performs the sacrifice everywhere; that which is Śiva, I am indeed that. [This is the dismissal.
Then, having worshipped Śiva with the eightfold offering of flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), [one should perform the special...]
