Having offered the *arghya* with "Hāṃ Hauṃ Śivāya," and having offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya* with the weapon-mantra ending in "Huṃ Phaṭ," one should dissolve the limbs of Śiva into their respective locations, beginning with the heart, by means of the flower-arrow mudrā while reciting: "Oṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva (*śivamūrti*)."
Having reflected upon my thousands of offenses committed day and night,
you should forgive me, thinking "This one is a servant," O you who are compassionate toward devotees.
Having thus made this request,

having sealed [the offering] with the root mantra using the *nirodhamudrā*, and having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā* with the *śaktimantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should offer it] with devotion.

"One should pay homage" means a dismissal with expectation (*sāpekṣavisarjana*). Immediately after the consecration with nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), one should join [the deity] to the portion of power (*śaktyaṃśa*) within the light-liṅga situated in the middle of the heart-lotus by means of the heart-mantra through inhalation and withdrawal.
This is the dismissal without expectation (*anupekṣavisarjana*). Following that, one should offer the *arghya* for the face-averting rite (*parāṅmukha*) to the Guru and others in reverse order.
|| Caṇḍapūjā || The Worship of Caṇḍa
Then, in the intermediate direction between the secondary northeast and the main east, on pure ground: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍāsana, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ!
Hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍamūrti, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ! Having thus worshipped [him], [one should meditate upon] Caṇḍa, who is born from Rudra-Agni, resembling lampblack, and terrifying.
He was fierce, possessing four faces and four arms, and bearing a trident and an axe.
With great flames issuing from his mouth, twelve blood-red eyes,
and a crest-jewel upon his matted locks, he is adorned with jeweled bracelets.

Having meditated thus: [upon him] who has a serpent as his sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), who holds a rosary, a sacred thread, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), who is seated upon a white lotus throne, and who destroys the suffering of those devoted to him. (47a, 1st line)
*Caṇḍanetrebhyo huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* ... *anyasya dhuru caṇḍeśvarāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having thus invoked [the deity], [one offers]: *caṇḍahṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *caṇḍabandhaśirase huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*;
*caṇḍaśikhāyai huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *caṇḍakavacāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *caṇḍāstrāya huṃ*.

"Phaṇṇamaḥ. Having thus performed the sakalīkaraṇa with these limbs, one should worship. Alternatively, having invoked [the deity] with only the seat-mantra (*āsana*), the form-mantra (*mūrti*), and the root-mantra (*mūla*), and having worshipped, offered the *arghya*, presented the food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth, and given the previously set-out *nirmālya*, [one offers] foods to be licked, sucked, and drunk, as well as betel, unguents, and ointments.
"The offering of remains (nirmālya) has been bestowed upon you by the command of Śiva.
Having thus informed [the deity], or else having recited the Śakti-mantra and offered it, one should say:
"All this ritual section (kriyākāṇḍa) has been performed by me, O Caṇḍa, at your command."

"Whatever has been done deficiently or in excess through delusion, may it always be complete for me. Having thus made this request, he should offer the *arghya* water with his face turned away. Then, having raised the limbs [of the deity] and joined them to the form [of the image] with the *mūrti-mantra*, he should dissolve [the deity] into his own heart using the root mantra accompanied by the *pūraka* breath-retention and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. All of this should be performed in the monastery (*maṭha*).
And this concerns the topic of the signs (*liṅga*) pertaining to the authority honored by the teacher, not the signs for one's own personal use. Then,

having raised the mantras residing in the *arghya* vessel, withdrawn them, and deposited them in the heart-lotus, one should remove the floral remains (*nirmālya*) and [smear] the ground with cow dung.
Having purified [the area], one should sprinkle it with water. Then, having washed one's feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
and having bathed with pure ashes and performed the rite of sakalīkaraṇa, one should recite the Aghora mantra twenty-one times for the sake of obtaining the fruit of the entire worship.
(Kapilā-pūjā) Then, having worshipped the Kapilā cow with perfumes, unbroken grains, and flowers.
O Surabhi, born from the churning of the nectar of immortality, you who sustain the world;
accept this morsel of food, for this is my supreme vow.

Having thus offered the morsel, one who worships with a *kāmya-mantra* should recite it according to the method prescribed for that particular ritual (*kalpa*). Thus [ends] the procedure for worship for those who are dispassionate (*virakta*).

But for one who is dispassionate, O Maheśvarī, there is neither knowledge, nor recitation, nor worship, nor fire-oblation, nor even virtuous conduct; no ritual duties involving the sacred fires need be performed by him.
For him, there is no observance of rules regarding fields or sacred seats,
nor worship, nor rites for the ancestors, nor pilgrimages, nor vows.
There is no fruit of merit or demerit, no guest-reception, and no worldly activities.
He should renounce all worldly activities without exception, as well as the entirety of conventional conduct and worldly wealth, having accomplished all that was to be done.

"One should not engage in conceptualization or discursive thought, nor in other sectarian practices, nor in trivial rites such as the worship of wood or stone"— such is the scriptural authority (āgama) from this statement.

Thus, for one who lacks the capacity for such steadfastness in the aforementioned worship of knowledge (*jñānapūjā*), external worship is also prescribed, according to the maxim: "Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people do as well. (4th line) There are three kinds of ascetics (*yatayaḥ*): the practitioner of austerity (*tapasvī*), the distinguished one (*viśiṣṭhaḥ*), and the wise one (*vidvān*).
As it is stated in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:

"Ascetics are to be known as being of three kinds: the practitioner (*tapasvin*), the scholar (*vidvas*), and likewise the realized one (*vidvān*); these are declared to be threefold. Hear now their distinctions in due order."
To one who is devoted to austerity and is an ascetic,
his wife of virtuous vows must not study, nor form any resolve, nor listen to anything whatsoever.
He should not engage in the gathering of disciples nor in the public proclamation of his learning;
he should not speak in refined Sanskrit, nor carry a staff or a water-pot.
Having worshipped the Liṅga for a moment, endowed with mere devotion,
he should remain alone at the foot of a tree or in a forest devoid of water.
Filled with fear from birth, he should live depending primarily on his arms;
while living there, he should obtain food and drink from whomever it may be.
"Using only his hands as a bowl, he shall subsist on food obtained by begging"—
since it is stated thus, such an ascetic would be a mere *sādhaka* bearing the name of a *yati*;
for according to this statement, neither the seeker of knowledge (*vividiṣu*) nor the man of realization (*vidvān*) has their method of worship been described.

"Therefore, having abandoned all the gods led by Brahmā, one should worship Virūpākṣa, who resides within the Ādityas. According to this statement, having first worshipped Śiva in the maṇḍala and performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), [one should place Him] on the ornamented throne of Śiva.
In the northwest, one should worship Vighneśvara facing south;
in the northeast, the Guru facing south;
and [then] Śiva according to the previously mentioned procedure, excluding the door-enclosure, the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), the offering of oblations (*bali*), and the presentation to Caṇḍeśvara.
One should perform worship.
Now, the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the Vedānta is prescribed there for the three [upper] castes;
the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the meaning of the Āgamas and the Purāṇas is for the Śūdra caste.
"Through service to those who have heard [the scriptures], there is mastery in all the treatises by means of philosophical insight.
The livelihoods of Śūdras should be explained through the meanings of the Śruti and the meanings of the Āgamas.
For others who are detached, the knowledge of reality comes through the spoken word. Thus [it is said].
Now, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"Some learned men say that for a Śūdra there is knowledge through the Purāṇas alone by means of service;
they declare that women are equal to Śūdras."
"For all others as well, the practice of knowledge is prescribed;
through another language and over time, that too will be beneficial for them.
Thus, by these words from the Skanda Purāṇa which explain the established doctrine.

Until midday, one should engage in the study and teaching of the Śiva-āgamas, or perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), recitation (japa), and meditation (dhyāna) according to the methods to be described hereafter. (The sequence of prāṇāyāma)
Herein is the sequence of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). In a place that is soundless, secluded, and fearless;
free from cold, wind, and heat; devoid of flies, mosquitoes, women, ants, scorpions, snakes, and the like;
in a plastered chamber or a pleasant spot upon a thick tiger skin—[one should practice].
Having arranged a soft seat and spread *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing north upon it, one should sit there; having properly assumed the *padmāsana*,
*muktāsana*, or *siddhāsana*, [one should worship] Kṣetrapāla, Gaṇeśa, the Guru, Śiva, and the Goddess.
Having praised and bowed to Vāyu, and having restrained the breath after first purifying the channels (*nāḍī*), one should perform *prāṇāyāma*.
(The procedure for *prāṇāyāma* is as follows: namely, by means of contraction, using the root-wind (*mūlavāyu*), one [draws] the fire situated at the *mūlādhāra* between the anus and the genitals.

Uttering the seed-syllable *vaṃ* (the fire with its bindu), one should raise [the *kuṇḍalinī*] from the navel— [therein] the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), which is shaped like the fruit of the *kośātaki* plant and constitutes the root of all channels— and having closed its downward-facing opening, one should cause both the wind and the fire arising from the *mūlādhāra* to enter that wheel of channels by means of the *iḍā* [nostril], performing a retention (*kumbhaka*) of the air alone.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*) together with the nasal bindu (*ṃ*) through all the channels,

having caused the wind and fire to enter, having exhaled through *piṅgalā*, and having again filled [the breath] through *piṅgalā* and performed retention (*kumbhaka*), then having exhaled through *iḍā* and again filled [the breath] through *iḍā* and performed retention— in this manner, by these six methods, [one practices] the seed-syllable of fire together with the bindu... (3rd line)
While reciting [the mantra], one should meditate upon Rudra as the presiding deity of the fire and purify the channel.
Now—
O Sage, for those who are dispassionate, the awakened, as well as for Vaiśyas, Śūdras,
and likewise for women,
the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) is performed with either the Śiva-mantra ending in "namaḥ" or the Vaiṣṇava-mantra, and not otherwise.
"One should always perform sixteen *prāṇāyāmas* in this manner," according to this statement.

Having performed the *kārābhādinyāsa*— consisting of the sage (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*devatā*), power (*śakti*), seed-syllable (*bīja*), letter (*varṇa*), field (*kṣetra*), and application (*viniyoga*)— of the five-syllabled mantra in the manner that will be described hereafter.
Uttering the *namaḥ*-*anta* Śiva-mantra sixteen times, one should fill [the breath] through the *iḍā* [nāḍī].

Having retained the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) in any one of the locations—the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, or the *brahmarandhra*—according to one's practice, and having meditated upon Śiva, one should recite the *namaḥ*-*anta* Śiva-mantra sixty-four times during the retention (*kumbhaka*). Then, slowly...

One should exhale by means of the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] through the recitation of the thirty-two-syllable [mantra]. In this way, one should perform sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) daily. There is spiritual advancement (*abhyudaya*) in performing more than this. Alternatively, [one may do so] by means of the *ajapā*.
Or one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the *Prāsāda* [mantra].
This has been stated in the *Prāsādaparamākṣaranirṇaya*:
By the sound *ha* it goes out, and by the sound *sa* it enters again;
the *haṃsa* moves upward, and this is known as the transition (*saṃkrānti*) at Capricorn (*makara*).
Then, practiced at six finger-breadths from the transition of the pitcher (*kumbha*),
it again transitions into Pisces (*mīna*) above the throat of the other.
Having left [the breath] from the middle of the throat up to the palate, one should enter Aries;
the transition extends to the end of the nose for eight finger-breadths.
Then, having abandoned the tip of the nose, the life-giving swan gradually enters Taurus.
Having left six finger-breadths [behind], one should again enter the sign of Gemini.
The transition (*saṃkrānti*) is situated in Gemini;

such is the sequence here. Having meditated upon Śiva, one should [expel] the wind residing in the abdomen through the channel *piṅgalā* by the utterance of the syllable *ha*, for thirty-two *mātrās*.

Having retained [the breath] and again meditated upon the Śakti while pronouncing the syllable *sa*, one should fill [the body] through the *iḍā* for sixteen *mātrās*; then, mentally pronouncing "so'haṃ," one should direct the wind into any one of the following locations:
the heart, the pit of the throat, the middle of the throat, the root of the palate, the tip of the palate, the middle of the eyebrows, or the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Because of the progressive excellence [of each stage]:
(4th line) Having retained the vital breath for sixty-four *mātrās* according to one's practice, one should perform *kumbhaka* with the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of Paraśiva.
Regarding the seven locations beginning with the heart, excluding the *brahmarandhra*, there are six locations pertaining to the internal self (*ādhyātmika*). (5th line)

The transition to Kauttaraṇāyana constitutes this very group of six stages of supreme liberation pertaining to the presiding deities (*adhidaivika*). Above that, however, is the stage of ultimate liberation (*paramokṣa*). Therefore, one should practice with effort so that the vital air (*vāyu*) may become stable within the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

(The sequence of breath control for the *Prāsāda* mantra): Then, having filled [the body] through the *iḍā* channel in the previously described manner, one should mentally recite the *Prāsāda* mantra while following the path of the *suṣumnā*.

With a mind purified by the heart and other centers, joined with the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), and having abandoned the sequence of deities beginning with Brahmā— starting from the letter *A* and so forth—

one proceeds as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Having restrained the vital breath there, one goes with the mind to the end of the *samāna* wind, and therein effects the dissolution of the mind.

Having performed [this], they consider that when the supreme Śiva— who is indivisible in form, being-existence-consciousness-bliss, non-dual, and perfectly full— has become a lake and remains [there], if the wind moves downward,
one should exhale through the Piṅgalā, fill [the lungs] again through the Iḍā, and perform *kumbhaka* (retention).

Having performed this, one should practice sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). Now, we shall demonstrate the characteristics of the locations beginning with the heart, their colors, vowels, deities, and so forth. Twelve finger-breadths above the navel is the heart, measuring four finger-breadths. Therein is the vowel *e* (*medhā-svara*), which has the luster of a flame of fire, possesses three measures (*mātra*), and is associated with the twenty-four principles (*tattva*), with Brahmā as its presiding deity. Above that, at the throat—

Eight finger-breadths [above], there is the letter *U*, possessing a radiance equal to the moon and sun, abiding for two morae (*mātrā*); it is conjoined with the six principles (*tattva*), and Viṣṇu is its presiding deity. Then, at the palate, four finger-breadths [above], there is the letter *M*, possessing a brilliance like lightning, abiding for one mora.

Rudra, conjoined with the principle of Māyā, is its presiding deity. Thereafter, at a distance of two finger-breadths between the eyebrows, there resides a point (*bindu*) the size of half a mora, circular in shape and resembling a lamp-flame; it is conjoined with the principles known as Śuddhavidyā and Īśvara, and Īśvara is its presiding deity. On the forehead, at a distance of one quarter [of a finger-breadth], there is the form of a half-moon, possessing the luster of the moon in the sky; it is situated above the *bindu*.
Endowed with the principle of Sādākhya, Sadāśiva is the presiding deity.
Above that is Nirodhinī, possessing one-eighth of a mātrā; the principle of Bindu has Śakti as its supreme deity. Above that—

Extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), it has the luster and radiance arising from a mass of jewels in the form of a staff; it is sixteen parts in measure, abiding as the *nāda*, with Śakti as its presiding deity. Thence, eleven finger-breadths above the eyebrows at the aperture of Brahmā on Mount Meru, there is a light resembling the brilliance of lightning flashing from a mountain peak.
The Ci-chakti is situated with a measure of thirty-two parts; then, one finger-breadth above that at the crown of the head, the Śakti is situated with a measure of sixty-four parts;
and three finger-breadths further above that is the Vyāpinī, with a measure of one hundred and twenty-eight parts.

[The state] is situated there; four *aṅgulas* above that, it remains at the measure of two hundred and fifty-six parts (*bhāga*). Four *aṅgulas* above that is the *manomātra*; beyond that is the *unmanā*. Then, [there is] Śiva, who shines forth—pervading internally, externally, below, and above, of undivided form, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and knowable solely through the experience of non-duality. Having thus understood correctly by means of the mouth of the Guru...
One should perform *prāṇāyāma*.
This has been stated in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:
"The heart is four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) above the navel, at a distance of one span (*vitasti*). (9th line)
At its end stands Medhā, whose voice has the luster of a flame of fire.
Brahmā, the cause, possesses three measures (*mātra*) and is joined with twenty-four principles (*tattva*);
the Lord of Speech (*Vācaspati*) is at the throat, measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), possessing two measures and the luster of the sun and moon.
Viṣṇu is joined with six principles and resides in the heart, measuring four [finger-breadths].
O Rudra, the principle of Māyā is poison; it is a single measure, possessing the brilliance of a mountain slope.
Between the eyebrows is the letter *a*, two finger-breadths in length, resembling a lamp and measuring half a mora;
it is conjoined with the two principles (*tattva*) and is infinite. On the forehead is the letter *ā*, measuring one quarter-mora.
The *nirodhinī* consists of one-eighth of the portion of light above the upper half of the circle;
it is said that from the dawn [of consciousness] comes the *daṇḍa*, which is one-sixteenth [of the portion] and has the luster of a jewel.
The thirty-second part, ending at the tip of the staff, is like the flash of lightning within the cavity;
it extends from the upper opening of the two ladles (*sruva*) for a measure of eleven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The power of sixty-four parts resides in the head at one finger-breadth;
the pervasive power (*vyāpinī*) consists of one hundred and twenty-eight parts over three finger-breadths;
and the power of fifty-two hundred and sixty parts extends over four finger-breadths.
Equal [in size] and extending upwards, it consists of mind alone and is four finger-breadths in height.
"Up to the end of Samānā is the net of bonds; beyond Unmanā is Supreme Śiva.
Now follows the sequence of recitation (*japa*).

The five-syllabled [mantra] is of six types, distinguished as the gross, the subtle, the mixed, and the pure, beginning with Tārā’s grace (*tārāprasāda*). Among these, for the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*), there is the five-syllabled Tārā beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ). For those among the Śūdras who are virtuous (*sacchūdra*), there is the five-syllabled grace beginning with the short *praṇava* (hrīṃ).

For those engaged in the initiation for the elevation from birth, there is the "Initial Gross Five-Syllabled" mantra: *nama ādipañcākṣaram*. For Śūdras who follow the general rules of conduct (*sāmānya-samayāyin*), there is the "Mixed Five-Syllabled" mantra: *namaśśivāya śivāya namaḥ*. For those of mixed castes (*saṅkara-jāti*), there is the "Subtle Five-Syllabled" mantra ending with *namaḥ*.

For those who are dispassionate, having abandoned the word "namas," [the mantra] "I am Śiva" is the pure five-syllabled [mantra]. This is stated for those beyond the stages of life (ativarṇāśramin) in the *Siddhāntabodha*: *viraktānām| namaḥ padaṃ vihāya śivohamasmīti śuddhapañcākṣaram| ativarṇāśramiṇām taduktaṃ siddhāntabodhe* || 8 ||
The five-syllabled mantra has six varieties: the *tāra*, the *prāsāda*, and their combinations;
it is gross, subtle, and pure. Listen now to the sequence of its utterance (*uccāra*): therein, "Unnamaḥ Śivāya" constitutes the five-syllabled *tāra*.
"Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ"—this is the five-syllabled *prāsāda* mantra. "Namaḥ śivāya" is both gross-gross and subtle; "namaśśivāya śivāya namaḥ" is gross-subtle.
The subtle [mantra] ending with "namaḥ" is said to be the pure five-syllabled one; having omitted the word "namaḥ," it is called "śivāya."

This pure five-syllabled [mantra] has been revealed through one's own direct experience; within that [mantra], the five syllables denote the Lord, the fetter, and the bound soul. In the midst of those, one should distinguish the two known as *mala* and *māyā* for the sake of realizing the Self.
And it is pure, natural, and conducive to the bliss of absolute liberation.

"That state, I am He"—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "I am Śiva. (Third line) In the Vedānta, however, it is taught that "I am He" is the five-syllabled *Tāra*, wherein the three syllables are prescribed.
A Śūdra should mutter this mantra, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, using the *prāsāda* [mantra].

For those joined with the general initiation, the gross five-syllabled mantra is prescribed; for the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation, the mixed [mantra] is declared for those who have not yet taken formal vows. Among those, the subtle five-syllabled mantra is prescribed for yogis and men of knowledge.
"But for those who have transcended the castes and stages of life (ati-varṇāśrama), the pure five-syllabled mantra is prescribed.
Now, regarding the statement that the *tāra-pañcākṣara* is for the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) alone, while the *prāsāda-pañcākṣara* is for Śūdras— and concerning this *prāsāda-pañcākṣara*:

Because the *praṇava* exists [in the mantra]. If it is asked, "How can this be for Śūdras?", the answer is true. For Śūdras, there is the qualification to recite the short *praṇava* in the *jātyuddhāra* [mantra]; however, since the short *praṇava* is impossible within the five-syllabled *tāra*, they have no qualification for that.
Since the short *praṇava* is possible within the five-syllabled *prāsāda*, they have qualification for that.
Then, from before noon, facing east, [one should sit] on seats such as a black antelope skin;

immediately thereafter, facing north, one should assume any one of the postures (āsanas) according to one's practice on seats such as a cloth mat. Having bound [the body], [one should recite] the five-syllabled mantra appropriate to each respective qualification.

One should recite [the mantra] after meditating upon Śiva in the locations beginning with the heart—accompanied by the meter, deity, power (*śakti*), seed-syllable (*bīja*), place of origin, and phonemes—as well as the hand-gestures (*kara*) and limb-assignments (*aṅganyāsa*) which are about to be described. Herein is the sequence of the assignment (*nyāsakrama*). To the Goddess, the Lord said: (9th line) This five-syllabled mantra, together with the *praṇava*, is my heart.
This is more secret than the secret, the manifest, unsurpassed knowledge of liberation.
And I shall declare for this mantra the seer (ṛṣi), the metre (chandas), and the presiding deity (adhidevatā);
as well as the seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), the vowel, the phoneme (varṇa), and the specific location for each syllable.
Vāmadeva by name is the seer; the metre is declared to be Paṅkti.
O fair-faced one, I am the deity Sadāśiva of this mantra of mine.
The seed-syllables beginning with 'a' consist of the five elements;
one should contemplate oneself as the Praṇava, the seed-syllable that is all-pervading and imperishable.
O Goddess of gods, you alone are Śakti, saluted by all the deities.
For every syllable, there is a seer (ṛṣi), a meter (chandas), and a deity;
likewise, there is a phoneme-deity (varṇadaiva), as well as Śakti, the support (ādhāra), and the meter itself.
The abode of the Ṛṣi—these seven are spoken of as individual syllables.
Listen now to the sequence of colors and so forth among the divisions of the five gross elements:
the color of the letter *na* is yellow, and Brahmā is its presiding deity (*adhidevatā*).
It is endowed with the power of the hand and has the earth as its support;
it is joined with the Anuṣṭubh metre, and Vasiṣṭha is likewise its seer.
The western face is said to be the syllable *ma*, the locus;
its color is white, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity there.
Endowed with the power of Lakṣmī, with water as its support,
joined with the Triṣṭubh metre, and likewise having Viśvāmitra as its seer.
The place is to the north, its face is turned upward, and it is said to be the syllable *Śi*.
Its color is red; Rudra is the presiding deity there.
Furthermore, Rudra, Gaurī, Śakti, the support, and Fire [are also present].
It is joined with the Triṣṭubh metre and likewise has Jamadagni as its seer (ṛṣi).
The syllable *va* is said to be the face on the right side;
it is blue in color, and Maheśvara is its presiding deity.
Joined with the power of Maheśa and having Vāyu as its support, it is conjoined with the Bṛhatī meter;
its seer is said to be Kāśyapa.
The place is indeed facing east and is called Tatpuruṣa;
the letter Ya is the color of crystal, and the deity has the form of Sadāśiva.
The support is conjoined with the Manonmanī Śakti, and likewise the ether;
it is joined with the Jagatī metre and has Bhāradvāja as its seer.
Above that is the station of Īśāna, which is said to be the syllable *ya*.
Thus the expressive has been indicated; now hear the sequence of the expressed.
The letter Śa is the form of Śiva, while the letter Va is said to be Śakti;
the letter Ya is the form of the Self (Ātman), and the letter Na is the form of the knot (granthi).
The letter Ma is the form of impurity (mala); such is the meaning of the five letters.
I shall now proclaim its ritual placement (nyāsa), which is auspicious and brings about all accomplishments.

For the student, the householder, and the ascetic, there is a sequential order. The birth of the stages is traditionally held to belong to the student and the householder; for the ascetics, however, there is only the dissolution [of the self] through the rite of renunciation, and not otherwise.
It will be explained to you, O fair-faced one, through its various divisions such as the upward flight and so forth.
One should first perform the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), immediately followed by the placement of the body (*dehanyāsa*).
Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) according to the prescribed sequence of the syllables.
This is called the "placement of origination" (*utpattinyāsa*), extending from the head down to the feet.
O Dear One, the dissolution occurs from the feet up to the crown of the head.
The placement [of mantras] from the heart onwards is declared to be the Nyāsasthiti-nyāsa;
it is auspicious for celibates, householders, and ascetics alike.
Then one should touch the entire body, including the head, with the mantra;
this is called the "placement upon the body" (sadehanyāsa), which is the same for everyone.
Beginning from the right thumb and ending at the left thumb—this is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*);
its arising is according to that sequence, while the reverse is the withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*).
One should indeed perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on both hands, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger;
this "placement of stability" (*sthitinyāsa*) bestows exceedingly great enjoyment upon the householder.
Having first performed the placement on the hands, one should immediately thereafter perform the placement on the body.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa); this is the general rule for the deity.
Having encased the syllable *oṃ*, one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) upon all the limbs,
and likewise upon both hands and their ten fingers in due order.
First, O fair-faced one, one should remember the seer, the meter, the deity, the seed-syllable,
the power, the Supreme Self, and Rudra.
Having touched the hands with the mantra, one should place the Praṇava upon the two palms.
And likewise on all the fingers, at both the first and the last joints.
May those five central seed-syllables be accomplished during the lunar nodes;
one should install them in sequence according to the stages of life, through the various divisions beginning with "arising" (*utpatti*).
Then, with both hands, [one should touch] from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
One should touch the deity with the mantra, encased within the Praṇava itself.

One should likewise place [the mantras] beginning with the *praṇava* on the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the feet, as well as on the throat, according to their respective divisions.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should indeed fashion the faces;
thereafter, O beautiful one, one should place the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in their respective locations.
One should know the *praṇava* to be the heart, and the syllable *nakāra* is said to be Śiva.
The crest-mantra consists of the syllable *ma*, and likewise, the syllable *śi* is the armor.
The letter *va* is the eye, while the letter *ya* is proclaimed to be the weapon.
Having thus performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-vinyāsa*), one should then bind the directions.
In this regard, for the twice-born alone there is the encapsulation by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), whereas for the *śūdras*, there is only the letter *va*.
Vighneśa, the Mothers, Durgā, and Kṣetrajña [are to be placed] in the directions in due order;
likewise, in all four corners starting from the southeast, in sequence.
Having established them with auspicious faces by means of the tips of the thumb and forefinger, O auspicious one.
And having said, "Forgive me," one should offer salutations individually to each.

The wise practitioner should thus perform the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) in sequence: on the palm, the middle of the hand, the thumb, the forefinger, and the other fingers, using the thumb.

Thus has this auspicious nyāsa been proclaimed, which removes all sins, brings about all accomplishments, is meritorious, provides all protection, and is auspicious. When this is performed upon the auspicious weapon [mantra], one becomes like Śaṅkara himself.
Sin committed in previous lives is destroyed at that very moment by performing this rite.
Having done so, the wise one— pure in appearance and firm in his vows—
should mutter the six-syllable mantra, having received it through the grace of the preceptor.
(The Place for Recitation) He states the place for recitation:
one should know that recitation performed in a house yields an equal [result]; in a cow-pen, it becomes a hundredfold.
A hundred thousand [recitations] by a river, and an infinite amount in the presence of Śiva;
on the seashore, in a temple of the gods, in sacred groves,
and in all holy hermitages, the recitation becomes ten million times more meritorious.
In the presence of Śiva, as well as of the Sun, Fire, and the Guru,
the practice of recitation for the reciter is now demonstrated.
O fair-faced one, one should know that the counting of finger-japa is by single units;
by the lines [of the hand], one knows eight, and by the fruits of the life-force (jīva-phala), ten.
A hundred [is the value] with conch-shell gems; a thousand with *laśca* stones;
ten thousand with crystal; and a hundred thousand is said to be the value with pearls.

With *patmākṣa* beads, ten lakhs [of recitations] are performed; with golden beads, it is said to be ten million (*koṭi*). With *kuśa*-grass knots and *rudrākṣa* beads, it becomes multiplied infinitely. Twenty-five [beads] are for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*), and twenty-seven are for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
The thirty [day] is the attainment of wealth, and the fifteenth is for malevolent rites.
One should know that the thumb bestows liberation; the index finger destroys enemies;
the middle finger brings about the destruction of poverty; and this ring finger effects peace.
The little finger is to be protected; it is the jewel of the hand for recitation, O beautiful one. One should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers.
Since an action performed without the thumb is fruitless, listen:
among all sacrifices, the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is superior.
Those who engage in violence through the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*),
as well as those running after sacrifices of action (*karmayajña*), vows, and austerities—
all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is proclaimed as belonging solely to one who possesses great-souled wisdom.
Therefore, it is taught that the *upāṃśu* [recitation] is a hundredfold [more effective] than that, and the mental (*mānasa*) is a thousandfold;
[this is so] when [the recitation is performed] with words in high, low, and circumflex tones, with clear syllables and distinct words.
In the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), one should utter the mantra with speech; that is called *vācaka*.
One should utter the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly. One should know that which is barely audible within the range of one's own ears as *upāṃśu*; that is remembered as *japa*.
One should further contemplate the meaning of the words; that is called mental recitation (mānasa-japa).
Among the three types of recitation-sacrifices (*japayajña*), each subsequent one is superior to the preceding. (8th line) [The Rule for the Practice of Recitation:
He states the rule for the practitioner of recitation (*jāpaka*).
One should never recite while wearing a turban, or while wearing a bodice, or naked, or with loose hair, or covered by a shawl;
nor while the hands are unpurified, nor while impure, nor while talking idly.
Anger, lethargy, hunger, spitting, yawning, seeing a dog, and sleep must be avoided there; indeed, the twice-born should recite [the mantra] while avoiding these.
Even when these [obstacles] occur, one should look at the sun and so forth;
or, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should recite the remainder [of the mantra], or perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
The sun, fire, the moon, as well as the planets, lunar mansions, and stars—

These have been declared by the learned Brahmins to be the luminaries. One should not recite [the mantra] with feet outstretched, nor while in the cock-posture, nor without a seat, nor while lying down, nor on a road, nor in the presence of a Śūdra.
A practitioner of recitation should not recite on barren ground or in a hole;
seated properly, he should recite the mantra with his mind focused inwardly.
Now follows the sequence of meditation.

One should meditate on that which is called the descent of power (sādākhyam) of Amūrta, or the descent of power of Śiva, either between the eyebrows or at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). If one is unable to do so, one should meditate upon it in the locations such as Mālādhāra and the rest. For example:
(The Meditation on Vināyaka):
In the center of a four-petaled lotus at the *mūlādhāra*, one should meditate on Vināyaka,
who has the face of an elephant, is red in luster, possesses three eyes, and has a large belly.
I worship the son of Mahādeva, whose four arms are beautiful with the elephant-goad, the hook, and the *apūpa* cake,
and who is the embodiment of the root mantra.
(Meditation on Brahmā)
And in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, upon a six-petalled lotus, [one should meditate on] the all-pervading Lord Vāṇīpati.
Having the form of gold, four-faced, wearing white garments and a sacred thread,
with four beautiful arms holding a deer, a rosary, a water-pot, and a staff.
I eternally revere the Grandfather (Brahmā), who is endowed with eyes and lips.
(This is the meditation on Viṣṇu.
And in the lotus known as Maṇipūraka, which has ten petals... (line 7)
And [he saw] the Lord, whose lower lip was like Lakṣmī’s, possessing a dark-blue luster, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
marked with the Śrīvatsa, and resplendent in yellow garments.
I bow to the unwearied Viṣṇu, who wears a forest garland, a crown, and earrings;
who grants fearlessness to all the gods; who has lotus-like eyes; who is free from ailment;
and who resembles many suns.
(Rudradhyāna:
One should meditate upon Maheśvara in the center of a twelve-petaled lotus in the Anāhata [cakra].
Having the luster of milk, with a dark throat, three eyes, and the moon as his crest-jewel;
[he is] the abode of the Gaṅgā, four-armed, and endowed with a trident, fire, and the gesture of granting boons.
The god who holds the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā), whose bracelets are made of the lords of serpents,
who bears the white lotus and the deer-skin, and whose body is adorned with sacred ashes.
I bow to Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the creator of dissolution and emergence.
(Maheśvara-dhyāna:
One should meditate upon Maheśvara in the lotus of eight petals known as Viśuddha.
Richly adorned with the splendor of a conch, a jasmine flower, and the moon; clothed in a tiger skin;
with the moon, the Gaṅgā, and matted locks as his crest; known as Maheśa; possessed of great radiance;
having the sun, moon, and fire as his eyes; with a dark throat; and free from all ailment.
Resembling ten million fierce suns, he wore a serpent as his sacred sacrificial thread.
I bow to the god Maheśvara, who possesses left and right arms enriched with the beauty of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
who holds the supreme Śaṅkha and the deer, and who is embodied in his own form,
accompanied on the left by Māheśvarī.
(Contemplation on Sadāśiva):
In the command-center, within a two-petaled lotus, [one should meditate upon] the imperishable Supreme Self.
Resembling pure crystal, endowed with the thirty-two marks,
seated upon a bound lotus, possessing five-colored faces and captivating the mind;
having fifteen eyes and the crescent moon as his crest, he is the bringer of auspiciousness.
Possessing ten arms, with a variegated body, and clad in the skin of an antelope.
His left and right hands are joined in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*);
[he holds] a trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, an axe, and likewise a noose.
[He is] Nāśa, Vahni, Ghaṇṭā, Dhārin, and Śāntarūpin;
endowed with the five enclosures, devoted to the fivefold ritual acts,
the God supreme in the five syllables, whose great body consists of the five mantras.
Endowed with thirty-eight kalās, it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
I salute the god Sadāśiva, who is the primordial lord of the sciences (*vidyās*), endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*,
complete with all ornaments, the leader of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*),
and united with Manonmanī.
(Meditation on the Form of the Guru):
Above the six supports, at the crown of the head, in the thousand-petaled lotus.
The Lord Guru, the embodiment of compassion, resembling a hibiscus flower,
with two eyes and two arms, peaceful, and clad in red garments and smeared with red unguents.
Always holding a red lotus, radiant with a crown of rubies,
he is beyond the principles of reality (tattva), the supreme power, the manifest bestower of liberation.
I bow to the teacher of the true path, whose form is existence-consciousness-bliss.
|| The Ritual for Begging Alms ||

But one who is dispassionate (*virakta*), whether in the middle stage or as before, [performs] the worship of Śiva during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth; or he should wander for alms (*bhikṣā*). Alms are of four types, distinguished as those from a family (*sāntānikī*), those not asked for (*ayācitā*), the "madhūkarika" type, and the "kaṇa" type. Among these, the *sāntānikī* is for the teacher (*ācārya*), as it is stated in the *Sādākhyasaṃhitā*.
The lineage of Śiva beginning with the disciple and so forth is what has been declared;
whatever substance is offered to the Guru, that indeed is remembered as *sāntānikī* alms.

Alms ranging from food to the very ground are known to belong to one’s own continuum (*sāntānika*). However, for the ascetic, it is only that which has been gathered [by himself]. As it is said in that very same place:
"By hunters, actors, fishermen, cowherds, executioners, and so forth..."
One should abandon a gift that has been offered by those who have fallen from their caste or those who are accused of heinous crimes, even if it was solicited.

Let there be pure food obtained unasked, accompanied by due respect; for one who desires knowledge, let the practice of *mādhūkaravṛtti* alone be the rule. Herein is the sequence: following the midday worship, having first washed [the hands], sipped water (*ācamana*), and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), therein—at the beginning, the five metals—

Having washed with water from the heart-mantra a vessel made of *udumbara* or other sacrificial trees, or a vessel made of unprohibited materials such as *palāśa*, *madhūka*, *kadamba*, or *amṛtabhaka*.
Having consecrated it through gazing and other rites, and having placed there the non-terrible (*aghora*) heart-mantra which resembles a blazing fire, one should display the *dhenumudrā*.
Then, upon the concealing cloth, one should place the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) on a staff that is as thick as a thumb and reaches only to the forehead.

Having performed the ritual placement of the weapon-mantra (*astranyāsa*), having prostrated before Śiva and the Guru, and having received permission, he should take the alms-bowl in his right hand and the staff in his left hand and proceed toward the temple of Śiva. At the time of wandering for food, he should recite the mantra of Śiva mentally for the welfare of all living beings.

Not looking toward any other direction, with his gaze fixed upon the big toe of his foot, remaining silent, and avoiding spitting, touching, saluting, showing impatience, or stepping over those who are under accusation, outcasts, and [other] Brahmins— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)

Having gone to a pure courtyard in the house of a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya, or in the houses of virtuous Śūdras who have undergone the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of Śiva that elevate their caste, and standing there for the duration of milking a cow, [one should avoid] a pregnant woman, a sick woman, an impure woman, one wearing soiled clothes, a hired laborer, or a female slave.

When a noble woman has bathed after her menses, one should sprinkle with the *astra-mantra* the food brought by her— whether placed on a ladle, in her hand, or in a bronze vessel— and having received the alms, saying "To Śiva," one should depart for another house during the time it takes to milk a cow. At the moment of departure, [one should leave].

If he has entered within the courtyard, he should stand right there and receive alms; if he has gone outside, he should proceed silently to another house. Having wandered thus until he has obtained enough to fill his belly, he should return to his own hermitage. Thereafter, having placed the alms-bowl on clean ground, [he should wash] his feet.

Having washed [the hands] and sipped water, performed the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), sipped water again, and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should worship Śiva with the eightfold flower offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā). Then, setting aside a portion of the alms-food for the inner controller Śiva, one should set apart some for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa); the remaining food [is then purified] by means of inspection and other rites.

Having purified it, he should offer it to Śiva. If, while on the road, there occurs contact with common people or others, he should bathe, purify his alms-bowl by means of inspection and other rites, perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) and so forth as before, and offer it to Śiva. If the alms-food has been touched by *caṇḍālas* or similar outcasts, [it must be purified].
Having discarded [the leftovers], one should bathe. If one is in the presence of the guru, one should offer it in his presence and consume that which has been granted as a favor.
(The rule for eating;
here is the sequence. (6th line)

Having prepared a square mandala measuring one cubit with cow-dung water, and having drawn one, two, three, or four lines with white powder for the initiate, the spiritual son, the practitioner, and the preceptor, he should face the east; there,
having washed a vessel fashioned from leaves of a single species such as the *palāśa* that are not prohibited, and having applied the mantra, he should place it [there].

Having consecrated it with the gazing and other rites, and having empowered it seven times with the Aghora mantra, one should meditate upon Mṛtyuñjaya— food not offered to Śiva, free from impurities, and resembling the autumnal moon.

(... "JRAṂ SAḤ MṚTYUÑJAYĀYA VAUṢAṬ. Having consecrated [the vessel] seven times with water, having placed it in the vessel, and having purified it with [the rites of] *niṣeka* and so forth, having sprinkled it with the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, and having empowered it seven times with the *Mṛtyuñjaya* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [it is] surrounded by water with the *Kavaca* mantra. (Leaves 55 to 65 missing)
(The Ritual for the Installation of the Pavitra) (66a, 1st line):
Having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, as before... having accomplished [the rite], one should divide it as previously described.

Then, having offered the *caru* oblation to Sūrya, and having gratified his door-keeper Gaṇapati and the gurus with the *pavitra*, one should recite the mantra beginning with "O Soul of Time" (*kālātman*) while specifying the name of Sūrya; having offered the *pavitras* with the Sūrya-mantra,

and having likewise offered the *pavitra* to the eight planets beginning with Soma who constitute his limbs, one should perform *japa*, offer the oblation, and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa; having offered the pavitra to Śānti and the others,

having recited the mantra, having presented the offering, and having sipped water (ācamana), having performed the sakalīkaraṇa, having offered the pavitra to Nandi and the others, [and] to Vāstoṣpati and Mahālakṣmī—

Having offered the *pavitra* to the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*), and having placed it upon the *kumbha* and *vardhanī*, and upon Gaṇapati and the Gurus; having presented the *caru* oblation and recited "Obeisance to you, O Soul of Time" (*namaḥ kālātmane*) and so forth; and having thus placed the *pavitras* upon the Blessed One residing in the mandala, one should worship Śiva and [place] the limbs of the vow-practice (*vratacaryā*) and other components in their respective places.

(5th line) Having offered the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) increased on that day, and having worshipped as usual the two door-keepers, Gaṇapati, the two Gurus, and the seat of Śiva with the purifying thread (*pavitra*), [one worships] the God.

Having meditated upon Śiva, who is of the nature of Time (*kālātmaka*), who is adorned by the splendor of his own primordial mandala, and who is intent on bestowing boons, one should remember him as having a body whose dimensions consist of years, solstices, months, fortnights, days, watches (*yāma*), and ghaṭikās;
who is the sole cause of the functioning of all the senses, the body, and their objects; and who has cast off all that was done or left undone.

Taking up purifying substances and fumigating them slightly, one should address the Lord— who is the sole witness of the final rite (*iṣṭakarma*), the protector of the field, the sovereign, the refuge, and the pure-minded— while facing him: "O God,
that which has been seen by you, whose nature is Time, within my ritual..."
It was performed, afflicted, abandoned, delighted, offered, protected, and excised.
Thereafter, by your will, all that was done— whether afflicted or unafflicted, performed or not performed— was rendered pure by the sage Śambhu through his entire being.
"Fill! Fill!"—

having uttered "Svāhā to the Lord of the Observances of Sacrificial Vows," and having uttered "Hāṃ Hauṃ, Svāhā to Śiva, the Lord of the Ātmatattva, up to Māyā"— [in the Ātmatattva] which extends to the end of Prakṛti and is protected by Brahmā as its cause.

In the *vidyā-tattva*, which extends up to the end of the *śuddhavidyā-tattva* and is protected by Viṣṇu as its cause, one should utter "HĀṂ HAUṂ, to Śiva, the lord of the *vidyā-tattva*, svāhā," ending with Īśvara; then, in the *śiva-tattva*, which extends up to the end of Śiva and is protected by Rudra as its cause—

Having uttered "Hāṃ Hauṃ, to Śiva, the Lord of the Śiva-tattva, Svāhā," ending with the word "Śiva," one who desires liberation should place the *pavitra* upon the top of the *liṅga* together with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), following the sequence; however, one who desires worldly enjoyment should offer it after uttering "the Śiva-tattva" and so forth. After that, [one offers] to the All-tattva protected by all causes, saying: "Hāṃ Hauṃ, to Śiva, the Lord of all tattvas, Svāhā."

Having recited [the mantra] up to the point of dissolution (*layānta*), having offered the descent of the Gaṅgā which consists of all the principles (*sarvatattvātmaka*), and having offered the purifiers (*pavitrāṇi*) to the limbs of Brahmā,
one should recite the root mantra up to the point of dissolution and offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva.
Having rendered [the deity] supreme through the Mahāmudrā and joining the palms in a gesture of offering flowers, one should address him with devotion:
“You are the refuge of all beings, abiding within all that is stable and moving;
you are the Supreme Lord, the witness of all beings who move within.”
In deed, thought, or word, there is no other refuge for me but you;
whatever has been performed by me that was deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in materials—[may it all be perfected through your grace].

O Maheśvara, fulfill that which has been left unaccomplished by me daily for you—devoid of recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, and lacking the proper words. You are my son, O Lord of the Gods; [grant this] which is purifying and destructive of sin.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, has been purified by you.
"O Lord, my vow has been broken due to the occurrence of an imperfection.

May all that [merit] become unified for all living beings who are strung together by the thread of Your command. Having thus made this request, he offered incense, lamps, the *ārātrika* lamp, sacred ash, a mirror, an umbrella, and chowries.

Having visualized [the deity] as satisfied, being measured by the three earths beginning with Nandi, and having performed the rites of *amṛtīkaraṇa* and *paramīkaraṇa*, one should recite [the mantra], offer it, and after reciting a tenth part for the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (*aṅga*), one should present it.
The Preceptor should then apply the *pavitra* to all the deities; the practitioner likewise [should apply it] to the mantra to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

One should give [the offering]. Having praised the Deity with hymns, bowed down, and asked for forgiveness, one should come near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), offer the purifiers (*pavitra*) to the Blessed One residing in the fire, and perform more than a hundred oblations for the sake of filling any deficiencies, completing the rite, and ensuring its stability. (9th line)

Then, having offered the *caru* oblation for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, having presented the food offering (*naivedya*), water for rinsing the mouth, betel leaf, and so forth, having applied sacred ash and sandalwood paste, and having confined Śiva, one should present the purifying thread (*pavitra*) to Agni and confine him.

Having offered oblations into the fire, performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, and offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation; having given the *bali* offering along with the *pavitra* to those [deities] situated upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass (*viṣṭara*); and having likewise given the external *bali* along with the *pavitra* while restraining [the breath]; and having performed the ritual unification (*sakaḷīkaraṇa*) preceded by the salutation of the ears;
and having given the perfected *pavitra* to the Guru and to the books; and having restrained the fire—
Having worshipped and completed [the rite] for the one situated in the maṇḍala... having fully worshipped the one situated in the liṅga and the one situated in the water-pot,
and having restrained the world-protectors (lokapālas) for the protection of the sacrifice,
and having honored those initiated according to their capacity with food, clothing, and so forth.

Having satisfied the poor, the blind, the wretched, the helpless, children, the elderly, the emaciated, the afflicted, and others, he should say: "By this [act], may Sadāśiva be pleased with me. Then, he should eat together with his disciples.

On the following day, having bathed and performed the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*), one should fetch all the purifying substances from Śiva, place them in a pure vessel as on the previous day, worship the Lord with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*),

complete the two daily rituals (*nityāhnika*), and perform the occasional twilight rite (*naimittikī saṃdhyā*) starting from the east and ending in the northeast, followed by the worship of the Sun and others, concluding with the worship of Śiva.
Having performed the libation with mantras into the fire for the purpose of completion (*nirvartya*), having prepared the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and offered it,

one should offer the sacred threads (*pavitra*) to Sūrya and the other deities as before; then, after first offering the ritual substances to Śiva, one should likewise offer the sacred threads to him as previously done.

Having completed the ritual actions up to the end of the *japa*, having offered libations even to that which resides in the fire, and having presented the *caru* oblation, one should perform a hundred recitations with the root mantra, the *astra* mantra, or the *aghora* mantra for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, if one desires worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*), one should say: "O Blessed One, may there be for me the attainment of the fruit."

One should dedicate one's conduct to Śiva. However, one who desires liberation, having offered this action with the thought, "O Lord, may this action not be a cause of bondage for me," and having given the food offering, water for sipping, sandalwood paste, and betel leaf to the Fire residing [within], and having performed the salutation of the ashes, should enter the fire and offer the eight flowers.
By means of the yoga of the channels (*nāḍīyoga*), having joined you— who reside in the fire and abide in the maṇḍala— into the Root Śiva, one should withdraw the mantras of the fire,

lead them to the *dvādaśānta*, and after they have emerged, place them within one’s own heart and then dismiss even that [deity]. Alternatively, at the conclusion of the worship of Caṇḍa, having worshipped him as well and offered oblations according to one's capacity, one should dismiss him.

Having removed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass (*viṣṭara*), and having offered the oblation (*bali*), one should perform the ritual integration (*sakaḷīkaraṇa*) preceded by hymns of praise and salutations. Then, having joined even that which resides in the mandala into the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*),
and having withdrawn the mantras of the water-jar (*kumbha*), the weapon (*astra*), and the *vardhinī* vessel, one should join them into the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśvara*).

One should dismiss [the deities] with the words "forgive me" while maintaining a sense of dependence [on them]. Having worshipped others with the *aṣṭapuṣpikā* offering and dismissed them— either with or without a sense of dependence according to the specific ritual context— one should worship the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*) as usual with the *Śivagāyatrī*, and [offer] the purifying substances (*pavitrāṇi*) for the sake of Caṇḍa.
Having protected the deity, having bathed him again, worshipped him, and dismissed the Sun as is appropriate,
he should then dismiss the guardians of the directions, the door-keepers, and others in reverse order; then, having taken the pure pavitra-strands from the deity according to the rule.

In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, a mobile liṅga, a metal liṅga, a jewel liṅga, a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga, and in all images, Caṇḍa shall be the authorized official. [In a mobile liṅga, a metal liṅga, a Bāṇaliṅga, and a self-manifested one...]

"And a fierce attendant (caṇḍa) is not appointed there specifically because it is a *ratnaliṅga*, according to the statements in the *Somaśambhupaddhati* and other texts. (4th line) In the case of liṅgas other than this, the householder should offer what has been presented to Caṇḍa. Having worshipped Caṇḍa upon a mandala or a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and having placed the purificatory threads (*pavitra*), the remainder is as before. (5th line)
Having offered the floral remains (*nirmālya*) and the sacred threads (*pavitra*), one should address him thus:
"Whatever annual rite has been performed by me, whether deficient or excessive, may it become complete through your command, O Caṇḍanātha. Thus.

Thereafter, having praised and bowed, and having propitiated Caṇḍāgni, one should offer a hundred oblations, dismiss [the deity], cast the *nirmālya* into a half-well or similar place, place the *pavitra* offerings into the fire,
and dismiss [the deity] into the fire. Then, [one should smear] the ground with cow dung.

Having purified himself, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite, he should bathe and worship the deity again. Immediately during the consecration (*adhivāsa*), following the previously mentioned sequence for the Sun and other deities worshipped in the pavilion, after offering the fragrant *pavitra*, he should offer a pure *pavitra*; likewise, he should offer a fragrant *pavitra* to the deity as well.

Afterwards, having offered eight flowers and placed the pure pavitras upon them, and having also placed the fragrant pavitras and the pure pavitras into the fire, one should perform the remainder as before and dismiss [the deity] with the mantra "yām" as previously stated. Then, one should have [the disciple] consume the pure five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
The Guru is to be worshipped like Śiva with garments, wealth, and ornaments;
when the Lord Guru is satisfied, Śaṅkara himself becomes satisfied.
And all his ritual activities and so forth for the year shall bear fruit, he whose Guru is completely satisfied;
thus spoke the Supreme Lord.

Even if situated five yojanas away, a pure disciple should perform [the rite] in the presence of the Guru. Beyond that distance, if he is unable to go, he should perform it together with the elders of his own lineage. In their absence, he should perform it himself. If he is unable to perform the purification (*pavitrakaraṇa*), he should consume the *śivakūrca* and observe a diet of milk.
One should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times while remaining in the prescribed posture. Thus ends the procedure for the Pavitrārohaṇa rite.
The Cāturmāsya Vow (The Four-Monthly Observance)

Now, a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) should perform the Cāturmāsya vow. It is as follows: beginning from the pure twelfth day of the month of Mithuna and ending with the pure twelfth day of Tulā is the period of Viṣṇu’s sleep. If there are two new moon days in the month of Mithuna, it is due to the distinction of an intercalary month, resulting in a double Āṣāḍha.
It occurs as follows: then, beginning from the pure twelfth day of Cancer and ending with the pure twelfth day of Scorpio, that is the period of sleep (*svāpakāla*).
This is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
The sleep of Viṣṇu occurs during the month of Mithuna on the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight;
when the sun is situated in Mithuna, it touches upon two new moon days.
That [period] should be known as Dvirāṣāḍha; Karkaṭa is the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, during the time of Viṣṇu’s sleep, the ascetic must certainly perform the Cāturmāsya vow, which is of the nature of Śiva:
"The Cāturmāsya and the vow of the nature of Śiva must be performed with diligence."
Or else, it should be performed according to one's own capacity by both householders and those committed to the ascetic life.

For one who subsists on physical food, the rule consists of eating only once a day and avoiding alkaline substances, salt, and the like. Having first occupied a favorable location, one should procure earth, ashes, tooth-sticks, and other necessary items.
As it is said in the Pauṣkara:
Having resolved upon the desired place for the four months, one should dwell there and, according to the rules, take possession of clay, ashes, and so forth. (As stated in the *Suprabheda*)
One should collect earth, ashes, wood from tooth-sticks, and the *bhūta-sūtra* and so forth.
Thus, first, is the procedure for collecting ashes:
either the dung of a tawny cow, or the dung of a cow possessing the characteristics previously described, or the dung of a white bull, during either the spring or the summer.
Leaving aside the portions to be discarded from the front and back, one should take the hard central portion released upon the ground with the *sadyojāta* mantra onto a lotus leaf;
having placed it on a ground smeared with cow dung and purified it, one should fashion the *piṇḍas* with the *vāmadeva* mantra and [offer them] with the *aghora* mantra.
Having dried it in the Śiva-fire, having placed it with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra, having covered it with heaps of chaff and burned it,
having collected [the ashes] with the *īśāna* mantra and cast them into black earth, one should purify them with a clean cloth that has been consecrated.

Having poured [the substances] with a new pitcher... one should perfume it with kṛṣṇagandha, camphor, uśīra, hrībera, ketaka, campaka, damanaka, and so forth. Alternatively, having collected wild cow-dung and stones, ground them, sprinkled them with fresh *sadyojāta* cow's urine, and performed the remainder as before. [The fire for] the festival-Śiva...

Or, having taken either dust from a windless place or ashes from a fire that has gone out, one should cause [the disciple] to dwell [there] as previously described. Then, for the sake of purification, one should procure earth for bathing accompanied by mantras—possessing the characteristics mentioned before—and tooth-sticks, all accompanied by mantras. (4th line)
Then,
a girdle consisting of three parts, joined with fifty threads and hanging down by one-third [of its length],
should be made eight finger-breadths wide, or according to the measurement of one's own hips.
It should be made one finger-breadth wider than the measurement of one's own hips;
it should be avoided from afar if it is too thick, too thin, cut, having many joints, covered with growths, dirty, or abounding in other defects.
It produces impure sin and, when consumed, brings about fear of the king.

A thick [cloth] causes disease; a mixed one is of middling quality; a thin one causes the depletion of wealth. One that has been torn at the edge results in death, while one that has been mended brings about abdominal tumors.
"From this [material], one should obtain that which is free from knots, hair, and other defects, being stainless and firm"— according to this statement,

one should prepare a waist-string (*kaṭisūtra*) devoid of such flaws. Then, the loincloth (*kaupīna*) should be one cubit or two cubits in length, with a border (*saṃhisita*) of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

One should procure an uncut saffron-colored loincloth (*kāṣāya-kaupīna*) made of cotton or similar material, fashioned independently, measuring ten or eight finger-breadths in length and width according to the proportions of one's own body; one should also procure a waist-band (*kaṭiveṣṭana*).
This has been stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"The support for the loincloth (*kaupīna*) may be one cubit or even two cubits;
its width should be twelve finger-breadths, or ten, or eight."
The loincloth (*kaupīna*) is thus described as being made from materials such as *kārpāsa* (cotton) and the like.
Having thus prepared these items for the disciple and others,

on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha— or, if there is a partial lunar day (*khaṇḍatithi*), on that which is pervaded by the sunrise— the master [should act] with the disciples and others.

"We shall perform service with the foot soldiers we have assembled according to our ability; staying right here, the Cāturmāsya vow must be observed. Having been thus requested, [the preceptor] consented, saying, "We shall do exactly so, provided there is no obstacle.
Then, having shaved his head, bathed according to the rules, sipped water (ācamana), and performed the daily worship and other rites, he—

In the presence of the Guru, or in the presence of the elders (jyeṣṭha), or in the presence of Śiva, according to the requirements of place and time, [the practice should be performed] for four months, three months, two months, one month, one fortnight, seven days, five days, three days, or a single day, under the guidance of the Guru.

Or, having fixed a specific time, and having obtained permission after resolving upon one [of the fruits] from among milk, fruit, or *mādhūka* according to the rule, he should perform the worship of Vrateśvara. This has been stated in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*:
For four, three, two, or one night;
for half a month, or even for seven days, five nights, three days, or a single day;
having undertaken the observance as instructed by the Guru.
Then, with milk, or even with fruit, or else with alms-food, the self-restrained one [should subsist].
One should spend the months of the rainy season eating only once a day according to the rule;
and during the four months of the summer, O bird, one should spend them according to the rule eating only at night.
The observance (niyama) must also be performed as a constituent part of the ritual action; otherwise, a fault would arise.

And during the period following the month of Moha-guru, O Lord, having been commanded with "By my order, you shall perform the Cāturmāsya vow and the religious observances according to your ability," one should carry that out. Thus it is said.
Herein is the sequence for the worship of Vrateśvara:

having performed the midday bath and other preliminary rites, one enters a pavilion adorned with cloths and garlands of flowers— either in a temple of Śiva or elsewhere— and [worships] Śiva within the solar disc situated between Indra and Agni.

Having worshipped [the deity], washed his feet, sipped water (ācamana), and bathed with holy ashes, he should sit upon a seat such as a black antelope skin on the right side of a square altar measuring two cubits and eight finger-breadths high in the middle of the pavilion; then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma).

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the five Brahmans, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*), and having established the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), the special water offering (*viśeṣārghya*), the obstructing water offering (*nirodhārghya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) as before, one should perform the purification of substances and oneself, and then invoke Vighneśvara in the north-western corner of the site.

Having worshipped the Lord and requested, "O Master, I shall perform the Cāturmāsya vow; please grant that it be free from obstacles," and having worshipped his own guru as Śiva with the Śiva-mantra while regarding him as Śiva himself according to the Īśāna [face], he says: "O Master, I shall perform the Cāturmāsya vow and the worship of Vrateśvara according to the path taught by you. Grant me permission. Having thus requested and received permission, [he proceeds].
To the west of that, having worshipped with scents, flowers, and so forth the Sage who is the primordial Guru of those respective lineages, using [his name] in the dative case, [one should recite]:
"The four stages of life have been proclaimed, characterized by the primary conduct."
And for those four, there are likewise four sages who are their preservers.

According to the statement, "Dadhīci, Gautama, Agastya, and Durvāsas in due order," one should thereafter face the Lord [Śiva] and worship the preceptor of the renunciant stage (saṃnyāsāśrama), the sage Durvāsas, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having worshipped [it], one should construct a square maṇḍala to its south by laying out lines; then, by further laying out lines,
one should divide that [square] into ten parts on all sides and fashion in the center a white lotus with two petals, a yellow pericarp, and filaments.

Having established the moon-segment and made it red-hued, one should fashion four lotuses— yellow, red, black, and white— with two petals each in the east, south, west, and north-west, including their filaments and pericarp; then,
having made the path-gate yellow-gold by its own portion, [one should place] four sets of two squares each as the images of the Lokanāthas.
Having made the doors provided with necks and side-panels, one should make the four corners variegated. Then,
[one should place] the lotus situated in the maṇḍala of Vrateśvara, and upon those lotuses, the five Brahmās of the Vrateśvaras, beginning with Īśāna.

Having offered the seat and other honors with their respective mantras and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the forms beginning with Īśāna, one should [visualize] those [deities] situated in the center of the lotus,
two-armed, single-faced, three-eyed, with the moon as their crest-jewel, and sequentially colored saffron, black, reddish-brown, and white.

Having meditated upon the Lords of Vows (Vrateśvaras), who hold a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*), a trident (*triśūla*), the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a sword (*khaḍga*), a shield (*kheṭaka*), an iron arrow (*nārāca*), a bow (*kārmuka*), a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and a citron (*bījapūra*),
and having worshipped them with the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, and having offered incense and a lamp— in the west,
one should take earth with the *Sadyojāta* mantra ending in *namaḥ*, or with the Heart-mantra; in the north, one should take *āmalaka* fruit with the *Vāmadeva* mantra or with the Head-mantra.

On the south, with the Aghora mantra and the Śikhā-mantra, [he should place] the rosary, the loincloth, the waist-thread, the lower garment, and the alms-bowl; on the east, with the Tatpuruṣa mantra and the Kavaca-mantra, the tooth-sticks; and in the northeast, with the Īśāna mantra or the Mūla-mantra, having set down the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having again worshipped the lords of the *punarvrata* with the *aṣṭapuṣpikā* offering,

having presented various kinds of food brought by the disciples— namely, solid foods (*bhakṣya*), soft foods (*bhojya*), foods to be licked (*lehya*), foods to be sucked (*coṣya*), and drinks (*pānīya*)— and having given hand-cleansers, mouth-perfumes, betel, and so forth, he should offer incense, lamps, and the waving of lights (*ārātrika*).
Having recited the *vṛtti-mantra* one hundred and eight times, having offered [the oblation], having performed three circumambulations, and having prostrated with the eight limbs twelve times,
one should thereafter [consume] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) as previously described.
Having consumed [the sacrificial food], washed his feet, sipped water, and bathed with ashes,

he should sit facing north in the presence of Vrateśvara as before and perform, according to his capacity, sixteen *prāṇāyāmas* up to two hundred and forty *prāṇāyāmas*, preceded by the syllable *AṂ*. Then—
Having meditated upon the form of Aghora within the heart-lotus and having recited the Aghora mantra one thousand and eight times,
one should engage in such activities as listening to the Siddhānta scriptures. Then, in the evening, having performed the ritual bath and other duties—
(fourth line)
Having fasted during the night in the presence of Vrateśvara, one should perform the vigil (*jāgara*). Then, having risen in the morning and completed the preliminary rites and so forth as before,
[one should worship] Śiva situated within the solar disc, just as on the previous day.

Having worshipped Vighneśvara, the Guru, the lineage-gurus (santānādiguru), the gurus of the [four] stages of life (āśramaguru), and the Lords of Vows (vrateśvara), and having performed hymns of praise, circumambulation, breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and so forth, one should dismiss them preceded by the offering of water for the face (parāṅmukhārghya).
Then, one should wear the loincloth, waist-thread, waist-band, and other items that were offered to the Guru. Thereafter—

Having remained in that very place until the completion of the vow by means of a restriction on food such as milk and so forth, one should, at the conclusion of the vow, worship the Lords of Vows (Vrateśvaras), the sage Durvāsas, and the Guru as before; then, on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), one may go wherever one desires. This [is the procedure].

All this is to be done in the absence of the guru; however, when the guru is present, one should perform the worship as previously described, honoring him as the guru. At the conclusion of the worship, having arranged a lion-throne in the northeast within a flower-pavilion possessing the characteristics to be described, one should worship one's own guru there—facing south—as Śiva himself, using the Śiva-mantra and offerings such as a seat.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, and having performed three circumambulations, one should prostrate with the eight limbs twelve times;
then, placing the two lotus-feet of the Guru upon one’s head, one should satisfy him with hymns of praise. The Guru [then performs] the five [limbs]... (70b, 1st line)

If he is situated in the midst of people, he should go to that very place, worship him alone, and remaining right there in the manner prescribed by him, perform the Cāturmāsya vow. If he is even further away than that, he should perform the Cāturmāsya vow together with the eldest member of his own lineage, having placed him at the forefront; [he should do so] in his own hermitage.

If an elder brother from another lineage is present, one should salute him and, having received his permission, perform the Cāturmāsya vow. [Thus ends the section on those beyond the stages of life (ativarṇāśrama) in the *Kriyādīpikā*,
composed by Śivāgrayogin, the protector of the Śaiva tradition.]
The third chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for the Pavitrāropaṇa and the Cāturmāsya Vow.
[Now begins] the Sequence of Initiations (Dīkṣākrama).

Now we shall explain the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*). For only one who is endowed with the initiations of the rules (*samaya*) and so forth has the authority (*adhikāra*) over the sections on conduct (*caryā*), ritual action (*kriyā*), yoga (*yoga*), and knowledge (*jñāna*). A devotee of Śiva, having approached a true Guru and received initiation, proceeds according to his authority in the practices of conduct and the rest.
Without initiation, there can be no liberation for living beings here through spiritual practices;
and there is no practice without a teacher; therefore, one should take refuge in a guide.
First, he states the characteristics of a true guru. In the *Suprabheda*:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are born of pure lineage—these indeed should be known as teachers (*ācāryas*), and never others."
And in the *Dviśatikālottara*:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are pure are the practitioners (*sādhaka*s);
O Six-faced One, the teachers (*ācārya*s), however, follow the sequence according to their own respective castes."
One who is proficient in the *kriyāpāda*, follows the *caryāpāda*,
has practiced the *yogapāda*, and is devoted to the *jñānapāda*—
the wise should accept those who are endowed with these qualities.
In the Vāyavīya [Tantra],
those who are fully conversant with the Śiva-śāstra and averse to the Paśu-śāstras—
namely the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas— are proclaimed as Ācāryas.
In the *Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*, the etymological definition of the title "Ācārya" is as follows:
Because he is fit for the perfect practice of knowledge (*jñāna*), yoga (*yoga*), and ritual action (*kriyā*), he is indeed called an *ācārya* for the benefit of all living beings. (10th line)
Two types of teachers are declared: the first is dispassionate (virakta), while the second is materialistic (bhautika); however, there are specific distinctions regarding the first.
