One who is a lifelong celibate student (*ājanmabrahmacārī*) and, immediately thereafter, an ascetic (*yati*); thus, these two constitute the first [stage], while the second stage consists of the householder (*gṛhastha*) and the forest-dweller (*vanastha*). In these two [subsequent] actions, there are likewise two [stages].
In the Sūtasamhitā:
"The wise man should know that the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, the mendicant,
and the one who has transcended the stages of life (ativarṇāśramī) are superior in successive order."
The one who has transcended the castes and stages of life is declared to be the Guru for all who possess authority;
no one shall be his disciple, just as I, Puruṣottama, am not.
One who has transcended the castes and stages of life is said to be the manifest teacher of teachers;
there is no doubt that in this world there is none equal to him, nor indeed any superior.
That man who, having passed beyond his own stages and castes, abides in the Self alone.
Thus he is declared to be one who transcends the castes and stages of life by those who perceive the meaning of all the Vedas.
The most excellent of gurus is one who has studied a hundred thousand verses and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
or else, through his instruction, the guru becomes one who is devoted to the Saṃhitā.
O observer of noble vows, listen to the characteristics of these teachers within the inconceivable tradition known as Viśvasādākhya:
they are non-violent, speakers of truth, and devoted to compassion for all living beings.
He is patient and tranquil in mind, capable of both restraint and favor;
he is endowed with right conduct, skillful, and devoted to recitation and meditation.
One who is joined with the initiation of consciousness (*vijñāna-dīkṣā*), proficient in devotion to the Guru,
and a knower of the internal scripture consisting of the four pillars of knowledge, yoga, ritual action,
and conduct; one who is free from deceitful behavior and has abandoned trivial activities.
He is discerning regarding the virtues and faults of his disciples and has conquered his senses.
Completely free from attachment and aversion, endowed with compassion,
and the upholder and protector of the foundation of all commitments.

Endowed with the experience of Śiva, his doubts were dispelled; free from diseases such as consumption and leprosy, he was exceedingly beautiful. Free from possessiveness, free from ego, devoid of cruelty, and free from conceptual construction.
Free from darkness, he is a knower of the scriptures and a contemplator of the ultimate truth.
One endowed with such characteristics is called an excellent preceptor (*ācāryavara*);
even one who is material (*bhautika*) is so designated specifically when he is accompanied by a lawful wife.
One possessed of the previously mentioned characteristics is called a material preceptor (*bhautikācārya*).
One should become initiated into the renunciant stage of life (sannyāsāśrama), which is the most supreme of all.
In the Devīkālottara (line 10): "Even if he is devoid of all [physical] characteristics, a guru who possesses knowledge is desired. In the Svacchandabhairava: [text missing].
A wise man should choose that very Guru by whose mere glance even supreme bliss (*parānanda*) arises; he should not choose another.
(Ajite)
He whose guru is remembered as the accomplisher of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—
just as darkness vanishes in the presence of the sun.
By the mere glance of the Guru, one is liberated from all sins;
whoever he touches with his hand or whoever he beholds with his eye [is likewise purified].
All that becomes auspicious solely through the grace of Śiva;
he is not smeared by impurity, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Therefore, the Guru is declared by Śiva to be the power of the Guru, Manonmanī;
he has even performed initiation for sinners a hundred thousand times.
If the knowledge of Śiva has arisen in one's heart, one should resort to him for the sake of that knowledge;
for having obtained a teacher devoid of knowledge, how can the [divine] form be attained?
Just as a stone resting upon another stone does not reach the other shore,
therefore one should, with every effort, take refuge in one who has reached the further shore of knowledge.
(From the *Sūtasamhitā*)
The teacher who lacks the continuity of knowledge and is devoid of wisdom goes to a terrible hell; of this there is no cause for doubt.
He who, being devoid of the knowledge of the lineage of the Vidyā, should act as a teacher,
will not remove even a minor ailment by merely consuming the air.
He who, being devoid of the knowledge of the lineage of the Vidyā, should act as a teacher...
He obtains oil even from sesame seeds that are not [properly prepared], and likewise from sand.
One who lacks realization of the perfected state,
who is devoid of knowledge of the scriptures, and who is bereft of the [proper] castes and stages of life;
for whom the three types of seeking arise through the eightfold transformations beginning with desire.
One who is immoral, ill-disposed, of wicked conduct, possessed of evil qualities, or unworthy of receiving gifts;

one who lacks authority over mantras and tantras and is devoid of the knowledge of yoga— such a person, contrary to the stated characteristics, shall not perform the rites beginning with the *samaya* and ending with the fifth initiation (*pañcadīkṣā*).
Under the guise of worship and ornaments, with dances characterized by the hunger for wealth.
Especially when one honors a teacher merely for the sake of alleviating the affliction of hunger,
initiation under such a teacher leads disciples indeed to hell.
For the path is never seen at all by one who is blind.
Therefore, having approached a virtuous teacher, one should attend upon him according to the prescribed characteristics.
Then, the teacher, endowed with the characteristics previously described,

having examined for a period of at least one year his own dependent disciples— who possess the characteristics to be described hereafter— should initiate them according to their respective capacities.
The Characteristics of a Disciple
In the Raurava [Tantra],
it is said: "If a Guru should perform initiation for those who do not know reality and are devoid of devotion,
they go to a non-Śiva state, and the Guru shall become one who goes to the Nīraya hell."
In the Sūtasaṃhitā:
"By instructing foolish disciples, by pride in one's learning, or by betraying the guru, even an omniscient person falls into a blind well. (2nd line)
Therefore, a disciple should be tested for one year;
moreover, a teacher should test his dependent disciples for one year, except in other cases.
Those who employ the best men for low tasks and the base for noble deeds,
and who do not fall into despondency even when dragged or beaten—
they are the fit, steadfast heroes for the rite of auspicious consecration.

Born among the four castes, he was a proponent of the knowledge of the scriptures; through the cessation of attachment and ignorance, he was always wise and possessed of moral conduct. He was a pursuer of the goals of human life, a diligent agent, and always possessed of a discerning intellect.
And he was skillful in service, exerting himself diligently in the tasks of his preceptor.

Constantly devoted to service for his guru and fearful of transgressing his commands—one who is endowed with these characteristics is [fit]; and this is also the characteristic of those possessing self-restraint (*saṃyama*). (From the *Parākhyatantra*)

However, for those Rudras who abstain from intoxicants, who are devoted to purity, proper conduct, and ritual observances, and who are devotees of Śiva—for them the initiation should be performed; otherwise, it certainly should not.
Listen now to the superior quality common to all disciples.
Devotion, trust, non-malice, and steadfastness in obeying the teacher's command.
Faith, tranquility, forgiveness, truthfulness, as well as purity, austerity, sacred learning, and gratitude— whichever disciple possesses this twelvefold set,
he is the foremost among disciples; others are not considered foremost by comparison with him.

All this, characterized as described above, pertains to the domain of the special initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*), according to the statement: "One should examine [the candidate] by means of the rule (*samaya*). (8th line) He should initiate even a Śūdra who is free from defects such as the great sins (*mahāpātaka*).
(The Descent of Power, *śaktinipāta*)

Since only one who is joined with the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*) has the qualification for initiation into *nirvāṇa*, [the teacher], having examined the very mild, milder, and very intense descents of power in his disciples, should initiate them and then unite them with the higher or lower liberations according to those [powers]. What is called the "descent of power" is the falling away of the power of the *āṇava* impurity.

And when the power of the Lord is manifested within the self, to the extent that the power of the Lord is manifested, to that same extent there is the cessation of the power of the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of individuality).
This has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
O Śiva, when the dominion of the power of darkness ceases and that [power] falls away, You manifest the bliss of misdeeds within the ocean of worldly bondage.
And in the *Parākhyatantra* it is said:
"In a small [receptacle], the small is manifested; the great resides within the great.
Whatever [the receptacle] may be like, such [is the manifestation], just as a lamp [appears differently] in darkness."
And in the *Svāyambhuva*,
it is said that by the will of Śiva, Parānandā bestows the meaning of Śaivism;
she is the primordial Śakti who descends upon a person in his final birth.
From that union, his impurity—the cause of saṃsāra—is discharged.
When that is exhausted, he becomes fit for supreme liberation. Having approached a teacher, his bonds are severed by initiation.
He proceeds, free from all affliction, to the stainless state of union with Śiva.
By this sequential yoga, having attained supreme isolation (*kevalatā*),
one reaches no further state of existence (*bhava*) because of being devoid of beginningless impurity.
As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
As long as she possesses the power of unfolding, united with passion for Śiva,
she falls [upon him] most intensely radiant, ever characterized by grace.
And from that conjunction, even for such an ignorant person who possesses desire,
there arises an understanding that functions through the discernment of the Self.
In one who possesses discernment and is dispassionate, the desire to know arises;
and that consciousness endowed with the desire to know [rescues] the bound soul from the ocean of saṃsāra.
The Lord, desiring to consume [the world], yokes him; once yoked, the Sovereign impels him.
In this impelling, the illustrious King of Mantras is the impeller of both.
Because the discipline of the one to be favored and likewise the compassion of the one who favors are both required, their conjunction is very difficult to obtain. Thus,
when the power of the Lord is manifested only slightly within the self, due to the extremely feeble descent of that power, at that time, of the self—

The power by which the Lord effects the cessation of saṃsāra is indeed the power called *nivṛtti*. That very [power] is the locus of the Lord in cessation (*nivṛttīśvara*). And its Lord is the Lord of Cessation (*nivṛttīśa*), in whom the descent of power is even milder than in the former due to a greater manifestation; for the suffix *-tarap* expresses a comparative degree of deficiency or excess. In this case, however, it denotes the excess.

Thus, for one who has not yet turned back, that power of establishment (*pratiṣṭhā-śakti*) establishes [the self] again with intensity according to its capacity. That very power of establishment is the station of the Lord of Establishment (*pratiṣṭheśvara*). He is the Lord of Establishment in relation to that. Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of even greater [power] than that—

The descent of intense power (*tīvraśaktinipāta*). At that time, having liberated the animal-like cognition regarding the sphere of objects according to one's capacity, it manifests the knowledge of Śiva (*śivajñāna*). That power is *vidyā*, and she herself is the station of the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*); her lord is the Lord of Knowledge. (73a, 1st line) Therefore, the intensity in the full manifestation of the knowledge of Śiva is the descent of power.

At that time, the power by which one releases all bonds, such as the three-fold suffering, and bestows supreme peace—that power is *Śānti*. That very [power] is the abode of Śāntīśvara, and its Lord is Śāntīśa.
As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
That by which he causes beings to turn back is his "causing-to-turn-back" [power];
that state is called "cessation," and the Lord there is also possessed of cessation.
That which is the movement again of one who has ceased, characterized by falling away, is his [power of] "falling."
That which is deposited is the foundation; that is the locus, and its possessor is the master thereof.
By means of that [foundation], He bestows knowledge upon the individual soul regarding the object that is to be reached by the self once it has abandoned [all else].
She is his field of knowledge, and Hara is the Lord of Knowledge and its master;
by her, Hara effects the pacification of all his sufferings.
"By performing that seven-step [rite] for peace, he too becomes possessed of peace. Thus,
in the *Mṛgendra*, he describes the signs of one who has been struck by the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*).
For those embodied beings whose power falls away so as not to return, that is their sign: longing for liberation and aversion toward worldly existence.
Devotion toward the devotees of Śiva, faith in the ritual prescribed by him,
as well as elsewhere; likewise, the falling of the body and trembling upon the experience of supreme bliss and joy.
The bristling of hair on the body—this is the sign of the descent of power (śaktipāta).
"In Pauṣkara, when shall I behold the Lord of Gods? When shall I be liberated from bondage?
Who will show me Śambhu?"—such a thought arises within him.

Thus, having recognized the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*) through the signs of the disciple, one should initiate a householder who desires worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*). However, one who is dispassionate (*virakta*)—whether desiring enjoyment or desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*)—one should initiate.
As it is said in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"The naiṣṭhika [initiates] should initiate both naiṣṭhikas and householders in due order;
however, the bhautika should initiate householders, but no one else should perform initiation.
(9th line) Thus it is said.
(The Determination of the Time for Initiation) Regarding the determination of the time for initiation, the *Makuṭa* states:
"During the period of the northern solstice, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day..."
One should perform the initiation at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction of the planets.
According to the *Kālottara*:
"The conjunction of autumn and spring is the best for the ritual procedure of initiation."
In the absence of those two, the rainy season is recommended even elsewhere.
In initiation and consecration, likewise in the reception of mantras,
in the undertaking and release of vows, and in rites performed with the acquisition of ritual substances;
On the full moon days of Kārttika and Vaiśākha, as well as at the sight of the sun and the moon,
and on those other lunar days (tithis) remembered as being joined with the "gaps" (chidra) of the day and so forth.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the beginnings of the six aśītis,
during the conjunctions of planets and lunar mansions, at the equinoxes, and also on festive occasions;

In all solstices, it grants the fulfillment of all goals through sacrifice. Among the lunar days, excluding the fourth, ninth, sixth, non-sixth (i.e., fifth), fourteenth, and full moon, all the remaining days are beneficial for those desiring worldly enjoyment.
For the sake of prosperity, one should avoid the days of Āditya (Sunday), Maṅgala (Tuesday), and Saurī (Saturday).
The three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Mūla, and Revatī.
Abhijit and Śravaṇa—these are the fourteen [asterisms] in the Śiva-sacrifice.
Furthermore, know the yogas to be: Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Śubha, Sukarman, Dhṛti, Sādhya, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa.
That Śiva is the most excellent Siddha, as are the sixteen [Siddhas] beginning with Brahmā and Indra.
The auspicious lunar days (*viṣṭi*) excluded, all other causes that are favorable for a person are praised for the sake of liberation.

At the time prescribed, in a sacred field (*puṇyakṣetra*), near a holy ford (*puṇyatīrtha*), in a monastery (*maṭha*), or in a pavilion previously constructed, one should perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The Characteristics of the Maṇḍapa (Pavilion)
Now, he speaks of the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-lakṣaṇa*) in the *Suprabheda*: [text].
The pavilion is considered to be of three kinds: the best is nine cubits [in extent], the middling is seven cubits, and the lowest is five cubits.
A wise person should have it constructed with sixteen pillars or even twelve, making it free of gaps in every cardinal and intermediate direction;
it should be provided with four doors and adorned with four archways.
The ground should be as high as a palm tree, or otherwise six finger-breadths.
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned it with flower garlands,
one should cover the top with canopies and decorate it with strings of pearls.
One should designate one-third of that [area] for the center of the altar (*vedi*).
(The acquisition of ground for the purpose of the pavilion.
The acquisition of ground for the purpose of the pavilion. (Line 10)
It is said:
[the ground] that is pure, not saline, burnt, and free from proximity to cremation grounds or outcaste settlements— whether it be of superior or middling quality—
one should level it into a perfect square at the prescribed time and auspicious moment using a cord.

Having fixed a wooden stake (*śaṅku*) three cubits in length, having dug [the ground] and cast the earth outside, and having removed hair, bones, thorns, ashes, husks, and so forth, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and scented water while reciting the *Śiva-mantra*; thus purified by stones, water, and so on...
(line 2).

Having filled the pit with sand, men who had bathed and were wearing washed garments, using mallets fitted with *palāśa* branches, pounded the ground until it resembled the surface of a mirror, and then [covered it] with stones.
One should have a pavilion constructed with bricks or pure timber; or else, in a beautiful temple,
having prepared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring five cubits or more by means of laying out the lines, and having provided it with four doors,
[one should proceed] again.

Having divided [the area] into nine parts by means of the laying of the cord, one should divide the intermediate quarter and the side-altar within that [area] into four parts by the laying of the cord using three of those parts; then, having set aside one part in the middle of the altar, one should prepare either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the characteristics to be described.
One should perform [the rite].
Now follows the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

In pavilions measuring nine, seven, or five cubits respectively, one should construct the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the eastern direction of the altar (*vedikā*), at a distance of one cubit, a fist-breadth, or a *ratni* respectively; leaving aside one-fourth of that space, one should make it for those [pavilions], specifically for the pit of one cubit.

One should fashion girdles (*mekhalā*) measuring four, three, or two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) for a [pillar] of one cubit (*aratni*) in length; for one of a fist’s length or one cubit, girdles measuring two, one, or half a finger-breadth; and for others, one should likewise fashion girdles. Above that, one should fashion a shape resembling a *pippala* leaf, an elephant’s trunk, or a vulva (*yoni*).

(8th line) One should mark the center of the *kuṇḍa* with a *vajra* or a lotus. We shall describe the ten types of *kuṇḍas* according to their characteristics later on. In the case of a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), it should be one cubit (*hasta*) in measure, or one *aratni*, or the depth of the hollow (*muṣṭi*) or one *aratni*. (9th line)

One should construct [the altar] four fingers high and perfectly square, using pure and purified sand. Having thus adorned the pavilion and other areas, one should bestow the initiation of the pledges (*samaya*) and so forth upon a disciple endowed with devotion and detachment. Herein is the sequence:
The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of the Maṇḍapa.

Having completed the two daily rituals (*āhnika*) in the pavilion, one should worship Śiva— who is the solar orb— within [the mandala] dedicated to Indra, Agni, and the others, as if it were a daily rite; then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and the ritual placement of mantras (*nyāsa*), [one should purify with] the general offering water (*sāmānyārghya*) using the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having sprinkled the gates in the east, south, west, and north, [one should recite]: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the gate of the Śāntikalā; Hāṃ, obeisance to the gate of the Vidyākalā; Hāṃ, obeisance to the gate of the Nivṛttikalā; Hāṃ, obeisance to the gate of the Pratiṣṭhākalā. Thus for the gates starting from the east.
One should worship [the deities] either in water-pots or on sacrificial altars. Following that, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and those situated above all the doors. The mantras are:
Hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Hāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī; Hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī.

In the east, south, west, and north, one should worship Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa, Vināyaka, Vṛṣabha, Kārttikeya, Gaurīśa, and Caṇḍeśvara, respectively, two by two, either with water-pots (*kalaśa*) or upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). The mantras, however, are: *Hāṃ Nandīśvarāya namaḥ*, and so forth.

Having thus worshipped all these with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having requested, "You should remain here with great devotion as protectors of the sacrifice," he should close the eastern, southern, western, and northern doors with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
At the western gate,
having worshipped the gatekeepers as usual and having expelled the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial obstacles, one enters within; there,
having worshipped the *Astra* [weapon] on the *udumbara* pillar for the sake of *Ṛkṣā*, one should gaze with *Avalokitā*.

Having performed the circumambulation while observing the vow regarding the materials and implements for the ritual, he should worship in the southwest with the mantra: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāstoṣpati Brahmā. Then, having protected the sacrificial hall by means of the enclosures of the *astra*, the *kavaca*, and the *avakuṇṭhana* [mantras].
Seated on the south of the altar facing north, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*),

and having sequentially executed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) of the phonemes, words, mantras, principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and kalās upon the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), he established the acts of worship, oblation, and meditation in the heart, the navel, and the point between the eyebrows (*bindu*).

Having prepared the special *arghya* and performed self-worship (*ātmapūjā*), one should sprinkle the ritual substances with the water from the special *arghya* while reciting the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having placed the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*) upon one's own head, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva. Thereafter, [one should perform] the triple clapping of the hands (*tālatraya*) and so forth.

Having protected the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and sipping (*ācamana*) during the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*), one should set aside the *arghya* for the purpose of restraint (*nirodha*). Then, for the sprinkling of the sacrificial animal (*paśu-prokṣaṇa*), one should place the *arghya* for the animal consecrated with the *saṃhitā-mantra*.
Thereafter, [one prepares] parched grain (*lāja*), sandalwood (*candana*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), ashes (*bhasma*), dūrvā grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), kuśa grass, and flowers.

Having consecrated [the substances] seven times with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should place the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth. Thereafter,
one should [consecrate] the sword of gnosis (*jñānāsi*) in the form of a braid made of thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

One should consecrate it seven times. In the context of the *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*, [one should recite] "Bhrūṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śakti" nine times... [and so forth]... having consecrated the ritual tool (*karmanī*) seven times with "Huṃ Haḥ, obeisance to the Weapon (*astra*)," using the mantras of the *kalās* beginning with *śāntyatītā*.
Having consecrated the white, yellow, black, reddish-brown, and green powders with mantras, one should perform purification. Thereafter, grasping the sword of wisdom in the armpit,
standing in the southwest facing north, one should sprinkle the sacrificial hall with the *arghya* water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having consecrated the sacrificial hall through inspection and other rites,

one should scatter various types of grains such as parched rice (*lāja*)— previously consecrated with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*— to destroy obstacles; then, having strewn sand, one should sweep up the scattered parched rice and other materials with a bundle of *kuśa* grass using the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

One should place [the vessel] for the sake of the *vardhanī* seat in the northeast (*īśāna*). Thereafter, having drawn the *vāstu-maṇḍala* with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in the southwest (*nairṛta*), one should worship Vāstoṣpati along with his retinue there. Then, having performed worship in the water-pot (*kalaśa*) or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with the mantra: "Obeisance to Vāstoṣpati, to Brahmā, and to his retinue," [one should proceed].

One should worship Mahālakṣmī, who is seated upon a lion, whose form is that of a pavilion, and who fills the sacrificial hall with all kinds of jewels. Following that, one should place the Śiva-pitcher in the northeast on a seat consisting of the seven grains— sesame, mustard, mung bean, black gram, hāḍhaka, rice, and barley.
Having established the *vardhanī* on its right side, and having placed it upon a seat of parched grain (*lāja*) and other materials gathered together with a bundle of *kuśa* grass,

one should worship the seat of the *śiva-kumbha* with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha. Then, having worshipped Śiva in the *śiva-kumbha* with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one worships the seat of the *vardhanī* with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Siṃhāsanā," and there [worships] Vanīśvarī.
Having visualized [the deity] in the form of a sword: *Haḥ astrāsanāya namaḥ*; *Haḥ astramūrtaye namaḥ*; *Haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *Haḥ astrahṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. (9th line)

HAḤ Astra-śiras-e HUṂ PHAṆṆAMAḤ | AḤ Astra-śikhāyai HUṂ PHAṆṆAMAḤ | AḤ Astra-kavacāya HUṂ PHAṆṆAMAḤ | HAḤ Astrāya HUṂ PHAṆṆAMAḤ—thus one should worship. Thereafter, HĀṂ Indrāya vajra-hastāya Airā... [10th line]

...to the one of [white] color, together with his retinue, obeisance! Hāṃ, to Agni, who holds a spear in his hand, who is mounted upon a ram, who is red in color, together with his retinue, obeisance! Hāṃ, to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand, who is mounted upon a buffalo, who is black...

(…………)ya namaḥ | Hāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti, who holds a sword in his hand, is mounted upon a corpse, is blue in color, and is accompanied by his retinue. Hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand, is mounted upon a crocodile, is white in color, and is accompanied by his retinue. Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand, is mounted upon a deer, and is smoke-colored.

Salutation to [him] together with his retinue. Hāṃ! Salutation to Kubera, who holds a mace in his hand, who is eternally free from affliction, together with his retinue. Hāṃ! Salutation to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand, who is mounted upon a bull, who is white in color, together with his retinue. Having thus worshipped [these deities] in the jars or on the sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) in the directions starting from the east, [one recites] "Hāṃ..."

(Third line) Salutation to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand, is mounted upon a swan, is yellow in color, and is accompanied by his retinue. Hāṃ! Salutation to Ananta, who holds a discus in his hand, is mounted upon Garuḍa, is dark green in color, and is accompanied by his retinue. (Fourth line)

Thus, one should worship Īśāna in the upper direction, Nṛti in the south, and [the other deities] in the east according to their respective directions. Thereafter, taking the *vardhanī* vessel and placing it behind the *śivakumbha*,
one should [pour water] in an unbroken stream while reciting the root mantra.
Having recited [this] and circumambulated [the site], moving clockwise, [he said]:
"For the sake of protecting the sacrifice and for the destruction of obstacles,
you all must stand ready with your respective mounts and weapons by the command of Śiva."
This Śiva-sacrifice has commenced by the command of Śiva for the sake of his devotees;
O Guardians of the World, you must protect it from obstacles with focused minds.

Thus one should proclaim the command of Śiva. Alternatively: "O Śakra, for the pacification of obstacles in your own quarter, you must remain vigilant until the conclusion of the rite by the command of Śiva. One should proclaim the command of Śiva to each [deity] individually. Then, having first established the Śiva-kumbha, one should subsequently establish the vardhanī.

Having worshipped Śiva in the Śivakumbha with the *sthirāsana* and other rites as usual, one should worship Paśupatāstra in the Vardhanī vessel. Thus: "Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the weapon, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ; Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the weapon, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
Having thus worshipped—
He has five faces, is most terrible, possesses ten arms and three eyes;
he is described as deformed, radiant like the sun, with tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair.
Holding in his hands a sword, a shield, an iron arrow, a bow, a measuring cord, and a water-pot;
equipped with a spear, a trident, an axe, and the Brahma-staff;
standing on one foot, two feet, or with feet evenly placed, he blazes brilliantly.
Having meditated thus: "Endowed with serpents on all his limbs, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread," one should invoke [the deity] with "glīṃ (...
phaṭ, obeisance to the Pāśupata weapon," and having worshipped him, [one should worship] the Heart of the Weapon with "huṃ phaṇṇama."

Having performed worship with devotion, one should touch the *kumbha* and *vardhanī* vessels while reciting: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śakti and Śiva" for the sake of attainment (*bhukti*), and "Ham, obeisance to Śiva and Śakti" for the sake of liberation (*mukti*). Thus says the *Āgama*: "One should touch the *kumbha* with the thumb, and the *vardhanī* with the fist."
"Those who have first eaten for the sake of liberation—[one] should touch the *vardhanī* with the fist.
Following that:
"For this form of yours is the immovable presiding lordship (*patitva*) over this sacrifice."
This sword of knowledge is yours; take up your own weapon.
Having made this request, one should place the *jñāna-nāsikallara* with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Thus says the Āgama:
"In the right hand of Śiva, the *vardhanī* and the weapon [are] duly measured."
Therefore, for the sake of protecting that sacrifice, one should place it in the ritual pitcher at the beginning of the sacrifice.
Thereafter, having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times and the limb mantras ten times each,
and having offered them into the Śiva-pitcher; and having recited the Pāśupata-weapon mantra ten times and offered it into the Vardhanī vessel.
This sacrifice of yours has been set in motion by me, a performer of rituals;
it must not be interrupted until its completion.
To Umā, who possesses the form of the *bhaga* and who bears the form of the *liṅga*.
Salutations to you, Śaṅkara, who bestows grace upon your devotees.

Having thus made this request, one should worship Gaṇeśa in the northwest (vāyukoṇa) and the Guru in the northeast (īśāna). Thereafter, having worshipped Śiva in the maṇḍala or in the chosen liṅga according to the daily rite (nityavat), one should inform Him, saying, "O Lord,
I shall perform the fire-rite (agnikārya)," and having obtained permission, [proceed] with the tips of the thumb and ring finger.

Having placed the root mantra upon the two eyes and having gazed at the collection of materials required for the fire sacrifice, one should sit comfortably on a seat to the south of the sacrificial pit and perform the extensive fire ritual (*bṛhadagnikārya*).
(The extensive fire ritual.)
"Hāṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva"—with this, there is the inspection of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

With the Weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, there is sprinkling and striking; with the Armor mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, there is pouring over. With the Weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, there is digging and lifting [the earth]. With the Heart mantra ending in *namaḥ*, there is filling and leveling; with the Armor mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, there is moistening.

Having performed the pulverizing [of obstacles] with the Weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and the cleansing and smearing with the Armor-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should place the mantras of the Kalās— such as Śāntyatītā and the others— in the center, east, south, north, and [other directions] within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) during the material initiation (*bhautikadīkṣā*). When performing the initiation, one should place them in the west, north, south, east, and center.
One should arrange the portions consisting of the digits beginning with Nivṛtti, ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, having encircled the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *namaḥ*, one should worship the pit with the mantra: *hāṃ kalāmayāya kuṇḍāya namaḥ*.
Then, with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, using *kuśa* grass, [one should draw lines] in the middle of the pit in the sequence from west to east.
One should draw four lines from south to north and from west to east with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Then, using three blades of *kuśa* grass in the shape of a trident at both ends, one should transform them into a *vajra*. With the *hṛdaya-mantra* ending in *namaḥ*, [one should do so] using two *kuśa* blades with their tips pointing east and north.

One should also provide a gift at the crossroads. Having thus performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should place four *kuśa* blades at the neck of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) using the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending with "namas. Then, saying "Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara," one should place a seat (*viṣṭara*) in the form of a *kuśa*-cross in the center of the pit, and there—

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the form with the mantra "Hāṃ! Salutation to the forms of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara," one should worship them with the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, using the mantra "Salutation to the splendor of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara. Thereafter, having taken up the fire as before and placed it in the southeast corner of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should proceed].

Having expelled the portion of the fire-element belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) toward the southwest corner with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having purified the fire through the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, one should say: *Hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of fire*.
Then, having grasped the fire—which has the appearance of a shimmering star—by means of the *iḍā* channel and the filling breath using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*:
Having joined the fire,

which resembles a falling sun, with the fire situated in the *bindu* by means of *kumbhaka*, and having joined that fire with the fire situated in the sacrificial pit of the navel, [one should recite] "Bhrūṃ,
obeisance to the consciousness of fire" for the fire that is like the midday sun amidst the mass of flames.

Having expelled [the fire] outward through the *piṅgalā* channel by means of the *recaka* breath, one should place it upon a heap of charcoal devoid of embers, situated in a vessel such as a copper bowl.
(The *saṃskāras* beginning with *garbhādhāna*) Having thus unified the fire, one should consecrate it with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*). (10th line)

Having rendered [the offering] nectar-like by means of the *śakti*-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, having enveloped it with the *kavaca* [mantra], protected it with the *astra* [mantra], and worshipped it with the *hṛdaya* [mantra] ending in *namaḥ*, one should rotate it three times clockwise above the *kuṇḍa* for the sake of non-disturbance, [reciting]: "O Vāgīśī and Vāgīśvara, enter! (yo viśataḥ).

Having visualized the clear meeting of the head of the sky and the earth, and having meditated on the seed-syllable of Śiva with the mantra "Hāṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to the seed-syllable of Śiva," one should visualize the fire being cast by the Lord into the channel within the womb of Vāgīśvarī, while standing on the ground with the right knee [bent].

Having placed the fire in the pit facing oneself, having gathered with the heart-mantra the embers scattered here and there, and having visualized the enclosure of the surrounding fence (*paridhi*), one should offer water for purification and sipping (*śaucācamana*) with the *arghya* water, saying "Hāṃ, svadhā to Vāgīśvarī," and having covered it with fuel sticks while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should kindle it with a fan while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*) ending in "huṃ phaṭ."

Having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Garbhāgni," one should empower a blade of kuśa grass seven times with the Astra-mantra ending in "hūṃ phaṭ" and bind it to the right hand of Vāgīśvarī. Thereafter, [one should worship] with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta."

Having worshipped with the heart-mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should offer five oblations of sesame seeds; this is the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite). Having worshipped with "Hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva," and having offered five oblations of sesame seeds at the end of *svāhā*, [one recites] "Hāṃ, obeisance to the body of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka-deha*)."

Thus, one should offer a drop of water from the general *arghya*. This is the *puṃsavana* rite. Having worshipped with "Huṃ, obeisance to Aghora," and having offered five oblations of sesame seeds with the *śikhā-mantra* ending in *svāhā*, [one performs the rite] for the purpose of establishing the boundaries of the limbs and faces.

And for the purpose of expiation for the lifting of the *lpanot* (the ritual obstruction), one should offer five oblations of sesame seeds with the *śikhā-mantra* ending in *svāhā*. This is the *sīmantonnayana* rite. Having worshipped [the deity] with "Hoṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa," and having offered five oblations of sesame seeds with the *kavaca-mantra* ending in *svāhā*, one should gaze at the fire upon the *kuśa* grass with the *varman-mantra* for the immediate pacification of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).

Having sprinkled both the interior and exterior of the sacrificial pit with the *arghya* water while reciting the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should sprinkle the Goddess, the fire that has been produced, and Vāgīśvarī for the sake of their ablution, using the ordinary *arghya* water while reciting: *hāṃ vāgīśvaryai svāhā*.

Having visualized her as one who has discarded the darbha-grass bracelet and is adorned with garments and ornaments, one should worship Vāgīśvarī with the mantra "Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī" and contemplate her as being well-pleased. This is the *jātakarma* rite. Then, for the purpose of removing the fire's saliva, [one should use] a blade of *palāśa* or similar wood, free from sap.
The five kinds of fuel-sticks (*samidh*)— smooth, free from worm-holes, twelve finger-breadths long, as thick as the little finger, and smeared with ghee—
should be offered with the Astra-mantra ending in *svāhā*.

One should perform this oblation for the removal of saliva. Thereafter, having strewn *kuśa* grass with tips pointing eastward upon the girdles in the four directions using the *astra-mantra*, and having placed seats (*viṣṭara*) upon the eastern, western, southern, and northern girdles using the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should offer: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā;
Hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Hāṃ... [third line].

"Salutation to Rudra; Hāṃ, salutation to Ananteśvara. Having worshipped them in this sequence, and having worshipped the eight world-protectors beginning with Indra, together with their respective mounts and weapons stationed in the east, south, west, and north.
Having worshipped Brahmā to the south-east and Viṣṇu to the east of Nairṛti,
the best of preceptors should cause [the deities] to hear the command of Śiva: "O gods, well-armed, do not harm this child by the command of Śiva."

Thereafter (line 5), having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles— which have been perfected through the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*)— and holding them with both hands joined in the *kuśa* grass, one should heat them three times in the fire with the Heart-mantra in order to remove their wooden nature; then, in the case of the material initiation (*bhautikadīkṣā*) (line 6).
With the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, having touched the tip, middle, and base of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the tips, middles, and bases of *kuśa* grass, [one recites]:
*hṛṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ*; *hṛṃ śivatattvādhipataye rudrāya namaḥ*; *hīṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ*; *hīṃ*... [7th line].

Having worshipped the tips, middles, and bases of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the mantras: "Obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*); hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the self (*ātma-tattva*); hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self," one places the *sruk* and *sruva* on the right.

Having placed [the ladles] upon *kuśa* grass with the mantra "Hāṃ, obeisance to Śakti and Śiva," one should offer the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. However, for one who is performing the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should consecrate the *sruk* and *sruva* according to the sequence of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*). Having wrapped their handles with a three-stranded thread while reciting the *Kavaca* mantra, one should worship them with perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings. Then, cow's ghee placed in a vessel made of gold or other materials—

Having purified [the materials] by means of inspection and other rites, one should whirl them three times above the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). This is the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire). Having meditated upon one's own body as consisting of Brahman, and having offered oblations into the southeast corner of the fire-pit with "Hāṃ, svāhā to Brahman," one should offer drops of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade.

One should perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*). Having meditated upon this body of one's own as being composed of Viṣṇu (*tāpanaṃ svadehaṃ viṣṇumayaṃ dhyātvā*), and having [meditated] on that clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇe*), one should offer a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, saying: "Hrīṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu. This is the act of placing [the vessel] over the fire (*adhiśrayaṇam*). One's own body...

Having meditated upon Rudra, and having visualized him at the navel of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, reciting: "Hāṃ Hāṃ, Svāhā to Rudra. This is the dismissal (*udvāsana*). [One should take] two *kuśa* blades, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length, with a *brahmagranthi* knot tied in the middle.

Taking [the two *kuśa* blades] with the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands, one says: *haiṃ kavacāya svāhā*. Having cast two drops of clarified butter into the mouth of the fire, one should throw those two *kuśa* blades—releasing the knot—into the fire. This is the *utplava* offering. Again, taking two *kuśa* blades according to the prescribed method for the location, one says: *hāṃ hṛdayāya svāhā*.
(4th line) Having thrown two drops of clarified butter facing oneself, one should cast those two *kuśa* blades with their knots released into the fire.
This is the "equal immersion" (*samaplava*). Saying "Hāṃ, homage to the heart," one should cast the *kuśa* blade facing upward into the clarified butter and then into the fire. (5th line)

This is the purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*). Having churned the clarified butter with the blazing *kuśa* grass using the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should cast the *kuśa* into the fire. This is the lustration (*nīrājana*). With the weapon-mantra (*astra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, that [should be performed]. (The sixth line is omitted; the seventh line follows).

Having visualized the bright and dark fortnights in the right and left portions respectively, one should establish the triad of channels—piṅgalā, iḍā, and suṣumnā—in the right, left, and middle portions thereof. Having visualized [them], in the right portion...
(8th line)

Taking ghee with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, [one offers] "Hāṃ! To Agni, Svāhā! into the right eye of the fire; "Hāṃ! into the southern part of the ghee. Taking clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva* into the left part, [one offers] "Hāṃ! To Soma, Svāhā" into the left eye; "Hāṃ! into the northern part of the clarified butter. Taking clarified butter with the *sruva* into the middle part, [one offers] "Hāṃ! To Agni and Soma, Svāhā."

Thus, with "HĀṂ" at the fire’s forehead-eye, and with "HĀṂ" in the middle portion of the fire divided into three parts, one should take clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon and offer it into the mouth of the fire with "HĀṂ AGNAYE SVIṢṬAKṚTE SVĀHĀ"; then, with "HĀṂ," one should offer the three portions of clarified butter. In this manner, [the rite is performed] in the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight.

Then one should offer oblations in reverse order; that is the opening [of the seal]. Having consecrated it with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), having veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), having protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having rendered it nectarine by means of the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*), one purifies the non-ghee by sprinkling drops of clarified butter, and takes up the sacrificial butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva* ladle.
Haṃ sadyojātāya svāhā, hiṃ vāmadevāya svāhā, huṃ aghorāya svāhā, heṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā, hoṃ īśānāya svāhā. Thus is the illumination of the faces. Haṃ hiṃ. (Third line)
*svāhā* to *Sadyojāta* and *Vāmadeva*, *hiṃ* *huṃ*! *svāhā* to *Vāmadeva* and *Aghora*, *huṃ* *heṃ*!

*svāhā* to *Aghora* and *Tatpuruṣa*, *heṃ* *hoṃ*! *svāhā* to *Tatpuruṣa* and *Īśāna*. Thus is the joining of the faces. *haṃ* *hiṃ* *huṃ* *heṃ* *hoṃ* [to] *Sadyojāta*, *Vāmadeva*, *Aghora*, *Tatpuruṣa*, and *Īśāna*.

Svāhā! Thus, one should pour a stream of clarified butter from the southeast corner to the northwest corner, and from the southwest corner to the northeast corner. This is the unification of the faces; such is the *jātakarman* (birth rite).

Having turned [the fire] back and worshipped it with "Hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna," one should offer five oblations with the Astra-mantra ending in Svāhā, and then assign the name: "O Consumer of Oblations, you are the Śiva-fire. Thereafter, having offered ten sesame oblations each with "Hāṃ, Svāhā to Vāgīśvarī" and "Hāṃ, Svāhā to Vāgīśvara," [one worships] Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara.
One should dismiss [the deity] with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, having filled the *sruk* with clarified butter (*ājya*), placed the *sruva* over the *sruk* facing downwards, and having placed a flower on the tip of the *sruk*,
one should [perform the rite] with the right and left hands in the mudrā resembling a conch shell.

Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and risen, he should place their base at his own navel; with his eyes fixed on the tip of the *sruk*, restraining his inhalation and exhalation, and having dismissed the Lords who are the causes beginning with Brahmā through the path of the *suṣumṇā* channel by means of the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, he should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) which fulfills all rites. By this—
The rites of the first feeding of solid food, the first outing, the tonsure ceremony, the initiation, and the godāna concluding the vows have been performed.
As it is stated in the Kālottara: [text follows].
For the successful completion of the remaining consecratory rites, one should subsequently cause the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to be offered;
likewise, for one free from desire, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) and the initiation of vows (vratabandha) should be performed.

"Up to the cutting of the top-knot and the giving of the cow, [the rite] was performed with fullness. Thus, having extracted a small fire for the purpose of the *caru* oblation, one should mark it out in another place. Thereafter, for the nourishment of the fire, one should offer sixteen palāśa fuel-sticks with the mantra: *hrūṃ agnaye svāhā*.
(On the meditation on the fire, etc.):
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the fire.
As it has been said in the *Acintya*:
He has one heart, two faces, two nostrils, and six eyes;
he possesses three girdles, three feet, and is surrounded by seven tongues of flame.
Seated upon four peaks, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
he has four hands on the right side and three hands on the left.
With his other hands on the right, he holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a spear, and fire.
A spear, a fan, and likewise a vessel of clarified butter.
Having thus meditated upon [the fire] as it flows forth, one should worship it with the seed-syllable of fire (*agni-bīja*).
Following that, having fully worshipped the fire with "Hrūṃ, obeisance to Agni," [one recites]:
"O Agni, you are the sovereign splendor, for you are the supreme purifier."
"Therefore, having established [the deity] within the lotus of your heart, we shall offer libations.
Thus one should pray; thereafter, one should perform the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). Such is the scripture.
One should contemplate the channel resembling a woolen thread, which has emerged from the risen [breath] and enters back into the unrisen; having emerged with the risen, it likewise enters again.
The Guru should not think of [the disciple] entering while he himself has not yet entered;
thus,
having subsequently entered the form of fire through the path of the channels (*nāḍī*), [he enters] into the middle of the heart-lotus of the fire.

Having first performed the postures beginning with the *ādhāra-śakti*, and having worshipped Śiva—who is fire-colored due to the limiting adjunct of his abode (*āśrayopādhi*)—along with the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) and the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), by means of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth; and having prayed, "O Blessed One, I satisfy you; grant me your command."

Having contemplated the identity of the mouth of Śiva and the mouth of fire, and having entered one's own body, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) in the Īśāna face for liberation; in the Puruṣa face, for the powers such as *aṇimā*;
in the Aghora face, for expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and the like; and likewise, in the Vāma face, for cruel deeds.
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the Vāmadeva face for the purpose of subduing, attracting, and deluding;

and in the western [face], one should cause the purification of the disciple and the daily oblation (*nityahoma*) to be performed. According to this statement, one should contemplate the seven tongues [of fire] in the Sadyojāta face.
They are as follows: Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā; these are proclaimed as the seven tongues.
In the directions of Īśāna, the East, Agni, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Vāyu, as well as in the center, the seven tongues of fire are situated in sequence:
Hiraṇyā, which has the luster of molten gold; Kanakā, which has the radiance of silver; and [the others].
The red [light] has the appearance of an exceedingly fresh dawn, while the black [light] has the luster of a sapphire.
Suprabhā is like a pearl, Dyotā is exceedingly red like a ruby,
and Bahurūpiṇī possesses a radiance like the moonstone or the autumnal moon.
Kanaka is the foremost for universal attraction and for the paralyzing of enemies; Rakta is used for causing enmity and delusion; Kṛṣṇā is for the rite of killing;
Suprabhā is declared for pacification, and Suraktā is considered for expulsion.
She is indeed one, yet manifold in form, bestowing the fruits of all desires.
If the letters ending in *ha* are without the *repha* (*ra*) and are joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*),
and further conjoined with *nāda* and the *bindu*, they are proclaimed as the *jihvā-mantras*.

Thereafter, one should perform the rites of kindling (*dīpana*), unification (*sandhāna*), and integration (*ekīkaraṇa*) for each of those tongues, either with a single oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-huti*) or with three oblations of sesame seeds (*tila-huti*) for each. It is as follows: *Yūṃ* to Hiraṇyā, *svāhā*; *Eṃ* to Kanakā, *svāhā*; *Āṃ* to Raktā, *svāhā*.
ŚŪṂ to Kṛṣṇā, Svāhā! ṢŪṂ to Suprabhā, Svāhā!
SŪṂ to Atiraktā, Svāhā! HŪṂ to Bahurūpā, Svāhā! Thus is the illumination. YŪṂ LŪṂ to Hiraṇya and Kanaka, Svāhā! LŪṂ VŪṂ... (7th line)

*kanakāraktābhyāṃ svāhā*. *Ghrūṃ* to the red and black ones, *svāhā*. *Śūṃ sūṃ* to the black and radiant (*suprabha*) ones, *svāhā*. *Ṣūṃ sūṃ* to the radiant and excessive (*atirikta*) ones, *svāhā*. *Sūṃ hūṃ* to the excessive and multiform (*bahurūpa*) ones, *svāhā*. This is the conjunction (*sandhāna*). *Yū lūṃ pūṃ śūṃ hūṃ sūṃ huṃ*.

"Hiraṇyakana-kāraktā-kuṣṇā-suprabhātiriktā-bahurūpābhyas svāhā"— this is the unification (*ekīkaraṇa*). Thereafter, having visualized the inclusion of Hiraṇyā and the others within Bahurūpā, [one should offer] with the root mantra using the available substances.

One hundred and eight oblations should be offered with [mantras] ending in *svāhā*. Having offered a tenth part of that with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) ending in *svāhā*, one should present the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, for the purpose of removing defects regarding place, time, and ill omens, and for the attainment of auspicious omens— [80a, line 1]

Having performed two hundred or half of that [number] with the *mūla-mantra*, the *aghora-mantra*, or the *astra-mantra*, together with a *pūrṇāhuti*, one should offer for each disciple one hundred oblations with the *mūla-mantra* along with a *pūrṇāhuti* for the purpose of the disciple’s entry. Thereafter: *hāṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā hāṃ*.

*Hṛdayāya svāhā*. *Hīṃ śirase svāhā*. *Huṃ śikhāyai svāhā*. *Oṃ heṃ kavacāya svāhā*. *Haḥ astrāya svāhā*—thus is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). *Hūṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya huṃphaṭ*. *Haṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya haṃ hīṃ phaṭ*. *Oṃ haṃ hīṃ śirase huṃphaṭ*. *Hūṃ haṃ*.
*Śikhāyai haṃ haṃ huṃ phaṭ | Hraṃ haiṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṭ | Haṃ haḥ astrāya [huṃ phaṭ]*—thus is the illumination (*dīpana*). According to the *Āgama*:
"With clarified butter (*ājya*), there shall be a single libation (*tarpaṇa*) for all mantras, ending with *svāhā*."
The illumination [of the mantra] is performed with the seed-syllables enclosed by the *śikhā* and ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus [ends] the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* (5th line).

Having washed a vessel made of iron, lead, tarnished copper, or clay—which is free from defects such as cracks—with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and having protected it with the Kavaca-mantra;
having purified it through the four refinements beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*);

having smeared it with sandalwood paste and the like and fumigated it; [one should place] around its neck a triple-threaded cord and *kuśa* grass over which the Astra and Kavaca mantras have been recited.

Having wrapped [the vessel] upon a mandala smeared with cow-dung, sprinkled with the *astra-mantra*, and shielded by the *kavaca-mantra*, and having placed *darbha* grass arranged with the *astra-mantra* upon it, one should worship the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsanam*). Having placed the vessel, which has become the embodiment [of the deity], upon that [seat], one should worship the Blessed One along with his limbs (*sāṅga*) therein, up to the stage of dissolution (*layāṅga*).

Having removed the flowers and other offerings, and having anointed [the vessel] with ghee from cow-products over which the scriptures have been recited, one should fill it with cow’s milk that has been purified by inspection and other rites and consecrated a hundred times with the *prāsāda* mantra. Then, for the sake of many disciples, one should place into it sacrificial rice grains (*yājñīya-dhānya-taṇḍula*) measuring five handfuls (*prasṛti*), increasing up to twelve handfuls; [having done so], [one prepares] the hearth (*cullī*) and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
In the southern, eastern, or western direction,
having scratched [the ground] facing west with the Astra-mantra,
one should [prepare] a seat for Dharma and Adharma, which has been sprinkled with that same mantra, enveloped by the Kavaca-mantra, swept clean, and smeared with [cow-dung].
Having fashioned [the vessel] with all its parts complete, having placed the seed-syllable *haṃ* upon it, and having consecrated it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*),
one should worship it with the previously extracted fire of Śiva. Having offered a seat consisting of the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and placed the pot upon it,

one should perform the inspection of the eastern side by moving and opening it with the weapon-mantra, and then perform the closing again with the eye-mantra (*netramantra*) and the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).

(Second line) One should cook the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) in a small fire-pit (*hrasvaprāsāda*) until it is well-cooked. If the cooking is too slow or too intense, the disease of "fivefold destruction" (*pañcatāvyādhi*) occurs. To pacify that, one should perform a hundred oblations (*āhuti*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Upon its completion, having performed the sprinkling with hot clarified butter while reciting the mantra-text ending in *svāhā*— saying "become well-steamed"— and having performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites upon the maṇḍala prepared with the *astra-mantra* and worshipped as before,
one should perform the scraping (*ullekhana*) with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, saying "become very cool" while reciting the mantra-text ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
One should perform the cooling sprinkling (*śītābhighāra*).
(Regarding the initiation of the pledge, *samayadīkṣā*:
Thereafter, having released the fire situated on the hearth by means of the heart-mantra and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mantra], one should then wipe away the clay from the outside with water and earth.

Having placed [the vessel] upon a seat raised six steps in the western portion of the mandala of the *kumbha*, having worshipped it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and having consecrated it in the fire with the *saṃhitā-mantra* followed by "svāhā," one should perform the *saṃpāta-homa* by shaking the *sruva*-ladle and pouring the remaining clarified butter over the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).

Then, having consecrated the *caru* with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*), veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and rendered it nectarine (*amṛtīkṛta*) by means of the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*),
one should divide the *caru* into three parts using the ladle (*darvī*) that pierces the distinctions between the deity, the fire, and the self; [of these], two portions—

Having offered a portion of one's own self to Śiva and Agni, one should preserve [the remainder]. Then, having made a circular maṇḍala with cow dung between the water-pot (kumbha) and the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), one should offer a bali-oblation in that maṇḍala with the mantra "svāhā" to those dwelling in the directions starting from the east—the lords of the directions (digīśas), spirits (bhūtas), the host of mothers (mātṛgaṇas), Rudras, the field-protectors (kṣetrapālas), and so forth. One should also offer the bali-oblation for the planets into the fire.

One should satisfy the deities of the sacrifice with offerings up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Thereafter, having worshipped Śiva—who resides in the fire, in the water-pot (*kumbha*), and in the mandala—with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*):
"For whose sake this sacrifice was commenced by me today..."
These sacrificial animals stand here, restrained because they have been pacified.
"In this matter, I have been commanded by you, who are the embodiment of the Guru:
'Therefore, having now empowered me, perform the favor for these [beings].'"
"May the Blessed Lord himself, the Sovereign who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, perform [this]," thus one should request.
Then the Preceptor, having adorned himself, should place the Hand of Śiva upon his own head and contemplate, "I am Śiva."
As it is said in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"One should place a white turban (*śvetoṣṇīṣa*), consecrated with the root mantra, upon the head;
the upper garment with the *gāyatrī*, and the lower garment with the *sadyojāta* [mantra]."
The preceptor should especially adorn himself with camphor powder mixed with sandalwood and flowers, as well as with fragrant ashes and ornaments that are utterly pure.
And with linen garments, pure clothes, and various ornaments and such.
The Guru should draw a mandala with fragrant substances on the right hand;
having worshipped Īśa therein, together with his limbs and his retinue.
Having placed that most excellent [mantra] upon his own head with the Śiva-mantra,
he should always contemplate himself as the agent, non-different from Īśvara.
Acting as a witness, he should observe the rites within the mandala;
likewise, he should cause the fire to consume the oblations offered in the hearth with the mantra "O golden-jawed one, protect [him].
Therein, he should especially effect the liberation from the multitude of bonds for the disciple.
"Having been graced within his own self, Maheśvara is the fivefold support;
'I am that very teacher,' thus one should maintain this state of being.

Thus, having prepared the sacrificial water for the bound soul (*paśu*)—which pervades the principles from the *ādhāra* up to *Puruṣa*—by means of the "eight flowers," and having taken it, [one proceeds].

(6th line) Having emerged from the sacrificial hall, one should prepare two maṇḍalas for the Bhautika [deity] facing the western door, measuring one cubit and square at the ends, situated in the west and east, using cow dung and the Astra-mantra. One performs the ritual placement (sanyāsa). (7th line)

One should fashion two mandalas situated from south to north. Then, in the initiation for the material elements (bhautika-dīkṣā), having laid down kusha grass with its tips pointing eastward upon the two mandalas, [one should place] the sixfold arising seat (ṣaḍutthāsana) there.
Having performed the worship and the circumambulation, and having placed the material disciple— who has fasted, bathed, and put on festive garments— facing east within the western mandala,
he himself stands facing west within the eastern mandala.
Having gazed with divine vision upon [the disciple] from the head down to the feet while the root mantra is being placed [therein],
one should again sprinkle the *arghya* with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; then, having struck the disciple’s heart with ashes using that same mantra,
one should again sprinkle it three times with the *arghya* water using that same mantra.

Having sprinkled [the site] with the Armor mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should scratch it three times above and below the navel with the tips and roots of *kuśa* grass while reciting the Weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*). Then, having placed *kuśa* grass with unbroken rice grains and their tips pointing north upon two circles— one to the south and one to the north— one should sit there upon the seat of the sixfold purity (*ṣaḍāsana*).
Having performed the worship, and having placed the disciple— who has completed the preliminary ablutions, is wearing clean garments, and is maintaining the vow of renunciation—
facing north upon the southern mandala, [the preceptor] himself stands facing south upon the northern mandala; then, with his divine vision fixed by the root mantra...

Having gazed from the feet up to the top of the head, one should again sprinkle the *arghya* water with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having struck the disciple’s heart with ashes using that same mantra,
and having sprinkled it again three times with water using that same mantra, one should drench [him] with the armor mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, proceeding in order from below the navel upward.

One should mark [the site] three times with the root and tip of *kuśa* grass using the Weapon-mantra (*astra*). Then, having visualized the solar, lunar, and fiery energy-mandalas (*maṇḍala*) within the lotus-heart of the disciple,
one should visualize the individual soul (*jīva*) situated there in the form of a shimmering star.
Having struck the disciple’s self with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having restrained him with the mantra *hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmamūrtaye namaḥ*,

one should worship Śiva on the disciple’s head with the eightfold flower-offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) using white flowers and the like, and apply a mark (*tilaka*) with sandalwood paste on his forehead while reciting the *hṛdaya* [mantra].

Then, having placed a flower in his joined palms, one should— after making the eye-cloth, whether of silk (*dukūla*), cotton (*kārpāsa*), or a new cloth, pure by means of inspection and other rites, consecrated with the root-mantra, veiled with the armor-mantra (*varma*), and protected by the weapon-mantra (*astra*)—
bind his eyes with that cloth using the eye-mantra. Thus says the Āgama:
That eye-bandage which was given so that you might not see others—
that very perception [of them] becomes for you once again the seed of the fetter.
"Therefore, because of that binding of the eyes, there is the shattering of the fetters of the bound soul (paśu).
Having said this, he should then lead the disciple clockwise around and seat him upon the sixfold throne to the right of the Deity.
This self is worthy of attaining the state of Śiva;
with its bonds loosened by my own power, it remains under my control even while it is still caught within the fetters.
I am Śiva, the Lord of boons, who— possessing the form of a liberated mango tree and being worthy of the manifestation of my own qualities— resemble a jewel upon the altar of touch.
Having quickly purified it through contact, like refined gold,
I shall always make it an ornament for my head, endowed with all virtues.
Having thus made this request,

one should strike the disciple’s heart with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* using a flower released from the thumb and forefinger; then, entering his body through the path of the nose, one should purify the disciple’s body— just as in the purification by the five-fold concentration (*pañcadhāraṇā*)— and transform it into the body of Śiva.
Having visualized the offerings, oblations, and meditations within the drops at the navel, one should then approach the Self; then,
having formed a fragrant mandala with the thumb and the palm of the left hand, one should worship Śiva there.
Having recited the root mantra from the heart and other centers up to the knot of the crown, reaching as far as Paraśiva, and having placed the Hand of Śiva upon the head of the disciple;

and having rendered the disciple—who has entered the aperture of Brahmā with the splendor of Śiva—entirely purified of the impurities of the hands by means of that splendor; one should then sit while reciting the root mantra.
Having removed the eye-blindfold,

having caused the disciple to offer a flower to the Goddess Śivā while reciting "In myself," and having led him to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he should seat the disciple on a six-fold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) to his right; then, placing the base of a *kuśa* blade consecrated with the root mantra into the disciple's right hand, [he should place] its tip...

(4th line) He should apply it to his own calf; then, as he renounces [the world], having placed the tip of the *kuśa* grass in his hand, he should apply the root of the *kuśa* grass to his own calf. Thereafter—

Having visualized the three channels as having emerged from the body of the disciple and merged into one's own body, and having worshipped Śiva residing within the fire, one should satisfy the three channels with the mantras: *hāṃ iḍāyai svāhā*, *hāṃ piṅgalāyai svāhā*, and *hāṃ suṣumnāyai svāhā*.
Then, for the sake of stabilizing the Hand of Śiva, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times with *svāhā* at the end.
Having offered oblations amounting to one-tenth of that with the Brahmāṅga mantras ending in *svāhā*, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,

one should offer one hundred and eight oblations along with the *pūrṇāhuti* using the Astra mantra ending in *svāhā* for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Then, by the disciple, [in the presence of] Śiva...

One should perform worship with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). By this, one becomes qualified for the service of the Guru who belongs to the common level of commitment (*sāmānyasamayī*) and so forth. At the end of the body, one attains the world of Śiva. Thus is the procedure for the initiation of the committed practitioner (*samayadīkṣāvidhi*). (8th line) Furthermore, the committed practitioner (*samayī*) is of two kinds: the worldly householder (*laukika*) and the one who has entered the Śaiva stage of life (*śivāśramī*). The Teacher (*deśika*) should instruct both in their common duties. [The first is] another's wife...
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable for others, attachment to what should not be done, speaking untruth,
speaking words that are unwholesome or unpleasant, slandering others, backbiting, eating forbidden food, violence, and adultery with another's wife.
Having abandoned the twelve kinds of sin— divided into mental, verbal, and physical types, such as the seizing of another's property—
one should practice one’s own respective conduct as will be described; therein, according to worldly custom, one should perform the morning *saṃdhyā* worship.
And [he should say] to the one who has entered the Śiva-āśrama: "Worship the gods, the guru, the twice-born, and the devotees of Śiva according to your ability. To the god:
[82b, 1st line]...
for the sake of the god.

One should instruct: "Perform the sweeping and anointing of flower gardens and temples, the offering of lamps, the construction of shrines, the recitation of hymns, circumambulation, and prostration; and serve Śiva, the Guru, and those devoted to them. (Second line)
The Ritual Procedure for the Special Initiation (Viśeṣadīkṣāvidhi)
Now the special initiation (viśeṣadīkṣā) is described:

"Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī; Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvara. Having invoked [the deities] into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and worshipped them, one should offer five oblations for the sake of their presence.
Upon the couch called the principle of Māyā, with the pure path as its pillow,
well-supported by the mattress of the crooked power (kuṭilā-śakti) and the lamp of knowledge (vidyā-dīpa).
The preeminent teacher, being either red or dark-complexioned, should contemplate Śiva.

Then, having sprinkled the disciple with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, he should [strike him] seven times with a flower consecrated by the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, using the mantra: *hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane haḥ huṃ phaṭ*.

Having performed the striking of the heart and the piercing with that very mantra, one enters by means of the *vāmā* [power] with the mantra "hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane haḥ huṃ phaṭ namaḥ"; then, having separated [the soul] by means of the *jyeṣṭhā* [power] with "hāṃ ātmane haḥ huṃ phaṭ", [one recites] "hāṃ haṃ ātmane haḥ".

With the mantra *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* and the goad mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*), the fierce one (*raudrī*) draws [the breath] upward; with *huṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ*, [one says] "I take [it] for myself. Having grasped it with *huṃ phaṭ*, one leads it to the *dvādaśānta* with the mantra *hāṃ haṃ hāṃ namaḥ ātmane* and the goad mudrā.

Having grasped oneself with the *saṃhāramudrā* and, by means of the left [nostril] during inhalation (*pūraka*), having established [the self] within one's own being, and having brought it into a state of aesthetic flavor (*samarasa*) with Śiva through breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), one should lead it— resembling a flaming spark of fire— from the heart and other locations by piercing the knots, up to the end of the upward-pointing power (*ūrdhvaśakti*), while abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, by means of the tip of the root mantra.

(8th line) Having gathered [the breath] with the *pūraka-saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], one should offer salutation to the Self with the mantra "Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ Ātmane Namaḥ" by means of the *udbhava-mudrā* and the *recaka* [breath] through the left [nostril].

Having meditated upon the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva and having properly joined it within the womb of Vāgīśvara for the sake of the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) and so forth, one should visualize it being cast into the womb of Vāgīśvarī, worship it, and—both for the purpose of its presence and for satisfaction—offer five oblations each with the root mantra or with one's own personal mantra (*svāṇu*). Now, [one might ask]: "But how can this be done for the Self (*ātman*), which is partless and all-pervading?"

If it is argued that going and coming are possible because [the Self] is delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the form of a city and the like, and thus movement and arrival are logically established— that is incorrect; for [the Lord] is crooked in His approach to the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) upon the couch of Māyā.

If it were possible for the self to be joined with Śiva—who is stainless, peaceful, and consists of consciousness—while situated upon the covering of the *śakti*, along with the *puryaṣṭaka* which is the effect of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), then let darkness be joined with the sun; therefore, the conjunction of the self with the body of the *puryaṣṭaka* in Śiva is not tenable. Hence, this secret [must be learned] from the mouth of a traditional guru.

One should know [this]. Then, one should infer the sin committed by the disciple from the signs of the fire. Thus says the Āgama: "If there is a foul odor, he is a stealer of land, a killer of a Brahmin, a violator of the Guru’s bed, a drinker of liquor, a slayer of his teacher, a killer of a cow, and a destroyer of what has been done."
If the smoke is black, or smells like a corpse, it portends the destruction of the fetus and the husband.
The fire wanders about when a woman is killed; it trembles when gold is stolen;
it bursts forth when a child is killed; and it becomes lusterless when an embryo is destroyed.
Having recognized the disciple’s impurity by such signs as these,
[he assumed] the form of the deity Pāpabhakṣaṇa, with a luster like crushed collyrium—
licking [his lips], invincible, roaring like a cloud, and exceedingly difficult to conquer.
With mouth wide open and large fangs, wearing red garments and possessing three eyes,
his matted locks and crest were reddish-yellow, and he was adorned with a circle of serpents.
Holding a trident and a sword, terrifying, with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
clad in a tiger skin, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
One should meditate upon the Lord, the destroyer of terrible sins, seated in the *baddhapadmāsana* posture;

having thus meditated upon the deity whose form is the devourer of sin, and having invoked and worshipped Him with the mantra: "To the devourer of sins, who possesses the sky, the earth, the six realms, the forest, and the mountain—svāhā."
One should offer more than a hundred oblations in accordance with the gravity or lightness of that sin.

"O Sadāśiva, through your grace toward sentient beings, may this twice-born man—purified in his disposition and food, and possessing purity of seed and womb—become a portion of Rudra. Thus [he prays].
Thereafter, he should inform [the disciple] and consecrate the disciple with the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *garbhādhāna*. For example:
"Whatever sentient beings there may be, who abide within all principles (*tattva*)."
So many indeed are the divisions recorded for the bodiless one who resides within the body.
O Six-faced One, whatever be the form of their names and origins here,
one should know that Śiva exists within those bodies in a form corresponding to them—
gross like a shadow-form, yet subtler than the subtle.
He is the formless one, utterly beyond form, through his partless and exceedingly subtle forms.
Furthermore, for the purpose of effecting his status as a twice-born, there is the meditation upon him as a portion of Rudra;
likewise, there is the seed-syllable, the purification of food, the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), and the rite of male-creation (*puṃsavana*).
In the *sīmantonnayana*, the *jātakarman*, and the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*),

one should offer oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred times for each of the five Brahmans. At the conclusion of the naming ceremony oblation, [the teacher should place] a flower with the hand of the disciple within the mandala of the five Brahmans and six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Having caused those flowers to fall, one should assign a name according to the mantra corresponding to that mandala, up to the end of the [deity’s] name.
Likewise, at the time of the exit, the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony (caulakarma), [the name should be assigned].
At the initiation, the instruction of vows, the godāna ceremony, and the rite of ritual bathing.
O Nandikeśvara, in the case of marriage, forest-dwelling, and the state of a mendicant,
