one should perform a fire-offering (*homa*) for each with the fifty-syllable root mantra immediately after the consecration of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-saṃskāra*) and the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*).

The preeminent teacher should offer oblations with the root mantra as before for those who have visited both the household and the forest stages, and especially for those who have reached the state of a householder.
For those established in the four stages of life, the limit [of the rite] corresponds to the specific duration of each respective stage.
"One should indeed perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*); from this point onward, one should not cause it to be performed.

Following that, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, having gone by way of the *vāmā* or the *raudrī*, having extracted oneself from the womb of Vāgīśī, having placed one's own self within oneself by means of the *vāmā*, and having made it of one flavor with the *jyeṣṭhā*—
Having led [the breath] through Raudrī to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], and having performed the purificatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*,

one should duly unite the Self, in the form of a throbbing light, with the body of the disciple. Then, having offered a drop of water from the *arghya* vessel for nourishment upon the disciple’s head,
and having worshipped and gratified Vāgīśī and Vāgīśvara, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*.

Having performed one hundred and eight oblations with the Astra-mantra, together with the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), for the sake of expiation, [the preceptor] says: "You have become fit for the study and hearing of the Siddhānta, as well as for the worship of Śiva, the Fire, and the Guru. Having spoken thus, he gives a *bāṇaliṅga* for the purpose of worship.
[One should not abandon] Śiva, the Śiva-scripture, the Śiva-fire, and likewise the Guru.
One should not transgress even the shadow of those who are censurable, under any circumstances whatsoever.
"One should instruct: 'The worship of Śiva, Agni, and the Guru must be performed for as long as one lives.

Thereafter, one should purify children, the ignorant, the elderly, and the sick according to the rule, as follows: HĀṂ, obeisance to Ananta and the other Lords of Knowledge; HĀṂ, obeisance to Nandin and the other Gaṇas; HĀṂ, obeisance to Indra and the other World-Protectors. (84a)

Having worshipped with "namaḥ" in the fire, having gratified each [deity] with one oblation of clarified butter, and having offered a hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purification of the observance (*samaya*), he should offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
"O Blessed One, this transgression in the observance of the conduct of the samaya is not worthy [of you].
Therefore, through this fire-offering (*homa*), may you grant forgiveness for all of that. Thus one should petition.
And elsewhere:
Having thus made the lords of knowledge, the lords of the hosts, fire, and the world-protectors his witnesses,
the best of teachers should purify his observance (*samaya*);
[this concludes] the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-vrata*).
Thereafter, if he desires the vow of lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*), one should grant him the [appropriate] conduct.
"The wearing of matted hair (*jaṭā*) and the smearing with ashes belong to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriya, there is the triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*) and a single lock of matted hair. Thus [it is said].
According to the scriptural injunction,
he should wear a single sacred thread (*upavīta*). In the manner to be described hereafter, he should tie his hair into a single braid (*jaṭā*), or alternatively,
he should perform a complete tonsure.
"By merely wearing the Vedic mantras on the topknot and the sacred thread,
a Śūdra brings about the destruction of the king and the kingdom through the reversal of their proper purpose.
Thus it is stated in the scripture.

Based on the statement, "For a Śūdra, a single-strand [cord] is prescribed by means of an Āgama mantra," the sacred thread (*upavīta*) consists of a single strand. The matted locks, the sacred thread, ashes, the loincloth, and the staff— the water-pot being an auxiliary of the vow— constitute this vow for the ascetic.
"Because of the statement: 'The entire sixfold set of limbs of the vow, as well as the matted hair and so forth, are indeed appropriate.

Having placed the staff, loincloth, ashes, sacred thread, and crest-jewel into the vessel and consecrated them with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, one performs the *sampātahoma* with the *Śivasaṃhitā* ending in *svāhā*, and [offers] the limb of the vow to the Śiva-pitcher for a moment."
Having requested, "O Blessed One, grant me permission, saying, 'I shall bestow this vow upon him after establishing him for protection,'" and having received that authorization,
he should bestow it upon him. He too, having prostrated before the preceptor and undertaken the ancillaries of the vow, should remain a practitioner of the vow for as long as he lives,
or else for a specified period of time after making a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

When the determined period has concluded, one should immediately worship Vrateśvara. Having resolved upon the duration according to the previously mentioned rule, including the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one should perform the sacrifice to Vrateśvara at the end and thereafter proceed with marriage. According to this statement, one should maintain [the vow] either for as long as one lives or for twelve years, having made the formal resolution (*saṃkalpa*). When that resolved period has come to an end...
(10th line) Having fully worshipped Īśvara, one should perform the marriage ceremony.
[The author] now states the sequence for the vow of lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya-vrata*).
In the inconceivable [reality] called Viśvasādākhya, celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is indeed twofold: the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*) and the temporary (*bhautika*).
Lifelong celibacy lasts from birth until the end of life.
Or else, he may have matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot;
during the month of Pauṣa, he should wear a girdle, a sacred thread, and carry a staff, his body smeared with ashes.
One whose body is marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) and adorned with rudrākṣa beads,
who is disciplined in his senses and engaged in ritual bathing— whether at the three times of day or once a day—
who speaks the truth, sleeps on the ground, is endowed with forbearance, and is firm in his vows; ||| (2nd line) ||| [he is a true devotee].
He was devoted to the service of his guru and intent on carrying out his commands.
Subsisting on alms for the sake of maintaining the body, he should eat only once a day at the house of his guru;
likewise, he should avoid betel, collyrium, bathing, turmeric, salt, wooden sandals, a crown, perfumes, and garlands.
One should always dwell in the place of the Guru; one should not sleep in another's house.
Having abandoned the doctrine of autonomy, one who is united with the autonomy of the Guru [attains] the field of merit, the sacred ford, meditation, and likewise ritual action and so forth.
Furthermore, even the constant display of great compassion and all such acts as austerity and charity are fruitless if they are devoid of the Guru’s command.
Therefore, with every effort, one should observe the command of the guru;
for this is lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*). Thus concludes the procedure for the special initiation (*viśeṣa-dīkṣā*).
Now, the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*) is described.

The initiation into Nirvāṇa is twofold: the worldly and that which possesses the nature of Śiva. That which is without the cutting of the topknot is to be known as possessing the nature of the world of light (Sālokadharmiṇī).
The initiation associated with the cutting of the topknot is that which conforms to the Śiva-dharma;
for the worldly initiation, the Guru should initiate those belonging to the material elements.
Having performed the initiation previously described, which purifies the observances (*samaya*) and so forth,
one should contemplate the enjoyment within the pure path in the supreme reality of dissolution.

The naiṣṭhikī initiation is likewise twofold, according to whether it follows the path of Śivadharmī or the naiṣṭhika path. The Guru should initiate one into the naiṣṭhika state when the path up to Māyā has been purified, or when the path is entirely pure.
That initiation which is performed with desire is called "with seed" (sabījā); at the end of its portion, it bestows liberation.
But that initiation of one who is free from desire, which occurs without ritual action on the path, is the destroyer of all fetters; it is seedless (*nirbījā*) and bestows non-duality.
In that case, the fruit previously acquired reaches the state of having its seeds burnt away.
The darkness that has overwhelmed him must be suppressed like the potency of poison;
once his body has begun to dissolve through the enjoyment [of the fruits of karma], he shall go to the state of Śiva.

Immediately after the initiation into the specific *samaya*, once the Lord of the Sacrifice (*yāgeśa*) has been dismissed, for the disciple who desires the initiation into *nirvāṇa*, one should again perform the initiation into the specific *samaya* and then effect the satisfaction and illumination of the mantra by means of the piercing of his bonds. In the sacrifice... (85a, 1st line).
But when the mantra-satiating and mantra-illumination rites have not yet been released, the disciple, having gone into the presence of Śiva and worshipped Śiva, [says]:
"O Blessed One, this one has been examined by me while you were presiding over the assembly;
he is of noble birth, a portion of Rudra for a very long time, and established in the observance."
One who is afflicted yet desires nirvāṇa, tormented by the suffering of existence, and whose mind is pure—
over this person, O Lord of Radiance, bestow your empowerment for the sake of liberation.

Having thus made this request and having meditated, "I am Śiva," one should place the initiate— who has bathed, fasted, joined his palms in reverence, and faces east— upon the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) in the southern mandala of both the sacrificial pit and oneself;
then, placing him facing north with his body upright, [one should apply mantras] to the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet of that initiate.

He should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *kalās* beginning with Śāntyatītā, using their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), [conceiving them] as containing the syllables of the minister (*mantrin*), the feet, the worlds (*bhuvana*), and the principles (*tattva*). Having performed the placement on the feet, the private parts, the heart, the face, and the head,
he should then perform the placement of the *kalās* beginning with Nivṛtti.
As it is said in the *Anirvāṇottara*:
"In this world, mantras are pervaded on all sides by words, which in turn consist of phonemes;
those [words] are pervaded by the worlds, and those [worlds] are pervaded by the principles (*tattva*)."
"The genus of the principles is likewise pervaded by the kalās;
therefore, having conceived their internal inclusion, the kalās must be purified with effort.
Thus [it is said].

(The binding with the noose-thread, etc. Thereafter, the triple-stranded thread prepared by a brahmin maiden is folded three times over; the noose-thread is washed and dried with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and then sprinkled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and scented water using that same mantra.

Having sprinkled [the disciple] with *arghya* water and worshipped him with the root mantra, one should bind the lock of hair (*śikhā*) of the worldly seeker (*bhautika*) with the mantra "Hauṃ, obeisance to Śakti," and then let it hang down as far as his big toe. For the sake of liberation, for one who is renouncing,
[it should hang] from the big toe up to the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Having extended it, one should bind it at the crest-lock [of the disciple] with the mantra "Hauṃ Śaktaye Namaḥ.
Then, having integrated that entire thread with the mantras, one should contemplate the cord of bonds as the form of the disciple's representative image. Thus says the Āgama.

"Those nooses are both to be cut and unbreakable in the context of the Sūtra-sthāna and in the disputation; therefore, the body composed of the thread must be meditated upon by the teachers. Following that, [one says]: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Kriyā-śakti. Having worshipped [the deity] within the disciple's body and having drawn the Self [into it] by means of striking and other rites, [one places it] upon the thread.

Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) and worship, having restrained [the breath] and worshipped in the fire, having restrained it again and enveloped it (*avakuṇṭhya*), one should worship and offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) in the fire. Then, within that body, one should worship with: "Hāṃ, obeisance to Iḍā; Hāṃ, obeisance to Piṅgalā; Hāṃ, obeisance to Suṣumnā. (85b, 1st line)

Having performed the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), and after the specific entry through the striking and piercing [of the centers] with mantras such as "HĀM IḌĀYAI HUṂPHAṬ," one should take [the consciousness] from the disciple’s body— which resembles a lotus fiber— by means of the *pūraka* and *saṃhāriṇī* [breaths], and place it upon the thread.

Having joined [the breaths], worshipped, restrained, and veiled [them], having fully worshipped [the fire] and projected the Self [into it], and having satiated the channels within it—having thus projected [the mantras] with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā; Hīṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; Hūṃ, obeisance to Raudrī"—one should worship in the fire.

Having worshipped [the thread] and offered five oblations each for the purpose of satiation (*tarpaṇa*) and for bringing [the deity] into proximity (*sannidhi*), one should again place it upon the thread, conceal it (*avakuṇṭhya*), and perform the separation of the fetters (*piśa-śleṣaṇādika*) with those [oblations]. Thus says the Āgama: "The three powers of Śambhu are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. (4th line)
"In the extraction of the union and separation [of phonemes], his vigor remains unimpeded everywhere.
(This is the sequence for the placement of power in the Sūtra.
Thereafter, having worshipped the triad of mandalas beginning with the Sun within the lotus of the disciple's heart with the Heart-mantra.

Having performed *pūraka* [inhalation], having placed the Self situated in the fire within the three threads (*trisūtra*), having worshipped it, restrained it, and veiled it, and having worshipped it also in the fire, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and offered libations, one should worship with "Hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" (*vidyādeha*), and then, taking it up by means of striking and other rites, [place it] upon the thread.

Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should prepare the water for offering (*arghya*) and so forth. (This is the sequence for self-consecration according to the *Sūtra*. Then, having sprinkled the disciple with the water for offering and consecrated him seven times with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [one should recite] *hāṃ haṃ*.

Saying "Hāṃ! To the self, Haḥ! Uṃ Phaṭ!", one should strike the disciple’s heart with a flower. Having visualized the hand and oneself as this [mantra], and having performed the piercing (*vibheda*) with that very mantra, one should visualize the self as moving from the calyx of the heart-lotus. Then, saying "Huṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ Haḥ Huṃ Phaṭ Namaḥ," [the self] exits from one's own body by means of the exhalation (*recaka*) and enters that [disciple].

Having entered that heart with the *pūraka* [breath] by means of the two *ayā*s, saying "Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ Ātmane Haḥ Huṃ Phaṭ," one should separate the Self from the calyx of that heart-lotus by means of the *kumbhaka* [retention] through the *jyeṣṭhā* [finger], saying "Huṃ Hāṃ Huṃ Ātmane."

Having drawn [the deity] in with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* while reciting "Namaḥ svāhā," and having led it to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *raudrī* breath through exhalation (*recaka*), one should grasp it with the mantra "Huṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmānaṃ gṛhṇāmi haḥ huṃ phaṭ. Then, saying "Hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ," one should take up the self situated within the power at the end of dissolution (*layānta-śakti*) and, by means of the *svapāmā* [mudrā], place it within one's own self; finally, making it of one flavor (*samarasīkṛtya*) through retention (*kumbhaka*).

Having separated [the self] from the *jyeṣṭhā* [power] by means of the *raudrī* [power] through exhalation (*recaka*), one should lead the self— situated at the tip of the root-mantra as *hāṃ*, resembling a blazing fire— in sequence, by piercing the knots of the heart and other centers, up to the end of the upward-pointing power (*ūrdhva-śakti*) at one's own *dvādaśānta*.

Having gathered [the self] from there by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [breath] through *pūraka*, having led it to the space between the eyebrows by means of the *sṛṣṭi* [breath], and having expelled it through the *piṅgalā* by means of *recaka* with the mantra "Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Self," one performs the burning of the bonds such as impurity (*mala*) in the fire-pit. Having joined the black self, which is the body of the thread, by means of the *udbhava-mudrā*, one should contemplate the self as pervading the thread.

Having worshipped [the deity], restrained [the breath], and enveloped [it with the armor-mantra], one should worship [the fire] and offer libations; then, one should present five oblations for the purpose of invoking the presence, following which one worships in the fire with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā;
Hīṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; Hrūṃ, obeisance to Raudrī," ending each with *svāhā*.
(Third line) One should offer five oblations for each [deity].
(In the Sūtra: the sequence for joining the nooses, such as the garland and so forth.)

Following that: *Hāṃ*, obeisance to the impurity-noose (*malapāśa*), the cause of the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). *Hāṃ*, obeisance to the black-colored karma-nooses (*karmapāśa*), the causes for the experience of pleasure and pain. *Hāṃ*, obeisance to the white and black forms, the illusion-noose (*māyāpāśa*), the cause of the body and its objects. *Hāṃ*, [obeisance to] camphor, the power (*śakti*) presiding over the impurity-noose.

Having taken the form of *tamas* from the disciple with the syllable *namaḥ*, having joined it to the thread, having worshipped it, restrained it, and enveloped it, and having worshipped it in the fire, one should offer five oblations for each of the three impurities (*mala*) for the sake of their presence.

Thereafter, [reciting] "Hāṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (vidyādeha)," one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the body of knowledge. Then, having joined [the mantra] "Hāṃ, obeisance to Tirobhāvikā and Kuṭilāśakti" to the crest-lock (śikhā) on the sacrificial thread (iṣvāsūtra), and having worshipped, restrained, and encircled it, and having worshipped it in the fire, one should offer five oblations for the sake of its presence (sannidhāna).

(The sequence for joining the *śāntyatīta* power to the consciousness residing in the thread: One should join the *śāntyatīta* [power] to the consciousness residing in the thread. For example: *hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ*.

Having observed, "Salutation to the noose of the *śāntyatīta* power," [one joins it] directly to the principles of *nāda*, *tattva*, and *bindu*, because they are presided over by the Śiva-principle and its Power (*śakti*).

In this Śivatattva, which is designated as both Śivatattva and Śaktitattva, there are the worlds of the Śaktikalā: Anāśritā, Anāthā, Anantā, Vyomarūpā, Vyāpinī, and Ūrdhvagāminī. Then there are the worlds of the Nādakalā: Rocikā, Mocikā, Dīpikā, and Iṇḍikā. Within the Śivatattva, there are the worlds of the Bindukalā: Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Vṛtti. (Lines 8–9)

In the Śakti-tattva, there are fifteen worlds with names identical to those of the Rudras. The sixteen phonemes are: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ. The first syllable, Oṃ, is a single word. The eleven words beginning with the Praṇava are to be meditated upon by the intermediate Śaivas within the five Kalās. [This does not apply to] the Ācāryas. [The mantras are]: hauṃ, hoṃ, haḥ.
The mantras of Śiva, Īśāna, and Astra; the *nāda* and *hakāra* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*). *Ku* and *kū* are the two channels (*nāḍī*), namely Śaṅkhinī, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.

The two winds are Vāk and Śrotrendriya; the object (*viṣaya*) is sound (*śabda*). Sound is the quality (*guṇa*). The figure (*vṛtta*) is the circle (*maṇḍala*). The state is that which transcends the fourth (*turyātītāvasthā*).

Sadāśiva; the Lord of Causes. Having meditated upon the Kalā Śāntyatītā as joined with these [deities], [one recites]: *Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ*, obeisance to the noose of the Kalā Śāntyatītā. *Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ*, obeisance to the two principles of Śakti and Śiva. *Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ*, [obeisance] to the fifteen worlds presided over by the powers beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Nivṛtti.

Namaḥ | Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ Akārādiḥ | (3rd line) Namaḥ to the sixteen phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *a*. Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ Namaḥ to the *yoṅkāra* word of the Transcendent (*sarvātīta*) and the Beyond-Transcendent (*turyātīta*). Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ Haḥ Namaḥ to the mantras of Śiva, Īśāna, and the Weapon (*astra*). Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ | (4th line)

Salutation to the seed-syllable *Ha*. Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the two channels, Kuhū and Śaṅkhinī. Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the two vital airs, Devadatta and Dhanañjaya. Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the two sense organs, hearing and speech. Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ... (5th line)
Salutation to the word of the object (*viṣaya-śabda*).

Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the quality of sound (*dhvani-guṇa*). Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the sphere of space (*vyoma-maṇḍala*), which is crystal-like in form and whose essence is the void (*avakāśātman*). Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the power of the point and resonance (*bindu-nāda-śakti*), which is self-spherical.
Salutation to her whose measure is ten thousand, one hundred thousand, and ten million *yojanas*. Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva, the Cause.
Having worshipped those whose nature consists of the *pratīkha* [the reverse], who are white, and who possess the crescent moon, the bindu, the nāda, and the *kuṭila* [the curved] form;
and having grasped them with the *pūraka-saṃhāriṇī* [the breath-retention that withdraws], one should join them to the thread extending from the crown of the head to the forehead and worship them.
Having extinguished [the fire], covered it, and worshipped it, one should offer five oblations for the sake of its presence.
(This is the sequence for the conjunction with the Śāntikalā.
Thereafter, *hāṃ hyaiṃ* (the eighth line).

Having observed with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the Śāntikalā," one should first [visualize] the Sadāśiva-tattva; above that, however, there is another auspicious reality consisting of all sovereignty—
the supreme Sadāśiva-tattva, as pure as clear crystal.
There dwells the Blessed Lord Hara, the master of all principles;
he is Sadāśiva himself, pervading the world, the supreme one whose form consists of mantra.
Endowed with infinite splendor, possessing an immeasurable succession of qualities,
enjoying infinite power, and seated upon an infinite throne;
(10th line) Sadāśiva’s world is one, while within the principle of Sadāśiva is the second, the principle of Īśvara.
Then, above that, there is yet another enclosure, that of the Vidyeshas;
it has the luster of a blazing fire, slightly red, and perfectly pure.
The eight Vidyeśvaras and Skanda abide therein, bestowing sovereign powers;
they resemble sparks of fire, blazing with smokeless rays.
Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin—
these are the eight worlds of the Vidyeśvaras within the principle of Īśvara. Above that, O Six-faced One, there exists another principle, the principle of Vidyā.
Resembling the pomegranate flower, it is somewhat yellow and perfectly pure.
In that regard, the lords of knowledge (*vidyādhipas*) should be known as having a radiance equal to the red lotus;
they are intensely blazing, stainless, subtle, all-pervading, and facing in every direction.

Mandomanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, Balapramathinī, Balavikaraṇī, Kalavikaraṇī, Kālī, Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Yāmā— these are the nine worlds within the principle of Śuddhavidyā. Thus, there are eighteen worlds associated with the Rudras.
The letters ka, kha, and ga share the same names and places of articulation. [Salutation] to Vyomavyāpin, whose form is space;
to Śiva, the all-pervading, the infinite, the lordless, the non-dependent, the fixed, the eternal, who is established upon the seat of yoga, the perpetual yogin whose nourishment is meditation.

Thus, these are the twelve words: *hema* and *haima*, the *tatpuruṣa* and *kavaca* mantras. (Line 6) The seed-syllables are the bindu and the letter *ya*. The channels are the *alambuṣā* and *yaśasvinī*. The winds are the *kṛkara* and *kūrma*. The sense organs are the skin and the feet. The object of perception is touch.

The qualities are sound and touch; the fourth state; the hexagon, a black circle. (7th line) The Lord who is the cause of Īśvara. Having meditated upon the Śāntikalā together with these, [one recites]: *Hāṃ Haiṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the Śāntikalā*.
*Hāṃ Hyaiṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and the principle of Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā-tattva)*.
HĀṂ HYAIṂ:

Salutation to the eighteen worlds presided over by the powers beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Vāmā. HĀṂ HAIṂ HĀṂ: Salutation to the phonemes Ka, Kha, Ga, and Va. HĀṂ HAIṂ HĀṂ: To those endowed with the Bindu and the Fourth State, O Vyomavyāpin.

Salutation to the twelve words ending with *dhyānahārānta* and beginning with *ityādi*. Salutation to the two mantras of Tatpuruṣa and Kavaca: *hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ*. Salutation to the seed-syllable (*bīja*) *hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ*. Salutation to Alampuruṣa and Īśāna and the others: *hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ*. (10th line)

Hāṃ Hyaiṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the black wind-maṇḍala, possessing six dots (ṣaṭbindu), hexagonal in shape, and measuring one hundred thousand crores of yojanas. Hāṃ Hyaiṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the cause that is Īśvara. Having worshipped Śyāmala— (87b, first line)

Having taken [the breath] through the *pūraka* and *saṃhāriṇī* [processes], one should join it to the thread from the mouth to the heart, worship it, restrain it, and veil it; then, having worshipped it in the fire as well, one should offer five oblations for the sake of its presence.
(This is the sequence for the conjunction with the *vidyā-kalā*.)
Thereafter,
having first observed the *māyā-tattva* with "HĀṂ HRŪṂ HĀṂ VIDYĀKALĀPĀŚĀYA NAMAḤ," he describes that portion which is the nature of the impure *māyā*, the agitated part.
But above and below, there is another principle, Māyā, which is very difficult to traverse;
it pierces the shell of the cosmic egg and possesses a luster like that of yellow orpiment.
He describes the nature of that power of ego-inflation (*abhimāna-śakti*):
"In its center resides the Goddess Māyā, who possesses many forms, by whom indeed the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—is deluded. (4th line)
Resembling sapphire in appearance and enveloped by a network of rays,
it was surrounded by thousands and tens of millions of shimmering drops amidst the darkness.

Therein, the names of the eight Rudras are: Bhuvana, Gopati, Trikāla, Mahāvīrya, Daśana, Haya, Hali, and Asādhya; these are the names equal [to those] of the Rudras. The second is the principle of Time (Kālatattva), resembling a dark cloud and possessing a luster like blue collyrium.

In its center stands Time (Kāla), the fierce one who brings an end to all people. With formidable fangs, a terrible mouth, tawny eyebrows, and blood-red pupils, he is crestless and the sole hero. Thus, there are two worlds within the state of Time (kālagata). The third is the principle of Necessity (niyati-tattva); the fourth is the principle of Limited Agency (kalā-tattva).
There is an inseparable connection between destiny (niyati) and limited agency (kalā). Now, above that, there is another [sheath] known as the covering of limited agency (kalā-āvaraṇa).
O Guha, it is white, yellow, red, black, and in some places a mixture of these colors.
In its center, one should know there is a digit (kalā), anointed with variegated colors;
she is rich in diverse ornaments and jewels, and fond of various garlands and garments.
Therein resides Rudra, the all-pervading, the omnipresent, the omniscient, the illuminator of knowledge;
he is blue and red in color, yet in some respects resembles the white moon.
The end of the five is Śuddhavidyā; these two worlds belong to the principle of Niyati.
Having withdrawn the two luminous worlds, there are the two worlds within Kāla. The fifth is the principle of Vidyā.
Now, that which exists above this is known as Vidyeśvara.
Resembling the wrath of Indra and in some places possessing the luster of gold,
in its center resides the Vidyā— pervasive, universal in form,
multiform, the protectress of the universe, and she who moves within the secret state.

Her limbs are variegated with the foundation of the mandala; her long eyes are restless in meditation; her breath is the true essence of the scriptures; and her mass of hair is composed of medicinal herbs. Then, Śiva alone stands above them all.

Caṇḍa and Krodha—these two worlds belong to Vidyā; the sixth principle is Rāga. Below and above, however, there is another known as Rāgāvaraṇa, which resembles saffron water and has the appearance of saffron pollen.
There dwells the Blessed One Passion, resembling a hibiscus flower;
he is the colorer of all principles, the object of knowledge, and exceedingly difficult to conquer.

Īśāna, Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa, Udbhava, Bhaya, and Vāmadeva—these five are the worlds within the principle of Rāga. The seventh is the principle of Puruṣa. Ekavīra, Pañcāntaka, Piṅgasūra-ga, Jyotis, Caṇḍasaṃvarta, and the one called Krodheśa—these six [are the worlds] within the principle of Krodha.

(4th line) The worlds [exist] within the principle of Puruṣa. Because the principle of Puruṣa—the Self—exists as the very essence of the Self, endowed with qualities, and because it abides by way of connection within the Self itself under the name of the "impurity of masculinity" (*puṃstvamala*), they exist precisely upon the head of Prakṛti through the sense of proximity; thus, there are twenty-seven.

(5th line) [The worlds] with the Rudras; names that are identical; the seven phonemes are ghaṃ, ḍa, ca, cha, ja, jña, and tra. Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, the source of all, to Śiva whose head is Īśāna, whose face is Tatpuruṣa, and whose heart is Aghora. (6th line)

To the one whose secret is Vāmadeva, whose form is Sadyojāta— Oṃ, salutations again and again! To the one whose secret consists of the qualities and so forth, to the Protector, to the giver of the unestablished, to the one presiding over all yoga, to the Lord of all sciences, to the one whose nature is light, to the Supreme Lord of Rāma—
in the sky of the conscious and the unconscious, in the sky, in the sky!

Thus, these twenty-one words, *huṃ phaṭ*, are the two mantras of Aghoraśikha. The seed-syllables are *ma* and *ra*. Pūṣan is the hand; the tongue and the channel (*nāḍī*). Vyāna is the navel; Vāyu is the eye, the hand, and the sense-organ (*indriya*). (8th line) The objects are form (*rūpa*); sound, touch, and form are the qualities (*guṇa*). The triangle is the red-colored fire-mandala.

The state of deep sleep is Rudra, the Lord of the Cause. Having meditated upon the Vidyā-kalā as accompanied by these [deities], [one should offer salutation] with *hrāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ* to the noose of the Vidyā-kalā with the mantra:
*vidyākalāpāśāya namaḥ*.

Hrūṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seven principles beginning with Māyā and ending with Puruṣa-tattva. Hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, salutation to the twenty-seven worlds of peace, beginning with Gopatya and ending with Krodha. Hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seven phonemes beginning with the letter *gha* and ending with the letter *ña*. Hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, together with the letter *ma*...

Salutation to those accompanied by Suṣṭhupati. Salutation to the twenty-one words beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *vyomin*. (88b, first line) Salutation to the two mantras *hāṃ hrūṃ huṃ hrūṃ hāṃ* and *agho...*. Salutation to the seed-syllable *hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ raṃ*. Salutation to the two channels, Puruṣa and Hastijihvā. Salutation to Vyāna and the Nāga wind.

Namaḥ | Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ (second line) | Homage to the two sense organs of sight and hand. Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ | Homage to the object of form. Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ | Homage to the qualities of sound, touch, and form. Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ | To the red fire-maṇḍala.

Homage to the one who desires his own burning and food, who is triangular, and whose measure is ten million times ten thousand yojanas; homage to the cause of Rudra, Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ. Having thus worshipped the author of the Itihāsas.

Having [performed] the *pūraka* and *saṃhāriṇī* [breaths], having joined [the deity] along the thread from the heart to the end of the navel, having worshipped, restrained, and concealed [the deity], and having worshipped [him] in the fire, one should offer five oblations for the sake of making [the deity] present.
(The sequence for joining the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*)

Thereafter, having first observed with "Hāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the bond of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā," [one should contemplate: Nature (*prakṛti*), the manifest (*vyakta*), and the Great One (*mahat*)—
the state known as the severing of the qualities (*guṇacchitta*)— are a single reality (*tattva*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇātmaka*).
Above that, however, there is another [element] known as the veil of qualities (guṇāvaraṇa),
which has the form of pure crystal and great sapphire gems.
Residing within the worlds corresponding to those [three] colors are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
whose forms are presided over by the qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva respectively.
The Śrīkaṇṭha, Aumikau māra, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Bhairava, and Kṛta worlds—

these eight worlds situated in the directions starting from Īśāna and ending with the East constitute the second [layer]. Furthermore, above that is another [layer] known as the Buddhyāvaraṇa, which is the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*).
Resembling the rising sun and possessing a luster equal to the glow of twilight,
the Intellect (*buddhi*) stands in its midst— pervasive, universal in form,
endowed with the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇiman*, and possessed of the energy of contentment (*tuṣṭi*).
The Brahma, the Prajeśvara, the Saumya, the Aindra, and the Gandharva [astras].

The eight classes of divine beings—namely the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas—are situated in the directions starting from Īśāna and ending with the East. At the summit of the intellect associated with the qualities (guṇas) is the third principle, the ego (ahaṅkāra).
O Six-faced One, both the lower and the upper realms consist of that which is produced by the ego (ahaṅkārya).
Resembling a blazing fire, it was terrifying in its roar and difficult to approach.
The great *liṅga* Sthūleśvara, Mahātejā, Nīlakaṇṭha, Śrīkaṇṭha, Mahān, Utkaṭa, Ūrdhvaretas, and Kapardin—

these are the eight worlds situated in the directions starting from Īśāna and ending with the East, consisting of the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), the sense organs (*indriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

In the principle of *ahaṃkāra*, which serves as the cause, is the fourth principle, the *manas* (mind). [The faculties are] the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose; speech, the feet, the hands, the anus, and the generative organ; and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. [Then there is] the principle of *ākāśa*.
Furthermore, above and below... (2nd line)
It would be established as being like the sky—immeasurable and indescribable, like another state of liberation.
There dwells the Blessed Lord, the Great Lord Maheśvara, whose form is the ether;
he is subtle in nature yet vast, and is surrounded by the eight purifiers.
Sthāṇu is the thousand-eyed one; Śiva is the one of great strength. Rudramūrti is the great yogin Bhava—these are Īśāna and the others.
The eight worlds situated at the eastern end and so forth reside in the element of space (*ākāśatva*). Then there is the element of air (*vāyutatva*).
Above that, there shall be another, the enclosure of air (*vāyavyāvaraṇa*).
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with a luster like that of crushed collyrium.
There dwells your lord Vāyu, black-hued like collyrium, fortunate, able to assume any form at will, and surrounded by the eight secret ones:
Mahābhīma, Mahānāda, Viśeṣa, Ugra, Svayambhu, Pitāmaha, Kāmarūpin, and Subhaga.

The eight worlds situated in the directions starting from Īśāna and ending with the East reside within the element of air (*vāyutatva*). Then there is the element of fire (*tejastatva*). Having taken up the pure space (*ākāśa*) which possesses the sound of thundering clouds, the Blessed Lord Agni dwells there, surrounded by the eight secret ones (*guhyāṣṭaka*).
Resembling a ruby (*padmarāga*) and blazing with that splendor,

[he is] Bhairava, Kedāra, Īśāna, Mahākāla, Sūkṣma, Triśūlī, Tripuraghna, and Hara— these are the eight worlds situated in the directions starting from Īśāna and ending with the East, within the principle of fire (*tejastattva*). The principle of water (*aptattva*).
Resounding with the noise of crashing waves and agitated by whirlpools and billows,
there dwells the Blessed Lord Varuṇa, born of nectar—
Lakuṭīśvara, Bhārabhūti, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍī, Āṣāḍha, Bhojagandha, Devadeva, and Śaśibhūṣaṇa.

The syllable *oṃ* [is the first]. From Īśāna to the eastern end, the locations of the directions (*diksthāna*) are likewise fifty-six worlds (*bhuvana*) within the element of water (*aptattva*), possessing names identical to those of the Rudras. The phonemes (*varṇa*) are twenty-three: *aṃ, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha*. [They are] formless (*arūpin*)... [and so on]... the first of the first; light upon light (*tejastejaḥ*). (10th line)
Light of lights; formless; without fire; smokeless; ashless; without food; manifold, manifold; dhū-dhū dhū-dhū; Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ suvaḥ;
without end, without end; source of the end; Śiva; Śarva; Supreme Self; Maheśvara; Mahādeva.

Sat-bhāveśvara, Mahātejas, Yogādhipati, muñca muñca, prathama prathama, śarva śarva—these are the thirty-two words. Hiṃ hīṃ. Vāmadeva and Śaśarasumantra. Vu va (.. are the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Gāndhārī and Suṣumnā are the channels (*nāḍī*).

Udāna and Samāna; the organs of wind, tongue, and anus; the element of taste; the objects of sound, touch, form, and taste; the qualities; the subtle body (*śūkṣma-deha*); the half-moon mandala; the state of dream; Viṣṇu as the Lord of Causes—together with these...
Having meditated upon the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā:

HĀṂ BHAṂ (HAṂ) HĀṂ, obeisance to the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā. HĀṂ HĪṂ HĀṂ, obeisance to the twenty-three principles beginning with *citta* and ending with *jala*. HĀṂ HLĪṂ HĀṂ, [obeisance] to the fifty-six [deities] beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with Oṃkāra.
(4th line) Salutation to the worlds!
Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, salutation to the twenty-three syllables beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*! Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to those accompanied by the dreams of the letter *U*. Salutation to the thirty-two words beginning with "Vyāpin" and ending with "Śarva. Salutation to the two mantras of Vāmadeva and Śira: *Hāṃ Hlīṃ Hiṃ Hīṃ Hāṃ*. Salutation to the seed-syllable *Ya*: *Hāṃ Hlīṃ Hāṃ Ya*. [Salutation to] Gandhārī-Suṣumnā: *Hāṃ Hlīṃ Hāṃ*.
Salutation to the two *nāḍīs*. Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, salutation to the *udāna* and *samāna* vital airs. Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, salutation to the organs of the tongue and the anus.
Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, salutation to the object of taste. (7th line)

Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, salutation to the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste. Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, salutation to the white water-maṇḍala, whose essence is fluidity, which is shaped like a half-moon and measures one thousand million *yojanas*. Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the cause. Having worshipped these white [elements], one should take them up through the *pūraka-saṃhāriṇī* [breath-retention].

Having joined [the thread] at the inner part of the knees, having worshipped, restrained, and veiled it, and having worshipped it over the fire, one should offer five oblations for the purpose of bringing about the presence [of the deity].
(The sequence for joining the *nivṛtti* level.)

Thereafter, having visualized with "Hāṃ Hlāṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the Nivṛtti-kalā," one perceives the single Earth-tattva. This Earth-tattva is golden, possessing a brilliance equal to ten thousand suns, shaped like a hen’s egg; this is called the Brahmāṇḍa.

The principle of the earth (*urvī-tattva*), which has the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) together with the fourteen worlds— namely Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Rasātala, Mahātala, Talātala, Pātāla, Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—
has as its presiding deity the Earth Goddess (*bhū-devī*). Herein, the manifestation is Bhadrakālī.
Vīrabhadra; pure beyond the cosmic egg; the sky, the bull, and the dot; marriage and the conveyance; lord of the thirty gods, the three-eyed one;
chief of the Gaṇas, the all-pervading Śambhu.

Thus, in the upward direction [there are] ten: Balipriya, Bhūtapāla, Īśāna, Piṅgekṣaṇa, Prabhu, Śiva, Sarvakṛt, Sarvajña, Sarva, and Sarvavidyādhipa—these are the ten in Īśāna. [In the northeast are] Karmarūpadṛklakṣmīvān, Aprakāśa, Prakāśa, Saumyadeha, Rūpavān, and Nidhīśa.

Adorned with various jewels, wearing a crown of matted hair—these ten in the north: Śibi, Śoṣaṇa, Vegavān, Tīkṣṇa, Sūkṣma, Vāyu, Sarvagandhavān, Sarvaga, Meghasañcārī, and Kapardī—these ten in the northwest. (Fifth line)

Bhīta, Vaḍabāmukha, Jalāntaka, Dīrghabāhu, Jayabhadra, Śveta, Mahābala, Pāśahasta, Atibala, and Bala—these are the ten in the quarter of Varuṇa. Daṃṣṭravān, Lohita, Dhūmra, Virūpākṣa, Ūrdhvaśepha, Bhayānaka, Krūradṛṣṭi, Hantṛ, Māraṇa, and Nairṛta—these are the ten in the quarter of Nirṛti. [Then there is] Dharmapati.
Dharma, Raudra, Kāla, Kartṛ, Vidhātṛ, Dhātṛ, Hara, Mṛtyu, and Yāmya—
these ten are in the southern direction.
Kṣayāntaka, Bhasmāntaka, Babhru, Dahana, Jvalana, Hara, Khādaka, Puṅgala, and Hutāśin.

In the southeast, there are ten [deities] beginning with Agnirudra: Tridaśādhipa, Pinākī, Śāstā, Avyaya, Vibhūti, Pramardana, Vajradeha, Buddha, Aja, and Kapa(lī)śa. In the east, there are ten [beginning with]:
Vaḍabāmukha, Grasta, Vīra, Vṛṣadhara, Vṛṣa, Viṣalocana, Viṣāgni, Vīra, and Pālaka.
Ananta and the others are ten; Rudra;

(9th line) Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hāṭaka, Kūśmāṇḍa, and Kālāgni—thus [are the worlds] within the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa). Above and below, there are one hundred and eight worlds. They have names identical to those of the Rudras. The phoneme is *kṣa*. Bhava, Bhava.

Bestower of happiness upon all beings in both existence and non-existence; maker of all things present; supreme over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; unworshipped by the unworshipped; unstudied by the unstudied;
abiding from of old, abiding from of old; witness, witness; *turu turu*; O bird, O bird; O tawny one, O tawny one.

Jñāna jñāna | Śabda śabda | Sūkṣma sūkṣma | Śiva śiva sarva sarvada | Oṃ namaḥ śivāya | Oṃ | Namaḥ | Namaḥ śivāya namaḥ | Namaḥ | Om | These are the twenty-eight words; *haṃ hāṃ* is known as the Heart of Sadyojāta.

The two mantras are the syllables *a* and *la*. The two seeds are the *piṅgalā* and *iḍā* channels. The two winds are *apāna* and *prāṇa*. The two organs are the nose and the genitals. The object is smell.
The qualities are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. The state is waking. [The seed-syllable] is yellow, square, and marked with a thunderbolt.

The circle of the earth; Brahmā, the Lord of Causes. Having meditated upon the *nivṛtti-kalā* accompanied by these: *Hāṃ rhāṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the noose of the *nivṛtti-kalā*; *Hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the principle (*tattva*) of earth; *Hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*... (4th)

Salutation to the one hundred and eight worlds beginning with Bhadrakālī and ending with Kālāgni. Hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter *kṣa*. Hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, salutation to those accompanied by the waking state born from the aggregate of the letter *a* (or *ṭa*). Bhava...

Salutation to the twenty-eight syllables beginning with *bhava* and ending with *oṃ*. Salutation to the two mantras of Sadyojāta’s heart: *hāṃ hlāṃ haṃ haṃ hāṃ*. Salutation to the seed-syllable *la*: *hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*. *Hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*.
Salutation to the object of smell. Hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ:
salutation to the five groups of five qualities beginning with sound and ending with smell. Hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ: salutation to the yellow, vajra-marked, square mandala of earth.

"Salutation to the one measuring one hundred *koṭi* yojanas; *hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the cause of Brahmā. Having thus worshipped those of golden luster, and having taken [the breath] through the *pūraka* and *saṃhāriṇī* [processes], one should join it to the thread extending from the knees to the big toes of the feet, and worship it.
Having suppressed [the breath], having covered [the disciple], and having worshipped even in the fire, one should offer five oblations for the sake of [the deity’s] presence.
(Regarding the differences in visualization in initiation with seed-syllables, etc.:
in the case of initiation with seed-syllables for one who desires enjoyment or liberation, [the results depend on] the merit and demerit commenced by the current body.)

One should contemplate all that consists of dharma and adharma— other than the results attached to these two [types of action] prescribed by the rites that bring about the conduct of the *samaya*— as being contained within the thread of the noose of karma. However, in the case of seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*),
[one considers only] the merit and demerit commenced by the present body.

And this is distinct from the incidental fruit. One should contemplate all karma—comprising both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), accompanied by the seeds of action that bring about the conduct of the *samaya*—as being contained within the thread of the fetters (*pāśasūtra*).
This occurs for the householder due to the power of *prārabdha* karma. [The result is] experience (*bhoga*).

And there is an equal desire for both [liberations]. One should contemplate all karma—excluding that which consists of *dharma* and pervades the three *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*—as being situated within the thread of the bonds (*pāśasūtra*). For a disciple who possesses the descent of the most intense power (*śakti*), in the case of immediate initiation into liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), all karma consisting of accumulated and commenced *dharma* and *adharma* is situated within the thread of the bonds.
One should meditate upon this:
(the relationship of pervaded and pervader among the paths).
All this consists of the mantras of the fivefold path. By means of the words, the words [are to be contemplated]. (3rd line)

The castes are pervaded by the colors, and the worlds are pervaded by the tattvas. Having directly perceived that *kalā* pervades impurity (*mala*) and karma, as well as *māyā* together with its products (*māyeya*), along with the piercing of the thread that binds the disciple’s body, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of the bond of *kalā* (4th line);

salutation to the power of the Supreme Lord. Having thus meditated, having taken up [the breath] through the *pūraka* and *saṃhāra* [breaths], and having placed it upon the thread, one should worship it.
Having extinguished [the fire], having covered it, and having worshipped it in the fire with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*, one should offer five oblations.
(5th line) But surely here the purpose is for the Lord of the Path (*adhvapati*), for Śiva, for the Self, or for the noose; because of the perfection of the Supreme Śiva, whose form is indivisible.

Since there is an absence of going and coming, the noose does not depend on a path; moreover, because the noose is insentient (*jaḍa*), such [movement] is even more impossible for it. If it is argued that, by process of elimination, going and coming are possible for the self because it is delimited by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), that too is not so, because the self is all-pervasive (*vibhu*) while the subtle body is localized (*prādeśika*).

Since it is impossible for there to be a delimitation of the self in its entirety, it is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) alone that possesses the nature of going and coming, but not the self. If it is asked, "Then to whom does this path belong?"—to this it is replied: [it belongs] to the self. (8th line)

Mantras and the like are metaphorically designated as "paths" because they serve as the means for acquiring merit and demerit— which are the causes of the experience of form, pleasure, and pain— just as [the paths] of time are. For example, this occurs through the correct pronunciation of the words and syllables of a mantra.

Furthermore, [there is transgression] through the incorrect pronunciation of mantras due to the inversion of vowels and other elements; through the worship or disparagement of the deities presiding over those respective mantras;

through benefiting or harming their worshippers; through the worship or the theft of the emblems (*liṅga*) of the Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*) situated on the earth; and through bathing in the sacred fords located near them.
And through the performance of rites at those sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and the commission of faults therein;
through the benefit or harm done to their devotees by means of the principles (*tatva*) such as the mind (*manas*); through the performance of prescribed or prohibited actions;
through the worship or disparagement of the five powers (*śakti*) which are the causes of the *kalās*; and through the benefit or harm done to their worshippers—[these constitute] merit and demerit.
[This] belongs to you.
(Second line) Karma, consisting of merit and demerit, perishes in its gross form, yet [remains] in a subtle form as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

The latent impression of karma (karmavāsanā) resides in those worlds pervaded by the three kalās that are the sites for the arising of their respective fruits; however, it resides in the intellect (buddhi). He now provides support for the view that the lords of the worlds act as the presiding deities over the liṅgas situated in the world of mortals (bhūrloka).
In the *Sarvajñānottara*,
there are the eight Rudras of the primary secret (*ādiguhyāṣṭaka*), likewise the eight of the supreme secret (*atiguhyāṣṭaka*),
the eight of the secret of secrets (*guhyātiguhyāṣṭaka*), and the eight purifiers (*pavitrāṣṭaka*).
These five—the Sthāṇus and the Aṣṭakas—dwell upon the earth by command;
for the sake of favoring the worlds, they remain established as manifest signs (liṅgas).
O Six-faced One, whatever water is situated in the immediate vicinity of those very [shrines], that is a supremely meritorious *tīrtha*; having bathed there, one shall go to Śiva. Thus it is said.

(The Satiating of the Kalās) Thereafter, one should perform the satiation and other rites with the *kalā* mantras and so forth. It is as follows: HĀṂ HAUṂ HĀṂ, svāhā to the bond of the *kalā* Beyond Peace (*śāntyatīta*). HĀṂ HAIṂ HĀṂ, [svāhā] to the bond of the *kalā* of Peace (*śānti*). (6th line)

Svāhā! Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ, svāhā to the noose of the Vidyā-kalā! Hāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ, svāhā to the noose of the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā! Hāṃ Hlāṃ Hāṃ, svāhā to the noose of the Nivṛtti-kalā! Thus is the libation (tarpaṇa).
(The kindling.)
Hrūṃ hauṃ hrūṃ, for the noose of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta-kalā-pāśa*);
haṃ phaṃ hūṃ hyaiṃ hūṃ, for the noose of the *kalā* of peace (*śānti-kalā-pāśa*), huṃ phaṭ; hraṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ, for the noose of the *kalā* of knowledge (*vidyā-kalā-pāśa*), huṃ huṃ phaṭ;
hūṃ hvīṃ haṃ, for the noose of the *kalā* of establishment (*pratiṣṭhā-kalā-pāśa*), huṃ huṃ phaṭ.

HŪṂ HLĀṂ HŪṂ NIVṚTTIKALĀPĀŚĀYA HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ. Thus is the illumination (*dīpana*). (The offerings of color and the fire-sacrifice): One should dye [the thread] with white and other colors for the sake of awakening it through the pervasion of the thread at the crest-lock, forehead, heart, navel, and knees. This is the coloring (*rakti*). Then:

On the head of the disciple (9th line), having worshipped Śiva together with his limbs and his mantra, and having offered one hundred oblations into the fire with the root mantra, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Thus end the worship and the fire-oblation.
(The inspection.)

Thereafter, having visualized [the impurities] within the disciple’s body by means of one's own pervasive [consciousness], one should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*: "Hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the companion consisting of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantras, composed of impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and *amāyā*, whose form is feminine and whose nature is the principle; obeisance to the bond of impurity belonging to the state of cessation (*nivṛtti*). Then: "Hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ. (92a, 1st line)

Having visualized that body through its own pervasion with the mantra "Obeisance to the one who possesses the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and the adjuncts of *māyā*; to the one whose form is the principle of woman (*strīrūpa-tattva*); to the bond of the *kalā* of *pratiṣṭhā*," he should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*. Hāṃ Hrūṃ Hāṃ. (Second line)

"Salutation to the one who possesses as attendants the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras (*mantra*), impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and that which is born of *māyā* (*māyeya*), and who has the form of the principle of woman (*strīrūpa-tattva-rūpa*) and the noose of knowledge and limited agency (*vidyā-kalā-pāśa*). Having thus beheld [the deity] within his body through his own pervasion, he should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*. (Third line)

"Hāṃ haiṃ hāṃ! Salutation to the one who is the essence of the principles, the worlds, the phonemes, the words, and the mantras; to the one who is the impurity of the bindu; to the minister; to the one whose form is the female principle and whose nature is the reality; to the noose of the peaceful kalā. Having thus beheld that body through his own pervasion, [he should offer oblation] with that [mantra] ending in svāhā.

One should offer five oblations. Having visualized [the deity] within the body of the disciple through one's own pervasive presence with the mantra: "Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ! Salutation to the one who is accompanied by the Tattvas, Bhuvanas, Varṇas, Padas, Mantras, and Malas; to the one whose form is the female principle (strī-rūpa) and the Tattvas; to the noose of the Kalā beyond Śānti," one should offer five oblations ending with "svāhā. This visualization is impossible for oneself [to perform].

(Sandhāna) HĀṂ HLĀṂ HLĪṂ HĀṂ. To the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantras; to the impurities (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and the assistants of *māyā*; to those in the form of women and in the form of the principles; to the [kalās] Nivṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā. (5th line)
Having performed the conjunction by pronouncing "bhyāṃ namaḥ" with short and long vowels, and having worshipped [the deity] even in the fire,

one should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*: *hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ* [to] the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras (*mantra*), impurity (*mala*), illusion (*māyā*), and the ministers of illusion (*māyeya-saciva*).

Having performed the conjunction by pronouncing the long *ha* and *sa* sounds— namely, "namaḥ" through the forms of the female principle (*strī-rūpa*) and the reality-principle (*tattva-rūpa*), corresponding to the categories of *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, *kalā*, and *paśu*— and having worshipped [the deity] in the fire, one should offer oblations with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*.

One should offer five oblations with the mantra: *hāṃ hrūṃ hyeṃ hāṃ namas* to the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras (*mantra*), impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, that which pertains to *māyā*, and the lunar drop (*bindu*), as well as to the two ministers in the form of woman and the form of the principles, and to the two digits (*kalā*) of knowledge (*vidyā*) and peace (*śānti*).

Having performed the conjunction (*sandhāna*) by pronouncing the short and long vowels, and having worshipped [the deity] in the fire, one should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*. With the pronunciation of the short and long vowels: *hāṃ hyaiṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*, [one says]: "Obeisance to the Tattva-Bhuvana-Varṇa-Pada-Mantra-Mala-Aindava, together with the two attendants, who are of the form of the female principle (*strī-tattva*) and the form of the principle (*tattva-rūpa*), and who are the bonds of the *kalās* of Śānti and Śāntyatīta. Thus [with the short and long vowels].
Having performed the reconnection (*sandhāna*) and worshipped the fire, one should offer five oblations ending with *svāhā*. Thus ends the reconnection.
(The Piercing: *hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*. (Line 10)

Having performed the piercing with "haṃ huṃ phaṭ" directed toward the principles (*tattva*), worlds, phonemes, words, mantras, impurities, karma, *māyā*, the effects of *māyā*, and their attendants, as well as toward the principle of the female form and the noose of the *kalā* of cessation (*nivṛtti*), one should offer five oblations with that same mantra ending in *svāhā*.

Having performed the piercing with "HĀM HĪM HĀM TATTVABHUVANAVARṆAPADAMANTRAMALAKARMAMĀYĀMĀYEYASACIVĀYA STRĪRŪPĀYA TATVARŪPĀYA PRATIKALĀPĀŚĀYA HAḤ | HUṂ PHAṬ," one should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in SVĀHĀ.

Having performed the piercing with "HĀṂ HRŪṂ HĀṂ" and "HAḤ HUṂ PHAṬ," [one should act] by means of that [mantra] ending in SVĀHĀ, [addressed] to the one who possesses the principles, the worlds, the mantra-words, the mantra, impure karma, Māyā, and the attendants of Māyā, and who has the form of the principle of the female form, and who is the noose of the Kalās of Vidyā.

One should offer five oblations. Having performed the piercing with "HĀṂ HYAIṂ HĀṂ TATTVABHUVANAVARṆAPADAMANTRAMALABAINDAVĀYA SACIVĀYA STRĪRŪPATATVARŪPĀYA ŚĀNTIKALĀPĀŚĀYA HAḤ HUṂPHAṬ," one should offer five oblations with that same mantra ending in "SVĀHĀ. HĀṂ HAUṂ HĀṂ.

Having performed the piercing with "haḥ huṃ phaṭ" directed toward the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, impurities (*mala*), and the lunar point (*bindu*), as well as toward the minister (*saciva*), the female form (*strīrūpa*), the principle of the female form (*tatvarūpa*), and the noose of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*), one should offer five oblations with that same mantra ending in "svāhā. This is the piercing.

(Tāḍana: Hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ! Salutation to the one who consists of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantras; to the impurity of action (*mala-karma*); to the one associated with the *bindu*; to the minister (*saciva*); to the one whose nature is the essence of sound (*svarūpa*) and the essence of the principles (*tattvarūpa*); to the one who has transcended the fetters of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*). [Thus,] pervading its own locus, from the principles (*tattva*) and so forth up to the *bindu*.
Having meditated upon and visualized [the deity], one should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*.

In the same way, one should also meditate upon and visualize Śāntyatītā and the others as pervading their respective locations, from the principles (*tattva*) up to the end of the bindu, and offer five oblations with their respective mantras ending in *svāhā*. One should also [offer oblations] for *hrūṃ* and the rest.

Having meditated upon and visualized [the deity] as endowed with the nine [categories] beginning with *tattva* and ending with *māyā*, one should offer five oblations for each of those respective mantras, ending with *svāhā*. This is the rite of *īkṣaṇa*. *Hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ tattva-bhuvana-arṇava-damana-mantra-mala-aindavāya sacivāya...* (9th line)

Having struck [the target] with the *nārāca* mudrā accompanied by flowers, using the mantra *haḥ huṃ phaṭ* directed toward the one whose form consists of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras (*mantra*), impurities (*mala*), and the *bindu*,

one should offer five oblations (*āhuti*) ending with *svāhā*. Then, [one offers] *hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ* to the one who possesses the impurities of the principles, worlds, phonemes, words, mantras, and the *bindu*.

To the minister, whose form is the reality of the female form, who has severed the noose of the kalās beyond peace, [one should offer] *haḥ*. Having struck him with the mantra *huṃ phaṭ* accompanied by the flower-arrow mudrā, one should offer five oblations with that mantra ending in *svāhā*:

*hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ*, [to the one] whose form is the reality of the female form—consisting of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, impurities (*mala*), bonds (*pāśa*), actions (*karman*), *māyā*, and that which pertains to *māyā*.

With the mantra *haḥ* for the noose of the *vidyā-kalā*, having struck [the victim] with the *sapuṣpa-nārāca-mudrā* while uttering *huṃ phaṭ*, one should offer five oblations (*pañcāhutīḥ*) with that same mantra ending in *svāhā*. [The mantra is: *hāṃ hvīṃ hāṃ*, [to the one] whose impurities are the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantras (*mantra*), as well as karma, *māyā*, and the assistants of *māyā*; [to the one] whose form is the female principle (*strī-rūpa-tattva*).
With the mantra *haḥ huṃ phaṭ* and the flower-arrow mudrā (*sapuṣpanārācamudrā*),

one should strike [the bonds] and offer five oblations with that same mantra ending in *svāhā*: *hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ*, to the bond of the *nivṛtti-kalā* consisting of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras (*mantra*), impurities (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and the *māyeya* assistants, as well as the female deities (*strī*) and the sacrificial cakes (*pūpa*).

Having struck [the victim] with the *sapuṣpanārāca-mudrā* while reciting "HAḤ | HUṂ PHAṬ," one should offer five oblations (*pañcāhuti*) with that same mantra ending in *svāhā*. This is the striking (*tāḍana*).
(Seizing, yoking, and binding:

HĀṂ HAUM HĀṂ! To the one who is the essence of the principles (*tattva*), the worlds, the mantra-syllables, the mantra-words, and the pure *bindu*; to the minister; to the one whose form is the female principle (*strītattva*); to the noose of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*).

"Namaḥ"—having entered [the fire], one should offer five oblations with that mantra ending in *svāhā*. The same applies to *śānti* and the others. Having entered, one should offer five oblations for each of those respective mantras ending in *svāhā*. This is the entry (*praveśa*). Hāṃ haṃ hāṃ hauṃ, [salutation] to the one who possesses the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantras (*mantra*), who is free from impurity (*mala*), who belongs to the *bindu*, who is accompanied by his attendants (*saciva*), and whose form is both feminine and that of the principles (*tatvarūpa*).

I grasp the noose of the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta) here with "haṃ huṃ phaṭ," having grasped it by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [breath] through inhalation; then with "hauṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ hauṃ," [I grasp] that which possesses the principles, worlds, phonemes, words, mantras, and impurities, belonging to the Bindu, accompanied by its attendants, and having the form of the female principle (*strī-tattva*).
I join [the thread] for the sake of the noose of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*). With the mantra *haṃ huṃ phaṭ*, having joined it to the thread by means of the *recaka-udbhava-mudrā*,
[I join] *hauṃ hāṃ*— [which is] the companion to the *tattva*, *bhuvana*, *varṇa*, *pada*, *mantra*, *mala*, and *bindu*, and which has the form of the female principle (*strīrūpa-tattva-rūpa*).

Having performed the binding with "Haḥ! I bind here! Huṃ Phaṭ!", one should offer five oblations ending in *svāhā* to the one who consists of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, impurities (*mala*), and the *bindu*, using [the mantra]:
*Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ Hyaiṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ*.

I take the minister, who is the form of the *tattva*, whose nature is reality, and whose noose is the power of peace: *haḥ huṃ phaṭ*. Having grasped [it] through the inhalation (*pūraka*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), [I offer it] to the minister of the *tattva*, world, mantra, impurity, and *bindu*: *hauṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.
I join the bond of the peaceful *kalā* whose form is the reality of the female form: *haḥ huṃ bha phaṭ*. This is the mudrā arising from exhalation (*recaka*).
Having joined [it] in the third [position], [one recites]: *hauṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.

I bind the one who possesses the principles (*tattva*), worlds, phonemes, words, mantras, and the impurities of the *bindu*; who has a female form as his companion; whose nature is the principles; and who is bound by the noose of the *śānti-kalā*. *Haḥ*! Having performed the binding with *huṃ phaṭ*, one should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*: *hauṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.

I grasp the noose of *vidyā* and *kalā*, consisting of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and that which is born of *māyā* (.... in the form of a woman (...), with the mantra *haḥ huṃ phaṭ* by means of the *pūraka* [breathing technique] and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā];
having grasped it with *hauṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.
I join the reality of the worlds, phonemes, words, mantras, impurities, karma, Māyā, and that which is governed by Māyā—
along with the reality of the female form and the fetters of Vidyā and Kalā— with the mantra *haḥ huṃ phaṭ* using the *recaka-utthāna-mudrā* upon the thread.
Having joined [the syllables] *haum hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ haum*, [one should say]:

"I bind the bonds of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and the adjuncts of *māyā*—which are of feminine form and the nature of the principles, and which consist of the bonds of *vidyā* and *kalā*—*haḥ huṃ phaṭ*. Having thus performed the binding, [one concludes] with *svāhā*.
With that, one should offer five oblations: *Hauṃ Hlāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ*.

[This is for] the fetter of the *kalā* of *Pratiṣṭhā*, which consists of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, impure karma, the *sāyā* [time-period], *māyā*, its attendant, the female form, the form of the principles, and the fetter of the *kalā* of *Pratiṣṭhā*.
I seize with "Haḥ | Huṃ Phaṭ," by means of the *pūraka-saṃhāriṇī* [breath-retention]. Having seized it with "Hauṃ Hāṃ Hvīṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ," [one seizes] the *tattva*,

*bhuvana*, *varṇa*, *pada*, *mantra*, impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and the assistants of *māyā*, as well as the *pāśa* of the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā* which has the form of the female principle (*strī-rūpa-tattva*).

I join [it] with *haḥ* *huṃ phaṭ*. Having joined it to the thread by means of the *recakodbhava-mudrā*, [I join] *hauṃ* *hlāṃ* *hvīṃ* *hāṃ* *hauṃ*—[the bonds of] the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras (*mantra*), impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and the assistants of *māyā*, as well as the principle in the form of woman (*strīrūpa-tattva-rūpa*). (8th line) I bind the bond of the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā* with *haḥ*.

Having performed the binding with "huṃ phaṭ," one should offer five oblations with that [mantra] ending in "svāhā. With "hauṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ hauṃ," one joins the bond of the *nivṛtti*-kalā— consisting of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, impure karma (*malakarman*), Māyā, and its attendants (*māyeyasaciva*), as well as the principle of the female form (*strīrūpatatvarūpa*)— to the thread by means of the *recakodbhava-mudrā* with "haḥ huṃ phaṭ."

Having joined *hauṃ hlāṃ hāṃ hauṃ* with the world (*bhuvana*), phoneme (*varṇa*), word (*pada*), mantra, impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and *amāyā*—[and] *vaṃ*, which is the form of the female principle (*strīrūpa-tattva*)—I bind the noose of the *nivṛtti-kalā*: *haḥ huṃ phaṭ*. Having thus performed the binding.
One should offer five oblations ending with "svāhā. Thus [are described] the seizing, yoking, and binding.
(In the Sūtra, there are the worship of the Kalās and so forth.
HĀṂ HAUṂ HĀṂ. (Second line)

One should worship with the mantra "Obeisance to the one who possesses the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, and impurities (*mala*), as well as the *bindu*; to the minister; to the one whose form is the female principle (*strītattva*); to the one who has transcended the bond of the *kalā* of *śāntyatīta*. In this manner, one should also worship *śānti* and the others within the thread (*sūtra*). Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ. Obeisance to the one who possesses the principles, worlds, phonemes, words, mantras, and impurities, as well as the *bindu*. (Third line)

One should offer five oblations with the mantra: *sacivāya strīrūpatattvarūpāya śāntyatītakalāpāśāya svāhā*. In this same manner, one should also offer five oblations each for Śānti and the others. Having joined [the mantra] to the thread with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Lord’s Power who presides over the fetters of the Kalās," and having worshipped it, one should worship it in the fire as well.

With that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*, one should offer five oblations (*āhuti*). Then, having placed the cord of bonds (*pāśasūtra*) upon the shoulder of the disciple, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra for the sake of liberation from defects of deficiency or excess, and then present the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
(The placement of the cord of bonds on the head of the disciple, etc.)

Then, having seated the disciple and placed the *pāśasūtra* upon his head, one should perform the *saṃpātahoma* twenty-one times with the mantra "Hauṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ haḥ śivāya svāhā. Then, having removed the *pāśasūtra* from his head, [one should place it] in a vessel made of copper or similar material for the person.
Having placed the noose-thread, the vessel for the Praṇīta water, and the women,

and having formed the *saṃpuṭa* of the *astra*, *kavaca*, and *hṛdaya* mantras, he should worship with the *hṛdaya* mantra as before; then, having performed the *saṃpāta* rite, he should wrap the initiate with a five-colored thread, show him to the *liṅga* by the command of the Guru, and consign him to the jar.

Thereafter, having fully worshipped the guardians of the quarters, Kumbha, and the others, one should cause three mandalas to be prepared outside the pavilion, facing the door, for the householder who is about to deposit [the substances] to the east of the eastern [direction], extending southward and northward.
(The procedure for consuming the five products of the cow,
etc. Thereafter, having seated the householder in the western mandala facing east in the kukkuṭāsana posture, the preceptor [should act] toward him who holds kuśa grass in his hand.

One with *kuśa* grass in hand should offer the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) three times. He, too, should consume the *pañcagavya*, sipping water for purification in between. Having seated him in the eastern part of the mandala as before, one should give him three morsels of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), each the size of a peacock’s egg. He, too, should eat the *caru*, sipping water for purification in between.

Having first seated [the disciple] in the eastern maṇḍala according to the previous procedure, the preceptor should empower with the *hṛdaya-mantra* a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics and give it to him. The disciple, having brushed his teeth with it and rinsed his mouth, should cast it upward while facing upwards.
The preceptor [observes] the falling of the tooth-stick...

If the [arrow] falls in an auspicious direction—namely, the east, west, north, or northeast—one should cause satisfaction. If it falls in a direction other than these, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Astra-mantra to dispel that defect, and then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Having seated [the disciple] in the three mandalas—the southern, middle, and northern—as before, one should perform the rites accordingly.
(The pacification of physical and other deficiencies:

Then, having offered seven hundred oblations with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). For the removal of defects of body, speech, and mind, one should offer one hundred oblations with the *Śiva-aghora-astra* mantras, and then [offer] with the root mantra.

Or one may give a full hundred [oblations]. Then, having offered a small portion of *caru* to Śivāgni, one should pray: "O Lord, from the time of the rite of installation (*ādhāna*) until the end of the lineage (*santāna*), whatever has been performed by you for the severance of bonds (*pāśa-hāna*)—herein there is no further presence [of the deity]. Having thus prayed, one should [dismiss] Śiva residing in the fire by offering the *nirodha-arghya*.

One should restrain [the breath]. Alternatively, having joined Śiva residing in the fire with Śiva residing in the *śivakumbha* by means of the connection of the channels (*nāḍī*), one should restrain it. Following that, the four *vyāhṛtis* and the four beginning with fire have not been written because they pertain to the subject of the Brāhmaṇas. Having offered two oblations (*bali*)... (5th line)
Having entrusted the ritual action to the Lord of the Maṇḍala, one should restrain the world-protectors and others by offering the *nirodhārghya*.
(This is the procedure for the sleep [of the deity] and the preliminary rite for the initiation into Nirvāṇa.

Then, in the sacrificial pavilion, on ground smeared with cow dung, [the disciple] should be made to lie down upon a bed of *darbha* grass over which the *astra-mantra* has been recited a hundred times, with his head toward the east.

(6th line) Having placed him upon a bed of ashes with his head to the south, and having performed the ritual installation (*nyāsa*) of the paths to be purified (*śodhyādhvan*), one should worship him with flower-offerings (*puṣpikā*) and bind his topknot (*śikhā*) with the *śikhā-mantra*.
Holding a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), the excellent mudrā, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*),

with a dream-child and tawny matted locks, and adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament— having thus meditated, one should say: "Obeisance to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul."
Salutation to Vāma, who possesses all forms, the lord of dreams.

"Speak, O Lord of the gods of gods; I have come for refuge to your presence. (8th line) Having thus informed [the deity] that all the tasks intended for the heart are indeed present, one should recite "hrīṃ hili hili śūlapāṇaye svāhā," cover [the image] with a cloth consecrated by the *vajra-mantra*, and cause it to sleep.

Then, having surrounded the colored powder in its four enclosures on all four sides with ashes, sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and white mustard seeds using mantras ending in *huṃ phaṭ* as the weapon-mantra, and having himself gone outside to offer the *bali* oblation to the lords of the directions, he should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and effect the ritual integration of his own body (*sakalīkaraṇa*).

(10th line) Consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth in sequence, accompanied by his companions, having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) and ritual sipping (*ācamana*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), he should cast straw and other materials into the fire for its protection until the completion of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), while maintaining the presence of the fire.

One should remember the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā). If a bad dream is seen by either the disciple or the guru, they should mutter the root mantra together with Śiva-Śakti and sleep again. Thus ends the ritual for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of Nirvāṇa-dīkṣā.
(Nirvāṇadīkṣā): Immediately after entering the pavilion, the Guru—
or the disciple— should perform the initiation even if there is the occurrence of birth or death impurity (*sūtaka*).
(The Pacification of Bad Dreams) Then,

at dawn, the preceptor, having risen, performs his daily and occasional rites— including the bath and so forth— concluding with the purification by mantras as before; then, holding the general *arghya* water...

Having first completed the rites beginning with the worship of the gatekeepers and ending with the propitiation and illumination of the mantras, standing before the mandala, one should sprinkle it with water, purify it through the rites of gazing and so forth, and then arrange the five kalās upon the colored powders according to their respective colors.

Having covered [the area] with the *kavaca* mantra and protected it with the *astra* mantra, one should consecrate it by reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times for the pacification of the defects of menstrual impurity (*rajodoṣa*). Having worshipped the *astra* in the directions beginning with the east, one should worship Śiva with incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Then, having fully worshipped Śiva residing in the fire with flowers and other offerings—

One should perform the rites for averting obstacles on the journey and so forth. Then, having rejoiced in [the merit] within a dream, one should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*) upon seeing an evil dream.
The fruit of the dream is as follows:
One should contemplate curd, rice, meat, wine, and other such excellent foods;
mounting an elephant or similar vehicle; grain; being enveloped in white garments;
and a bright mountain, a river, the ocean, or even mud.
He who delights in the midst of this most terrible and great difficulty attains success.
For them, there will occur, by way of adverse results, disease, death, fear, or even imprisonment, loss of wealth,
