Having offered five oblations with "svāhā," saying, "Take the female form and the true form, the mind and the dried drop," one should surrender the office.
"O Sadāśiva, you must remain bound by the year for this child whose bonds have been completely burnt away;
thus you should cause him to hear the command of Śiva.
Then, having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should dismiss Sadāśiva with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Then...

Having said, "I perform the extraction of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*)," and having offered five oblations with the root mantra, one proceeds with the *Vāmā* [power], separates [the soul] from the *Jyeṣṭhā*, and extracts it from the *Raudrī* pit. Thus purified, blazing,
and possessing a radiance like the full autumn moon, the self is rendered fit for the manifestation of omniscience and the six divine qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
Meditating [on the Self] and having established it within one's own self through the initiation of *hauti*, even though it has been extracted from the gross and subtle *liṅga* bodies,
it is like curd [remaining] for the sake of experiencing the remnants of *prārabdha* karma, due to contact with other substances such as the action of the razor and the *pāka*.
Having performed that [ritual] and having churned it, one should extract the butter (*navanīta*) and, as if placing it back into the whey (*takra*), deposit it into the heart-lotus of the disciple;

in the case of the *naiṣṭhika* initiation, one should join it to the body of the thread at the location of the topknot (*śikhā*). Then, for the sake of stabilizing the self, [one should recite] with the root mantra.

Having offered five oblations for the nourishment of the disciple, one should place on his head, by means of the ring finger, water from the *arghya* vessel consisting of drops of nectar with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; then,
having satiated Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara with ten oblations each.
"O parents, that which was urged by me during the initiation of my disciples—out of compassion, forgive that; now go to your own abode."
Having thus made this request and dismissed [the deity], one should offer the *pūrṇā* oblation with the mantra: *HĀṂ HAUṂ ŚĀNTYATĪTAKALĀŚIKHĀŚAKTIBHYĀṂ NAMAḤ*.

Then, having gazed upon the power of the purification of the *śāntyatītakalā*, one should establish the lineage (*santāna*) by uttering the short and long vowels, and for its stabilization, [one should perform it] with the root mantra (*mūla*).
One should offer five oblations; this is the purification of the Śāntyatīta-kalā.
The Ritual for the Cutting of the Topknot (Śikhācchedavidhi)

Thereafter, according to the procedure to be described, one should unite the disciple— who is composed of the elements and abides in the worldly order— with [the supreme reality]. Then, for the lifelong disciple who abides in the Śiva-order, one should [sever] the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), which stands at the end of the path, pervades all paths, and acts as an auxiliary to impurity (*mala*).

Having meditated upon her as being of the nature of the left-hand power (*vāmaśakti*), one should recite the mantra "haṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ" seven times over the scissors and consecrate them. Thus says the *Āgama*:
"The scissors shall be the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*); in this way, it cuts the fetter."
That supreme *kalā* is exceedingly subtle, the highest awakener of mantras.
It should be understood by the best of teachers as the *kartarī* in the form of the agent (*kartṛ*).
Following that, [one should utter] *huṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ hrūṃ*, the power of concealment (*tirobhāvikā*).

Having cut the topknot with a pair of scissors while reciting the mantra "Kuṭilāśakti... haḥ huṃ phaṭ," and having purified the sacrificial altar with cow dung, one should offer the topknot as an oblation while reciting "Śivā...

haṃ hāṃ hauṃ... kalāśakti hoṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Thereafter, one should consecrate it with five oblations using the Astra-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ. Following that, the disciple, having immersed himself in water and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), becomes pure.
Thus ends the procedure for the cutting of the topknot (śikhā).
"I am Śiva" (beginning with this contemplation).

Thereafter, the preceptor also, having bathed with water or ash and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and having placed the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*) upon his own head, should intensely contemplate, "I am Śiva. The disciple also [should do the same].

Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and placed the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*) upon his own head, he should salute the Lord as the Preceptor (*deśika*) does. Then the Preceptor, together with the disciple, having worshipped Śiva and performed the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) and illumination (*dīpana*) of the mantras in the blazing fire, [says]: "O Blessed One, by Your grace, [I shall perform] that which is established within the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*)."
Having seized the sacrificial animal and purified it, ending with the cutting of its crest-lock.
"You must perform even a small portion of the rites prescribed for sacrifices according to my instruction;
by that power of yours, O Śiva, you shall go to the pure state of Śiva.
Now, as one who follows your command, this is what must be done by me."
Therefore, O Lord, grant me your command; I shall purify the disciple.

Having thus made this request and taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, having washed them with warm water, and having worshipped those two—which consist of Śiva and Śakti—with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should contemplate them as being composed of Śiva and Śakti. Thus says the Āgama:
"This vessel at the base of the handle is the *kalaśa*; the handle is the *maṇḍala*, extending to the end of the *kalās*."

The *daṇḍāgrasaṃpuṭa* is *māyā*; the altar (*vedi*) is the forgotten *vidyā*. The mantras are situated upon the variegated petals; the corner is the stream (*srota*), the binding. That which is the hollow is the support (*ādhāra*), the lotus established as the seat (*āsana*).
That [channel] has the shape of a conch-shell at the ear and the mouth of the tube; it is the form of the power (*śakti*) of the [central channel].
This power, which pervades all the paths, is fashioned as a tube.
It has the form of a thread, and its staff-like axis is the circular rotation of the point (*bindu*).
"The *sruva* and *sruk* [ladles] are Sadāśiva, the mass of power (*śaktipiṇḍa*), whose domain is all-pervasive. (This concludes the "Joining of the Disciple to Śiva").
Then, on his own left side, [he should place] that which stands upon the mandala.

Having sprinkled the disciple with arghya water together with the fire, and having performed the continuity of the channels (*nāḍīsantāna*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) in his presence, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra for the sake of obstructing the ritual acts that follow initiation, and then offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Thereafter, one should heat the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles three times with fire to turn them away from their wooden nature. Then—

The central channel, which is like a staff emerging from the jar-like bulb (kanda) filled with the nectar of supreme bliss, has its openings clearly manifest at the heart-lotus, the palate, and the throat.

Having meditated upon the inner form of the *sruk* as a stream of nectar flowing from the expansion at the tip of the *bindu*, one then anoints the *sruk* and *sruva* with sandalwood paste. Having worshipped Śakti and Śiva within them and meditated upon them as being of the nature of Śakti and Śiva who pervade all levels of existence (*adhvan*), one takes hold of them; [thus] Śakti, her body agitated by Śiva, flows with nectar.
Holding [the two vessels] filled with clarified butter outside [the maṇḍala] with the conch-like mudrā,

one takes the consciousness of the disciple situated in the maṇḍala on one's left by means of the sequence beginning with striking, brings it into one's own self, and effects a state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*).
Having performed [the preliminary rites], with a slight smile and mouth slightly opened, with a serene mind, placing the tip of the tongue against the palate,
slightly closing the eyes, and adopting the divine posture (*divyakaraṇa*) while maintaining the natural height of the body; (108a, first line)

Having performed inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), one should block all the gates with exhalation (*recaka*) using the syllables *huṃ* and *haḥ*. Having established a connection between the teeth and the channels (*nāḍī*), one takes [the essence] from the mandala, the jar, the fire, the disciple, and oneself through the conduits (*praṇāḍikā*). Having taken it from the jar and placed it at the tip of the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*), one performs inhalation and retention.

With the mantra *huṃ haṃ huṃ phaṭ* during the exhalation (*recaka*), the preceptor pierces the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Then, while reciting the root-mantra (*mūla*) once, he [performs] the sevenfold equinox (*viṣuva*) within the temple-palace located inside the lotus and the conch.
Having recollected [this]:

"But when one is joined to that which is inexpressible, supportless, ungraspable, devoid of the conceit of 'I', and beyond all conceptual existence—that, according to the scripture, is liberation. (4th line)
According to this statement,

having transcended the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), while contemplating the disciple’s self as being in a state of aesthetic unification (*samarasībhāva*) with Śiva— the supreme bliss of the mass of consciousness— one should proceed gradually.
One should perform the *pūrṇā* [offering]... for the sake of stability, one should again give a *pūrṇā*.

Following that—[beginning with the attainment of the sixfold qualities]—one should [unite] the disciple’s self, which resides at the *dvādaśānta*, with Paramaśiva by means of the recitation of the previously mentioned mantra.

Following the sequence of the full inhalation (*pūrakāgamana*), one should visualize— along the path of the root power (*mūlaśakti*) within the nectar-filled clarified butter— the central channel attached to the navel, which is joined with the sacrificial ladles (*sruc*) that pervade everything from the element of earth up to the principle of power (*śaktitattva*). Then, having first uttered the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), [one should proceed].
Having joined the disciple’s self at the tip of the flame of fire with a full stream of clarified butter, [one recites]: "Hāṃ! O Self, become conscious;
svāhā! Hīṃ! O Self, become eternally satisfied; svāhā! Hūṃ! O Self..."

"NĀDIBODHO BHAVA SVĀHĀ! HYAIṂ TVAMĀTMAN SVATANTRŌ BHAVA SVĀHĀ! HAUṂ TVAMĀTMAN ALUPTAŚAKTIRBHAVA SVĀHĀ! HAḤ TVAMĀTMAN ANANTAŚAKTIRBHAVA SVĀHĀ!"—with these three oblations each, having manifested the innate Śaiva qualities of the self, one should extract the self from the fire.

When that body has been purified by means of the *dhāraṇās*, one should engage it for the sake of experiencing the *prārabdha* karma. Then, to pacify the exhaustion produced by the impact of the extremely intense power (*śakti*) of the mantra, one should offer a handful of water (*arghya*) consisting of drops of nectar upon its head.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the worship of Śiva in this manner: one should prostrate to Śiva, to the Self, and to the Fire. Then, of Śiva...
Having established the disciple with a serene countenance within his own right mandala, [the preceptor says]:
"This one has been graced by you alone, having assumed my very form."
Therefore, one should increase devotion toward the Lord, who is like a god, a fire, and a guru.
By your grace, may this [work] reach its completion with uninterrupted activity;
O Lord, let no fault arising from negligence become a cause for its obstruction.

Having thus informed Śiva and gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess;

then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the weapon mantra (*astra*) as an atonement (*prāyaścitta*), and say the blessing over the disciple: "May there be welfare, O ancestors! (*śreyo vā pitaras tu*).
(The dismissal of the sacrifice):
Thereafter, one should dismiss the sacrifice. For example: having worshipped Śiva residing in the fire, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the root mantra;
having offered a tenth part of that with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), one should offer three final oblations with the root mantra and several mouthfuls with the limb-mantras.

Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the pacification of defects of deficiency or excess, and having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *astra-mantra* for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*),
and having offered the final full oblation, he should worship [the deity] with the eightfold flower-offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*).
Then, having offered the *arghya* facing away [from the deity], the practitioner should unite the mantra within the image through the path of the channels (*nāḍīmārga*).
Having joined Śiva, who resides in the fire, with Śivā, who resides in the mandala, and having bid farewell to Brahmā and the others, one should worship and dismiss the fire with "Hāṃ Hrūṃ,
obeisance to Agni," and then, having drawn two mandalas in the south-east corner of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having worshipped Rudra, the groups of Mothers, and the Yakṣas in the eastern and other directions at the edge of the western mandala,

and having worshipped the planets starting with Īśāna in the intermediate directions, as well as the Asuras, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas, one should [worship] in the corners starting from Īśāna in the center of the mandala.

Having worshipped the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the zodiac signs (*rāśi*), the guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapāla*), and the Viśvedevas, one should offer a *bali* to Rudra and the others with their respective mantras— preceded by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the word "Brahman" (*brahman*) and ending in *svāhā*— using food mixed with water. Then, having dismissed them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should worship the guardians of the ten worlds, beginning with the East, within the previously prepared mandala, and in the center of that, worship Nīlalohita, using food mixed with water.

Having offered the *bali* to Indra and the other deities with their respective name-mantras preceded by the seed-syllable *brahma* (Oṃ) and ending in *svāhā*, one should dismiss them with the *hṛdaya*-mantra.

Then, [one offers] *svāhā* to those dwelling in the eastern and other directions—namely, the lords of the directions, the spirits, the hosts of mothers, Rudra, the *kṣetrapālas*, and so forth. In this way, having offered the *bali* in all directions according to the distinction of their names.

Having offered the bali with the mantra, "Hāṃ, to the crows and others who violate the samaya, svāhā," and having informed [the deities] with the two verses beginning with "Those Rudras of fierce deeds," one should pay obeisance and ask for forgiveness. Then, having gone near Śiva, prostrated, and worshipped him with the mūrti-mantra...
Having meditated upon the dissolution of the limbs of Sadāśiva into the locations beginning with the heart by means of the *divyamudrā*,

and having offered a flower with the root mantra preceded by "Oṃ" while saying "Forgive me," one should, with devotion, display the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā* using the *śaktimantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Having paid obeisance to Śiva, one should dissolve [the deity] into one's own self. However, in the case of initiation into the *iṣṭaliṅga*, after saying "Forgive me," one should block [the deity] with the root mantra using the *nirodhamudrā*, display the *mahāmudrā*, and pay obeisance with devotion. Thereafter—

In the northeastern quarter or in a mandala marked with a svastika, one should perform the avabhṛtha bath first with the water from the Śiva-kumbha, then with the water from the weapon-vessel (astrakumbha), and finally with the water from the weapon-vessel itself. Then, having worshipped Caṇḍeśvara in the fire with the remnants of the sacrifice, such as clarified butter and other offerings—
Having gratified Caṇḍeśvara with a thousand or a hundred oblations, one should dismiss him with the words, "Forgive me.

In the case of initiation according to worldly custom (*lokadharmiṇī dīkṣā*), however, one should perform the remainder of the rite except for the cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*). Thus ends the procedure for the *nirvāṇadīkṣā* pertaining to the Hotṛ priest.
(The Classification of the Initiation into Nirvāṇa) This initiation into nirvāṇa is twofold, according to the distinction between knowledge and action,
for the renunciant. (7th line)

Because the external fire has been superimposed upon the sublime fire, one should perform initiation through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) without the ritual of the fire-offering (*agnikārya*). Furthermore, if the householder teacher possesses the direct realization of Śiva and the disciple is highly advanced,
he should bestow upon him the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*).
Thus it is stated in the Vāruṇapaddhati:
"The initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā) is one, while the other is remembered as being accompanied by ritual action (kriyāvatī);
[the latter] is devoid of sacrifice, fire-rites, and so forth, consisting merely of [physical] activity."

"Initiation is said to be possessed of knowledge, arising from the correct awakening to reality; that which possesses the fire of truth is born from skill in ritual action. Thus, for those of mixed caste, having performed the *samaya* and other rites—excluding the *hautrī* [initiation] and [the rites involving] the eye and so forth—one performs worship, *homa*, and [other rituals].

(10th line) Without hearing the Kāgama, having established the qualification for service, mental devotion, and worship, one should cause [the disciple] to understand the nature of the three categories by means of the Bhāṣāstra.
The Sequence of the Initiation of Knowledge (Jñānadīkṣākrama)
Now, the sequence of the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) is described.
In the initiation of the true state (*bhāvasaddīkṣā*), there is a slight distinction:
it has been established in the scriptures that this must be performed by a teacher of knowledge (*jñānācārya*).

The procedure here is as follows: the preceptor, having performed the two daily rites of morning and midday, having executed the *ṣaḍadhvan* placement (*nyāsa*), and having become pure, exits by means of his own exhaling breath; he enters the heart of the disciple by means of the disciple’s inhaling breath, seizes the disciple’s consciousness, and exits by means of the disciple’s exhaling breath; then, entering his own heart by means of his own inhaling breath—

Having established the disciple’s consciousness within the consciousness of Śiva by means of the *kumbhaka* (retention), and having visualized the disciple’s consciousness emerging through the *recaka* (exhalation) and entering that [disciple’s] body via the *pūraka* (inhalation) breath,
one should treat the disciple— who has performed obeisance— as previously described.

In both maṇḍalas, the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) should be performed with the *praṇava* for the members of the three higher castes alone, since its consumption is prescribed only for them;

however, having caused the Śūdras to consume it with the *haṃsa* mantra or the mixed five-syllabled mantra, one should have them perform the cleaning of the teeth and the pure sipping of water (*ācamana*). Then, having seated the disciple on a seat of *darbha* grass in a clean place, [one should proceed].
One should worship Śiva with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) upon the disciple’s head, which is [visualized as] a seat consisting of six [lotuses].
This has been stated in the *Varuṇapaddhati*:
But as for the internal initiation, which is the daily rite according to rule,
the teacher brings it to completion while remaining in the form of the mantra-body.

Having himself established in the state of Śiva, he should, according to the prescribed rite, install the consciousness of this [image]— which is the form of the mantra— by means of the *pūraka* breath.
Having grasped [the breath] with Śiva residing in one's own mind, one should join it with that [Śiva];
then, having supported it within the disciple's body, one should expel it through the upward-moving breaths (recakas).
One should again cause this five-fold cow-product (pañcagavya), over which obeisance has been performed, to be drunk;
then, one should [administer] the mantra with the *haṃsa* syllable or with the *praṇava*.

Furthermore, the wise one who should perform [the rite] together with the five-syllable [mantra], this is declared to be the consecration (adhivāsa); he should carry it out in each respective location. Thus ends the procedure for the consecration.
Now, the initiation.
Then, in a secluded room adorned with variegated canopies and garlands,
its floor smeared with pure cow dung and decorated with darbha grass;
The teacher himself, having bathed, his body smeared with ashes,
wearing rudrākṣa beads on all his limbs, and having performed the worship of Śiva;
Having had the disciple, who has performed his salutation, stand before him,
the Guru himself should pay homage to Śiva; then, having received permission, the Guru—
standing in the center of the mandala and facing either south or east— [proceeds].
Facing east, his mind was intent on meditating upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
The specific rule regarding this is as follows: during the initiation for Nirvāṇa, one faces the south;
during the two initiations for the specific pledges (*samaya*), one faces the east.
One should be equipped with a lower garment and an upper cloth, and wear a yogic belt (*yogapaṭṭikā*).
On an auspicious seat of darbha grass, one should visualize the fire of the mūlādhāra at a distance of four finger-breadths.
Having raised up the lunar disc,
the instructor should imagine it as remaining stable within the body of the disciple, as appropriate, in the locations of the elements.
The path of mantra, the path of word, the path of phoneme, the worlds, and the path of kalā—
this sixfold division is always pervaded by the paths.
Having caused [the soul] to enter into the state of withdrawal, which is the cause within the paths,
and having likewise severed the bound karma with the sharp sword of knowledge;
The Guru, through various means, should purify the path of the wise by means of the pure [practice];
having rendered [the disciple's state] consisting of Mahāmāyā, which obstructs the consciousness of the disciple,
he should contemplate that Āṇava-śakti of his with his eye.
Then, having seen him, he separated the consciousness from the excellent body.
Having then applied a continuous contemplation upon that [state], which is exceedingly pure like the moon released from Rāhu and uttered as the state of Śiva,
together with the mantra of the temple characterized by its proper measures; (6th line)
Having duly imparted instruction on the three categories of principles.

Having appropriately conceived the body, the object, and the vital breath as being one with Śiva through the initiation known as *anāmaya*, [the disciple] places them first into water and then into the hand of the Guru.
Whatever is offered and whatever remains near your body, O disciple, all that belongs to me alone; you should always conduct yourself with the sense of "this is mine."
Having spoken thus, he should cause the disciple to perform three prostrations before the Guru Śambhu. Then, the pure-souled one himself should perform the worship of the Guru as Śiva;
having praised him with supreme hymns, he should thus conclude the worship. Having performed the worship himself, the disciple [should proceed] before the Guru...

Endowed with faith, together with flowers superior to those of the gods and Gandharvas, as well as incense, lamps, and other offerings, you are not capable here of destroying the torment of the Lord within the cycle of worldly existence. O Embodiment of Compassion, there is no one higher than You; protect me, O Lord of Teachers!
Having thus praised Him and bowed down, even to the eldest [ancestors], with palms joined in reverence, he should feed his own ancestors and elders. He himself...
Having himself eaten the remaining food, he should perform a salutation to the Guru.
This is declared to be the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*); now hear the procedure for the *Dīkṣottara*.
Thus it is said.
Now, in Raurava, or on the bank of a river, in a monastery, or in an auspicious place such as a temple of the Guru—
On a mountain peak, in a pure place, one should have a pavilion constructed there.
Having measured out four fingers [in width], there is a fine altar four cubits [in length];
it is provided with four doors and endowed with four archways.

One should construct a small pavilion above, adorned with fine cotton cloths, variegated silk fabrics, and strings of pearls, and decorated with fragrant flowers. Having applied a coating of cow dung, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having relied upon what was called "place" (sthāna) and likewise upon "time" (kāla) as it is conceived, [the following is stated].
On a day when there is an auspicious conjunction of stars, his initiation should be received;
having appointed the eldest [son], who is endowed with the initiation of knowledge, as the domestic priest (*purohita*),
one should eat only once on that day and consume products of the cow (*gavya*) during that night.
On that day, one should observe a fast, endowed with ritual bathing and purity.
By means of the form of impure *māyā*, she is called Kālarātri;
for it is at the final station of the principle of *māyā* that the nature of consciousness is perceived.
The form is pure at the end of *māyā*, because it transcends the determination of objects;
it is the dissolution of the duality of *māyā* into a single form, wherein the concealment and non-concealment of existence are both invisible and clearly visible.
Through these combined times, it is established as the "Night of Time" (Kālarātri);
she who causes destruction at midnight remains in the night for constant withdrawal.
Since one who is not attached to the body, senses, and so forth dissolves [into the self] at night,
for those who know the scriptures, this constitutes the most excellent time for the night.
At the proper time, having had [the disciple] enter the pavilion and having prepared the sixteen offering substances such as perfumes and flowers, [the preceptor], standing facing north,
should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*), and so forth, as well as the *arghya* and other rites.
The length of the four-pitch [structure] should be thirty-six finger-breadths, and its height likewise.
One should apply fragrant unguents with a mind prepared according to the prescribed rite;
one should worship that which consists of the form of the mantra, beginning with earth and ending with the family (kula).
Well-bathed with scented water and clad in red silk garments,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās, accompanied by the contemplation "I am That."
Having taken refuge in the knowledge-eye, one should grasp the divine lotus-feet;
indeed, having consecrated the two feet with the fragrant substances prescribed in the scriptures.
Having wiped them with a white cloth,
one should offer the water-lilies upon a birch-leaf or a stone slab that has been smeared with fragrant unguents;
having first inscribed the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should then write "namaḥ" in the center of it.
Having meditated upon the impurity of concealment (tirodhānamala), one should cast it onto the seat of the Guru's feet.
One should worship with various divine fragrances and garlands of flowers;
having offered incense and lamps, one should present the *sthālīpāka* oblation.
The disciple, moreover, should contemplate the Guru in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
For this is the liberation from the bonds of existence for the disciple by means of the Guru.
Through the two initiations of vision and knowledge, he performs his duty in due order;
by means of the nature of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), the earth is [perceived] as being only knee-deep.
The earth extends as far as the limit of primordial nature (prakṛti) and has water as its navel;
fire, however, pervades the principle of the Lord of Earth (pṛthivīśvara-tattva) and reaches up to the throat.
The earth is Sadāśiva; the element of air [emerges] from the forehead. (4th line) The earth is the Śakti-tattva, and space [emerges] from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The sixfold form beginning with Mantra, as well as the elements (bhūta) and so forth, exist in pairs;
in these well-concealed locations, the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti shall come into being.
Thus, having become a perfected master, I shall burn away the karma accumulated throughout the paths with the fire of knowledge; that shall be the purification of the paths.
The nature of pure *māyā* and likewise the impurity called *āṇava* remain from beginningless time, existing precisely by obstructing the power of the Self (*ātmaśakti*).
One should observe this with the vision of knowledge; indeed, such a one is called "pure."
One should place the palm of one's own hand upon the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) of the disciple.
Just as the moon becomes stainless at the end of its well-being through the subduing of Rāhu,
so too is the union of consciousness with Śiva the manifestation of that state of Śiva.
Thereafter, one should demonstrate the identity of Śiva and the self by means of the root mantra.
Having placed the disciple directly in front of him, [he should likewise place] his own two feet there.
The Guru should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the head and other parts [of the body] with the nature of Śiva and Śakti. Furthermore,
the disciple who is to be graced should offer to the true Gurus his wealth, his means of knowledge, and his sense of self-importance, through speech, mind, and action.
For this very reason, one should be devoid of independence. Thus,
within the context of the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*), he describes the sixteen purifications (*saṃskāra*) by way of the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*).
In the inconceivable state known as Viśvasādākhya,
when the bonds have become loosened, that which is the elevation of the Self into Śakti and its being conceived as the son of Rudra is called *garbhādhāna* (the rite of conception). (10th line)
The manifestation of qualities such as sovereignty constitutes the birth of the person here;
through the discernment between Māyā and the Self, it is the expansion of the parturient line of knowledge.
The acceptance of Śiva and other entities, whether existent or non-existent, constitutes "generation" (*janana*).
That which is the awakening of one who is worthy of Śiva-nature by means of Śiva-nature itself is called "awakening" (*bodhana*).
Indeed, the entry into Śiva-nature is termed "emergence" (*niṣkrāmaṇa*).
The enjoyment of supreme bliss is called the first feeding with solid food.
That which constitutes the supreme excellence of Śiva is the *cūḍākara* (the topknot);
the sacred thread (*upavītaka*) is the connection with the sūtra of the knowledge of Nirvāṇa.
And the restraint of the senses is remembered as the chosen place (*vṛtā deśa*).
The renunciation of rebirth is celebrated as the "gift of a cow" (godāna).
The state of being independent toward all things is called the "bath" (*snāna*);
the union with infinite power is proclaimed as "marriage" (*vivāha*).
The union with the internal power is held to be the state of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha);
if one were to point out "you" as being solely the true nature of Śiva, that would be so.

One should discard the top-knot and the external sacred thread for the sake of the ascetic. Thus ends the procedure for the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*). This very [initiation] is the *sāmbavadīkṣā*.
(Now, the procedure for Śaiva renunciation:
Now, one should perform renunciation for the sake of pacifying all defects and for the sake of attaining supreme liberation. Thus says the Āgama:
Whatever defects arise from the junctions [of rebirth] and whatever may originate from past actions—
renunciation burns away those defects as fire consumes chaff.
Thirty years beyond, thirty years below, and thirty years further beyond that.

By renunciation alone, one immediately rescues one's ancestors from hell. A wise man should go forth as a wandering mendicant either while still a student, or from the state of a householder, or from the forest; whether he be free from illness or deeply afflicted by suffering.
Furthermore, there is an absence of the act of giving; one whose wife has died may wander as a mendicant.
Forest-dwellers, having shaken off their sins, might resort to a sinful place.
The sage Aṅgiras declared that for one who has encountered a calamity or is threatened by fear in a place frequented by thieves, tigers, and the like, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is prescribed;
for those who are afflicted by illness, there is neither the ritual procedure nor any [other] formal act through renunciation.
Having uttered the syllable "Prāuṣ" alone, one should complete the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) therein.
The destination that is proclaimed for an ascetic who has stayed but a single night cannot be attained by a householder even through hundreds of sacrifices.
He who is attached to the Supreme Self and detached from the Supreme Self,
being liberated from all actions, is worthy to eat even alms.
One who has entered the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) should perform four *kūrca* penances;
however, one still remaining in a [prior] stage of life (*āśramin*) becomes eligible for renunciation only after performing one *kṛcchra* penance.

Now follows the procedure for Śaiva renunciation (*śaivasannyāsakrama*), together with its rules of conduct (*samayācāra*). Having resided in one of the three stages of life (*āśrama*) previously, or being devoid of the stage of life characterized by the rules of conduct, one should perform the fourfold *kṛśra* and then perform the *jīvaśrāddha*.

(The Ritual for the Śrāddha of the Living Being). It is as follows: Having invited twenty Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva—whether they have performed their daily ablutions or [are otherwise prepared]—and having seated them, (second line).

Having washed his feet, sipped water for purification, and sat down facing east in the presence of a Brāhmaṇa, he should first remember Śiva, perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and listen to the sacred syllable *Tath*. Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the *jīvaśrāddha*, which is a limb of my own renunciation (*sannyāsa*)," [he proceeds].

From this point until the conclusion, having become an *upavītī* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder), one should perform the rites with *akṣata* grains alone. Then, for the sake of the Viśvedevas known as Satyavasu, the moment (*kṣaṇa*) should be graciously accepted by you two. For the sake of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, [the moment should be graciously accepted] by you two.

A moment should be granted; for the sake of the celestial sages (*devarṣi*), the Brahman-sages (*brahmarṣi*), and the royal sages (*rājarṣi*), a moment should be granted by you both. For the sake of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, a moment should be granted by you both.
For the sake of Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, and Sanatkumāra—(line 5).

Your time should be graciously granted; for the sake of the great elements, earth and the rest, your time should be graciously granted; for the sake of my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, your time should be graciously granted.
(Line 6)
For the sake of your mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother, you two should grant me the opportunity.

For the sake of yourself, your father, and your paternal grandfather, you two should grant me the opportunity. For the sake of your maternal grandfather and maternal great-grandfather, you two should grant me the opportunity. Thus, two by two.

Having consulted with the Brahmins, and having drawn circles starting from the south and proceeding toward the north, and having worshipped them, one should address the two Brahmins by name in the vocative case and say, "This is the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) for you both," while placing it at their feet within the circle.

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) with *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and water while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), and having washed their feet and then his own feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*),
he should call out the names of those seated in order in the genitive case and offer seats and other items during the *jīvaśrāddha*.
Having offered perfumes, flowers, and garments to each of all those who have attained the [highest] state, saying "I am [their] moment," one should say, "May the worship be complete.
In the case of the father, mother, and others, the worship is performed with their lineage names (*gotra*) and personal names; otherwise, it is performed with their names alone. Then—
Having placed rice with side-dishes and betel-leaf in the bowls, and having strewn the bowls with *kuśa* grass, [he should offer] water together with the Brahmins.

Having sprinkled water clockwise around [the vessel], holding the bowl with the left hand, and grasping unbroken rice (*akṣata*) along with water together with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the right hand, one should offer it to each of them individually using the dative case ending. Then, having propitiated them by saying, "May the *jīva-śrāddha* performed by me be as prescribed," and having prostrated like a staff, one should meditate on Śiva. Thereafter, [one should touch] the feet...

Having washed his hands and sipped water, and having washed the place for placing the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) with cow-dung and water, he should face the east, perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the offering of rice-balls in the *jīva-śrāddha*. Then, having drawn nine lines from south to north... (third line).
Having spread darbha grass upon them in sequence and silently poured water into the five locations beginning with that of the deities,

one should offer water for sipping (*kakṣata*) at the locations of the paternal ancestors, maternal ancestors, and so forth, using their respective names. Then, in sequence, [one should do so] for the deities and others by means of their names ending in the dative case.

For each group, one should give three balls made of wheat flour. Then, having washed his feet and sipped water, he should perform circumambulation, prostration, and other rites toward the Brahmins; after causing them to wash [the hair], he should dismiss them.
(The procedure for shaving and so forth.)

Then, having washed his feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, he should have [the hair] shaved after first clipping the nails of both hands; having established a crest (*śikhā*) measuring seven hairs above the ears, he should have it shorn. Then, having bathed—

Having smeared oneself with ashes by means of the *saṃhārī* [mudrā], having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the deity’s abode, in a temple, a fire-sanctuary, a cow-pen, a forest, or a monastery, facing east and joining the palms in reverence (*brahmāñjali*), one should say: "Salutation to Brahmā;
salutation to Indra; salutation to Sūrya; salutation to the Self (*ātman*); salutation to the Infinite Self (*anantātman*); salutation to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)."

Having recited "Obeisance to the Self of Consciousness," one should offer three handfuls of roasted grain flour (*saktu*)—prepared with barley, wild rice (*nīvāra*), wheat, millet (*ślāmāka*), or *vrīhi*—into the root-fire raised by the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, while reciting: "To the Self, svāhā! To the Infinite Self, svāhā!
To the Supreme Self, svāhā! Then, having sipped water and formed the *parigha-mudrā*, one should consecrate it with that same mantra.

Having performed the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā*) in the presence of Śiva, one should keep a vigil by listening to discourses on Śiva and other such activities. Then, the disciple, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed his daily personal rites, should fully worship the preceptor of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-deśika*).

Having prostrated with the eight limbs, having made his request, having adorned himself, having sipped water for purification, and having sat down facing north upon a seat of *darbha* grass, he should take a handful of *darbha*, perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), meditate upon Śiva and Śivā, and then announce the lunar day (*tithi*).

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the Śaiva renunciation," one should bow to the preceptor (deśika). Thereafter, the preceptor, having adorned the pavilion or the temple with flower garlands and other ornaments, having smeared the site with cow dung, and having made it square by the laying of lines,
and again making it square by the laying of lines, [he should divide] it tenfold on all sides by the laying of lines.
Having divided [the area] and constructed a lotus in the center with two white squares for the pericarp and yellow stamens, according to the lunar portion (one-sixteenth),
and having made it red-hued, one should fashion four lotuses in the four directions starting from the east, each consisting of two by two squares, colored yellow, black, white, and red respectively.

Having performed the rite of emanation according to the portion of Indra, and having fashioned [the image] with a golden luster, one should then begin the worship of Śiva as the solar orb in the northeast.

It has been stated that one should worship the Guru; having performed [the preliminary rites] as before, and having prepared the lotus situated within the mandala of the Vratas, one should offer the seat and other honors to the five Brahmans—Vrateśvara, Svarūpa, Īśāna, and so forth—upon the petals with their respective mantras.
Then, having installed the forms beginning with Īśāna, one should [visualize] the deity in the center of the lotus as two-armed, one-faced, and three-eyed.
One should worship the Candraśekharas in sequence— [those] white, saffron-colored, black, white, and reddish like the moon—
holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), rosary, trident, gesture of fearlessness, sword, shield, iron arrow, bow, blue lotus, and citron.
Having meditated upon the Lords of Vows (Vrateśvaras) and worshipped them with their vehicles and other offerings,
having presented incense, lamps, food offerings, water for drinking, water for sipping, hand-unguents, mouth-perfumes, betel, and so forth,
and having recited each mantra one hundred and eight times, he should offer it and prostrate himself with the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
(The Fire Ritual, etc.
Then the disciple, having requested permission for the fire ritual and received it, goes near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), sits down, and begins the consecration of the pit.

One should offer the full oblation that fulfills all rites. Having performed everything up to this point as previously described, one should extract and protect the fire for the sake of the *caru* offering; then, having performed the fuel-oblation (*idhmahoma*), meditated upon the fire, worshipped it, and prayed to it, one should perform the joining of the reeds (*naḍīsandhāna*).

Having entered the body of the fire through that path, and having worshipped the Lords of Vows (vrateśvaras) in the center of the heart-lotus of the fire, one should request permission, saying, "O Blessed Ones,
I satisfy the Blessed One," and then,
having meditated upon the unity of the Brahma-face and the Fire-face, enter one's own body through the Sadyojāta-face.

Having performed the kindling, joining, and unification of the seven tongues of flame, and having visualized the inclusion of Bahurūpā, Nāyaka, Hiraṇya, and the others, one should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) one hundred and eight times for each of the five Brahmās.

(Śaiva Sannyāsa Procedure) Then the preceptor, having worshipped the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) upon a cow-dung mandala provided with north-pointing *kuśa* grass and unbroken rice grains, [should initiate] the one being ordained there.

Having positioned the disciple with his face upward and directed toward the zenith, while the teacher himself stands otherwise, he should consecrate him with the *saṃhāriṇī* staff-gesture and gaze upon him with divine vision from the feet up to the crown of the head. Then, the disciple [stands] in water reaching the navel in the presence of the Guru.
Standing facing north,
[he recites] the mantra: "Having abandoned mother, father, son, wife, the sacred thread, Śiva, and everything else that has been renounced by me here."

Uttering [the mantra] five times softly, five times moderately, and five times loudly, having extracted the topknot with the left hand while the right hand is held in the *upavīta* position, and having thrown it into the water,
he should loosen his waist-cloth, raise both hands, and say: "Fearlessness to all beings."
Uttering this loudly, facing north, observing silence, and wearing only his loincloth, he should proceed.
Then the preceptor accepts the waist-thread, the loincloth, and other items characterized as mentioned above, for the sake of worldly convention.
(6th line) One should give these to him. Namely: with the mantra ending in *namaḥ sadyojātāya*, one should present the saffron-colored garments, the waist-thread, the loincloth, and the waist-band.
Having accepted them, the ascetic should wash his feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and [approach] the Guru. (7th line)

He should prostrate. Then the preceptor, having seated the disciple facing him nearby, [should mark] with the *namaḥ-antāstra* mantra seven or nine times, measuring only as far as the space between the eyebrows, with a circumference of one thumb, variegated in color, and free from defects such as the *yonimudrā*.
He should bestow a bamboo staff; a begging bowl with its characteristics as previously described, preceded by a salutation at its head; a covering for it with the *kavaca* mantra;
a vessel for alms with the five-syllabled mantra; a *śivaliṅga*; and a book of the knowledge of Śiva—[he should give these] for as long as Śiva [remains].

"One should say: 'Direct realization shall become firm; for that long, one must perform the hearing of the Śiva-śāstras and so forth. Then the disciple, having accepted these [instructions], goes elsewhere, washes his feet, and performs ācamana.
[He then applies] ash consecrated by the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti."
Having dusted [the disciple] with ashes according to the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta at the feet and so forth, and having sipped water and performed the *saṃhāranyāsa*,
one should worship the Preceptor with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and prostrate before him.
(The Instruction on the Great Sayings of the Siddhānta)
Then the preceptor, having placed the Hand of Śiva upon the head of the disciple—
just as water poured into water, a razor into a razor, or ghee into ghee.
In that same way, there would be no distinction between the individual self and the supreme self.

Having thus joined [the disciple] with that which is meaningful according to the words—[namely] the indivisible form, the non-dual, perfect plenitude of Being-Consciousness-Bliss—he should instruct him, saying, "Thou art Śiva. The disciple, too, having contemplated this, should declare, "I am Śiva. Thereafter, having risen, [he should approach] the Guru...
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman—salutations to that illustrious Guru.
Having offered such praises, one should perform three circumambulations and twelve prostrations.
(The Conduct of the Ascetic) Now, the Preceptor shall instruct the ascetic in his conduct. (Line 4)
Thus is the traditional teaching: the teacher, endowed with compassion, should speak thus to that disciple:
"I am Śiva," being possessed of contemplation and endowed with both external and internal purity.
Engaged in bathing at the three times of day, yet restricted to a single time;
with his entire body smeared with sacred ash, clad in washed saffron robes;
equipped with a loincloth and a staff, he is devoted solely to the worship of the Liṅga.
Endowed with the yoga of Śiva, he was entirely devoted to the meditation upon Śiva.
Endowed with the experience of Śiva, he is free from all afflictions;
he is equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, regarding a clod of earth and gold as the same.
Possessing a state of universal loving-kindness and always endowed with contentment,
one should view a woman as a corpse while being fully imbued with the spirit of Śiva;
free from sorrow, one enters into the sufferings of others, becoming united with their joy and pain.
In that very same way, he who is pained by the suffering of others is enveloped [by it].
Endowed with such qualities, even for those who are like children, madmen, or Piśācas,
one should daily recite the root mantra while being solely intent on the meditation of Śiva.
When the recitation comes to an end, one should likewise take recourse in meditation.
Having ceased from meditation and being composed, one should always thereafter mutter the root mantra.
Like medicine, one should consume food, drink, and so forth for the sake of pacifying the affliction of hunger;
for the purpose of alms, one should enter a village, or else [dwell] at the foot of a tree or in a monastery cell.
He may reside in a monastery or similar dwelling constructed by another;
furthermore, for ascetics, the twilight worship (sandhyā-vandana) is performed through the twilight of knowledge (jñāna-sandhyā).
In the Devīkālottara (10th line):
"O Goddess, conduct (ācāra) is now being described; listen to it from me.
There is no [need for] knowledge, no recitation, no worship, no fire-oblation, and no ritual practice."
No fire-rituals are to be performed; he has no Great Goddess (Maheśvarī).
He has no observance (*niyama*), nor service at the sacred fields (*kṣetra*) and seats (*pīṭha*). There is no worship, no ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*), no pilgrimages, and no vows.
There is no fruit of merit or demerit, nor is there any practice of extreme asceticism or worldly activity.

One should renounce all ritual actions and worldly conduct without exception; having fulfilled one's duties, one should relinquish even the wealth associated with the complete observance of conventional rules.
When conceptualization, discursive thought, and other family-specific rites,
as well as various forms of supernatural accomplishments and elixirs such as those of Pātāla,
are obtained through direct perception, the practitioner should not grasp them at all.
Apart from this all-pervading nature of consciousness, there is no higher liberation through these [other means].
In every way, animal sacrifices lead to the lower paths;

by whatever guise one may be, in every state, one is separated from consciousness. If there is curiosity, one should abandon the body while dwelling in the sacred field (*kṣetra*) or the seat (*pīṭha*).
Then, O Goddess, [he created] worms, insects, moths, and the lords of the forest.
One should not pulverize or destroy [anything], just as the intellect does not do so regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
one should not uproot the very root, and one should avoid cutting even a blade of grass.
One should not pluck flowers from a natural pedestal;
if worship is to be performed, it should be done with flowers that have fallen of their own accord.
[One should avoid] rites such as killing, driving away, creating enmity, and likewise paralyzing.
It effects the subjugation, summoning, and delusion of those possessed by fever-demons.
One should not perform minor rites such as the worship of wood or stone;

nor should one offer hand-gestures (*mudrā*) or sacrifices to the deities of the sacred fields (*kṣetra*) or seats (*pīṭha*). Having abandoned all conditioned mental impressions (*vāsanā*), one should take refuge in all-pervading awakening (*bodha*).
Equanimity, freedom from passion, and likewise equality toward pleasure and pain.
Being equal toward both friend and foe, and regarding a clod of earth and gold as the same,
the yogi then becomes fearless, free from desire, and established in the Self.
Being equal toward blame and praise, always equal toward all beings,
one should maintain an impartial vision, regarding others exactly as oneself.
One should avoid dispute, worldly gossip, and quarrel;
one should not engage in scholarly debate concerning ill-spoken or well-spoken words.
One should also avoid envy, calumny, hypocrisy, passion, and even malice.
One should gradually abandon all desire, anger, fear, and sorrow.
Completely liberated from all dualities and perpetually free from people,
omniscience is attained by means of this very body.
When liberation is attained through knowledge alone, then supernatural power (siddhi) is useless;
nevertheless, practitioners desire both enjoyment and supernatural power.
In the *Sūtasamhitā*, within the section on the three-fold path of knowledge and yoga (*jñānayogakhaṇḍa*):
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsāśrama*).
Monks are to be known as fourfold, according to the distinctions in their conduct."
O best of sages, I shall describe to you the conduct of the Kuṭīcaka, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsa. The Kuṭīcaka, having renounced, should always remain in his own house.
Having taken alms, he should eat them either here or at his own kinsmen's place.
He should wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*);
he should possess the purifier (*pavitra*) and wear ochre robes (*kāṣāya*), and should always recite the *Gāyatrī*.
He should perform the smearing of ashes over all his limbs and apply the three marks (*tripuṇḍra*) at the three junctions of the day.
One should perform the worship of the Śivaliṅga every single day with faith alone.
In the Bahūdaka stage of renunciation, one who is devoid of kinsmen, sons, and the like,
should wander for alms among seven houses and avoid food obtained by purchase. He should be well-bound with a cow’s tail-hair rope and possess three garments and a water-pot.
A bowl, a water-strainer, a loincloth, and a water-pot.
A covering garment, as well as a shoulder-cloth, sandals, an excellent umbrella,
a sacred antelope skin, a needle, a water-strainer, a rosary of beads,
a yogic staff, a spade, and a hand-drum.
In that same manner, one should apply the smearing of all the limbs as well as the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Wearing the topknot and the sacred thread, devoted to the worship of the deity,
he should always abandon all speech during his private recitation, remaining intent upon meditation. At the time of the twilights, he should perform the ritual of muttering the Sāvitrī mantra.
The haṃsa [carries] a water-pot, a white cloth, and likewise an alms-bowl.
Having covered his shoulders and private parts with a garment, and wearing a necklace of beads outside his feet,
he should always carry a single bamboo staff with due reverence.
He should apply the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with holy ashes and worship the *śivaliṅga*.
One should always eat eight mouthfuls at once; he shall plant auspiciousness.
At the time of twilight, one should perform the recitation of the Sāvitrī, meditation on the inner self,
service at sacred fords, as well as insignificant tasks and the study of the Ājñāyaṇa and other texts;
one should practice these according to the rule of staying for only one night in a village.
A parahaṃsa carries a triple staff and a rope made of cowhair.
The white rosary, the sacred thread, the *kalandhava* [water-pot],
the skin of the *vaṅkṣiṇī* deer, the *sravi*, and that sacred thread for the hand—
Śivā [the consort] and the sacrificial thread; one should abandon these as part of the daily ritual (*nityakarman*).
A loincloth for covering, a garment for the shoulders, and a cloak to ward off the cold.
One should take up the yogic garment, the outer cloth, the sandals,
the sacrificial seat, the rosary, and the unyielding bamboo staff;
then, with joy, one should perform the smearing of ashes with the mantras beginning with "agniriti" and so forth.
Having spoken thus to Miḍa, he then applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) with the *haṃsa* mantra.
One should take a vessel made of clay, or one of bell-metal, or indeed one of wood or bamboo; likewise, having sipped water for purification, one should take a vessel for the stomach [to hold food].
The Śruti declares that he should not employ a bell-metal vessel, but rather an earthen one;
likewise, the Parahaṃsa should wander with a single staff. Indeed, there is no yoga for one who is not disciplined, nor is there liberation for one who lacks yoga.
Therefore, the Paramahaṃsa should enjoy [alms] from one who possesses virtues through yoga;
having purified one who is accused, he should practice [this] among all castes.
Upon attaining each subsequent stage, one should relinquish each preceding one;
through constant service to the Guru, one should thoroughly practice self-knowledge.
[One should observe] bathing, purity, meditation, and truthfulness free from falsehood.
The abandonment of desire and anger, free from joy and wrath.
The exponents of Brahman declare that for all [ascetics], there is the renunciation of greed and delusion, free from ritual grass, darbha, and the like, as well as the Cāturmāsya vow.
There are the Kuṭīcaka, the Haṃsa, and likewise the Bahūdaka.
O Goddess, let there be the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* for those who have conquered their senses;
nevertheless, one is liberated when purified by the direct realization of the Lord.
"Śiva resides right here within this body composed of the five elements;
from Śiva down to the earth, this world has Śaṅkara as its very essence. (2nd line)
He states the characteristics of the three types of Śaiva renunciants:
In the inconceivable state known as Viśvasāda, three types of ascetics are to be known: the practitioner of austerity (*tapasvin*), the learned one (*vidvan*), and likewise the knower (*vidvān*).
These are declared to be threefold; hear their distinctions in due order.
To him who was devoted to austerity and was an ascetic, Suvratā provided his livelihood;
for him there was no study, no ritual resolve, and nothing whatsoever to be heard.
He should not engage in the gathering of disciples nor in the public exposition of knowledge;
he should not speak in the Sanskrit language, nor carry a staff or a water-pot.
Having worshipped the *liṅga* for a moment, he remains endowed with the path of devotion.
Alone at the foot of a tree, or in a forest devoid of people.
Filled with fear, he should dwell among people using his own arm as a pillow;
likewise, he should subsist on whatever clothing, food, and drink may be available.
"Subsisting on food obtained by begging, with the hand as the bowl and the stomach as the bag—

such a person is called a *tapasvin* (ascetic), while one who possesses the name of a *yati* (renunciant) is a *sāyaka*. O Nandikeśvara, this is the mode of conduct for both those who desire knowledge (*vividiṣu*) and those who are united [in realization]."
Teaching, studying, listening, and likewise reflecting;

There is a distinction between a *vidvat* and a *yati*: [the former] consists of exposition (*vyākhyāna*) and reflection (*cintana*). One who is endowed with the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of a true teacher is designated as a *vidvat*. For *yatis*, there are three types, and for Śaivas, there are four stages of life (*āśrama*).
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for Śaiva renunciation.
(The Ritual for the Initiation of the Master). Next is the ritual for the initiation of the material master (the characteristics of those qualified for initiation, etc.):
"The three categories and four feet, which give rise to the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. (8th line)
The disciple who thoroughly understands the Saṃhitā is worthy of initiation.
Devoted to the vow of truth, peaceful, endowed with renunciation, and full of compassion;
with a serene countenance, skillful, devoted to his guru, and firm in his vows.
One who is fully endowed with purity and proper conduct, disciplined in yoga, having conquered the senses,
a devotee of Śiva, ever self-restrained, and one who has mastered the tantra— such a person is a fit disciple.

Having performed the previously mentioned initiation and having cleared the path, the knower of mantras should then perform that consecration for one who discriminates between what is appropriate and inappropriate.
Here (the tenth line),
the sequence is as follows: having adorned the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) according to the previously mentioned method,

and having caused the consecration pavilion (*abhiṣekamaṇḍapa*) to be constructed and adorned according to the method to be described hereafter, one who has performed his daily obligatory rites [should proceed] between Indra and Agni.

Having worshipped Śiva, who resides within the solar disc, as before, and having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), with the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*) in hand, one should complete the ritual actions— beginning with the worship of the gatekeepers and the archway (*toraṇa*) and ending with the satiation and illumination of the mantras— as previously described.
For the purpose of removing ill omens that cause one to leave the country and for establishing auspicious signs,
one should perform the oblation as before. Then, in another case, for one who has been initiated elsewhere, or for a disciple who, immediately after initiation,
is joined with a deficiency in conduct, there is again an immediate consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Having performed the rites beginning with the *samaya* and ending with the initiation into *nirvāṇa*, one should confer the *ācāryābhiṣeka*. (The sequence for obtaining Śiva’s authorization:
Then, having gone into the presence of Śiva...
"O Lord of excellent vows, I have been thus commanded by you, who are the very embodiment of the Guru: 'This yoga of initiation and exposition must be maintained without interruption by you,
who possess perfect knowledge and whose conduct is circularly complete.'"
It should be given to one's own disciple immediately after the consecration of the head.
"By your grace, this [opportunity] has now come to me;
with your permission, I shall bestow upon him the yoga.
Having thus made his request and received permission, the disciple—having performed his daily rites—performed the worship of the deities beginning with Indra and ending with Agni.
One should cause [it] to be made.
(The procedure for the placement of the consecration jar.
Thereafter, to the north of the pavilion—or to the east or west—one should face either the east or the north.
Or, having caused a bathing pavilion to be constructed and adorned it with canopies, garlands of flowers, and so forth, one should have two square altars built there, situated from south to north,
each two cubits in width and eight finger-breadths in height.
Having smeared the two altars with cow dung and strewn them with barley and unbroken rice grains, one should proceed there to the lotus and svastika [designs].
Having drawn [the mandala] on a level altar and having worshipped six raised seats upon five heaps of grain,
one should place the water-pots (kumbhas) upon them. Herein is the sequence:
In the inconceivable [space] called Viśvasāda,
one should first place the jars upon heaps of grain; among them, one should set down the Śiva-jar, and to its left, the Vardhanī jar, consecrated with the Śakti-mantra.
One should place the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) outside of that;
likewise, one should place a single-leafed *bhadra* tree and a *vaikaṅkata* tree together with the Goddesses.
Viṣṇukrānti—these five are known as the "five medicinal herbs" (pañcauṣadha). Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, hirihera, and māṃsī [are the other five].
Saffron, the root of *uśīra*, lac, and *jātī*— these,
combined with the five jewels and medicinal herbs, and joined with *śāli* rice grains;
He offered eight oceans as gifts: those filled with pure water and adorned with mango sprouts;
and among them, the salt ocean, the ocean of curd, the ocean of milk, the ocean of wine, the ocean of clarified butter, the ocean of sugarcane juice, the ocean of honey, and the ocean of pure water.
In the center of the ocean of Śiva, within the Vardhanī, is the ocean of Śakti.
Having invoked and worshipped the eight Vidyeśvaras in sequence,
one should worship everything according to the rules, joined with eight recitations of the root mantra. Then,
by means of the five pitchers associated with the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, [one should perform the ritual].
Alternatively, one may perform the consecration with a single copper vessel.
One should install two Vidyeshas in each of the five jars;
likewise, one should also install a pair of Samudras in the same manner.
In the center, however, [one should place] the Śiva-vessel and likewise the Śiva-water-ocean;
and at its side, the Vardhanī vessel, accompanied by the Śakti-water-ocean.
The preeminent teacher should place Śiva and Śakti, as well as the lords of the vidyās, into a single pitcher; he should also place the ten mudrās therein.

Then, for the sake of enjoyment (*bhukti*), one should consecrate the *śāntyatīta-kalā* and the others in the central, eastern, southern, northern, and western pitchers; and for the sake of liberation (*mukti*), one should consecrate the *nivṛtti-kalā* and the others in the western, northern, southern, eastern, and central pitchers. [For the sake of] enjoyment, [one should perform the rite] through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) starting from the Ocean of Śiva (*śivasāgara*) and continuing through the oceans such as the *anantara*.
Having invoked and worshipped the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), for the sake of liberation, one should invoke the eight oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk into the jars;
having invoked and worshipped them, one should invoke the Ocean of Śiva into the central jar and worship it, and likewise invoke the Lords of Knowledge into the jars.

Having worshipped Śiva, together with His limbs (*aṅga*) and retinues (*āvaraṇa*), in the central jar according to the daily rite (*nityavat*), one should then consecrate [the offerings] one hundred and eight times with the root mantra and perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) until its completion according to the prescribed number of recitations (*japa*). Alternatively—
Having established either five jars or a single jar in the manner described, one should worship them.
(The procedure for the initiation of the disciple) Then... (line 7)

Having worshipped the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) upon an auspicious throne made of *śrīparṇa* wood and other materials, one should have the initiate (*bhautika*) sit facing east and the lifelong practitioner (*naiṣṭhika*) facing north; then, having performed the ritual of integration (*sakaḷīkaraṇa*), one should worship them with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) according to the sequence beginning with Indra.

Having protected the disciple with divine garments such as the vajra-cloth, and having cleansed him with all the nectars— namely ashes, cow dung, sour gruel, boiled rice, white mustard seeds, and water from the beloved [vessel]— and having enveloped him three times with the water of the armor-mantra, one should place the jars endowed with the retention of nectar for the purpose of consumption.

For the sake of liberation, having lifted [the disciple] by way of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama), one should consecrate the perfected Lord of Knowledge (vidyeśa) with the sounds of Vedic chanting (brahmaghoṣa) and auspicious musical instruments,
using the root mantra and the mantras to be accomplished. Thereafter, [one should apply] the water clinging to his limbs...

Having wiped [the disciple] with a clean cloth, having caused him to rise [from his seat] with clarified butter, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should establish the disciple upon the sixfold raised seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) at the southern altar; having worshipped him as Śiva and having encircled him three times with three handfuls of *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and so forth, for the sake of accomplishing the eight auspicious signs (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*).
One should offer gorocanā, sandalwood, dūrvā grass,
flowers, curd, milk-rice, barley, and white mustard seeds, and then pay one's respects.

(The Procedure for Bestowing the Self-Composed Text, etc. Then the Preceptor, having taken hold of the disciple with his left hand, leads him into the sacrificial pavilion; having caused him to perform three circumambulations, he places him to the south of the mandala.
Having worshipped the sixfold arising seat (ṣaḍutthāsana) arranged upon the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], and having seated the disciple there and honored him;
having seated the disciple there and worshipped him, [he should offer] his own Saṃhitā, the rosary, the three [sacraments], and the yogapaṭṭikā.
A water-pot, sandals, a needle-case, and a thread-cutter.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a finger-ring, *darbha* grass, an elephant, a horse, a palanquin, and so forth,
as well as a turban and a crown—
one should present these to the preceptor who is a householder.
The uṣṇīṣa crown, the parasol, the sandals, the chowries, and so forth.
"One should present these to the most excellent lifelong preceptor.
(The procedure for the worship of Caṇḍeśvara and others).
Then, having worshipped [the deity] together with Caṇḍeśvara, one should [worship] Sadāśiva, Ananta, and Hara in the eight directions starting from the east of that [deity] with the Heart-mantra.

Having worshipped the Goddess, Acyuta, Kamalāsana, Skanda, and his own guru, and having likewise caused the disciple to perform the worship of Caṇḍeśvara and offered libations to Caṇḍeśvara and the others in the fire, the preceptor, placing a flower in the hand of the disciple,
[stands] in the presence of the worshipped guru.
And you, my child, being an authorized recipient, [should maintain] the supreme reality and the pledges witnessed by Caṇḍeśa and the Guru, which have come down through the lineage of the Gurus.
"From this day forward, the residents of that region must always perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, having reflected well upon them by the command of Śiva.
Thus (line 8) he should cause the command of Śiva to be heard. The Guru should salute the disciple who has been consecrated for the surrender of his own authority.

Then, the preceptor, though not yet qualified [to initiate others], having gone to the presence of the fire and offered one hundred and eight oblations ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* using the root mantra for the sake of his own initiation, should seat the disciple— who has joined his palms in reverence— to his right, and worship him with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) for the satisfaction of the mantra.

Having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra until the end is complete, one should mark the little fingers of the disciple’s right hand with burnt *darbha* grass while reciting the mantras, in order to produce a state of heat (*ūṣmatva*). Then, having first joined the channels (*nāḍī*), one should place the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*) upon his head and [transfer] that which resides in the fire.
Having invoked Śiva and having offered libations, one should perform the worship— beginning with the ritual vessel (*kumbha*) and ending with one's own self— for Śiva;
this constitutes the procedure for the initiation of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and so forth.

The procedure for initiation is also applicable to the initiation of a practitioner (*sādhaka*), though it is accompanied by the mantra of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and is devoid of the ritual instruments such as the *uṣṇīṣa* and the *kartarī*. For a Śaiva renunciant (*śaivasannyāsī*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) shall perform the remainder of the *ācāryābhiṣeka* after the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), except for the Śaiva renunciation itself.
As it has been stated in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*: "The procedure for the fire-ritual of Śiva has been taught as being independent of [worldly] ascetics;
therefore, the rites of the Śaiva path must be performed especially by an ascetic."
Indeed, there is a slight distinction among the Ācāryas and the Yatis;
likewise, there is a distinction between the Parahaṃsa Yatis and those who have renounced through austerity (tapas-nyāsins).
"The eligibility of these two for fire-rituals is not prescribed;
thus, for them, consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is ordained instead of the *homa*.
Thus ends the [work] composed by Śivāgrayogin, the preeminent teacher beyond the castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśrama*), the protector of the Śaiva tradition.
[The fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Initiation of the Preceptor," in the Kriyādīpikā.]
|| The Final Rite ||
(5th line) Now,
the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) is described— the so-called funeral rite.
The final supreme reality, the state of being desired, and the entry [into it]—
this is designated as the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) according to the rule of the path of yoga.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*,
the procedure for the final funeral rites (*anty-eṣṭi-vidhāna*) is now briefly described by me:
here, the yogin who has passed away through the process of transference (*utkrānti*), having burnt away all his impurities, [attains liberation].
One should burn his pure body, consisting of mantra, with the fire of Śiva. Neither the rite of the funeral cake (*piṇḍakriyā*) nor the rite of water (*udakakriyā*) should be performed for him.
However, at that time, the disciples must perform the worship of Śiva in order to discharge their debt.
In this context, it is stated how that [attainment] occurs for all others as well.
For those men who are established in the reality [of the teachings] through initiation, who possess constant right conduct,
who are skilled in the meaning of the Siddhānta, and whose [worldly] selves have been dissolved by time;
One may burn the body with the fire of Śiva, yet there is no ritual action for that;
rather, purification of the path is ordained for those who have failed in conduct and vows.
He who violates the rules of conduct (*samaya*) at any time subsequent to initiation shall become a partaker of great sin (*mahāpātaka*) toward the deity and the gurus;
this applies to those who have not abandoned doubt and to others whose nature is defiled.
O Guha, for the sake of removing their sins, the funeral rites have been prescribed;
yet by transgressing the rules and other commitments, one attains only the abode of the bound.
For those who have resorted to other scriptures and likewise for those whose rites have been neglected, the funeral ceremony (antyeṣṭi) must be performed with effort;
otherwise, one shall not attain the supreme state.
One should perform the purification of the paths for the most excellent practitioners and teachers;
however, one should not do so for one who abides by the commitments (*samaya*) or for one who desires liberation.
Whether it be an Ācārya, a Sādhaka, a Putraka, or a Samayin—
whether they be observers of vows or householders— one should place the deceased and adorn them, according to the Kāmika.
When the time known as the departure of life has arrived for a living being,
he should perform the ritual bath and prepare his body with the protective mantras of Agni.
And for one desiring liberation, having prepared the mantra-body as it should be known,
and having worshipped the God with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) out of a desire for liberation,
[one should worship] with sandalwood and other substances using both hands, which have been rendered serviceable by oneself.
Having established Maheśvara in the form of a liṅga within his heart.
Having touched his head with joined palms and placed them there,
he should speak these words for that purpose in the presence of the Lord of Gods.
"O Lord, this one who is devoted to the welfare of all worlds and is the observer of Śiva’s command has been initiated by you; he shall be led to the state of Śiva without delay."
Having thus informed the Lord of the Gods, one should establish him in his own place;
one may perform this rite either once or many times.
At the time of the soul's departure (*utkrānti*), one should recite the *saṃhitā* near the ear;
specifically, the *Śiva-mantra* or the five-syllabled (*pañcākṣara*) mantra.
All of this should be performed by either the preceptor (*deśika*) or another [qualified person].
That [deceased] should be addressed by one who knows his lineage, or by another, with the ritual action that is about to be described.
Now, [the procedure for bringing to the cremation ground] one who has passed away— whether by departing [from the body] or otherwise:
having laid the deceased householder down and adorned him, one should bind his two well-joined big toes with a white thread.

Having performed the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) in the manner that will be described, and having placed [the image] upon a temporary scaffold made of sacrificial wood during the winter season, one should mount it onto a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) resembling a staircase to heaven, adorned with red garments, banners, flowers, and garlands; then, placing the fire accompanied by smoke in front, [The remainder of the sentence follows: ...one should proceed.

Having had [the object] carried by those initiated into the same class as himself, who recite the *astra-mantra* and possess the seal of the pledge (*samaya-mudrā*), and having scattered an offering (*bali*) in the directions along the path toward the target amidst the resounding blasts of conchs, cymbals, drums, and other instruments, [he should offer] powdered incense, betel, and parched grain at night.
Having scattered [the remains] toward the north, the northeast, or another direction, one should reach a cremation ground near water and lower [the body] there with its head facing south.
(The procedure for constructing the pavilion.)
Then,
