In the tongue: *hāṃ*, homage to the reality of the tongue (*jihvātattva*); *hāṃ*, homage to Mahāvaktra, the lord of the reality of the tongue (*jihvātattvādhipa*). In the nose: *hāṃ*. (9th line)
Homage to the reality of the nose. Hāṃ, homage to Vilambaka, the lord of the reality of the nose. In the mouth: Hāṃ, homage to the reality of speech.
Hāṃ, homage to Dundubhi, the lord of the reality of speech. In the two hands: Hāṃ, homage to the reality of the hands.
Hāṃ... (130a, first line)

To the Lord of the principle of the hands, Samadāya, homage! At the two feet: (–) *hāṃ*, homage to the principle of the feet (*pādatattva*). *Hāṃ*, homage to Ramaṇa, the Lord of the principle of the feet (*pādatattvādhipa*). At the anus: (–) *hāṃ*, homage to the principle of the anus (*pāyutattva*). *Hāṃ*, homage to Tūrṇakṛt, the Lord of the principle of the anus (*pāyutattvādhipa*). At the generative organ: (–) (second line).

Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the generative organ (upastha-tattva). Hāṃ, obeisance to Ghanānanda, the presiding deity of the principle of the generative organ. Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of sound (śabda-tattva). Hāṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣmānanda, the presiding deity of the principle of sound. Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of touch (sparśa-tattva).
Hāṃ, obeisance to Balavattara, the presiding deity of the principle of touch. (Third Line)
Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of form (rūpa-tattva). Hāṃ, obeisance to Bhānumat, the lord of the principle of form. Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of taste (rasa-tattva).

Hāṃ, obeisance to Jalada, the lord of the principle of taste. Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of smell (gandha-tattva). Hāṃ, obeisance to Gandhāṅga, the lord of the principle of smell. In the Yoni: (–) Hāṃ. (4th line)

Salutation to the element of space (*vyomatattva*). Hāṃ, salutation to Sūkṣma, the lord of the element of space. In that very place, Hāṃ, salutation to the element of air (*vāyutattva*). Salutation to Mātariśvan, the lord of the element of air. Within the womb, in the location of the navel, Hāṃ, salutation to the element of fire (*agnitattva*). Hāṃ. (5th line)
Salutation to the Lord of the fire-element (*tejas-tattva*), the repository of splendors. Then, [down to] the knees: *Hāṃ*, salutation to the water-element (*jala-tattva*);

*Hāṃ*, salutation to the Lord of the water-element, the Lord of Waters (*jaleśa*). Below the knees: *Hāṃ*, salutation to the earth-element (*pṛthivī-tattva*); *Hāṃ*, salutation to the Lord of the earth-element, Śrīkaṇṭha. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by including the worlds beginning with the hells and Pātāla within these elements.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings and meditated upon that form, [one should contemplate] within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, in the left, right, and middle [channels],
the triad of channels known as Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā; and within those, the triad of powers known as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, as well as merit and demerit.
Having thus disposed [the elements] and having invoked and established oneself by means of that name through the application of the Great Net (*mahājāla*),

one should perform everything up to the stage of conjunction (*yojanikā*) as before and cremate [the body] as previously described. At the conclusion of that cremation, having offered three oblations of the principles (*tattva*), one should dismiss the fire, collect the ashes, and cast them into deep water.
He now states the expiation for an untimely death.
Now, for those whose lives have been taken through negligence, or by thieves, snakes, fire,
elephants, tigers, the force of a river, or in battle;
Having extracted [the consciousness] from others who are devoid of self and whose bodies are subject to death,
one should first burn their body silently with the fire of Śiva.

Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred thousand times, and having offered the Rudra-bali as prescribed, one should worship the Rudras on the Raudra ground and likewise worship those Kṣetrapālas.
May those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes,
as well as the other Kṣetrapālas, Piśācas, Dānavas,
and so forth— may they all, with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering.
Through the power of a violent death, he has attained the state of a piśāca.
Having requested, "Release [them]," one should cast down a handful of offerings:
*Hāṃ!
Salutation to Rudra, Raudra, Kṣetrapāla, Piśāca, Rākṣasa, Dānava, Bhūta, Graha, Kūśmāṇḍa, and the others who desire the offering.*

The application of mantras for worship, the offering of oblations, and so forth, ends with "svāhā. Having bathed, sipped water, and returned, one should feed eight ascetics who observe the great vow, or those belonging to the Pāśupata and other such orders.
Having gratified her with garments and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should dismiss her;
having fashioned an effigy (*puttalikā*) out of *darbha* grass, serving as a replica of her body.
Having written his name upon a leaf, having tied it around his neck and rubbed it [with ashes],
and having performed the remaining rites as before, one should unite him in the stainless state.
[Thus ends the section] composed by the venerable Ativarṇāśramācāryavarya, the protector of the Śaiva tradition, the foremost yogin Śiva.
[In the Kriyādīpikā, the sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Final Rites" (Antyeṣṭividhi):
(The Procedure for Digging)] Now, [regarding] the renunciants (sannyāsins)... (6th line)

The procedure for entering the cremation ground is now described: A renunciant (*sannyāsī*) who is firmly established in absolute dispassion (*atyantavairāgya*), yet unable to endure the latent impressions of the body (*dehavāsanā*), should go to a sacred site of Śiva (*śivakṣetra*) and abandon the body through deliberate effort for the sake of liberation.
As it is said in the *Śaiva Purāṇa*: [text omitted].
And that mortal who, though subject to death, has repeatedly seen both the desirable and the undesirable, should, being devoted to the practice of yoga, take refuge in the abode of Śiva.
Within a hundred cubits in every direction from the linga is the sacred field of Śiva;
for embodied beings who die there, it is the cause of attaining union with Śiva.
This measurement of the sacred field is prescribed for a *liṅga* installed by humans;
for a self-manifested (*svayambhu*) one, it should be a thousand [units], and for one established by sages (*ārṣa*), it should be half of that.
Since even one of evil conduct who dies therein goes to Śiva,
therefore one should construct a dwelling in the vicinity of a sacred field of Śiva;
indeed, one should personally renounce even one's life-breaths through yoga and other such means.
Having thus observed a fast and offered his body into the fire of Śiva, he departed.
Or, having cast his own body into the sacred waters of Śiva (*śivatīrtha*) and immersed himself therein,
he who should renounce his life according to the procedure prescribed in the Śiva scriptures shall be liberated immediately; nor is such a person a suicide.
"Nevertheless, they desire death through fasting and other such means.

These [statements] refer to the practitioner (*sādhaka*). However, for one who has attained realization through knowledge (*jñānasiddha*), there is no dependence on death in a specific sacred field (*viśiṣṭakṣetra*) through wisdom (*prajñā*)... [text fragment]. Thus says the *Āgama*.
"At a sacred ford, in the house of a dog-eater, or even with memory lost, one may cast off the body;
liberated at the very moment of knowledge, he attains absolute isolation (kaivalya), his sorrow destroyed. Thus [it is said].
Now, whether by means of departure from the body or otherwise, for those who have become pure within the fire of the womb...

Since it is heard in scripture that there is a fault in cremating Śaiva renunciants who have maintained the sacred fire of Śiva, one should instead perform their excavation (khanana). As it is said in the *Siddhāntabodha*:
"Of the knowers, the yogis, and those performing austerities who possess the form of ascetics..."
Indeed, the characteristic sign for the falling of people’s bodies is as follows:
one should dig a pit measuring four cubits in size, shaped like a hollowed-out *śībhala* fruit,
and fill it sequentially with two cubits of turmeric powder and salt.
Having placed Śiva upon that auspicious lotus-seat,
[one should place him] with salt along with [other substances] in the ground-area of the side directions;
filling it with one cubit [of space], [leaving] a portion of one cubit for the other side.
And one should make it level with the clay; therefore, when the ground has been leveled, [one should proceed].
Others, having properly prepared a pedestal,
[worship] others through the sequence of single forms on a pedestal made of clay or stone, provided it is joined with three girdles.
Then, having installed the liṅga, perform the ritual of digging in due order with perfumes,
flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth.
"Having worshipped according to the rule, one should perform [the rite] that brings great increase to the king and the kingdom;
or else, if one should perform the cremation, it will bring about the destruction of the king and the kingdom. Thus it is said in the *Suprabheda*.
"The procedure for cremation is prescribed for the three stages beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*);
however, one should not perform cremation for ascetics (*yatis*), nor the rite of digging a pit.
Thus [it is stated] in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
"Having previously deposited the world-fire into the fire of the stomach,
and because of the absence of external fire-rituals, one should cover [the body] with salt. (This is the procedure for the digging and transporting to the burial site.)

For example, his disciple or another devotee of Śiva, having bathed with ashes, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and effected the ritual integration of the self (*sakalīkaraṇa*), shall wash the body of the Śiva-yogin; having bathed the body of the Śiva-yogin with ashes in the manner to be described, changed his loincloth, and adorned him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, [he should offer it] to the devotees of Śiva.
One should offer riches, perfumes, unbroken grains, and betel. Then, having placed the body of the Śiva-yogin in a pure palanquin or in the previously mentioned celestial chariot (*vimāna*),
and having had it carried by initiated persons of equal caste, [one should proceed].

Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, trumpets, auspicious drums, and the like, and together with the scattering of flowers and parched grain, one should slowly lead [the body] toward the eastern or northern direction and place the body of the Śiva-yogin in a pure location on the bank of a river or at the root of an Aśvattha tree, with the head facing south.

In a temple, a cow-pen, at the root of a sacred tree (*brahmavṛkṣa*), or at the root of a *bīra* tree, one should sprinkle the ground with milk and dig a pit (*avaṭa*) two cubits wide, four cubits long, and half a cubit deep. Then,
having smeared the pit with cow-dung, one should spread a layer of sand upon it.
Having spread pure *darbha* grass, one should worship silently with perfumes and other offerings. (This is the procedure for the rites of digging and consecration.

Then, having sprinkled the body of the Śiva-yogin with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, one should bathe it with water from sacred sites while reciting the *Śivasaṃhitā* ending with the word *svāhā*.

One should bathe [the disciple]. Then, having exchanged the loincloth and the waist-thread, one should sprinkle the feet, the private parts, the heart, the mouth, and the head with the five mantras beginning with *Sadyojāta* and ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having sprinkled the western, northern, southern, eastern, and central locations of his head with those [mantras] ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should do so] with those [mantras] ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Having scattered the six limbs with the six parts [of the mantra] (line 5), and having scattered all the limbs with the *prāsāda* mantra, one should perform the consecration of ashes upon his head with the *śivasaṃhitā* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, change his loincloth (*kaupīna*), and adorn him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth (line 6).

Having properly placed the body of the auspicious yogi upon a funeral pyre amidst the sounds of great drums and auspicious musical instruments, having applied ashes to his armpits and placed a bamboo staff in his hand, having worshipped him with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) consisting of bilva leaves and other items, and having recited the root mantra over his heart— (line 7)
Alternatively, having worshipped Avaṭa with bilva leaves or salt, one should install a Śiva-liṅga or his image in the area near it and worship it with the rites of invocation and so forth.
This is stated in the Kāmika: (–)
If the corpse is accompanied by the departure [of consciousness], the yogin should,
having adorned it with all those pure ornaments, cause it to be carried out.
And let them place the corpse upon such a pure palanquin,
followed by attendants with loudly resounding musical instruments playing high-pitched notes.
Having been honored by those standing behind him,
he was welcomed with the sound of conch shells accompanied by a tumultuous variety of other musical sounds.
Having had [the corpse] carried slowly by those initiated of the same caste, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), or by others reciting the *astra-mantra*,
one should lead it to a very pure spot of ground with its head facing south.
Having established it, one should construct a pit in a cremation ground on pure ground.
For *yatis* there should be only a staff; for *munis*, only a water-pot (*arman*).

Whether they be *yatis* or *munis*, their ritual action should be performed with a pure mind. And as for the rite at the pit, having performed the purification of the body, it should be smeared [with cow-dung].
Having spread pure darbha grass over a layer of sand, the preceptor—
There, one should properly perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and fill [the vessel] with *bilva* leaves;
or else, one should fill the area near it with salt. Right there, one should install either a pedestal (*pīṭha*) or a *liṅga*, provided it is joined with its temple-shrine (*ālaya*).
Having assumed the form of a boy or his own natural form, one should bathe him and worship him.
In that regard, the *piṇḍodaka* śrāddha, as well as anything else, is not desired; nor is the binding of the thumb, nor the spitting of betel-juice. And [this applies] in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
The length of the pit should be one cubit (devakara);
its width at the bottom should be two cubits, and it should be dug four cubits deep.
Without the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), one should perform all other rites as before;
and in that place, one may also cause the installation of a *liṅga* or the like.
That may be an image, or a pedestal, or even a painting on a wall.
One should have a temple or a pavilion constructed in that place;
there, one should perform worship beginning with the invocation and ending with the offering of oblations (bali), or alternatively, ending with the lamps.
And in the *Suprabheda*,
it is said: "Having carried [the image] in palanquins and other vehicles to the accompaniment of the great sounds of musical instruments,
the wise man should cause all auspicious rites to be performed."
Having dug a pit to the depth of a staff, with its head toward the east and its shoulders first [buried],
one should not perform a bath there, nor should one perform water-libation rites for the impure.
(From the *Śaivapurāṇa*)
Whether he has duly attained the purification of the six paths or is one who practices asceticism,
one should not perform funeral rites for him here on earth, as one would for ordinary bound souls (paśus).
Impurity would not apply at all, especially in the case of a son and others;
for there is no burning of what has already been burnt, just as there is no cooking of what has already been cooked.
For those whose seeds have been consumed by the fire of Śiva, there is neither śrāddha nor ritual action;
yet, if one desires to perform a rite even on their behalf, it may be done.
One should perform auspicious deeds according to one's ability and satisfy those who are devoted;
[this refers to the installation of lingas and so forth at the site of excavation], and elsewhere as well. (9th line)
In this very manner, one should cause the ritual of digging to be performed according to the rules;
however, the fire-ritual must not be performed, for digging is the prescribed rule for ascetics.
Having dug in the eastern direction to the depth of a staff's length,
one should face eastward there and prepare the seat and other requisites.
Having placed it upon a seat, one should worship it in due order with perfumes and other offerings;
then, having dismissed the disciples and others, one should fill [the vessel] with salt.
One should fill it with smooth clay and dig firmly there;
above that, one should construct a pedestal (*pīṭha*) or a pinnacle (*kūṭa*). The wise man should worship [the deity] at the three joints (*trisandhi*).
Thereafter, having constructed a temple in the forest according to the instructions given by the preceptor;
One should fashion either a *liṅga*, or an image, or even a pedestal.
Regarding the image,
it should have two arms and two eyes, and be endowed with all the [auspicious] characteristics.
O wise one, perform the consecration of the entire [image] according to the path already described.
One should construct the height of the pedestal according to the prescribed rule, making it equal to three cubits, two cubits, or even one cubit, in accordance with its width.
Having thus invoked the deity from the *pīṭha*, one should install him according to the prescribed rite;
there, one should cause a temple, a pavilion, or a peaked roof structure to be constructed.
One should cause the enclosure wall, the gate-tower, and all the surrounding structures to be constructed out of stone, baked bricks, and so forth, in accordance with the prescribed ritual rules.

Then, one should perform the daily worship according to the procedure prescribed for the ritual of adoration. The wise practitioner should offer the bali-oblation and maintain the perpetual sacred fire.
Furthermore, the daily festival should be celebrated, and the monthly festival should be arranged.
Then, he should perform the Abda-utsava according to this prescribed ritual.

One should worship [the deity] with offerings ending in lamps, or ending in oblations (*havis*), or ending in sacrificial cakes (*bali*); likewise, there is the ritual of ascending the *pavitra* and the ritual of ascending the *damana*. Furthermore, there are the two rites involving clarified butter (*ghṛtakarma*) and the ninefold offering of food (*naivedya*) and so forth.
(Definition of those entitled to receive the wealth and other assets of a Śaiva ascetic:

If there is an accumulation of wealth and so forth belonging to a Śaiva teacher who observes the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*), it belongs to his disciples alone after the fall of that body; in the absence of disciples, it belongs to Śiva himself.
But this does not apply to one whose lineage has previously been devoid of cattle.
As it is said in the Kāmika:
"One should divide [the property] in this manner for Dhananta, provided that there exists a Śaiva lineage."
"If it does not exist, one should give it to Śiva, but one should not give it to the lineage of bound souls.
(The Procedure for Worshipping the Guru).
Now, one should perform the worship of the guru. It is as follows: (line 7)

On the lunar day following the Guru’s feet, having performed the two daily rites every year, bathed with sacred ash, sipped water for purification, and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should,
in a clean place within a pavilion adorned with canopies, garlands, and the like, prepare a well-rounded circle one cubit in size using powders of five colors.
Having drawn five lotuses (*padma*) as in the previously described *Vrateśvara-maṇḍala*, and having worshipped the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*) therein,
one should place the form of the Guru upon that seat, invoke Śiva, and worship him according to the daily rite (*nityavat*).
Then, for the sake of the Guru, the Paramaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru, [one should worship] those endowed with virtuous conduct...

Having summoned three Brahmins who are endowed with various teachers' empowerments, one should prepare three mandalas with cow dung; there, having worshipped the sixfold seat with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and flowers, and having seated the Brahmins therein, [one should wash] their feet with scented water.

Having personally washed his feet, sipped water for purification (ācamana), and performed the preliminary worship, he should draw three mandalas with cow dung in the vicinity of Śiva— either from west to east or from south to north— and having worshipped the sixfold seats (ṣaḍutthāsana) upon them, he should sit... (133a, 1st line)

Having seated the Brahmins facing either south or east, and having invoked and worshipped the Guru, Upaguru, Guruparamaguru, and Parameṣṭhiguru in order from west to east or from south to north, he should offer rice, side dishes, betel, and so forth to each one individually in their respective forms, and perform the feeding of Hari. If the performer is a householder, he should do so with the root mantra.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations into the perpetual fire; then, having circumambulated and paid obeisance to the Brahmins, one should follow them.

Having said, "Go to your respective places," he should wash his feet, perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), and carry out the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). He should worship Śiva residing in the fire, merge him into Śiva who resides in the form of the Guru within the mandala, and then join that [Guru] as well to the Guru-mandala at the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus upon his own head. Then, [he should place] himself... (4th line)

Having fed the elders of his own lineage as well as other members of the Śiva-āśrama belonging to other lineages, he should afterwards eat the food offered to the Guru himself. In the absence of a recipient possessing the aforementioned characteristics, he should [feed] Śiva-devoted Brāhmaṇas in the presence of the Guru situated within the maṇḍala.

Having honored guests and visitors with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should provide rice and other provisions in abundance for their meal. Likewise, during the propitiation of the Guru, pilgrimages to deities, weddings, the instruction of mantras, the commencement of Śiva-yāga, and in rites concerning those already perfected or yet to be accomplished, [one should act accordingly].
For the purpose of pacifying bad dreams and for the attainment of the fruits of good dreams, [the rite] should be performed in the form of Nādi.
As it is said in the *Kālottara*: "O son of Pārvatī, I shall explain the Guru-yāga in brief."

Likewise, this [rite] should be performed when beholding a deity, as well as when accomplishing a perfected practice; at the time of a wedding procession, upon seeing a bad dream, upon obtaining a [divine] dream,
and especially at the commencement of a mantra-ritual or a sacrifice.
One should fashion that auspicious lotus, measuring exactly one cubit in circumference.
Having prepared a seat there, one should place the Lord Śiva in embodied form.
One should then invoke the Supreme Śiva there, together with Brahmā and his limbs (the mantras).
One should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the root mantra.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times, he should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having meditated upon the Guru as Sadāśiva and prostrated before him again and again,
the disciple, having requested his permission and offered [the oblation], should perform the sacrifice and other rites.
This procedure has been declared for when the Guru has passed away to the state of Śiva.
If one should worship the Guru even when he is present, as before,
then, having diligently received his command, one should perform the ritual action.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of the act of excavation for Śaiva renunciants.
The Procedure for Covering the Nakedness of Others.

When even a householder has been liberated through the initiation into Nirvāṇa, his son or other descendant must, for the sake of maintaining the duties of his own stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*), perform the subsequent *tantra* following the covering of the nakedness [of the deceased].
Regarding the case of a householder—

Then the performer, having given clothing to cover the nakedness [of the deceased], shall bathe day by day from the first day until the end of the tenth day; wearing wet clothes, he shall worship Śiva daily as usual,
and having worshipped him especially on behalf of the deceased, immediately—

Having gratified him with each of the mantras— Vāmā, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna, Hṛdaya, Śiras, Śikhā, Kavaca, and Astra— each joined with his initiation name in the dative case and ending in *svāhā*, he should then invite three Brahmins, wash their feet, worship them, and offer rice mixed with lentils (*daṇḍula*) and other foods for their meal.

One should offer [the rice balls]. Starting from the second day until the tenth day, one should perform the rite with an increase of one each day. Then, having offered the final rice ball oneself, one should eat once at another's house, avoiding salt, liquids, and the like.
(5th line) || Now, one should collect the bones.
Thus is the traditional teaching:
one should pile [the fire-altar] while reciting the Astra mantra on the third or the fourth day;
or else on the first, the third, the fifth, or even the seventh day.

"Or rather, the collection of bones (*asthisañcayana*) should be performed by the twice-born on the ninth day. Regarding that, it is said: "If one should perform the collection of bones on Sunday, Saturday, Thursday, or Friday, it will cause the destruction of the family. Here, "Sunday" (*āravāra*) refers to the day of the Sun; "Saturday" (*sauravāra*) refers to the day of Saturn.
If the funeral pyre fire has been extinguished, one should generate the Śiva-fire near it and, for the sake of expiation, offer a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra;
then, preceded by the worship of the principles beginning with Earth, one should offer three oblations to each of them as follows: *Hāṃ* to the Earth-principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*).

Homage! Hāṃ, homage to the element of water. Hāṃ, homage to the element of fire. Hāṃ, homage to the element of wind. Hāṃ, homage to the element of space. Hāṃ, homage to the element of smell. Hāṃ, homage to the element of taste. Hāṃ, homage to the element of form. Hāṃ, homage to the element of touch. Hāṃ... (8th line)

Homage to the principle of sound. Hāṃ, homage to the principle of the generative organ. Hāṃ, homage to the principle of the anus. Hāṃ, homage to the principle of the feet. Hāṃ, homage to the principle of the hands. Hāṃ, homage to the principle of speech. Hāṃ, homage to the principle of the nose. Hāṃ, homage to the principle of the tongue. Hāṃ... (9th line)

Hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the eye; hāṃ, salutation to the principle of speech; hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the ear; hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the mind; hāṃ, salutation to the principle of ego; hāṃ, salutation to the principle of intellect; hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the qualities;
hāṃ, salutation to the principle of primordial nature.

Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Puruṣa; Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Rāga; Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Niyati; Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Vidyā; Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Kalā; Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Kāla; Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Māyā.

"Hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā-tattva); hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Īśvara; hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Sadāśiva; hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Śakti; hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Śiva. Having thus worshipped, one should offer three oblations for each, ending with "svāhā. Then:

Having extracted the bones from the feet, private parts, heart, mouth, and head with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras, one should place them inside a jar filled with milk situated upon a tripod of three wooden sticks;
thereafter, one should set it down in a pure location on the ground, or else in the water of a sacred ford such as the ocean.
One should cast it; one should throw the ashes into deep water. (4th line) Now begins the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
|| The Procedure for the *Ekoddiṣṭa* Rite ||

On the day the impurity (*āśauca*) ceases—beginning from the eleventh day and so forth—after the purification of the house and other such matters has been performed, [the rite] should be carried out. For that purpose, on the preceding day, one should invite a *deśika*, a *sādhaka*, or a *putraka* who is a Brāhmaṇa; or, in the absence of these, a Brāhmaṇa who is solely a devotee of Śiva and possesses the aforementioned characteristics.

Having seated [the elder] upon a seat facing west, honoring the younger [relative] with affectionate words by touching his elder shank and grasping the tips of his lotus-like hands, and having presented the offering,
[one performs] the Śiva-śrāddha for the sake of such-and-such deity who has become Śiva.
One should pray, "It must be performed.

He [the candidate] should also respond, "So be it," granting permission. Now, one might object: since even Śūdras who have received the Śiva-saṃskāra are heard to possess the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*) in the absence of any one of these—namely, an Ācārya, a Sādhaka, or a Putraka—among the twice-born, why [seek an Ācārya] from among them?
One should choose either a practitioner (*sādhaka*) or a spiritual son (*putraka*). If it is asked, "Why search for a Brāhmaṇa?", that is incorrect;

because even a Kṣatriya who has undergone the sacraments from conception (*niṣeka*) up to the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) lacks the qualification to accept gifts for ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and so forth, let alone others—this follows by the logic of the "how much more" argument (*kaimutikanyāya*).
Even for a Śūdra who has undergone the Śiva-consecration (*śivasaṃskāra*), there is an even greater lack of qualification.

Therefore, in the absence of any one of the [three types of] practitioners—the *ācārya*, the *sādhaka*, or the *putraka*—the teacher should select only a Brāhmaṇa who is a general devotee of Śiva for the funeral rites (*śrāddha*) and other ceremonies. As for the intermediate Śaivas...

Immediately after the *sapiṇḍana* ceremony, one should feed [the Brahmins] for the sake of pleasing Śiva. Thereafter, remembering the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) throughout that night, one should restrain the collection of the senses as much as possible. On the following day, having performed the daily rites such as bathing and so forth, one should remain without food during the forenoon.
Having performed his daily rites such as bathing and having honored him with rising from his seat and other marks of respect upon his arrival,

he should prepare two circular maṇḍalas smeared with cow-dung on the courtyard floor, arranged east-west and north-south with a space between them, and then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīti*), [proceeds].

Having arranged the ritual placement in reverse order with the hands holding the general *arghya* water, one should scatter *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds with their tips pointing south within those two mandalas;

having worshipped and offered the *arghya* with white flowers using the *astra-mantra* in the southern mandala, and having placed earth for washing the feet, one should worship in the northern [mandala] with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and offer the *arghya*.
Having given [the offering] and established the invited [deity] in the southern maṇḍala with sesame seeds,

one should offer the arghya water with the name of the initiation preceded by the word *svadhā* as the sign; then, having washed the feet with clay and water using the name of the initiation preceded by the seed-syllable of Vāmadeva, one should enter within after performing the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) in the northern maṇḍala.

Having himself sipped water and entered within, he should seat [the disciple] upon a pure seat or similar surface, facing either west or north. With his sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) in reverse order, he should wash the arghya vessel with the Astra-mantra, fill it with pure water from [his own] head, cast sesame seeds into it, and [place] a purifying offering (pavitra) provided with sandalwood paste, dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, using the Sadyojāta-mantra.

Having deposited [the water] with the *śikhā* mantra, consecrated it with the *hṛdaya*, and protected it, one should sprinkle the ritual substances (*dravya*) with that water; then, having consecrated the fragrance with the *hṛdaya*, the flower with the *śiras*, the incense and lamp with the *śikhā*, and the mouth-cloth (*vaktra*), sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth with the *kavaca*, and having protected them, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha.

Having thus prayed, when told by him, "Do so," he should offer him a seat with its tips pointing south, made of double-folded *darbha* grass, while performing the ritual with the *sadyojāta* mantra and keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). Then, having requested, "I invoke [the deity]," he should perform the invocation. Being thus instructed, he should invoke [the deity] using the name of the initiation (*dīkṣā-nāman*) joined with the root mantra, ending in the dative case and followed by "namas. Having performed the triad beginning with installation (*sthāpana*) with the left hand, [he proceeds].

Having performed the protection rite with sesame seeds while circumambulating counter-clockwise using the Īśāna mantra, one should offer the *sānnidhya-arghya*—consisting of water with flowers, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*)—while kneeling on the ground with the Īśāna mantra.
One should say, "May it be complete," and the other should reply, "May it be complete. Then, [one should take] the *arghya* water together with the *pavitra*.
Having placed that [water] in his hand, one should take the water flowing from it into some vessel; then, saying "Obeisance to the Pitṛs in the north-west," one should pour it into another vessel.

Then, for the sake of eating, on a purified ground where the sweeping and other rites have been performed, [one should place] rice grains [along with] the prescribed forms and all the people. (Leaf 135).
(As if missing) (136a,
first line) || The Sequence of the Varieties of Initiation ||
In the *Svāyambhuva*, it is said: "The true nature of knowledge is bestowed and the three impurities are destroyed;
through this conjunction of bestowing and destroying, initiation brings about purification for those whose selves are [prepared]."
Among those to be graced within the universe of the thinkable (*cintyaviśva*), there are three: the *pralayākala* who possesses knowledge of the scriptures, and the third is the *sakala*;
the first, moreover, consists of *mala* alone.
Those joined with impurity and karma are the *pralayākala*s,
and the *sakala* possesses the *kalā*s beginning with *nivṛtti* and ending with *vṛtti*.
The different types of initiation will now be explained according to their modes of grace:
that which has a support (*sādhārā*), that which is without support (*nirādhārā*), that which possesses seeds (*sabījā*), and that which is devoid of seeds (*bījavarjitā*).
It should be understood that there is also another type, which has an officiant (*sādhikārā*), as well as one that is without an officiant (*niradhikāriṇī*).
Indeed, O Śivadharmiṇī, it is both dependent and independent.
The initiation pertaining to worldly dharmas, the temporary, and likewise the lifelong; that which grants immediate nirvāṇa, and the supreme one which grants nirvāṇa after a long time.
Listen now to these as they exist within the *Kriyāvatī* and the *Jñānavatī*.
The visual initiation, the tactile initiation, as well as the vocal and the mental [initiations].
The Śāstrī, the Yogavatī, the Hautrī, and likewise the Śāmbhavī; the Śāktimatī and so forth, as well as the Tīvra and the Tīvratarā.
The division of initiation into twenty-eight types which has been proclaimed in the *Mṛgendra*— namely,
the initiation for the accomplishment of one's desired aims— is that which has issued from the mouth of the Supreme Lord.
Although it is shared, it is without support; yet it is the support of all.
O Nandikeśvara, according to the rule, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the activity for all those who possess thought within the universe.
Having taken refuge in the form of the Guru, by means of the gradual descent of the intense [descent of power] and so forth.
The Lord performs this [creation] as a whole; the wise know it as "with support" (sādhārāntā).
And for the learned and the capable, it is proclaimed as "with seed" (sabījā).

The *sabījā* [samādhi] is proclaimed as that which includes the *prārabdha* karma, along with the conduct of the observances (*samayācāra*) and its secondary consequences, as well as the portion of accumulated (*sañcita*) karma that remains distinct. (Svacchanda Tantra, 136b,
first line)
That [initiation] should be known as "with seed" (sabījā) even for the spiritual son and the teacher;
furthermore, it is so when one initiates a householder or a forest-dweller without having made a formal resolve (asaṃkalpya).
O Dear One, this sacrifice of the assemblies is proclaimed as having seeds;
it bestows grace upon those who are joined with the conduct of the *samaya*.
Those who abide in the mantra are proclaimed to possess the specific conduct of the *samaya*.
But in the case of nirvāṇa with seed, [the soul] perishes due to the absence of bonds.
Indeed, the initiate who maintains the bond of the conduct of the *samaya* shall be purified by those very bonds; that [initiation] is proclaimed as "with seed" (*sabījā*).
(From the *Cintyaviśva*)

But for those who are incapable [of practice], it is seedless; however, for those whose souls delight in enjoyment, that which has been accumulated through the conduct of the observance (samaya) is purified, and thus it is considered "seedless."
Even in the *Kriyākaraṇamaṇḍana*,
it is stated that for those who are incapable, initiation is seedless; however, for those whose souls delight in worldly enjoyment,
the initiation with the fire-seed (*agnibīja*) is better for both the initiate (*samayin*) and the son (*putraka*).
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*:

"For children, eunuchs, the elderly, women, those who indulge in sensual pleasures, and those afflicted by disease, there may be a seedless initiation (*nirbījakā dīkṣā*) that is devoid of the conduct of the rules (*samayācāra*). (5th line)
Likewise, according to the rule, blindness, deafness, and so forth are prescribed for women and children;
yet in the scripture, a distinction is stated even for those desiring liberation:
"He whose karma has been burnt by the fire of initiation and whose bonds have been severed by Māyā..."

Having reached the supreme state of steadfastness in knowledge, he remains established in Śiva as one who is seedless (*nirbīja*). For him, there is no need for religious observances, nor for the worship of external symbols;
neither is there need for journeys to sacred fords and fields, nor for bodily restraints.
"Prārabdha-karma perishes through experience; sañcita-karma is destroyed by initiation;
and āgāmi-karma [is destroyed] by worship—such is the certainty of the scripture," as stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.
That [initiation] which possesses authority and possesses seed is that by which one becomes an *adhikārin*;
for it is through this that the status of the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya* is attained in the rites of initiation and consecration.
Even in the *Kriyākaraṇamaṇḍana*,
it is stated that for rites consisting of obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) acts, as well as those such as expiatory rituals (*prāyaścitta*),
that [initiation] shall be one that possesses authority (*sādhikārā*) and is suitable for both the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*).
Because she is qualified in all respects, she is indeed "with qualification" for those two;
she is remembered as "with qualification" because she possesses the capacity for qualification.
However, for the Samayin and the Putraka, when there is no qualification, initiation is "seedless."
Because it pertains exclusively to the eternal, initiation is without any [temporal] qualification.
In the *Mṛgendra*,

it is stated by the wise that the observance of the rules and so forth which has passed beyond its time, yet persists, is called "dependent" (*sāpekṣa*) when it consists primarily of distinguished personal qualities.
That which is incapable of [performing] sacrifice and so forth, such as an old man or a eunuch,
is called "independent" because it does not depend on those [auxiliaries].
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*, [the lineage] is twofold, distinguished by its seed-syllables (*sabījā*); the first is characterized by Śiva.
The existence of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*) [is established] through the distinctions of place, time, and so forth.
Wherein action consisting of merit and demerit, which was performed previously and is manifold,
and that which has been accumulated, is lamented— that indeed is called the state characterized by Śiva.
That initiation which is accompanied by the cutting of the top-knot is the Śivadharmiṇī.
Furthermore, in the Āgama:
"Whether one follows worldly or Vedic conduct, he who possesses devotion to Śiva [is qualified]."
The practice of the Śivadharmas [leads to] that [state], but it occurs immediately after the enjoyment of those [fruits].
That state which consists of omniscience and so forth is said to reside in one who possesses the nature of Śiva;
as it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"When one should indeed initiate those whose wealth is austerity into the initiation of the nature of Śiva..."
In the *Skandakaulottara* it is also said:
"The initiation associated with the cutting of the top-knot (*śikhā*) is that which conforms to the nature of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*).
If the initiation conforming to the nature of Śiva is performed, it shall unite [the soul] with the stainless state."
Liberation shall occur at the fall of the body through the observance of the conduct of the *samaya*.
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*, it is said:
"The second [type of practitioner] is one who is purified merely from unrighteousness and abides by worldly dharma."
The Guru should initiate householders by means of the initiation pertaining to the worldly order.
Where there is no cutting of the top-knot (*śikhā*), that initiation belongs to the worldly way (*lokadharminī*).
Even in the *Svacchanda*,
[it is said] that the past and future karma is that which brings about the destruction of unrighteousness (*adharma*).
Engaged in the rites of sacrifice and public works according to the worldly dharma, he was initiated.
One who performs actions while desiring their fruit, being fixed solely on the auspicious or seeking the inauspicious—
such a person should be known as one who follows worldly dharma and is devoid of the propitiation of mantras.

But upon the dissolution of the body that was begun, having offered [the senses] into the fire and having experienced the enjoyments such as aṇimā and the rest, he shall go upward to where he has been directed by his Guru.
Whether in the state with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*), it occurs according to the status of the disciple and the teacher.
Even in the *Kriyākaraṇamaṇḍana*, having established the one who follows worldly conventions within the doctrine of the *Bhuvanakartarī* [Tantra], [the following is stated].
One should perform that [rite] for the sake of Śiva, or for one who desires the [initiation with the] knife, by means of the descent of those qualities.
Those who have been born within the circle of Gaṇapati and the Guru, purified by initiation, abide in the reality of Sadāśiva; likewise, they dwell in his supreme state.
By means of the mantras of the Siddhas, their bodies shine like the orb of the young sun.

Having consumed [the offerings] or [drunk] the sugarcane juice, those who are endowed with the splendor of the pure state of immortality, being freed from longing, become partakers of the sovereignty of the station of Supreme Śiva.
Thus, in the *Pañcāvaraṇastotra*:

And to those practitioners of the Supreme Lord who, desiring a share in the arising of pure manifestation, worship you with various modes of sacrifice— to them, having given [this], [one should give]...
It bestows enjoyments and immediately thereafter liberation.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"That state of one who follows the path of Śiva is twofold: the material (*bhautika*) and the ultimate (*naiṣṭhika*)."
That which is conjoined with the release from vows is called the *bhautika* (elemental) [state].
You have described the material initiation (*bhautikī-dīkṣā*) for the wise as being accompanied by seed (*sabījā*).

For those observing the lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhika-vratī*), it is considered to be witnessed at the time of the body's fall. Others, however, hold that the lifelong initiation (*naiṣṭhikī-dīkṣā*) pertains to those who are incapable [of the former].

The intention here is as follows: having undertaken initiation (*dīkṣā*) and observed the vow for some time according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures until everything is completed, that is the *bhautikī* [initiation]. That initiation which consists of the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) until the fall of the body is the *naiṣṭhikī*.
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*:
"Now, initiation without seed (*nirbījaka*) is said to be twofold according to its division; the first bestows immediate liberation, while the latter is the supreme bestower of liberation. (7th line)
The web of karma—consisting of that which has begun, that which has been accumulated, and that which is yet to come—is completely dissolved;
for those who have renounced and are dispassionate, it is pure and immediately bestows liberation.
In the *Svacchanda* as well, when there is the intention to discuss the bonds of conventional conduct (*samayācāra*) and so forth, one should purify [them];
by initiation alone the form [is purified], and always through devotion alone to the Guru.
By virtue of initiation (dīkṣā), one may abandon the body and proceed to the supreme state;
yet, she [the soul] experiences the fruition of her prārabdha-karmas until liberation (mukti).
Even fools and others go [to liberation], and it shall grant nirvāṇa according to one's own desire,
just as the initiation involving ritual action (*kriyāvatī-dīkṣā*) is preceded by the [drawing of the] *kuṇḍala* and the *maṇḍala*.

In the *Svacchanda*, it is said: "Thus, in accordance with the disposition of the disciples and the gurus, a fruit of manifold forms is always brought to fruition through a perfect initiation. (2nd line)
Indeed, the inconceivable power of mantra, which has issued from the mouth of the Supreme Lord,
should be employed by the Guru at the time of ritual action, preceded by devotion.
In the Cintyaviśva,
I shall proclaim the initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā) correctly and in due order, by Virūṇaśiva.
The *Chāyā-śāstra* is considered to consist of ninety [verses] and is regarded as being merely a mental operation (*manovyāpāra*).
It is said to be of many kinds; its detailed exposition is now set forth.
Having meditated upon that reality, one should open the eyes of the disciple who desires [initiation];
for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the fetters, the initiation known as "visual" (cākṣuṣī) is prescribed.
Having placed Śiva, conjoined with the limbs of Brahmā, in his right hand,
and having placed it upon the head of the disciple, this shall be the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*).
Having concentrated the mind upon reality with a splendor that has reached its culmination, the Guru should recite the mantra; thus is the Mantra-initiation accomplished.
One should utter the mantras with speech; that initiation is considered to be the Vācaka (the vocal).
By the bestowing of the Śiva-scripture, the initiation into the scripture (śāstradīkṣā) has been fully accomplished.

Through yoga, there shall be initiation by yoga; established in the state of Śiva, the initiation consisting of the fire-rite and the recitation of mantras is thus described. (Vāmadevaśivāgama, 6th line)
In the Śiva-āgama, initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as being threefold: the Śāmbhavī, the Śākta, and the Māntrī.
Through the mere sight, touch, or even conversation with the Guru,
the wise one immediately attains that which brings about the destruction of the flood of bonds.
That initiation is declared to be Sāmbhavī;
it is further divided into two types, namely "intense" and "extremely intense," according to the degree of destruction of the flood of bonds.
That [intensity] by which cessation occurs immediately is considered the most intense;
however, the intense [intensity] serves for a person's liberation while living, releasing them from their bonds.
The initiation consisting of the power of knowledge (śāktijñāna) is performed by the Guru, having entered the body of the disciple through the path of yoga and with the eye of wisdom.
Initiation, accompanied by the performance of mantras and preceded by the sacrificial pit and the mandala,
is capable of bestowing grace upon disciples in accordance with the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
And by the Guru alone is the primary initiation for all traditionally remembered;
therein lies the yoga of the state of Rudra, and therein lies the yoga of the state of Īśvara.
Where there is no cutting of the topknot (*śikhā*), that initiation is the *samayī*; it is of two kinds.
Also, in the *Pūrvakāmika*, in the chapter on *samayī* initiation, having performed the perfuming with scents (*gandhādhivāsita*) while holding [the substance] in one's own right hand—
It was presided over by Śiva, who, together with his teaching and his body, had pierced through the obstacles of ignorance.
Having meditated upon the Hand of Śiva as both with and without expectation,
one should lead it from the region of the heart to the station of the eyebrows— tranquil and reaching as far as the hollow of the cupped palms.
Along with the movement through the palace that pierces all knots,
one should place [the mudrā] upon the head, which bestows the attainment of the state of Rudreśvara.
The disciple should perform the rite of anointing all the limbs, especially [the head].
O sages, through such fitness, human beings attain the Rudra-maheṣa state,
wherein there is the severing of the bonds and the crest-lock, and where yoga resides in the supreme state of the living soul.
That very [wisdom] is called Nirvāṇa; it is not [attained] by a son through consecration.
Together with the empowerment of the mantra, it is proclaimed for the practitioner;
through the empowerment of all the vidyās, it pertains to the domain of the master.
The bestowal of that state of Śiva-ness which belongs to one endowed with the Śiva-consecration (śivasaṃskāra) is considered to be accomplished entirely through ritual action,
or through power, or through initiation (dīkṣā).
Through initiation (*dīkṣā*), the embodied soul is liberated from the threefold bond of worldly existence.
In the *Cintyaviśva*,
there are forty Vedic purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) performed in sequence.
Indeed, for one possessing ritual action, it leads to the increase of impurities by way of the path of liberation.
Therefore, the destruction of impurity does not occur through the Vedic path;
rather, it is brought about by initiation according to the path taught in the Śaiva Āgamas, which has liberation as its cause.
The Guru, through his grace, should purify the bonds of the disciple and unite him [with the divine].
Now follows the purification through initiation (dīkṣā-śuddhi).
Now, at the time of initiation, learn from me their purificatory rites in due order:
one should establish the principle of Śakti, the world-sphere, and Śakti herself.
Having performed the ritual offering of incense for them in due order,
one should likewise [offer it] for Ananta, Kālāgni, and the hells in their proper sequence.

Then, O fair-faced one, one should awaken the netherworlds (*pātāla*) and those above them in successive order; thereafter, one should perform the service (*upasthāna*) for the world of the earth (*bhūloka*).
Then, having worshipped the deity Vāgīśvarī with flowers and other offerings,
and having consecrated the sacrificial victim (paśu) and performed its ritual separation (viśleṣa).
Chodana, ākarṣaṇa, grahaṇa, and likewise yojana;
as well as garbhādhāna, janana, and adhikāra.
Yoga, enjoyment, and dissolution, as well as the purification of the womb—these are the fourteen parts; I shall explain them to you in their proper sequence.
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra;
likewise the Prājāpatya, Saumya, and the Brāhma is recorded as the eighth.

In the sacrificial rite (adhvara), those belonging to the lower path— beasts, birds, wild animals, as well as those possessing life-force and breaths— should be purified by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
The fifth is to be known as the stationary, and the sixth is born from the human womb;
that which is joined with the divine womb is declared to be the circle of worldly existence.
One should purify the fourteenfold world of mortals;
for this Self transmigrates within the sphere of Māyā and the rest. Therefore, it is called "saṃsāra" (transmigration), because it is seen moving here and there.
Indeed, while traveling along the path, one experiences pleasure, pain, and likewise delusion.
Traversed by the three bonds and presided over by the Vāma-śakti,
[the soul] proceeds along the path of emanation and reabsorption by means of Īśvara as its instrumental cause.
Furthermore, in the midst of that path, it is joined with auspicious and inauspicious [experiences].
Likewise, those [powers] which exist in the midst of the path and at the end of the bonds, numbering infinite crores.

Up to the state that is unconditioned (*anāśrita*), through the distinction between the primary and the secondary qualities, one should thus understand the cause of the bondage of the path. Furthermore, that which is called the fourteen-fold circle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*)— *Note: The asterisks (*) indicate the placement of the verse number 7 within the source text.*
Its divisions are indeed infinite, as they are differentiated according to the diversity of karma.
For the bonds of karma are indeed endless, and one holds authority over the practice of karma;
by oneself the self is bound, and by oneself the self is liberated.
Just as a silkworm encases itself within a cocoon, so does it surround itself separately.
(…) he cannot deceive [them], nor can his own nature be made otherwise than it truly is.
Just as all transmigrating beings are bound by the fetters of saṃsāra, yet these bound souls are not able to liberate themselves from their bonds, so too are they like animals caught in snares.
And indeed, as long as one has not beheld Śiva himself,
[beings] are purified from the bonds of the fetters by the descent of Śiva’s power.
O Goddess, that which was previously described by me as the fourteen-fold mandala of saṃsāra should be purified upon the surface of the earth;
I shall now explain all of that in due order, according to how it is to be purified in the sacrifice of Śiva.
One should purify [the world] by proceeding through the sequence from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
One should purify, in due order, the Brahma-sphere, as well as the Saumya,
Aindra, Gandharva, Yakṣa, and thereafter the Rākṣasa;
then the Paiśāca, the human, and likewise the stationary.
Vāsuki is likewise the king of all stationary beings and of those born from sweat.
One should purify Garuḍa among birds, the lion among wild beasts, the cow among domestic animals, and the Brāhmaṇa among men as the final one; likewise,
the outcaste among those born of the lowest order, and the Brāhmaṇa as the last among the Brahmin, Vaiśya, and Kṣatriya castes.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should purify the body with the Brahma-mantras.
By means of the application of ten oblations for each, from the lowest castes up to the Brāhmaṇas,
one should perform forty-eight oblations for the Brāhmaṇa’s eight rites of entitlement:
the conception rite (*garbha*), the rite for ensuring a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and the birth rite (*jātakarman*).
Namely, the rite of departure from the womb, the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony.
By this very means, O lady of excellent limbs, that which is to be purified is proclaimed;
O Goddess, by these [means], one then certainly attains liberation.
In the ninth [chapter], the binding of the vows (vratabandha) is proclaimed as its constituent part;
I shall now duly explain those constituent parts in their proper sequence.
The girdle, the tooth-stick, the deerskin, the three-fold staff, as well as the twilight devotions, the worship of the fire, and alms-gathering— they know these indeed to be the seven.
O fair-faced one, at the time of initiation, a student of sacred knowledge should employ these seven primary restraints, beginning with the girdle.
They know Bhūteśa, Pūṣpatya, Gaṇa, and Gaṇeśvara,
as well as Unmatta, Asidhāra, and Vrateśa as the seventh.
These seven are indeed the principal vows for those living the life of a student;
they are to be known as the "Heavenly Vows" (dayāvratas) and are proclaimed as being auxiliary to the Vedas.
But for one who has come together with these, the ninth [stage] is the binding of the vow;
included within that is what has been described as the seventh vow.
The four Vedic vows must undoubtedly be offered:
the Āstika, the Pārvaṇa, the Bhautika, and likewise the Saumika.
The four Vrateśvaras are Brahmacārī, Niyantrika, [and the others];
one should know the thirteenth to be Devabhājana.
Then, O beloved, there is Godāna, which is the fourteenth.
O dear one, he should marry a maiden who has attained knowledge and perfection.
Having fashioned a wife out of darbha grass, one should likewise perform sacrifices together with her;
that is to be known as the fifteenth [rite]. Next, however, are the *pākamukha* rites;
they are said to be occasional (*naimittika*), which I shall now describe in brief.
The Śrāddha on the Aṣṭakā festival, as well as those on the Śrāvaṇī and Āgrāyaṇī days;
Caitrī and Āśvayujī are to be known as the seven cooking vessels;
the seeds combined with these are twenty-two in number.
Then there is this [offering], the Agnihotra, and after that, the Darśa.
Likewise, the full moon day (Paurṇamāsī) and the four-month festival (Cāturmāsya) should be known in the same way.
Following this, the Sautrāmaṇī is designated as the Animal Sacrifice (*paśubandha*).
These are declared to be the seven, or alternatively nine, known as the Havis sacrifices.
Through these, one should understand the twenty-nine sacraments (*saṃskāras*).
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the Agniṣṭoma; likewise, the Ṣoḍaśin is offered at dawn.
The Vājapeya is an Atirātra, and the Āptoryāma is the seventh;
thus the Soma-sacrifices are fully described as thirty-six in number.
Indeed, first [is] Pāda, then Guhyahiraṇyadhṛk,
Haraṇyamoha, Hiraṇyamānābhi, and likewise Nirhiraṇyagarbha.
Hiraṇyabhrātṛ, Hiraṇyatvak, Cirakṣata, likewise Hiraṇyajihva,
and Hiraṇyaśṛṅga— these are proclaimed as the ten knowers of the sacrifice.
But when one understands each of these vows individually,
all thirty-seven of them are purified by a thousand [repetitions].
Thereafter, one should perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and the fire oblation (homa) in due order;
thus, by all these means, there shall be prosperity.
Or else, having performed the supreme thirty-eighth [rite], there shall then be a *prastha* [of merit];
thereafter, by performing the funeral rites for a wandering mendicant (*parivrāja*), one shall attain the state of a Brahmin.
But there are forty formative factors (*saṃskāra*) together with which one cognizes;
therefore, I shall briefly explain the eight qualities of the self (*ātman*).
Likewise, for one who possesses patience toward all beings,
purity, freedom from exertion, and supreme auspiciousness follow thereafter.
Freedom from meanness and lack of craving—these are remembered as the eight qualities of the self (*ātma-guṇa*). Likewise, forty-eight formative factors (*saṃskāra*) have been proclaimed.
O observer of excellent vows, even if they are innumerable, these [impurities] are purified by these pure [rites];
therefore, having indeed performed the funeral oblation (antyeṣṭi), one should bestow qualities upon the child.
One should offer five oblations for each of the five [deities] in their proper sequence with the Brahma-mantras;
having offered sesame seeds and clarified butter at the feet, one should then direct them upward.
Or, with the word "ūrdhva," one should perform the conjunction in that which is proclaimed as pure in sequence; and that is prescribed elsewhere as well.
Therefore, one should not perform an extraction nor a removal anywhere;
rather, whatever procedure is required here, that alone should be applied there as well.
Then, for the sake of one's own enjoyment, the powers beginning with *aṇimā* should be invoked by the Brahmās in due order, using the practice of uttering "Huṃ."
That which is supported by the world of the living (*bhūrloka*) should be known by the term "upward power" (*ūrdhvaśakti*);
and that is to be accomplished by one who is disciplined, and never in any other way.
As long as one experiences the fruits of karma, how can there be yoga while that karma has not yet been extracted?
His application [to yoga] is designated by the term "exertion" because his mind is focused solely upon each respective action.
The Great Goddess is thus brought forth; thereafter, one should offer oblations for expiation.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Śiva-mantra, one should then [offer] to the lords of the worlds.
Having purified the dwellings up to the end of the worlds and the worlds themselves in their proper order by means of the oblation alone, one should then separate the consciousness.
Then, one should perform meditation up to the *pūrṇāhuti* and remain established therein in due order;
thereafter, having offered the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*), [the rite] is performed for the arising of knowledge.
In this very sequence, one should purify [the path] up to the end of the watch;
it is the supreme means of deliverance for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, like a boat.
When, however, through a cause, the power that brings about liberation emerges from the realm of ignorance and the beast-like state of illusion and delusion, [then it occurs].
By the will of Śiva, one should attain the auspicious initiation endowed with knowledge, consisting of the application of mantras; then the bound soul (paśu) shall go to liberation.
They do not attain liberation otherwise, even through hundreds of [other] forms of knowledge,
for everything is illuminated within by Śiva, who exists as their inner form.
He alone attains liberation— he is Śiva and he is Maheśvara—
having received initiation on the path of Śiva through the grace of the Guru, O Goddess of the Gods.
By the mere glance of the Guru, the destruction of all sins occurs,
just as darkness perishes in the presence of the sun.
One is not smeared by impurity at all, like a lotus leaf by water.
Thus ends the compendium of the sequence of the various types of initiation.
The Manual of Varuṇa.
Homage to Śambhu, who is the Moon and the seed of the three types of nirvāṇa.
Now, the two seeds of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) are summarized.
Just as that which is called the state of Śiva is defined as the liberation from the three bonds,
so too is that ritual action described as initiation, characterized by devotion and dispassion.
Therefore, knowledge, devotion, and dispassion are the marks of the self that has been initiated here; these do not belong directly to the bound soul (paśu).
The individual soul (paśu) is one who possesses limited knowledge, is impure, is subject to division, is the agent and enjoyer of its own actions,
is distinct from the body, is all-pervading, eternal, capable of being refined by sacraments, and is under the governance of a Lord.
The fetters are also to be known as threefold: impurity (*mala*), illusion (*māyā*), and action (*karman*).
Impurity is impurity and ignorance; it is that which obstructs consciousness.
That collection of principles beginning with Māyā and ending with Kalā,
as well as karma consisting of merit and demerit— by these fetters the bound soul (paśu) is joined.
Due to the ignorance of the bound soul (paśu), there is the application of illusion for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karmas;
the will of the Lord proceeds equally [toward all], because it cannot be otherwise.

Then, due to his past karma, that transmigrating soul— bound, yet possessing mastery, and still joined with the three fetters— is liberated and enjoys the entirety of experience, such as pleasure and the like.
This [individual soul] is to be favored in three ways: as *sakala*, *pralayākala*, and *vijñānākala*. Now, their essential natures are described.
He who is born from the impurity of karma and māyā is designated as *sakala* (the bound soul with parts).
He who is enveloped by the impurity of karma is the *pralayākala* (the soul in a state of dissolution).
The bond of the "Malai-kabandha" is said to be the bond of ignorance (*vijñāna-ākalu*).

Furthermore, the grace (*anugraha*) of Śiva is twofold: that which is without support (*nirādhāra*) and that which has a support (*sādhāra*). Śiva, independent of a teacher, [bestows grace] in two ways through the descent of His power (*śakti-nipātana*).
He himself bestows grace upon the Vijñānakalas and Pralayākalas.
Assuming the form of the Teacher through the fourfold descent of power (*śaktipāta*),
the Blessed One bestows grace upon all beings.
Through the grace of Śiva, initiation arises for those who have performed their prescribed duties.
And that [nature] is said to be of many kinds; its detailed exposition is now being stated.
The initiation of sight, the initiation of touch, the verbal initiation, the mental initiation,

the scriptural initiation, the initiation of yoga, the initiation of the *hautra* priest, and so forth— [it is] manifold. When, having opened the eyes, the disciple is gazed upon by means of that reality...
This initiation shall be visual for the purpose of liberation from bondage by the noose.
Having placed Śiva, conjoined with the Brahma-aṅgas, in his right hand, he should touch the disciple from the crown of the head downwards; this shall be the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*).
Having concentrated the mind on the *tattva* and expanded [his own] internal radiance through that splendor...
One should recite the Saṃhitā mantras; this is proclaimed as the initiation of speech (vāgdīkṣā).

Resorting to a mental procedure, it is called "mental initiation. By the transmission of the scripture, the "initiation of the scripture" is proclaimed. Through yoga, there shall be the "initiation of yoga," which is established in the state of Śiva-hood.
Rajaḥ and Kuṇḍavatī are said to be the two divisions of Bhautī.
In brief, this initiation is said by the knowers of reality here to be of two kinds:
one is known as consisting of knowledge, and the other is remembered as consisting of ritual action.
[The latter] occurs merely through mental activity, such as the rites of worship, fire-offerings, and so forth.
Initiation is said to be possessed of knowledge, arising from the correct awakening to reality.
That which possesses sacrifice and fire, arising from skill in ritual action,
is manifold— both with action and without seed, as well as with seed and without seed.
In that regard, the seedless [initiation] is to be applied for the Samayin and the Putraka;
however, the seeded initiation should be for the Sādhaka and the Ācārya as well.
Now, the seedless initiation (nirbījikā-dīkṣā) has been described; it is of two kinds:
one bestows liberation immediately, and the second [bestows it] upon the falling away of the body.
For children, the very young, the elderly, women, those addicted to sensual enjoyments, and those afflicted by disease,
there may be a seedless initiation (*nirbījikā-dīkṣā*) that is devoid of the conduct of the pledges (*samaya*).
For those who are wise and capable, it is proclaimed as "with seed" (sabījā).
This "with seed" [initiation] is divided into two types; the first is that which conforms to the nature of Śiva (śivadharmiṇī).
The second [type of action] is said to belong to both the teacher and the disciple; it is purified by the mother of non-dharma and distinguished by differences of place, time, and so forth.
Action, consisting of both dharma and adharma, is manifold and extends into the future.
That state in which one grieves after having reflected [on the past] is called the "one characterized by the nature of Śiva" (śivadharmiṇī).
The second [initiation] is purified by mere non-dharma and pertains to worldly life;
through this worldly initiation, the Guru should initiate householders.

Because the entitlement belongs exclusively to those who are permanent [initiates], initiation for one who is merely observing the rules (samayin) or for one who is not a son [of the lineage] is indeed devoid of entitlement; it is merely occasional and lacks authority.
Since both the practitioner and the teacher possess authority in all rites— whether daily, occasional, or optional— that [wisdom] belongs to them as something possessing such authority.
Wherein there is yoga in the state of Rudra, and wherein there is yoga in the state of Īśvara; wherein there is no severing of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*) for the *samayin* and the *putraka*.
Where there is the severing of the bonds and the crest-lock, and the yoga pertaining to the state of Śiva occurs—
that very thing is called Nirvāṇa through the consecration of the Putraka.
She is proclaimed as being for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) through the consecration of the mantra of the adept (*sādhva-mantra*).
Through the consecration of all vidyās, she belongs to the domain of the master (*ācārya*).
The bestowal of the state of Śiva upon one who is joined with the purificatory rites of Śiva is considered by all to occur either through ritual action, or through power, or through initiation.

By initiation (*dīkṣā*), the embodied soul is liberated from the threefold bondage of existence. That initiation is purified through the path (*adhvan*), and that path is traditionally taught to be sixfold.
The path of mantra, the path of word, the path of phoneme consisting of the worlds,
the path of principle, and the path of aspect— these twenty enter into the single state of Śiva.
Mantras, words, and phonemes are here pervaded on all sides.
The castes are pervaded by the worlds, and those worlds are pervaded by the principles (tattvas).
The tattvas are pervaded here by the kalās in their respective order;
having thus contemplated them, one should purify those which are proclaimed as five, five, and a half.
These are Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and the fifth, Śāntyatītā, belonging to the ether.
[The sequence] proceeds in order from the *kalā* [cakra] up to the heart, throat, palate, eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Upon cessation, the single, patient, imperishable royal principle (pārthiva-tattva) is to be meditated upon;
however, there are one hundred and eight cities belonging to Kālāgni and the others.
O Mahādeva, from the final word down to the first word in reverse order,
there are twenty-eight *vyomavyāpin* words by count.
Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya are proclaimed as the two mantras;
the qualities beginning with smell and ending with sound, along with the five Brahmans, constitute the cause.
In the *Pratiṣṭhā*, the principles beginning with *Ābādi* and numbering twenty-three,
ending with *Prakṛti*, are to be known from within one's own womb (*svagarbha*).
The twenty-three phonemes beginning with *ha* and ending with *ṭa* are to be known in reverse order;
furthermore, there are fifty-six cities beginning with Amareśa.
There are twenty-one words beginning with Maheśvara and ending with Arūpa.
The two mantras are Śiras and Vāma; the qualities are considered to be four, beginning with rasa and ending with the word śabda; and Viṣṇu is the cause here.
In the Vidyā [tattva], there are seven principles (*tattvas*) in the sequence beginning with Puruṣa;
furthermore, from Vāmā up to Bhuvana, twenty-seven [principles] are to be known.
The mantras consist of twenty words beginning with "dhyānāhārāyaparyantā vyāpinn iti";
these are established as the crest (śikhā) and the two knees (khora).
The seven letters beginning with *ja* and ending with *sa* are in reverse order;
their qualities are form, touch, and sound, and Rudra is their cause.
In the case of pacification (śānti), however, there are three principles: Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, and [Īśvara];
and the three phonemes ga, kha, and ka, which constitute the two mantras born of the mouth and the body.
The eighteen principal Purāṇas by number,
and the eleven words beginning with "nityayoginaḥ" and so forth.
The [mantras] ending with "vyomavyāpinaḥ" have been stated here in reverse order;
[the elements] are quality, touch, and sound, while the Lord (Īśvara) is the cause.
In the Kalā beyond Śānti, however, two principles are established;
here, the five and ten ancient worlds, beginning with Nivṛtti, exist.
The single word "Om" is the mantra; herein, the sixteen phonemes beginning with the Visarga and ending with the letter 'A' are proclaimed as the weapons of Īśāna and Śiva.
"Your *ṛg* is the quality (*guṇa*), while the cause is Sadāśiva.
Having thus contemplated the path, [one should contemplate] the Supreme Goddess who pervades the six paths.
Having meditated upon Śakti, one should then contemplate the Supreme State above her;
then, in due order, the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) which are employed for initiation.
Thus, the summary is stated according to its threefold division:
[the faces] are Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Mahāghora, Puruṣa, Īśāna, and Kṛti.
The crest-lock (*śikhā*), armor (*varma*), and weapon (*astra*) are declared to be the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*).
*Oṃ vyomavyāpine vyomarūpāya sarvavyāpine śivāya anantāya anāthāya anāśritāya dhruvāya śāśvatāya yogapīṭhasaṃsthitāya nityayogine.* (11)
To the one whose food is meditation; obeisance to Śiva; to the source of all; to Śiva; to the one whose head is Īśāna; to the one whose face is Tatpuruṣa;

(fourth line) to the one whose heart is Aghora; to the one whose secret parts are Vāmadeva; to the one whose form is Sadyojāta; obeisance, obeisance! To the one more secret than the secret; to the Protector.
To the one who is without end;

to the one presiding over all yogas; to the lord of all vidyās; to the one whose form is light; to the Supreme Lord. (5th line) O insentient one, O insentient one! O sky, O sky! O pervasive one, O pervasive one! 20. O formless one, O formless one! O primordial one, O primordial one! O splendor, O splendor!

Light of lights; formless; without fire; smokeless; ashless; without beginning; manifold, manifold; (sixth line) *dhū dhū dhū dhū*; *oṃ bhūḥ*; *oṃ bhuvaḥ*; *oṃ suvaḥ*; without end; the end; source of the end; *śiva*; *śarva*; Supreme Self; *maheśvara*; 21; *mahādeva*; Lord of true being; of great splendor; Lord of yoga; release, release; (seventh line)

First, first! Śarva, Śarva! Bhava, Bhava! O source of existence! O bestower of happiness upon all beings! O maker of all things present! O supreme one beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra! Unbound, unbound! Unconditioned, unconditioned! You who abide from of old!
O witness, witness present from of old! *Turu turu*! O sun-bird (*pataṅga*), sun-bird!
O tawny one (*piṅga*), tawny one! O knowledge, knowledge! O sound, sound! O subtle one, subtle one!
Śiva! Śarva! Bestower of all! *Oṃ namo namaḥ*. *Oṃ*, salutations again and again to Śiva. *Oṃ*. 28.
Thus, the path of words (*padādhvā*) is proclaimed to consist of exactly eighty-one words;
it is declared to begin with the letter *a* and end with the letter *kṣa*.
The worlds of Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brahmavaiṣṇava,
and Raudra— these six are situated within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Kapālī, Īśa, Tvaja, Buddha, Vaktrabheda, Pramardana,
[Vihati...], Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa.
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Pādaka, Hara,
Jvalana, Dahana, Bava, Bhṛ, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka.
By that river [flowed] Mṛtyu, Hara, Vidhātṛ, as well as Para;
Akṣaya, Viyoktṛ, Dharma, and likewise Dharmapati.
Niṛti, the slayer and killer, of cruel gaze and terrifying appearance;
with erect phallus, deformed eyes, and smoke-colored red fangs;
Bala, Atibala, and Mahābala, holding nooses in their hands.
Then Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka.
Meghanāda and Sunāda are proclaimed as the tenth;
[the others are] Śīghra, Laghu, Vāyuvega, Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, Kṣaya, and Antaka.
The ender of the five, the one with five tufts of hair, the one with matted locks, the one whose vehicle is the clouds;
the lord of treasures, the beautiful, the fortunate, the one of gentle form, the wearer of matted hair.
Lakṣmīdhṛk, Ratnadhṛk, Śrīdhṛk, Prasāda,
Prakāmada, Vidyādhipa, Īśa, Sarvajña, Jñānabhū, and Vedapāraga.
Sureśa, Śarva, Jyeṣṭha, Bhūtapāla,
Balipriya, Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, and Mārutāśana.
Grasana, Udumbara, Śaucaphaṇīndra, Vajradaṃṣṭrin;
Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, Tridaśeśvara;
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Nabholipsu, and Trilocana. (Verse 10)
Vīrabhadra and Bhadrakālī [occupy] the two worlds at the very top of all.
Kapālīśa and the others are in the east; Agnirudra and the others are in the southeast;
Yāmya and the others are in the southern quarter; Nairṛta and the others are in the southwest;
Balā and the others are in the western quarter; and Ghrīghra and the others are in the northwest.
And in the north are Nidhīśa and the others; in the northeast are Vidyādhipa and the others.
Vṛṣa and the others are situated in the lower region, while Śambhu and the principal deities occupy the celestial regions;
they are established in the ten directions outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Thus, by way of enumeration, [are described] the ancient cities of Kālāgni and the others.
In the kalā called Nivṛtti, however, one hundred and eight [deities] are to be known.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiśa, Puṣkara, Ṣaḍī, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍi, Bhārabhūti,
Valkuleśvara, Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Kalpeśa, and Ādikeśvara.
In the middle [region] are Śomaga, Kāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava;
