Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākhalo, and likewise Nakhava; Vimaleśa, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīmakeśvara.
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, Sthāṇu,
Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Kāṭa, and Maṇḍaleśvara.
Kālajña, Śaṅkhukarṇa, Dhūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara; the Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra, Saumya, Prājeśvara, and the eighth is proclaimed as Brāhma. || 8 || 8 ||
Akṛta, Kṛta, Bhairava, Brāhma,
Vaiṣṇava, Kaumāra, Cauma, and Śrīkaṇṭha as the eighth; likewise Amareśa and the others in the state of authority, and Hari in the splendor of the moon and other luminaries.
And in the reality of the wind at Gayā and other such places, as well as in the sky, there are the words "vastra" and so forth.
The egoity [of the city] beginning with Chagaṇḍala is situated in the intellect, while that beginning with Paiśāca resides in primordial nature;
likewise, there are fifty-six cities beginning with Akṛta in primordial nature.
In the Pratiṣṭhā [kalpa], they are to be known by the names Amareśa and the others;
Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhaveśa, and Ekavīraka.
Pracaṇḍa, Māti, Ajona, Taika, and Śiva;
Krodha, Caṇḍa, Muni, Saṃvarta, and Sruva.
Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, Śikheda of great splendor,
Vāmadeva, Bhava, Bhavodbhava, and also Ekapiṅgala.
Likewise, Ekokṣaṇa and Īśāna, as well as Aṅguṣṭhamātraka;
in Vāma, Ādi, Puruṣa, and Rāga, there is the group of five beginning with Pracaṇḍa and Āditya.
In Niyati and the others, as well as in Krodha, Mahādyuti, Māyika,
and the ancient cities of Vāmā and the rest, there are twenty-seven [deities] within the Vidyā-tattva.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī,
as well as Balavikaraṇī and Balapramathinī.
Sarvabhūtadamanī, Manonmanī,
Anantaka, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, and Rudra are the three forms [of the goddess].
Śrīkaṇṭha, Śikhaṇḍin, and likewise another, Sadāśiva;
[the powers] beginning with Vāmā reside within Śuddhavidyā, while those beginning with Anta reside within Īśvara.
In the Śānti [Kalā], there are eighteen worlds with faces turned to the left:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
In Śāntyātīta, there are Ambikā, Dīpikā, and likewise Rocikā;
[and] Ūrdhvagā, Vyāpinī, and Vyomarūpiṇī.
Anantā, Anāthā, Aśrā, Anāśritā, and likewise Parā;
these are the fifteen cities of the past, beginning with Nivṛtti.
Thus, the fivefold Kalā is the speaker of the hundreds of worlds...
which has been described as exceeding [that number] on the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*).

Now, when the thirty-six principles have been reached—earth, water, fire, air, and space; odor, form, taste, touch, and sound; the organs of generation and excretion; ||| ... [and so forth] ||| [The remaining elements and faculties continue as follows: ||| [The mind, intellect, ego, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras); the ten organs of perception and action; the five gross elements; the three qualities (guṇas); time, destiny, and nature. ||| Thus, these are the thirty-six principles. ||| [Note: The provided fragment contains the first portion of a traditional list of the thirty-six tattvas (principles) of the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava systems.]
The feet, the hands, speech, the nose, the tongue, the eyes, the skin, and the ears;
the mind, the ego, and the intellect; as well as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).

Passion (rāga), necessity (niyati), knowledge (vidyā), limited agency (kalā), time (kāla), and the deluding power (mohinī); then knowledge (vidyā), the Lord (īśvara), and the Indefinable (sādākhya); [these are the categories], while Power (śakti) and Śiva are traditionally remembered as the ultimate principles.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and the supreme Atītā—know these to be the divisions (*kalā*) of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*); this is the brief exposition. Now follows the procedure for Pratiṣṭhā.
The offering of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) into the linga which consists of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti),
and the union with the pedestal (pīṭha) according to the prescribed rule— that is consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and it is fivefold.
Pratiṣṭhā, sthāpana, and indeed sthitasthāpana—
these [rites] are to be applied to the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) following the placement of the *brahmaśilā* upon the *liṅga*.
In the case of [images such as] Bāṇa and others, when the separate pedestal has decayed, they are to be applied according to the sequence [of the specific rite] once it has become manifest.
The arrangement of the forms and the heads of the lords, accompanied by the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras).
Where the foundation is eightfold or fivefold, that is the rule in some cases;
when the portion of Rudra is divided into three according to the line of Brahmā,
one should hang two lower parts as a mark down to the water-reservoir.
In the measurement of the liṅga, however, the width of the base (lakṣma) is one part out of the total extent.
The earth-line is low, and its extension is one-ninth of the width;
from half the *lakṣma* mark, two wing-lines are drawn, divided by one-eighth of that field.
By revolving through six and seven parts on the back, their junction is formed below by subtraction.
But when that field is divided by fire (three), it is [formed] by rotating two and a half parts.
The characteristic mark is for the purpose of continuity [of the line], by excluding the lower half;
this applies in the case of a common rule, but otherwise when there is a distinction in the ritual action.

The opening of the eyes, the manifestation [of form], and the characteristic of being manifest or unmanifest do not occur through arrows and the like, nor by means of a moving object, nor even by one made of iron or born of jewels.

In the middle of the aperture, shaped like a vulva with its tip pointing upward, it rests upon the seat of Lakṣmī; by dividing the aperture into one or two parts, a circular line is drawn at its base.
One should then conceive of the pervasion of the principles (tattvas) in sequence within the liṅga, the pedestal, and the stone slab;
furthermore, one should fashion it as three sections ending with Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva.
O Goddess, that which is proclaimed as Māyā is the power of Śakti-Śiva;
she resides, in sequence, within the word, the mind, the seat, the pedestal, and the stone.
The triad of the principle of Māyā is proclaimed as the pervasion of the heart-vessel;
furthermore, the path of the three sections consists of the digit of consciousness (citta-kalā) ending with Māyā.

The path of the three sections belongs to the Person (*puruṣa*), and the cognition of sound extends as far as the Person. The pervasion of the gates, the palaces, and the pinnacles is said to be characterized by the Linga.
There, one should sequentially place the three principles (tattvas) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa,
which are endowed with their own respective principles and consist of the nature of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
Whether as eightfold or fivefold, it is endowed with the forms and the lords of the forms; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are indeed the presiding deities over the three principles within the Liṅga.
The eight forms— Earth, Fire, Sacrifice, Measure, Sun, Moon, Wind, and Sky— should be installed in each section.
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra,
Bhava, Īśāna, Mahādeva, and Bhīma— these are the guardians of the eight forms.
For one desiring enjoyment (bubhukṣu), Śuddhavartinī resides from Śuddhavidyā up to the end of Śakti;
for the practitioner (sādhaka), however, Ananta and the others are the presiding deities (mūrtipās) within the level of Pratiṣṭhā.
Ananta, Śuddhasaṃjña, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and then Śikhaṇḍin—
at the end of this sequence of Puruṣīdaka, within the Sound (dhvani) of the pure and impure paths.
Furthermore, the Rudras who protect the forms should be known as being the size of a thumb.
The Lord is the size of a thumb, with one eye and one tawny hair;
he is Udbhava, Bhava, Vāmadeva, and the one of great splendor.
In the impure [tattva], from the stage of sound (dhvani) up to the end of Pradhāna,
are established the eight Mūrtipas of the hundred Rudras who embody the ten directions.
Kapālīśa, Agnirudra, the one known as Yāmya, the one named Nairṛta,
Bala, Śīghra, Nidhīśa, and Vidyādhipati is the eighth.
In some places, Indra and the other guardians of the world are considered to be the lords of the [divine] forms;
likewise, the Bhairavas are well-known even in minor rites.
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍaka, Unmatta-bhairava,
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra is remembered as the eighth.
In the ritual installation (*nyāsa*) consisting of the five forms (*pañcamūrti*), the elements are earth, water, fire, air, and ether;

these are the forms in the *liṅga*, whose guardians are the five forms beginning with Brahmā. Alternatively, for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the forms in the installation are those beginning with Nivṛtti.
Sadyojāta and the others are considered the five lords of that [liṅga].
In this manner, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed upon the seat and the stone by the one who explains it.
Action (*kriyā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and will (*icchā*)—these three principles are considered the Lords (*īśvara*).
(9th line) [She is] radiant, beautiful to behold, moonlight-like, and preeminent in power.
Dhātrī, Vibhvī, and Trimūrtīśā are considered to be present within the sphere of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth.

In the consecration of the practitioner, at the seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth, the lords of the [five] elements shall be Ananta and the others, having arrived as the protectors of the women. From the perspective of the fivefold division, they are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānī, and Icchā.
The lords of the five forms on the seats and so forth are said to have names beginning with "Ugra" and ending with "abdhi."
Tamas, Moha, Kṣaya, Niṣṭhā, Mṛtyu, Māyā, Bhaya, Jvara—these are the eight [aspects] in the five-fold group; Tamas, Moha, Ghorā, Atighorā, and Parajvara.
These [qualities] belong to all five forms, even in their liṅgas, pīṭhas, and śilās.
One should thus contemplate the differentiation [of the paths] through their pervasion of the levels of reality (tattva) in due order.
The fire [element] ends with passion (rāga), the earth, water, and time; knowledge (vidyā) ends with the fire.
The wind extends as far as Īśvara, and from the Liṅga of Space (vyoma-liṅga) it extends as far as Śiva. From the Puruṣa [principle] down to earth, water, and time, the fire [element] ends with Māyā.
The wind [element] ends with Śuddhavidyā, and the sky [element] extends from the seat of Vyoma to Śakti.

[The letters] ending with *bha*, *ta*, *kṣa*, *m*, *a*, *mbu* (water), and *śabda* (sound); [those] ending with fire (*va*), the organs of action (*ka*), and the organs of perception (*ba*); [and those] ending with wind (*ya*) and ether (*ha*), up to the intellect (*ma*) in the stone (*śa*).
In the eight-fold arrangement, however, the forms beginning with earth (*m*) and so forth are placed from the east to the northeast.
In the five-fold system, those facing north, south, east, and west are situated.
This entire sequence should be understood to apply to images as well;
having meditated upon the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the name of the Form (*mūrti*) and the Lord of Forms (*mūrtīśvara*), etc.,
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) everywhere according to the established procedure.
The earth remains established in its state of reliability, as do water and the other elements, each in its own respective domain.
Above the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) are situated the two, Soma and Sūrya;
above those, at the cheeks, is situated Śarva, who is called Dharma.
Rudra Paśupati resides in the sphere of ego within the element of form;
Rudra is to be understood as being right there, while Bhava resides in the subtle element of taste.
Īśāna resides in the subtle element of touch, and Mahādeva is situated in the mind.
And Bhīma is established in the subtle element of sound; such is the arrangement of the Lords of Form.

The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are to be known as established within the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva). Brahmā extends from the earth element up to the individual soul (puruṣa); Hari extends from the earth up to Māyā;
Rudra extends from the earth up to Vidyā; and Īśvara extends from the earth up to the Bindu.
When [the universe] is dissolved by means of the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Sādākhya, Śakti remains as the ultimate limit of Earth and the other elements.

The ten incarnate forms of Viṣṇu reside within the element of earth; they are situated in the heart, intellect, and ego of beings, and are accessible through the secondary [means] and the lords of primordial matter (*pradhāna*). (In the eighth line:
Mitra and the others, Keśava and the others, and Tryambaka and the others are recorded as the ten.
And Vighnarāja is in the state called Sādākhya; likewise is the goddess Sarasvatī.
Nanda and the others reside in Śuddhavidyā; Lakṣmī resides in the sphere of Īśvara; people abide in Prakṛti; the Śāktas are established in Buddhi;
those who know the Pañcarātra reside in Puruṣa; and Sūrya is established in Śiva.
Apsaras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, vidyādharas, and indeed kinnaras;
The spirits, vetālas, and ḍākinīs; the planets, lunar mansions, and zodiac signs;
the oceans, the guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapāla*), and others; the sages, Brahmā, and the lords of the directions;
as well as those born from a womb, from an egg, or from sprouts—all these are known to abide within the essence of the earth.
For others as well, among the principles (tattvas), each is established in its respective place.
The placement (*nyāsa*) is the tooth; her supreme station is that very same thing.
She has four faces and eight arms, and is yellow, wearing yellow garments and ornaments. Seated upon a tortoise, she is of gentle form and is surrounded by serpents, oceans, and rivers.
The Fire-god, mounted upon a ram, with blazing flames and a spear in his hand, appeared.
Shaped like a sacrificial pit with its mouth turned upward, blazing with the splendor of the sun,
possessing black horns and heat, and joined with a beautiful girdle on the left.
The sacrificer is proclaimed as one whose limbs are smeared with fresh butter;
he is the Sun, mounted upon his chariot, clad in armor, wearing earrings, and bearing a banner.
Wearing a crown, with a lotus in his hand, adorned with anklets and a charioteer,
he is four-armed by nature and decorated with all ornaments.
Varuṇa holds a noose and a heart; he is the lord of aquatic creatures, whose banner is the makara. He has four arms, four faces, is smoke-colored, and possesses great strength.
Seated upon a deer, with a slender waist, full-bodied, and with arched eyebrows, his movement is ever gentle;
he is Soma, the mild one, stationed in a celestial chariot, holding a mace and a conch, and bestowing boons.
Resembling a jewel of universal form, joined with the nectar of the jar,
he has four arms and four faces, bearing a trident and sounding a hand-drum.
Possessing the splendor of the moon, conch, jasmine, crystal,
and snow, she is endowed with the qualities of a world-guardian and distinguished by the weapon appropriate to her own direction.
Those beginning with Śarva, who possess bodies described by Vidyā, are considered to be drinkers of the vital energy (*ūrjapā*).
Their hands are like molten gold, they have four faces, and they are adorned with many ornaments.
Nivṛtti is proclaimed as having a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a rosary, and a lotus;
she resembles pure crystal, has one face, and four arms.
Holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she is the goddess Pratiṣṭhā, adorned with jewels;
she is red in color, has a single chignon, three faces, and four arms.
Holding a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she resembles a blazing fire;
she has four faces, four arms, a dark complexion, and great strength.
Śānti has a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus;
she wears the sacred thread across her shoulder, resembles pure crystal, and has five faces and four arms.
Śāntyatītā holds a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a water-lily, and bestows boons;
she is three-eyed, stands in the attire of a youth, is full-bodied, and has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
He was watery, adorned with earrings, instantly resembling a white lotus in his eyes,
gentle-faced, serene, and decorated with lovely ornaments.
Adorned with the crescent moon, possessing plump and beautiful limbs, with eyes like those of a deer,
he has tawny eyebrows and beard, round eyes, matted locks, and is decorated with the moon.
Fanged, licking his tongue, resembling the Destroyer (*Kṛtānta*),
with a face possessing a pot-shaped forehead, eyebrows, and beard, he was endowed with the heat of youth and possessed the vigor of the wind.
With a face graced by beautiful eyebrows and a smile, adorned with serpents,
skulls, and snakes, yellow in color, with matted hair like the moon, he is known as Tatpuruṣa in the east.
The Lord of Mantras lies supine and white upon his head, each presiding over his own respective direction;
adorned with earrings, three-eyed, wearing a crown, and possessing the radiant luster of a youth.
He was then joined by all the Maruts, who were filled with lotuses as blue as sapphire;
in their left hands they held skull-topped staffs (khaṭvāṅgas), spears, tridents, and displayed the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The Vidyeśvaras have four faces and ten arms like Hara;
they wear the crescent moon upon their heads, stand upon lotuses with their right hands, and bear various weapons:
the sword, shield, bow, arrow, water-pot, and rosary.
Their hands are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and they hold tridents and lotuses.
Śakra, the thousand-eyed one, is mounted upon a bull and accompanied by Marut; Agni is mounted upon a goat;
Yama, the terrible one, holds a staff and has a buffalo as his vehicle;
Nirṛti, with a gaping mouth, a sword, and fierce eyes, is mounted upon a corpse.
Gadī Vaiśravaṇa is stout and adorned with a large belly.

Īśāna is like a jasmine flower, the moon, or snow; he is seated upon a bull, bears the crescent moon, is equipped with weapons such as the *vidyujjvālā* and the *aśoka*, and is adorned with a necklace of skulls. Brahmā has four faces, is yellow in color, and is adorned with four staff-like arms.
He is equipped with a sacrificial ladle, a staff, and kusha grass; he wears a crown and has a swan as his vehicle.
Viṣṇu has four arms and wears a garland; he holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
He resembles a dark blue cloud and is seated upon Garuḍa.
He has five faces and fifteen eyes, ten arms, and is adorned with the moon.
Seated upon a bull, wearing the sacred thread, Rudra is as pure as the kunda flower and the moon.
The Lord of the World should be known as having eight arms, four faces, and three eyes, with the luster of crystal, wearing a serpent as his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
pure as a jasmine flower or the moon, the deity of the five mantras and of great form.
He has ten arms, a serene face, five faces, and is Sadāśiva.
Four-armed and four-faced, seated upon a square lotus,
this is known as the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self), possessing the luster of molten gold.
[The *vidyātattva*] resembles a dark blue cloud, blue in color, and endowed with eight faces and eight arms.
Having one face and a gentle countenance, it is proclaimed as the principle of Vidyā.
This Śiva-tattva is remembered as resembling a jasmine flower or the moon, containing within it all the paths (*adhvan*);
it has five faces and four arms.
Thus, when performed in its own place and time, the sacrifice bestows the fruit of its presiding authority.
In another place and at another time, those very same things become causes of what is undesirable.
One should perform the formal undertaking (*upādāna*) according to the place and time for which it is intended;
one should worship the place in the south-eastern direction (*āgneyī*) and the time in the eastern direction (*aindrī*).
Having invoked the deity of the eighth [direction] (the northwest), one should establish the place as one's own.
Or who else could have completed a year by means of his own twelve [fingers]? And I am he.
The five [principles] beginning with Space (Ākāśa) reside in the Earth and the other elements; then the eight [deities] beginning with Īśāna follow in sequence.
Time, beginning with Prabhava, occurs through the application of the twelve-fold order.
In these five [elements], the five Lords of Causes (Kāraṇeśvaras), beginning with Brahmā, reside in sequence.
And others, situated within that pervasion, [arise] through the connection with place and so forth.
Now, in connection with the [discussion of] regions, the deities of the site (vāstudevatāḥ) are seen:
Brāhma, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendra,
Āravi, Satyaka, Bhṛśa, Antarikṣa, Saptārdhi, Pūṣan, and the one named Avitatha.
Graha, Kṣata, Pretapa, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅganā (Bṛga).
Pitṛ, Dauvāri, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Pracetas;
the Asura, Śoṣa, and Roga; Vāyu, Nāga, and Mukhyaka;
Bhallāṭa, that deity, Aditi, and Diti.
Marīci, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Dharādhara;
Āpa, Āpavat, Ḍauḍavitā, Sāvitra, Indrajit,
Tamā, Rudra, then Rudradāsa,
Carakī, Vidāri, Pūtanā, the two sinful Rākṣasīs, Skanda, Aryaman, and Jambhaka.
Thus, fifty-three [syllables] are declared as the *pilipiccha* meter, followed by the *upadaṃ* (the concluding phrase).
The various lines extending eastward and northward constitute eighteen *nāḍīs*;
the two diagonal beams (*vaṃśas*) and the eight cords (*rajjus*) consist of twelve squares each.
Thus, by this incidental description, the site (*vāstu*) consists of sixty-four squares.
Fifty-three deities are enumerated here in their proper sequence.
Brahmā is in the center with four feet; Marīci is in the east with six feet;
Rudra is below the northwest corner with seven feet, and further below him is Rudradā;
in the direction of the Lord of Yakṣas, within Guptā, is Dharādhara with six feet.
The waters are below Īśāna, and they flow downward even further than that.
Starting from the half-step of Īśa and extending as far as the end of Īśāna,
at the extremities from Īśāna to Śakra, there are thirty-two [deities] in the southern sequence:
Marīci, Vivadhvān, Mitra, and Bhūdhara, each occupying six steps.
Āpa, Apāpavatsa, Savitṛ, Sāvitra, Indra, and Indrajittama.

Rudra and his servant should each consist of two quarters, while the others are single-quartered. These two seed-syllables (*bīja*)— namely *Dīkṣā* and *Pratiṣṭhā*— should be grasped by the preceptor at the proper time, with the desire for their successful accomplishment.

Thus, the venerable teacher Somaśambhu, whose name is proclaimed as containing the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) that signify being gazed upon by the Eye at the end of time, has extracted [this] from two hundred scriptures of the Āgamas. The *Varuṇapaddhati* is hereby completed. He who is named Varuṇa should be known as Varuṇaśambhu.

**The Characteristic of the Equinox** (147a) By uniting the self with the mind through the vital breaths, the equinox occurs. This is declared to be the "equinox of the breath" (*prāṇa-viṣuva*), as well as that of the disciple and one's own mind.
Having meditated upon the dissolution of the self within the *nāda* from the *kanda*,
through the conjunction and subsequent separation of the phonemes beginning with *a* and *u*,
one should cause that which is designated as mantra to flow upward from the heart to the end of the *bilā*.
Above the penis are the kanda and the navel; then the heart and the pit of the throat.
The tip of the throat, the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā, the Śakti,
and the end of the twelve—
having pierced these ten knots in succession with the trident of the root mantra, the Nāda proceeds forth.
Through the union of sound and the channel, that channel is considered the equinox (viṣuva).
Having abandoned the phonemes *a* and *u*, the phoneme *ma* known as the *bindu*,
and [the stages] joined with *nāda* and *nādānta* in their respective order among Brahmā and the others,
one should lead the disciple’s self into dissolution within the seventh [stage], the center of Śakti.
One should know that to be the state of perfect peace, which is beyond the range of the senses through tranquility.
The *nāda* situated in the midst of the *śakti* extends as far as the end of the *manas*;
that is declared the *viṣuva* of *śakti*, and it is called the *kālya-viṣuva*. That duration of time which is merely the twinkling of an eye is proclaimed as a *truṭi*.
Having thus understood time as threefold with respect to the vital breath, perform it likewise in a threefold manner.
Another is the sixteenth, up to the seventeenth which is both prior and subsequent;
but that time which follows it, O Dear One, is remembered as the eighteenth.
Having thus understood the breath as threefold time, perform the ritual action accordingly.
The other [time] consists of sixteen parts;
the third, ending at *samanā*, is called the equinox (*viṣuva*).
That which ends with the unmanī state is then declared to be the principle known as the Viṣuva.
This definition of the *viṣuva* [equinox] should also be observed in the *Prāsādacandrikā* and in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*, though by a different method. (147b blank;
148–157 missing).
Regarding the installation of the Śiva-liṅga:

(86a, 1st line) The disciples, those connected to the guru, and those related to the guru should perform the ritual for three days, including recitation (*japa*) and other rites, except for the obligatory daily ones.
In the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
"For the knower who possesses the seed of purification and performs the proper rites,
that [impurity] may last for only a moment, and it is removed simply by bathing."
Devotion, knowledge, and dispassion— or even one of these—
if they should be properly present in someone, by him, as a holder of the pledges (samayin), the worship should be performed.
Even for one for whom these three are either slow or very slow,
the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) must also be performed at the conclusion over two days.

"Or for one day, subsisting on barley, one should recite the Aghora mantra a thousand times at the conclusion of the bath, and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part [of that number]. Thus [it is said].
(4th line)
The procedure for the funeral rites and other ceremonies, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara, is completed.

The Lord of the Gaṇas, who plays with the intent of experiencing the graceful sport of the lotus-like hands, and who sports at the feet of his mother with a sense of joy, [is the one who] destroys the tree of obstacles.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the offering of finger-gestures (mudrās).

On whichever day the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsakarma*) is performed for the sake of the subjects and so forth, omitting that one day, on the ninth, seventh, or [other specified] day prior, or immediately, one should place a jar adorned with heaps of grain upon a pure ground divided into sixteen sections; having placed it in the central group of four squares, [one proceeds] with the squares starting from the northeast (*īśāna*).

Having arranged twelve clay-filled small jars, pots, and bowls, and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, distinguished by the word "Mahādeva," and having performed the ritual of complete identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should worship Soma in the central jar with the mantra: *oṃ raṃ paṃ vaṃ yaṃ saṃ ṣīṃ hāṃ śrīṃ amṛteśvarāya namaḥ*, using the central seed-syllable.

Having worshipped the limbs [of the deity], one should worship the twelve Ādityas in the pitchers starting from the east and ending in the northeast, using their own names in the dative case, joined with the *praṇava* and the word "namaskāra. For example: (—)
Vaikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi,
Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama.
Āditya, Sūrya, Aṃśumālin, and Divākara—
having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) to these, one should worship them in pure vessel-milk with the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ śaktaye namaḥ*.
In that [vessel], having prepared wild rice, mung beans, sesame, black gram, pigeon pea, *niṣpāva*,

and mustard seeds with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), and having worshipped them with the *Saṃhitā* while intending them to be the "seed of Śiva" (*śivabīja*), and having placed them into the *pālikā* and other vessels, one should worship the *Ādhāraśakti* and offer incense, lamps, and so forth.
Preceded by the auspicious sound of conchs, one should cast the seed-syllables with milk— either with the heart-mantra or with the root and limb-mantras—
and nourish them with water from the moon-pitcher (*candrakumbha*). Then, day after day, one should nourish them again with water from the pitcher.

One should fill the pitcher with pure water. At the conclusion of the designated day, one should release the pitcher. If the sprouts are straight and bright, they bring about all prosperity. (Sixth line) If they are smoky-colored or crooked, considering them to be obstacles to well-being, one should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*).
Now follows the procedure for the preliminary consecration of the water.

In the pavilion for the removal of marks (*lakṣaṇoddhāra-maṇḍapa*), having first performed the ritual bathing and then carried out the removal of marks as will be described [in the seventh line], the Guru should bathe [the image] once more, adorn it, place it upon a chariot or similar vehicle, perform a circumambulation of the village and so forth, and then establish it on the bank of a river; in this manner, he should prepare two sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having placed the God and Goddess upon the auspicious throne in due order,
and having covered them with a new cloth provided with hanging fringes,
one should set down eight jars all around and offer them to the World-Protectors.
Afterwards, one should place the God and the Goddess together with their feet within the water;
or else, one should lay them upon a wooden plank with their heads toward the east and their faces turned upward.
One should consecrate the deity, together with its pedestal, in water for three nights,

two nights, one night, or even for a single day, or for a mere watch (yāma). And every day, [the rite should be performed] along with sacrificial offerings, dance, Vedic chanting, music, and so forth.

Having performed the ritual immersion (*adhivāsa*) in water and brought it from that place to the bathing pavilion (*snānamaṇḍapa*), one should perform the purification of the form upon the eastern altar. Then, having brought the *liṅga* together with its pedestal to the northern altar (*uttaravedikā*) and adorned it, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth using the general mantra, or tie the protective thread (*kautuka*). [It should be placed] in a vessel filled with pure rice.
Having worshipped the Ādhāra-śakti, who is the color of the milk-ocean and has the form of a seed-sprout, in a vessel made of gold or other materials;
and having visualized within her the Kuṭilā-śakti, who resembles the milk-ocean and is as slender as a stalk of wild rice (nīvāra);
and having placed a protective cloth—chosen from among those made of gold, silver, or linen—over it; and having worshipped it and circumambulated the temple.

(5th line) Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) accompanied by all musical instruments, and having wiped [the forehead] three times with ashes using the thumb and ring finger while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra, at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction (*sulagna*), [one should perform the rite].
One should bind the thread upon the portion of Rudra with the mantra of Īśāna;
and upon the stalk of the pedestal, one should bind the *kautuka* with the *hṛdaya* [mantra].
With the *Tryambaka* mantra, one should contemplate the protection of the two fragrances.
Then the wise man should cause betel to be distributed to all the people. To the east of the pavilion, he should perform the propitiatory rite accompanied by the touching of the linga,
and he should also have the chanting of Vedic mantras performed, either through others or himself.

"O Rudra, for whomsoever this portion of yours is intended, together with Ambikā and the thousand sisters, may you accept it... [and so forth]. Having recited this, one should tie the *kautuka* (sacred thread). This may be done at night, at the time of the *sadyas* [immediate] rite, or even during the day.
Thus ends the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*jalādhivāsa*).
(The Entrance Offering:
Having performed the worship of Vāstu preceded by the worship of Vināyaka in the pavilion,
and having performed the sprinkling with the "Auspicious Day" water preceded by the circumambulation with fire using that same fire;

One should decorate the pavilion with canopies, garlands of *darbha* grass, and other ornaments. However, in the case of the consecration of a metal image, one should first perform the ritual placement of gems (*ratnanyāsa*),
then construct a very firm lotus-base (*padmabandha*), and only thereafter carry out the removal of defects (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*) and other rites.

Then, for the sake of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the selection of the stone, on an auspicious day, having worshipped Śiva and offered prayers, and having obtained permission at an appropriate moment, accompanied by artisans and assistants, he should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), recollect the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) in his heart, and proceed to the desired site of the stone. Having arrived—

Having ascertained the stone according to the previously stated characteristics— its thighs, back, head, feet, and so forth— and having worshipped Śiva upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated to its north, having generated the fire in the southeast, performed the libation with mantras, and offered the internal oblation (*antarbali*), one should sprinkle the stone with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*.

Having enveloped [the image] with the *varman* mantra and worshipped it with the *praṇava*, and having consecrated the artisan, his assistants, the chisel, the hammer, and so forth with the *astra* mantra and worshipped them with the *praṇava*, one should likewise offer a hundred oblations into the fire with the *astra* mantra, seal [the site], and while reciting the *svapnamāṇava* mantra, one who subsists on sacrificial porridge (*caru*) should proceed.

He should sleep as the Piṅga Māṇavaka, holding a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), the supreme mudrā, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya); he wears matted hair and has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Oṃ liṣṭilihi śūlapāṇaye svāhā.
Oṃ, salutation to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
salutation to the Auspicious One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams.
"Speak, O Lord of the Gods of gods! I have sought refuge at your feet.
In my dream, all my duties and the fears residing in my heart [were revealed].
Having thus risen in the morning, having worshipped Śiva, and having rejoiced in the auspicious dream, [one should perform the rite] with the Astra-mantra for the sake of peace.
Having offered a hundred oblations, one should strike a stone slab— whose head is toward the northeast and which is joined with a bull—
make it square, dismiss the deities and the fire, place it upon a vehicle, bring it back, and have it conveyed to the workshop located in the northern part of the palace.
In the absence [of such a stone], one may instead bring and take up another stone.

Thereafter, one should fashion the liṅga, the pedestal, the Brahmaśilā, the bull, and Caṇḍeśvara, having caused them to be made with their proper characteristics as prescribed in the scriptures. Then, having obtained ground possessing the stated characteristics, at night during an auspicious moment,
[one should perform the rites] with the water of the general arghya.

Having sprinkled [the site] with scents and other offerings and worshipped it, one should divide it into nine parts. Having offered a *bali* in the sections beginning with the Brahma-place with the mantra: "Oṃ, svāhā to all beings, ghosts, piśācas, rākṣasas, and so forth," one should recite: "O beings, ghosts, piśācas, and rākṣasas who dwell upon this earth, depart at your will, leaving this place; I take possession of this ground."
"Having made the request, one should dismiss [the deities]"— this refers to the offering for entry (*praveśabali*).
Then, the Guru, together with the artisans, [should go] to the northeast.

Having prepared a single water-pot like that of Śiva, and having placed Viśvakarman there as well as those [deities] possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, and having worshipped them and sprinkled with that water, at an auspicious moment,
one should strike the ground in the corners starting from the southeast, having first marked it with portions, with the mantra: "Om, to all those belonging to Agni, and to others who..."
Dependent upon them,
let all those who are desired accept from me this excellent, meritorious *modana* offering, joined with the utterance of *svāhā*.
The lord of the Nairṛtas and the Rākṣasas who belong to the Nairṛta quarter.
I offer this oblation to them; may they accept it with joyful minds. This is the meritorious rice-offering: Oṃ! To all the Rudras and to those others who depend upon them.
"I offer this oblation to them; may they accept it with joyful minds. Thus one should present the oblation.
This concludes the installation of the Śaṅku.
Next is the ritual for the formal acceptance (*parigraha*).
Then, desiring to construct a palace according to the prescribed characteristics, one should examine the ground by means of digging and other tests and take possession of it.

Having caused a pavilion together with sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) to be built there according to the instructions, and having performed the ritual beginning with the worship of the doors and their guardians up to the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) with mantras, one should perform a thousand recitations with the *tacchāntīśa* mantra for the purpose of producing color in the garments, fibers, substances, and metals.

For the sake of purifying the ground, one should offer a thousand oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra; then, having leveled the center of the site and smeared it [with cow dung], one should establish the directions using a conch-shell or similar instrument. Having drawn a clockwise line with gold, curd, and unbroken rice, one should place [the vessel] upon all kinds of grain in the northeast corner from the center, filled with water consecrated by mantras.

Having worshipped the jar— which is adorned at its mouth with auspicious medicinal herbs, gems, mango sprouts, *aśvattha* shoots, *bījapūra* fruits, and so forth, covered with a pair of white thread-cloths, and presided over by the Blessed One together with his retinue— [one should proceed].
Having worshipped the Vāstu deity,

having bathed the spade and other implements with water from the ritual pitcher, and having offered the directional oblation (*digbali*) outside the Vāstu site according to the procedure for the house of the Rākṣasas,
one should transfer the worship performed for the Vāstu into the pitcher when the auspicious moment (*lagna*) arrives.
Having consecrated the *āgneyī* [direction] with honey-anointed earth dug to the depth of a cubit using a spade, having cast that soil toward the *nairṛta* [direction],

having filled the pit with water from a jar, and having sprinkled the ground, one should bathe the spade and other implements and worship them. Furthermore, one should place a full jar covered with a pair of cloths upon the right shoulder of a Brāhmaṇa.

Having set down the musical instruments and the like, accompanied by the sound of Vedic chanting, he should lead [the image] in the presence of many witnesses as far as desired toward the eastern boundary of the city. Having stayed there for a mere moment, he should circumambulate it,
sprinkling the boundary markers all around.

One should cause [the vessel] to revolve as far as the domain of Īśāna. Having thus performed the ritual seizure of the ground (*bhūparigraha*) by means of this taking possession of the auspicious jar (*bhadrakumbhaparigraha*), one should dismiss the sacrifice.

Immediately thereafter, for the sake of removing the disciples' doubts regarding the site of the temple, one should dig down to the water-level and fill it with earth until it rises eight finger-breadths above the hand.
Having filled the area up to three paces [from the center] with other soft earth mixed with water and struck down with a mallet,
one should prepare the ground so that it is level, well-compacted, smooth, and extending toward the northeast; then, having established the desired square [area].
One should commence the laying of the foundation stones (śilānyāsa).

There, on an auspicious day, the Guru, accompanied by the image-keepers (mūrtipas), should perform in the pavilion— from the worship of the doors onwards— up to the libation with mantras, as will be described.

Having performed the ritual acts, having brought about the pacification of ill omens and the induction of auspicious signs regarding the site and the time, and having gone to the bathing pavilion honored by the patron, one should commence the bathing of the stones.
Those stones, for a temple made of stone, should be square-shaped and [measured] in cubits.

They are half as wide [as the stones] and eight *aṅgulas* high; or else, in the case of a structure made of bricks, the bricks should be of that same measure, marked with the *vajra* and other symbols, and provided with nine lotus-marks—or five, in the case of five. Having made marks on those corner-stones (*vidik-śilā*) and having offered the seat of the *praṇava* to them without distinction, and having placed *darbha* grass upon them, [one should place it] in the center.

The stone named Śrī and the jar called Uttarā at its side; in the eight directions beginning with the east, the stones named Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Pūrṇā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Vijayā, Maṅgalā, and so forth;
and at their sides, those known as Subhadrā, Vibhadrā, Sunandā, Puṣpanaṣṭakā, Jayā, Vijayā, Kumbha, and Pūrṇa.

(8th line) One should arrange the jars in sequence. In the five-jar arrangement, the jar called "Ocean" is placed in the center, and the four jars named Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Āruntī are placed in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneyī). (89b, 1st line)

Having placed jars made of stone, lotus, great-lotus, conch, emerald, and so forth near those [images], one should scrape them with the *astra-mantra*, encircle them with the *varma-mantra*, and perform the purification of their form with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, using earth, cow dung, cow urine, decoction-water, and scented water; then [one should place] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the scented water in between.

Having bathed [the deity] with water from the ocean of milk and other waters, using jewels, gold, flowers, grain, cow-horns, and [other substances], preceded by the syllable *praṇava* and ending with the personal name followed by a salutation (*namaskāra*); having anointed it with sandalwood paste, covered it with red garments,
circumambulated the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), and entered through the western door, [he places it] upon the altar.
On a bed of leveled ground strewn with *śāli* rice and other grains,

preceded by six prostrations, one should lay [the image] down from the center toward its respective directions with the head facing east while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*; then, having covered it with a cloth over which the *varma-mantra* has been recited, one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) while mentally tracing the path from the crown of the head down to the feet.

One should install the principles (*tattva*) and their respective lords, beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*), as follows: *Oṃ hāṃ namas to the principle of the intellect.* *Oṃ hāṃ namas to the Buddha, the lord of the principle of the intellect.* *Oṃ hāṃ namas to the principle of egoity (*ahaṅkāra*).* *Oṃ hāṃ namas to Ahaṅkṛta, the lord of the principle of egoity.* *Oṃ hāṃ namas to the principle of the mind (*manas*).* *Oṃ hāṃ...*

Salutation to the Lord of the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*), the conceptualizer (*saṅkalpa*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of hearing (*śrotra-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the principle of hearing, the one who moves through space (*vayomacāra*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of touch (*tvak-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the principle of touch, the one whose limbs are all-pervading (*sarvāṅga*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of sight (*cakṣus-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ...

Homage to the Lord of the Principle of the Eye for the sake of illumination. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Principle of the Tongue. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahāvaktra, the Lord of the Principle of the Tongue. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Principle of the Nose. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the Principle of the Nose. (90a, 1st line; 152a)
Homage to Vilambaka. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of speech. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dundubhi, the lord of the principle of speech.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the hand. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Samādāna, the lord of the principle of the hand. Oṃ hāṃ... (second line).

Salutation to the principle of the feet. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ramaṇa, the presiding deity of the principle of the feet. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the anus. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Tūrṇakṛt, the presiding deity of the principle of the anus. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the generative organ. Oṃ hāṃ, [salutation to the presiding deity] of the principle of the generative organ. (Third line)
Salutation to Ghanānanda. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of sound (śabda-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the principle of sound, Sūkṣmanāda.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of touch (sparśa-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the principle of touch, Balavattara. (4th line)

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of form (*rūpatattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhānumat, the lord of the principle of form. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of taste (*rasatattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jalada, the lord of the principle of taste. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of smell (*gandhatattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gandhāṅga, the lord of the principle of smell. Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to the principle of space (*vyoma-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sūkṣma, the lord of the principle of space.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of air (*vāyu-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mātariśvan, the lord of the principle of air. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of fire (*agni-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, [salutation to the lord of the principle of fire].

Salutation to the storehouse of splendors. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the water-element (jala-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the water-element, the Lord of Waters (jaleśa). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the earth-element (pṛthivī-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the lord of the earth-element. Having thus consecrated the central stone and the others in sequence, one should distribute the flower garland.

On the three-part stones (*trikhaṇḍāsu*), from intellect (*buddhi*) up to the mind (*manas*): *oṃ huṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ | oṃ huṃ śivatattvādhipataye rudrāya namaḥ*. Up to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*): *oṃ hrīṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ | oṃ hrīṃ vidyātattvādhipataye...* [90b]

(First line) *Viṣṇave namaḥ*. Up to the end of the earth: *Oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvādhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ*. Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), [one places] *Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ* in each respective part in the directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast. (Second line) *Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ*... [continues].

Salutation to the form of Earth. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śarva, the lord of the form of Earth. Oṃ hāṃ īṃ, salutation to the form of Fire. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Paśupati, the lord of the form of Fire. Oṃ hāṃ śūṃ, salutation to the form of the Sacrificer. (Third line)
Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ugra, the presiding deity of the Sacrificer-form. Oṃ hāṃ ṣūṃ, salutation to the Sun-form.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the presiding deity of the Fire-form. Oṃ hāṃ pūṃ, salutation to the Water-form. Oṃ hāṃ... (fourth line).
Salutation to Bhava, the lord of the water-form.

Oṃ hāṃ yūṃ, salutation to the wind-form. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśvara, the lord of the wind-form. Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, salutation to the moon-form. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to [the lord] of the moon-form. (Fifth line)

Salutation to Mahādeva. Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, salutation to Khamūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhīma, the lord of Khamūrti. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight forms and their respective lords, [one should place] those [liṅgas] which have been worshipped with ghee, honey, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), metals, gems, minerals, seeds, and medicinal herbs, and whose necks are bound with triple-stranded threads and the like.

Having consecrated with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) the jars placed upon the sections of the stone foundation, one should worship them with the mantras beginning with Śakra and ending with Ananta. In the five-pakṣa system, in the western, northern, southern, eastern, and northeastern directions, [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ pṛthivīmūrtaye*.
Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the earth-form.

(8th line) Oṃ hāṃ pūṃ, salutation to the water-form. Oṃ hāṃ pūṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the water-form. Oṃ hāṃ rūṃ, salutation to the fire-form. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fire-form.
Oṃ hāṃ yūṃ, homage to Vāyumūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśvara, the lord of Vāyumūrti. Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, homage to Ākāśamūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sadāśiva, the lord of Ākāśamūrti. Then, [second line]...
The five jars should be worshipped with their respective names beginning with "Ṣaṣṭha. Then, having restrained them with the Niṣṭhura-mudrā and worshipped them,
one should place the Nidrā-jar on the region of the head, consecrate it a hundred times with the Astra-mantra, and [construct] a triple enclosure with ashes, darbha grass, and sesame seeds.

Having performed the ritual preparations, the preceptor goes near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), sits down, consecrates the *śāntikumbha* by reciting the *astra-mantra* one hundred times, and purifies it with the residual drops (*saṃpāta*). Having worshipped within the middle of the pit with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," he offers three oblations (*āhuti*) and [worships] with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ātmatattva; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Ātmatattva."
"Salutation to Brahmā. Having thus worshipped and gratified [the deity] with oblations, [one should offer]: "Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ, salutation to the Earth-form (kṣmāmūrti).
(5th line) "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śarva, the lord of the Earth-form. Following this sequence: "Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ, salutation to the Earth-form (pṛthivīmūrti). Oṃ hāṃ..."

Or, having worshipped the forms and the lords of the forms with the mantra "Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the earth-form," and having gratified them with oblations, one should offer [the fire] in sequence— either a hundred, a thousand, or half that number— with the root mantra, the limb mantras, and the Brahmā mantras, ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*, according to the quality of the materials. The guardians of the forms [should worship] starting from the east, each their own...

Having worshipped the Mūrtīśvaras in their respective directions with their own Brahmāṅga mantras, preceded by the ritual placement of the Ādhāraśakti, they should perform [the rite] according to the time and materials for the *homa*.
Alternatively, they may perform it using a tenth part of the *homa* performed by the Guru. Then... (8th line)

The Guru, assuming a physical form, goes near the stone, sprinkles it with the waters from his respective *śānti*-vases, touches the portion belonging to Brahmā with the root of a *kuśa* blade, performs a recitation (*japa*) equal in number to the *homa* offerings, and having sprinkled it again, effects the union of the pure and impure— the *ātmatattva* and *vidyātattva*— as well as that of the *mūrti* and the *mūrtīśvaras*.
Having performed the reconnection (*sandhāna*) of the pure and impure [elements], one should go again near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and recite: *oṃ hāṃ hīṃ namaḥ ātmatattvavidyātattvābhyām*.

Having offered oblations for the purpose of joining the *tattvas* and for the purpose of joining the *mūrti* and the *mūrtīśvara*, and having established, worshipped, and again offered oblations as before to the *vidyātattva*, its presiding deity Viṣṇu, and the *mūrti* and *mūrtīśvara*s; then, having gone to the stone slab, performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and recitation (*japa*) as before, touched the middle of the stone with the middle of the *kuśa* grass, and having thoroughly sprinkled it, he should perform the joining (*sandhāna*) once more.

Having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the unification of the principles (*tattvasandhāna*) with the formula: "Oṃ hīṃ hūṃ, salutation to the Principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*) and the Principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*)," and likewise perform the unification of the Form (*mūrti*) and the Lord of the Form (*mūrtīśvara*). Then, having offered oblations, [one should worship] the Principle of Śiva and its presiding lord.

Having installed Rudra and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvaras*), having worshipped them and gratified them with oblations (*āhuti*), one should go near the stone. As before, having performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the recitation (*japa*), and having touched the edge of the stone with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, one should proclaim the command of Śiva: "O Lords of the Principles (*tatveśvaras*)!"

Having requested, "May you be present together with the embodied and unembodied lords by the command of Śiva," one should worship the five Navakumārabhās with the mantras of the world-protectors (lokapālas), either by their respective names or [generally], perform a fire-oblation (homa) for the sake of their presence, and then meditate upon the presiding deities (adhidevatās).
Embodied as knowledge, having performed their ablutions, golden-hued, with smiling faces,
endowed with all ornaments, they are the presiding deities of the stone slabs.

Thus, for the sake of expiation and for the purification of the site, one should offer one hundred oblations accompanied by the *pūrṇāhuti* using the Astra-mantra. Then, having divided the temple-site into eight parts and created sixty-four squares—
Having laid out the vertical beam from the northeast to the southwest and the horizontal beam from the southeast to the northwest,

and having placed eight lines consisting of two and six squares, one should [install] the thirty-two deities starting from the half-square at the northeast corner of the outer row and extending to its midpoint: Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendra, Ravi, Satyaka, Bhṛśa...
Vyāma, Pāvaka, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Graha, Kṣata, Yama, Gandharva, Bhṛṅga, Dṛk, Mṛga, Pitṛ, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Jalādhipa, Asura,
Śoṣa, Roga, Vāyu, Nāgamukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, Ṛk, Aditi, and Diti.
Thus, one should invoke Āpa in the northeast square outside the four central squares; Āpavatsa in that same northeast square;
Marīci in the six squares within the two rows located in the east; Savitṛ in the southeast square;
Sāvitra in the corner square inside that; and Vivasvat in the six squares within the two rows located in the south.
In the northwest, one should worship [the deity] at the end of that; in the two corner squares, Indra and Indrajaya; in the west, as before;
in the northwest corner square situated in the six squares, Mitra; in the north, as before; in the two corner squares at the end of that, Rudra and Rudradāsaka;
and in the center of the four squares, Brahmā—having worshipped these with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Or, having offered an oblation (*bali*) with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, curd, and unbroken rice grains while walking outside the site in the directions starting from the northeast (*īśāna*),

one should worship and offer oblations to Skanda, Vidārī, Aryaman, Pūtanā, Jambhaka, the evil *rākṣasī*, and Pilipiñca. Then, having offered three oblations for each deity to ensure their presence and having concluded the rites, [one should proceed] at the auspicious moment (*lagne*).
Taking a stone slab and water-pots, one should go to the temple and, having placed the *ādhāraśakti* in the central pit, install the one named Ananta along with a water-pot, reciting:
*oṃ lauṃ anantāya namaḥ*. Having installed the ocean-pot (*samudrakumbha*) or other vessels with their respective mantras, [one proceeds] up to the *vidyā*.

Having meditated upon [the site] as pervaded by his own feet, and having uttered "oṃ hāṃ śivāya svāhā" or ending with "namaḥ," he should place the previously mentioned earth or stone— with its head toward the northeast— by means of the root mantra in the eight directions beginning with the east.

Having placed the *ādhāra-śakti* within the hollows situated in the middle of the walls, one should install the auspicious jars (*kumbha*) and so forth with the syllables *lūṃ rūṃ śūṃ ṣūṃ sūṃ yūṃ śrūṃ hūṃ*,

and by means of the aforementioned names of Indra and the other [directional deities]. Then, one should sequentially place the slabs (*śilā*) beginning with Nandā, [consecrated] with Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, and Bhava.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantras of Maheśvara, Mahādeva, and Bhīma, and having performed the placement by way of presiding over *dharma*, *jñāna*, *vairāgya*, and *aiśvarya*, one should restrain [the breath]. In the five-fold system, in the cavities of the fire-altar and so forth, one should place the lotuses and other vessels; in each of those [locations], [one should place them].

Having installed other stones with the mantras of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, and having installed them as the presiding deities of virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and having worshipped them,
one should address the stone: "May you remain in this temple for as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist, fulfilling the desires of the mind."
O Vows, may you always bring about the accomplishment of all goals—either individually or collectively.
Oṃ! You are the fullness, O Great Knowledge, characterized by the gathering of all things;
O daughter of Aṅgiras, make everything here completely fulfilled. Oṃ. (6th line)
O Nandinī, I establish you here in this palace for the delight of men, remaining exceedingly joyful as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
"Grant long life and prosperity, or [grant] it to those who possess bodies;
you must always provide protection for this palace with great effort."
Oṃ Bhadre! Always bring auspiciousness to the worlds;
O Goddess, grant desires and always be the bestower of prosperity. Oṃ Jayā! O Goddess, you have been installed here by me with constant devotion.
O Bhārgavī, always be for the victory and prosperity of your master!
Oṃ, O you who are empty, O destroyer of faults, O bestower of accomplishment and liberation,
O auspicious one, O you who abide in all places at all times, I am established in you, O you whose form is Hrīṃ!
Having meditated upon the palace in the sky, having placed therein the three principles together with the Lord, and having contemplated the pervasive Śiva.

Having paid obeisance and gone to the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa), one should perform the expiation and then dismiss the sacrifice. Thus ends the procedure for the laying of the foundation stone (śilānyāsavidhi).
Now follows the ritual procedure for the installation of the Śiva-liṅga.
When a specific proximity is indeed brought about for the pervasive [deity] through meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) and mantras within a physical form,
that is designated as "consecration" (pratiṣṭhā).
One who knows the method of Śiva-yoga and contemplates the yoga of the equinox (viṣu),
being one who undertakes nothing among all undertakings, should contemplate the nature of Nāda.
Now, the procedure for the installation of the Śiva-liṅga:
having prepared a ground in front of the temple measuring that same size—[specifically] three, eight, nine, or ten cubits for the smallest liṅgas;
and for others, starting from four cubits, increasing by two cubits up to twelve cubits, or increasing by two cubits at a time.

In the case of the *liṅgas* such as the *pādavṛddha* and others, having constructed a pavilion from among these according to one's own capacity— using materials such as bamboo as available and in accordance with the prescribed measurements— and having divided that [area] into nine parts,
one should prepare an altar (*vedi*) eight finger-breadths high in the central portion, or for those measuring two cubits and upwards, increasing the height by two finger-breadths at each stage.
Having placed that interval between those [points],

one should construct five fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) in the eight directions starting from the east— specifically in the middle between the northeast (*īśāna*) and the north— or else one pit in the direction of Śiva (the north) or the east; or [if there is only one], it should be circular in the direction of Śiva or the east.

Having constructed a square pavilion, one should prepare a bathing pavilion to its east, north, or northeast, measuring half its size and provided with two altars and an auspicious throne; having adorned both of these with canopies, garlands of *darbha* grass, and other ornaments, one should install the arches (*toraṇas*) according to their prescribed characteristics in the directions starting from the east within the preliminary consecration pavilion (*adhivāsa-maṇḍapa*).
The banners— resembling Indra’s bow, black, smoke-colored,
moon-bright, white-hued, golden, and like crystal—
should be arranged starting from the east; and a spear is to be placed in the station of Brahmā.
The blue Ananta is in the southwest, or else Citra or Śitā is in the center.

Having thus placed these eight banners, [one should place] the pitchers for the gate-keepers of the archways, such as Praśānta and Śaśira; the vessels for Lokeśa, Vāstu, Lakṣmī, Gaṇeśa, Guru, Dharma, and the other Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara);
and the Śiva-pitcher and the *vardhanī*—all these being endowed with the proper characteristics and accompanied by their ritual threads.
Having offered streams consisting of cloth, purified gold, jewels, fruits, food, various grains, and the five products [of the cow] according to their respective places,

he should bring forth the collection of implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. Then, having performed his bath and daily rites, accompanied by two [assistants], the preceptor, and the image-protectors (*mūrtipāḥ*), he should proceed to the sacrificial hall.

Having gone there, performed the worship of the Sun, sipped water (ācamana), and performed the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa), one should prepare the general offering (sāmānyārghya). With that water, one should sprinkle the archways (toraṇas) starting from the east with the Astra-mantra and veil them with the Kavaca-mantra. [Then recite: "Obeisance to the Peaceful Archway in the East; obeisance to the Door of the Peaceful Kalā."
On the two branches to the left and right: to Nandin, to Mahākāla, to Praśānta, and to Śiśira. On the right:
to Bhūtitoraṇa, to Vidyākalādvāra, and on the two branches: to Bhṛṅgin, to Vināyaka, to Parjanya, and to Aśoka.
In the west: to the western archway;
to the door of the *nivṛtti* stage; to Vṛṣabha; to Skanda; to Bhūtasañjīvana; to Amṛta. In the north: to the northern archway;
to the door of the *pratiṣṭhā* stage; to Devī; to Caṇḍa; to Dhanada.

In the west, [he should say]: "O bestowers of prosperity! Having worshipped and offered *arghya* to the gatekeepers as if they were permanent residents, you must remain here with great devotion as the protectors of this sacrifice. Thus he should inform them.
In the case of the extensive ritual (*vistārapakṣa*), [the procedure is as follows].

Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the Astra-mantra, [one should worship] in the eastern arch-gate jar: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Peaceful Arch-gate*. Above: *Oṃ, obeisance to the Ṛgveda*; *Oṃ, obeisance to the Kṛta Yuga*. On the trident: *Oṃ, obeisance to Pūṣan*; *Oṃ, obeisance to Dhātṛ*.

Oṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ. [Offerings] at the base of the western branch and the two jars: Oṃ, salutation to Praśānta; Oṃ, salutation to Śiśira; Oṃ, salutation to Bhūloka; Oṃ, salutation to Bhuvarloka; Oṃ, salutation to Pratyuṣas; Oṃ, salutation to Prabhāsa; Oṃ, salutation to Soma; Oṃ, salutation to Bhauma. Again, at the door-jars: Oṃ Hāṃ.

Salutation to the door of the Śāntikalā. At the upper *udumbara* [post]: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. On the two branches to the right and left: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nandin; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla; Oṃ hāṃ... [fifth line].

Salutation to Yamunā. Oṃ Haḥ, salutation to the Guardian of the Weapon-Door. Oṃ, salutation to the *ka*-group. Oṃ, salutation to the *kha*-group. As the presiding deity: Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Īśvara, the Lord of Causes. As the presiding controller... (6th line).

Oṃ Heṃ, obeisance to the Face of Tatpuruṣa; on the southern arch-pot. Oṃ, obeisance to the Arch of the Earth. Above, Oṃ, obeisance to the Yajurveda. Oṃ, obeisance to the Tretā Age. On the trident, Oṃ, obeisance to Bhaga. Oṃ, obeisance to Parjanya. Oṃ, obeisance to Indra. On the two pots at the branches, Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Parjanya.

Oṃ, homage to Aśoka. Oṃ, homage to Svarloka. Oṃ, homage to Maharloka. (8th line) Oṃ, homage to Ajaghanya. Oṃ, homage to Jaghanya. Oṃ, homage to Budha. Oṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati. Again, at the door-pitcher: Oṃ Hāṃ, homage to the door of the Vidyā-kalā. At the upper udumbara (94b, 1st line).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī.
[On] the two branches and pots: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhṛṅgin. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahī. Oṃ hāṃ... (second line).

Salutation to Vināyaka. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Narmadā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Astra, the guardian of the door. Oṃ, salutation to the *ca*-group. Oṃ, salutation to the *ṭa*-group. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the Lord of Causes. Oṃ huṃ. (Third Line)
Salutation to Aghora-hṛdaya; on the western arch-pot: Oṃ, salutation to Bala-toraṇa. Above: Oṃ, salutation to Sāmaveda;
Oṃ, salutation to Dvāpara. On the trident: Oṃ, salutation to Aryaman; Oṃ, salutation to Mitra.

Oṃ, salutation to Tvaṣṭṛ. [At] the branch and the jar: Oṃ, salutation to Bhūtasañjīvana; Oṃ, salutation to Amṛta; Oṃ, salutation to Janaloka; Oṃ, salutation to Tapaloka; Oṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ; (fifth line) Oṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ; Oṃ, salutation to Bhārgava; Oṃ, salutation to Śanaiścara. Now, at the door and the jar: Oṃ Hāṃ.
Salutation to the door of the Nivṛttikalā. Above: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. On the two side-branches: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabha; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sindhu; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Skanda; Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Sarasvatī. Oṃ Haḥ, salutation to the Guardian of the Weapon-Door. Oṃ, salutation to the Ca-group. Oṃ, salutation to the Pa-group. Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the Lord of Causes. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the Sadyojāta form.

On the northern arch-pot: *oṃ ārogyatoraṇāya namaḥ*. Above: *atharvavedāya namaḥ*. *oṃ kaliyugāya namaḥ*. On the trident: *oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*, *oṃ savitre namaḥ*, *oṃ aṃśumate namaḥ*. On the two pots at the branches: *oṃ dhanadāya*.

Namaḥ! Oṃ, salutation to Śrīprada. Oṃ, salutation to Satyaloka. Oṃ, salutation to Dhruvaloka. Oṃ, salutation to Āvāhana. Oṃ, salutation to Vivāha. Oṃ, salutation to Ketu. Now, at the door-pitcher: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the door of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā.

Salutation! Above: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. On the two branches of the pitcher: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Devī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Payoṣṇī;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Caṇḍa; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Tāpī; Oṃ haḥ, salutation to the Weapon-Guardian of the Door.

Oṃ, salutation to the *yavarga* (the palatal class). Oṃ, salutation to the *śavarga* (the retroflex class). Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Causes. Oṃ Hiṃ, salutation to the secret [form] of Vāmadeva. Having thus worshipped and offered the *arghya*, inform them: "You must remain here with great attentiveness as the protectors of this sacrifice. Thus he instructs them.

In the banners of the eastern and other directions: Oṃ vajrāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ śāntyai hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ daṇḍāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ khaṭvāṅgāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ pāśāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ dhvajāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ gadāyai...
*Huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ*. *Oṃ triśūlāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ*, in the northeast (*īśāna*). *Oṃ padmāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ*, in the southwest (*nairṛta*). *Oṃ cakrāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ*, on the central banner.
Having worshipped the Aghora-weapon, [one should worship] upon the banners in the east and other directions.

Oṃ kauṃ, homage to Kumuda. Oṃ kauṃ, homage to Kumudākṣa. Oṃ pauṃ, homage to Puṇḍarīka. Oṃ vauṃ, homage to Vāmana. Oṃ śauṃ, homage to Śaṅkukarṇa. Oṃ sauṃ, homage to Sarvanetra. Oṃ sauṃ, homage to Sumukha. Oṃ sauṃ.

"Salutation to Supratiṣṭha. Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] in the directions starting from the east: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Hetuka; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Tripuraghna; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vahni; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Yamajihva;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kāla; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kālīna; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ekāṅghri; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhīma."
Homage!
All the field-protectors (*kṣetrapāla*) should be known as having fangs that are terrifying and possessing large bellies;
they are proclaimed to be headed by Hetuka and others, and are equipped with gongs and skull-topped staffs (*khaṭvāṅga*).

Having meditated thus, having worshipped the *kṣetrapālas*, and having visualized them as satisfied, [one should place offerings] in vessels made of bell-metal and the like situated above the pavilion: in a vessel of bell-metal, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Earth Principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sadyojāta form. In the grasses, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Water Principle (*ap-tattva*)."

Namaḥ | Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to the secret of Vāmadeva. In the bands (–): Oṃ hāṃ (5th line), salutation to the principle of fire (tejaḥ-tattva). Oṃ huṃ, salutation to the heart of Aghora. In the bamboo-staves (–): Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of air (vāyu-tattva).
Oṃ heṃ, salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa.
On the pillars: *oṃ hāṃ ākāśatattvāya namaḥ* | *oṃ hoṃ īśānamūrdhāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped, one should visualize the pavilion as pervading up to the level of the Sadāśiva-tattva;
then, looking with the vision of the Tattvas and closing the remaining doors, [one should worship] the door-keepers as usual.
Having worshipped at the western gate and dispelled the obstacles situated in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on the earth, and having worshipped the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) upon the threshold,
one should enter; then, proceeding by way of circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), one should worship the Lord of the Site (*vāstunātha*) in the southwest, to the south of the altar.

Sitting facing north, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*), the purification of the special *arghya* substances and mantras, and the preparation of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) as before, one should perform self-worship (*svātmapūjā*). Then, one should [place] *oṃ hūṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ* on one’s own forehead, throat, and the region of the feet. *Oṃ*...
Hāṃ, salutation to Rudra; Oṃ Hīṃ, salutation to the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva); Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the self (ātma-tattva);
Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), [one should proceed].

Having deposited the auspicious *sāsana*—which possesses the limbs of Brahmā—by means of its pervasion of the *tattvas*, and having placed the *śivahasta* upon it; having adorned oneself with the *samūrtika* [form] using a sacred thread, garments, a crown, and so forth;
having contemplated "I am Śiva"; and having taken up the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) and consecrated the scattered offerings (*vikira*), one stands in the southwest (*naiṛta*).

Having consecrated [the site] with the fourfold purificatory rites beginning with inspection and ending with the path-cleansing, having scattered the *vikira* offerings, having gathered them together with a bundle of *kuśa* grass,
and having laid down the cloth for the placement [of the deities], one should worship Vāstupati; then, at the western door, one should worship Lakṣmī as before.

Then, having worshipped the Śiva-kumbha, the Astra-vardhanī, and the movable seat, one should meditate upon the world-protectors beginning with Indra and ending with Viṣṇu, together with their vehicles and weapons, in the directions starting from the east.

Having worshipped him, one should address each [deity] individually, saying: "O Śakra, by your own command, you must remain in your respective quarter with vigilance until the end of the sacrifice for the sake of pacifying obstacles—so be it by the command of Śiva. Then, one should station Dharma and the others in the corners of the altar, or in the cardinal directions; and once again, one should proclaim the command of Śiva.

Recalling the *vardhanī*— which flows from the tip of the *kumbha* in an unbroken stream— as being the fortress of weapons (*astradurga*), one should first rotate it with the root mantra, then place the *kumbha* and subsequently the *vardhanī*,
and having established them on stable seats, worship both the *kumbha* and the *vardhanī*.

Having performed the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, and having made this petition: "O Lord of the World, protect [us] through compassion for your devotees," and having offered the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), accomplished the *nirodhārghya* offering, and presented it;
then, having cleared away all remaining obstacles from every side with the weapons arising from the *vardhanī*, the seat, and the scattering [of grain], [he worships] Gaṇeśa and the Guru.

Having performed worship [of the deities] and having worshipped Śiva in the mandala, or on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or in the pitcher (kumbha) situated in the northeast of the altar, one should go near the fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, by the command of the Guru, the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should each approach their respective pit and perform the consecration of the pit (kuṇḍasaṃskṛti).
The Guru, having approached the sacrificial pit in the northeast direction and placing the navel of the pit before him, should sit down facing either the east or the north.
There, he should gaze at the pit with his eyes fixed on the root mantra placed [there] by his ring finger and thumb, while reciting the Śiva-mantra.

Having performed the sprinkling with *kuśa* grass while reciting the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having carried out the digging, scattering, filling, leveling, moistening, pounding, sweeping, and smearing with the *khaṭvāṅga* while reciting the *kavaca-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*; [one should mark] in the center, east, south, north, and west of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having performed the nyāsa of the mantras of the Kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā, having visualized [the pit] as consisting of the Kalās, and having encircled it with the three-stranded cord and the arghya water, one should worship it with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the pit consisting of the Kalās. Then, using three blades of kuśa grass in the form of a trident at both ends, one should draw four lines—one extending eastward and one extending northward—together with a transverse line.
The vajrīkaraṇa [ritual] consists of laying down two *kuśa* grasses with their tips pointing east and north to form a crossroads using the *astra-mantra*.

Having constructed a protective screen (*akṣapāṭa*) all around with *kuśa* grasses standing upright using the *kavaca-mantra*, one should place a seat (*viṣṭara*) in the center in the form of a tuft of grass, saying:
"Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara. Then, upon that [seat]...
One should invoke the Goddess Vidyā, the Mother of the Universe, according to the prescribed rite;
having meditated upon the Mother as the Intellect, adorned with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon her who has a serene face and three eyes resembling lotus petals, one should worship Vāgīśvarī with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī," and likewise [worship] Vāgīśvara.

And: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvara*. Having thus worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should bring fire from a fire-drill, a sun-crystal, a Brahmin’s house, or one’s own house, and place it in an earthen or copper vessel in the south-east, north-east, or south-west. Then, having set aside a portion of the fire for the carnivorous spirits in the south-west, [one should purify the fire] by means of the four rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*).

Having purified it with the *saṃskāras*, one should take up the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of fire" (*vahnimūrtaye namaḥ*); then, having joined it with the heart-fire (*hṛdayāgni*) during retention (*kumbhaka*), and with the fire of the navel (*nābhyagni*) and the fire of the *bindu*, one should exhale (*recaka*).

Having extracted [the fire] with "Oṃ Hrūṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire," and having thus deposited it into the fire situated in the vessel, one should worship it with the *saṃhitā*, protect it, and veil it. Then, with the *Prāsāda* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should render it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*. Having taken [it] and whirled it three times clockwise above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should meditate upon it as the seed-syllable of Śiva.

(7th line) Meditating on the parents with their heads turned toward the eastern and western directions, and visualizing [the embryo] being cast by Vāgīśvara into the *garbhanāḍī* of Vāgīśvarī, one should place the knee upon the ground.
One should cast [the seed-syllable] facing oneself with the *mūla-mantra*.

Having gathered it at the region of the navel and visualized the covering of the lower garment, one should offer a drop of water for the purpose of purification and sipping with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, cover it with dense armor with the *kavaca-mantra*, and kindle it with the *astra-mantra*: "Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the fire of the womb."
