Having thus worshipped the fire of the womb, and having tied a bunch of *darbha* grass— over which mantras for the protection of the embryo have been recited— into the hand of the Goddess;
and having worshipped [the fire] with the *sadyojāta* mantra for the sake of conception (*garbhādhāna*), one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the *hṛdaya* mantra.

In the third month, for the sake of obtaining a male child, having worshipped with the *vāmadeva* mantra, one should offer three oblations with the head-mantra (*śiras*), sprinkle drops of water, and then,
for the purpose of the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) in the sixth month, having worshipped with the *aghora* mantra, one should offer three oblations with the crest-mantra (*śikhā*).
Having performed the formation of the faces and limbs as well as the expiation (*niṣkṛti*) using that same crest-mantra, [one performs the rite] in the tenth month for the sake of birth.
Having worshipped with the *puruṣasūkta* and offered three oblations with the *kavaca*, when the fetus has been born, for the purpose of bathing to remove the impurities of birth,

one should kindle the fire with the tips of *darbha* grass; then, having removed the *darbha* bracelet from the hand of the Goddess and meditating that the golden binding was performed by the Goddess, one should worship it immediately with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

To remove the impurity (*sūtaka*), one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra, strike it with a blade of *darbha* grass empowered by the *astra* mantra, and sprinkle it with water empowered by the *kavaca* mantra. Then, for the protection of the fire, one should spread *darbha* grass from east to west upon the eastern girdles (*mekhalā*) with their tips pointing northeast, using the *astra* mantra; having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the seat-grass (*viṣṭara*) upon them, [one proceeds] to the [offerings for] the faces.
For the removal of saliva and for the nourishment of the fire, one should offer five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) smeared with ghee into the fire from the root and the tip using a sword.
Then, in the eastern, western, southern, and northern directions, [one should offer oblations with]: *Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; *Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*; *Oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ*...
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara. Having thus worshipped those situated at the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one worships on the seats in the directions beginning with Indra: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra";
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni"; "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yama"; "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti"; "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa."
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā.

In the northeast: *Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped [the deities] in the southwest and offered them water for honor (*arghya*), one should ward off the host of obstacles and proclaim the command of Śiva: "Protect the child! (4th line). Then, having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles along with *kuśa* grass, with their bases upward and their mouths downward, one should sprinkle them with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
Having sprinkled [the water] with the *kavaca* mantra, having concealed it, having heated it over the fire, and having whirled it around while touching its tip with the tip of a *kuśa* blade;
then, having whirled it again and touched its middle with the middle [of the blade], and having whirled it once more and touched its root with the root [of the blade],
[one should touch] those parts of the two [blades] where they were touched by the *kuśa*.

Having sequentially assigned the three principles known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, together with their presiding deities named Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, using the syllables *oṃ*, *hūṃ*, *hīṃ*, *hāṃ*, and *śaṃ* along with their respective powers (*balaiḥ*), one should place the Sūcī-Śakti in the *sruva* ladle and Śambhu with the *varman* mantra.
Then, having wrapped it three times with thread, one should establish it upon *kuśa* grass on the left side of oneself by means of the root mantra.

One should worship with the *hṛdaya* mantra. Then, having brought the products of the cow (*gavya*) and purified them through the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, one should contemplate one’s own body as consisting of Brahman. First, having heated [the ladle] three times over the fire located above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and taking a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *darbha* blade, one should offer it with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*. Then, [one should contemplate it] as consisting of Viṣṇu.

In the activity of one's own body, having placed [the vessel] upon the northeast fire and having offered an oblation with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting "Oṃ Hīṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu," one should thereafter regard one's own form as consisting of Rudra; holding it at the navel and reciting "Oṃ Hāṃ,
svāhā to Rudra," one should offer a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, thus concluding the rite.
Taking with the thumb and ring finger a *pavitraka*— a strainer made from two tips of *darbha* grass, a span in length, and tied with a knot in the middle—

one should sprinkle the clarified butter (*ājya*) three times toward the fire while reciting the *astra-mantra*. Likewise, one should perform the sprinkling toward oneself while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Having tied that sacred thread (*pavitra-granthi*), one should untie it, cast it into the fire, and then, having consecrated with the *hṛdaya-mantra* a burning tuft of *darbha* grass, cast it into clarified butter while reciting the *astra-mantra*; having thus purified it, one should also cast that into the fire with the *astra-mantra*. (Line 5) Having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) over the fire with another blazing *darbha* blade while reciting the *kavaca-mantra*, and having kindled it further with another blazing blade while reciting the *astra-mantra*...

That too one should cast into the fire [like] a torch. Then, having placed two *kuśa* blades with a knot in their middle, measuring a span (*prādeśa*), into the midst of the clarified butter with the syllable *praṇava*, one should [visualize] the two fortnights— the bright and the dark— in the order of right and left,
and the three channels (*nāḍī*) beginning with *piṅgalā*, *iḍā*, and *suṣumnā* in the right, left, and middle parts.
Having made the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), taking clarified butter (*ājya*) from the left side with the *sruva* spoon, [he offers] "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā" into the right eye of the fire.
Taking clarified butter from the left side, [he offers] "Oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā" into the left eye of the fire.
Taking [clarified butter] from the center, [he offers] "Oṃ hāṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā" into the middle eye of the fire. [He offers] "Oṃ hāṃ agne sviṣṭakṛte... [into the mouth].

Saying "svāhā" into the mouth of Agni, having offered a small portion with the mantra "paśu," one should cast the remaining clarified butter into those respective portions of the Ājyabhāgas with the word "heti. In the bright fortnight, [the mantras are as follows]; however, in the dark fortnight: *oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ somāgnibhyāṃ svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ agnaye*...

Having offered oblations of clarified butter as before into the left, right, and middle eyes of the Fire-god, and into his mouth with the mantra "Sviṣṭakṛte svāhā," one should consecrate it with the *saṃhitā*, protect it, conceal it, transform it into nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā*, and worship it.

Then, by sprinkling drops of clarified butter while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should perform the purification of the remaining clarified butter. Following that, [one should offer]: "Oṃ hāṃ sadyojātāya svāhā" and "Oṃ hiṃ."

"Vāmadevāya svāhā, oṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā, oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā, oṃ hoṃ īśānāya svāhā"—with these offerings of clarified butter, one by one, [he performs] the āghāra oblation for the faces of the fire. "oṃ haṃ hiṃ... (the sixth line).
Svāhā to Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva; Oṃ Hiṃ Huṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva and Aghora; Oṃ Huṃ Heṃ, svāhā to Aghora and Tatpuruṣa; Oṃ Heṃ Hoṃ. (7th line)

One should perform the joining of the faces with the mantra "tatpuruṣeśānābhyāṃ svāhā. Then, one should effect the unification of the faces by means of an oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛtāhuti*)—which has moved from the fire to the northwest and then to the southwest—from the northeast, using the mantra: "oṃ haṃ hiṃ huṃ heṃ hoṃ sadyojātavāmadevāghoratatpuruṣeśānebhyaḥ svāhā. Thereafter...

For the purpose of naming [the fire], having worshipped with the *Īśa* mantra and offered three oblations with the *Astra* mantra, one should give the fire its name, saying "Oṃ Hāṃ, you are Śivāgni, the consumer of oblations. Then, having worshipped Vāgīśa and Vāgīśī with the *Hṛdaya* mantra and dismissed them, one should determine the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as desired and assign the faces [of the fire]; furthermore, for the sake of completing the purificatory rites up to the topknot (*cūḍānta-saṃskāra*) on the tongue—

(Third line) One should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, having divided the fire into nine or five parts, and having placed the fires situated in their respective directions into the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) located in those same directions, [one prepares] for the sake of the sacrificial pap (*caru*) and clarified butter (*ājya*). (Fourth line)

Having removed [the oblation] from the hearth and preserved it, one should kindle the central portion, perform the fuel-offering (*idhmahoma*), and having entered the fire, worship the Blessed One and perform the central libation (*madhyatarpaṇa*). Having worshipped Śiva in the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and the vessel (*sruc*) within the fire—surrounded by the limbs [of the rite] according to the mantras of their respective directions—and having performed the mantra-libation, they should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, [the ritual of] bestowing the region...
For the purpose of pacifying ill omens and bringing about auspicious signs at the time of the ritual application,

one should offer a hundred oblations for each [deity], prepare the sacrificial pap as before, and present it into each fire-pit. Then, having consecrated the peace-vases (*śāntikumbha*) one hundred times with the *astra-mantra* and performed the *sampāta*-oblation, [one proceeds] to the bathing pavilion.
They should proceed. At the time of the ritual bath, the initiated ones should recite the *saṃhitā-mantra* within the consecrated pavilion (*adhivāsa-maṇḍapa*) in all directions.
Uninitiated twice-born men (*dvija*) should recite the *śānti* outside. In that regard, the follower of the *Ṛgveda*—(8th line).

In the eastern quarter... it is said that one who brings evil should mutter the Maitraka, the Vṛṣākapi, the Devavrata, the Bhāruṇḍa, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Rathantara, and the Puruṣāgati; [this applies to] the Sāmavedin in the south.
In the Śrīkāmika [Tantra], that which has arisen by itself is declared to be the *svāyambhuva* (self-manifested) linga;
that which has been consecrated by Śiva is declared to be the *bāṇaliṅga*.

There is no fixed location or measurement for the *liṅgas* of Svāyambhuva and the others. However, regarding this location, the portion belonging to Brahmā and the portion belonging to Viṣṇu [are situated] above, while the portion belonging to Rudra is [situated] within the *aḍayāl* (the central cavity).
Thus, from [the base], the portion of Brahmā and the portion of Viṣṇu constitute the sacrificial offering (*pūjāmśa*) above, and the portion of Rudra [is below].
(With pride. From one cubit as the minimum, up to nine cubits is the height for wearing [the liṅga]).
(Because the Kriyāliṅga-pramāṇa applies, whereas for the Swayambhū-liṅga, the authority is the Śoṇikuṇḍārśama-puṣpa-pramāṇa).
(Therefore, it is nine cubits high—4th line).

(The Dīniyoliṅgavacana. Beginning from one cubit and increasing by one part at a time, up to the measure of nine cubits, the measurement of the liṅga is declared. (This is the statement regarding the measurement of the liṅga.)
Now, according to the words of the Bhagavat in the *Suprabheda*:
"The lower part should be square, and that which is in the middle should be octagonal."
Above that, the circular portion should likewise be divided into three equal parts.
(The sixth line:
[The end-point is a four-sided square; the left portion and the Viṣṇu-portion above are... the golden part.
(As for the Kriyāliṅga: creating the portion for Rudra in the correct measure (7th line);
in that very same [text].
In the twenty-four-fold [mandala], the square is seven parts;
the eight-sided is eight parts, while the circle is indeed nine parts.

This present linga is for Śiva; beyond that [is what] is considered [the next]. (153b) [This refers to the aforementioned *vaktaliṅga*, which is one full *mūrti* [measure], etc., up to the measure of a *mūla*.
From the measurement [of the body] that has been stated... [up to] seven, eight, and nine. (2nd line)
(The portion [of the altar] is the portion of Rudra;
one must construct it as a square, an octagon, and a circle. Elsewhere, there is another alternative: having divided the length into ten parts, [one should take] a square from three parts.
The octagon is formed by one-third [of the diameter], and the circle by four parts.
Thus,
the greatness of that Liṅga-vacana is indeed greater than Śiva’s in that very place.
The *liṅga* bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). (Thus ends the previous section on the *Amaramaṇi-haṅkāma-śāsana*).
Regarding the measurement of the *liṅga*, there are nine types; among them, those consisting of three or four [units] are of two kinds.
The *svastika-liṅga* is described in many ways. (5th line)
(The primordial *satyajātādi-mukhodaya-liṅga* which is the enjoyment for [the period of] nine thousand [years], etc., is the *svastika-liṅga*.
[Sixth line]) (The ninth, tenth, and eleventh: *samaliṅga*, *vardhamānaliṅga*, and *śivādhikyaliṅga* (nine thousand).
Whether it be one established by yourself as a self-manifested *liṅga*,
or one installed by the great [sages], or even one established by the gods— there is no form that does not exist within you; may you be pleased with this divine form.

The Yajurvedin should recite the Śrīrudra, the Puruṣasūkta, the Ślokādhyāya, and the Brahmāṇa in the west; the Atharvavedin should recite the Nīlarudra, the Sūktastava, and the Atharvaśiras in the north. Then, the ritual bathing takes place in the pavilion, which consists of nine compartments.

Having placed the Śiva-tattva in the center, the Sadāśiva-tattva in the east, the Īśvara-tattva in the southeast, the Vidyā-tattva in the south, the Māyā-tattva in the southwest, the Kāla-tattva in the west, the Niyati-tattva in the northwest, the Puruṣa-tattva in the north, and the Prakṛti-tattva in the northeast.
Milk in the center, curd in the east, clarified butter in the south, cow-dung in the west, and cow-urine in the north;
with attendants bringing the materials for the under-layer and the collection of offerings—incense, honey, and garments—in the southeast (4th line);
the lustration rite (nīrājana) in the northwest; the collection of astringents in the southwest; saffron in the northwest; and [in the northeast]—thus, the group of implements in the compartment.

Having arranged jars containing milk, *āmalaka* fruit, perfumes, gems, fruits, flowers, and grain— designated as the "oceans"— and having sprinkled them with the Astra-mantra and veiled them with the Kavaca-mantra, one should worship them with their respective names; elsewhere, one should place the oceans of salt water and so forth.
Having visualized other jars as well, having placed them outside, having consecrated them with the Astra-mantra and protected them by enveloping them with the Kavaca-mantra,

and having honored them together with the presiding deities (*mūrtipas*), one should install the *liṅga* upon a throne (*bhadrapīṭha*) marked with a lotus on the eastern altar, which is provided with a seat of the Praṇava; then, having struck it with the Astra-mantra and enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, one should firmly establish it.

Having performed worship with water, the group of decoctions, cow’s urine, another portion of water, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), cow dung interspersed with water, ash, and scented water;
having performed the purification of the site with the *huṃ phaṭ*-ending weapon-mantra (*astra*) and the letter *āḥ*; and having performed the general worship with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Having covered the pedestal, the *brahmaśilā*, and the bull with a cloth that has been sprinkled with water over which the *varma* mantra has been recited, and having bathed [the deity] in this manner, one should bring the *liṅga* to the northern altar (*uttaravedikā*). There,
having provided a bed and a seat with the *praṇava* and having settled it, [one should proceed] with the thread for the *kūlālipta*.
Having divided [the area] according to the path taught in the scriptures, the Guru should draw the characteristics with a golden stylus using the Aghora mantra. It is as follows:
(—) When the portion of Rudra has been divided into three parts following the Brahma-line, one should extend the mark (—) through the two lower sections down to the water-receptacle. (4th line)
In the length of the *liṅga*, which consists of nine parts, the width of the *lakṣma* (the central mark) is one part;
the earth is lower than that, and its line is one-ninth of that width.
From the half-measure of the *lakṣma*, two eyelash-lines (*pakṣmarekhā*) are formed; that field is divided into eight parts.
By means of the sequence of six, seven, and [eight] units on the back, their conjunction is produced through subtraction.
The opening of the eyes is the characteristic of the manifest and the unmanifest;
in the center of the aperture, it has the shape of a vulva, is triangular, and rests upon the seat of the mark.
One should fashion its secret part, characterized by secrecy, like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, resembling a bee at its base through its division;
[it should be] like the moon in the pedestal-base, with a width half that of the channel.
Two *yūkās* and five *likṣās* shall be the distance between two lines.
The state of being a *rekhāpuri* consists of two [units] plus one-quarter; likewise, there are two *likṣās* for the hair of the head.
One should increase each by one *yūkā* and one *likṣā* in the case of the *dvikṣā* and subsequent measures.
"One should not scratch the characteristic marks on the eye-ball; rather, one should scratch them there," so says the Bhārgava [Tantra].
Then the ophthalmic surgeon (*śippī*), using a sharp instrument, should scratch [the cornea].
Having filled the eyelid fissure with ghee and honey while reciting the *Mṛtyujit* mantra, he should give the vessel, probe, and other tools to the artisan.

Having seated her again on the seat and shown her a cow with its calf, eight or four women who are not widows and have sons, touching her with northward-pointed sprouts and applying auspicious *gorocanā* to her limbs, should perform the rites such as the lustration (*nīrājanā*) with turmeric.
One should dismiss them by giving gifts of molasses, salt, grain, turmeric, and so forth; immediately thereafter,
having struck them with the Astra-mantra, veiled them with the Varma-mantra, and worshipped them with either the Hṛdaya-mantra or the Praṇava, one should [perform the rite] preceded by the Liṅga.

One should commence the special ablution (*viśeṣasnāna*). In the meantime, having gone to a reservoir of water accompanied by the *liṅga*, and having performed the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and placed [the deity] in the water for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), some say that one should bring it from there to the bathing pavilion and perform the special ablution. In that regard, [one should use] earth, cow dung, cow urine, ashes, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and decoctions (*kaṣāya*).

Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and other waters, and having dried it with powders of *bilva*, wheat, and so forth, one should perform the ritual with water containing all medicinal herbs, with the juices of flowers and fruits, with water from golden and jeweled vessels, with water from the horns of a cow, with a thousand streams, with water from divine medicinal plants,
with water from holy fords such as the Gaṅgā, with scented water, and with jars from the salt ocean and other sources.
Having bathed [the deity] with water from the Śiva-pitcher and dried [him] with a clean cloth, having anointed [him] with fragrant sandalwood and other unguents,
having dressed [him] in two red garments, having worshipped [him] with the Brahma-mantras, and having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) with the *bahurūpa* mantra; then,

having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with the *hṛdaya*-mantra, having applied a protective mark (*rakṣā-tilaka*) with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and having raised [the deity] onto the chariot with the *hṛdaya*-mantra.
Having placed [the image] upon it and made it well-secured, accompanied by songs, instrumental music, dancing, and auspicious sounds such as the chanting of the *Brahma-ghoṣa*,

one should scatter parched grain, flowers, gold, and other offerings in a place consecrated by the Preceptor (*ācārya*). Then, with the patron (*yajamāna*) at the head, followed by artisans and others along the path of the chariot, one should enter the city, the town, the palace, or the pavilion.

Having circumambulated [the deity] together, having brought [him] to the western door of the sacrificial hall, and having offered an eight-limbed *arghya* with the heart-mantra accompanied by *vaṣaṭ* and *svāhā*, having caused [him] to descend from the chariot, having established [him] on the heart-seat,
and having worshipped [him].

When the rite for auspiciousness (*svastyayana*) has been performed, having caused [the image] to enter, [one should place it] upon a pedestal (*vedikā*) surrounded by a heap of rice; having spread *kuśa* grass and formed a *svastika*, one should arrange a couch or a wooden plank,

and having placed a small box covered with a pair of soft cloths, one should [place the deity] there with the *praṇava* upon the head, on the seat consisting of the elements beginning with earth and ending with *Śakti*.

In the western-facing temple, having placed the *liṅga* slightly to the east of the center of the altar, resting toward the northeast, with its head facing east, one should provide a pillow made of the *śikhā*, cover it with a garment consecrated by the recitation of the *varma* mantra, and [place it] upon a bed at the base of the *liṅga*.

One should install the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*), and the bull (*vṛṣa*). Alternatively, one should install the Brahma-stone at the base of the *liṅga*, the pedestal to its north, and the bull to the north of that. However, in a temple facing south (*pūṣāsya*), one should install them in reverse order.
One should cover the pedestal and the other items with red cloths. Then...

Having first sprinkled the water from the *śāntighaṭa* upon the *liṅga*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the forms beginning with Īśāna and ending with Brahmā upon the head and other parts [of the deity].

Then, having worshipped with flowers, incense, and so forth using the root mantra, and having prepared the food offering (*naivedya*) and other items, one should place at the feet of the deity the umbrella, chowries, sandals, the throne, household utensils, and whatever has fallen from the house and so forth. Therein—

Having established honey and ghee contained in a vessel intended for massaging the feet with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra near the head—[placing] the Śiva-pitcher [therein]—and having placed the sleep-pitcher obtained through the hundred-fold recitation of the Astra-mantra upon the seat of the Praṇava, [one should offer] into the pitchers in the directions starting from the east:
*oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ sūkṣmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ*... (fifth line).
Hāṃ, obeisance to Śivottama. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ekanetra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ekarudra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Trimūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śikhaṇḍin. (Sixth line)

Having thus worshipped and stood at the base of the *liṅga*, she should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-six auspicious principles (*tattva*) upon the *liṅga*, from the top of the head down to its base.
As follows, in the portion belonging to Rudra: *oṃ hāṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ*... [seventh line].

Salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Power (śaktitattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śaktimān, the lord of the principle of Power. In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Sadāśiva. Oṃ... (102b, first line)

Salutation to Brahmā, the presiding lord of the principle of Sadāśiva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Īśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ananta, the presiding lord of the principle of Īśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Śuddhavidyā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śambara, the presiding lord of the principle of Śuddhavidyā.
In the Brahmabhāga: (–) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Māyātattva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gahaneśa, the lord of the Māyātattva.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Kālatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kāla by name, the lord of the Kālatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Kalātattva. Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to the Lord of the principle of *kalā*, the drop of knowledge (*jñānabindu*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of necessity (*niyati-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the principle of necessity, the regulator (*niyāmaka*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*).

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the principle of knowledge, the specialized awareness of the Vedas (*veda-vijñāna*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ... (fifth line)
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the principle of *rāga* (attachment), the bestower of desires. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of *puruṣa* (the individual soul).

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), the Lord of the principle of *puruṣa*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of *prakṛti* (primordial nature). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the Lord of the principle of *prakṛti*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the *guṇas* (qualities). Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to the Lord of the principle of *guṇa*, who possesses three bodies. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of *buddhi*.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Buddha, the lord of the principle of *buddhi*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of *ahaṅkāra*. Oṃ hāṃ...

Obeisance to Ahaṅkṛta, the lord of the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāra-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Saṃkalpa, the lord of the principle of mind. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of hearing (*śrotra-tattva*).
Obeisance to Vyomacara, the lord of the principle of hearing. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of touch (*tvak-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, [obeisance] to the lord of the principle of touch...
(Second line) Salutation to Sarvāṅga.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the eye (cakṣustattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Prakāśa, the lord of the principle of the eye. Oṃ hāṃ.

Oṃ, salutation to the principle of the tongue. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the principle of the tongue, Mahāvaktra. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the nose. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the principle of the nose, Vilambaka. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of speech. Oṃ, salutation to the lord of the principle of speech, Dundubhi. Oṃ hāṃ... (fourth line).

Homage to Pāṇitatva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Samādāna, the lord of Pāṇitatvatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pādatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ramaṇa, the lord of Pādatattvatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pāyutattva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Tiṣṇakṛt, the lord of Pāyutattvatattva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Upasthatattva.
Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ghanānanda, the lord of the principle of the generative organ (upastha-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of sound (śabda-tattva).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sūkṣmanāda, the lord of the principle of sound. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of touch (sparśa-tattva).
Salutation to Balavattara, the lord of the principle of touch.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhānumat, the lord of the element of form. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of taste. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jalada, the lord of the element of taste. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the element of smell. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gandhāṅga, the lord of the element of smell.

Salutation to the element of space (*vyoma-tattva*). Salutation to the subtle lord of the element of space. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of air (*vāyu-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mātariśvan, the presiding deity of the element of air. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of fire (*agni-tattva*). (Second line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the repository of radiance, the presiding deity of the element of fire. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the element of water (*jala-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to the Lord of the water element, the Master of Waters. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the earth element. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord of the earth element. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*), and having offered a flower garland and a protective thread (*pratisara*) that indicates the three divisions, one should arrange the three sections; then, in the portion of Rudra, [one should place] up to the Śiva-tattva: Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva.

*Namaḥ*. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu, up to the end of the principle of Sadāśiva: Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of Knowledge. In the portion belonging to Brahmā... (fifth line).
Up to the end of the *māyā-tattva*: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the *ātma-tattva*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the *ātma-tattva*.
Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), then, for each division in the sequence starting from the east and ending with the northeast (*īśāna*):
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sūkṣmāmūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śarva, the lord of Sūkṣmāmūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, rūṃ..."
Salutation to the form of Agni.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Paśupati, the presiding lord of the form of Agni. Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, salutation to the form of the sacrificer. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ugra, the presiding lord of the form of the sacrificer. Oṃ hāṃ...
ṢŪṂ, obeisance to the Sun-form. OṂ HĀṂ, obeisance to Rudra, the presiding lord of the Sun-form.

OṂ HĀṂ PUṂ, obeisance to the Water-form. OṂ HĀṂ, obeisance to Bhava, the presiding lord of the Water-form. OṂ HĀṂ YŪṂ VŪṂ, obeisance to the Wind-form. OṂ HĀṂ, obeisance to Īśāna, the presiding lord of the Wind-form.

Oṃ hāṃ sruṃ, obeisance to Indra-mūrti. Oṃ hā ya, obeisance to Mahādeva, the lord of Indra-mūrti. Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Kha-mūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhīma, the lord of Kha-mūrti. Thus one should install the forms and their presiding deities.

Alternatively, in the five-fold system, in the western, northern, southern, eastern, and northeastern directions: *oṃ hāṃ lūṃ pṛthivīmūrtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ pṛthivīmūrtyadhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ yūṃ jalamūrtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ*... [fourth line].

Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the water-form. Oṃ hāṃ rūṃ, salutation to the fire-form. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fire-form. Oṃ hāṃ yūṃ, salutation to the wind-form. Oṃ hāṃ... (5th line)

Salutation to Īśvara, the lord of the wind-form. Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, salutation to the ether-form. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva, the lord of the ether-form. Having thus performed the placement for each section, one should restrain [the breath]. For the seeker of liberation, there are the forms known as Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatītā.

The guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) are known as Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. Alternatively, one should everywhere install the three principles (tritatva) together with their presiding deities (sādhipam). For in this case—
Following the teacher’s instruction, one should slowly utter the mantra from the *kanda* and other centers;
it is subtle, consisting of the power of resonance (*nāda-śakti*), and spreading like the sound of a bell.
Through the yoga of abandoning the causes, it has emerged from the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*),
possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns and a radiance equal to the flash of lightning.
With its shimmering rays forming a canopy that illuminated the quarters of space,
it was mentally pierced by the mantra, resulting in the emergence of the essence of bliss.
Having brought down from the *dvādaśānta* the partless, all-pervading Śiva,
who is endowed with thirty-eight *kalās* and blazes like a thousand rays;

Having meditated upon the orb of radiant energy (*tejobimba*) situated on the forehead as consisting of all powers (*sarvaśaktimaya*), accompanied by its limbs (*sāṅga*), and resembling a row [of lights], one should make it the door and lead it forth.
Having visualized it as having emerged through the *suṣumnā* channel, shimmering like a moving star, one should bring it to the door.
One should place it, fixed at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), pervading the entire body.
In this manner, the *jīvannyāsa* performed upon the *liṅga* accomplishes all goals;
it effects the installation, the presence, the confinement, and the immobilization.

Having consecrated [the deity] with these— [offering] a mudrā, the vision, water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, and flowers— and having worshipped [it], one should cover [it] with a cloth and construct three outer enclosures using ashes, darbha grass, and sesame seeds. Starting from the portion of the navel on the pedestal, [one should worship] "Oṃ hāṃ, to the Śakti-tattva."

*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Śaktimant, the lord of the principle of Śakti (*śaktitattva*). Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the principles starting from this point as before, up to the earth (*pṛthivī*), and having placed the lords of those principles, one should give a garland and an amulet for the purpose of showing the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*). Then, on the left side: *Oṃ haṃ*, salutation to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*); *Oṃ hāṃ*, [salutation] to the mistress of the principle of Śiva.

*icchāyai* (7th line), *namaḥ*. From the end of the *śakti-tattva* up to the upper part of the neck of the pedestal: *oṃ hīṃ vidyā-tattvāya namaḥ*. *oṃ hāṃ vidyā-tattvādhipāyai jñānyai namaḥ*. From the base of the pedestal up to the end of the *sadāśiva-tattva*: (105a, 1st) [line].

At the upper part of the throat: *oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvādhipāyai kriyāyai namaḥ*. One should thus perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the Māyātattva. Alternatively, the three principles (*tritattva*) are located at the lower part of the throat, at the throat itself, and above it.
And one should place the three principles (*tritattva*). Then, for each division in the directions starting from the east: *oṃ hāṃ kṣmāmūrtaye namaḥ*;
*oṃ hāṃ kṣmāmūrtyadhipāyai dhārikāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ agnimūrtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ* (third line).

Salutation to Dīptimatī, the presiding deity of the form of Agni. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of the Sacrificer. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Cetanā, the presiding deity of the form of the Sacrificer. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Balotkaṭā, the presiding deity of the form of Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of the Arrow.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dhātrī, the presiding deity of the arrow-form. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the ether-form. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the presiding deity of the ether-form. Alternatively, according to the five-fold system: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the earth-form. Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to Pāmā, the presiding deity of the earth-form; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the water-form;
oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭhā, the presiding deity of the water-form; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the fire-form; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of the fire-form.

Salutation to Kriyā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāyumūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jñānī, the presiding deity of Vāyumūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ākāśamūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Icchā, the presiding deity of Ākāśamūrti. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) and restrained [the breath], Oṃ hrīṃ...

Salutation to Kriyāśakti. Or else: *Oṃ hrīṃ saṃ mahāgauri rudradayite svāhā*. *Oṃ hraḥ kriyāśaktaye namaḥ*. Having uttered this mantra, having invoked [the deity], established [her], and restrained [her], one should likewise perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the bull (*vṛṣabha*). *Oṃ*... (second line).
"Hrīṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabha. Having thus invoked [the deity], one should restrain [the breath]. In this same manner, one should also perform the placement upon the foundation stone (*ādhāraśilā*).

This is the placement of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Sadāśiva. Having performed the placement of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*)—from Śabda, Citta, and Sada-Īśāna—as prescribed for the pedestal (*pīṭha*), [one recites]: *Oṃ srūṃ* (third line).

"Salutation to Ādhāraśakti. Having invoked [the deity] with "hrīṃ" or "vā," one should restrain [the breath]. One should then construct three outer enclosures using these [materials]: ashes, darbha grass, and sesame seeds. Afterwards, having worshipped the world-protectors situated in their respective directions for the sake of protection, one should proceed toward the central sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). There, in the center of the pit, [one should worship] the Supreme Lord, and upon the girdles (*mekhalā*)...

Having placed the four kalās beginning with Nivṛtti at the navel, Kriyā at the [heart], Śānti at the lips, and Nāda [at the palate], one should perform the union of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) together with the lords of the forms (mūrtipas) and with Śiva residing in the jar, on the sacrificial ground, and in the fire.
The *ūrṇā* hair, resembling a thread, having emerged through the channel with joy,
enters again with non-joy, and having emerged once more, it does so with joy.
One should contemplate her entering [the fire] by means of the *ātman* itself, even without it being uttered.

(6th line) For the purpose of uniting that, having offered three oblations into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," and having worshipped [her], one should offer three oblations; then, having worshipped the *ātmatattva* and its Lord (*tadīśa*), one should offer three oblations. (7th line)

Having assigned the forms and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*), having worshipped each with three oblations (*āhuti*) to satisfy them, one should offer the primary mantras (*mūla*) and the limbs (*aṅga*) of Brahman—
one hundred, one thousand, or half that number— along with the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then,

having placed the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*) and the others in their respective fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the rite for the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipāḥ*), numbering either eight or four.

Having performed the installation and propitiation of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), having installed the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*) along with its presiding deity and offered an oblation, and having installed the respective forms and their guardians in the sequence starting from the east and offering three oblations to each, one should worship the mantras beginning with Tatpuruṣa.

In accordance with their wealth and the time available, the preceptors should offer one hundred, one thousand, or half that number of oblations, or a tenth part of the total performed, accompanied by the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, all of them, together with the preceptor and holding the *śānti-kumbha* (peace-vessel) in their hands, shall go near the *liṅga* and stand in their respective directions.
The Guru, having first sprinkled [the area] with water from the *śāntikumbha* while reciting the root mantra, should touch the *brahmabhāga* with the roots of *kuśa* grass,

perform the recitation (*japa*) the number of times equal to the *homa*, and then sprinkle it with the waters of the *śāntikumbha*. Thereafter, the Guru [should do the same] with his own heart-mantra.

Having performed the rite of *sannidhi* for them, having enveloped [the deity] with the armor (*varman*) and restrained [it], one should cause the Lord of Reality (*tattvādhipa*) to hear the command: "O Brahmā, Lord of the Self-reality (*ātmatattva*), as long as this *liṅga* is free from all defects, so long must you remain right here through your presence. Then, [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ*.
"Oṃ, salutations to the principles of the Self and the principles of Knowledge.
Thus, one should worship up to Māyā by means of the utterance ending in Nāda. "Oṃ Āṃ Āṃ Hāṃ Hāṃ, salutations to the form of Vāk-kṣmā.
In this manner, [one worships] with the forms of Fire and the others, both pure and impure.

One should join [the mantras]: *oṃ lūṃ lūṃ rūṃ rūṃ śuṃ ṣuṃ āṃ āṃ yūṃ yūṃ sūṃ sūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, or else *oṃ lūṃ lūṃ hāṃ hāṃ* to the form (*mūrti*) of Earth (*kṣmā*). In this manner, one should join [the mantras] with the forms of Fire and the other elements, both pure and impure. [This applies to] the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipās*) and the two principles (*tattvas*).
They should perform the reintegration (*sandhāna*) of their own forms.

Then, having gone to the vicinity of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and worshipped in this manner, they should offer oblations for the sake of reintegration. Having worshipped and invoked the presence of Viṣṇu—the Lord of the *vidyā-tattva*—and having worshipped the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*), [they should proceed].

Having offered three oblations for each [deity], one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* as before. In the same manner, the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipās*) should also offer oblations as before. Afterwards, having gone near the *liṅga*, preceded by the sprinkling of water from the *śānti-kumbha* as before, one should touch the portion belonging to Viṣṇu with the middle blade of *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra, and then perform the recitation (*japa*) according to the number of oblations offered.

Having sprinkled [the image] with water of pacification while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and having performed the rites of *sannidhi* (presence), *avakuṇṭhana* (concealment), and *nirodhana* (restriction), one should announce the command to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu,
Lord of the Principle of Knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*), until he is completely freed from all defects..."
"O Liṅga, you must remain right here through your presence.
Then, having worshipped with "Oṃ Hīṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to the Vidya-tattva and Śiva-tattva," one should join the western side of the images as before.

Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and likewise offered oblations into the fire while maintaining the same mental focus, one should worship and invoke the presence of the Śiva-tattva and its Lord Rudra.

Having done so, one should offer three oblations each to the elements beginning with Earth (*kṣmādi*) and the deities beginning with Śarva, as well as to the forms (*mūrti*) and the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipā*).

After satiating them with a hundred or more oblations using the *saṃhitā-mantra*, and having the guardians of the forms offer oblations as before, one should go near the *liṅga* with the water of peace (*śāntijala*).

Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the root mantra using the tip of a *kuśa* blade, having touched the portion belonging to Rudra, having recited [the mantra] as many times as the number of oblations,

having sprinkled it with the water of pacification (*śāntyambu*), having effected presence (*sannidhi*) with the heart mantra, having performed the encircling protection (*avakuṇṭhana*), and having restrained [him], one should cause Rudra to hear the command: "O..."

"O Rudra, O Lord of the Śiva-principle, as long as this faultless Linga remains here, O Master, you must remain here by the command of Śiva. Thus, even in the case of the Piṇḍī, the stone, and the Vṛṣa, the Lord [establishes] the Self, Knowledge, the Śiva-principle, and so forth— namely, those called Will, Knowledge, and Action.

Having worshipped the forms beginning with Kṣmā, the Mistress of the forms beginning with Dhārikā (or the forms of Earth and so forth, or the Mistresses of the forms beginning with Vāmā), in the fire, and having gratified them with three oblations, [one should offer]: *oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ vākīyā śaktaye namaḥ*. *Oṃ*... (fourth line).

"Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha; Oṃ Srūṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. Having thus offered one hundred oblations for each [deity], including the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), together with the presiding priests (*mūrtipās*), he should go near [the deity], sprinkle it with the water of peace (*śāntyambhas*), touch it with the roots, middles, and tips of *kuśa* grass as before, and recite the mantra as many times as the number of oblations offered.
Having performed the synthesis of the pure and impure forms of those two principles, having gone, offered oblations, recited [mantras], and synthesized, and having gone,
synthesized, gone, and returned, one should perform everything as before. Then, for the purpose of removing defects such as omissions and the like:

Having offered one hundred oblations each with the *śiva*, *aghora*, and *asit* mantras along with the *pūrṇāhuti*, having presented the *caru*, performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, given water for sipping (*ācamana*) and betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) and so forth, having restrained Śiva, offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations,
presented the internal offering (*antarbali*), performed the salutation of the ears (*śrotravandana*), and performed the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
Having gone into the presence of Śiva, at the southern ear of Śiva, [he spoke] into the mouth of the Blessed One:
"O Lord, that which [occurred] through delusion regarding the three portions beginning with Brahmā..."
O you who are compassionate toward your devotees, I have performed my duty, whether it be deficient or excessive.
May all that be complete here in this sacrifice through your grace.
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the fierce Rudra; salutations be unto you.

"Whether the rite is complete or incomplete, let it be accepted as having been fulfilled according to my own capacity. Having thus informed the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and having performed its placement (*nyāsa*), one should restrain it. And [one should pray]: "O Blessed One, by Your grace, may the ritual action (*karman*) performed by me within the three parts of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) reach completion."

Having made this request with "Oṃ hrīṃ śaṅkari pūraya pūraya svāhā," one should install and restrain the *akriyā-śakti*. Having performed all rites upon the *brahmaśilā* and requested, "May it be accepted," one should offer salutation to the *ādhāraśakti* with "Oṃ hrūṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ. Having likewise requested the Bull (*vṛṣa*), [one should proceed] with "Oṃ... (fifth line).
"Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha"— with this, one should restrain the bull. With fire-offerings, the sounding of the Vedas and other scriptures, and great festivals of song and dance,
[one should perform this] with devotion for seven nights, or five nights, or three nights.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the deities for one night or immediately;
every day, one hundred oblations should be offered with their respective mantras.
One should perform the worship of the Śiva-pitcher and other vessels, and offer the oblation to the quarters;
then, having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances along with the sacrificial images and wealth, one should go to sleep.
In the case of a rite lasting many days, the officiant (mantrin) should eat pure food and sleep [in the ritual space],
and thereafter the image-bearers (mūrtipās).
Thus ends [the section] from the *Kriyākramadyotikā* composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara.
The ritual procedure for the consecration and perfuming is completed.

Then, in the morning, having performed the daily rites, [he should perform] the worship of the Sun and the Gatekeepers, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the consecration of the special materials for the *arghya* offering,
the *śivahasta*, the contemplation of Śiva (*śivabhāvanā*), and [the worship of] the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*), the *śivakumbha*, the *vardhanī*, Gaṇapati, and the Guru.

Having performed the worship of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), having worshipped the *liṅga* with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and having fully worshipped the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*), and the bull (*vṛṣa*), one should invoke Śiva into the fire as before, perform the libation of mantras (*mantratarpaṇa*), and [proceed] with the mantras of the pedestal and so forth.
And one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*).

The image-keepers (*mūrtipas*), having worshipped Śiva in their respective fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) and performed the libation, should satisfy their own mantras as well as the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) and other elements.
As for the officiant who is uninitiated (*adīkṣita*)— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]

One should initiate him here in the interim. Having prepared the *caru* oblation and offered it, one should present the ritual offering (*bali*). Then, having informed Śiva and received his permission, while reciting the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should go to the temple, expel the obstacles with the *astra-mantra*, and sprinkle [the site].
After examining the location of Brahmā and clearing a space with a barley grain or half a barley grain, one should take refuge slightly toward the northeast (*īśāna*) and [worship] Śivā.
One should place [the mantra] in the center:

*Oṃ sūṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*. Then, having installed the stone by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārgeṇa*) with the mantra *Oṃ namo* ... *vyā* ... *sthire acale āvelaṃ hmīṃ laṃ svāhā*, one should worship it.
You alone are the Supreme Power; you alone are the Lady who sits upon the seat. By the command of Śiva, O Goddess, you must remain here at all times.

Having thus informed [the deities] and worshipped them, and having emerged [from the mandala], one should visualize within the nine pits in its center—starting from the east—the [nine substances] consisting of jewels, metals, minerals, medicinal herbs, crops, radiance, physical form, vigor, health, and the power of satisfaction. Then, with the *lokapālas* and their consorts, [one recites]:
*lūṃ rūṃ śūṃ ṣūṃ pūṃ yūṃ sūṃ hūṃ*. [The nine substances are: diamond (*vajra*), sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), blue sapphire (*nīla*), great sapphire (*mahānīla*), and pearl (*mauktika*).
(Third line) Topaz, ruby, beryl, gems, gold, copper, black iron, tin, silver,
brass, bronze, and lead— these are the metals.

Haritāla, manaḥśilā, (4th line) gairika, svarṇamākṣika; pārada, gairika, galaka, and abhraka are the minerals (dhātavaḥ). Uśīra, viṣṇukrāntā, raktacandana, kṛṣṇāguru, śrīkaṇṭha, and śārivā. (5th line)
Having placed the medicinal herbs *kuṣṭha* and *śaṅkhapuṣpikā*, as well as the grains— rice, wheat, sesame, black gram,
green gram, barley, wild rice, and *śyāmāka*— in the center, one should place a golden tortoise and a golden lotus.
One should install facing the door a bull, the Earth, Lakṣmaṇā, and Sahadevā, using either the Ananta-mantra or the root-mantra.
Alternatively, in the absence of these, one should install a diamond, gold, yellow orpiment, sahadevā, barley, and sahadevā in all the pits; or, in every case, mercury.
Having laid down the seat beginning with the *ādhāra-śakti* and ending with the *śakti*,

having worshipped it, protected it with the *astra-mantra*, covered it with a cloth over which the *varma-mantra* has been recited, offered the bali-oblation to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and consecrated oneself (*sakalīkṛtya*), [one proceeds] with the *śiva-weapon* or the *sword* for the purpose of preventing any cracks that might arise in the thread upon the stone.
Having offered one hundred oblations together with the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should satisfy the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*) by offering a single oblation to each:
Brahmā, Īśa, Parjanya, Jaya, Indra, Arka, Satya,
Bhṛśa, Antarikṣa, Saptārcis, Pūṣan, and the one known as Vitatha.
Gṛhakṣata, Pretapati, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgaka, Mṛga,
Pitṛdaivatya, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Pracetas.
Asura, Śoṣa, Roga, Vāyu, Nāga, then Mukhyaka;
Bhallāṭa, Soma, Aditi, and Diti.
Marīci, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Dharādhara; Āpa, Apavatsa, Savitṛ, Sāvitra, Indra, and Indrajit;
(5th line) Rudra, then Rudradāsa, Carakī, and Vidārī as well.
Pūtanā, the sinful Rākṣasīs, Skanda, Aryaman, and Jambhaka;
Thus, the fifty-three deities, including Pilapiṇḍa, have been described.

Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, and having reached the temple of the host of gods—the abode of the Liṅga—one should inform [the deity] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*), raise him up, and offer the *arghya* with the head-mantra (*śiras-mantra*). Then, accompanied by the Blessed One, one should perform dance, song, instrumental music, and shouts of victory amidst the resounding sounds of auspicious instruments.
(7th line) [The officiant], his own kinsman, standing behind and touching Śiva; the preceptor, the presiding image-maker, standing in front, preceded by the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*),
while scattering gold, bell-metal, garments, jewels, and so forth— (109b, 1st line).

Having circumambulated the temple and brought [the Brahman] inside the door, he should place him facing the door upon an auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*). When told, "Be steady," he should offer the *arghya* water. Then, having opened the cavity of the *brahmaśilā* while reciting the *Mahāpāśupata* mantra, he should worship Śiva with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and other offerings, preceded by the sound of the fourth auspicious proclamation.
Having said, "Arise from the heart," the Guru, together with the guardians of the images, takes hold of the Liṅga along with its mechanical apparatus and examines it for vertical alignment.
[He meditates upon] the Supreme Lord, the possessor of power, who is the support of the Kaśilā and the source of all power;
he meditates on the supreme splendor arisen through meditation, the cause of all causes.

Having recited the root mantra up to its dissolution (*layānta*) and, by way of the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*), having established the form of Paraśiva in the shape of light within the cavity of the *liṅga*, one should cover that cavity with lead and other materials; then, saying "Be firm," once the *liṅga* has become stable, one should project [the deity] up to the top of the head and meditate upon it.

Having recited the mantra of the equinox (viṣuva) up to the sphere of the partless (niṣkala), one should deposit the partless [form] within that image, which consists of pure reality alone and embodies all forms.
Supported by the power of action and fashioned by the power of knowledge,
it should truly abide in the form of the substratum of the object of knowledge.
Having invoked [the deity] and visualized him face-to-face, and having performed the confinement of his presence (*sānnidhya-sannirodhana*),

one should offer the water of honor (*arghya*). Then, having awakened the *piṇḍī*, and having brought it as before, one should first secure the base on the double-knot pedestal (*dvibandha-pīṭha*), and straighten it with suspensions.

Regarding the characteristics of touching the marks of the *liṅga*: having recited the mantra of the Goddess, "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Umā, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)," one should bind the *piṇḍī*—which is the manifest form of the power of action—by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*). If there is wandering or movement of the *liṅga* and the *piṇḍī* in any particular direction, [one should perform] a hundred [recitations] with the mantras of the lords of those respective directions.

One should offer oblations together with the *pūrṇāhuti*. If there occurs the rising of sounds and other such disturbances, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra or the *aghora* mantra for their pacification. Therein, for the sake of satisfying the lords of the directions, one should give to the preceptor an elephant made of gold, a buffalo, a goat, a pearl, a brass cow, and silver. One should [seal] the joints on the sides of the pedestal with lead, diamond-paste, and so forth.

Having established the connection (*nissandhi*), the Guru, together with the image-worshippers (*mūrtipais*), should bathe the [deity] on its head with the water from the peace-vessel (*śāntikumbha*) and with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, while the artisans and others perform the rite for the pacification of touch. Then, reciting "Oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Kriyāśakti and Śiva" with the *liṅgamudrā*, [he unites] the pedestal and the *liṅga* for one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) or for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*).
(5th line) *Oṃ hauṃ hrīṃ, salutations to Śiva and Śakti*—having thus touched [the deity] on the pedestal of the *liṅga*, one should perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the six paths (*adhvan*).
In the portion of Rudra: *Śāntyatītā*; in the portion of Viṣṇu: *Śānti*; in the portion of Brahmā: (6th line) [Śāntikalā].

The path of the *kalās* (*kalādhvā*) consists of the cessation of the foundation of knowledge (*vidyā-pratiṣṭhā-nivṛtti*). In the portion belonging to Rudra, there are the principles (*tattva*) of Śiva and Śakti. In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu, there are the principles of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā.
In the portion belonging to Brahmā, there are Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, and Kalā. (7th line)

Knowledge (*vidyā*), passion (*rāga*), the person (*puruṣa*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the qualities (*guṇa*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), ear (*śrotra*), skin (*tvak*), eye (*cakṣus*), tongue (*jihvā*), nose (*ghrāṇa*), speech (*vāk*), hand (*pāṇi*), foot (*pāda*), anus (*pāyu*), generative organ (*upastha*), sound (*śabda*), touch (*sparśa*), form (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), smell (*gandha*), ether (*ākāśa*), wind (*vāyu*), fire (*agni*), water (*jala*), and earth (*pṛthivī*): these are the principles (*tattvārtha*). In the portion of Rudra are Anāśritā, Anāthā, Anantā, and Vyomarūpā.
Vyāpinī, Ūrdhvagāminī, Śocikā, Mocikā, Dīpikā, Śāntyatītā; (second line) Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, Nivṛtti. In the portion of Viṣṇu: Sadāśiva, Śikhaṇḍin, Śrīkaṇṭha, Trimūrti, Ekarudra.
Ekanetra, Śivottama, Sūkṣma, Ananta, Manonmanī, Sarvabhūtadamani, Balapramathinī,
Balavikariṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Kālī, Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā—
[these reside] in the portion of Brahmā. Aṅguṣṭhamātra, Bhuvaneśa, Īśāna, Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa, Udbhava, Vāmadeva— [these reside] in the fourth line.
Mahātejā, Śikheḍa, Ekavīra, Pañcāntaka, Śūra, Saṃvarta, Jyotis, Caṇḍa, Karodha, Ekaśiva, Ananta, Aja, Umāpati, Pracaṇḍa, Ekavīra, Īśāna, Bhava, Ugra,
Bhīma, Vāma, Śrīkaṇṭha, Auma, Kaumāra, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Bhairava, Kṛta, Akṛta, Brāhma.
Prājeśa, Saumya, Aindra, Gandharva, Yākṣa, Rākṣasa,
Paiśāca, Sthaleśvara, Sthūleśvara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Kālañjara, Maṇḍaleśvara, Mākoṭa, Dviraṇḍa, and Chagalaṇḍa.
Sthāṇu, Svarṇākṣa, Bhadrakarṇa, Gokarṇa, Mahālaya, Avimukta, Rudrakoṭi,
Vastrāpada, Bhīmeśvara, Mahendra, Aṭṭahāsa, Vimaleśvara, Nakhala, Nākhala, Kurukṣetra, Gayā, Bhairava, Kedāra, Mahākāla, and Madhyameśvara.
Āmrādikeśvara, Jalpeśvara, Śrīśaila, Hariścandra, Lakulīśvara, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍi, Bhārabhūti, Āṣāḍhi, Puṣkara, Naimiśa, Prabhāsa, Amareśa, Bhadrakālī, Vīrabhadra, Trilocana, Lipsu, Nabhas,
Vivāha, Saṃvāha, Tridaśeśvara, Tryakṣa, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Vibhu, Śambhu, Daṃṣṭrin, and Vajrin.

Lord of Serpents, Lord of Udumbara, Swallower, Wind-eater, Wrathful One, Ananta, Bull-bearer, Bull, Lover of Bali; (third line) Protector of Beings, Pāṭala, Jyeṣṭha, Śarva, Sovereign of the Gods, Master of the Vedas, Consumer of Knowledge, Omniscient One, Lord, Master of Wisdom, Radiance, Grace, Bearer of Fortune, Bearer of Jewels, Bearer of Lakṣmī, Bearer of Matted Locks, Gentle-bodied One, Blessed One; (fourth line)

The embodied one; Lord of the lunar days; He whose vehicle is the clouds; the one with matted hair; the five-crested one; the destroyer of the five; the ender of destruction; the sharp; the subtle; the one with the speed of wind; the light; the swift; the one of beautiful sound; the one who sounds like a thundercloud; the ender of the waters; the long-armed; the auspicious one of the waters; the white; the one of great strength.
Noose-in-hand, exceedingly powerful, possessing strength, fanged, red, smoke-colored, odd-eyed, with an erect phallus, terrifying, of cruel gaze, slayer, destroyer,
(6th line) Nirṛti, Lord of Dharma, Dharma, disjoiner, uniter, ordainer, creator, Hara, Death, Yama’s servant, ender of destruction.

Bhasmāntaka, Babhru, Dahana, Jvalana, Hara, Khādaka, Piṅgala, Hutāśana, Agnirudra, Tridaśādhipa, Pinākin, Śāstra, Avyaya, Vibhūti, Pramardana, Vajradeha, Buddha, Aja, Kapālīśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hāṭaka, Kūśmāṇḍa.
The path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) consists of the names of the Kālāgnis.
In the portion belonging to Rudra: *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *am*, *aḥ*.
In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu: *ka*, *kha*, *ga*.

In the portion of Brahmā: gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha, ḷ, kṣa—this is the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*).
In the portion of Rudra: oṃ. In the portion of Viṣṇu: vyo(ma)vyāpine, vyomarūpāya, sarvavyāpine, śivāya. (Third line)

To the infinite, to the protectorless, to the supportless, to the firm, to the eternal, to him who is established upon the seat of yoga, to the perpetual yogin, to him whose food is meditation, to the portion of Brahman—Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva! To the source of all, to Śiva! (4th line)

To the one whose head is Īśāna; to the one whose face is Tatpuruṣa; to the one whose heart is Aghora; to the one whose secret organ is Vāmadeva; to the one whose form is Sadyojāta; *oṃ* salutations, salutations! To the one more secret than the secret; to the protector; to the imperishable; (5th line) to the one presiding over all yoga; to the lord of all sciences; to the one whose nature is light; to the Supreme Lord; O conscious-unconscious one, O sky!
Pervading the sky, pervading;
formless, formless; primordial, primordial; splendor, splendor; light, light; formless; without fire; without smoke; without ashes; without beginning; manifold, manifold.
Dhū-dhū dhū-dhūḥ | Oṃ bhūḥ | Oṃ bhuvaḥ | Oṃ suvaḥ | Anidhana | Nidhana | Nidhanodbhava | Śiva | Śarva | Paramātman | Maheśvara | Mahādeva | Satbhāveśvara | Mahātejaḥ | Yogādhipate | Muñca.
Release! First, first! Śarva, Śarva! Bhava, Bhava! Origin of existence!
Bestower of happiness upon all beings! Maker of presence for all! Supreme over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra! Honored by the unhonored! Unrefined by the refined! Abiding from before!

*pūrvasthita*, *sākṣi*, *sākṣi*, *turuturu*, *pataṅga*, *pataṅga*, *piṅga*, *piṅga*, *jñāna*, *jñāna*, *śabda*, *śabda*, *sūkṣma*, *sūkṣma*, *śiva*, *śarva*, *sarvada*, *oṃ namaśśivāya*, *namo namaḥ*, *śivāya namo namaḥ*, *oṃ*. Thus is the path of words (*padādhvan*).
In the portion of Rudra: Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva; Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to the head of Īśāna.
In the portion of Viṣṇu: Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa.
In the portion of Brahmā: (fourth line)

Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the heart of Aghora. Oṃ hiṃ, homage to the secret of Vāmadeva. Oṃ haṃ, homage to the form of Sadyojāta. In the Brahma-quarter: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the heart. Oṃ hīṃ, homage to the head. Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the crest-lock.
In the portion of Viṣṇu: Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ.
In the portion of Rudra: Oṃ hauṃ netrebhyo namaḥ. Oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ. Thus (line 6) is the path of mantra (mantrādhvā). In the portion of Rudra: the principle of Śiva (śivatatva); [and] Rudra.
Having assigned the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) as Viṣṇu in the portion of Viṣṇu,
and the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*) as Brahmā in the portion of Brahmā, [one should do so] for each section. (Line 7)
The forms [of Śiva] consist of Earth, Fire, the Sacrificer, the Sun, Water, and the faces beginning with that of the Lord of Elephants;
and [the names] Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, and Īśvara.

One should install the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*) as Mahādeva and Bhīma. Then, on the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should place the *śivatattva* in the upper portion; *icchā* at the throat; the *vidyātattva* and *jñāna*; and below, the *ātmattattva* and *kriyā*.
The eightfold forms beginning with Earth and Fire are each assigned a portion.
The placement of Daṇḍabhaṅginī and Muṇḍabhaṅginī is as follows:
Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, Cetā, and Balotkaṭā.
One should install Dhātrī, Vibhavī, and Mūrtīśvarī.

In this manner, one should also install the foundation stone (*ādhāraśilā*). If the subject consists of five aspects, one should install the Lords of the Forms (*mūrtīśvaras*)— namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— upon the pedestal stone and the foundation stone, representing the forms of earth, water, fire, air, and ether.

One should install the five forms beginning with Earth— namely Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānī, and the Mistress of Forms known as Icchā. Then, having installed the mantras of the seat (*āsana*) consisting of the principles (*tattva*) of the powers beginning with Ādhāra-śakti upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should install the Form (*mūrti*) upon the *liṅga*, and the Brahmans [the five faces] upon the head, face, heart, and secret place.

Having performed the placement upon all the limbs by means of the *daṇḍabhaṅgī* method, and having performed the placement upon the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western faces by means of the *vaktrabhaṅgī* method, one should perform the placement by means of the *kalābhaṅgī* method as follows: Oṃ, *Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām*, obeisance to Śaśinī; [this is] on the upper head.

Oṃ, to Īśvara, the Lord of omniscience, salutation to Aṅgadā; on the eastern head. Oṃ, to Brahmādhipati, the Lord of Brahmā, the Brahmā of the sacrifice, salutation to Iṣṭā; on the southern head. Oṃ, may Śiva be mine;
salutation to Marīci; on the northern head.

Oṃ, obeisance to Sadāśivajvālinī; on the western head. Thus are the Īśāna-kalās. Afterwards: Oṃ, obeisance to Avyaktakalā; on the upper face. Oṃ, we know Tatpuruṣa, obeisance to Śānti; on the eastern face. Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva, obeisance to Vidyā; on the southern face. Oṃ, may that Rudra [bestow] upon us, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhā.
In the northern face: *Oṃ pracodayāt*, salutation to Nivṛtti. In the western face: [thus] these are the four [faces], Tatpuruṣa and Kālī.

Oṃ aghorebhyaḥ tamāyai namaḥ | In the heart. Oṃ atha ghorebhyaḥ mohāyai namaḥ | In the neck. Oṃ ghorarakṣāyai namaḥ | On the right shoulder. Oṃ ghoratarebhyaḥ ca nidrātvaṣṭhāyai namaḥ | On the left shoulder.
Oṃ, obeisance to Sarvada, to Sarvamṛtyu; at the navel. Oṃ, obeisance to all, to Māyā;
at the belly. Oṃ, obeisance to you, to Rudrabhayā; at the back. Oṃ, obeisance to forms, to Jarā; at the chest.
The eight verses on the terrible Kalās.

Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Rajā. (5th line) [At] the secret place. Oṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭha; salutation to Rakṣā. At the liṅga. Oṃ, salutation to Rudra; salutation to Ratī. On the right thigh.
Oṃ, salutation to Kāla; salutation to Pālī—on the left thigh. Oṃ (6th line), salutation to Kalakāmā—on the right knee. Oṃ, salutation to Vikaraṇa; salutation to Saṃyamani—on the left knee.

Oṃ, salutation to Balakriyā; on the right shank. Oṃ, salutation to Vikaraṇa (7th line), salutation to Buddhi; on the left shank. Oṃ, salutation to Balakārī; on the right buttock. Oṃ, salutation to Pramathana, salutation to Dhātrī.
On the left buttock: *Oṃ*, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana;

salutation to Brahmaṇī. On the hip: *Oṃ*, salutation to Manamohinī. On the right side: *Oṃ*, salutation to Unmana; salutation to Bhavā. On the left side: *Oṃ*, salutation to Unmana; salutation to Bhavā. These are the thirteen digits (*kalā*) of Vāmadeva.
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation to Siddhi. [On] the right foot. Oṃ, salutation indeed to Sadyojāta;
salutation to Ṛddhi. [On] the left foot. Oṃ, salutation to Bhava and Dyuti. [On] the right hand.
Oṃ, salutation to Abhava and Lakṣmī. [On] the left hand. Oṃ, salutation to Anādibhava and Medhā. [On] the nose. Oṃ...
"Bhajasva māṃ kāntyai namaḥ" on the head. "Oṃ bhaja svadhāyai namaḥ" on the right arm.

(Fourth line) "Oṃ udbhavāya namo dhṛtyai namaḥ" on the left arm. Thus ends the eightfold *kalā*-installation of Sadyojāta. Having thus performed the installation of the thirty-eight *kalās* with their respective *mudrās*, [one should proceed].
Having attained the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*),

and after the placement of the eyes (*netranyāsa*), one should invoke the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), establish it, bring it into proximity, restrain it, and having assigned the limbs (*aṅga*) to their respective places, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and flowers.

Oṃ sauṃ, salutation to Jñānaśakti; [place this] on the *liṅga* in the portion of Rudra, and everywhere on the *pīṭha*. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Kriyāśakti—having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and restrained [the senses], and having displayed incense and lamps, one should consecrate the *vajra* and other implements made from cow-dung paste and so forth with their respective mantras, or with the *astra-mantra*.
Having established [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth— using twenty-five, one hundred and eight, or a thousand jars—

and having thoroughly anointed it all over with sandalwood paste and other substances, clothed it in garments, adorned it with necklaces, earrings, crowns, sacred threads, ribbons, and the like, worshipped it, and offered incense, [one performs] the dissolution-limb (*layāṅga*).
Having worshipped the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) on the petals beginning with Īśāna,
and having worshipped them at the tips of the petals, one should worship the eight [forms]: Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin.

Having worshipped the eight deities— Nandi, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vināyaka, Vṛṣaskanda, Devī, Caṇḍa, and Ānanda— at the neck of the pedestal in the directions starting from the east, and having worshipped Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu at the feet of the pedestal in their respective directions, [one should proceed] upon the *brahma-śilā*.

Having worshipped and offered *arghya* to the weapons— the *vajra*, *śakti*, staff (*daṇḍa*), sword (*khaḍga*), noose (*pāśa*), banner (*dhvaja*), mace (*gadā*), trident (*śūla*), lotus (*padma*), and discus (*cakra*)— in their respective directions, and having presented food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth, [one should worship] with the sacred thread (*pavitra*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), and the *ārātrika* rite, as well as with mirrors, parasols, fly-whisks (*cāmara*), songs, dances, and other such performances.

Having satisfied [the deity], performed the recitation (*japa*), and offered the oblation, one should offer the food under the name of the patron, the Goddess, Hari, and Sūrya, ending with the name of the Lord as "Bhagavate Amukeśvara," and then pray:
"O Lord, together with the Lords of Mantras and the Guardians of the Forms, you should remain here at your own will for as long as the moon, the stars, and the constellations endure."

Regarding the word "temple" (*mandira*): having obtained permission for that, and having prostrated like a staff with eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-daṇḍavat*), he goes outside, mentally establishes the Bull (*vṛṣa*) with the *praṇava*, bathes it, and worships it. Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) together with the presiding priests (*mūrtipās*), for the sake of pacification (*śānti*) and for the propitiation of the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, and Nārka, [he proceeds].

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations each of *grāsa* (or *lāśaka*), *vāpāmārga*, *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *śamī*, *dūrvā*, *kuśa*, or sesame seeds; having offered one hundred oblations of clay, cow dung, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) while reciting the root mantra and the *māmantra*; and having offered one hundred oblations with either the root mantra or the *aghora* mantra for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should present the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), followed by water for sipping (*ācamana*), sandalwood paste, and so forth.
Having given [the offerings], having restrained [the senses], having offered oblations of parched grain and so forth, having presented the *bali* offering, having entered within,

and having circumambulated and prostrated, [one should confess]: "Whatever has been prescribed by the scriptures that I have not performed— whether through ignorance or lack of knowledge— with respect to the stone, the *liṅga*, the *piṇḍī*, and the bull..."

"In this sacrifice within my abode, whatever deficiency has occurred through fault in action, speech, body, or mind—O Lord, may all that become complete for me through Your grace. Thus he should inform [the deity]. Then the king or other performer [should offer] everything from gold and land down to male and female slaves for the sake of worship, as well as dance, song, and so forth.

One should offer it, saying, "For the sake of Amukeśvara. One who is not a king should offer a sixth part of the merit to the public. One should provide food for the preceptor and others, as well as for the blind, the destitute, and the miserable, and hold a great festival every day for four days. Then, on the second day, having performed the daily obligatory rites...

Having performed the worship of the gatekeepers, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the inner sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the consecration of the special *arghya* materials, the worship of Śiva, the water-pot (*kumbha*), and so forth,

as well as the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), Gaṇapati, and the Guru, the worship of the Liṅga, and the preparation of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*), he went to the vicinity of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and took hold [of the ritual] together with the image-bearers (*mūrtipa*) for the purpose of completing the rite.

One should offer oblations one hundred times each with the *aghora* and *śiva* mantras. In the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) to the east, south, north, and west, one should offer oblations using the root-mantras of the *śivāstra*, *aghorāstra*, and *pāśupatāstra*. Alternatively, in the pits starting from the southeast (*āgneya*), one should offer oblations separately—one thousand, five hundred, or one hundred times—with the *aghorāstra*, *sāvitrī*, *gāyatrī*, and *pratyaṅgirā* mantras.
Therein, the mantras are as follows: Oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ | The Śivāstra.
Oṃ prasphura sphura ghora-ghoratara-tanurūpa caṭacaṭa pracaṭa kaha kaha vama vama ghātaya ghātaya huṃ phaṭ | The Aghorāstra. Oṃ ślīṃ paśuṃ huṃ phaṭ | The Paśvastra.
The Pāśupata Weapon: Oṃ, let us know Vyomavyoman; let us meditate upon Sūkṣmasūkṣma; may that Rudra inspire us. The Śivasāvitrī: Oṃ, let us know that Maheśa; let us meditate upon Vāgviśuddha;
may that Śiva inspire us. The Śivagāyatrī: Oṃ Āṃ Īṃ Ūṃ, O Rudrāsthiśṛṅkhalā, hūṃ, from all sides!
O auspicious one, O hut, O Rudrapacana, O Vidhāri, protect, protect me, O Pratyangirā!

O abode, O abode! O light, O light! I invoke heaven, I invoke the celestial realm! I invoke the earthly realm, I invoke the intermediate realm! Protect me, I am immortal; I am the divine truth, threefold.

"Obeisance to you who delight in the foot of Lakṣmī; let that very [power] enter Kirikeya through this great vow. Obeisance, obeisance, svāhā! Thus ends the Praty-aṅgirā. Then, on the third day, having offered a hundred oblations with the Rūpiṇāsinī mantra, [one should perform the rites] belonging to Indra, Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti.

For the sake of pacification, one should offer a thousand or half that number of oblations into the ten directions— namely Vāruṇī, Vāyavī, Kauberī, Aiśānī, and so forth— into the fire for Tvaṣṭṛ using their respective mantras. Then, on the fourth day,

having worshipped the Blessed One according to one's ability with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), and having offered a hundred oblations with the Aghora mantra, one should [proceed] with the Vāgīśvarī mantra accompanied by its own Brahma-aṅgas, beginning with *Oṃ*.

Having offered oblations into each fire-pit— either one thousand, five hundred, or one hundred, including the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*)— with the mantra "Kirikiri Kumārike Svāhā," and having prepared the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and presented it to the Deity, the guardians of the images (*mūrtipāḥ*) should offer oblations according to their capacity. Then,
having established two jars upon the altar in the same manner as the jar of Śiva and having worshipped them, [the ritual continues].

Having gone to Śiva, one should offer the oblation (*homa*). For four days here, there is no defect in the object that has been mounted upon the image, whether it be crushed, stepped over, given away, or smelled. Then, [one should perform] the Vedic recitation...
Having celebrated the fourth-day auspiciousness with musical instruments, having worshipped with the Gāyatrī mantra, having removed the *nirmālya* from the *liṅga*,
having placed the offerings, the *nirmālya*, and so forth into a vessel, and having performed the purification of the site,
one should sprinkle everywhere with the water of the *arghya* offering, bathe the *liṅga*, worship it, and, in the case of a common *liṅga*, bid it farewell with the words, "Forgive me."

Having worshipped Caṇḍa in the northeast corner of the Puṇḍarīka, and having taken him and installed him in the sanctuary, one should worship the Liṅga and perform seven oblations beginning with the *sthira* mantra. Alternatively, in the case of a common (*sādhāraṇa*) Liṅga, one should dismiss the presiding consciousness (*caitanya*) and release one's own mantra; then, having invoked Caṇḍeśvara into that [Liṅga], one should worship him.
