In the previously mentioned pavilion, after the conclusion of the mantra-satisfaction (*mantratṛpti*), having performed the placement of the *nyāsa* on the head and other parts as before, and having performed the purification of the hands preceded by meditation, [one should perform] the opening of the eyes, the re-bathing, the entry into the sacrificial seat (*śayyāniveśana*), and the *tritattva-nyāsa* and others.

In the northeast, on the outer *jagatī*, at the site of the temple’s central sanctum (*garbha*) where the form of Caṇḍa is established, one should bring Caṇḍa—who resides in the *liṅga*—into the state of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), unite him with the Self, and having installed and specially bathed him according to the rules, one should worship him with the appropriate mantras and limbs (*brahmāṅgas*). *Oṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*. *Oṃ anantāsanāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ...*
Homage to Dharma. Oṃ, homage to Jñāna. Oṃ, homage to Vairāgya. Oṃ, homage to Aiśvarya. (Fourth line) Oṃ, homage to Padma.
Oṃ Caṇḍāsanāya huṃ phaṭ, homage. Oṃ Oṃ Caṇḍamūrtaye huṃ phaṭ, homage. O Coṃ, homage to Īśāna.

Hūṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ caṃ caṇḍanetrebhyo hūṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ (5th line) dhvanicaṇḍeśvarāya hūṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ cuṃ aghorāya hūṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ ciṃ vāmadevāya hūṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ caṃ sadyojātāya hūṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ caṃ caṇḍanetrebhyo...
huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | oṃ (6th line) dhvanicaṇḍeśvarāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | oṃ cāṃ caṇḍahṛdayāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | oṃ cīṃ caṇḍaśirase huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | oṃ cuṃ

Oṃ caṇḍaśikhāyai huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ caiṃ caṇḍakavacāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ caḥ caṇḍāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Having worshipped with these [mantras] using the five offerings up until the end of the recitation, one should present the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*).
One should say to him: "O guardian of Śiva’s property, remain here in the presence of Śiva;
having set aside garments, wealth, and ornaments, the remains of the offerings [nirmālya] shall be your sustenance."
O Lord Caṇḍeśa, as long as you are present, so long may you remain present;
whatever has been done by me through ignorance, whether deficient or excessive,
please fulfill all of that through your grace.
Having made this request, he should go outside and bathe; or else, having performed the washing of the feet, the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*),
and the ritual of making oneself whole (*sakalīkaraṇa*), he should go into the presence of Śiva and bathe Śiva with one of the two jars previously set out.

The *praṇava*, *mātṛkā*, *māyā*, *vyomavyāpin*, the six-syllabled [mantra], *prāsāda*, and *bahurūpa*— these seven are remembered as common [mantras]. Since it has been stated thus, one should perform the specific [worship] with any one of these general mantras, including the five offerings, up until the end of the recitation (*japa*).
Having performed worship and gone to the vicinity of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer seven oblations beginning with *sthira*:
*oṃ namaḥ śivāya sthiro bhava svāhā*, *oṃ namaḥ śivāya svāpako bhava svāhā*, *oṃ namaḥ śivāya aprameyo bhava svāhā*, *oṃ namaḥ śivāya anādibodho*... [svāhā].
"Become [existent], svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva; become eternal, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva; become indestructible, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva; become satisfied, svāhā!
Thus, even for one endowed with attributes such as eternity and so forth—

One should offer seven oblations for the sake of completing the ritual actions of the Blessed One. For the sake of completing the performed and unperformed actions, one should again offer a hundred, a thousand, or half [of that] with the *oghora* and *asi* mantras; having offered a hundred oblations each together with the *mūrtipas*, and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should perform the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), the offering of sandalwood paste, betel, and ashes, and the salutation, and then dismiss the *bali*.
Having given [the offerings] and dismissed the pitcher and other items by throwing water held in one's own hand upwards,

having dismissed the pavilion, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should go before Śiva, offer the ritual service, and conclude the rite.
Having informed Rudra and the others and offered them the sacrificial oblation (bali), one should restrain them:
"For as long as Mahādeva remains stationed here, having taken recourse to this linga,
for that same length of time you must all remain forever for the sake of protection."

Having thus informed [the deity], dismissed [him], and prostrated, he should request [permission] and, being protected, go outside. Then, having established the patron (yajamāna) together with his kinsmen, his wife, and his retinue in a pure place,
he should bathe him with the waters from the jar of the peaceful rite (śāntighaṭa) remaining from the ritual, as well as with the water from the jar previously installed.

Even while seeking victory, one should honor the consecrator like Maheśvara himself and provide him with ornaments such as land, gold, and the like, without any stinginess regarding wealth. According to the number of finger-joints on the hand of the Liṅga or other object thus installed—
Kings should devoutly give two or three times the weight of pure gold as a gift.
One should give [the gift] equal in number to that, beginning with the eldest, as an offering;
for the guru is to be honored in such a way that he attains satisfaction.
Since the fruit of that [action] would not accrue to the performer if the preceptor were dissatisfied,

one should subsequently honor and gratify the image-keepers (*mūrtipas*), the reciters (*jāpakas*), and likewise the Brahmins, according to the rules; and having worshipped the astrologer and the artisan with devotion, one should gratify them according to one's capacity.
But for those who bear the form [of the deity] and recite the weapon-mantra, it is one-quarter less than that quarter.
There should be worship with wine for the pervasive deities, the experts, and the artisans;
and the consecrator, being satisfied, shall then manifest the fruit to the patron.
For as many units of measurement as there are in the image, the linga, or the pedestal,
for that many thousands of yugas shall they enjoy the fruit of their merit. This merit has been declared regarding an uncooked earthen linga.
It is said that [the merit] is tenfold when [the recipient] is cooked [in hell], and ten times more than that when [the recipient] is made of wood.
On stone, the fruit is tenfold; on iron, it is eight times ten times more;
and for objects born of jewels, the fruit is declared to be ten times that of gold.
Even therein, the superiority of the fruit is proclaimed according to the excellence of each specific object.
In a Bāṇa Liṅga it is ten million-fold, and in a Rasa Liṅga it is ten billion-fold.
Who is able to describe the virtues of the bull-emblem of Śaṅkara?
(*)(4th line) It is stated that [the merit] is attached everywhere:
whatever fruit exists in all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred fords, and the Vedas, [is obtained by this].
Having established that fruit multiplied ten millionfold, a man shall obtain a liṅga.
Liberation is established in the *liṅga*, as are uninterrupted worldly prosperities;
for one who marries a woman, there arises [the debt] born of his father and that born of his mother.
"Having ascended through twenty-one lineages, one shall thereafter go to the supreme goal.
Thus [it is said]. Whatever was perceived by me here in the presence of the Blessed One, O Lord, ocean of compassion, please forgive all of that for me.

To the patron who has thus offered this request, the true guru should, with his own hand, bestow the merit-accumulation of the consecration— which is radiant like shimmering stars— accompanied by *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains.
The wretched, the blind, the miserable, the protectorless, the young, the old, the emaciated, and the afflicted.
And one should worship all those who are present at this rite.
Then the Guru, having recited the Pāśupatāstra mantra and circumambulated the Supreme Lord, shall return to his own abode.
The preceptor should take possession of the sacrificial pavilion equipped with garments and other articles;
likewise, the artisan [should take] all the implements and the ablution pavilion.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the installation of the Śivaliṅga.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the consecration of the door.
Then,

as before, having performed the rites beginning with the worship of the door-keepers at the entrance of the pavilion and ending with the libation of mantras, one should bathe the limbs of the door with astringent decoctions and the like, cover them with a red cloth, and place them upon the bed beneath the *udumbara* wood.

Having worshipped Brahmā, the principle of Ātman ending with Māyā, upon the upper branches of the body; Viṣṇu, the principle of Vidyā ending with Sadāśiva, upon the upper Udumbara fruit; and Rudra, the principle of Śiva ending with Śakti, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the forms and their presiding lords.
Or one may perform [the rite]. Having removed the ashes with *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and so forth,

and having established protection by means of a triple enclosure, one should go near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), worship the Lord of the Principles (*tatveśāna*) as before, satisfy him with three oblations, and [recite] the *saṃhitā*.

Having performed the oblation and sprinkled [the site] with water from the *śāntighaṭa* obtained through the *astra-mantra*, one should touch the various sections with the roots, middles, and tips of *kuśa* grass respectively; having purified them by reciting the mantra as many times as the number of oblations, one should worship Vāstu at the entrance, offer individual oblations, and having placed the five items beginning with jewels with the *ananta-mantra*, [one prepares] the seat of the *praṇava*.
Having offered [the oblation] with the *praṇava* and having assigned [the mantra] to the door situated in the northeast (*īśāna*), [one recites]:
"Yava, Siddhārthaka, Kānti, Ṛddhi, Vṛddhi, Sahā, and Anilā."
The characteristics of the supreme lord of diseases, which cause delusion, are like cow-dung, earth, and Darada; [this is] Amṛtā.
Having made a packet (poṭṭalikā) from yellow pigment (rocanā), lac (rasadhā), dūrvā grass, and burnt kuśa grass,
and having tied it upward with the syllable Om (praṇava) for the sake of protection against Śambara, one should offer seven oblations beginning with the "sthirā" mantra.
It is stable, as well as the object of knowledge, and likewise beginningless consciousness;
it is eternal, all-pervading, indestructible, and indeed satisfied.

(3rd line) Having offered the previous [oblations] such as the *dāma* and so forth, one should assign the three principles (*tattva*) to their respective parts, and [place] Nandin, Mahākāla, and Gaṅgā upon the branches.

Having installed Gaṇeśa, Sarasvatī, and Śrī upon an Udumbara tree on the banks of the Yamunā, and having restrained them by the command of Śiva with their respective names, one should offer oblations a hundred or fifty times. Then, for the sake of expiation, having offered a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra and having given the directional offerings (digbali), one should dismiss the sacrifice. [The Guru...]
The performer should honor [the officiant] with gifts of gold, clothing, and food.
This is the procedure for the installation of the sacrificial knife (sṛk).
Having performed the rites up to the satisfaction of the mantras in the pavilion as previously described, one should bathe a golden image of a person and a copper jar,
anoint them with sandalwood paste, cover them with cloths, and place them upon a bed on top of the altar.
Having prepared a pitcher filled with honey and milk, into which the five [substances] beginning with gems have been placed,
and having brought from the *dvādaśānta* a single drop of the *pralaya-kaḷama* [nectar] awakened by the word of Śiva’s command for the person, [recite]: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ*.

"By the command of Ātmaśiva, you must remain here in this body"—having thus deposited [this] with the *recaka* breath, one should deposit the most protective body: *oṃ hāṃ kalāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ kalādhipāya jñānabindave namaḥ*.
"O Lord of Kalā, perform the pervasion of agency (*kartṛtva-vyāpti*), perform it! *oṃ hāṃ kālāya namaḥ*. *oṃ* (second line).

Hāṃ, obeisance to Kālādhipa, named Kāla. O Kālādhipa, impel me toward enjoyments, impel me! Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidyā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidyādhipa, the knowledge of the Vedas. O Vidyādhipa, [impel] me... (third line).
Manifest knowledge, manifest it! Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rāga. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rāgādhipa, the granter of desires.

O Rāgādhipa, produce passion for his sense objects, produce it! Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Niyati. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Niyatyadhipa, the controller. O Niyatyadhipa, [establish] the regulation of his enjoyments.

kurukuru | oṃ hāṃ puruṣāya namaḥ | oṃ hāṃ puruṣādhipāya sūkṣmadehāya namaḥ | (5th line) puruṣādhipāya sūkṣmadehāya namaḥ | puruṣādhipāsya sūkṣmadehabhogaṃ kurukuru | oṃ hāṃ prakṛtyai namaḥ | oṃ hāṃ prakṛtyadhipāya pradhānakāya namaḥ | (6th line)

O Sovereign of Nature, fulfill your office; perform, perform! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Guṇa! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Guṇādhipa, the Three-Body One! O Sovereign of the Qualities, impel the sattva; perform, perform! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Buddhi! (7th line)

Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Buddha, the lord of the intellect (*buddhi*). Awaken the intellect of this [being]; for the sake of the objects of sense, manifest form, manifest form! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the ego, the one who has become ego. Produce the conceit of the lord of the ego, produce it! Oṃ hāṃ, to the mind (*manas*)...

Namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the mind, to Saṃkalpa; O lord of the mind, perform, perform the state of conceptualization and discursive thought! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two ears! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the ears, to Vyomacara; O lord of the ears, perform, perform the function of perceiving sound! Oṃ...

Hāṃ, homage to the tongue. (3rd line) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the Tongue, the Great Mouth. Perform, perform the function of perceiving tastes for the Lord of the Tongue! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the nose. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Lord of the Nose, Vilumbaka. (4th line)
To the Lord of the Nose: perform the grasping of odors, *kuru kuru*. *Oṃ vāce namaḥ*. *Oṃ vāgadhipāya dundubhaye namaḥ*. To the Lord of Speech: grant speech, *kuru kuru*.
*Oṃ hāṃ pāṇibhyāṃ namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ* (5th line).

Homage to Pāṇyadhipa Samadana! O Pāṇyadhipa, perform the grasping of objects for me; perform it, perform it! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Padbhyā! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Padadhipa Ramaṇa! O Padadhipa, perform the impelling of movement for me; perform it, perform it! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pāyava! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pāyvadhipa Tūrṇakṛt!

Homage! To the lord of the anus, perform, perform the evacuation! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the anus! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of the anus, the bliss! To the lord of the anus, bestow, bestow bliss! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to sound! Oṃ hāṃ...

Homage to the subtle sound, the lord of sound. (120a, 1st line) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to touch. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of touch, the most powerful one. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to form. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lord of form, the radiant one. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to taste. Oṃ hāṃ (2nd line)

Salutation to the lord of taste, the giver of water. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to fragrance. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of fragrance, the limb of fragrance. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the ether. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lord of the ether, the subtle one. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the wind. (Third line)

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mātariśvan, the lord of wind. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni. Oṃ, obeisance to the lord of fire, the repository of splendors. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to water. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lord of water, the master of the waters.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the earth. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha, the lord of the earth.

"Thus, may the presiding deities of sound and the other [objects] act as aids to his enjoyment; act, act! Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) and made this request, one should perform the placement of the ten channels (*nāḍī*) and the ten excretory organs (*pāyu*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Iḍā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Piṅgalā.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Suṣumnā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gandhā. (6th line)
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śaṅkhinī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kuhū. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yaśasvinī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Hastijihvā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pūṣā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Alaṃpūṣā. (7th line)

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Prāṇa. Oṃ, homage to Apāna. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Samāna. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Udāna. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vyāna. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nāga. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kūrma. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kṛkara. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Devadatta. Oṃ hāṃ...

"Salutation to Dhanañjaya. Thus, by means of the filler of one's own transformations, [one should contemplate] Māyā as the regulator of time; through the mantra beginning with *aṃ yaṃ* and so forth, she is established as the self-accomplisher of one's own practice.

Having installed the Blessed Lord Śiva by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) and pervasion (*vyāpaka*), and having restrained [the breath], one should install the principles of the Self (*ātmatattva*), Knowledge (*vidyātattva*),

and Śiva (*śivatattva*), as well as Māyā, Sadāśiva, and Śiva. Then, having performed the protection rite with *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains, one should worship and satisfy the Support Power (*ādhāraśakti*) within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having attained the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā*, one should worship as before, satisfy [the deities] with three oblations (*āhuti*), and having satisfied the lords of each principle (*tattveśvara*), perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.
Having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to the number of oblations, one should proclaim the command:
"By the command of Śiva, the presiding lords of *kalā* and the others, together with their respective sovereigns [are authorized]."

One should restrain [the breath] until the end of the stream by means of this path, thinking, "It must remain as long as the palace stands. This was stated for the purpose of making it known in the region of the heart.
The seat is equal to the pedestal; like the foot of the abode, it is considered a foot.
The *prastara* is his hip; the *pātha* is his thigh. Another *prastara* is his heart; the *veda* is his shoulder and the *gala* is his throat.
The head is his head; the *śikhā* is the pinnacle (*sthūpī*), and the temple (*prāsāda*) is the deity—to him, obeisance!
Then, above the pure nose, on the eastern altar within the interior of the wall, having established the *kumbha* with the heart-mantra as if it were a heart-lotus,
and having established the *puruṣa* therein, one should restrain [the breath]. Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)...
Having performed the expiation with the Astra-mantra, one should conclude the sacrifice.
Then the performer should give the preceptor a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) equal to three-quarters of the principal amount.
This is the procedure for the consecration of the *culikā* and other [structures].

As before, having performed the rite beginning with the worship of the Sun at the gate and the propitiation of the gatekeepers by means of mantras, up until the end, one should bathe [the image] with a handful of water accompanied by the *śikhipāda* mantra,
bring it to the consecration pavilion (*adhivāsamaṇḍapa*), and place it upon the bed with its head toward the east, in the circular section.

Having assigned the Śivatattva—Rudra ending with Śakti—to the eight-cornered portion; the Vidyātattva—Viṣṇu ending with Sadāśiva—to the four-cornered portion; and the Ātmatattva—Brahmā ending with Māyā—to [the center];
[one should assign] the voids (*khāni*) to earth (*kṣmā*), fire, the sacrificer, the sun, water, and wind.
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, and Maheśvara.
Having sequentially assigned Mahādeva and Bhīma as the presiding deities of the forms for each section, and having restrained [the breath],
preceded by the placement of the power of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa-śakti*),

one should offer oblations in each part as before, and having gone there, recited [mantras], and performed everything, [one should place them] above the neck in the location where the temple has been constructed.

Having performed the placement according to the sequence of creation, part by part: the Śivatattva, from Rudra to Śakti, at the throat; the Vidyātattva, from Viṣṇu to Sadāśiva, in the shanks; and the Ātmatattva, from Brahmā to Māyā, as before, [one should place] the forms and the guardians of the forms.

Having performed the cessation as before, having offered the oblation, gone, touched, and recited, and having performed everything [else], one should place the five substances such as jewels and so forth into the hollow of the joined palms with the root mantra, set the palms together, and then [perform] what is appropriate for the occasion.
A coconut fruit, two oranges, a pomegranate,
a citron, and a cluster of plantains and jackfruits.
Having filled the jars with these [substances], one should perform the fruit-bath (*phala-snāna*) for the temple.

Then, having bathed the staff (*daṇḍa*), sprinkled the banner (*dhvaja*) with the *astra-mantra*, and protected it with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should place it upon the bed on the northern altar (*uttaravedikā*) of the temple; as before, for both [the staff and the banner], one should [meditate] upon the *ātmatattva* and *vidyātattva*.

Having projected the Śiva-tattva together with Īśvara, as well as the embodied and unembodied lords, onto the staff and the banner through the process of emanation; having restrained them, performed the fire-oblation, gone there, touched them, and recited mantras; and having purified everything as before, one should place the Sakala-Śiva upon the staff and the Niṣkala-Śiva upon the banner.

One should also assign the limbs. Having placed the sixfold arising seat upon the base of the flagstaff, having assigned the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), and having established the staff as the embodied form, one should worship the Aghora-weapon with:
(5th line) *oṃ prasphura sphura ghora ghoratara tanurūpa caṭacaṭa pracaṭa praṭaca kaha kaha vama vama*.

Slay, slay! Hūṃ phaṇnamaḥ! Oṃ prasphura sphura, homage to the heart! Oṃ ghorataraśivarase, homage! Oṃ tanurūpaśivāyai, homage! Oṃ caṭacaṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa, homage to the armor! Oṃ kaha kaha vama vama, homage to the eyes! Oṃ ghātaya... (line 7)

"Obliterate! *Huṃ Phaṭ*—salutation to the Weapon (*astra*). Having thus worshipped and fixed the banner (*dhvaja*) therein, one should worship the Pāśupata weapon there with: *Oṃ astrāsanāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ*. *Oṃ oṃ astramūrtaye huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ*. *Oṃ ślīṃ paśūṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ oṃ hṛdayāya huṃ*.
Oṃ śvīṃ śirase huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ paṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ śūṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ hūṃ netrebhyo huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ phaṭ astrāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ |

*Phaṇṇamaḥ*. Having thus worshipped, one should offer the perfumes and other articles with the *vidyāṅga* mantras: *Oṃ parameśvaraparāya brahmaśirase namaḥ*. Thus, the perfume (*gandha*). *Oṃ sarvayogādhikṛtāya vidyādhipāya namaḥ*. Thus, the flower (*puṣpa*). *Oṃ jyotirūpāya rudrāṇyai namaḥ*. Thus, the lamp (*dīpa*). *Oṃ goptre*... [fourth line]
"Salutation to the one praised by many. With this, the food offering (*naivedya*).

"Oṃ, salutation to the first, the first Pāśupata weapon. With this, the incense (*dhūpa*). Having worshipped with these ritual services (*upacāra*), one should meditate [on Him] who resembles ten million suns and whose roar is like the clouds at the dissolution of the universe.
He has three eyes, a serpent for a sacred thread, four faces, and four arms;
the tips of his teeth are blazing, and his eyebrows, beard, and hair are aflame.
Holding a spear, a mallet, a trident, and a sword in his hands, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
he is the crusher of the arrogant gods, dānavas, and daityas.
Having thus prostrated, one should meditate upon the palace as consisting of all principles (*sarvatattva*).
Having visualized Ananta and Kālarudra at the lotus feet, and having visualized Kūṣmāṇḍa and Hāṭaka upon the pedestal together with the subterranean realms and hells; ||| (7th line)
Having meditated upon the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) as surrounded by the worlds, the guardians of the quarters, the hundred Rudras, and so forth, one should contemplate it within the shank;
[it is] endowed with the five elements— water, fire, wind, and space— and the eight [worlds].
And that which is known as the enclosure of the womb, endowed with the eightfold birthplaces, is the intellect (buddhi).
One should contemplate the three qualities (guṇas) ending with the nose, joined with the eightfold yoga, as well as the Puruṣa situated in the jar, the lion, and passion;
and upon the pedestal of the flower-cluster, the fourfold group beginning with Vidyā.
One should know Māyā at the throat and the ocean at the *vidyā* level; the *vidyā* at the *amalasāraka*, and the jar (*kalaśa*) together with the *vidyeśvara* and the upper dot (*bindu*).
One should know the matted locks (*jaṭā*) and the crest (*cūḍā*), as well as the trident in the form of the half-moon.
And having meditated upon the three powers and the resonance (nāda) within that very staff;
One should contemplate the abode as the coiled power (*kuṇḍalinī-śakti*) upon the banner,

just as the *liṅga* is joined with its pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) by means of the world-ground (*jagatī*). Having thus meditated and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of Śiva as the all-pervading one, one approaches the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the sake of expiation with the *Aghora* mantra and the *astra* mantra of Śiva, one should conclude the sacrifice. The performer should gratify the Guru with gifts of gold, clothing, and food.
Now follows the procedure for the restoration of a dilapidated [shrine] (*jīrṇoddhāra*).
To the south-east outside the temple,
having constructed a single-arched gateway pavilion for the western door,
one should perform the worship of the door and so forth there, while the worship of Śiva is performed upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having performed the satiation of the mantras and worshipped the deities of the site (vāstudeva), and having offered three oblations for each,

one should offer a thousand oblations with the Aghora weapon-mantra for the purpose of causing the liṅga to move; then, having given the directional offerings (dik-bali) outside and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and having satisfied those bearing the *liṅga* with food and other offerings, the assistant shall enter within and inform Śiva: "O Lord, this *liṅga* is defiled by faults; it is a *liṅga* of impurity (*mala*). Your word is that there shall be peace through its extraction. Therefore, in this procedure..."
"O Maheśvara, preside over me.

Having thus petitioned [the deity] and received permission, for the sake of pacification, he should offer one hundred and eight oblations with honey, clarified butter, milk, and *dūrvā* grass using the root mantra, followed by a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, having entered within, he should worship the *liṅga*, bathe it, and perform worship. [He should provide] the seat of the *praṇava*.

Having offered [the oblation], [recite]: *oṃ vyāpakeśvara ehyehi namaḥ | oṃ vyāpakeśvarahṛdayāya namaḥ | oṃ vyāpakeśvaraśirase svāhā | oṃ vyāpakeśvaraśikhāyai vaṣaṭ | oṃ vyāpakeśvarakavacāya huṃ | oṃ*...

Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes of Vyāpakeśvara! Oṃ Phaṭ to the weapon of Vyāpakeśvara! Having thus worshipped [the deity] together with the limbs, one should cause the being residing within the liṅga to hear these words: "O being, whatever fear may exist, let it depart from this liṅga; by the command of Śiva, let it go wherever it desires, leaving the liṅga behind."

"Śambhu will become a Yakṣa here through the Vidyās and the Lords of Vidyās. Having spoken thus, he should offer the *arghya* with the Mahāstra and then dismiss [the deity]. Then, having offered a thousand oblations for each portion with the Pāśupata-weapon, he should sprinkle it with water for peace and touch it with *kuśa* grass.
Having recited [the mantra] and offered the *arghya* in reverse order,

one should dismiss the principles (*tatva*), the lords of the principles (*tatveśvara*), the forms (*mūrti*), and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*). Having dismissed the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the mantras of the seat (*pīṭhamantra*), the mantras of the three parts of the *liṅga*,
the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), and the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), and having also dismissed that *Caṇḍeśa*, [one should act] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and the spade (*khanitra*).

Having dug [the pit] and rinsed it, one should place the *liṅga* in a golden vessel, fasten a cloth around its neck, mount it upon the shoulder of a bull, and while reciting "Śivam astu," carry it outside together with the people and cast it into the water of a river or a lake with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). Thereafter, for the sake of pacification—

Having offered one hundred oblations of *dūrvā* grass smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), and having offered oblations with the respective mantras of the lords of the directions for the sake of their satisfaction,

and having offered oblations with the *astra-mantra* for the purification of the site of the temple (*prāsādavāstuśuddhi*), one should protect the temple with the *pāśupatāstra*. There, one should prepare and install the *liṅga* or other objects established according to the previously determined measurements.
This very same rite applies to the removal of a dilapidated temple;
having installed the groups of mantras upon the sword, one should cause another temple to be constructed. One should worship the Śambaras associated with the sword until the temple is completed.

One should perform the protection of the *liṅga* according to the previous measurement. It is declared that if it is too narrow, death results; if too wide, there is loss of wealth. That material, whether it be a superior substance or otherwise, should be prepared according to those same proportions.
(Regarding the Svāyambhuva-pratiṣṭhā:
In the Svāyambhuva-pratiṣṭhā, the consecration is performed upon the pedestal itself;

the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the principles (tattva), the lords of the principles (tattveśa), and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśa), as well as the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites, are to be performed as previously described.
Since the *liṅga* is divine by its very nature, bathing and other rites are prescribed for it;
one should perform the recitation of the *saṃhitā*, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, and fire-oblations for the sake of peace.
Since the self-manifested Bāṇaliṅga was previously consecrated by the gods, one should not engrave a mark upon it;
otherwise, there would be no [merit], and the assumption of harm and so forth would arise.

In this case, for the sake of enjoyment and other goals, there is no fourth stage, nor is there the fierce (caṇḍa) visualization. Upon the growth [of the liṅga], the presence of consciousness should be established; the consecration is like that of a *bāṇaliṅga*.
Whether it be a self-manifested (*svayambhu*) or a *bāṇaliṅga*, it bestows both enjoyment and liberation upon all.
The fruit resulting from the installation and worship [of an image] is a thousandfold greater than that of other [meritorious acts].
Well-proportioned or deformed, it brings all accomplishments to men;
the procedure for consecration has been declared, which is called the installation of the chariot.
In the case of a mobile liṅga on a separate pedestal,
one should place two parts, or one part, out of five or three parts respectively, into the cavity of the piṇḍikā.

In that case, the portion for the image (*arcā*) shall be three parts, two parts, or one part, according to one's own *śambara* [tradition]. When the arrow has been consecrated as before, and the movable pedestal (*cala-pīṭha*) has also been consecrated;
One should sequentially assign the powers of knowledge and action, and so forth, as previously described.
Thus, the installation (*sthāpana*) has been explained; now the "installation of the established" (*sthitasthāpana*) is being discussed.
This applies to a mobile linga together with its pedestal, such as one made of crystal and other materials, by virtue of its inherent nature.
The entire ritual procedure is as before, but here it concerns the liṅga and its pedestal.

Because there is no distinction between them, the consecration (*saṃskṛti*) should be performed either in the pavilion or in the house. Furthermore, one should mentally conceive the placement of the Brahma-stone, the jewels, and the abundance [of the materials], as well as the joining of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
Even when [the deity] has moved, the consecration (*saṃskṛti*) is as before, whether at a Bāṇaliṅga or a Rauhaka,
in a pavilion or a house, or on a funeral pyre (*cita*) which is the support for all seats (*pīṭha*).

The method of installation for the *sthirabāṇa* and others mentioned previously is also remembered here. One should install a fixed *vallī-liṅga* made of metal, gemstone, stone, or even other non-organic materials, according to one's mental inclination.

Due to the abundance of ritual applications, the action is described here: one should perform the installation in the previously mentioned pavilion, in a house, or in the initiation pavilion (*dīkṣā-maṇḍapa*), upon a pedestal (*pīṭha*) or a linga as previously stated. There, having bathed the linga and its pedestal with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances as before, having anointed them with sandalwood paste and the like, and having placed them upon the pedestal or similar base—in the case of a *bāṇaliṅga*—[one should proceed].

Having worshipped [the deity] preceded by the placement of mantras according to the *Saṃhitā*, one should offer oblations a hundred, a thousand, or half that number. Or, having performed the *jīvanyāsa* upon a *liṅga* grown from a river or the sea, one should perform the *saṃhitānyāsa* and the fire-oblation (*homa*). Alternatively, because it is preceded by the placement of the principles (*tattva*) and their respective lords, one should perform the thirty-six principles as before, including the *jīvanyāsa*.
Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the *sādhipas*— namely the *śivatattva*, *vidyātattva*, *ātmatattva*, as well as Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā—

and having placed the forms (*mūrti*) known as earth, water, fire, air, and ether, along with their respective lords, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, in each section starting from the west, one should perform the placement of the living soul (*jīvanyāsa*) and provide protection with sesame seeds, *darbha* grass, and so forth.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] as before, having gratified [the deity] with three oblations, and having offered a hundred, a thousand,

or half that number of oblations with the *saṃhitā-mantra*, having sprinkled [the vessel], touched it with *darbha* grass, recited [the mantra], and joined [the breaths], one should perform everything as previously described.

One should purify. On the seat, as before, one should perform the *jīvanyāsa* by depositing the principles of Śiva (*śivatattva*), Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), and the Self (*ātmatattva*), along with their presiding deities—Will (*icchā*), Knowledge (*jñāna*), and Action (*kriyā*)—and for each section, the forms known as Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether, along with their presiding deities: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānī, and Icchā. Having performed this, one recites: "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Power of Action (*kriyāśakti*). Thus, having performed the *jīvanyāsa*.

Having protected [the site] as before, having offered oblations, having recited [mantras], and having performed everything else, one should project the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) into the *liṅga* and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) into the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Then, having mentally performed the placement of the foundation stone (*brahmaśilā*), the jewels, and so forth, and the joining of the pedestal with the *liṅga*, one effects the union of the vulva and the phallus (*bhagaliṅgasamāyoga*) between the pedestal and the *liṅga*.

Having performed the placement of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavinyāsa*) with the *Śakti* and *Śiva* mantras, and having placed the mantras of the throne (*āsana*)—beginning with *Ādhāraśakti* and ending with *Śakti*—upon the pedestal; and having placed the *mūrti*, the *vidyādeha*, and the *netra* upon the *liṅga*; one should invoke [the deity] with the root mantra and worship, as before, with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).

Having completed the worship at the end of the recitation (*japa*), having bestowed the name "Amukeśvara," and having made the request, "Be present here as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure," one should bow down and offer sesame seeds a hundred times while reciting both the root mantra and the *umā-mantra*.

Having offered one hundred oblations with milk-rice and one hundred with the *mṛtyujit* mantra, and having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra.
The patron (*yajamāna*), having resolved to perform worship for as long as he lives, should perform the worship of the Guru and then worship daily as previously described.
By means of the consecration through visualization and other rites of temporary lingas produced from clay, ashes, cow dung, flour, pieces of fragrant substances,
and so forth;
Having purified [the vessel] according to the rule, one obtains the fruit of this world through constant worship;
at the end of the year, one should release it and cast it into the water.
One should perform the ritual bathing of cloth paintings, manuscripts, and clay models in a mirror;
for the installation of clay models and murals, purification is achieved through meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*).
The mere opening of the lids is intended for the arrangement of the seats and so forth;
below those, one should perform worship and other rites with flowers and the like, without touching them. Incense alone does not cause any fault, as the seats may be made of stone, gems, and so on.
That which is called *sthitasthāpana* is here termed *āsthāpana*.
And even for the manifest [deities], one should follow the previously mentioned procedure, excluding Caṇḍeśvara;
as for that which was taught beginning with Kūrma and that which is the Ratnaka.
One should deposit [the materials] into the pits of the pedestals, excluding the Brahma-stone;
having divided the interior space into six parts, one should leave out the part at the back.
The installation [of the deity] during the day is determined by dividing [the time] into eight parts and taking the fifth part;
likewise, for images, the installation in the seventh part brings happiness.
The Installation of Gaurī

In the consecration of Gaurī, having performed the rites in the pavilion as before up to the satisfaction of the mantra, one should bathe the Goddess as previously described with the *hṛdaya* and other [limb-mantras], perform the opening of her eyes (*netronmīlana*), and bathe her again.
Having placed [the deity] upon the bed, set down the jar of sleep, and performed worship, having provided everything from the food offering (*naivedya*) up to the household utensils,

standing at the foot of the bed, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth and ending with Śakti; then, at the position of the knees and the position of the throat.

Having bestowed the protective amulet (*mālā-pratisara*) for the purpose of beholding the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for each section: the *śivatattva* ending with the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) above the neck; the *vidyātattva* ending with Sadāśiva and the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) above the heart; and the *ātmatattva* ending with Māyā and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) in the region below the knees.
Earth, Fire, Sacrificer, Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Ether;
Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, Cetā, and Balotkaṭā.
One should place Dhātrī and Vibhavī.

In the fivefold [system], one should place the forms of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; and their presiding goddesses—Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānī, and the one called Icchā—one should place. Alternatively, one may place the ether-form up to the forehead, and the will (icchā) up to the heart.

Having placed the Fire-form (Agni-mūrti), the Jñāna [kalā], up to the navel; the Water-form (Jala-mūrti), the Jyeṣṭhā [kalā], up to the knees; and the Earth-form (Pṛthivī-mūrti), the Vāmā [kalā], up to the knees;
one should then place the three principles (tri-tattva) and the Lords of the Principles (tattveśvarīs) reaching down to the knees: *Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ Mahāgaurī Rudradayite*.

(Third line) Having performed the *jīvanyāsa* with the word "svāhā," and having established the enclosure of sesame seeds, *darbha* grass, and so forth, one should also place upon the pedestal the three principles (*tattva*) situated within the three sections— extending from Māyā through Śuddhavidyā to Sadāśiva— together with the Goddesses of Sovereignty (*Īśvarīs*). Then, [placing] "oṃ hrīṃ" (Fourth line...)
Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Kriyā-śakti" and having kindled the fire, one should likewise install Ādhāra-śakti in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
and then, as before, satisfy the *tattva* and *tattveśvarī*, the *mūrti* and *mūrtīśvarī*, with their respective mantras and the *saṃhitā*.

Having approached the Goddess, touched her, recited [the mantra], and focused [the mind] as before, having divided [the site] into sections, and having entered the womb at an auspicious moment (*sulagna*), one should examine the center as before and [worship] the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) with: "Oṃ sūṃ, salutation to Kriyā-śakti. (6th line)
Having placed the jewels and other items there, and having worshipped the seat with the mantras beginning with "aindrī" and "āgneyī," one should place the form of Gaurī,

ending with Śakti, there in the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Having placed [the mantra] "Oṃ srūṃ, obeisance to Kriyāśakti" on the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and [the mantra] "Oṃ sīṃ, obeisance to Jñānaśakti" on the form of Gaurī, one should then invoke the supreme Śakti, who is her vessel (*vāpikā*).
Having established [the deity] and conceived of her with the name "Amukeśī," one should worship her. The mantras are as follows:
(126b, 1st line) Oṃ Āṃ, obeisance to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti). Oṃ Īṃ, obeisance to the Bulb (Kanda). Oṃ Ūṃ, obeisance to the Stem (Nāla). Oṃ Ṛṃ...

Salutation to Dharma. Oṃ Ṛṃ, salutation to Knowledge. Oṃ Ḷṃ, salutation to Dispassion. Oṃ Ḹṃ, salutation to Sovereignty. Oṃ Eṃ, salutation to Non-dharma. Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Ignorance. Oṃ Oṃ, salutation to Non-dispassion. Oṃ Auṃ, salutation to Non-sovereignty. Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to the Lower Covering.

Oṃ aḥ (third line), obeisance to the upper covering. Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the lotus. Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to the filaments. Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to the pericarp. Oṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to the petals. Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to the stalk. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the wise one.
Homage! (4th line) Oṃ hrūṃ, homage to Kriyā. Oṃ hreṃ, homage to Vāk. Oṃ hraiṃ, homage to Vācī. Oṃ hauṃ, homage to Jvālinī. Au auṃ, homage to Vāmā. Oṃ hrūṃ, homage to Jyeṣṭhā. (5th line)

*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrūṃ*, salutation to Raudrī. Thus are the nine Śaktis. *Oṃ gāṃ*, salutation to the seat of Gaurī. *Oṃ gauṃ*, salutation to the form of Gaurī. *Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ*, O Mahāgaurī, beloved of Rudra, *svāhā*. *Oṃ* (sixth line).

*gāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ gīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *Oṃ gūṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *namaḥ*. *Oṃ gaiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *namaḥ*. *Oṃ gaṃ* to the eyes, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ gaḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *namaḥ*. Or: *Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hraṃ hraḥ*. *Oṃ skāṃ* to Subhagā, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ sha* to Lalitā, *namaḥ*. *Sruṃ*.

"Salutation to Kāminī. Oṃ sbhoṃ, salutation to Kāmamālinī. (127a, 1st line) Having thus worshipped the companions of Gaurī with five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) up until the end of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the rite of atonement (*prāyaścitta*). Except for Caṇḍā, one should perform the rites beginning with the dative case (*caturthī*) as before.

The Ritual for the Installation of the Sun (Saurapratiṣṭhāvidhi): On a seat or bed at the end of the day, one who has performed the ritual bathing and other preliminary rites should install the Sun there,
along with the three principles including the Lord (Īśvara), as previously described.
One should place Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā within the sky, wind, fire, water, and earth, ending with Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, and Sadāśiva. Then,
[one should perform] the *jīvanyāsa* with the mantra "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Sūrya," and [place] Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, and Sadāśiva upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

Having established [the deity] from all sides according to the ritual procedure by means of the power of the conceptualization of the three sections, the Guru should then duly install the Sun, ending with the Śakti, along with the Sthāṇu-mantra. The mantras of the Sun are as prescribed for the daily rite.
[This concludes] the installation of Gaṇapati.

Having seated the group who have performed their ablutions and other rites upon the seat and bed of the *vidyā* [mantra], one should place the three principles (*tattva*) together with their presiding deities: Māyā, Vidyā, and Sadeśaga.
One should place the void, wind, fire, water, and earth [elements] ending at the knees, throat, head, and so forth;
likewise Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
Alternatively, one may place earth, fire, the sacrificer, sun, water, wind, moon, and the void.
Āmoda, Pramoda, Sumukha, and likewise Durmukha.
With the *avivena* [mantra], one worships Vighnarāja, who has five hands and eats all kinds of food;
these are known as the eight presiding deities (*mūrtipās*) of the mantras, born from the syllables of the mantras.
The arrangement of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*) on the seat extends up to Māyā and Vidyeśvara.
Regarding the consecration of Skanda:
having performed the auspicious rites such as bathing upon the bed and seat ending with Māyā.
And that which is called Ātma-vidyā-śiva extends up to the knees, the throat, and the head.
Having performed the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the Egg-cognition up to Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) within the pentad beginning with the Form (*mūrti*), [one proceeds] as before;
however, in the eightfold [system], there are the lords of the Vidyeśvaras beginning with Earth (*kṣmā*).
[These are] Ṣaṇmukha, Śaktipāṇi, Kārttikeya, and Guha.
Skanda shall have a peacock as his vehicle, and Viśākha shall be the commander of the army.
One should apply the *mohinī* mark up to its edge; the conceptualization of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍakalpanā*) occurs on the pedestal.
A hexagonal sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is desired, located either in the northeast or in the southeast.
O Lord of the dance of Puruṣa, one should perform even the primary *liṅgas* and others as if they were the principal ones;
that which is not explicitly mentioned here should be practiced according to the general rule established [in the scriptures].
Or else:
One should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) through the ritual of pervasion (vyāpti), extending as far as the station of Sadāśiva.
As before, one should place Durgā upon the altar-bed (vedi-śayyā), beginning with the ritual bathing and other rites.

One should place that which is called Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, reaching up to the knees, throat, and head; and Māyā, Sadeśa, and Śakti, ending at those points, just as [one places] the elements beginning with earth.
Earth, fire, the sacrificer, the sun, water, wind, the moon, and ether;
darkness, delusion, decay, the end, death, illusion, [Bha]... the supreme.
Or else, the five are darkness, delusion, the terrible, attachment, and the supreme fever.
Or else, there are three activities: the knower, the seeker, and the leader.
One should place the Self and so forth within the three principles of intense form;
from Māyā, Vidyā, up to Sadeśa, this is the conception of the triple-sectioned seat upon the pedestal.
In the consecration of Dakṣiṇāmūrti:
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha—
these sages are stationed to the south of the Lord of the South.
Bharadvāja, Agastya, Gautama, and Atri—
these lords of sages are stationed to the south of the Lord of the South (Yama), though they are themselves beyond the need for sacrificial fees.
From the very crown of matted hair down to the tips of the nipples are the *golonta* [limbs];
the principles (*tattvas*) are as before in the God, and likewise as described among the sages.
In the principle of Earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*), one should conceive of a triad of principles;
one should install the Lord as the Self (*ātman*), the Inner Self (*antarātman*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Furthermore, in the consecration of a beautiful body (*sudeha-pratiṣṭhā*), this triad of principles is to be known again.
On that seat as well, up to Prakṛti, and up to Prajñā on the stone, it is as before.
The subtle elements, Pradhāna, and the principle of the Person—this triad belongs to Hari;
[it consists of] Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Trivikrama.
Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Dāmodara, and likewise the eight guardians of the forms, beginning with Earth; furthermore,
in the fivefold system, Sadyojāta, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and so forth.
Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Śrīdhara are likewise his forms.
One should place the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) which pervades up to the limit of *prakṛti* by means of the subtle object (*lakṣyāṇu*).
The three principles (*tritattva*)—the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and *pradhāna*—are the station of Brahmā.
The conceptualization of the three sections on the seat extends from the cosmic egg up to the ego-sense and the intellect;

for Ardhanārīśvara, the cosmic egg, the intellect, and Māyā are established [therein]. One should conceive of these three principles on the seat, reaching as far as the cosmic egg, the intellect, and the kalās.
In this same manner, Harihareśa should also be installed by the most excellent gurus.
In the half of Hari, as before, the ritual actions and mantras are to be understood according to the rule;
in the Kṣetrapāla [mantra], there is the conceptualization of the principles (tattvas) from the Egg (aṇḍa) up to Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
One should visualize the wise one entering within the seat according to the procedure as before:
Hetuka, Tripuraghna, Vahni, Yamajihvaka,
Kāla, Karālika, and also Ekāṅghri.
Alternatively:
Anala, Agnikeśa, Karāla as the third,
Ghaṇṭārava, Mahākrodha, and the sixth is indeed Piśitāśana.
The seventh is Piṅgalākṣa, and the eighth is Ūrdhvakeśa;
these are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), and they are remembered as the embodiments of Earth, Fire, Water, and Iron.
In the consecration of Nandin and the others, one should likewise conceive of this pervasion;
for the conceptualization of the three sections for the seven Mothers is exactly the same.
The wise one should fashion the images of Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī,
Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍī, Vīrabhadraka, Vīravighna,
and Vighneśa.
The seed-syllables ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, and ha belong to Gaṇeśa. Gaṃ is also [the seed-syllable] of Gaṇapati.
Joined with the fire of Māyā and endowed with Bindu and Nāda, this is declared to be their mantra; one should fashion the limbs from the long vowels.
The deposition of the jewels should be performed either on all [the goddesses] or specifically upon the pedestal.
Having established Brāhmī in the center, one should place Māheśvarī in the east;
one should place Kaumārī in the western region and Vaiṣṇavī in the south.
And one should place Vārāhī and Indrāṇī in the west.
One should install Cāmuṇḍī in the northwest, Vīrabhadra in the north,
and Gaṇapati in the northeast, or else according to the [specific] tradition.
The best of preceptors should install the image of the Hero there facing west,
and install the Goddess facing north;
then he should likewise install Vighneśa facing east.
The Installation of Devotees
It should be joined with the first vowel [A], ending in the letter *Sa*, and provided with the *bindu*.
This is known as the *ātman-mantra*, the word *Haṃsa*, followed by *Vāma* (the left).
One should fashion the limbs of Brahmā using that very same syllable ending in *Sa*.
One should also place the limbs of the Vidyā, beginning with the letter 'A', as well as the mantra consisting of the lunar days (tithis).

The syllable *hrīṃ* is established as the female principle; by means of it, the conceptualization of the limbs of Brahmā is performed. Furthermore, the triad of principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva has been proclaimed.

One should sequentially establish the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self as the presiding lords over the three principles. (5th line) For women as well, it should be exactly thus; the elements beginning with earth are considered their forms.
In the fivefold scheme, there are eight [elements], whereas in the fivefold [classification], there are indeed only the five beginning with earth.
In one view, Indra and the others are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipāḥ), while in another, Nivṛtti and the others are the guardians of the forms;
having assigned the respective Brahmās, one should assign those respective forms to the body.
The letters from *a* to *kṣa*, together with the *śa*, are to be placed in sequence upon the head and the other [parts of the body].
One should place the letter *a* on the head as Śrīkaṇṭha; *āṃ* as Ananta on the forehead;
*iṃ* as Sūkṣma in the right eye; and *ī* as Trimūrti in the left.
One should place "ma-he" in the right ear, and "yī-śva-ra" in the left ear and on the feet.
One should place *ṛm* on the right ear, *ṛ* on the right nostril, *īm* on the mind, and *īśvara* on the left nostril; then *ḷm* on the right cheek, *sthāṇu*, *hara*, and *caru* on the left cheek.
One should place Nandīśa on the upper lip, and likewise Emi on the lower lip;
one should place Jātaumau on the upper teeth and Anugraheśvara on the lower teeth;
one should place Kūra on the crest-lock and Mahāsena on the mouth.
One should place Krodhīśvara on the right arm and Caṇḍa on the right upper arm.
One should place *pañcāntaka* on the right wrist and *śivottama* on the right forearm;
*ghaṃ* on the palm of the right hand, and *darudraka* on the tips of its fingers.
One should place *kūrma* on the left arm, *ekanetra* and *cha* on the elbow,
*brahmā* at the wrist-joint, and *nandīśvara* at the end of the hand. Then, *jña* and *indu* at the tip of that hand, and *someśa* and *aṃ* on the right thigh.
Lāṃ is on the right knee, while Ḍaṃ and Dāruka are at the tips of the shanks.
One should place Ardhanārīśvaraṇḍa on the sole of the right foot;
Ṇaṃ-Umākāntaṇḍi on the tip of the foot, and Ḍiṇḍīśantama on the left thigh.
One should place *ḍiṇḍittha* on the left knee, and the thirty letters beginning with *ña* at the tips of the shanks;
*dha* (or *ya*) and *īśāna* on the sole of the foot, *na* and *meṣa* at the front of the feet;
*lohitapaṃ* on the right side, and *phaṃ* and *śikhiṃ* on the left side.
One should place the syllable *baka* and the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) upon the back portion.
One should place *bhaṃ* and *dviraṇḍaṃ* at the navel; *kālakam*, which destroys the vital points (*marmans*), in the heart;
*yaṃ* on the skin; *vālinam* likewise; and one should place *raṃ* and *bhujagam* in the blood.
One should place Pinākin in the flesh and Khaḍgīśa in the fat;
having placed Aṣṭhibaka in the bone, one should place Ṣaṃ Śveta in the marrow. One should place Bhṛgu in the semen, Lakulīśa in the phlegm, and Haṃ in the heart.
The syllable *laṃ* is the form of *tamas* in the *liṅga*, and *kṣaṃ* is the operative [syllable] in its organ.
"Ma, ṣa, a, kha, ca, and akṣāḥ" constitute the group of letters belonging to the limbs of the Mātṛkā;
(second line) "ma, a, aṃ, ka, ca, i, ī, kṣaḥ" are the limbs of the Mātṛkā.

Ma is the heart; A is the head; Aṃ is the crest-lock; Ka is the armor; I and Ī are the eyes; Kṣaḥ is the weapon. Having performed the placement of the vital breath (*jīvanyāsa*) with one's own mantra, one should then place the limbs (*aṅga*).
Having offered oblations in sequence up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for each of the principles (tattvas) and their respective lords,
one should likewise offer three oblations for each of the forms (mūrtis) together with their lords.
Having purified it, one should place it upon a pedestal provided with the installation of jewels and other ornaments;
having performed a hundred oblations with the *ghorānu* mantra for the sake of making [the rite] free from defects, as is appropriate.
The Foundation of Humanity.
Whether joined with the first letter of one's own name or with the second, let it be taken;
[take] the second of the seventh [group] and the fourteenth of the first.
The human seed-syllable is said to be conjoined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*. The short vowels are declared to be the Brahmās; one should fashion the limbs (*aṅgas*) by means of the long vowels.
And likewise the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, gods, and Siddhas.
One should likewise station the vehicles of the gods in this very manner;
then, one should place the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) there within the body.
One should place the image in the upper region and install the sleep-vessel (*nidrākumbha*).
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, as well as Suṣumnā; Gāndhārī, Hāhā, Jihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī;
Alaṃbuṣā, Kuhu, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
Then, one should place these very channels (nāḍīs) within that form:
Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna;
as well as Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
The three principles (tattvas) ending with the knees and the neck are the objects of perception for that [the subtle body].
One should install the Self (*ātman*), the Inner Self (*antarātman*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as the presiding deities;
then the Guru should perform the installation of the living soul (*jīvanyāsa*) using the previously mentioned mantra.
Having purified it, one should establish it upon a pedestal provided with the installation of jewels and other elements.
[The Sprinkling: Having been consecrated and worshipped for a year or half a year, it is established.
The liṅga is generally inhabited by dogs, crows, and other such creatures.
That [object], when worshipped in this world, produces thousands of great evils;
yet, the refinement (saṃskāra) of one who remains fixed therein is here described.
First, one should have the pavilion and other structures constructed according to the previously mentioned procedure;
then, having bathed the weapon [deity] with clay and other substances using the Weapon-mantra as before,
or else with the three principles (*tritattva*) preceded by the triad of principles beginning with Form (*mūrti*).
Having anointed the installed linga as before, one should worship it.

Having offered oblations for each portion as before, and having recited the mantra as many times as the number of offerings made during the rising rite, one should then present [the offering] with the water from the peace-vessel.
At the end of the *pūrṇāhuti*, as before, one should mentally place the five types of stones and jewels;
having installed the previously mentioned seat, upon that, as before,
[one should place] the *liṅga* endowed with the *mūrti-mantra* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the *pīṭha-mantra*.
Having realized Śiva and having performed the ritual installation (samāropa), one should then assign his limbs (aṅgas).
Having offered the arghya as before, and having performed the worship and the fire-oblation,
the preceptor should perform the rite of the fourth day and the dismissal of his own mantra.
Thus has the ritual sprinkling been declared; it was taught for those who have performed worship for six months or more.
It effects the purification of the liṅga and bestows the fruits of the root image.
Thus, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), including the *liṅga* and other objects up to the attendant deities,
has been performed entirely without dependence on others for the sake of awakening the disciples.
The characteristics of the limbs (*aṅga*) for initiation (*dīkṣā*) and installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) have not been stated here;
rather, this shall serve as a technical exposition (*paribhāṣā*) for the *Kriyākramavibodha*.
[This was composed] by the venerable Śrīnetraśivārya, the conqueror of Tāraka, the foremost among the hosts of teachers known as the stainless Śrīśāna-Śiva and his predecessors.
And he was delighted.
The illustrious and excellent teacher named Ghorashiva— knower of the sacred self and of knowledge— who is none other than the Supreme Lord himself,
shone forth in the southern region like the risen sun, accompanied by the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs.
He whose intellect is well-refined by the *Susaṃskṛta*, whose fuel for debate is his skill in composition, who thrice knows the scriptures, who is the best among the best of men,
an ocean of the treatises on logic (*nyāya*) and other sciences, an expert in the knowledge of speech, foremost in the exposition of the Śiva doctrine— he [expresses] gratitude...
The ritual procedure for consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is taught in four directions regarding one’s own self and the supreme gurus.
The lineage (gotra) is to be known as fourfold, and the spheres of activity (gocara) are recorded as sixteen.
There are four sages of the lineages, and their stations are fourfold.
Thirty-six of them are proclaimed as brothers who were sages;
fifteen monasteries are mentioned, and four trees are said to exist.
Sāvitrī, known as Gāyatrī, as well as Bhāratī and Manonmanī—these are said to be the Śaktis of Śiva; some [also mention] the gotras.
Śiva and the others are the presiding deities of the Gāyatrī and other mantras, and likewise their respective objects of perception;
those which are the divisions of these, such as the Prājāpatya and so forth, should be known.
Due to the differentiation of the objects to be presided over, they perceive something of the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
For the state of being a lineage (gotra) belongs to its subdivisions, whereas its primary status is that of a quality (guṇa).
The *gotras*, their presiding deities such as Śiva and others, and the *gocarās* are distinct.
If it is held that the *gocarās* are indeed distinct from the *gotras*,
then let it be understood that their respective functions (*vṛttis*) are the *gocarās*.
The best of teachers, who know the established doctrine, consider this to be correct.

The term *gocara* is said to mean "family" (*kula*) because it is established as a synonym for lineage (*gotra*), ancestry (*anvaya*), family (*kula*), and so forth, according to the work of Śrīkaraṇa.

The lineage (*gotra*) known as Sāvitrī is established as the auspicious crest-light (*śivaśikhājyotis*); it is conceived as being presided over by *bindu*, *nāda*, gross *bindu*, and *nāda*. From Śiva, through Śakti, there arises the fourfold *bindu* and *nāda*.
The lineage is a station consisting of light; in some places, it is the fivefold state of the gurus.
In Śālmala, the one known as Śāka, Puṣkara, and the one named Kuśa—
these four are situated respectively in all the other continents.
Due to the division of each [deity] into four forms, there are sixteen spheres of experience (*gocara*).
O Śivā, the *prājāpatya*, the *pālās*, the *kapolas*, and the *granthikas* are in the *śikhā*-family;
likewise, the *kuṭikās* and the *vetālās* are in the *padmagṛha*.
The Dhṛtarāṣṭras, Bakas, Kākas, and Gopālas are recorded as belonging to the sphere of light.
The Tuṭikāmāras, the Śuddhikas, and others, the Daṇḍins;
Bhāradvāja in the Śivakula, and Kuśika in the one called Śiva;
Kāśyapa is to be known in Jyotiṣa, and the sage Gautama in Sāvitra.
The parasol of Bhāradvāja was black, and that of Kuśika was white.
The *nāgara* [mantra] was taught by Kāśyapa; that which arises from the nails belongs to Gautama. The lords of the *gotras* are thus declared, as are the brothers.
Śaṅkha, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, the one known as Pāṇḍarāśvabhra,
the one named Śuka, Śunaka, Manu, and Kṛṣṇapiṅgala—
these nine are remembered as the younger brothers of Bhāradvāja.
Namuci, Dakṣa by name, Bhṛgu, and the two delights of Vālmīki.
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Bodhāyana, and Sanātana—
these brothers of Kuśika are proclaimed as the nine in the Śikhā lineage.
Aṅgiras, he who is known as Sthūla, Śāṇḍilya who is without a [specific] name,
Āpastamba, Uśanābhūti, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Virājaka—
these nine brothers of Kāśyapa are proclaimed in the third [generation].
Bāḍaba, Gārgya by name, Vasiṣṭha, Māṭhara, Atri,
Gārgala, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Kātyāyana, and Uśanas;
Sāvitrī was born within the range of Gautama’s gaze, and she had two brothers.
The monastery named Kailāsa is proclaimed as the first, and the Pālāśa is the second.
Valāhaka shall be the third, and Kalpagrāma the fourth;
Badarikā is to be known as the fifth, and after that, Devadāruvana.
Then the *Kakambasaptama*, followed by the *Śaṅkhottarāraṇyaka*;
after that the *Dakṣiṇāraṇyaka*, and beyond that the *Govindāna*.
The Āmarda, Mattamayūra, Adraṇabhadra, Golaki,
Kadamba, Aru, Aśvattha, Vaṭa, and Amaṃ-vibhūṣaṇa.
This is common to all and is called the "evenly continuous" [breathing],
provided that the breath is not forced into the hollow [of the navel] and is attached to something other than that which is intent upon Śiva.
The family of Śiva has manifested, presided over by the power of Gāyatrī;
from that [family] proceed, in sequence, the Great Lords of Mantra, the Gaṇas, the deities, and so forth.
The family of Śiva, characterized by the yoga of the channels (*nāḍī*), the wheels (*cakra*), self-knowledge, and the seed-syllables (*bīja*),
descended into the great sage Durvāsas.
It became the abode of those who were favored by him alone, such as the Mṛṣyādins.
It is the illustrious place named Āmardaka, adorned with kadamba and mango trees.
At that time, there was a place on the earth in Bhārata, the land of liberation, which arose from the lineage of the venerable Āmardaka-sandhāma. (Verse 5)
I bow to the sage Durvāsas, the awakener of the knowledge of Śiva,
from whom [the lineage] beginning with the one named Paiṅgala proceeded in succession through the line of gurus.
Then, having been transferred by way of livelihood to the human being named Paitāmaha,
four spheres of activity (*gocara*) arose, designated as Prājāpatya and the others.
Through non-violence, service to the teacher, self-study, purity, and self-restraint—
by these qualities they are characterized as true, arising from the sphere of the Prajāpati state.
The lineage of gurus arose, centered upon the distinguished mantra of Śiva.
Vyāpakaśiva, the excellent teacher of Lāṭa, was the supreme guru among them;
he became the lord of the monastery known as Āmarda, just like the venerable Durvāsas.
His disciple was Sarveśa Paṇḍita, the foremost among the Gauḍas.
The Guru established his residence at Nīlavāṭāgha in Pattana.
Then there was Somaśiva, born there, who was a lord of ascetics belonging to that region.
Then Pūrṇaśivācārya, honored by the king in Vārāṇasī,
[departed] from there.
From him [came] Vidyeśānaśiva; from him, Āryavratīśvara;
from him, the one known as Vidyāntaśiva, born in the land of Cola.
In Vārāṇasī was Nṛpācārya, a master who had reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge;
from him came Brahmaśivācārya, an ascetic and the preeminent leader of the Lāṭas.
From him came Mūrtiśiva, who resided in the city named Vijaya.
In Māyāpurī, the teacher who is the self of all resides, having taken birth there.
His disciple was Gauḍavṛṣabha, the venerable teacher Śrīkaṇṭhaśiva,
who resembled the face of the Lord of the illustrious Darbha assembly and who had gone to the river-bank.
The illustrious King Vikramāditya installed him as his own preceptor;
thereafter, the venerable Dhyānaśiva became the preeminent leader of Gauḍa.
This teacher was skilled in the exposition of the twenty-eight Tantras.
Having worshipped Coleśvara, he then worshipped Sabheśa.
Therefore,
there arose one named Hṛdayaśaṅku, who had mastered all the Āgamas and possessed a pure disposition;
he was the foremost descendant of my grandfather’s paternal uncle, renowned on earth as Śaivādhirāja.
The younger brother of our father’s maternal uncle was Parameśvara;
he was favored by the illustrious Dhyānaśiva and made his preceptor. (133b, 1st line)

I bow to that one who possesses the eye of the Śiva-tantras, the supreme among the sciences beginning with the Vedas, who is delighted by the power of the sun-like Śiva directly perceived, and who is the manifest bestower of grace; there,
he is the Jewel of the Lineage (Anvayaratna), praised by all, and a dweller in Kāñcī.
The wise one, who touches the glory of his own abode, who is named the Supreme Lord, and who severs the bonds of worldly existence—
known on earth by that very name— he favored me [for the sake of Śarajanman].
The Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, the ocean of compassion, spoke thus.
In those compendia known as the *Kālottara*, three hundred and fifty [verses] were composed by the author,
who [composed another work] with ten hundred [verses].
Whatever has not been stated here has merely been hinted at, not fully revealed.
And having consulted another extensive compendium, the Saṃhitā.
Furthermore, the daily and occasional rites have been performed by our ancient and most excellent gurus according to the *Uttuṅgaśivapaddhati*.
This has been performed according to the *Siddhāntasārapaddhati*, together with its oral instructions,
received from our most excellent Guru, the venerable Sarvātmaśiva. Thus,
the daily rites and so forth have been explained along with their underlying reasoning, out of reverence.
Having heard this, I have composed this illumination of the sequence of ritual actions.
Since this was composed by me at the command of my venerable master,
may the wise gurus not find fault with it herein.

In the year of Śaka, composed for those seeking to know the Nāda, this *Dyotikā*, which elucidates the sequence of ritual action (*kriyākrama*), consisting of one thousand five hundred [verses], has been fashioned. Thus [ends] the work composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara.
The ritual procedure for consecration in the *Kriyākramadyotikā* is completed.
As consisting of *bindu* and *nāda*, Śiva— who is indefinable and imperishable—
shines forth for those engaged in yoga whose selves have been washed by the waters of *śakti*.

At the commencement of all undertakings, one who is free from all worldly exertion should contemplate the Self as consisting of *nāda*, shaped like a *kadamba* flower bud and flashing with rays of power (*śakti*).
Hari Om. May there be auspiciousness. Salutations to Sāmbaśiva. Salutations to Gaṇapati.
The virtuous ought to forgive the offense committed by me. Homage to Skanda!
The *liṅga* is the seat of Sadāśiva, while the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) is the seat of the *liṅga*. Viṣṇu is the seat of the pedestal, and from that, Brahmā is the seat of Viṣṇu.
The Brahmāsana is indeed the tortoise; thus the fivefold seat is prescribed.
Inspection is performed with the root mantra, and sprinkling with the weapon mantra.
Striking is done with the weapon mantra, and sprinkling should be performed with the armor mantra.
Having formed the *gokarṇa* (cow-ear) hand gesture, one should drink water in which a *māṣa* bean has been submerged.
Having surely drunk that water excessively, it would turn into blood;
Brahmā himself [held] the wrist-bind, while Śatakratu [held] the thumb.
Īśvara is said to be on the index finger, Mādhava as the deity on the middle finger,
Ananta on the ring finger, and Bhāskara on the little finger.
The palm is indeed all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), O Sāvitrī;
the presiding deity is the lineage of the disciple (*śiṣyagotra*), while the womb (*yoni*) is the tongue of the Guru, and the *liṅga* is the same.
Through the union of mantra and bindu, the disciple is ordained as a son.
Now follows the application of the Great Net (Mahājāla).

This network of channels has been described; now hear about the "Great Net" (mahājāla), which is proclaimed to be the form of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth, as well as the "knots of the net."
Whatever color the letter 'A' may have, that same color is said to belong to the jewel;
the cord used for the net is traditionally known as dharma and adharma.
Like one standing on the bank of a river with a net cast without effort,
he perceives the power of the fish-net as it enters into the midst of the water.
With his left hand placed upon the water-vessel on the pedestal,
the preceptor, manifesting the mantra-body, should utter the name of initiation.
Having drawn in the self by means of the net of mantras with the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*),
and having seized it with the withdrawal-gesture (*saṃhāriṇī*), one should unite it with the mantra-body.
Afterwards, at the conclusion of the ritual action, one should join [the breath] according to the path of the higher [realities]:

the *ātmatattva* reaches the end of the navel, the *vidyātattva* reaches the end of the throat, and the *śivatattva* should reach the end of the twelve fingers (*dvādaśānta*). Having drunk the [nectar], one becomes pure.

Having thus drunk it three times, one should touch [the mouth] twice with the thumb. Regarding the "knowable through sound" (*nādajñeya*): *na* is the single location; *da* is the ten locations; *ña* is the hundred locations; *ya* is the thousand locations; *stra* is the location of the stake (*śūlasthāna*); *stra* is the location of emptiness (*śūnyasthāna*).
And therefore: [it is said that] "he performed the *kiyākrama* at Tadakayila for eighty-nine thousand years.
This is the procedure for the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣāvidhi*).
[Kāmika, 135a (197a)].
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall describe the initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā),
especially on an auspicious day, a favorable lunar fortnight, and at a particularly propitious moment.
In a solitary and secluded place at midnight,
a true teacher should especially bestow awakening upon worthy disciples.
[This should be done] in a temple of Śiva, in the abode of the Guru, on a Śakti-pīṭha, in a monastery, or in a house.
Seated comfortably in a pure place, [one should contemplate] those things arising from the five objects of sense.

On an auspicious day, upon a seat of darbha grass, a tiger skin, or a six-legged stool in the center of the pedestal— the dwelling place of the True Guru and the abode of happiness for men— [one should perform the rite].
Having worshipped [the deity] in the center of the yoga-pīṭha with the services of bathing, garlands, all kinds of ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, [one should proceed].
One should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*apūpa*), and betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*);
one should worship at the feet of the Guru with the sixteen modes of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).
The most excellent and true teacher should especially perform the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*).
One should offer one's body, wealth, and vital breath to the true gurus.
In the presence of the guru, one who is shameless should not commit even a long transgression.
That teacher should especially bring about awakening for one who is a true disciple.

The compassionate teacher should cause a vessel of perfumes and flowers to be placed upon the heads of each respective disciple; having offered it in the midst of their heads, he should place his foot [upon them].
Thereafter, one should awaken the disciple to this true nature of knowledge:
first is the essential form of reality (*tattvarūpa*), second is the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*),
third is the body of reality (*tattvaśarīra*), and fourth is the characteristic of the self (*ātmalakṣaṇa*).
The fifth is the self-contemplation, and the sixth should be the self-purification.
The seventh is called the Śivarūpa; the eighth is the Śivadarśana;
the ninth is the Śivayoga; and the tenth is the Śivabhoga. By means of the fourth [chapter], which consists of three groups of three divisions, [he explains] the triad of Pati, Pāśa, and Paśu.
Revealed through the path of the guru’s word by one who is liberated while living.
"Thus is the path of knowledge that reveals the meaning prescribed. So it is stated in the Kāmika (135b, first line).
Then, in the Sūkṣma:
"Hereafter I shall proclaim the rite of initiation through knowledge; listen to the procedure."
For one whose body is bound by impurity, that [impurity] is burnt away by the initiation of knowledge.
The wise one knows that knowledge which is like the sun, as described in the *Andhakārapada*,
as well as the mantra, the words and syllables, the world, the principle (*tattva*),
the digit (*kalā*), and the self; when these are purified, for him there is no further birth.
Thus, at its conclusion, one is united with Nirvana through the initiation of knowledge.
Then the Guru should perform the initiation and instruct one who has been fully prepared;
having smeared the ground with cow dung, it should be adorned with various patterns made of flour.
Above that, one should place a lion-throne endowed with the proper characteristics,
adorned with perfumes and flowers, and provided with hair arranged in braided locks.
Adorned with pearls, linen garments, and fragrant pastes, and provided with lotuses, blue water-lilies, *āragvadha*, *bilva*, *śamī*, and *dūrvā* grass—
the Preceptor [should perform the rites].
Having adorned him with dukūla garments and an upper cloth over his turban,
having decorated him with all ornaments and anointed him with fragrant sandalwood paste,
he was further embellished with ashes, rudrākṣa beads, and a yogic belt.
Having adorned [the image] with flower garlands and recollecting its nature as the deity's form,
the Guru, facing south, should place it upon a throne provided with hanging footrests for Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
The disciple,
having performed the purification and other rites upon his body, adorned with clean garments,
marked with the signs of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and reciting the Śiva-mantra; (line 7)
Having approached the presence of the Guru with hands joined in añjali and facing north, one should stand and proclaim one's knowledge.
The Preceptor,
by gazing with the vision of wisdom from the crown of the head down to the feet,
[purifies] the accumulated impurity at that moment; thereafter, the remainder is [cleansed] in due order.
The disciple:
one should perform the pure consecration from the knees down to the feet,
and one should also consecrate him with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Endowed with the pure consecration and the lifting up of the cloth,
