one should worship according to the ritual procedure, applying perfumes and sandalwood paste, as well as the disciple.
The disciple should duly offer milk-rice as the sacrificial food, accompanied by fruits, cakes, and *gilas*, together with incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering.
One should worship the feet of the Guru with the sixteenfold service;
at that time, the presence of the [deity] shall abide within the body of the disciple.
Having performed circumambulation and prostration as before, the Guru stands at the head [of the disciple]—
the Ācārya—
and should place the Śiva-hand upon the disciple’s head and impart the subtle mantra.
Thereafter, the Guru should duly place the Śrīpāda [mantra] on the head, the mouth, the heart, the eyes, the ears, or the arms, according to the prescribed rite.
In this way, the *prārabdha* impurity alone remains before the Sun like a house-lamp;
having rendered it devoid of light, the impurity likewise [remains].
Then, because the village was burnt by the five impurities, the Guru should awaken that disciple through the sequence of the ten tasks, starting with the installation of the feet of Śiva.
His knowledge is exceedingly subtle, its domain transcending both speech and mind.
It is a secret, exceedingly hidden, subtler than the subtle, and composed of Śiva.
"The disciple should offer his body, wealth, and life to the true gurus.
At the conclusion of that [initiation], the name "Giri" is prescribed for one who is perfected in knowledge; thus it is stated in the *Sūkṣmāgama* and the *Kriyākaraṇamaṇḍana*.
In gardens, in temples of Śiva, on the banks of rivers, in the abode of lotuses, in Kāñcīpura, on the sands of the ocean, on Mount Jalpeśvara, in a cow-pen,
in the houses of one’s preceptor, or in the temple of the illustrious Kālahastīśvara—
In Gokarṇa, amidst the vast forest, is your initiation ground for embodied beings, O Lord of the Site.
He states the time for initiation: "At the time of the northern solstice, during the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day."
One should perform the rite of initiation at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction of planets.
In the *Kālottara*,

the practice regarding the procedure for the rite of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*) is that the conjunction of autumn and spring is the proper time. In the absence of those two seasons, it is possible [to perform it] at other times as well, even without regard for the year.
During initiation, consecration, as well as the formal reception of mantras, at the commencement and conclusion of a vow, during the acquisition of ritual materials, and during ritual action;
on the full moon day of Kārttika, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, and also upon the appearance of the sun [at the new moon]; [one should not study].
And that which is joined with the concealment of the day, as well as the other states (sthiti) that are traditionally taught.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods,
during the conjunctions of planets and lunar mansions, and even on the festivals of the Viṣṇu days.
In all solstices, a sacrifice grants the fulfillment of all aims;
[one should avoid] the fourth, ninth, sixth, eighth, and fourteenth [lunar days].
For those desiring prosperity, all the remaining [days] except for the full moon day are auspicious for those seeking enjoyment,
provided one avoids the days of the Sun, Mars, and Saturn.
The three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Karka, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Hasta, Svātī, Anurādhā, Makhā, Mūla,
Revatī, Abhijit, and Śravaṇa— these constitute the Śiva-yoga on the fourteenth day.
And Yoga, Prīti, Āyuṣmat, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, and Śubhā.
Sukarman, Vadhṛti, Vṛddhi, Sravas, Siddhi, Harṣaṇa,
Varīyān, Śiva, and Siddha— these sixteen [were born] from the Brāhmaṇas.
The instruments [are] empty, auspicious, and all those which are eternal are praised for the sake of liberation.
(7th line) The ritual procedure for the worship of knowledge. (137a, 1st line)
(199a) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the worship of gnosis (*jñāna*).
How does gnosis— which is exceedingly difficult to attain— arise within persons?
That knowledge is to be known as twofold, through the division of the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*).
The first is the supreme knowledge, which reveals the Lord (*pati*), the fetter (*pāśa*), and the self (*ātman*);
the second is the lower knowledge, which reveals only the fetter.
Just as in the example [given], it is seen at night in the eyes of both a man and a cat.
Thus, this supreme and subordinate knowledge is characterized by such distinctions;
for whatever [karma] one performs in another birth through the specific ripening of that action, [it results in this].
Through the glance of the Preceptor of Knowledge, the wise one who knows the three categories and the means of valid cognition,
having attained the object of knowledge through knowledge, should commence the worship of knowledge. Having risen early in the morning, he should contemplate Śiva at the conclusion [of his duties].
One should perform the daily rites according to the prescriptions of the ritual section.
At the time of bathing, having meditated upon the water as an ocean of supreme nectar,
one should contemplate Śiva— who is partless, stainless, manifest, and eternally liberated.
Having bathed, if one is joined with Vedic rites, one should perform the Sandhyā worship;
one should contemplate the immutable Doer, the witness of all actions.
(6th line) One should perform the Ācamana rite together with the mantras beginning with the Tattvas of the Self and ending with Śiva.
Having meditated upon the supreme light, one should wear the ashes with the five-syllabled mantra.

Or one may perform [the rite] by means of the method of smearing ashes (*uddhūlana*) or by the method of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*). Through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, one effects the exit of sin from within.
Having filled [the body] with that consciousness of Śiva and performed the kumbhaka (retention) thereof,
one should purify the palms and the backs of the hands by means of the Praṇava alone.

Having performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the five syllables together with the *āsana* and the root-form (*mūrti*) in sequence, one should thereafter perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
One should meditate upon Śiva, who is both with parts and without parts, eternal, and consisting of consciousness and bliss;
one should satisfy the eight deities who protect the forms beginning with Śarva, as well as the Guru.
Having meditated upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should offer three oblations to him with the root mantra.
The satisfaction of the lineage-preceptor occurs through the path of each respective continuum.
One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the embodiments of the *samayācāra* according to the prescribed rule;
one should offer the respectful water (*arghya*) with their respective personal-name mantras,
but [the offering] to Śiva should be made with the mantra ending in *svāhā*, in due order, and one should satisfy them with that water.
Having sprinkled oneself with water while reciting the root mantra and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one becomes fully consecrated (sakalīkṛta).
Having meditated upon Śiva, he should then not show the place and other surroundings to the temple;
having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should enter the place of worship.
Facing north and seated upon a beautiful seat,
having applied sacred ash, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras on the hands (karanyāsa) and the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Having prepared the *arghya* offering and having performed purification everywhere, especially [within the ritual space],
one should bathe the Supreme Lord after worshipping him according to the prescribed rule.
Then, until midday, one should remain established in samādhi,
[visualizing] the *liṅga* consisting of the light of consciousness, as radiant as the autumnal moon; there,
situated in the middle of the throat (*kaṇṭha*), one should join the mind and the vital breaths.
The yogi, whose time for absorption has arrived, should gradually lead the mind toward emptiness.
When the mind has perished, the supreme bliss of consciousness shines forth by itself;
this indeed is called samādhi, the abode of the qualities such as aṇimā and the rest.
If one is unable to do so, then having meditated upon Śiva and the other [deities],
beginning with the first, according to the path taught by the Guru, [one should recite] the Śiva-mantra.
In the absence of that, having performed recitation (*japa*) and listened to the scriptures with devotion,
the teacher of knowledge should then commence the midday worship.
Taking recourse at the southern gate, one should perform the worship of knowledge;
worship facing south is supreme, for it is the cause of attaining the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
Abiding in the form of the Preceptor (*ācārya*), Hara faces the south.
One should provide instruction in knowledge for the sake of destroying the bonds of living beings.
Therefore, the worship of the southern face shall be endowed with wisdom;
having commenced the worship there, one should indeed perform the application of sacred ash.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord;
having recited the five-syllabled mantra once and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa),
one should offer arghya with that water and sprinkle the collection of substances at the door and elsewhere with the Śiva-mantra.
Then, having performed the worship of the doors with the mantras of the lineage preceptors, |||
Having placed the rosary in the southeast and the vessel for ashes in the southwest,
and having set down the scriptures of Śiva in the west, one should then worship them.
In the north, one should thoroughly honor the foremost among the devotees of Śiva.
Having prostrated and designated [the deity] as the witness of the worship, one should sprinkle [the materials] and meditate upon Śiva.

Having purified the self and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should meditate with palms joined together upon [the deity] who is conjoined with the principles (tattva) and sub-principles (upatattva), and characterized by both the gross and the subtle.
One should contemplate each of the principles (*tattva*s), beginning with earth, as being distinct within this body which is joined to the paths;
and one should contemplate [the soul] as the enjoyer of the fruits of *prārabdha* karma, acting under the command of Śiva.
That body, having perished by its own will through inquiry, [is destroyed] in an instant.
Having abandoned his ancient home, he attained a new one;
having cast off his body, a divine splendor manifested.
One should not contemplate the nine [worlds] as eternal, composed of consciousness and bliss;
rather, one should contemplate them within one's own stainless body as being pervaded by the power of Kṣuṇḍa,
possessing bodies consisting of the abode of Śiva and vehicles of abundant nectar.
Then, one should contemplate the Self residing in that ālaya as being of the nature of Śiva.
The internal sacrifice (antaryāga) should be performed within that stainless Self;
one should offer oblation at the navel and contemplate the partless, all-pervading Śiva between the eyebrows as the locus of worship,
whose nature is the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā-tattva).
Having dispelled the net of nooses with divine vision through the splendor of Śiva.
Having filled it right here, one should meditate upon the arghya vessel,
having washed it with the *bahurūpa* mantra and with the *śiva* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
One should fill [the vessel] with pure water and arrange the perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
one should worship it with the five-syllabled mantra for eleven times (the number of Rudras).
Having performed the binding of the directions and so forth, one should consecrate [the offering] by means of the cow-seal (dhenumudrā) as nectar.
One should sprinkle the collections of liquids and purify them through the rites of gazing and so forth.
Reciting the Śiva-mantra ten times over the flowers and casting them away, one achieves purification according to the Tantra, preceded by the three *tālas*.
By means of the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and other rites, the site is rendered an immersion in nectar (*amṛta*).
One should contemplate both the exterior and the interior as being filled with auspicious splendor.
Having taken the *liṅga* with the root mantra, one should discard any stale flowers;
having consecrated it with the weapon mantra, one should perform the ablution with the previously offered water of honor (*arghya*).
One should worship that [seat] with the seat-mantra and the form-mantra;
having invoked Śiva with the root-mantra, one should offer perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having offered incense and lamps with the heart-mantra, one should present the arghya with the root-mantra.
Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth.
Having bathed Śiva with perfumed water, pure water, the root mantra, and arghya water,
and having wiped him dry with a clean cloth, one should place him upon the seat.
Having offered these, one should present drops of ash, flowers, and *arghya*.
(Third line) [One should worship] the form whose posture is curved at the ends, consisting of will, knowledge, and action.
Having thus meditated upon Lakulīśvara as identical with Śiva through the root mantra,
one should again worship him with both the seat and the image using the root mantra alone,
while contemplating the bliss of Śiva, which is eternally arisen and imperishable.

One should offer the triad beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*)— namely, water for the feet, water for sipping (*arghya*), and water for the face— respectively upon the foot consisting of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), the mouth consisting of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and the head consisting of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).
One should worship Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with garlands.
Having sacrificed to the bull in front and to the lords of sages at the two sides,
and having worshipped Agastya and the others, one should then honor the Guru.
Having offered incense and a lamp to Śiva, one should present three handfuls of flowers.
One should cause to be offered an oblation of food endowed with the six flavors along with side dishes;
having given water for drinking and sipping, one should then present betel leaf.
Having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should worship Śiva until the end of the recitation;
having praised Mahādeva with mantras and bowed again and again with devotion,
one should offer the entire fruit of that worship into the water.
There, one should pray for one's desired object and worship Śiva with flowers.
Having offered the *arghya* with its face turned away and having rendered it supreme by means of the root mantra,
one should meditate upon [the deity] as partless and stainless, and then install him in his proper place.
Having worshipped, praised, and bowed to one's own guru upon the seat, one should bid him farewell; one should contemplate the Lord Śiva— the supreme auspiciousness, partless, stainless,
consisting of consciousness and bliss, eternal, and whose form is splendor.
One should eat what has been offered to him; there is no such thing as his discarded floral remains (nirmālya).
In this manner, the devoted man performed the worship endowed with knowledge;
he shall become wealthy and glorious in this very life, and at the end, he shall attain liberation.
[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the worship of knowledge in the Jñānapāda of the great tantra called the Vātula.]
May it be auspicious.
(140a, 1st line) || The Ritual for the Worship of Gnosis (Jñānapūjāvidhi) in the Kāmika [Tantra]. ||
One should worship the God Nandin during the day, and never at night;
one should worship the God constantly during the day, and avoid it at night.

Thus is the sequence of the worship of knowledge (*jñānapūjākrama*). Purity of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is the absence of pride regarding the distinctions between the forms of the elements. Purity of substances (*dravyaśuddhi*) is the absence of longing for sense objects. Alternatively, purity of the elements is the perception of the eightfold form (*aṣṭamūrti*) of Śiva; purity of substances is the perception of Śiva’s permeation into all substances. [This occurs] in the five-syllabled [mantra] consisting of three words.

Having abandoned the two syllables of the word following "pāśa" and understood the two syllables of the word following the meaning of "pati," as well as the single syllable of the word following the meaning of "paśu," one should abandon the verbal and mental [conceptions] and practice the contemplation of the identity of the signified.
The purification of the mantra:
as it is stated in the *Siddhāntabodha*:
"Having omitted the word 'namaḥ', when [the name] is proclaimed as 'to Śiva'..."
"This pure five-syllabled [mantra] reveals one's own direct experience.
Thus, having perceived one's own true nature through the knowledge of Śiva, abiding as one with that [nature] is self-purification (*ātmaśuddhi*).

The purification of the *liṅga* consists of the contemplation of Śiva, whose nature is indivisible form (*akhaṇḍākāra*), existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), and who is to be known through experience alone.
Now, the seat and so forth are described: the Self is the seat of Śiva;
the Form is truth, knowledge, and the unobscured; the Root is supreme bliss. Next, the invocation (*āvāhana*) is described.
In this context, the manifestation of Śiva alone is traditionally known as "invocation" (āvahana). Immobility is "establishment" (sthāpana), facing toward [the deity] is "proximity" (sannidhāna),
and the cessation of dissolution, distraction, and effusion is called "firm fixation" (sannirodhana).
Hereafter, I shall explain the worship of Śiva beginning with the water for the feet (pādya).

The dissolution of the two-fold illusion is the water for the feet; likewise, the water for sipping is the destruction of the threefold karma. The water for the guest-offering is the liberation from ignorance. The great consecration is the removal of the floral garland; the pure garment is the state of being unconditioned.
Nirlepana, śrīgandha, dvivarāga, and prasūnaka.
The destruction of the latent impressions of ignorance is the incense; self-luminosity is the lamp;
the experience of Śiva is the food offering; and the well-perfumed water is the drinking water.
The removal of impurities from the teeth by means of liquids or powders is called *bhasmodvartana*;
chewing betel leaf, which produces a cleansing effect and fragrance for the mouth, is known as *mukhavāsana*.
The dissolution (*laya*) of the sound known as *āhata* is said to be located there;
it is circumambulatory and all-pervading together with Śambhu.
Just as water becomes of one taste through its union with rivers and oceans,
so too is the union of the Self and Śiva proclaimed as a salutation.
Just as the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge become submerged [in oneness], so it is for you.
They say that the water for the guest (arghya) offered with one's face turned away is an offering made to oneself.
Thus ends the worship of knowledge according to the method of the intermediate Śaiva tradition.
The Procedure for Initiation (*Dīkṣākrama*) according to the *Śaivasannyāsapaddhati*.

The Preceptor (*ācārya*), having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the phonemes, words, liberated energies (*muktakalā*), and mantras, and having contemplated "I am Śiva," becoming immersed in supreme bliss, should perform the initiation regarding the rules (*samaya*) and so forth for the disciples. [He should initiate] the disciples...

Having examined those who have served for the duration of a year through their devotion, and having discerned— by means of their merit toward Śiva, their worship of Śiva, their detachment from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and their desire for liberation— their capacities ranging from very weak to very intense, as well as whether they are endowed with *nipāta* [initiation], he should perform the initiation of the *samaya* and other rites in accordance with that capacity.
As it is said in the *Kālottara*:
"The Guru should examine his dependent disciples for one year through commands such as the giving of his own life-force or wealth, and by means of both equal and unequal [tasks]."
If those who, having made even the lowliest perform the highest deeds,
do not fall into despondency when drawn away or even insulted; and if they are intent on the practice of the work that refines the arrow— then [they are truly disciplined].
In the Raurava [tantra], the teacher, having caused the disciple to be joined with the descent of the intense power (tīvraśakti),
becomes immersed within for a moment in supreme bliss.
Having become one with the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), one should look [upon the disciple] for the sake of the removal of bonds.
Now follows the procedure for initiation into the communal observance (*samayadīkṣā*).
The teacher should adorn himself with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
This has been stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"With sandalwood mixed with camphor powder, as well as with saffron..."

The preceptor, being wise, should especially adorn himself with ash mixed with fragrances, as well as with ornaments— specifically with garments of linen and silk, and various pure ornaments and the like. Then, in the presence of the teacher, the measurement of the hand...

One should prepare two circles with cow dung using the Astra-mantra; the space between them should be square, oriented from south to north. However, in the case of the *bhautikī* initiation, one should prepare two circles oriented from west to east. In the case of the initiation for those committed to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-naiṣṭhika*), [the orientation is as follows].
In both mandalas, having arranged kusha grass with unbroken grains and tips pointing upward, one should worship the sixfold arising seat there; then,
[one should place] upon it the candidate who has been examined, who has fasted,
and who has consumed the five products of the cow.

Having been requested by the first disciple, he should cause the disciple to stand facing north; then, having gazed from the feet to the crown of the head with divine vision established by the root mantra, and having sprinkled [the disciple] with the water of the general *arghya* using the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
[he should perform the rite for] the disciple.
Having struck the heart with that same mantra using ashes, having sprinkled it three times again with arghya water using that same mantra,
and having sprinkled it with the armor-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should [strike] below and above the navel in sequence with the roots and tips of *kuśa* grass using the weapon-mantra.
One should recite [the mantra] three times. In the initiation of the elemental (bhautika) type, having placed *kuśa* grass with rice grains upon two mandalas with their tips pointing eastward,

and having worshipped the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) there, one should establish the elemental disciple— whose body is straight from the big toes to the head and whose hands are joined in *añjali*— before the Preceptor, who is composed of light, and then [address] him.
Having gazed with divine vision established by the root mantra from the head down to the feet, one should perform sprinkling as before,
followed by striking with the hand, sprinkling again, and the *asūkṣaṇa* rite; then, with the tips of *kuśa* grass, one should proceed in order above the navel.

One should mark [the disciple] three times with the *astra-mantra* using *kuśa* roots. Then, having visualized the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, Fire, and Śakti within the heart-lotus of the disciple, and having visualized the individual soul (*jīva*) situated there in the form of a shimmering star, one should strike the disciple’s self with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and bind it with: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ namas to the form of the Self*.

Having worshipped Śiva on the head of the disciple with the eight-fold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) consisting of white flowers and other such items, and having applied a *tilaka* mark on his forehead, he should place half of that [offering] upon his heart and cast the flowers into his two hands while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having prepared a blindfold made of silk, fine linen, or cotton— a new cloth endowed with the fourfold accomplishment beginning with inspection—

and having consecrated it with the root mantra, veiled it with the armor-mantra (*varman*), and protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should bind the disciple's eyes with that cloth while reciting the eye-mantra (*netramantra*). Thus says the Āgama:
He was given a blindfold so that he could not see the others;
yet, from the very sight [of them], that same latent impression (vāsanā) arises once more as a bond.
Therefore, because [the disciple] is bound by those eyes, there is the "shattering of the bonds of the bound" (*paśu-pāśa-vighaṭṭana*).

Then, having led the disciple clockwise around, he should place him— whether a *sannyāsin* or a *naiṣṭhika*— in the northern mandala, and a *bhautika* in the eastern mandala, upon the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) as before.
This base self, whose bonds have been loosened so that it is worthy of attaining Śiva-hood, is under my control;
for even this entire multitude of fetters is subject to me alone through my own power.
The final consecration here is that which is suitable for the arising of one's own qualities;
and I, the stone, am the excellent and sovereign Lord, resembling a jewel upon the altar of touch.
"Having purified it through touch, as if instantly cleansing a water-pot,
I shall make him endowed with virtues and an ornament upon the heads of the virtuous.
Having thus informed [the disciple], he should strike the disciple's heart with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, using a flower released from the thumb and forefinger.

Having struck [the disciple] and entered his body through the path of the *nāḍīs*, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) by means of the five-fold concentration (*pañcadhāraṇā*), thoroughly cleansing the disciple’s body and making it a body of Śiva (*śivatanu*). Having seated him there, one should contemplate the worship, oblation, and meditation upon the *dadhat*, *lāḍī*, and *bindu* syllables; then, having brought the Self from that [state], one should worship the disciple with the left thumb.

Having prepared a fragrant mandala on the palm of the left hand, having worshipped Śiva there along with his limbs, his retinue, and his progeny, and having recited the root mantra from the piercing of the knots of the heart and other centers up to Paraśiva, [one should place it] upon the head of the disciple.

Having placed the *śivahasta* [upon the disciple] and purified the impurities of the disciple’s hands by means of the seated splendor of Śiva from the *brahmarandhra*, and having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkṛtya*), he should— if the disciple belongs to one of the three higher castes—instruct him in the six-syllabled mantra ending in the dative case; if he belongs to the fourth caste, he should instruct him in the five-syllabled mantra ending in the dative case. Then, having removed the eye-band, [he should contemplate] the three channels (*nāḍītraya*).

Having emerged from the body of the disciple and visualized [the disciple] as absorbed into one's own pure body, and having caused [the disciple] to bow before Śiva after first offering a handful of flowers for his favor, one should instruct him in the conduct of the Samaya, such as service to the Guru and so forth.
One should unite [the disciple] with the state of Śrīkaṇṭha.

Likewise, in the *Svāyambhuva*, having prepared the offering of perfumes and so forth (*gandhādyaṅgāraṃ*)— that is, the decoration beginning with perfume— one should [touch] the right [hand] with the left thumb.
One should assign the five [faces], beginning with Sadyojāta, to the five fingers, starting from the little finger.
Having worshipped Śiva along with his limbs in due order upon the palm of the hand,
he should touch that disciple with that hand on the head and the heart.
Thereafter, the Guru should perform the rite of sakalīkaraṇa with his heart.
Thus ends the procedure for the initiation of the pledge (samayadīkṣā).
Thus it should also be understood in the *Īśvaraśivācāryapaddhati*.
[Section on] the Special Initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*).

One should consecrate the disciple, who has been purified by the initiation of the *samaya* and has worshipped the maṇḍala of the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) as previously taught, with the initiation for the extraction of the knower of the Śiva-hermitage (*śivāśramin*). For it is stated [in the scripture]: "The extraction of birth is said to be twofold—general and particular—and likewise external and internal"—and thus, without the general procedure...
One should consecrate [the disciple] as follows:

having sprinkled the disciple with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), one should [sprinkle him] seven times with flowers consecrated by the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [reciting]: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmadeha huṃ phaṭ*.

Having performed the piercing (*bhedana*) in the heart with this very mantra, having entered by means of the *vāmā* [channel], having loosened [the knot] by means of the *jyeṣṭhā*, having drawn it out by means of the *raudrī* with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, and having grasped it with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* and led it to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.

Having grasped the self with the left [nostril] during inhalation (*pūraka*), having established it within one's own self, and having made it of one flavor through retention (*kumbhaka*), one should contemplate the self as the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva. Thus purified by the offering of contemplation, one possesses the purification of the body of the seed-syllable.
By your grace, may this twice-born one become Sadāśiva, an emanation of Rudra.
Having made this request, one should consecrate [the disciple] with the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *jātakarman*. Thereafter,
having entered the body of the disciple and performed the purification of the subtle and gross bodies as before, [one should proceed].
Having bathed the body of the bindu with a profuse stream of nectar overflowing from the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), and having emerged from the body of the disciple,
one leads the Self— which has been purified by the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* and which has the form of a shimmering star— from its own twelve [fingers] by means of *raudrī*.

Having gathered [the disciple's consciousness] with the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], having led it to the *brahmarandhra*, and having caused it to pervade the path of the *suṣumṇā*, one should unite the luminous Self within the heart; then, for the sake of nourishment, one should place a drop of clarified butter and water upon the head of the disciple. Thereafter, having prepared a mandala with cow dung—

There, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus and having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of Brahmā upon five of the petals with the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) into that mandala and bestow a name upon him using the formula beginning with the syllable *pa* (the first fallen flower), followed by the word *mūrti*, and ending with the word *śiva*.
Having performed the rite of emergence through the contemplation of entering into the state of Śiva,
the first feeding of solid food through the contemplation of being an enjoyer of supreme bliss, and the tonsure ceremony through the contemplation of the excellence of Śiva’s grace,
one should complete [the rites] by adding five, three, two, or one [additional elements].

One should wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) according to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. For a disciple established in a stage of life (*āśrama*) such as studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) up to the limit of that particular stage of life.
As stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*: [text omitted].
The sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta-sūtra*) for a Brahmin is traditionally prescribed as having five strands;
for a Kṣatriya it is said to have three strands, and for a Vaiśya it is traditionally prescribed as having two strands.
"The single-thread [sacred thread] is to be known as the constant and unswerving [rule] for the Śūdra.
In this regard, since the wearing of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is not established for the Śūdra by the general scripture, he states the restriction regarding the time [of its performance].
"In worship, in the fire-ritual, and at the time of the twilight prayers, and not otherwise. Thus,
in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, regarding the four stages of life (*caturāśrama*), the limit for each respective stage is [defined].
"One should perform the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*) in this manner; henceforth, one should not cause it to be performed.

Following that, having instructed the disciple in the five-syllable mantra of the temple (*prāsāda*), [he should engage him] in listening to the Siddhānta and in the worship of Śiva, the Fire, and the Guru.

Furthermore, one who knows the principles of conduct (*nītijña*) should not appoint someone who lacks the fitness for the initiation into *nirvāṇa* to that office. In this context, the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) refers to the head of the impure *māyā*-kalās presided over by the Lord. Subsequently, for those who are powerless—such as worldly people, children, and so forth—one should purify them according to their stage of life (*samaya*) and instruct them in the path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*). For those who are empowered, however, [one should instruct] the one established in the *śiva-āśrama*.
One should instruct him in the dharma of the Śiva-āśrama and the path of *prapatti*. Thus says the Āgama:
"Having done this, the best of teachers should purify his [disciple] for a year. (*Note: The text in parentheses appears to be a marginal or interlinear correction.*)
The best of gurus should cause the disciple to hear all the Samayas.

One must never lead away Śiva, the Śiva-scripture, the Śiva-fire, or likewise the Guru; nor should one ever cast even their shadow, under any circumstances. Worship of Śiva, the fire, and the Guru must be performed as long as one lives.
Now follows the procedure for the vow.
Thus it is said in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"Henceforth, I shall describe the vow for those who have been initiated;
indeed, the vow is of two kinds: Vaidika and Śaiva. (4th line)
The Vedic rites, such as the wearing of the sacred thread (upavīta) and so forth, are the duties of the three twice-born castes;
however, Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā) is the primary [duty], and everything else is exceedingly superior.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—brahmacarya is indeed twofold: the lifelong (naiṣṭhika) and likewise the temporary (bhautika).
Maintaining lifelong celibacy until the end of life,
wearing the sacred thread and carrying a staff, his body smeared with ashes,
his person marked with the triple horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra), and adorned with rudrākṣa beads.
Whether three times a day or at a single time, he should be engaged in bathing and have his senses subdued.
Speaking the truth, sleeping on the ground, endowed with patience, firm in his vows,
devoted to serving his guru, and intent on carrying out his guru’s commands;
eating only alms for the sake of sustaining the body once a day at the house of his guru.
One should likewise offer that very pūjāla, collyrium, turmeric, and salt.
One should avoid wearing shoes with leather soles and should abstain from perfumes, garlands, and the like.
One should always dwell in a cow-pen and never sleep in another's house.
Having abandoned one's own independence and so forth, and being joined with dependence upon the Guru,
[one attains] the field of merit, the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), as well as desire and the rest; indeed, everything,
and the vision of the Guru’s compassion again and again.
But austerity, charity, and so forth, when devoid of the guru's command, are fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should observe the command of the Guru.
Now hear the rule for lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya) for those who belong to the material realm.
Having determined the duration according to the prescribed rule as before, he should observe celibacy;
at the end, having performed the sacrifice to Vrateśvara, he should then proceed with the marriage.
A devotee of Śiva should grow matted hair, increasing those matted locks day by day out of devotion.
By that, the single fruit of eternity is attained; there is no doubt in this matter.
"Having become a practitioner of the vow for as long as life lasts, one who is self-restrained should determine the duration;
when the determined time has concluded, he should immediately worship Vrateśvara.
Thus it is said.
In the *Kiraṇa*,
it is stated that for others [the Śaivas], the topknot (*śikhā*) consists of the ash of a dull-witted twice-born,
whereas for a Brāhmaṇa, the ash-smearing itself constitutes the triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*) and the topknot.
But for the triad beginning with the Kṣatriya, [the measurements are] as follows:
the gross [measurement] should be known as double that, and the interval for the Kṣatriya is indeed [double].
What crest-lock is prescribed for the Vaiśya, and likewise what is proclaimed for the Śūdra?
When there is a great number [of locks], the rule regarding their number is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"By means of the number of the Tattvas, Mantras, and Mantreśvaras, which are purified by the power of the Kalās."

Thus, the statement beginning with "Jaṭāṃśo bitrayāditya" refers to the subject of renunciation (*sannyāsa*). This is the rule for the triple staff (*tridanda*). In this way, the sequence of the special initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*) is completed.
Likewise, it should be understood regarding the Lord Śiva and the teacher (*ācārya*) as well as the two vows (*vrata*).
Now the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*) is described.
(141a–145a) The initiation of liberation is twofold: that which conforms to worldly norms (*laukikī*) and that which conforms to the nature of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*).
O child, that which is known as conforming to worldly norms is to be understood as being without the cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*).
Initiation conjoined with the cutting of the top-knot is that which pertains to the Śiva-dharma.
By means of initiation pertaining to the world-dharma, the Guru should initiate those who are materialistic;
likewise, by means of initiation pertaining to the Śiva-dharma, the Guru should initiate those who are lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika).
But for those who are incapable, it is seedless; furthermore, it is for those whose souls delight in worldly enjoyment.

Having performed the initiation previously described, which purifies the *samaya* and other elements, one should effect [the transition] into the supreme reality; one should contemplate enjoyment upon the path of purification.
The Śivadharmiṇī is of two kinds:
the naiṣṭhikī, which lasts until the fall of the body, and the bhautikī, which ends with the release from the vow.
For both of these, initiation may or may not be accompanied by further office (*adhikāra*).
The perpetual [initiation] is of two kinds:
that which, through illusion (*māyā*), bestows enjoyment on the pure path during the purification of the paths;
that is called "with seed" (*sabījā*) and, at the end of enjoyment, shall become the bestower of liberation.
But that initiation of one who is free from desire, performed without previously commenced ritual action, is the destroyer of all fetters; it is seedless and bestows non-duality.

"The fruit previously accumulated therein, once burnt, may take on the state of a seed; its future fruit must be suppressed like the potency of poison. By means of that [body] already begun, at the end of its experience, one shall go to the state of Śiva. Thus it is said.

Then, for a disciple who desires the initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*) immediately following the initiation into the specific [level] of equality (*samatva-viśeṣa-dīkṣā*), one should perform the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*).

This is as follows: having determined a time conjoined with an auspicious lunar mansion and other favorable factors, one should first cause the disciple to take only a single meal on the preceding day.
One should perform ten thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra. Then, at night, having laid the disciple upon darbha grass with his head to the east if he seeks worldly prosperity,
or upon ashes with his head to the south if he seeks liberation, one should wake him during the Brāhma-muhūrta,
ask him about the dream seen during the night, and, if it is auspicious, satisfy him.

When the presence of defects exists that correspond to those [defects], one should cause the recitation of the Aghora mantra to be performed ten thousand times up to a hundred thousand times. Then, once the disciple has bathed and performed his daily rites, the Preceptor, abiding in the realization "I am Śiva," should, by means of a vowel and through the inhalation (*pūraka*) of the disciple, place [the mantra] within that disciple's body.
To the west of that pavilion, having produced three mandalas from east to west,
[one should offer] the *brahmakūrca* to the third-caste renunciant in the western mandala with the *haṃsa* mantra, and to both seekers of liberation with the five-syllabled mantra.

Having made [the disciple] drink the middle [mixture], and having first performed the cleaning of the teeth within the maṇḍala, one should cause him to wash his feet and perform the pure *ācamana* rite in the maṇḍala; on that day, one should cause him to observe the vow of fasting. This is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*). Thus it is stated in the *Vāruṇapaddhati*:
And at the beginning of the observance (samaya) and during initiation, having completed the daily rite according to the rule,
the preceptor [should worship] him who abides as the very form of the mantra.
Having oneself established in the state of Śiva, one should, according to the prescribed rite,
install the consciousness of this [image]— which is the embodiment of the mantra— by means of the vital breath through inhalation (pūraka).
Having grasped it with Śiva residing in his own mind, he should unite it;
having held it there during the kumbhaka, he should [expel] it from the disciple's body by means of the recakas.
One should again perform the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) after having made obeisance;
then, having caused [the disciple] to drink it with the mantra *haṃsa* or the *praṇava*.

Furthermore, the wise one who performs [the rite] together with the five-syllable [mantra], this is called the *adhivāsa* (preliminary consecration), according to the statement: "This is to be known as the *adhivāsa*.
Thereafter, the preceptor, having said, "Become qualified for that *nirvāṇadīkṣā*," [addresses] his respective first disciple.
Having brought him [there], one should say: "Prepare the requisites for the purpose of his initiation into Nirvāṇa.
Regarding the characteristics of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*):
in one's own house, in a monastery (*maṭha*), on a riverbank, on a mountain peak, in a temple of the Guru, or in any pure place.

Having dug four finger-breadths deep and cleared the site, one should prepare a pavilion four cubits square, with four doors and four archways, shaped like a celestial mansion (*vimāna*), adorned with variegated cloths such as fine linen, fragrant flower garlands, and other ornaments; then, having smeared it with cow dung, [one should sprinkle] it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Having sprinkled [the site] and smeared it with fragrant paste, one should have [it prepared]. Thereafter, at midnight, having appointed his own eldest priest as endowed with the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*),
he should sit facing north upon a seat of *darbha* grass on the southern side of the pavilion.

Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the ritual placement of the digits (*kalānyāsa*), and the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*);

having set out the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the offering (*arghya*); and having purified the materials for worship such as perfumes and flowers; [one should prepare] a square throne of mantras (*mantrasiṃhāsana*) consisting of the layers beginning with Earth, smeared with fragrance and thirty-six finger-breadths high, ending with the peak of the *kuṭilā*.

Having worshipped with scented water, and having requested permission from the Knowledge-Teacher (Jñānācārya) who has bathed and is seated upon the lion-throne, saying, "O Lord, I worship you," he— having received permission— [proceeds] with ghee and the like, [offering it] into the Knowledge itself.
For the sake of favoring his disciples,

he meditated upon himself as having arisen with two arms, one face, and three eyes, with the moon as his crest-jewel, appearing like crystal; then, having meditated upon himself as having arisen with the luster of red crystal, consisting of the nature of Śakti and Śiva.

Having grasped the pair of lotus-feet, which have the luster of red crystal, and having consecrated them with water mixed with perfumes and other substances while reciting the Śiva-mantra, and having wiped them with a fine silk cloth, one should write the Praṇava on a birch-bark leaf or a stone slab smeared with perfume. (142b, 1st line; 146b)

In the center of that, having written the name of Manoratha, whose nature is the impurity of concealment (*tirodhāna-mala*), one should place the seat for the right foot of the Knowledge-Teacher (*jñānācārya*). Then, [one should place] the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti seated upon the throne of the Hero (*vīrasiṃhāsana*).

Having worshipped [the deity] with divine perfumes, flowers, and ornaments, as well as divine garments, crowns, and diadems, using the Śiva-mantra; and having offered incense and lamps according to the rules, one should present the prepared *sthālīpāka* along with side dishes, ghee, milk, honey, sugar, cakes, and water.

Having offered the food together with fruits and other items into a vessel made of gold or similar material, using the *Śiva-mantra* ending in *svāhā*, and having set aside the food to be offered elsewhere in a pure place as well as the water for the foot-bath, one should perform the purification of the site (*sthalashuddhi*) and offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and scents for the eyes and mouth (*kṣimukhavāsa*).

Having given [these], he should offer incense, lamps, the *ārātrika* lamp, an umbrella, chowries, a fan, and a mirror. Then the preceptor, having accepted the worship offered by the disciple through the contemplation "I am Śiva," should purify the *kalās* of the disciple.

Here is the village [of the ritual]. Having seated the disciple facing north upon the sixfold seat within the mandala, one should contemplate him from the crest-lock down to the feet as consisting of the mantra-words, phonemes, worlds, and principles (*tattva*), by means of the kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā and ending with Nivṛtti; one should then reflect upon the impurities of *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman* as pervading those kalās.

Namely: at the head, within the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), there are two [aspects] in the *śāntyatītakalā*: the power of coolness (*śitatvaśakti*) and the principle of reality (*tatva*). [These are] Anāśritā, Anāthā, Anantā, Avyomarūpā, Vyāpinī, Ūrdhvagāminī, Śocikā, Mocikā, Dīpikā, and Indhikā; these are the worlds of the *nādakalā* within the principle of Śiva. [This is] the *śāntyatītā*.
Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti—these are the worlds of the *bindu-kalā* within the principle of Śakti (*śakti-tattva*).
There are fifteen lords of these worlds, bearing these very names.
The sixteen phonemes are: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, and aḥ. The first [of these], the syllable *oṃ*, constitutes a single word.

The mantras for the garments of Śiva and Īśāna: (second line) The seed-syllables are *nāda* and *hakāra*. The channels (*nāḍī*) are *śikhī* and *nī*. The winds (*vāyu*) are *dha*, *na*, *ja*, and *ya*, namely Devadatta. The sense organs (*indriya*) are hearing and speech. The object (*viṣaya*) is sound. The quality (*guṇa*) is resonance (*dhvani*). The mandala is sprinkled. [The syllables] *va*, *ju*, *jñāṃ*, and *kitam*. (third line)
One should contemplate: "The state beyond the fourth (turyātītāvasthā); Sadāśiva, the Lord of Causes.

Thereafter, within the mouth, in the *śāntikalā*, there are the three principles (*tattva*) of Sadāśiveśvara and Śuddhavidyā; the world of Sadāśiva (*sadāśivabhuvana*) is within the principle of Sadāśiva. [Śikhaṇḍī] (4th line).

Śrīkaṇṭhī, Trimūrti, and Ekarudra; Kanetrā, Śivottama, Sūkṣma, and Ananta—these eight worlds are in the principle of Īśvara. Manonmanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, Balapramathanī, Balavikaraṇī, Kalavikaraṇī, Kālī, Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Vāmā—these nine worlds are in the principle of Śuddhavidyā.
These very [deities] are the eighteen Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśvaras*), whose names consist of the phonemes *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *ña*.

(6th line) To Śiva, who is all-pervading like space, whose form is space, who pervades everything, who is infinite, who is without protector, who is without support, who is fixed, who is eternal, who is established upon the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*), who is the eternally united one, and who steals away through meditation—thus [are the twelve]. (7th line)
The two mantras are the Puruṣa and Kavaca. Vindu is the causal seed-syllable (*kāraṇabīja*). The root is for Puruṣa; there are two channels (*nāḍī*).

The winds are Kūrma and Kṛkara. The skin and the hand are the sense organs. Touch is the object. Sound and touch are the qualities. (143b, 1st line–147b) [The seat is] black and hexagonal, marked with six dots.
The maṇḍala is perishable; the meaning is that it is the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśa*). Following that, within the heart, in the category of *vidyā* (knowledge), there are seven principles (*tattva*):
*māyā*, *kāla* (time), *niyati* (restriction), *kāla* (time), *vidyā*, *rāga* (attachment), and *puruṣa*.
Like [the thumb-sized Lord], there are eight [deities] known as Īśa, Īśāna, Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa, Udbhava, Vāmadeva, and Mahātejas.

In Māyā: Śikheda and Ekavīra; in Kalā: Pañca and Anta; in Śuddhavidyā: Niyata, Saṃvarta, Jala, and Iti; in Īśvara: Caṇḍa and Krodha; in Vidya: Ekaśiva and Śivānta; and [the mantras] ending with Jomāpati and Praṇava.
The five worlds are in *rāga*.

(4th line) The six worlds named Ekavīra, Īśāna, Bhava, Ugra, Bhīma, and Vāma are in *puruṣa*. These are indeed the seventeen Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*). The seven phonemes are *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, and *ña*. *Oṃ namaśśivāya*. [This is] for the Source of All (*sarvaprabhu*).

(5th line) To Śiva, whose head is Īśāna, whose face is Tatpuruṣa, whose heart is Aghora, whose secret part is Vāmadeva, and whose form is Sadyojāta; Oṃ, salutations, salutations to Kha, the most secret of secrets, to Golatra. (6th line)

To the one without beginning or end, the presiding authority over all yogas, whose form is light, who is devoted to the Supreme Lord, [is addressed] with twenty-one words: "cetanā-cetane" (the conscious and the unconscious), "vyomin-vyomin" (in the ether, in the ether). These are the *mantra*s of Aghoraśikhā; "ma-ra-la" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Pūṣan is the tongue; the two channels (*nāḍī*) are the hands. Vyāna is the wind; the eyes are the feet, which are the sense organs. Form is the object; [these are] sound, touch, and form.
The qualities (*guṇas*): a red triangular mandala marked with a svastika.

(144a, 1st line) The state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Rudra is the Lord of the Cause (*kāraṇeśa*). Thus one should meditate. Then, at the navel, within the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā, [one should contemplate] the qualities (*guṇa*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the senses of hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell. (2nd line)

The twenty-three principles consist of speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, air, fire, water, earth, and that which is called power (*bala*). In the *guṇa* [tattva], there is the group of eight wombs known as Śrīkaṇṭhya, Saumya, Kaumāra, Vaiṣṇava, Brahmā, Bhairava, Kṛta, and Akṛta.
The eightfold divine birth—namely Brāhma, Vyāja, Īśa, Saumya, Aindra, Gāndharva, Yākṣa, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca—is located in the intellect (*buddhi*).
Sthaleśvara is in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Sthūleśvara is in the mind (*manas*). Śaṅkukarṇa is in the pentad of the sense organs of cognition, beginning with the ear.

In the pentad of the organs of action beginning with speech, in the pentad of sound and the other [objects], and in the pentad of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), there are the following: Kālañjara, Maṇḍaleśvara, Mākoṭa, Dviṇḍa, Ghacchagalaṇḍa, and others; the five *sthāṇu*s; Svarṇākṣa, Bhabhṛka, Gokarṇa, Mahālaya, Avimukta, Rudrakoṭi, and the one named Vastrāpada.

There are eight worlds in the element of space (ākāśa-tattva). In the element of air (vāyu-tattva), there are eight worlds known as Bhīmeśvara, Mahendra, Aṭṭahāsa, Vimale, Vimaleśvara, Nakha, Lanākhala, Gurukṣetra, and Gada;
[and] Bhairava and Kedāra.
The eight worlds named Mahāla, Madhyārjuna, Atrīśvara, Jalpeśvara, Śrīśaila, Hara, Candra, and [the eighth] are in the principle of fire (*tejastattva*).
The eight worlds named Lakulīśa, Bhārabhūti, Diṇḍi, Muṇḍa, Āṣāḍhi, Puṣkara, Naimiśa, and Prabhāsa-amareśa are in the principle of water (*aptattva*). Thus, there are fifty-six [worlds].

The worlds: thus, there are fifty-six Lords of the Worlds (bhuvaneśvaras) with these very names. [The seed-syllables are] ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha—these twenty-three syllables. Vyāpin, Vyāpin.

Formless yet possessing form, first among the first, heat within heat, light within light; O you who are without fire, without exertion, and without ashes; (third line) without beginning; manifold, manifold; *dhū-dhū* *dhū-dhū*; *oṃ bhūḥ*; *oṃ bhuvaḥ*; *oṃ suvaḥ*; without end; the end; the source of the end; Śiva, Śarva, Supreme Self.

Maheśvara, Mahādeva, Sadbhāveśvara, Mahātejas, Yogādhipate, Mumuñca Mumuñca, Prathama Prathama, Śarva Śarva—these are the thirty-two words. These two mantras are on the head of Vāmadeva; the syllables *U* and *Va* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Among the Gāndhāras... (fifth line).
(... Its [deities] are the *udāna* and *samāna* breaths; the tongue is its organ; taste is its object; sound, touch, form, and taste are its qualities;
the white half-moon, the lotus, and the water-pot are its symbols;
and Viṣṇu is its presiding deity during the state of dream.
One should meditate on him as the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśa*). Thereafter, upon the two knees in the *nivṛtti*-kalā, there is the single earth-element, Bhadrakālī, and Vīrabhadra.
Above Brahmā... [there is] a pair [of elements].

The sky is for one desiring the three eyes. Śambhu—the all-pervading lord of the thirty gods, the master of the Gaṇas, and the three-eyed one—is present in the ten directions above the marriage-assembly.
Daṃṣṭrin, Vaktrin, Paṇīndra, Udumbarīśa, Sanamāruta, Aśanākrodhana, Anantavṛṣadhara, Vṛṣa— these ten below; Baripriya, Bhūtapāla, Bheṣṭha, Śarva, Sureśa, Depāṅgajñānabhuk.
In the northeast (Īśāna), there are ten [names]: Sarvajña, Īśa, Vidyādhipa, Prakāmada, Prasāda, Śrīdhara, Lakṣmīdhara, Dhanamūrti, Dhaneśvara, and Saumyadeha.
In the north (Uttara), there are ten [names]: Nidhīśa, Meghavāhana, Kapardin, Pañcaśikha, Pañcāntaka, Kṣayāntaka, [Kṣayāntaka], ... [Dhānyarūpavān].
"Sharp, subtle, wind-speed, light, swift"— these are the ten [names] for Vāyu.
"Beautiful-sounding, cloud-sounding, water-born, ender-of-water, long-armed, victorious, auspicious, white, great-strength, noose-in-hand, and so forth, powerful-army"— these are for Varuṇa.

O slayer of Māra, ten-faced one with ten fangs, red and smoky, with deformed eyes, erect phallus, terrifying and cruel gaze— protect me from the Nairṛtas who destroy human fame! O Lord of Dharma, [protect me] from those who separate one from dharma!

In the southern [direction], there are ten: Saṃyoktṛ, Kartṛ, Vidhātṛ, Bharatṛ, [and so forth]. In the southeastern [direction], there are ten: Kṣayāntaka, Yāntaka, Bhasmānta, Satradahana, Jvalana, Harakhānaka, Piṅgala, Hutāśana, Agni, and Rudra.
In the eastern [direction], there are ten: Tridaśādhipa, Pināki, Śāstravyadha, Vibhūtipramardana, Vajradeha, Buddhāja, and Kapālīśa.
The group of six known as Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Aṭaka, Kūśmāṇḍa, and Kālāgni (145b, l. 1–149b–211).
Thus, within the Egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*), there are one hundred and eight worlds. These are the Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*) bearing these names. The phoneme is *kṣa*.
O Bhava, Bhava, you who arise from Bhava, bestower of happiness upon all beings, maker of all things present! (2nd line)

O you who are beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; unadorned, yet adorned; unconsecrated, yet consecrated; abiding from before, abiding from before; witness, witness; fly, fly; tawny, tawny; knowledge, knowledge; sound, sound; subtle, subtle; Śiva! (3rd line)

*Sarva sarva | Oṃ namaḥ śivāya oṃ namaḥ namaḥ oṃ*—these are the twenty-eight words. The two mantras are named Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya. The seed-syllables (*bīja*) are *ka* and *la*. Piṅgalā and Dhānādhya are the two channels. Apāna and Prāṇa are the two vital winds (*vāyu*). Ghṛṇi and Indra are the two senses. Smell is the object (*viṣaya*). Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the qualities (*guṇa*).

One should meditate upon a yellow, square vajra and a water-pot, representing the waking state, Brahmā, and the Lord of Causes. Thereafter, one should contemplate the relationship of pervader and pervaded among the mantras and so forth, as follows: the mantras are pervaded by the words (*pada*), and the words are pervaded by the phonemes (*varṇa*).

One should contemplate that the *varṇas* [are purified] by the *bhuvanas*, the *bhuvanas* by the *tattvas*, the *karmas* by those *tattvas*, and those *tattvas* by the two *māyās*; those two by *mala*, and *mala* by the *kalās*. Having thus visualized them, one should purify the limited souls (*śakalas*).
Thereafter, having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara within the *nābhikuṇḍa* of the disciple... (146a, 1st line; 212–150a).
If one is qualified for the conduct of the *samaya* through initiation with seed (*sabījadīkṣā*),

then all other karma— other than the dharma that produces the present body, such as sacrifices and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*) along with their secondary consequences, and the conduct of the *samaya*— is simultaneously ripened.

Having performed the union of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara and visualized it, one should imagine the disciple’s self situated within that [union] and born simultaneously from all wombs; then, having caused all karma— consisting of merit and demerit and pervading the three times—
to be consumed simultaneously, like the power of poison neutralized by mantras and herbs, one should visualize the obstruction of ignorance as being removed.

By means of the process of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, one should unite [the disciple] in the state of Śiva; having manifested the sixfold attributes such as omniscience, one should cause him to attain equality with Śiva. If [the disciple] lacks the capacity for the conduct of the *samaya*, then there is the seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*), which [removes] the incidental dharmas that initiate the body.
Having purified all ritual action (*sarvakarma*) together with one's own specific pledges and conduct (*samayācāra*), one should cause it to attain the state of Śiva as previously described.
In both cases, if one is desirous of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), all action— which consists of *dharma* pervading the three periods of time— [should be purified] within the present body.
Having envisioned [the disciple] as the bestower of enjoyments and as consisting of all superfluous impurities (*adharmas*), one should purify him;

then, by means of the sequential abandonment of the causal principles beginning with Brahmā, having joined him to his intended station and placed the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*) upon the head of the disciple, one should instruct him in the entire temple (*prāsāda*) endowed with the characteristics of the measures (*mātrā*). This is the alternative procedure (*vikalpa*) for this stage.

If a practitioner (*sādhaka*)— who has been initiated for the sake of [attaining] discipleship and the next world, who is intent upon *iṣṭāpūrta* and other such merits, and whose [karmic] portion has been exhausted by the Śaiva mantra— should reach the end of his body, [the Lord] shall cause him to attain the unsurpassed *siddhis*,
such as *aṇimā* and so forth; however, this does not apply to the practices of those yogins who have attained success through the treatises composed by Patañjali and others.
The supernatural powers (*siddhi*s). As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"When the portion of [karmic] misdeeds has been exhausted in all the lands of enjoyment,
for the sake of intoxication, [the body] remains in the remaining worlds characterized by the dharma of the desired [beings].
Thus, [it remains] always in those lords of the worlds intended by him.

When [this] is performed for you, then— having established within that [space], in its midst, in that world-sphere (*bhuvaneśvara*), and together with its power (*śakti*) whatever path belongs to whom and to whatever extent, and having uttered the mantra denoting that [deity] ending in *nāda*—

[one should know that] because it was previously stated that "it destroys all evil deeds," one remains in the place of suffering, untouched by the suffering consisting of the experience of inauspiciousness.

One should unite the disciple’s self [with the deity]. Having united him with each respective [state], one should effect the attainment of its attributes (*taddharmāpādana*). The meaning is that one should cause him to attain the qualities residing therein, such as omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth. Now, if after such enjoyment the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) desires to depart for the next world, then for him—who has been initiated into the state characterized by the other world—the abodes (*dhāma*) and so forth do not exist as objects of enjoyment.

When all future portions [of karma] have been [rendered] such that the portion of evil deeds is destroyed and the portion of auspicious deeds is established, for one who desires liberation—after the body has passed away and while residing in the [various] worlds (*bhuvana*) consisting of what has been experienced and what is yet to be experienced—one should unite the hundredfold Self with the Supreme Lord for the sake of attaining Śiva. As it is said in that very [text]: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific details of the worlds mentioned in the original source.*

"Having superimposed the worldly one upon the Earth as the agent in the [meditative] view, one should effect the attainment of its qualities; or, for one desiring liberation, [one should do so] upon Śilā. Thus it is said.
Herein, the aforementioned Lords of the Worlds are Gaurī, Bhāskara, and the others.
As it is said in that very same place:
"In this very way, once that path has been purified, the devotee should attain union with Ambikā, Sūrya, Smara, Viṣṇu, and Prajāpati. (2nd line)

"The path for others and for the gods is indeed exactly thus; in the higher [world], there is the means with its superior [result], while in the worldly [realm], there is the activity of desired objects. Regarding that [half-verse], it follows the previously mentioned sequence: "Gaurī, Ravi, Manobhava... (3rd line).

Regarding the subject of those whose duty pertains to the other world: one who is devoted to Keśava, Brahmā, and others—those deities stationed at every stage along the path—should be initiated; once that path has been purified, he is to be led to union (*sāyujya*) with each respective deity. (4th line)

Now, regarding the previously mentioned liberation pertaining to the next world— which consists of union with Śiva— one who possesses devotion and seeks that union is one for whom there is a "superior means" (*sottaropāya*). This superior means is that which is conjoined with initiation (*dīkṣā*) independent [of other rites], together with the procedure for removing the transgression of violating the conduct of the *samaya*.

This means that he is to be led to union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*). Here, the word *indha* (in the sixth line) should be understood as the "kindling wood" (*indhaka*) for the world-sphere situated below Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), or for the world-sphere of Sadāśiva. Now, regarding those initiated by means of the material initiation (*bhautikadīkṣā*) in the other compartments:
If [the soul] is a seeker of enjoyment, then wherever in the world there is a desire for enjoyment,
a union with a desired body must be brought about for the sake of enjoyments suitable to that body, even for a living being who has begun an action that results in a physical form.

For the sake of protecting the body from falling [into ruin], one should protect it by fulfilling the conduct of the *samaya*. All other activities beyond that—whether they be fearsome or fearful results—one should burn away in the fire of knowledge (*jñānāgni*).

Any other ritual action should be performed according to the rules for the final initiation (*naiṣṭhika-dīkṣā*). Now, if one has been initiated by means of the initiation pertaining to the elements of others (*parabhautika-dīkṣā*)... [and] desires [to proceed further].
The noble one [attains] union at the end of the state beginning with Earth and ending with Māyā— which is the state of *bhava* (existence), the "grindstone"—

and at the end of the state beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Īśvara— which is the state of *abhava* (non-existence), the "grindstone" [itself]— within the principle of Sadākhya, namely Sadāśiva. As it is said in that very same [text]:
In the *Śrī Mṛgendra*,
it is said that through this very yoga of action (*kriyāyoga*), even one who is on the earth attains the supreme and the lower [states].
However, for the sake of not abandoning the body, the embodied soul must exhaust its *prārabdha* karma.
Having formed an alliance with the one to be accomplished by means of the Śaiva practitioner, he should protect him;
he should burn everything else along with its consequences in the blazing fire of initiation.
When the five lords of the Sādhya reside at the end of the syllables of the *kaṣṭa* and *akaṣṭa* [mantras], [the rite is performed].
Yoga occurs when there is the desire for a different form in the case of one who teaches grammar.
Now, if one who has been initiated by the *aparanaiṣṭhika* initiation is desirous of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*),
then— being the cause for attaining the goals of human existence— he assumes a divine body of his own choosing after the dissolution of the [current] physical body.
Having enjoyed the objects of the various terrestrial realms as he desires, he subsequently attains the state of Śiva’s *samaya*.

The desire to attain, greed, and lack of discernment—[one should] cause that [stream of consciousness] to reach those [states]. This means that after the enjoyment of the worlds, such as the world of Sadāśiva and others, one should attain equality with Sadāśiva. (148a, 1st line) (152a – 214) This is the initiation for the non-final (*aparanaiṣṭhika*) stage, pertaining to the mind during the practice of sacrifice and so forth, and not that which is called "seedless" (*nirbījika*). Thus it is.

Having initiated [the disciple] as appropriate through the fivefold initiation, distinguished by the seeded (*sabīja*) and seedless (*nirbīja*) types, if [the disciple] is a seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), then— as previously described— he should be joined to the respective desired locations, such as the *Śuddhavidyā-tattva* and so forth among the worlds, or to the worlds ending with the *Īśvara-tattva*. Then,
placing the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*) upon the head of the disciple, [he should perform the rite] conjoined with the characteristics of the *mātrās*.

One should instruct on the entire temple. If the candidate for initiation is one who desires liberation (*umukṣu*) after having experienced the enjoyments of the state to be initiated into, then, following the purification of such actions,
one should contemplate— as before— the obstruction caused by ignorance.

Having joined the disciple to the eternal reality of Sadāśiva through the sequential abandonment of the causal principles beginning with Brahmā, and having placed the Hand of Śiva upon the disciple’s head, he should instruct him in the partless temple (*niṣkalaprāsāda*) endowed with the characteristics of the *mātrā*s. If the one to be initiated is a seeker of liberation, then for him— desiring no enjoyments anywhere— the initiation is that of the seedless, innate, supreme, and ultimate type.

Having manifested the sixfold attributes such as omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) and so forth, he should cause [the disciple] to reach the reality known as the *Ṣaḍākhya* in the presence of Sadāśiva. Likewise, having initiated him through the higher ritual (*uparikriyā*), the teacher should lead the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) to that same vision.

"Averse to worldly conduct, he is solely intent upon the performance of auspicious rites. Thus, although the officiants of the constituent parts of the sacrifices and so forth in Śiva-initiations possess ownership [of the ritual],
these [initiations] are distinct because of the difference between teacher and disciple in their mutual agreement that "let such-and-such an initiation be performed for the disciple."
All initiations yield different results.
As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Even though these [initiations] are accomplished by the same agent, they convey different purposes due to the difference created by the intention of both the teacher and the disciple."
All of this refers to the domain characterized by the descent of powers such as *manda-bheda*, *manda-manda-bhedatara*, and so forth.
Now, regarding the domain of *tīvra* (intense), *manda*, *mandatara*, and so on, the initiation of knowledge (*jñāna-dīkṣā*) should be performed solely through the path of knowledge. For example:

now, one who stands as if situated in the *śāntyatīta-kalā* (the level beyond peace), having reached the ultimate limit and being indifferent to enjoyments, possesses an intense differentiation (*tīvra-bheda*).

If the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*) has occurred, the teacher, having for a moment become immersed in supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) and having become inwardly composed of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), closes his eyes; then, by means of the fire of his gaze, he consigns the disciple’s *prārabdha-karma* and all accumulated karma (*sañcita-karma*) residing within the constituent parts of the *kalās* to be consumed.

Having sequentially joined the mantra-words, phonemes, worlds, and principles to the *kalās* as previously described, one should join them to the five powers of the *kalās*. By means of this conjunction at the hands and the head, one should dismiss the two-fold *māyā* and [remove] the impurity of the self— which is shrouded by the *āṇava-mala*, remains like a knot at the tip of the nose, and persists for a long time.

Having joined the soul, along with the powers such as Jñānapriyā and the others, into the Supreme Power (parāśakti), one should then join it into the Supreme Śiva— who is of the nature of the Lower Power (aparāśakti)— like the waters of a river into the ocean, milk into milk, or clarified butter into clarified butter. Thereafter...

One should demonstrate the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme through either the *prāsāda* mantra or the five-syllabled (*pañcākṣara*) mantra. Thus united, the self remains in the body for the sake of experiencing the fruits of *prārabdha-karma*;
therefore, [the practice is undertaken] for the purpose of removing the afflictions of the five elements, the five senses, and the internal organ.

And for the sake of accomplishing the power of *samādhi*, one should touch with the two feet—which are the very nature of Śiva and Śakti—the *brahmarandhra*, the eyes, the heart, and the middle of the eyebrows. Since the *brahmarandhra* is the locus of space (*ākāśa*), and because the other four [elements] are contained within it, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) occurs through that contact; and by that purification, [the goal is attained].

Then there is the purification of the mind and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Now, among the physical organs and the senses, because the eye holds primacy, through its purification, the purification of the other four [senses] follows. Likewise, from the purification of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), the subsequent purification of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) ensues.
Because the heart is the locus of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), through its power, there is purification of the internal organ.

Because the space between the eyebrows is the locus of *samādhi*, through contact with it, *samādhi* is accomplished. Thereafter, one should purify [the disciple] through knowledge regarding the various sacraments (*saṃskāra*), beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and extending up to the respective stages of life (*āśrama*). Then the disciple, having risen, [honors] the Guru...
Having circumambulated, paid homage, and offered praise,
and having first presented his own body along with water to the Guru, he likewise [presented them] to the elders according to their respective caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).

Having prostrated, drunk the water from the Guru’s feet, and accepted some of the grace-bestowing *prasāda*, one should perform one's daily obligatory rites at dawn; then, having fed the Guru, the elders, the devotees of Śiva, and the Brahmins, one should afterwards eat the remnants of what the Guru has eaten.
Thereafter, one should hear from the mouth of the Guru the Śivāgama, beginning with the awakening of the knowledge of Śiva. This very [process] is the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*);
it should be understood as the *śāmbhavī* variety of initiation, which is the initiation consisting of the [nine] *āṇavas*. There is agreement regarding the stated meaning. (4th line)
In the venerable *Raurava*,
a slight distinction is made regarding initiation through mental cultivation (*manobhāvanādīkṣā*):
that which is to be performed by a teacher of knowledge (*jñānācārya*) is considered "consisting of knowledge" (*jñānavatī*).
I am that Guru, whose nature is the state of being, and who is the Lord skilled in the knowledge of the practices and so forth.
Having approached that Guru in this ocean of birth within saṃsāra, the disciple—
Bound by the threefold fetters of impurity, immersed in the experience of pleasure, pain, and the like,
now stupefied and unconscious— O Treasure of Compassion!—
the merit accumulated through many births has now entered into Your lotus feet.
O Supreme Lord, protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Thus the disciple should make this request with devotion and one-pointed mind. Having thus accepted the disciple through the actions of speech, mind, and body, [one should proceed].
Having observed within six months or a year his falling of power,
his retention, his inability to grasp, his practice, and his vision of the secret;
The Guru should cause the disciple to perceive the immovable form of knowledge as the object of apprehension;
indeed, he should [teach] the place, the location, the time, the ritual action, the meditative cultivation, and the vision.
Listen to my instruction on how to practice good conduct in due order:
in a sacred place (*tīrthabhūmi*) that is preeminent for Śiva, in a region endowed with a river;
or on a riverbank, in a monastery (*maṭha*), or in one’s own home, in the temple of the Guru.
On a mountain peak, in a pure place, one should have a pavilion constructed there.
Having measured out four fingers for the goddess of the four cubits,
[he should construct a temple] provided with four doors and endowed with four archways.
One should construct an elevated pavilion adorned with fine cotton cloths, variegated fabrics, strings of pearls,
and fragrant garlands of flowers;
having applied a coating of cow dung, one should perform a sprinkling with the five products of the cow.
Having relied upon what was called "place" and likewise upon "time" as it is conceptualized, [the following is stated].
On a day conjoined with an auspicious lunar mansion, his initiation should be performed;
having appointed the eldest, endowed with the initiation of knowledge, as the domestic priest.
On the following day, one should eat only once; for that night, the consumption of cow products is prescribed.
On the next day, staying by a well and endowed with ritual bathing and purification, one should proceed.
On that day, at midnight, one should receive the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*).
Kālarātri is declared to be the very nature of impure *māyā*.
In the place situated at the end of the principle of Māyā, one should gradually manifest the nature of consciousness;
for indeed, the nature of consciousness is the very certainty [of the Self] at the end of pure Māyā. It is the dissolution of the two Māyās and the contemplation of that which has a single form.
Concealment and non-concealment, as well as the showing and not showing [of the self].
When joined with these [planets], the Night of Time (Kālarātri) becomes especially distinguished;
at midnight, she is the "Destroyer of Destruction" (Kṣayakṛtyā), and there occurs the constant withdrawal [of all beings] during the night.
Since the activity of the body and the senses dissolves at night,
the lamp of knowledge should be observed during the nights, as it were, by means of a [physical] lamp.
For those learned in the scriptures, this shall be the best time for the night. At that time, having entered the pavilion, one should [worship] with sixteen [offerings] such as perfumes and flowers.
Having prepared the materials for worship and standing facing north,
