one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*), and so forth, as well as the offering of the *arghya* water and other rites. The [mandala] should be four *tālas* in length and thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height.
One should apply fragrant ointments and prepare a well-concealed seat according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the form of the Mantra, which begins with the Earth (Kṣiti) and ends with Kuṭilā,
well-bathed with scented water and adorned with jewels, garlands, and fine garments.
Endowed with the contemplation of the placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*,
and having taken refuge in the divine lotus-feet of the Teacher of Knowledge (*jñānadeśika*),
one should bathe those two feet with the ritual substances prescribed by the scriptures.
Having wiped them with a white cloth, one should offer the water-lilies.

On a birch-bark leaf, having smeared it with fragrant [substances] and written the *praṇava* (OM), one should then write "Nage" in its center. Having understood the concealment of impurity (*mala*), one should protect it at the feet of the Guru.
One should worship with various divine fragrances and garlands of flowers.
Having offered incense and lamps, one should present the *sthālīpāka* oblation;
one should then contemplate the Guru in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti and the disciple likewise.

Indeed, the supreme teacher, in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, should accept this devotion of the disciple— which consists of worship performed with faith for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the guru.
Having accepted such worship, he should release the bond of the disciple.
In the body of the disciple, at the locations of the elements as they are joined, the teacher [establishes] the path of mantra,
the path of word, the path of phoneme, and the worlds.
And the path of the *kalās*— thus, having introduced the paths along with their pervasions according to the sixfold division into the sacrificial rite (*adhvara*),
which is the cause of the afflictions of transmigratory existence,
one should likewise sever the karma that binds by means of the sharp-edged sword of knowledge.
The Guru should purify the path of the wise through the pure [initiation] according to the prescribed rite.

That teacher, having offered [the disciple] internally for a moment into the eternal fire of supreme bliss— having joined the disciple with the "moment of intense power" (tīvra-śakti-muhūrta) through the descent of the supreme [grace]— [proceeds].
Having become one with the Supreme Power for the sake of the bound soul (*paśu*) so that his fetters may be removed,
[the Guru] creates a power consisting of Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) which obstructs the consciousness of the disciple;
then, having perceived that *āṇava* power of his with his eye, [he proceeds].
Then, having separated consciousness from the moon by means of his vision, he—

Having applied continuous contemplation (*anusandhāna*) to that mind of the bound soul (*paśu*), which was exceedingly obstructed like Rāhu released from the moon and yet destined for the state of Śiva, it is indeed merged—
like water poured into water, or milk added to milk.
And having effected the unification of these two through their fulfillment, like the waters of a river into the ocean.
Having constructed a temple endowed with the characteristics of its dimensions according to the [relevant] sūtra,
and having provided instruction on the three categories of reality in accordance with the rule, the preceptor should appropriately determine the name for his initiation.
Then, having positioned the disciple facing him, the Guru should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the head and other parts with his two feet, which are of the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
The movement of the elements, beginning with earth, is said to be the quality of space;
having burned away [impurities] in the space of the Brahma-randhra, it is the destroyer of karma.
Of all the sense organs, the faculty of sight should be predominant;
therefore, there shall be two eyes, and one should touch with both feet.
That which is acquired through the organs of action must be disciplined within the activity of the organs of knowledge.
The intellect of the mind (manobuddhi) [produces] the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which sets all the sense organs into motion.
His karma is burnt away; one should always touch the region of the heart.
Returning once more, he attains the "I-am-ness" (so'ham) at the center of his own eyebrows.
Having performed this for the sake of destroying the impurity of *prārabdha* karma, that teacher—
Having withdrawn his foot from its own place, he prostrated himself like a staff once again.

Having purified the disciple through the various initiatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, according to the specific limits of each stage of life (*āśrama*), and having rendered him as Śiva, free from all affliction, by means of the purificatory rite of knowledge (*jñānasaṃskāra*).
One should bestow the Śivajñānabodha scripture and the contemplation of the Lord (pati) and so forth upon that disciple who is to be graced through the actions of speech, mind, and body.

Having first offered his body, wealth, and life into the hand of the Guru, the well-established disciple should always conduct himself with the thought: "Whatever is near to your person is indeed mine."
Having been addressed thus, the disciple should cause that Guru to perform the triple prostration.
"You are not able here to destroy the torment of the afflictions within my heart;
there is no other, O embodiment of compassion. Protect me, O Lord of Teachers!"
Having thus praised and bowed, one should complete the worship of the Guru.
Then, with a self purified by initiation, even toward the elders, one should join the palms in reverence;
having drunk the water from the Guru’s feet, one should accept his grace.
Then at dawn, the disciple, having performed his daily obligatory rites, [approached].
Having worshipped his own guru, and thereafter the gurus, elders, and others,
the supreme practitioner should then eat the remaining food after having fed them.
Then, together with those seeking spiritual lineage (*sāntānika*), one should contemplate the knowledge of Śiva (*śivajñāna*).
This is declared to be the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*); now hear the procedure for the *Dīkṣottara*.
Thus [it is said].

Thus, for one who has been struck by the descent of intense power (*tīvra-śakti-nipāta*) and whose self is now united with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), there might be a concern that—once again, for the sake of experiencing the fruits of *prārabdha* karma, he would become connected with a body born of *māyā*; and that, for the sake of experiencing the results of future karma consisting of both the beneficial and the harmful, there would once more be the risk of falling back into the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*). If this is the objection:

No; because he is united with Śiva, the base self is not tainted by future karma, and therefore [he does not experience rebirth]. Rather, he attains union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva. As it is said in that very *Raurava*, in the *Dīkṣottara-vidhi*:
Thus, initiation is said to be bodiless; even that body no longer possesses the nature of a body.
With all impurities burnt away, having attained complete ripeness and straightness, he is liberated, his mind fixed solely on Śiva.
Upon the fall of the body, he attains the bliss of consciousness and the state of being of one essence with Śiva.
Yet it does not undergo division, like the water of a river in the ocean.
"Just as darkness is swiftly destroyed upon the rising of the sun, so too, having obtained alms, both merit and demerit perish," and so forth. And elsewhere:
"In this way, having attained the Śaiva sacrifice arising from initiation and mantra..."
Furthermore, that initiated one, the best of men, does not undergo rebirth;
having become Śiva when the body is dissolved, and being endowed with the qualities of Śiva,
he attains the bliss of Śiva and becomes non-differentiated.
Furthermore,
[there is] the pride regarding existence and so forth; because of reporting [one's faults] to the gurus,
one is freed from independence and established in the conduct of the *samaya*.
Like a burnt cloth, the embodied one— having taken up this insubstantial body through the actions of speech, mind, and body— is satisfied by pure conduct.
Accompanied by the whirling of the *lolacakra* and the [wind] of the *arvāṇa*,
the vessel (*pātra*) becomes fragrant (*parimala*) through the process of refinement (*saṃskāra*).

"...even though he is intent upon those duties, rebirth does not exist for him," and so forth (159a, line 1). Now, even though this [person] is fully awakened to the experience of objects such as sound and the like, there is no bondage for him.
As it has been stated in the venerable *Śivadharmottara* and other texts:
Indeed, O evil one, even one endowed with the power of Indra is made to wander by the serpents of the three [worlds]...;
likewise, the wise man is not seen sporting with the serpents that are the sense-faculties.
Just as a lotus leaf is not stained by water, even by that which remains upon it,
so too the man of knowledge is not stained by the waters of the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest.
Just as poison that has been swallowed is cleansed away by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, [so is the mind purified].
In the same way, may all our actions be eclipsed in an instant by the splendor of the Sun.
"A fish situated in the salt ocean does not undergo the state of being weighed down by its burden;
likewise, the yogi is not defiled by the auspicious and inauspicious within the sense objects.
Thus, the procedure for the initiation of knowledge is completed.

May there be auspiciousness! (6th line)
At the parting of the hair, at the birth-rite, and at the naming ceremony;
One should offer oblations with the root mantra and each of the five Brahma-mantras one hundred times each,

O Nandikeśvara, [these apply] at the initiation, at the taking of vows, at the *godāna* ceremony, at the rite of ritual bathing, at marriage, at entering the forest life, and at becoming an ascetic.

One should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) for each [deity] with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) five times. One should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) among those established in the four stages of life (*āśrama*) according to their respective [rules] until the end of that [period]; one should not cause it to be performed beyond that.
To householders and forest-dwellers, and especially to those who have renounced worldly life (yatis).
The supreme preceptor should offer oblations with nine measures as before;
thus [ends the section] following the procedure for the purificatory rite of action.

The extraction of power from one whose bonds have become loosened is called the *garbhādhāna* (conception); likewise, the manifestation of the qualities such as sovereignty (*svātantrya*) constitutes the *puṃsavana* (the rite for ensuring a male child). (4th line)

The illusory nature [of the self] is discerned through discrimination; knowledge is the increase of the parting of the hair. The acceptance of the real and unreal entities beginning with Śiva constitutes "birth.

That which is the awakening to the state of Śiva is called "the naming" of one who is worthy of Śiva-hood. Indeed, the entry into the state of Śiva is described as "emerging" [from the womb]. The enjoyment of supreme bliss is called "the first feeding of solid food."
But that which constitutes the excellence of Śiva’s grace would be the act [of initiation];
the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is the connection with the sūtra of the knowledge of Nirvāṇa; and the purification of the senses is traditionally known as the instruction in the vows (*vrata*).

The renunciation of rebirth is proclaimed as the "gift of the cow" (*godāna*). Indifference toward all things is the "bath of true being" (*sadbhāvasnāna*) for the Śiva-ascetics (*śivasannyāsins*). [The Ritual for the Consecration of the Preceptor (*ācāryābhiṣeka*)].

If the renunciant (*sannyāsī*) belongs to one of the three higher castes (*trivarṇaka*), he should bind his matted hair (*jaṭā*); however, if he belongs to the fourth caste, he should perform a complete shaving of the head (*vapanam eva kuryāt*), based on such scriptural injunctions as "a Śūdra shall not wear matted hair. As for the statement that "a Śūdra has a single lock of hair" (*ekā jaṭā*), this refers specifically to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) or the religious student (*brahmacārī*).

Thus it is said in the Śivadharmottara: "Whether he be a Jaḍī, a Muṇḍī, or a Śikhī, subsisting on alms, free from longing, observing silence, and full of compassion, the ascetic should then practice tranquility."
"Even a Śūdra who is liberated from all attachments and devoted to Śiva, having performed the tonsure here, shall become a follower of the lords of yogins. Thus it is stated in the Kiraṇa.
If one is unable to practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he should resort to the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*).
Even one who dwells in the forest-dweller stage (*vānaprasthāśrama*) is superior to the householder;
indeed, that [householder] is distinguished as being even more excellent than those dwelling in the forest-dweller stage.
For these as well, renunciation is ordained as appropriate once liberation has been attained.

"One should become initiated into the renunciant stage (*sannyāsāśrama*), which is the ultimate and most excellent; for one who observes the vows there, there is no other cause for liberation than that. "One initiated [into the Vedic order] should not perform actions such as wandering on great highways, foolishness, fasting,
and so forth.
Since this is intended to prohibit Vedic ritual action, the term "renunciation" (*sannyāsa*) therein refers to the prohibition of performing the rites prescribed for that stage.
This is the statement. For this very reason, in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*, it says:
"One should enter [the path] through celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and one may also enter from the state of a householder."
"A wise man should depart from the forest," and so forth, is what has been prescribed. (...... (8th line) Now, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated:
"In the Śaiva tradition, there are only two stages of life: the householder and the student."
Indeed, these two wandering mendicants and ascetics are not the ones who act for the benefit of the world.

The visual initiation (*cākṣuṣī*), the tactile initiation (*sparśadīkṣā*), the verbal initiation (*vācakī*), and likewise the mental initiation (*mānasī*)—these are the initiations of condensed knowledge for women and others. Then, having brought the disciple face-to-face, the Guru should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the head and other parts with both feet, which are of the nature of Śiva and Śakti. Thus is the tactile initiation (*sparśadīkṣā*).

Having constructed a temple endowed with the characteristics of measurement together with the *prāsāda-mantra*, and having provided the instruction on the three categories (*tripadārtha*) according to the rule—this is the initiation of the reciter (*vācakī-dīkṣā*). and through the vision [of whom] and other means, supreme bliss (*parānanda*) arises."
"A wise man should choose that very guru and no other.

Upon the sacrificial ground, one should first place the jars: the jar of Śiva (*śivakumbha*) and the *vardhanī* vessel; one should install the *śakti* jar to its left. One should then install the lords of knowledge (*vidyeśas*) outside of that jar.
Or else, one may perform it with five medicinal herbs, or even with ten flowers, or with a chariot.

"Made of *sahadevī*, with a single leaf, or auspiciously made of *vaikaṅkata*," and so forth; up to "one should present these to the most excellent lifelong teacher"—this is well known in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*.
[This is stated] in the *Śrīmanmakuṭa* regarding the procedure for wearing the sacred ashes (*vibhūti*).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
[it is applied] on the forehead, the chest, the neck, and likewise on the ears.
One should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the chest, the arms, the navel, and likewise the back; then on the two thighs, the two knees, and the two feet.
Brahmā himself resides in the *brahmarandhra*, Subrahmaṇya on the forehead;
the god Vināyaka is in the ear, and Sūrya and Soma are in the two eyes.
Indra and Viṣṇu are in the arms, and likewise Īśvara is in the heart.
The goddess Durgā should be at the navel, and likewise the ancestors on the back.
One should sequentially place [the deities] upon the thighs, the knees, and the feet;
likewise, one should place the Nāgas and Nāga maidens upon the two thighs.

Furthermore, the sages and the wives of the sages are situated upon the pair of knees, while the seven oceans and all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) reside upon the two feet. The locations of the *tripuṇḍra* and the deities associated with them have thus been proclaimed.
In the [mandala] called Viśvasāda, which is to be meditated upon,
one should contemplate the God of gods, the Supreme Lord, in its center.
In the form of Sadāśiva, resembling pure crystal,
endowed with five faces, each face having three eyes,
joined with a crown of matted hair, and accompanied by the lords [of the directions].
In his right [hands], he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and the gestures of speech and fearlessness;
in his left, a noose, a serpent, a goad, a bell, and fire.
He is auspicious, possessing all limbs in their entirety, and wears divine garments.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial flowers.
"Adorned with all ornaments," and so forth, in the *Śrīmat Kāmika*.

In the ether of the *brahmarandhra*, it is to be pointed out as the destroyer of karma.
Among all the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), the visual faculty is preeminent;

having returned to the space between his own eyebrows, he would attain the realization "I am He.
Having withdrawn his foot to its own place, the Guru, prostrate like a staff, [should bestow the initiation].
And having purified him according to the rule by means of the initiation of meditative cultivation (bhāvanādīkṣā), |||
One should bestow the *Śivajñānabodha* scripture and the contemplation of the Lord and so forth upon that disciple who is to be favored through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
One should offer one’s wealth, life, and ego to the gurus;
for this very reason, one becomes devoid of independence.
Indeed, such a person, being devoid of independence, is fashioned according to the conduct of the *samaya*.
Like a cloth that has been burnt, the embodied soul [is purified] by the actions of speech, mind, and body.
Having grasped the coreless body, which is sustained by pure activities,
it revolves like a potter’s wheel, equipped with the bow and arrow.
In this way, having extracted [the essence] by means of those instruments, the vessel— endowed with objects such as sound and the rest—
becomes fragrant through refinement, like a bulbous root.
Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and rendered the physical actions perfectly motionless,
and having established silence, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the mind for the sake of removing defects.
Since all karma is destroyed for one who is intent on the meditation upon Śiva,
one should indeed contemplate Him in the form of light within the lotus of the heart, which is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
By means of vision, one perceives all objects like a lamp resting upon cotton.

"All sins [reside] in the body; upon the destruction of the body, it grants liberation. And again in that very same place, in the *Raurava*: "Having thus attained the Śaiva ritual path, which arises from initiation and mantra..."
Furthermore, that best of men who has been initiated does not undergo rebirth.
When the body has perished, having become Śiva and being endowed with the Śiva-dharma,
one attains the bliss of Śiva and becomes fit for non-duality.
Having reached the ocean, a river carrying joyful waters attains the state of salty water through the power of the great sea.
"In this way, indeed, one whose self is distinct from the body attains Śiva alone.
Thus,
within the context of the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*), he describes the sixteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) by means of the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*).
The passage beginning with "In the venerable Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra" and so forth should be recited.
This concludes the procedure for the performance [of rites] according to the *Śaivasannyāsapaddhati*.

Having performed the pure sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) three times—reciting the *praṇava* during inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*), and the *saṃhitā* during retention (*kumbhaka*)—and then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of dissolution (*saṃhāranyāsa*). Thus: having recited twice the mantra "Oṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ," one should [strike] the palm of the left hand twice with the right hand.
Having thoroughly purified this very mantra and recited it with a peaceful mind, one should purify the palm of the right hand once with the left hand; then,
visualizing both hands as imbued with the splendor of the *astra* [weapon-mantra] up to the wrists, one should join the palms together with the two thumbs positioned between them.

One should meditate on the Śakti-maṇḍala with the seed-syllable of nectar. Having sprinkled both hands with "Oṃ hauṃ śaktaye vauṣaṭ," one should contemplate the seat of Śiva within the cavity [of the hands] as an eight-petaled lotus in the form of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). Then, having honored it with "Oṃ hāṃ śivāsanāya namaḥ," one should [proceed with] "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ śivamūrtaye namaḥ."
Having projected a subtle form while reciting the mantra "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" (vidyādeha), one should project the form of Sadāśiva. [Then] with "Oṃ haṃ,
obeisance to Sadyojāta," [one places it] on the two little fingers.

Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva—thus on the two ring fingers. Oṃ huṃ, salutation to Aghora—thus on the two middle fingers. Oṃ heṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa—thus on the two index fingers. Oṃ hoṃ, salutation to Īśāna—thus on the two thumbs. Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the three eyes—thus [on the palms].

On the three middle fingers: *Oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*. On the two little fingers: *Oṃ hiṃ śirase namaḥ*. On the two ring fingers: *Oṃ huṃ śikhāyai namaḥ*. On the two middle fingers: *Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*. On the two index fingers: *Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*. On the two thumbs: *Oṃ haṃ astrāya phaṭ*. [With] the root mantra...
Having joined the palms and the backs of the hands together, having veiled [the deity] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and having placed [the mantra] at the navel with "Oṃ hāṃ,
obeisance to the seat of Śiva," one should then project the subtle form from that point up to the forehead with "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva."
Having meditated with "Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva)," and having meditated from the navel up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
one should place [the mantra] on the chest with the tips of the fingers; then, while reciting the root mantra at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta),
one should place it on the head and perform the placement in the manner of a shaven head (muṇḍabhaṅgyā).
"Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta"—with the tips of the little finger and the thumb, on the back part of the head;

"Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva"—with the thumb and the ring finger, on the left side of the head; "Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Aghora"—with the tips of the thumb and the middle finger, on the right side; "Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa."

With the tips of the thumb and forefinger, [one places it] on the two knees. With the mantra "Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to the secret organ of Vāmadeva, to the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā," with the tips of the thumb and ring finger, [one places it] on the secret organ. With the mantra "Oṃ huṃ, salutation to the heart of Aghora, to the Vidya-kalā."

With the tips of the thumb and middle finger at the heart: *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya śāntikalāyai namaḥ*. With the tips of the thumb and index finger at the face: *oṃ hāṃ īśānamūrdhāya śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ*.
Having formed a fist with the hand, [place it] on the head with the tip of the thumb: *oṃ hāṃ sarvajñaśaktidhāmne hṛdayāya*.
With the tips of the little finger and the thumb [saying] "namaḥ" at the heart; with "oṃ hiṃ tṛptiśaktidhāmne kavacāya huṃ."

With the two index fingers, one performs the *kavaca* (armor) mudrā from the throat down to the middle of the breasts by way of covering them. With the middle fingers, one performs the *netra* (eye) mudrā on the two eyes with the mantra: *Oṃ hauṃ alīptaśaktidhāmne netrattrayāya vauṣaṭ*. Then, with the mantra *Anantaśaktidhāmne astrāya huṃ phaṭ*, [one performs the *astra* (weapon) mudrā].

Having performed three *tāla* gestures and the binding of the ten directions by circling oneself clockwise with the *uṣṇīṣamudrā* while uttering "phaṭ," one should consecrate [the self] from the feet to the crown of the head with the root mantra.
Likewise, in the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"Creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—this is said to be the threefold ritual deposition (*nyāsa*).
The householder should follow the path of creation, while the student (*brahmacārī*) should practice maintenance."
For forest-dwellers and ascetics, however, renunciation is called *saṃhāra*;
if a forest-dweller is without a wife, it is called *saṃhāra-nyāsa*.
In the *Triśatikālottara*:
"One should purify the sole and the back of the hand with the seed-syllable of the Weapon (*astra*).
In the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*: [same].
Having thus recited the mantra twice, one should purify the left hand with the right hand,
and the right hand with the left hand.
Having recited that [mantra] once, O Lord of Naddika, one should purify [the hands],
while recollecting the two hands as endowed with the splendor of the weapon-mantra, extending as far as the wrists.
Having formed a hollowed cup with both hands, with the two thumbs placed between the middle fingers,
one should meditate upon the supreme mandala of Śakti by means of the seed-syllable of nectar (Amṛta).
Oṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ to Śakti. One should contemplate the two hands joined together in the form of a lotus within the cavity [of the palms], and in the center of that is the seat of Śiva.
Having first projected the subtle form and subsequently reciting the mantra,
one should thus project the form of Sadāśiva upon the head of the Lord, O Nandikeśvara;
[this is stated] in the Santānasaṃhitā.
One should assign Sadyojāta to the little finger, Vāmadeva to the ring finger,
Aghora to the middle finger, and Puruṣa to the forefinger.
O Goddess of the gods, one should likewise place Īśāna on the thumb;
this is called the Saṃhāranyāsa, extending from the feet up to the hair.
In the *Sārdhatriśatikālottara*:
"Beginning with the little finger and ending with the thumb,
one should place the Brahmā-mantras there, and likewise the [five] limbs in their proper order."
One should recite the [mantras] beginning with the Heart and ending with *namaḥ*, and then utter the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) ending with *phaṭ*. Thus it is said in the *Acintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"Thereafter, one should cause that supreme *īkāra* to be performed by means of the root-mantra."
Having enveloped [the body] with armor, one should again contemplate the subtle form from the navel up to the *bhellāṭa* [the crown of the head].
One attains the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) from the navel up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
From the upward movement to the *dvādaśānta*, one should perform the fourfold [rite] beginning with the seat (*āsana*).
One should place the heart upon the heart, and the head upon the head.
Having placed the crest-lock (*śikhā*) upon the crest-lock, one should place the armor (*tanutra*) in the middle of the body.
Having placed the Netra-mantra upon the eyes and the Astra-mantra upon the two hands,
With the *coṭikā* mudrā, he should perform the binding of the directions and intermediate directions;
then, having consecrated [the disciple] with the root mantra, he should subsequently display the *mahāmudrā* in due order.
One should touch [the body] from the feet up to the head with both hands.

This is the procedure for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the temple (*prāsāda*). As for the placement of the pure five-syllabled mantra (*śuddhapañcākṣara*), we shall explain it in the section on recitation following the worship (line 4).

Regarding the *sakala-prāsāda* [the temple with parts], the *saṃhitā* is: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ hu hūṃ heṃ haiṃ hoṃ hauṃ haḥ, obeisance to Śiva. Regarding the *niṣkala-prāsāda* [the partless temple], however, it is: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ... (5th line).

"Hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ haḥ, obeisance to Śiva"—this is the *saṃhitā*, which constitutes the procedure for ritual placement (*nyāsa*). The placement of the five syllables (*pañcākṣaranyāsa*) is to be observed in the section on recitation (*japa-prakaraṇa*) within the intermediate Śaiva manual (*avāntara-śaiva-paddhati*). (6th line) It is stated in the *Śaiva-saṃnyāsa-paddhati* that one should perform the rite of cremation (*dahanopasana*) after the worship. Likewise: "Now, the wise man..."

One should perform the meditation on the Fire (*dahanopāsanā*). It is as follows: within the Supreme Brahman, or in the center of the heart-lotus, one should contemplate the signified (*vācya*) or the signifier (*vācaka*), or indeed the object of cognition (*vādya*); for what [other] origin could there be? [It is] devoid of powers (*śakti*) and the like, stainless, devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), partless (*niravayava*), actionless (*nikriya*), supportless (*nirālamba*), and incomparable (*nirūpama*).
Meditating upon the non-dual space of consciousness, whose nature is truth, knowledge, and bliss, and relinquishing the states of knower, knowing, and known, one shall become immortal.
This has been stated in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:

Likewise, in the Śaiva Purāṇa, in the Śrī Rudra-saṃhitā, within the *Puṇḍarīkapura-māhātmya*, it says: "Then, in the city of Brahmaṇya, [he bestowed] that which belongs to Puṇḍarīka," and so forth. (165a, 1st line) Having performed the binding of the ten directions (*daśadigbandhana*), one should effect the supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) from the feet to the top of the head by means of the root mantra (*mūla*).
Likewise, in the *Santānasaṃhitā*:

"Creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—this threefold deposition (*nyāsa*) is taught. A householder should practice through the path of creation, and a student (*brahmacārī*) should practice maintenance."
For forest-dwellers and ascetics, however, renunciation is called *saṃhāra*. If a forest-dweller is without a wife, it is called *saṃhāra-nyāsa*.
In the *Triśatikālottara*, it says:
"Purify the sole and the back of the hand with the seed-syllable of the Weapon (*astra*).
Thus [it is stated].
Having thus recited the mantra twice in the inconceivable *viśvasādākhyam*, one should purify the left hand;
in the case of an action, one should use the right [hand] for the right [hand] and the left hand for the left.
Having recited that [mantra] once, O Nandikeśvara,
one should purify the hands while visualizing them joined with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) up to the wrists.
Having formed a hollowed cup with both hands, with the two thumbs placed between the middle fingers,
one should meditate upon the supreme mandala of Śakti by means of the seed-syllable of nectar (Amṛta).
Oṃ hauṃ, vaṣaṭ to Śakti. One should contemplate the two hands as being submerged and formed into the shape of a lotus bud; within that, one should visualize the seat of Śiva.
Having placed the subtle form there, and subsequently reciting the mantra, one thus [attains] the form of Sadāśiva.
Nandikeśvara, one should perform the placement according to the Santāna-saṃhitā:
Sadyojāta on the little finger, and Vāmadeva on the ring finger.
Having assigned Aghora to the middle finger, one should assign Puruṣa to the index finger.
And likewise, O Goddess of gods, one should place Īśāna on the big toe;
this is called the Saṃhāranyāsa, extending from the feet up to the hair.
In the *Sārdhatriśatikālottara*:
"Beginning with the little finger and ending with the thumb,
one should place the Brahmā-mantras there, and likewise the limbs (*aṅga*) in their proper order."
One should recite the heart-mantra and the others ending with *namaḥ*, and the weapon-mantra ending with *phaṭ*.
Then, in the inconceivable state known as Viśvasāda, one should subsequently cause the supreme *īkāra* to arise from the root mantra.
Having enveloped [the body] with armor, one should again contemplate the subtle form from the navel up to the *bhellāṭa* [the crown of the head].
The attainment of the *vidyā-deha* (wisdom-body) extends from the navel to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
From the upward resonance at the *dvādaśānta*, one should perform the fourfold [placement] beginning with the seat (*āsana*).
One should place the heart-mantra upon the heart;
having placed the crest-mantra (*śikhā*) on the crest, one should place the armor-mantra (*tanutra*) in the middle of the body.
Having placed the *netra* (eye-mantra) upon the eyes, and likewise the *astra* (weapon-mantra) upon the two hands.
With the *coṭikā* mudrā, perform the binding of the ten directions;
then, having consecrated [the site] with the root mantra, sequentially form the *mahāmudrā*.
"One should touch [the body] from the feet up to the head with both hands. Thus ends the procedure for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the temple.
As for the placement of the pure five-syllable mantra (*śuddhapañcākṣaranyāsa*), it is performed according to the section on recitation (*japa*) mentioned in the ritual of worship (line 4).
We shall explain [this] regarding the entire temple:
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ hu hūṃ hluṃ heṃ haiṃ hoṃ hauṃ haḥ, to Śiva.
The *saṃhitā* [reading] is "namaḥ.
However, regarding the Niṣkala Prāsāda,
it is "oṃ hāṃ hauṃ" (on the fifth line).

"Hāṃ hīṃ huṃ haiṃ haḥ, obeisance to Śiva"—this is the *saṃhitā* [mantra]; such is the procedure for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). The five-syllable *nyāsa* is to be found in the section on recitation (*japa*) within the intermediate *Śaiva-paddhati*. (6th line)

In the *Śaivasannyāsapaddhati*, it is stated that one should perform the meditation on cremation (*dahanopāsanā*) after the worship. As follows: "Now, the wise man should perform the meditation on cremation.
It is as follows: within the city of Brahman, in the center of the heart-lotus, [is] the statement consisting of the signified and the signifier... (line 7).

Meditating upon the non-dual space of consciousness (*citākāśa*), which is devoid of birth, destruction, and so forth, stainless, attributeless, partless, actionless, supportless, and incomparable, and whose nature is truth, knowledge, and bliss— one should cast off the states of knower, knowing, and known, and become immortal.
Thus it has been stated in the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas;
likewise in the Śiva Purāṇa, in the Puṇḍarīkapura-māhātmya of the Śrī Rudra-saṃhitā: "Now, that which is called Vasvaśma-puṇḍarīka in the city of Brahmāṇḍapura," and so forth. (166a, first order) Oṃ.

Hāṃ, svadhā to the principle of the Self (ātmatattva). Oṃ hīṃ, svadhā to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). Oṃ hūṃ, svadhā to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva). Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the Weapon (astra). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart (hṛdaya). Oṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to the Nivṛtti-kalā. Oṃ hvīṃ, obeisance to the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā.

Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the Vidyā-tattva. Oṃ hyaiṃ, obeisance to Śānti-kalā. (Second order) ... hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna-mūrdhan. Heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa-vaktra. Huṃ, obeisance to Aghora-hṛdaya. Hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva-guhya. Haṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta-mūrti. Hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart. Hīṃ, obeisance to the Head.

Namaḥ | Hūṃ, obeisance to the crest-lock (śikhā). (Third order) ... Hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes. Haḥ, obeisance to the weapon (astra). Hauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the power (śakti). Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva (śivāsana).
Hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva (śivamūrti). Hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (vidyādeha). Haṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ hūṃ.

Salutation to the Self. Hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ, to the Nivṛtti-kalā: Haḥ huṃ phaṭ; haiṃ, salutation to the armor (kavaca). (166b, first order) [Omission] ... to the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā: Haḥ huṃ phaṭ; hrūṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ, to the Vidyā-kalā: Haḥ huṃ phaṭ. Hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. Hāṃ, salutation to the Gurus. Hāṃ...
Salutation to the Power of the Support (*ādhāraśakti*). Hāṃ, salutation to Anantāsana. Hāṃ, salutation to Ananta.
Hāṃ, salutation to Dharma. Hāṃ, salutation to Jñāna. Hāṃ, salutation to Vairāgya. Hāṃ, salutation to Aiśvarya.
(Second order: Hāṃ, salutation to Adharma. Hāṃ, salutation to Ajñāna. Hāṃ, salutation to Avairāgya. Hāṃ...

Homage to Anaiśvarya. Hāṃ, homage to Adhacchadana. Hāṃ, homage to Ūrdhvacchadana. Hāṃ, homage to the Kanda. Hāṃ, homage to the Bīja. Hāṃ, homage to the Aṅkura. Hāṃ, homage to the Nāla. Hāṃ, homage to the Dala-s. Hāṃ, homage to the Kesara-s. Hāṃ, homage to the Sūryamaṇḍala.

Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala). Hāṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc (somamaṇḍala). Hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar disc. Hāṃ, obeisance to the fiery disc (agnimaṇḍala). Obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fiery disc. Hāṃ, obeisance to the power-disc (śaktimaṇḍala). Hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of the power-disc. Oṃ.
Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva. (167a, 1st line;
156a, 153) [This applies] during the consecration, the offering of food, and likewise during the ritual services;
one should avoid circumambulation, prostration, meditation, and salutation.

One should avoid prostration when the Lord of Gods has mounted his chariot— whether he is in front, behind, to the left, or likewise in the inner sanctum (garbhageha). One should likewise avoid it when the Lord of Gods has entered the street or the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa).

One should not attend upon the root-linga; merit earned through desire is destroyed. Even while seated in the outer pavilion during that festival, seeing the root-linga destroys previously accumulated merit.

Facing west or facing north, standing on the left side—that is, on the side other than that [of the deity]—one should perform the worship and prostrations to Īśāna; otherwise, they would lead to fault, for they would be fruitless.
This sacrificial fire, abundant with fuel and produced from the *viraja* wood, belongs only to the student (*varnin*) who maintains the sacred fires.

There is no other [way]. A Śūdra should apply the *tripuṇḍra* and perform the smearing with ashes using the mantra "Namaḥ" alone. For those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), it is prescribed that the white ash should be produced from the fire of cooking, or from the dust raised by the shaking of a garment. For others, they say the ash should be taken from a forest fire (*dāvāgni*) and applied while reciting the appropriate mantra.
Manifest power (vibhūti) is said to be twofold, distinguished as the higher and the lower.
The higher they call Sadāśiva, and the lower is remembered as being twofold.
That indeed is the common support for all [the deities] arising from the temple,
and it is also proclaimed as the sixfold uncommon [support].
Sixfold prosperity has been declared:
that arising from the Vedic sacrificial fires, that born from the fire free of passion (virajā), and likewise that produced by the Smārta fires.
[The fire] produced from the sacrificial fuel (samidh) is [for the purpose of...
(*); likewise, for pure Brahmins, it is that which arises from the domestic cooking fire (pacanāgni).
Transcendental knowledge of Brahman is derived from the scriptures, preceded by a teacher.
The direct realization of the Self, preceded by the verbal instruction of a teacher, burns away the sin committed intentionally, just as fire consumes blackness.
The latent impressions of saṃsāra are like a fierce sun to the darkness of ignorance.
Whether in a temple, in the midst of an assembly, in a cremation ground, or in the presence of a king, the recitation of mantras should be performed; it does not result in any fault.
In this regard, the rule for the application of the sacred ash (vibhūti) is as follows: before midday, it should be mixed with water; after midday, it should be used without water.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Saṃhitā]:
"With the very mantra 'Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya', one who is fond of service should always perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion. Thus it is said.
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*,
it is said that not even an atom’s worth of ash should fall upon the ground;
having collected it in this manner, one should perform the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*).
If one is unable even to perform the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana), one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and so forth.
Kālāgni is said to reside in the left thumb, while Mūlāgni is said to reside at its base.
The digestive fire is at the navel, the fire of desire is located in the middle of the eyes, and the fire of knowledge is at the end of the twelve; these are proclaimed as the five fires.

In adversity, self-restraint; in wonder, forbearance; in battle, valor that is as swift as a hundred Śivas; in calamity, devotion to the Lord of the Aśvins; in praise, the offering of ten million maidens; and as a great gift, the worship of Śiva with a single flower—this is the rite of salutation. (168a, 1st line)
With the chest, the head, the mind, and likewise with speech,
as well as with the feet, the two hands, and the two ears— this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).

One should meditate upon the god Maṅgalāyatanadeva, who is exceedingly beautiful like a field of barley, and upon the wielder of the Pināka bow arriving with the appearance of a grove of Kalpa trees. O Hari, he is indeed Maheśvara, the trident-bearer, the holder of the Pināka.
By the names Paśupati, Śiva, and Mahādeva.

The term "Mahādeva" is used here without a case-ending. Just as one might imagine a beautiful woman at the foot of a tree, one should worship the Blessed Lady on the left side of the Blessed One. The mantra for this is: *Oṃ nama ādir bhagavatyai śaṅkarapriyāyai namaḥ*. Thus (the third line).
The seven rites beginning with the fetching of clay are: the fetching of clay, kneading, consecration, placing [the image], bathing, worship, and dismissal thereafter;
these seven rites, beginning with the fetching of clay, are performed with the seven names starting with Hara, preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.

The meaning is that one should perform the worship of the earthen *liṅga*. Oṃ, salutation to Śarva, the embodiment of the earth; to Bhava, the embodiment of water; to Rudra, the embodiment of fire; to Ugra, the embodiment of air; to Bhīma, the embodiment of ether;
(fifth line) to Paśupati, the embodiment of the sacrificer; to Mahādeva, the embodiment of the moon; to Īśāna, the embodiment of the sun. Oṃ, salutation.
Salutation to the Blessed One, the beloved of Śaṅkara, the illustrious Gaurī.
(6th line) I invoke the illustrious Gaurī into the left side of the illustrious Rudra.
(168b, 1st line) Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Hoṃ Haṃsaḥ So'haṃ; may the vital breaths, accompanied by the Pināka-bow, be present here as the vital breaths.
The individual soul (*jīva*) situated here is joined with the Pināka; joined with the Pināka are all the sense organs (*indriya*);

joined with the Pināka are mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), consciousness (*citta*), earth (*pṛthivī*), water (*ap*), fire (*tejas*), air (*vāyu*), ether (*ākāśa*), sound (*śabda*), touch (*sparśa*), form (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), smell (*gandha*), ear (*śrotra*), skin (*tvak*), eye (*cakṣus*), and tongue (*jihvā*).
May [the senses of] smell, speech, hands, anus, and genitals, having come here itself, remain happily for a long time; svāhā!
Among these [deities], Vāyu, Agni, Varuṇa, Īśāna, Nṛti, Soma, and Yama—the seed-syllables *da*, *dha*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are to be known as belonging to them respectively.
Āṃ pāśam, kroṃ aṃ ta guram, hrīṃ the seed-syllable of Śakti. (169a,
first line) This is the mantra for the *Śaivasannyāsapaddhati* concerning the entire *Prāsāda*.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ huṃ hūṃ heṃ haiṃ hoṃ hauṃ haḥ śivāya namaḥ—this is the *saṃhitā*. Regarding the Niṣkala-prāsāda: (second line).
*Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ haḥ śivāya namaḥ*—this is the *saṃhitā*.
This is the distinction of the mantras for the ritual assignment of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
*Oṃ hiṃ vāmadevaguhyāya pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ*; *Oṃ huṃ aghorahṛdayāya* [the third].

Line) *vidyākalāyai namaḥ* | *oṃ heṃ* to the face of Tatpuruṣa, *śāntikalāyai namaḥ* | *oṃ hoṃ* to the head of Īśāna, *śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ* | *sadyojāta oṃ haṃ* to the form of Sadyojāta, *nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ*. (4th)
Now, the division of the limb-mantras:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart, the abode of the power of omniscience; Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the head, the abode of the power of satisfaction.

Svāhā! Oṃ hūṃ, to the abode of the power of primordial awakening, for the tuft of hair (śikhā), vaṣaṭ! (5th line) Oṃ heṃ, to the abode of the power of sovereignty, for the armor (kavaca), hūṃ! Oṃ hauṃ, to the abode of the power that is never lost, for the three eyes (netratraya), vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ haḥ, to the abode of infinite power, for the weapon (astra), hūṃ phaṭ! Thus. (6th line)

*Oṃ juṃ saḥ* is the *mṛtyuñjaya-mantra*. Regarding the cause of the hymn (*stotra*): the seventh letter of the sky (*kha*) joined with the ear (*ṛ*) and possessing the crescent moon above; the fifth letter of *ku* (*pa*) joined with two dots (*bindu*) and the upward breath (*ū*).

And Manu, capable of protecting his arrows, [uttered] the *mṛtyuñjaya* (conqueror of death) mantra for himself, which clearly fulfills one's desired aim; it consists of the letter *ma*, the seventh vowel (*ū*), joined with *karṇa* (*ra*) and *kāra* (*ka*), possessing the *ardhacandra* (half-moon), and the sound *na*; may the Earth protect [it] up to the fifth [vowel], ending with the seed-syllable *la*.
The letter *sa* protects the pair of thighs; the visarga protects the knees. (169b, first line) …… *ghṛta* is declared [as the offering].
This is the ritual for the eightfold binding for one's own sake in the *Dīptāgama*.

Having placed eight jars— namely the *kumbha* and the two *vardhanīkās*— around it according to the arrangement in the mandala, one should perform the worship of Śiva, Śivā, Vidyeśvara, and the others within those [jars] in due order. Then, having performed the binding with the thread (*sobhayabandhana*), the bathing with water and garments,
the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, and the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) for the jar, the pitcher, and the rest, one should then complete [the ceremony].

Having also placed that liṅga upon the auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha) and offered the food oblation (naivedya) and other items, one should then recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times as an expiation,
or alternatively, perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
[Then] the mirror should be removed.
The water-pot, the jar, the bull, the pair of fly-whisks, the śrīvatsa, the svastika, the conch, and the lamp—
these are the eight auspicious emblems of the gods.
This is the sequence for the monthly worship.
In Mārgaśīrṣa, ghee is prescribed for the crown; in Puṣya, honey is commended;
in Māgha, a woolen blanket; and in Phālguna, a meal of curd.
In the month of Caitra, the offering of *damanaka* is prescribed; in Vaiśākha, the worship of *bhaṅgā*;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, the fruit [of the offering]; and in Āṣāḍha, the worship with milk.
In Śrāvaṇa, the worship with sugar; and in Bhādrapada, the worship with cakes.
"In the month of Tulā there is no worship, and in Kārttika there is the worship of lamps.
(170a, 1st line) Cotton, silk, buffalo ghee, and fine sugar; lac, beeswax, and *kunduruṣka*;
saffron-dyed cloth, stone, and resin—these are equal [in measure] for the pedestal (*pīṭha*) of the *liṅga*, as well as for its base and the binding with bitumen. (Sembampu, Erumai)
(White pepper) (second line) (Long pepper, ginger, lime, *kundurukka*, *kāvikal*, and *vellam*—these are the eight medicinal ingredients as described above.
An alternative method: Then, the "eight-fold binding" (*aṣṭabandhana*).
One should prepare [a mixture] of sesame oil, resin, red ochre, bdellium, sand, sugar, shellac, and sal tree resin—
these eight ingredients constitute the *aṣṭāṅga* (eightfold) formula.
Next is the *pañcabandhana* (fivefold binding).
Sugar, resin of the *sarja* tree, *guggulu*, the fruit of the plantain,
and buffalo butter— this is proclaimed as the "five-fold bond" (*pañcabandha*).
Both this "eight-fold bond" (*aṣṭabandhana*) and the "five-fold bond" concern the interests of others.

The threefold bond for one's own sake is as follows: Blue *gulgulu* (5th line), along with sugar powder, combined with buffalo ghee; by means of the technique of cooking, it is pounded twice with a pestle on a mortar, resulting in a firm bond. (Here, *kuṅkumam* and lime [are also used]). (6th line)

(Along with white lead,) having combined [the ingredients] equally and ground them in a mortar with a bamboo pestle, one should mix the medicine according to the prescribed method and administer it as a powder.
(170b, first line)
When the sun has entered the month of Dhanus, the worship of Śiva performed at dawn—
accompanied by the recitation of [the] thousand[-name hymn]— is considered equal to a day's worship.
Śiva is eternally present in the *āragvadha* tree, in the *vilva*, in the *liṅga*,
in the form of Śiva, and in the body of a Śiva-yogin. [He dwells there] even amidst millions of minor offenses and tens of millions of murders of Brahmins.
The sight of a devotee of Śiva burns away all sins without exception.
Even at a very great distance, wherever there is a person devoted to Maheśvara, Śiva is present there with effort, even if he must be sought out.
Praise is ten million times more meritorious than ritual worship; recitation is ten million times more meritorious than praise.
Meditation is ten million times more effective than recitation; absorption is ten million times more effective than meditation.
The word *pū* is said to bestow enjoyment (*bhukti*), and likewise the word *jā* bestows liberation (*mukti*);
by means of these two, the word *pūjā* is here spoken of as granting both enjoyment and liberation.
O beautiful lady, he who takes his meal at night on a Monday dwells in my presence for seven thousand crores of years;
likewise, on the eleventh lunar day, it is as if ten thousand crores of lunar and solar eclipses have occurred.
Those who eat only once on a Monday do not deserve sixteen-fold Kaula food.
Through the teacher’s ascetic power, through the excellence of worship,
and through the likeness of his form and the image— by these three means, Śiva is present.
Having touched the penis of the bull and likewise having heard the words of Hara, and having beheld Śiva between the two horns, there is no rebirth.
(171a, 1st order) *Hāṃ Hauṃ*, salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*). *Hīṃ Hauṃ*, [salutation] to the lord of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*).
Salutation to Śiva. Hūṃ Hauṃ, salutation to Śiva, the Lord of the Śiva-tattva. Hāṃ Hauṃ, salutation to Śiva.
The mantra for the worship of the door:
Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī. Oṃ Hāṃ...

Salutation to Mahālakṣmī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nandin. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Yamunā. (Second order: Hāṃ, svāhā to all mantras. Hāṃ, svāhā to the gods. Hāṃ, salutation to all the ṛṣis. Hāṃ, salutation to all...

Vaṣaṭ to humans! Hāṃ, svadhā to all the ancestors! Hāṃ, svadhā to all the mothers! Hāṃ, svadhā to all the kinsmen! Hāṃ, svadhā to all the teachers! (Third Order) .................. Hāṃ, obeisance to the Subtle One! Hāṃ, obeisance to Śivottama!

Salutation! Hāṃ, salutation to Ekanetra; Hāṃ, salutation to Ekarudra; Hāṃ, salutation to Trimūrti; Hāṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha; Hāṃ, salutation to Śikhaṇḍin; Hāṃ, salutation to Devī. (Fourth Order) [........................ Hāṃ, salutation to Nandin; Hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla.

Hāṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin. Hāṃ, obeisance to Vināyaka. Hāṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha. Hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda. Hāṃ, obeisance to Indra. Hāṃ, obeisance to Agni. (171b, first order) …… Hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa. Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. Hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera. Hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā.

*Namaḥ*. *Hāṃ*, obeisance to Viṣṇu. (Second order) *Hāṃ*, obeisance to the Vajra; *hāṃ*, obeisance to the Śakti; *hāṃ*, obeisance to the Daṇḍa; *hāṃ*, obeisance to the Khaḍga; *hāṃ*, obeisance to the Pāśa; *hāṃ*, obeisance to the Aṅkuśa; *hāṃ*, obeisance to the Gadā; *hāṃ*, obeisance to the Triśūla. (Third order) *Hāṃ*, obeisance to the Padma.

*Namaḥ*. *Hāṃ*, obeisance to Cakra. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Vāmā. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Raudrī. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Kālī. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Balavikaraṇī. (Fourth Order) *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Balapramathinī. *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamanī. *Oṃ*...
Hāṃ, salutation to Manonmanī.

The seed-syllable of Sarasvatī is *saṃ*; the syllables of Sarasvatī are *aiṃ klīṃ sauṃ*. (172a, first order [no activity]) (……… *puṇagu*) The specific [trees] are: *ciribilva* (also *puṇugu*), *khadira* (the *kaṅkuraṅkāli* tree), *śirīṣa* (the *vākai* tree), and *arjuna* (the *marutu* tree).
The mango tree (*āmra*), trees with prohibited milky sap (*niṣiddhakṣīravṛkṣa*) such as the *āl*, the *vānīra* (water reed), the *yava* (barley, here referring to the *marudukārai* plant),
the *apāmārga* (swallow-wort), the *dhātrī* (myrobalan), the *śigru* (moringa), the *nimba* (neem), the *kataka* (soapberry),
the *tintiṇī* (tamarind), the *japā* (hibiscus), and the *iḍānāḍī* (third-order [plants]).
(Touching the big toe on the left side and moving up to the head: (With the *sūcīmukhī* [needle-mouthed] and *piṅgalā* [tawny] channels, moving backward two [units]:
*Piṅgalanāḍī*. (Touching the big toe on the right side: (Moving up to the *tata* [shoulder] with the *sūcīmukhī* and binding it... [it shall be established].

The procedure for flowers: *puṃnāga* (Punnāga), *droṇa* (Droṇa), *mādhavī* (Mādhavī), *kurava* and *kurumba* (Kurava and Kurumba), *jāti* and *mālā* (Jāti and Mālā), *dūrvā* (Dūrvā), and *bakapuṣpa* (Bakapuṣpa).
(Kokkurakuma-nāra), girikarṇī (white kākaṭuṅga flower), bhadrā (peyara), bhadrakamadu śrīpuṣpam (tālipu flower),
sinduvāra (nocci), lodhra (paṇṇilōti), hayadhāmāra (alari), suraktā, bṛhatī (red kaṭṭari), piṇḍītaka (marukānā tree), hemaśraddhrā (poṉṉūmattu), and asana (vaṅkai).

The *saṃkhinī* (the jasmine flower), the *vakula* (the mahiḻamaram tree, the flower of the *paṭṭikā-paṭṭiya*), (4th order) the *śrīvera* (ra mi ta... vo...), the *japā* (...*sī*), the *damanaka* (the marukkoḻuntu), the *sahakāra* (the mango blossom), the *śamīpuṣpa* (the vanmippū), the *pāṭalī* (the pādirī), and the *kanakāpuṣpa* (also known as *hemapuṣpam*, the *śeṇṇagam*).

*Ekapatrāravinda* (a single-petaled lotus), *aśara* (honey), *nāgadantikā*, *sahadevī*, *sītadevīyā* (red leadwort), *uśīra* (vetiver grass), *hiribera* (costus root), and *munipuṣpa*. (172b, first order) [………] *munipuṣpa*.
Kuraṇḍaka (known as golden jasmine), Brahmavṛkṣa (Palāśa or Māma), Gokṣura (Neruñcirappū),
Atasī (Kāsāmbū), Kośātakī (Pīrggu), Śrīvarṇabilva (Tāliyiṣa or the three types of Bilva), Vikaṅkata (Mucaikai), Jatu (Arakku),
Murā (Amukkūrā), and Māṃsī.

(Chadamāmāñji), vacā (vachampū), koṣṭhaṃ (cheṅkazu-nīrkoṭṭam), rajanīdvayaṃ (malaimañjalam, mañjal), nūcyam (ceviyamānakaḍiccāru), astam (koṉraṅkiḻaṅku), haridrā (mañjalam nirāyumadu), gairikaṃ (kaḷavikkal), śatarajas (mañjapodi). (Third order)

In the rite of initiation (dīkṣākarma), there are five stages: the fetter (saṃyojana), the generation (sañjanana), the enjoyment of enjoyments (bhogabhojana), the severing of the noose (pāśaccheda), and the subsequent extraction (uddhāra).

The sevenfold equinox shines forth in the *Siddhāntasārāvali* within the sixfold state of equal flavor (*ṣaḍvidhasamarasībhāva*). As for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to its circumference: having bound it with three girdles (*mekhalā*), the middle girdle is situated to the east, north, and west; the four cities (*pura*) extending to the east, south, west, and north form the sacrificial seat (*viṣṭara*). Thus it was clearly established.
(The Darbha grass placed at the four corners of the second Mekhalā [girdle], its tip reaching the single Mekhalā above—this is the Darbha grass used by the one who places it;
it occurs in the Antyeṣṭi [funeral rites]. The purification at the crossroads [the 14th] will appear in the Maṇḍapa-pūjā.)
Its ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is explained in the section on consecration (*pratiṣṭhāprakaraṇa*). || The procedure for circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇavidhi*). ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the circumambulation of Nidhaneśa,
which removes all sins, is meritorious, and bestows the fruits of all desires.
The letter *da* removes all fear and bestows one's desires;
the letter *kṣa* destroys sin, and the letter *ṇa* is the means to liberation. Whatever sins have been committed in other births—those too [are destroyed].
Those various [faults] perish at every single step as one proceeds clockwise.
Moving from foot to foot, with hands free from movement,
praise on the lips and meditation in the heart— this is the four-limbed circumambulation.
Just as a woman whose delivery is imminent walks slowly while carrying a water-filled jar,
so should one perform the circumambulation;
with a single prostration with the staff held upright and a single circumambulation.
A single prostration with one hand destroys previously accumulated merit.
In front, behind, to the left, or likewise within the inner sanctum,
one should never perform recitation, fire-offerings, or prostrations.
With the two feet, the two hands, the two fists, the two knees, the head, the chest,
as well as with the mind and speech— this is called the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*).
As many particles of dust as there are that adhere to the body of one whose limbs are covered in dust, [so many worlds does he conquer].
For that many thousands of years, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Even when a prostration is made before the Liṅga with disrespect, deceit, mockery, or guile,
there shall be the destruction of all sins;
likewise, when a devotee falls like a staff upon the ground before Paśupati.
All sins fall away together, but they do not rise up again.
Having covered his body with a cloth, the man should meditate [on me] and bow to me;
otherwise, he is born mute for three lifetimes and remains destitute for seven lifetimes.
While dancing before Śaṅkara, what position was taken from the beginning?
The birds of great sin situated within the body were driven upward.
As for the *añjali* gesture toward the gods, it is placed upon the forehead for the gurus.
For others, the prostration performed upon the chest is considered to be of three kinds.

In an appropriate place, he should always be served; however, when staying in his temple, he may be served according to the time. In one's own home, Hara should be constantly served, except at midnight.
Having performed three circumambulations with five prostrations,
and having circumambulated once more, rebirth is no longer found.
One [verse] has been taught for Vināyaka, while there should be six for Ṣaṇmukha;
O Lord, four [verses] are established for Keśava according to the Paddhati.
Three circumambulations are prescribed for Śiva, and seven for the Aśvattha tree; for other deities and trees, however, four circumambulations are taught.
Thus has the general rule been declared; what follows shall be the specific rule.
For ascetics it is to the right, but for students of sacred knowledge it is to the left.

The leftward path (*apasavya*) is for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*); however, in the case of the householder, it is prescribed that he should circumambulate the home clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*) when performing worship.
There too, having avoided at that time the shadow of the God of gods, the stepping over of his offerings (*nirmālya*),
and the path of the *somasūtra*,
one should perform that circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) by way of both the left and the right.
It may be half the measure of the mind-line, or it may be equal to the measure of the ground.
Having left [the center] in the north of the inner mandala, one should perform a circumambulation externally;
then, having gone to the left of the God of Gods, one should proceed with the thread and other materials.
Having reached the western side by way of the south, one should lead it back again into its vicinity;
thus, by moving alternately to the left and right, one should avoid the shadow of the watchtower.
Wherever, however, there is a sacrificial altar (*balipīṭha*) during the circumambulation, that is the place for the bull to stand.
In each of those places, one should perform circumambulations, keeping that as the primary focus.
Whether there are two bulls for the Lord of Gods, or if there are no bulls at the altar of the sacrificial offering (balipīṭha),
the performer, having circumambulated those situated outside, should perform the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa).
A wise person should not pass between the Lord of Devas and the Bull, nor between the two when they are on the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), as that constitutes a violation of the enclosure.
Circumambulating the Garbhagṛha yields the merit born of ten horse-sacrifices;
the merit in the region of the inner maṇḍala is ten times greater than that.

In the inner chambers and other such halls, each successive circumambulation shall be ten times greater than the preceding one. A single circumambulation performed at the site of the fifth enclosure is equal to ten million circumambulations of the earth consisting of the seven continents and oceans.
Pure from the rising of the sun until its setting.
By performing circumambulation with devotion, one shall attain the same world as Śiva;
if this circumambulation is performed limb by limb, it is the means for attaining union with Śiva.
A thousand circumambulations are equal to a single circumambulation of the limbs;
one should perform three circumambulations, which accomplish all desires and goals.
The fruit of five circumambulations is said to bestow victory;
with seven, there shall be the destruction of enemies, and with nine, the increase of sons.
Through eleven [verses] one gains longevity; through thirteen, one's desires;
through fifteen, the bestowal of prosperity; and through seventeen, wealth.
Through nineteen, it is said that health is attained and disease is destroyed.
Through twenty-one [means], the increase of knowledge for men shall come to pass.

The fruits are twenty-three and twenty-five [circumambulations], resulting respectively in happiness and strength; thus, those seeking desired objects should always perform the circumambulation. In the forenoon it shall destroy disease, and at midday it grants one's desired aims.
In the evening it destroys all sins; at the half-watch of night, it bestows liberation.
One should perform twenty-eight circumambulations up to one hundred and eight; for the sake of non-specific desires, however, they should be performed in increasing groups of ten, moving clockwise.
One should perform two hundred and eight circumambulations with devotion;
the fruit of this is equal to that of the Atirātra sacrifice in a single day, without a doubt.
If one performs three hundred and eight [recitations] with purity, one attains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, one should perform four hundred and eight [times];
one obtains the fruit of a Gomedha sacrifice. Likewise, for five hundred [times], one obtains the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice; and for six hundred and eight [times], the same result follows.
He who performs this [rite] certainly partakes of the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
To him who respectfully performs seven hundred circumambulations,
Śiva grants the fruit of the Naramedha sacrifice and bestows his affection.
If one performs eight hundred circumambulations with devotion, [he likewise attains the same].
He obtains the certain fruit of the merit from giving ten million cows.
If a pure person performs nine hundred [recitations] with devotion,
having obtained the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, he rejoices as one possessing great enjoyments.
But he who performs [it] one thousand and eight times preceded by devotion—
Having obtained the fruit of the eight initiations, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
One seeking knowledge [should recite] two thousand; one seeking a maiden, three thousand;
one seeking wealth, four thousand; and one seeking enjoyments, fifty thousand.
One who desires knowledge should perform it six thousand times; one who desires subjugation, seven thousand times;
one who desires dominion, eight thousand times; one who desires food, nine thousand times;
and for the sake of the prosperity of all attainments, one should perform it ten thousand times.
One should perform twenty thousand [repetitions] for the purification of the great sins (mahāpātaka).
With forty thousand [verses] one attains sālokya;
with sixty thousand, sāmīpya; indeed, through those thousands, one attains proximity.

Through the power of circumambulation, union with the divine is attained by eighty thousand, and the supreme state by one hundred thousand; everything is certainly obtained. Therefore, no merit equal to this exists even throughout the three worlds.
Having always risen early in the morning and bathed, one should perform circumambulation with devotion.
He who performs the circumambulation three times a day for a year without restriction shall obtain a hundred [merits] by walking within the inner circle as many times as there are vowels.
That man shall attain his desired success, which is difficult for mortals to achieve;
indeed, within six months, the earth yields its fruits to him.
Then, for the sake of destroying enemies, the king should have ten thousand [mantras] performed;
by practicing this for three months, the king will quickly come under his control—of this there is no doubt.
Any mortal who, seeking cattle, land, sons, or wealth, should perform this for a period of three months, shall obtain all of that; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He who performs circumambulations twenty-five times every single day—
A haunted house is liberated from Piśācas and the like by means of the three maṇḍalas.

One who is tormented by diseases such as consumption, leprosy, and skin ailments shall become free from them and partake in happiness after performing ten thousand circumambulations. What need is there for much speaking on this matter? Whatever a person undertakes while joined with [this practice], he attains it.
O God of gods, by circumambulating [thee], one attains the desired object without effort.
Five, ten, fifteen,
or twenty-five prostrations, performed with the eight limbs and accompanied by hymns of praise.
During a festival, a chariot procession, or at any auspicious time,
a wise person who performs circumambulation with devotion bestows great joy.
The man who, having circumambulated Śambhu, undertakes a pilgrimage,
shall have his desires fulfilled, become happy, and return once again.

Even for one who has abandoned all characteristics, who is devoid of action, and of low birth—whosoever shall circumambulate the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) and attain the foremost perfection of Kuṇḍalinī—the greatness of circumambulation has been described by me in detail. Furthermore, there is another type of circumambulation, limb-by-limb, from sunrise until sunset; of these two—
We are not worthy to describe the greatness of this merit:
first is the prostration with the staff, second is that with eight limbs,
third is that with five limbs, and fourth is that with three limbs.
Having performed the five-limbed dance, perform the sixth limb, which is the hymn of praise. Thus, the seventh limb is meditation, the eighth limb is the vision of the Liṅga,
the ninth limb is the pure Śakti, and the tenth limb is the vision of the Tāṇḍava dance.
Listen now to this other procedure, which consists of ten limbs and follows that specific sequence:
a man with a pure mind, having prostrated himself like a staff before Śiva,
shall experience the destruction of all his sins through [the Lord's] grace and attain all spiritual perfections.
The first limb has thus been declared; now hear the second limb:
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
mind, intellect, and ego—this is the certainty regarding the eight limbs.
The second limb has thus been declared; now hear the third limb.
Having sequentially placed the two knees, the two hands, and the head, one should utter the five-syllable mantra and then apply the five limbs.
The third limb has thus been declared; now hear the fourth limb.
The hands raised above the head with palms joined like buds, conjoined with the three-syllable Praṇava,
and fixed immovably upon the Self— this is remembered as the limb of the Praṇava.
The fourth limb has thus been declared; now hear of the five-limbed [rite].
Having performed the clapping of hands, perform the dance out of compassion.
By performing the dance of bliss, it is determined as a limb of the dance.
It should be known as having five limbs; now hear about the sixth limb from him.
Having attained a single-pointed mind through the hymn of praise to Compassion and through prostration— (5th line)—
he for whom this sixth-limbed hymn of praise is maintained shall proceed [on the path].
This should be known as the sixfold limb; now hear of the sevenfold limb.
These consist of mantras, words, phonemes, and the worlds in their true nature.
Through the non-union with the mixture of kalās, the wise one [attains] the limb of meditation.
It should be known as having seven limbs; now hear about the eight-limbed [path].
Having uttered the subtle mantra, one perceives the *liṅga* between the eyebrows;
this should be known as the eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*) [yoga], and now hear the nine-limbed (*navāṅga*).
By means of a state of pure wakefulness, one should cause [the mind] to enter the station of the fourth (*turya*).
This should be known as the nine-limbed [scripture]; now hear the ten-limbed.
In the Ādhāra [cakra], beginning with Brahmā, and above that Viṣṇu;
above Viṣṇu is Rudra, and above Rudra is Maheśvara.
Īśa is above, and Sādākhya is above that; and above that is Bindu alone.
Having beheld Dṛṣṭika above that, one should worship Śiva in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

Above that is the Tāṇḍava, which is proclaimed as having ten limbs. Even if a salutation is performed toward a Liṅga with disrespect, beginning with the letter Śa, or through jesting or deceit, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
For as many particles of dust as there are on his body covered by dust,
for that many thousands of years was Hara united with him.
For one who recites the six-syllabled mantra preceded by the *praṇava* three times as [Śiva] goes toward tranquility,
and who abides before Śiva, his life is fruitful.
In the *Dīpti* [mudrā] (third line):
having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one should offer the eight limbs—
the head, the two hands, the two ears, the chin, and the pair of arms.

Now hear concerning the eight-limbed and the five-limbed prostration. Having placed the head, the two hands, the two arms, and the two knees upon the ground—this is called the five-limbed [prostration]. (The head, the two hands, and the two knees constitute this five-limbed [prostration]).
Elsewhere it is also said: "The feet, knees, hands, thighs, navel, shoulders, heart, and head—these are called the eight-and-a-half limbs; with these one should perform prostration to Śiva."
With the chest, the head, the gaze, the mind, the speech,
the heart, the two thighs, and the two hands— this is called the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
Now, the ritual procedure for the Rudrākṣa:
For thousands of divine years my eyes remained closed;
they fell from my eyes upon the earth like drops of water.
The Rudrāśravindavas were born as great rudrākṣa trees; thus originated the birth of the rudrākṣa from the water of Rudra’s eyes. Since its fruit possesses the form of Rudra, it is called rudrākṣa.
If one who has placed rudrākṣa beads around his neck conquers even a dog, [then what need is there to mention others]?
He attains the state of Rudra; how much more so, then, humans and others?
Śiva himself, with his single face, directly removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The two-faced [mantra] of the God of gods certainly destroys the sin of killing a cow;
the three-faced [mantra], which is Fire itself, burns away the sin of killing a woman in an instant.

One who personally [worships] the four-faced [form] is Brahmā himself; such a person removes the sin of killing a human being. One who personally [worships] the five-faced [form] is Rudra himself, known by the name Kālāgni.
By wearing the five-faced [liṅga], one is liberated from all sins, even from going where one should not go and from eating what should not be eaten.
One should hold the six-faced Kārttikeya in the right hand;
the sin of killing an embryo and other such evils is destroyed—of this there is no doubt.
O Mahāsena, by [worshipping] the one with seven faces named Ananta,
a person is liberated from the sins of stealing gold and killing a cow.
In the great festival of Aṣṭavaktra, the god Vināyaka is present in person;
Viṣṇu likewise is Aṣṭavaktra, Navavaktra, and Caturmukha.
Mānakūṭa, Kūṭa, and likewise Sarvakūṭa;
with the back, belly, and hand, one should touch the wives of others.
O child, Daśavaktra is indeed the god Janārdana himself.
And likewise the grahas, piśācas, vetālas, and brahmarākṣasas.
By wearing it, all others—the serpents, the Garuḍas, and the rest—are destroyed.
One should always wear an eleven-faced Rudrākṣa on the crest; hear now the meritorious fruit thereof, for such a person is indeed the eleventh Rudra himself.
Or one may recite [the mantra] ten thousand times, or even a hundred times that number.
One should wear twelve rudrākṣas around the region of the neck; a mortal obtains that fruit which belongs to the gomedha, aśvamedha, and sacrifices involving much gold—
of this there is no need for doubt.
Furthermore, neither the fear of fire nor disease shall prevail.
O child, one should wear the thirteen-faced Rudrākṣa,
which grants desires, bestows success, and is known as the giver of all accomplishments.

O child, if one wears a fourteen-faced rudrākṣa, they shall destroy those who desire to drink mercury, elixirs, or the results of alchemical transmutations, as well as their mother, father, kinsmen, and brothers.
One should constantly hold the Śakti-bindu of Śiva upon the crown of the head.
Constantly honored by the gods, one attains supreme merit;
even for one's own body, that [merit] exists when a rudrākṣa is placed upon the head.
By holding [the breath] at the crest-lock (śikhā), one reaches thirty-six [finger-breadths]; likewise thirty-two at the head;
thirty-two at the region of the throat; and likewise fifty at the heart.
A man should always wear sixteen armlets, twelve bracelets at the wrists, and eight rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.
At every step, one undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
by wearing it on the crest, ten million [merits are gained], and at the two ears, ten billion;
at the throat, a thousand billion, and by wearing it on the arms, they are innumerable.
If, at the time of death, one has consumed a rudrākṣa and thus become immortal;
He too attains the state of Rudra; for him, there is no further rebirth—this applies to the man who performs one hundred and eight repetitions, or even half of that.
Alternatively, one seeking liberation should use a rosary of twenty-five beautiful Rudrākṣas; one seeking security, twenty-seven;
one seeking wealth, thirty; and one seeking long life, twenty-five.
Twenty-five [syllables] are for the purpose of liberation; twenty-seven are for nourishment.
The twenty-eighth is for the sake of desired objects, and the thirty-first is for wealth;
the letter *ja* destroys rebirth, while the letter *pa* destroys evil.
The letter *ma* is the release from impurity (*mala*), and likewise the letter *lā* is liberation (*mukti*).
The definition of the rosary (*japamālā*) is thus declared by the reciter.
The letter *ja* is the severance of rebirth (*janma*), and the letter *pa* is the destruction of sin (*pāpa*).
Since recitation removes death, it is for this reason that it is called "japa" here.
One should know that the fruit of audible recitation is single; that which is performed with teeth, palate, and lips is tenfold;
at the root of the tongue it is a hundredfold; and mental recitation is a hundred-thousandfold.
Mental recitation is the best, while that performed with dust [or in a dusty place] is middling.
Those who investigate the meaning of the scriptures declare that verbal [action] is the lowest.
Shaped like a cow’s tail-ring, each [coil] joined by a knot;
mouth joined with mouth, tail joined with tail.
The thumb is to be known as the liberator; the index finger destroys enemies;
the ring finger brings prosperity; and the middle finger leads to wealth.
O Six-faced One, for those who count by means of finger-joints, each single joint [counts as one];
by lines, it is eightfold; and by the fruits of the son-lamp, it is tenfold.
Facing east brings subjugation; facing south, malevolent rites;

facing west, the acquisition of wealth; and facing north, there shall be pacification. (6th line) In the southeast, there is affliction by disease; likewise, in the southwest, there is inciting hatred.
In the northwest, there is indeed plowing, and in the northeast, liberation itself.
With conch shells, the merit is a hundredfold; with crystal beads, it is a thousandfold.
From the Rudrākṣa tree, however, there exists a number corresponding exactly to that of one's sons.
The rosary is indeed the asterism; the Moon is its leader.
The knots are endowed with Viṣṇu and Śiva, while Brahmā is the presiding deity.
The root of that rudrākṣa is Brahman; its stalk is said to be Viṣṇu. Its face is called Rudra, and the drop (*bindu*) is all the deities.
Therefore, the form of the God is the direct means for attaining liberation;
by adorning it with Rudrākṣas at the beginning of worship and other rites, one bestows the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
[One should wear] a sacred thread of Rudrākṣas, a turban, and an upper garment [of the same].
And the ash [mark] of the non-Śaivas; these are proclaimed as the five mudrās.
An *ayuta*, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand,
