or a hundred thousand *rudrākṣas* that are cut or split are said to yield the fruit of *sārūpya*.
A man should strive for the swift destruction of the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes.
For seven thousand births, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
The rosary, the ash on the head, the smearing with ashes, the seat of animal skin,
the staff, and the sacred thread— these six mudrās are the characteristics of Śiva.
Listen now in due order to the rosaries for the neck, the arm, the hand, the head, and likewise the garland of hair on the head.
For those seeking liberation, the recitation with twenty-five rudrākṣas is prescribed.
Twenty-six [recitations] are for the sake of Śiva, for the sake of knowledge, and for the destruction of enemies.
For the sake of the twenty-seventh [deity], twenty-eight are proclaimed;
for one seeking a wife, thirty [are used], and fifteen for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
Thus indeed should the rosary for recitation be; now hear the characteristics of others:
a garland extending from the neck to the navel is of excellent quality.
[A garland] above the navel does not grant long life, while one below the navel causes the loss of ascetic merit.
Therefore, the Brahma-sūtra is not [merely] for the purpose of direct realization.
The head-garland is equal in measure to that [neck-garland], and the arm-garland is likewise;
the hand-garland is measured by the hand, and the throat-garland is equal to that.
Its sight pacifies evil, and its touch bestows all perfections.
One should always wear a Rudrākṣa, which is meritorious even before its consecration.
Whether pure or even impure, one should always wear the rudrākṣa;
for a practitioner who does not wear rudrākṣa, there is no worship of Śiva.
All that work becomes fruitless, like an oblation poured into ashes;
even if a dog were to die while wearing a rudrākṣa around its neck.
He attains the state of Rudra; how much more so, then, humans and others?
Therefore, with every effort, one should always wear the rudrākṣa.
By wearing [it], one attains heaven and is not subject to rebirth;
one should always wear it on the hands, ears, crest-lock, and the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*),
together with ashes, for the sake of pacifying all sins.
News of kings, news of merchants, and especially news of worldly affairs.

Merely by the movement of the rudrākṣa beads, it becomes as fruitful as a mantra. Those who always wear a rosary fashioned from a thousand rudrākṣas, which is the very form of Śiva, attain the supreme goal.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always wear the rudrākṣa.
Even a Mleccha or a Cāṇḍāla, though joined with grievous sins, becomes Rudra himself through the wearing of Rudrākṣas; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the Rudrākṣa. Thus it is written in the *Sakalāgamasāra*. (179a, line 1) [117] The Ritual Procedure for Sacred Ashes (*Bhasma-vidhi*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for the ash-bath:
the cow dung of a tawny cow is the best, while that of a white cow is middling.
That which is red or black is declared to be the lowest; one should take [clay] from a five-petaled [lotus].
One should take cow dung fallen upon a ground that is not scorched or black, using the *sadyojāta* mantra.
One should form the lumps with the *vāmadeva* mantra and consecrate them with the *aghora* mantra.
Having burned it with the Śiva-mantra, the wise one should then seize it with the Tatpuruṣa-mantra.
Having burned [the offering] with the Puruṣa-mantra, one should take possession [of it] with the Īśāna-mantra.
Likewise, [one should offer] Ketakī, Mallikā, Nāga, Campaka, and Pāṭala flowers.
Having placed lotus, palāśa, tulasī, apāmārga, the tips of kuśa grass,
and jasmine there, one should take them up in excellent vessels.
The wise one should cast it into a vessel made of gourd or into a stream of ashes;
having placed it in a new earthen jar, he should protect it with the *kavaca* mantra.
Taking that ash while recollecting the Śiva-mantra,
one should mutter the Vyomavyāpin mantra once, accompanied by the five Brahmans and the Śiva-aṅgas.
One should apply the sacred ash with both hands joined in the *brahmamudrā* gesture;
specifically, one should place it upon the left hand using the right hand alone.
Placing [the hand] upon the right knee, one should mutter the Śiva-mantra a hundred times;
having muttered the mantras once, perform the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*).
If one is unable even to perform the smearing, [one should apply] the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) on all the joints.
In the thirty-two junctions, or else in the sixteen.
Or the mantra-practitioner should apply the *tripuṇḍra* according to the rite upon the eight joints:
on the head, the forehead, the two ears, the two eyes, the two nostrils,
the neck, the two arms, and the two elbows.
And in the [treatise on] binding, [the locations are] the heart, the navel, the penis, and likewise the anus.
The thighs, knees, shanks, and likewise the calves, as well as the feet— these thirty-two joints are recited in their proper order.

In the same manner, one should assign [the mantras] to the heads and other parts of the eight-formed Lord, as well as to the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), and the Vasus. [Specifically:
the head on the forehead, the neck, the shoulders, the upper arms, and the forearms.
The heart, the belly, the navel, the two sides, and the back.
One established in the Śiva-āśrama should apply two triple-marks (*tripuṇḍra*) at each of the sixteen locations.
Likewise, one should apply them for the five forms beginning with Śiva, as well as for those beginning with Vāmā.
One should know that [the mark] is dear to Aśvinī; it should be fashioned starting from the head.
The head, the forehead, the throat, the two arms, and likewise the heart.
The navel and the back are to be known as the eight joints in sequence;
the head is [consecrated] by Īśāna alone, and the face by Tatpuruṣa.

One should mark the heart with the Ghora mantra, the secret place with the Vāma mantra, and all the limbs with the Sadyojāta mantra; thus one should perform the ritual sprinkling in sequence. Furthermore, one should apply marks upon the body using sandalwood mixed with ashes.
For initiated twice-born men, however, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be six finger-breadths in length.
The characteristics of the *tripuṇḍra* for one who is uninitiated shall now be described; listen.
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* using the middle, ring, and index fingers.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
they constitute the very nature of the triple mark as creation, preservation, and dissolution.
For Brāhmaṇas it is six finger-breadths in width, and for kings, four finger-breadths.
For Vaiśyas it is two finger-breadths, and for Śūdras one finger-breadth.
For all others as well, the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) should be like that of a *śūdra*. For kings and those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*), it should be made with sandalwood mixed with ashes.
Brahmā himself is at the aperture of the crown (*brahmarandhra*), and Subrahmaṇya is on the forehead.
The god Vināyaka is in the throat; the Sun and Moon are in the two eyes.
Indra and Viṣṇu are in the two arms; likewise, Īśvara is in the heart;
Durgādevī is in the navel; and the Pitṛs are in the back.
Upon his two thighs dwell the Nāgas and likewise the Nāga maidens;
upon the pair of his knees are the sages and the wives of the sages; and again, upon his feet reside the seven oceans and all the sacred fords (tīrthas).
The locations for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the deities associated with them have been fully proclaimed:
during the forenoon, at the time of eating, on the seat, and even while lying down, the triple mark should be made with ashes; this is ordained as a protection against all [evils].
It is used for the act of wearing, eating, dwelling, and plunging into water.
Having touched a Caṇḍāla, a Śūdra, or a woman, one should practice the Āgneya bath;
likewise after sleeping, eating, drinking water, or having performed the necessary bodily functions.
[One should also bathe after touching] a woman, a man, a neuter, a Śūdra, a cat, a heron, or a mouse.
Having touched such things, one should likewise practice the fire-related (āgneya) bath.
It brings prosperity and purity, destroys diseases and defects,
grants mastery over the world, and is meritorious, destroying sins day by day.
It provides protection for all mortals, and he goes to the world of Śiva.
Even by the sight of bad dreams or contact with wicked people... [for those] who are unable to bathe and for those who are always afflicted by illness.
They are purified by the ash-bath and become fit for worship.
(...... the planets and the spirits (bhūtas) (......).
Protection against epilepsy, sudden death, and youth [afflictions] is ordained for all.
Vain is the Veda, vain is the sacrifice, vain is the gift, and vain is the austerity;
vain also is the dwelling for one who does not wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).

Having performed a hundred ablutions with water, but a hundred thousand ablutions with mantras, and having smeared himself with ashes while reciting the mantra, he becomes Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
For those whose bodies are smeared with ashes from the soles of their feet to the crown of their heads, every single hair is a liṅga; that body is called the pīṭha.
In a *śrāddha*, a sacrifice, a recitation (*japa*), an oblation (*homa*), the *vaiśvadeva* rite, or the worship of the gods—
whatever one performs without wearing the *puṇḍra* mark shall all be fruitless.
The *tripuṇḍra* mark should be applied on the forehead and other limbs, not on the *śūlāṅga*.
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* three times a day, twice a day, or once a day,
in the presence of Śiva, [the sacred fire], and the Guru.
One should not perform the smearing with ashes on pure ground.
Having first offered the ashes with the *pratādāra* mantra and having prostrated before the ritual substance,
the person should then likewise prostrate and smear the ashes.
For as many thousands of years as there are particles of ash that fall upon the ground,
for that many years shall the perpetrator go to hell.
If ashes fall upon the ground through negligence, one should wipe them away with the hand and then place them on the head; thereafter, one should meditate upon Śiva.
O Śambhu’s son, have a linga-shaped object, a bilva fruit, a bamboo leaf,
as well as leaves of the aśvattha and udumbara trees, engraved.
The *liṅga* form, the lamp, the half-moon, the triple-ash mark (*tripuṇḍraka*),
and the circular smearing of ash— these six are the means for attaining Śiva.
In the midst of the rival [letters] imagined [there], lead [the two] into half a measure of the eyebrows;
that knowledge is obtained when the two and the two are joined. Again, half a dot, beautiful as a crescent moon, marked by one quarter of a measure, [is placed] on the forehead.

Beyond the cluster of the *rocanā* [mineral], there is no further luster; that [region] consists of one-eighth of a *mātrā*. A staff (*daṇḍa*) measuring sixteen parts, resembling a jewel, follows, and beyond that are the *tamasas*. Then, within the cavity of light that rivals the flash of a lightning-bud at the end of the staff, is the *brahman*;
in its center is the cavity of the eyebrows.

Having accepted that which is dear to the Truth within the measure of a finger-breadth (*bhavāṅgula*), the Lord Īśa, in that region, performs his own slaughter for the four-footed [deities] beginning with the half-moon.
Thereafter, in the space of one *aṅgula*, there is the Śakti consisting of a sixteenth part of a digit (*kalā*);
beyond that, it is double that portion, and above that, it is another three *aṅgulas*.

Marked by two pairs of ten lines, each consisting of fifty units endowed with six [dots], with a slender body and reaching as far as the attachment of the noose at four finger-breadths—that is Śakti; that Śakti triumphs at four finger-breadths, O Lord beyond the Unnameable! At the desired Śakti, Śiva, who is the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) and possesses the luster of ten million suns at the end of an aeon, is present.

The utterance of the seed-syllable is the waking state; the grasping of the bindu is the dream state; and the union with the nāda is deep sleep. One should perform this while maintaining awareness and joined with the vital breath (jīva).
At the end of the *samanā* stage, the noose-net is dissolved; [there] is the transcendent Śiva (*paraśiva*).

[He is] partless (*niṣkala*), adorned with the form of the individual soul (*pudgala*), possessing the moon, the mountain, the staff, and the power at its end—[this is] the Lord-yogi within the fourfold [state].
I bow down to Śaṅkara, who moves through the fingers of the ocean, who is devoid of [worldly] taste,
the lord of all mantras, who traverses the six paths,
who is adorned with the five primordial deaths, who is the rising sun of fragmented qualities and stages, and whose form is like the moon within the solar disc.
"Having the form of a plow, with a crest of rays and a staff...
[may] the Unmanifest protect [us], as well as the Supreme, the Sakalākala, and the Sakala Śiva.
This is stated as the method for the sixteen purificatory rites (*ṣoḍaśasaṃskāra*) in the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*).
In the inconceivable state known as Viśvasāda,
when the bonds have become loosened, that elevation of the self into the Śakti is called its conception as the son of Rudra.

The manifestation of qualities such as sovereignty constitutes the *puṃsavana* (the rite for ensuring a male child). Knowledge that discriminates between *māyā* and the Self is the *sīmantonnayana* (the parting of the hair).
The acceptance of the reality of entities, both existent and non-existent, beginning with Śiva, constitutes the *janana* (birth).
Awakening is that which, by virtue of its fitness for Śiva-hood, consists in the name "Śiva-hood";
for the entry into Śiva-hood is indeed intended as the "emergence" [from limitation].
The enjoyment of the bliss of the Supreme Self is called the "eating of food."
But that which excels through the grace of Śiva would be the *cūḍākara* (the rite of tonsure).
The upper garment is the connection [formed] by the thread of the knowledge of Nirvāṇa;
and the restraint of the senses is traditionally known as the instruction in the vows.
The renunciation of rebirth is celebrated as the "gift of the cow" (godāna);
indifference toward all things is called the state of being established in true existence (sadbhāva).
And he who is endowed with infinite power is celebrated as Vāha;
that which possesses infinite power is the union known as Vānaprastha.
"If one were to point out that 'you' are simply the true being of Śiva," (189a, first line).

If [the disciple] is empowered by the conduct of the *samaya* through initiation with seed (*sabījadīkṣā*), then all other ritual action—pertaining to the duties that characterize the present body, such as the previously desired [rites], and including their associated *samayācāra*—is performed simultaneously. (second line)

Having brought [the disciple] to maturity, and having joined him with the Lord of Speech (*vāgīśvara*), and having placed himself within that [disciple’s] womb, he should contemplate [himself] as born simultaneously from all wombs; then, having caused [the disciple] to consume simultaneously all karma— comprising both merit and demerit and pervading the three times— he should [extinguish] ignorance, like the power of poison neutralized by mantras and medicinal herbs.
Having visualized [the soul] as bound, one should unite it with the state of Śiva by means of the sequential abandonment of the causal principles beginning with Brahmā;

having manifested the manifestation of the sixfold attributes such as omniscience, one should cause it to attain equality with Śiva. If the recipient is a child or otherwise incapable of observing the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), one should perform the seedless initiation (*nirvījadīkṣā*).

One should purify all ritual action (*karma*) other than that which initiates the body and its incidental consequences, provided it is accompanied by the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*). Even in both cases where these belong to worldly dharma, if one is a seeker of liberation among those following the Śiva-dharma, then all action— consisting of the nature of dharma and pervading the three times— is [to be purified] from the destruction of the physical elements.
Having identified that which brings about the acquisition of portions within the present body as being entirely of the nature of *adharma*,

and having purified it by means of the sequential abandonment of the causal principles beginning with Brahmā, one should unite [the disciple] with either the principle of *Śuddhavidyā* or the principle of *Īśvara*.
Then, placing the Hand of Śiva upon the head of the disciple, one should impart the instruction on the entire temple (*prāsāda*) accompanied by its measures and characteristics.
If one is a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*),

having abandoned all action residing in the hands— namely, all action consisting of merit and demerit— and having purified [the self] as before by removing the obstruction of ignorance, [one proceeds] through the sequence of abandoning the causal chain beginning with Brahmā.

As before, having united [the disciple] with the state of Śiva, which is equality with Paraśiva, and having placed the Hand of Śiva upon the head of the disciple, one should instruct him in the Niṣkala-prāsāda, which is endowed with the characteristics of the *mātrās*. All of this pertains to disciples whose ripening of impurities (*mala*) is slight.

The ritual beginning with the *kriyā* [kalā] up to the *garbha* [mantra] must be performed in its entirety; then, however, [the rites] belonging to *jñāna*. Now, if the disciple has reached the worlds situated within the *kalā* of *śāntyatīta* and is indifferent to worldly enjoyments (*bhoga*), being joined with the descent of the power of light (*dīpya-praśakti-nipāta*), the teacher, having become immersed for a moment in supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), [should enter] the interior [of that disciple].
Having become one with the power of *māra*, opening his eyes, and by means of the fire of vision born from the knowledge of the manifestation of *prārabdha-karma*,

he burns away all karma residing within the *kalās* such as *nivṛtti* and the rest; then, having joined the mantra-words, phonemes, worlds, and principles (*tattvas*) in their proper sequence to the [subtle] channels (*nāḍīs*), and having assigned the five *kalās* to the five powers (*śaktis*), he [unites] the two *māyās* through the conjunction of hand and head.

Having cast off the impurity of the self— which, shrouded by the *āṇavamala*, remains like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu— and having removed that impurity by means of the powers of knowledge and action, one should unite the self with the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*).

Furthermore, one should unite oneself and the Supreme Power within the Supreme Śiva—who is non-dual in nature—like the waters of a river and the ocean, like milk with milk, or like clarified butter with clarified butter. Thereafter, one should instruct [the disciple] on the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme through either the *Prāsāda* mantra or the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*).
Thus united, the self [remains] for the sake of experiencing the fruits of *prārabdha* karma.
Because it resides within the body,

[the yogi] employs the two feet in the form of Śiva and Śakti toward the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the eyes, the heart, and the midpoint between the eyebrows, for the purpose of removing the afflictions of the five elements, the five senses, and the internal organ, and for the sake of attaining the power of *samādhi*.

One should touch [the crown]. Because the *brahmarandhra* is the locus of space (*ākāśa*), and because the other four elements are contained within it, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is accomplished by touching it. Because the center of the eyebrows is the locus of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the perfection of *samādhi* is attained by touching that. (Second line) Regarding the sacraments beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) which have not been performed, one should perform them by means of knowledge of the specific time appropriate for each stage of life (*āśrama*).
Then the disciple, having risen, circumambulated the Guru, bowed down, and offered praise; having offered his body, wealth, and himself along with water to the Guru,
and having also saluted those of senior status according to their caste and stage of life, he drank the water from the Guru’s feet, which bestows knowledge.

Having accepted some favor, and having performed his daily obligatory rites at dawn, he should worship the Guru; then, having fed the Guru, the elders, the Śiva-devotees, and the Brāhmaṇas, he should afterwards eat the remnants of what the Guru has eaten. Thereafter, [he should study] the Śivāgama.

One should hear the awakening of the knowledge of Śiva and so forth from the mouth of the Guru; this alone is the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*). This is my current consent for your sake. (5th line) (The initiation of mental cultivation, *manobhāvanadīkṣā*)

A slight distinction is made regarding the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the cultivation of the mind (*manobhāvanā*). The Knowledge-Teacher (*jñānācārya*) must perform the investigation of the scriptures and their transmissions; being skilled in the knowledge of conduct (*caryā*) and the rest, he is the Guru who consists of the nature of Being (*bhāvātmaka*). Having approached that Guru in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the disciple—

O ocean of compassion, I am now immersed in the ocean of birth, bound by the three fetters, deluded, and submerged in the experience of pleasure and pain; yet, having performed [meritorious deeds] over many lifetimes, I have now come to the lotus-feet of Your Honor.
I, who have sought refuge, offer myself [to You].
"The practitioner himself must protect [the disciple]"— having been thus instructed, the disciple who possesses devotion and understands one-pointedness of mind,
having accepted such a disciple through speech, mind, action, and body,
and having observed for six months or a year the descent of power (*śaktinipātana*), [he should proceed].
Retention is the means for attaining the power of grasping; it is the vision of the secret, the form of knowledge, and that which is to be favored. The wise know it to be immovable.
The place, the location, the time, the action, the cultivation, and the vision—these, along with right conduct, must be practiced; hear my teaching regarding desire.

In a sacred place (tīrtha), on a vast ground, or in a location preeminent for Śiva; or in a region endowed with those qualities, on a riverbank, in a monastery, or in one's own residence, within a temple of the Guru.
On a mountain peak, in a bright place, one should have a pavilion constructed there;
having examined the ground, a four-cubit altar should be made with a depth of four finger-breadths.
It should be provided with four doors and equipped with four archways;
it is adorned with fine cotton cloths, variegated fabrics, and single-strand garlands.
Above, one should construct a small pavilion decorated with fragrant flower garlands.
Having performed the smearing with cow dung, one should perform the sprinkling with the five products of the cow.
Having relied upon what has been called the "place" and also the time that has been determined,
his initiation should be performed on that day when it is joined with an auspicious lunar mansion.

Having appointed the eldest [son], who is endowed with the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*), as the family priest (*purohita*), one should eat only once on that day; for that night, the consumption of cow-products (*gavya*) is prescribed. Then, on the following day, staying by a well and endowed with ritual bathing and purification, [one should proceed].
O Kālarātri, whose nature is impure illusion, [I bow] always to you in my heart.
One should gradually show the forms of consciousness at the station immediately preceding the principle of Māyā;
and at the end of pure Māyā, the object is indeed determined as being of the nature of consciousness.
Māyā is twofold, consisting of the dissolution of two and the cultivation of a single form;
it is the beautiful vision that provides instruction on concealment and non-concealment.
When conjoined with the [constellation] Mṛgaśiras, the time is indeed distinguished as Kālarātri;
it occurs at midnight for the rite of destruction, and during the night for the constant withdrawal [of the world].
That which withdraws into itself during the night while the body and senses are active,
or like the appearance of a lamp in the darkness of night—
this is the supreme time of night for those who know the scriptures.
Having had her brought into the pavilion at the proper time, [he should worship her] with sixteen offerings, beginning with perfumes and flowers.
Having prepared the materials for worship, standing facing north,

one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*), and so forth, as well as the offering of the water of honor (*arghya*) and the other rites.
The length should be four tālas, and the height thirty-six finger-breadths.
One should perform the anointing with fragrant unguents according to the rules for the seat prescribed in the scripture.
One should worship that which consists of the mantra-form, beginning with the earth element and ending with the curved tip.
He performed the ritual placement of the thirty-eight *kalās*, accompanied by the meditation on the destruction of sorrow.
Having taken refuge in the divine lotus-feet of the Teacher of Wisdom,
one should perform the consecration with the substances of ritual service according to the mantra.
Having wiped it with a white cloth,
one should offer white water-lilies upon a birch-bark leaf that has been smoothed with stone and anointed with fragrant unguents.
Then, having written the Praṇava, one should write "Namaḥ" in its center.
Having meditated upon the impurity of concealment (tirodhānamala), one should cast it into the seat of the Guru's feet.
One should worship with various divine fragrances and garlands of flowers; then, having offered incense and lamps, one should present the *sthālīpāka* oblation.
The disciple should meditate upon the Guru in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
for this indeed is the liberation from bonds for the Guru by means of the disciple’s devotion.
Thus, [the Guru should accept] the worship performed by the disciple, which is endowed with purity.
"Having become filled with supreme bliss, the best of teachers should indeed receive [the offering] in the form of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having thus again accepted such a command, the teacher should purify the bonds of the disciple;
the teacher should apply [the purification] to the various locations within the body of the disciple as is appropriate.
The path of mantra, the path of word, the path of phoneme, the worlds,
and the path of kalā— these are the sixfold paths along with their pervasions.
Having caused [the disciple] to enter, and having then severed with the sharp sword of knowledge the bond of karma— which is the cause of the afflictions of saṃsāra—
the Guru should purify, according to the prescribed rite, the pure paths of the knowers.
Having made her of the nature of Mahāmāyā, she obstructs the consciousness of the disciple.
Having contemplated that *āṇavī* power of his, and having perceived it,
he then extracted the consciousness (*caitanya*),
which is like the moon released from Rāhu— exceedingly pure and worthy of the state of Śiva. (5th line)
Having established the connection for that very mind of the bound soul,

and having performed the instruction on the meaning of the three quarters according to the rule— endowed with the characteristics of the measures and accompanied by the grace of the Anu— he [proceeded].

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is defined as follows: having formed the singular thought that Śiva alone is real, one should offer the body, wealth, and vital breath into the hand of the Guru, preceded by water;
then, having established the disciple in a state of well-being, whatever belongs to you within the vicinity of the body [is likewise offered].
Considering all that as indeed my own, you should always conduct yourself accordingly.
Having spoken thus, he should cause him to perform prostration before the Guru Śambhu;
then, being himself of pure soul, he should perform the worship of the Guru as that of Śiva.
Having praised him supremely with hymns, one should thus complete the worship;
having performed this worship for the disciple, Gora, endowed with faith, [should conclude].
With flowers of superior color and fragrance, along with incense, lamps, and the like—you alone are capable here of destroying the torment of the afflictions of cyclic existence for us.
O embodiment of compassion, O Lord of Guides, there is no other; protect me!
Having thus addressed him and bowed down with her hands joined in reverence, Jyeṣṭhā remained without any sign of agitation.
One should feed those who are one's own, as well as one's elders and preceptors;
having eaten the remaining food oneself, one should perform a salutation to the preceptors.
"The initiation of knowledge has been fully described; now hear the procedure following the initiation.
And furthermore, in the Raurava [Tantra] it says:
"The initiation of knowledge through vision occurs, and he performs his duty in due order."
The earth is [equal to] one knee-joint in size relative to the nature of the universe.
The earth element extends up to the *prakṛti* as the navel;
the principle of the Lord of Earth (*pṛthivīśvara-tattva*) is pervasive, while fire resides in the two [regions] of the throat.
The earth is dissolved into Sadāśiva; the element of air is in the two eyebrows;
the earth and the triad of elements beginning with Śakti are [dissolved] there, while space is in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The sixfold form beginning with mantra consists of the pairs of elements and so forth;
by means of these well-concealed locations, one knows the limbs of the kalās, such as nivṛtti and the rest.

The teacher, having meditated upon the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), should effect the purification of the paths by relying on the burning of those karmas accumulated throughout the [three] paths with the fire of knowledge. (…) The consciousness of the disciple is to be contemplated as the form of the illusory sacrifice (*māyādhvara*).

The impurity known as *āṇava* remains obstructing the primordial power (*ādyaśakti*) from time immemorial; by observing this with the vision of knowledge (*jñānadṛṣṭi*), its stainlessness (*nirmalatva*) is proclaimed. By touching the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) in the disciple—through the absence of both [the lunar and solar] oblations and through the cessation of suppression—one attains the state of the Moon (*candratva*) as it is stainless. This is the unification of consciousness (*caitanyasandhāna*) within Śiva.

That state is the manifestation of Śiva-nature; therefore, one should demonstrate that there is no difference from the Śiva-stage by means of the Śūla-mantra. Having thus made oneself single-minded, the disciple remains established with a concentrated mind during the self-performed union.
Having given instruction in the manner that is liberated, consisting of syllables accompanied by palaces endowed with the characteristics of the measures (mātrā).
Through the specific performance of these rites, which arise from the *pāśa* and the *liṅga*,
there shall be liberation through the severing of the bonds during the ritual of the Atirātra.
Having placed [the disciple] before him with his two divine feet,
the Guru should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the head and other parts [of the body], [those feet] being the very nature of Śiva and Śakti.

The movement of the elements such as earth and the rest is said to be the quality of space (*ākāśa*). When [the self] is completely consumed within the space of the *brahmarandhra*, there is the destruction of karma.
Of all the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), the visual faculty is the most predominant;
therefore, one should have two eyes and likewise touch with both feet.
When the activity of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) is conquered and burnt away, it is absorbed into the function of the organs of knowledge.
The intellect of the mind (manobuddhi) impels the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and all the sense organs.
His karma is burnt; then one should touch the region of the heart with the foot.
Having returned to the space between one's own eyebrows, he shall attain the realization "I am He."
Having placed Śiva below, one should cause him to enter through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Having pressed his foot upon the spot, he should prostrate before the Guru like a staff.
Then, having purified this disciple by means of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the destruction of [impurities], he [the Guru]... [and so forth].
And one should give the Śivajñānabodha-śāstra and the Patyārcana.
But one who is to be favored, through the actions of speech, mind, and body as a disciple, should offer himself to the true gurus, who take pride in [bestowing] wealth and life.
For this reason, one should act; otherwise, one remains devoid of independence.
He is indeed devoid of independence and is fashioned by the conduct of the samaya.
Having pointed out the tracks of the words through the actions of speech, mind, and body,
he has grasped this essence-less body, which is sustained by pure deeds.
Abiding by means of these instruments— the spinning of a potter’s wheel and the drawing of a bow with an arrow—
one remains endowed with the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest.
The vessel, swollen with the desire for refinement, shall become fragrant;
having established oneself in the lotus posture, one is certain regarding the activities of the body.
By maintaining silence, the fault of speech perishes at that very moment;
remaining composed through breath control, one becomes intent on meditation upon Śiva.
One should contemplate the form of light within the lotus of the heart in the space of consciousness;
by this vision, all material objects [of the body] are consumed like a lamp situated within cotton,
and all sins are burnt away, bestowing liberation upon the destruction of the body.
In that very Raurava,
just as water poured into water or milk mixed with milk,
so too does the knower of mantras attain oneness through the initiation mantra.
Just as when a heap of incense is offered into a blazing fire, its fragrance pervades everywhere; it does not become an element of the fire itself.
Thus, having attained the Śaiva ritual arising from initiation and mantra,
that best of men who has been initiated does not undergo rebirth again.
When the body has dissolved, having become Śiva and endowed with the qualities of Śiva,
one attains the bliss of Śiva and is prepared for manifestation.
Having reached the ocean, a river carrying joyful waters attains the state of salty water through the power of the great sea.

"Thus indeed the self, once separated from the body, attains Śiva alone. Now, one might object: for the sake of experiencing the *prārabdha* karma of the self conjoined with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), there would again be a connection with a body belonging to *māyā*, and consequently, future karma consisting of both beneficial and harmful results [would arise].
If it is argued that there would be the consequence of rebirth for the sake of experiencing the fruits arising from that [past action], we say no;
because he is united with Śiva, the inferior self is not tainted by future karma.
Thus it is stated in the Raurava: [text follows].
The teacher, having caused the disciple to be joined with the descent of intense power,
should for a moment remain immersed within supreme bliss;
then, becoming one with the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), he should gaze [upon the disciple] for the sake of the removal of his bonds.
Upon the cessation of that [bondage], consciousness-bliss arises through union with Śiva.
Thus, one whose self is purified by initiation, though remaining in the body, does not belong to the body;
because all fetters have been burnt away, he is liberated while living, with his mind fixed solely on Śiva.
Upon the fall of the body, one attains the bliss of consciousness and becomes one with the singular essence of Śiva.
Yet it does not undergo division, like the water of a river in the ocean;
just as darkness quickly perishes upon encountering the rising sun.
Thus, having attained initiation, both merit and demerit perish;
just as the sun illuminates these worlds with its rays. (The Subrahmaṇya-kalpa as described in the Śāradātilaka).
*Tāram* (Om), *khaḍgīśvaraḥ* (Khaḍgīśvara), *kūrmaḥ* (Kūrma), *nisvaraḥ* (the soundless), *ṇāntarīritaḥ* (uttered with the nasal ṇa),
*bhuve* (to the earth), *natiḥ* (salutation)— this mantra, consisting of seven syllables, has Subrahmaṇya as its essence.
The ritual of the limbs (*aṅgakriyā*) is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) joined with the six long vowels.

[One should meditate on the deity] whose splendor is as red as vermilion, whose face is like the moon, whose body is adorned with divine ornaments such as armlets and necklaces, and who bestows the bliss of heaven.

We worship Subrahmaṇya, who holds a lotus, a gesture of fearlessness, and a spear, who is adorned with red unguents and garments, and who is intent on destroying the fears of those who bow before him.
Then, the practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with sacrificial oblations;
at the conclusion, he should offer a tenth part as a burnt offering and also feed the Brahmins.
On the seat imagined as Dharma and the other [elements], to the west of the fire-maṇḍala,
one should worship the deity according to the prescribed rite with the offerings as described.
The limb-worship (*aṅgapūjā*) should be performed upon the filaments (*kesara*), with these [deities] situated within the mantra:
the one named Jayanta, the fire-receptacle (*agnikośa*), the one known as Kṛttikāputra,
followed by Bhūtapati, Senānī, and the one known as Guha.
One should place Hemaśūla and Viśālākṣa, with Śakti and Vajra in their hands.
Furthermore, at the tips of the petals of the directions, starting from the east, [one should place] the commander of the gods' army;
then Vidyā, Medhā, and Vajra; and in the corners, Śakti and Kukkuṭī.

Having worshipped Mayūradvipa, one should place the Lokapālas on the exterior; the weapons [should be placed] in such a way that they become infinite when impelled by the worship of Subrahmaṇya. With sweet foods, edibles, and the like, one should satisfy the Lord on the sixth lunar day.
One should worship the deities with the intellect and the celibate youths (kumāras).

May Subrahmaṇya, who is worshipped by the gods, swiftly bestow upon the practitioner his station, victory, valor, protection, longevity, fortune, glory, seed, power, and form, as well as the *kīlaka*. [Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Śāradātilaka]. Of this...

Of the great mantra Subrahmaṇya, Brahmā-Viṣṇu [Śiva] is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter, *rāṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *nī* is the power (*śakti*), and *rūṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). [He holds] the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, as well as the noose and the goad.
The mace, the trident, the lotus, and the discus—these constitute the ten weapons.
One should join the sixth [syllable] with the end of the thirteenth [syllable] in the fifth;
this, conjoined with the cause and the effect, is here called the root mantra.

The sixth is the letter Ū. The end of the thirteenth [vowel] is the letter AU. The fifth is the sonorous syllable, which is the letter HA. [As for] the *yogaka* of *Tihariṇī*: [the sixth line] (HAUṂ ...
HAUṂ is the task). The Bindu is the cause; the Nāda is the means. Thus, by combination, [it becomes] OṂ HĀṂ HŪṂ HAUṂ.
One should say "Śivāya namaḥ" (along with the Praṇava).
The Heart-seed (Hrīṃ) is common to all mantras.
(Line 7) Having added the fourteen vowels, the eight consonants, the Bindu, and the Nāda, one should conclude with "Śivāya."
(“Namo naḥ kūrirmummal kūṭai... is the Tirumantra. (195a, 1st order) Salutations to Amareśvara. Salutations to Ārādhya. Salutations to Indrapurogama. Salutations to Īśaputra.

Salutation to the son of Umā. Salutation to the one whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*). Salutation to the beloved of the sages (*ṛṣipriya*). Salutation to the remover of debts (*ṛṇoddhara*). (Second order) Salutation to the one worthy of praise by *ḷ*. Salutation to the one worthy of praise by *ḹ* [elided]. Salutation to the sole leader (*ekanāyaka*). Salutation to the bestower of sovereignty (*aiśvaryaprada*). Salutation to the vigorous one (*ojasvin*). Salutation to the one free from birth (*autpattirahita*). Salutation to the one seated upon a lotus (*ambujāsana*). Salutation to the one whose brilliance is extinguished (*kṣīṇatejas*). Salutation to the bearer of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍaludhara*).

(Third Order) Homage to the one who holds a skull-topped staff in his hand (*khaṭvāṅgapāṇi*). Homage to the son of Gaṅgā. Homage to the one with a bell in his hand (*ghaṇṭahasta*). Homage to the one dear to the letter *ṅa*. Homage to the moon-crested one (*candraśekhara*). Homage to the one consisting of the meters (*chandomaya*). Homage to the source of the world (*jagadbhū*). (Fourth Order) Homage to the conqueror whose banner bears the fish (*jhaṣaketu*).
Salutation! Salutation to the embodiment of knowledge! Salutation to the one with the *caṅku* in hand! Salutation to the one whose nature is *ṭha*! Salutation to the deceptive one (*ḍambha*)!

Salutation to the one who loves the *ḍhakkā* drum! Salutation to the one who is not to be approached (*ṇagamyā*)! (Fifth group) Salutation to the one whose nature is reality (*tattva*)! Salutation to the most excellent (*thaviṣṭha*)! Salutation to the one with a staff in hand (*daṇḍapāṇi*)! Salutation to the one with a bow in hand (*dhanuṣpāṇi*)!

Salutation to the one who makes holes in the city (*nagarandhrakara*). Salutation to the one with a lotus in his hand (*padmahasta*). Salutation to the one whose vehicle is a ram (*bhaṇibhukvāhana*). Salutation to the son of Bahula (*bahulāputra*). (6th order) Salutation to the son of Bhava (*bhavātmaja*). Salutation to Mahāsena. Salutation to the embodiment of sacrifice (*yajñamūrti*). Salutation to the delightful one (*ramaṇīya*). Salutation to the large-bellied one (*lambodara*). Salutation to the four-armed one (*caturbhuja*). (195b, 1st order) Salutation to the one born from the arrow (*śarasambhava*).

Homage to the six-faced one! Homage to the lord of all worlds! Homage to the son of Hara! Homage to the one who possesses the syllable *la*! Homage to the field of forbearance! Thus ends the Mātṛkā-mantra. (196a)

The *Sat-subrahmaṇya-kavaca* I take refuge in the son of the Bearer of the Ganges, whose ears are made restless by the playful movements of bees wandering about, drawn by the streams of ichor flowing from his cheeks,
and who is celebrated in song by Gandharvas, Siddhas, gods, and Kinnaras.
O observer of noble vows, listen as I shall proclaim the armor of Subrahmaṇya;
it pacifies all sins and destroys all calamities.
The Brāhmī Anuṣṭubh is the metre; Subrahmaṇya is its deity.
By means of the long vowel *ṣāṃ*, one should perform the visualization of the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon a hexagon.
May Subrahmaṇya protect [me] from the front, and Senāni protect from behind.
May Guha protect you on the right; may the Fourfold Being protect you from the left.
May Mahāsena protect your head, and Skanda guard your forehead.
May the Twelve-syllabled One protect your eyes, and may Viśvabhū guard your ears.
May the Six-faced One protect my face; may the Son of Śaṅkara protect my nose;
may the Lord of the Creeper protect my lips; may the Six-syllabled One protect my tongue.
May the commander of the divine army, the son of Sahala, whose tusks are like *cupu* fruits, protect [me];
may he who conquered Tāraka and possesses twelve arms protect Karna.
May the wielder of the spear protect my hands, and may the one born from the arrow protect my chest.
May the Heart protect the region of Brahmā; may the Son of Ambikā protect the belly.
May he who is mounted upon an elephant protect my thighs; may the son of Jahnavī protect both my knees;
may Viśākha protect my shanks, and may he whose vehicle is the peacock protect my feet.
The Lord of the Poor [Viṣṇu] protects all my limbs, and the Son of Agni [Skanda] protects the seven bodily constituents.
At the time of twilight and at midnight, [may he protect me] from the difficult waters,
from the impassable great forest, and from the royal gate when I am without a helper.
In a place with bad roots, in the midst of battle, and among all wicked beasts and the like.
In cases of thieves and other non-divine beings, in the affliction of fever and disease,
in fear of malevolent planets and the like, and for the purpose of adorning oneself against ill fortune and such, [one should perform this rite].
And when missiles and weapons fall, may he who pierced the Krauñca mountain protect me;
whoever recites this *Subrahmaṇyaka* armor, which bestows the fulfillment of desired goals—for him there is no threefold suffering. This I speak as truth, the absolute truth.
One who seeks the Dharma obtains the Dharma, and one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth.
One who desires sensual pleasures shall obtain sensual pleasures; one who desires liberation shall attain liberation. Wherever one recites [this mantra], there Guha is ever present.
One should recite this at the time of worship, at the time of consecration, and at the time of recitation;
for them alone there is the attainment of fruit and the destruction of great sins.
Whoever should daily recite or listen with devotion in the presence of the God shall attain all desires and, at the end, go to the city of Skanda.
Thus ends the *Sat-subrahmaṇyaka-kavaca*.
Homage to the Guru.

The term *śānta* means the letter *sa*. Its long form is *sā*, and so forth. (197a, first line) May that [mantra], which bestows great merit, brings joy to all living beings, destroys evil through mere recitation, and grants the fruit of all desires, be for your sake.

This armor of Skanda, which wards off all afflictions, should be given to the lords of sages; it is to be worn and its recitation destroys disease. It pacifies the fire and eliminates the calamities of thieves.
By the mere recollection of this, it brings peace to those afflicted by piśācas, fear, and diseases.
This *Skandaka-vastra* has been proclaimed; when worn upon the heart by people, poverty and misfortune shall never befall them.
On earth, he shall attain the wealth of universal sovereignty, and in the end, he will obtain absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
He shall possess eternal longevity, truthfulness, and devotion to Skanda shall arise.
Kumāra Kārttikeya shall protect his topknot, and likewise his head.
The son of Pārvatī was the forehead, and likewise Viśākha was the pair of eyebrows.
Kauñcabhedin resides in the eyes, Śikhivāhana in the nose;
likewise, Śaktiyukta is in the ears, and Ṣaḍānana at the base of the throat.
May Senānī protect both lips; may Tārakāpahā protect the tongue;
may Guha always protect the tooth, as well as the chin of Gāṅgeya;
may Bhavodbhava protect the cheek, and may Śambhunandana protect speech.
The son of Pārvatī [Śiva] protects the neck and shoulders, and likewise Agnibhū [Skanda] protects the throat.
May Sābāhuleya protect the *nāḍikā*; likewise, may Skandha protect the six mothers (*ṣāṇmātura*). May Viśākha protect the pair of arms, and may Vaṇik protect the two hands.
May the younger brother of Vināyaka protect the finger adorned with nails;
may Subrahmaṇya always protect the belly, and may the slayer of the enemies of the gods provide protection.
The Lord of the universe protected the right breast with Vaikāsa and likewise the left with Āgneya;

the hero in battle guarded the heart, while the ocean of compassion protected the mind. The one being served by his disciples protected the belly, and he who is compassionate toward the multitude of devotees protected the waist.
But at the navel is the supreme practice, the womb-like [seat] that bestows all desires.

May the Moon-bearer protect the secret place; may Śipikṣeva, who has eyes as dark as a blue lotus, protect it as well. May the Son of Umā protect the thighs, and he who is fond of Vallikā protect the knees.
May the Lord of Wealth protect the shanks, and may the one of great strength protect the ankles.
May the destroyer of sins protect my feet; may he whose banner is the cock protect my entire body.
May the crest-jewel of the gods protect my fat, marrow, bones, blood, skin, intellect, semen, and wherever it may be cold, as well as my crown that rests upon the lotus.
May the one of great prowess, Kapardin, cherished by Śambhu, protect [us];
he who is the bliss of Śivā, the abode of treasures, and the one served by sages such as Buddhi and the rest.

May the All-Knowing One, the six-faced Lord, always protect the vital breaths and other winds; likewise may the Sovereign protect Lakṣmī, fame, virtues, lineage, wife, and sons. Furthermore, may He who grants fearlessness to all deities protect knowledge from below.
That place which is unprotected, empty, and devoid of armor.
May all that generally fall within the domain of youth be protected;
may there always be the accomplishment of the purpose of poetry—this armor arises from recollection.
It brings victory in battle and causes the triumph of all;
it is the destroyer of ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and the like, as well as of voids and obstacles.
May the Beloved of Śakti protect [me] in all directions, beginning with the east, within the center;
by reciting this, one shall obtain his own self, free from malevolent spells and the like.
He who constantly recites or even hears this armor of Skanda—
Having attained all auspicious fortunes, one shall obtain union with Guha.
This armor-mantra is also completed.
Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa of Subrahmaṇya:
Listen, O Kauśika, I shall declare the Mātṛkā of Subrahmaṇya,
which bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men and destroys all calamities.
One should place the vowels at the hairline, the circumference of the face, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils,
the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the head, and the mouth.
One should place the *ka*-group on the right hand and the *ca*-group on the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group on the right foot and the *ta*-group on the left foot. One should place *pa* and *pha* on the two sides and the letter *sa* on the region of the back.
One should place the syllable *bha* at the region of the navel and the syllable *ma* at the region of the belly.
One should place the letter *ya* in the heart; one should place *ra* and *la* at the two armpits;
one should place the letter *va* on the back of the neck, and one should place *śa* and *ṣa* on the two sides of the armpits.
One should place the letter *sa* on the penis and the secret organ, and the letter *ḷ* on the two arms;
the letter *kṣa*, which is all-pervading, belongs to these [limbs] and is known as the Mātṛkā named Subrahmaṇyā.
"These locations have been declared; now hear of the lords of the five staffs (*pañcadaṇḍeśvara*).
Thus ends the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. ... [At] the twelve-finger limit (*dvādaśānta*) [is] *paṇaṃ ca*; [at] the right eye, *annaṃ namaḥ*; [at] the left eye, *innaṃ namaḥ*.
*Īn namaḥ* (on the right ear), *Un namaḥ* (on the left ear), *Ūn namaḥ* (on the right nostril),
*Ṛn namaḥ* (on the left nostril), *Ṝn namaḥ* (on the right temple), *Ḷn namaḥ* (on the left temple).

*Ḷ* Namaḥ (on the upper palate), *e* Namaḥ (on the lower palate), *ai* Namaḥ (on the upper row of teeth), *o* Namaḥ (on the lower row of teeth), *au* Namaḥ (on the third line, i.e., the head), *aṃ* Namaḥ (in the mouth), *aḥ* Namaḥ (at the corner of the right ear, extending from the wrist to the navel).
(Kaṇiṣṭha as the īra: kaṇnamaḥ, khaṇnamaḥ, gaṇnamaḥ, ghaṇnamaḥ, ṅaṇnamaḥ (on the left hand ring finger).
(Following the ṭṭiraki-pāṃpa method: caṇnamaḥ, chaṇnamaḥ, jaṇnamaḥ, jhaṇnamaḥ, ñaṇnamaḥ (on the right foot).
(On the ankle, the calf, and the big toe: Ṭannamaḥ, Ṭhannamaḥ, Ḍannamaḥ, Ḍhannamaḥ, (fifth line) Ṇannamaḥ. (The same for the left leg.)

*Tannamaḥ* (right shoulder), *thannamaḥ*, *dannamaḥ*, *dhannamaḥ*, *nannamaḥ* (right clavicle); *pannamaḥ* (left clavicle); *phannamaḥ* (head); *bannamaḥ* (navel); *bhannamaḥ* (chest); *mannamaḥ* (heart); *yannamaḥ* (above the right elbow, below the shoulder); *rannamaḥ* (left).
(laṃ namaḥ) in the hand; (vaṃ namaḥ) in the stomach; (śaṃ namaḥ) in the right armpit; (ṣaṃ namaḥ) in the left armpit; (saṃ namaḥ) in the penis. (7th line)
(Below the navel: *haṃ namaḥ* (on the right shoulder: *ḷaṃ namaḥ* (on the left shoulder and the navel:
*kṣaṃ namaḥ*. (Perform it thus.
(199a, 1st line) *Namaḥ skandāya devāya namo brahmasvarūpiṇe.*
Salutation to the god Śikhidhvaja, whose true nature is illusion.
Salutations to the preceptor of Kumāra, whose nature is that of Sadāśiva;
salutations to you, Kārttikeya, who possesses the form of Vāyu.
Salutations to the god Guha; salutations to you who have the form of Agni;
salutations to you, the lord of the Gaṇas, the Sovereign; salutations again and again.
Salutations to you, the son of Gaṅgā; salutations to you who possess the form of Rudra. Salutations to you in the form of Varuṇa; salutations to you, the wielder of the spear.
Salutations to you, the enemy of the Daityas; salutations to you who possess the form of Viṣṇu.
Salutations to you, the lord of the five elements, the remover of sins.
Salutations, prostrations, to the one established in the Mūlādhāra, the root mantra.
Salutations to you who possess five colors; salutations to you who transcend all colors.
Salutations to you, the six-faced one; salutations to the soul of the six systems of philosophy. Salutations indeed to the one whose very nature is the Brahman-mantra, who has transcended *māyā*.
Salutations to you, whose essence is the mantra of Lakṣmī, the bestower of Lakṣmī;
salutations to you who take the form of living beings, salutations to you whose nature is Brahman.
(6th line) Salutations indeed to you whose essential nature is the meaning of the syllable *na*, and who possesses manifold colors.
Salutations to you whose self is Nārāyaṇa, whose essential nature is the meaning of the syllable *ma*, who have transcended *māyā*;
salutations to you whose form is the syllable *śi*, the blue-throated one, the Self.

Salutation to you, whose essential nature is the meaning of the syllable *va* and who transcends speech; salutation indeed to him whose essential nature is the meaning of the syllable *ya* and who is the very form of Yama.
Salutations to you, whose essential nature is the meaning of the syllable *sa*, the witness of all;
salutations indeed to him whose nature is [the essence of] ……, who has transcended time.
Salutations indeed to the one whose essential nature is the meaning of the letter *ta*, who has transcended all reality;
salutations to the one whose essential nature is the meaning of the letter *ya*, who is the very embodiment of sacrifice.
Salutations to you, whose form is the meaning of the seed-syllable of *māyā*, and who possesses the form of *māyā*.
Again, salutations again to the Person whose very nature is Lakṣmī.
Salutations to the one whose essential nature is the meaning of the syllable *na*, who is the self of Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to the one whose essential nature is the meaning of the syllable *ma*, who is the very form of the Mother.
Salutations indeed to the god Namaskāra, the Subrahmaṇya;
always pure at dawn, at midday, and in the evening,
wherever one may be, whether in a royal palace or a fortress.
Whether on uneven ground or even on a mountain, when afflicted by fear or oppressed by enemies.
Whoever recites with supreme devotion this excellent hymn spoken by me shall attain all desires and achieve union with Skanda.
O you who grant boons through compassion, protect me— who have come for refuge, who am afflicted, conquered by Māyā, and overwhelmed by desire—

by means of the beautiful and eternal *araka* born from the forest of reeds (*śara*), the destroyer of Māra. O treasure-house of joy for Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, and the gods, you whose lotus-like feet are cherished by the sprout-like hands of the daughter of Himavat, born from the essence of Hara.

O Protector, O Slayer of Tāraka, protect me! O Victorious Hero beloved by the people and the brahmins, salutations! O Auspicious One devoted to those who seek victory, salutations! Victory to Śākha, Viśākha, and Kumāra! Salutations! O Protector, O Slayer of Tāraka, protect me! O Son of Bahulā, [whose] arrow...
O you whose voice is broken with emotion, who possess the golden luster of the daughter of the celestial river (Gaṅgā), whose vehicle is the peacock with its crest-tufts,

O slayer of Tāraka, protect me! O slayer of Tāraka, protect me with your consort, who has a face like the autumnal moon, whose eyes are as beautiful as lotuses, who is free from all worldly attributes, and who is your own innate splendor.
Be before me, be my dispeller of distress on the path;
always resort to me and protect me who has come to you. O Slayer of Tāraka, cause victory to shine for me and protect me on all sides.
Thus [is it for] those who remember Kukkuṭaketu.
For those who recite this *Ṣaṇmukha-ṣaṭka* and for those who bow to it,
there exists nowhere among embodied beings any lack of both [merit and] the joy of the Nandana grove. The *Subrahmaṇya-stotra* is completed.

Now, the root [mantra] of the one hundred and eight-name mantra: For the divine one hundred and eight-name mantra of Subrahmaṇya, Gārgya is the great seer (*maharṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), Subrahmaṇya, the son of the Kṛttikās, is the deity (*devatā*), *Śrīm* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *Klīṃ* is the power (*śakti*). My application (*viniyoga*) is for meditation during recitation (*japa*) for the sake of attaining the grace of Skanda. [He who has] twelve arms...

I salute Kumāra, the six-faced son of Ambikā, whose splendor is equal to the sun, who is seated upon a peacock, born from fire, the commander of the army... Skanda, Guha, the six-faced one, the protector, the eye, the son, and the Lord.
The tawny one, son of the Kṛttikās, whose vehicle is the peacock, possessing twelve arms and twelve eyes;
the wielder of the spear, the eater of flesh, the manifestor of the universe;
the destroyer of the demon Tāraka and the crusher of the strength of the Rākṣasas.
Intoxicated, heedless, and mad, he is the protector of the excellent Saṅgha;
he is the wise commander of the celestial army, compassionate and affectionate toward his devotees.
The son of Umā, the wielder of the spear, Kumāra, the piercer of Krauñca;
the leader of the army, born from Agni, Viśākha, the son of Śaṅkara;
the lord of Śiva, the lord of the Gaṇas, the eternal lord of all.
He possesses infinite power, is unshakeable, and is the beloved son of Pārvatī.
The son of Gaṅgā, born from an arrow, the son of Fire, the oblation;
Jṛmbha, Prajṛmbha, Ujjṛmbha, Kamalāsana, and Unnata;
likewise, he who is of one color, two colors, and three colors.
He is of four colors, of five colors, and furthermore, he is Prajāpati.
He who contains fire within his womb, who contains the *śamī* tree within his womb, whose seed is all-pervading, the slayer of the enemies of the gods;
he who is the golden womb, the doer of auspicious deeds, the possessor of wealth, and the wearer of the form of a young brahmin.
Pūṣā, Agabhasti, Gagana, Candravarṇa, Kalādhara, Mayādhara,
Mahāmāyī, Kaivalya, and Kalātmaka;
Viśvayoni, Ameyātman, Tejonidhi, and Anāmaya.
Parameṣṭhin, Guru, Brahmā, Vedagarbha, Virāṭ, and Vasu.
The daughter of Pulinda, the husband who bestows great eloquence,
the giver of all to those who take refuge in him, the slayer of thieves, and the destroyer of diseases.
He of infinite power, blissful, whose banner is divided into many parts;
he is Dambha, Paramadambha, Mahādambha, and Vṛṣākapi;
he who has assumed a body through a cause, and whose form transcends all causes.
The lord of serpents, the immortal, the vital breath, the sustainer of life, the supreme and the inferior.
Viruddhahantā, Arivīraghna, Rakta, Śyāma, Piṅgala,
Bahuparṇa, Gopati, Dākṣiṇādya, Varaprada,
Sarveśvara, Lokaguru, and Asurānīkamardana.
O Sage, that which is secret among gurus here must not be imparted to just anyone.
Thus worshipped with these one hundred and eight names, Guha,
being well-pleased, will surely grant all desired objects.
One should thus recite the *Nāmāṣṭaśataka* when surrounded by thieves and the like,
at the king’s gate, in legal disputes, and during the three calamities.
In the event of affliction by spirits, vetālas, piśācas, or brahmarākṣasas, the wise man, endowed with devotion to his guru, should perform worship three times.
One should consecrate the ashes with mantras and wear that ash;
by the mere wearing of the ash, all afflictions are destroyed.
Upon seeing the Puruṣa at the conclusion of the recitation, one afflicted by a snake becomes well.
Both hot and cold fevers perish by the mere act of recitation.
By reciting for a full year, epilepsy is destroyed.
Within six months, even one afflicted by leprosy is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
It brings about the success of men's undertakings, and untimely death is destroyed;
it is like fire for the two pairs of names of the three-footed mantras.
Just as among all rivers, Gaṅgā is the foremost, so too is that which has become the name of the Rākṣasa.
The spring season is like the summer heat among all seasons, scorching with its fervor.
O Sage, listen to this *tattva* consisting of one hundred and eight [names];
endowed with devotion to Skanda, recite this constantly.
"Being well-pleased, the Son of Śiva makes his presence available through ascetic power.
Thus ends the one hundred and eight names of Subrahmaṇya. (Second line:
Śrīparvata is the location of the head, while Citambaram is the heart.
Śoṇācala is the location of the throat, while Pāṇa is the nose during the practice of kumbhaka.
Vārāṇasī and Kāñcī are the left and right eyes;

wherever the Gaṅgā river flows, it is [meritorious]. In Kāśī, even water from the northern bank yields great results despite much hardship. For the wise, there is no need for dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, darbha grass, unbroken rice, or funeral clay.
At the Kāverī, the Mausala bath bestows eightfold fruit;
one should perform the inspection with the root mantra and the sprinkling with the weapon mantra.
Striking with the weapon-mantra and the protection by the armor-mantra shall be instantaneous;
thus, O Jayacit, know that piercing is the gazing performed by the creation of Śiva.
"Sprinkling is the fitness [of] a substance distinct from the insentient;
therein the power of consciousness is like the striking of a stone. And:
"The production of the *liṅgas*, however, follows after the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*). Thus it is said.
O Śiva, that which exists for even a moment or half a moment becomes the bond of worldly activity.
The fruit of that is union with Śiva; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
What [other] vow is there for one who is diligent, self-controlled, and has conquered the senses?

What is wealth? Knowledge. What is unhappiness? Conversation with those who lack wisdom. What is loss? Lack of discipline. And what is skill? A mind directed toward liberation. Without causing distress to others and without entering one's own home...
Having thus directed oneself, even that which is very small becomes much.
In the *Kālottara*, in the chapter on the rules for the stages of life (*āśrama-vidhi-paṭala*), Lord (*Īśvara*) said:
"The student (*brahmacārī*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*)—the teacher (*deśika*) is considered to be of two kinds."
I shall tell you everything regarding what is to be avoided and what is not to be avoided by those two:
meat, the udumbara fruit, weapons, the avoidance of turmeric and collyrium,
as well as women, the refinement of passion, and dancing to the accompaniment of song and instrumental music.
Having made it a binding rule, one should diligently avoid [these] elsewhere;
eating twice a day, singing, and avoiding that [behavior] by means of a fence.
In the *Mṛgendra-tantra*, in the section on Conduct (*caryāpāda*), [it is stated]:
"The abandonment of meat, women, and honey; the observance of vows; sleeping on the ground.
In the commentary on this, [it says]: "And here, the abandonment of meat... (5th line).

It is written: "Since the prohibition [of certain acts] is established for others even when they have no means of livelihood, it applies only to the Śūdra. In inferior and unworthy places, the wise man should practice that which is Dharma; he should disregard [those places], just as one who offers all his taxes [does not honor unworthy recipients].
He should act toward cows and toward Brahmins even in [such] circumstances. (203a, 1st line) (204 in Tamil omitted).

(211a, first line) The ritual procedure for Gomukha.

(………) Having sprinkled [the vessel] and worshipped it with the Śivagāyatrī, the householder, using that water and the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, should offer the five-fold libation (*pañcārghya*) starting from the Īśāna face; however, one who is detached [from worldly life] should do so starting from the Sadyojāta face. Having performed the worship and placed that [water] upon the hand, the householder [should proceed].
In the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), one who is detached [from worldly things] should repeat the five Brahmans ending with *namaḥ* in the order of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*). Then,

carefully grasping a flower with the little finger and the ring finger, and removing the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya*) with the tips of the thumb and index finger while reciting the Weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having placed the previously taken flower upon the head of the deity with the little finger and the ring finger, one should offer the *nirmālya* to the seat of Caṇḍeśvara in the secondary northeast, saying: "Hāṃ, to Dhvanicaṇḍeśvara, Huṃ Phaṭ Namaḥ," using the Śiva-weapon mantra.

Having washed the *liṅga* with the *Pāśupatāstra* mantra and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) with the *Hṛdaya* mantra ending in *svāhā*, using the water of the general *arghya*, one should consecrate the deity [as described in the passage beginning with "devamabhiṣicya"]. Thus it should be understood. Now, regarding the *gomukha*: [the practitioner] should place Śiva facing north, as stated in the *Uḍai-tvāndara*.
(From the northern Kāyār...
[211b, 1st line]) (If the *gomukha* is situated to the east, it is not called *vaikacchoṇḍra*; that is the rule.
(Statement. Written in the *Tantrasāra*, in the chapter on the procedure for worship (*arcanāvidhipaṭala*), by one residing at Aruṇācala. (2nd line)

Alternatively, the worship of the retinue or the *nāla* should be performed on the left; or facing Soma, or toward the region of Īśa, [one should place] Vighnarāja. Here, with respect to the eastern junction, there is movement toward the western presence.

The face [is] toward the direction of Varuṇa... the retinue... [it is] Nālagomukhā. Of her, the *liṅga* facing east and the *liṅga* facing west—when moving toward these two sides, she is employed as Gomukhā. Toward the *liṅga* facing south...
By way of the left [side], the face is at the southeast; Soma is in the northern direction. It should be understood that she is the "Nālā" employed [there].
Indeed, it should be reflected upon as if it were to be known that the linga of the face is precisely on the left side in the north. Thus says Aṭṭabhaṇḍan.

(The face being directed northward at the [proper] time, the Liṅga with its face toward the south... [it is] lofty toward the south... (212a, 1st line). || *Gomukhā-nirṇayaḥ* || (|| *Āvāhana-nirṇayaḥ* ||) [Both are in the margin.]
In the Śrīmatkāmika [Tantra] it is said: "One should fashion a Gomukha at the north of the western eastern gate;
at the southern and northern gates, one should likewise fashion a Gomukha to the east. (Thus it is stated.)
The *nāla* (tube) should not be applied on the left side. [By Enrada: Facing south [second line], to the east of the *liṅga*, it should remain facing the *gomukha* [by Enrada];
or else, facing Soma [Enrada]—this is a specific instruction. Also, to the north of the south-facing *liṅga*, it should remain facing the *gomukha*. [Third line]
(From Kalāmēnrar’s work: (Thus it is said:
To the east of the liṅga facing south is Gomuka, and to the north is Gomukī. For this reason, [the one] whose garment is Śiva... [should place the betel nut] at Gomuka. (Line 4)
(He replied: "This is for the ritual worship of action (*kriyāpūjā*);

for the worship of knowledge [*jñānapūjā*], it is indeed excellent if the *gomukha* is situated to the north during the time of the *aṣṭabandhana* [the eighth lunar day] and remains in the northern direction.
(5th line)
In the *Śrīmadviśvasārottara*, in the chapter on the worship of the image (*pratimārcanapaṭala*), it is said:
"In the absence of the [mudrā] granting boons (*varada*) for the deity, there should be the boon-granting and the fear-dispelling [mudrās].
In the absence of those two, one should arrange their respective functions in those very places. Thus.
Alternatively, regarding the matter of the vehicles:
one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) while reciting the root mantra;
the installation (*sthāpana*) and subsequent rites are performed with the *Sadyojāta* and the triad beginning with *Vāmadeva*.
"The face-to-face *arghya* should be offered there by Īśāna.
By the word "upward" (*ūrdhve*), the face of Īśāna (the seventh) is indicated;
therein lies the procedure for invocation (*āvāhana*), because that [face] consists of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*).

Because it pervades the four faces beginning with Sadyojāta, for that very reason, the *sammukhārghya* (guest-offering), the *svāgatārghya* (welcome-offering), and the ritual of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth are prescribed there,
in the face of Īśāna. (212b, first line) [Having thus instructed this...]
In the venerable *Sarvajñānottara* it is said:
"There, however, [the offering] should be given above, facing forward and facing away.
And likewise in the venerable *Vātulaśuddha*: [it is said].
There is a certain distinction here regarding the upward-facing [face] among the six faces:
having visualized the root of that face, it is traditionally taught that its mouth is turned away.
At the time of worship, having meditated upon him as the worshipped, one should perform the ritual action like a mouth;
having thus resolved according to the rule, at the conclusion of the worship it should be as before. Thus [ends the section on] the Śrīmanmakuṭa.
Then one should invoke the God, who holds flowers in his hand and is seated on a comfortable throne;
having recollected the Root-mantra and known the Supreme Sadāśiva, who is all-pervading.
Having meditated upon the supreme Sadāśiva, one should invoke him with the Sadyojāta mantra;
the installation is performed with the Vāmadeva mantra, and the confinement with the Aghora mantra.
There should be the presence of the Puruṣa, while the worship should be performed by Īśāna.
Likewise, in the venerable *Skandakaulottara* it is said:
"Then the knower of mantras should invoke the deity with the *sadyojāta* mantra;
he should establish him with the *vāmadeva* mantra, and perform the confinement with the *aghora* mantra."
The presence [of the deity] is effected by the Puruṣa alone, and the worship is performed by Īśāna.
First, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to Śiva who has arrived at his feet.
"One should offer the sipping of water (ācamana) at the mouths and present it upon his head.
Thus [it is said]. Now, the venerable *ūrṇā*—having led it upward again through the *suṣumṇā* channel from behind—(6th line).
Then, having gradually brought [the disciple] together through the instruction taught by his own guru, |||
"Having invoked him into the heart with the root mantra, the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) should be performed. Thus,
according to the *Paddhati* composed by Aghoraśivācārya and others,
the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and confinement (*sannirodhana*) are to be performed using the Heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).
"...as stated [in the Pañcārthabhāṣya]... [and] in the *Triśatikālottara* and other [texts], O Six-faced One: 'Then one should invoke the God with the Heart-mantra;
likewise, there is the installation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamana*).'"
One should perform the installation and the worship with the *hṛdaya* [mantra];
whatever has been stated or not stated, all that is done with the *hṛdaya*.
Thus, this single enclosure alone accomplishes all desires and purposes. (As it was said:)

Now, regarding the "posture of the broken staff and the broken head" (*daṇḍabhaṅgimuṇḍabhaṅgi*), this is the worship of his form (*mūrtyarcana*) through the offering of the aesthetic sentiment of the broken head (*muṇḍabhaṅgikalārpaṇa*). Next, [the description of] the posture of the broken staff and the broken head...
In the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, regarding the ritual of consecration (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*):

having placed [the deities] all around upon the pedestal, one should place the *mūrti* in the *liṅga*, and the Brahmāṇīs on the head, face, heart, secret parts, and all limbs, in an upward sequence following the arrangement of the staff.

Having placed [the mantras] at the eastern, southern, western, and northern faces with a curved arrangement, one should place them with a digit-like (kalā) configuration. Likewise, in another manual (paddhati):
"The staff-like (daṇḍa) arrangement, however, is from the tip of the thumb of the fist; Īśāna is above. (5th line)
Saying "namaḥ," [one should touch] the head with the thumb and forefinger; saying "oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ," [one should touch] the mouth with the thumb and middle finger;
saying "oṃ huṃ aghorahṛdayāya namaḥ," [one should touch] the heart with the thumb and ring finger.

"Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to the secret Vāmadeva"—thus at the navel. With the thumb and little finger, "Oṃ haṃ, salutation to the Sadyojāta form"—thus one should place [the mantra] on the foot. Now, as for the placement of the Muṇḍabhaṅginī, [one should form] a fist... (7th line).
Having bound the *bhadramudrā* at the crown of the head, [one says]: "Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Thus, on the uppermost head.
With the thumb and forefinger: "Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa. Thus, on the eastern head. With the thumb and middle finger: "Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Aghora. Thus, on the southern head.

With the thumb and ring finger, saying "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva," one should place [the mudrā] on the northern head. With the thumb and little finger, saying "Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta," one should place it on the western head.
Thus [says] the Skandakālottara regarding the installation of the liṅga:
"Having established Sadyojāta in the west, and likewise Vāmadeva in the north."
Having established Aghora in the south, one should place Puruṣa in the east;
then, according to the path of emanation, one should place Īśāna as the head in the center.

[This refers to] the *muṇḍabhaṅgī*. Next, for the *daṇḍabhaṅgī*, one should place the *pañcabrahma* there and then place the *kalāpiṇḍa* in sequence. Thus, in that context, it is by way of the *śivādhvan*. (4th line)
In the [first] rite,
one should place Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna; then,
for the second rite, one should assign Īśāna and the others to the faces, the heart, the face, and the secret organ.
"Having placed Sadyojāta on the two feet, one should perform the placement with the seed-syllable of Brahma.
Thus it is said.
Sadyojāta has eight limbs, while Vāmadeva has thirteen.
"One should install the face of Aghora with eight [and] four [syllables], and Īśāna in five ways; thus one should install the thirty-eight kalās. Thus it is said in the *Amṛtamauli*.
The southern gate, however, is the best for the four castes in their respective order;
O Maheśvara, the eastern gate is praised for Brāhmaṇas.
The southern gate is for the Kṣatriyas, the auspicious northern one for the Vaiśyas, and the western gate for the Śūdras, O Maheśvara;
however, for all castes, the southern gate is the most excellent. Thus it is said.
